title: The Roadhouse by a Vanished Lake
place: Near Fulton and Divisadero streets (site of 1333 Fulton St)
hook: On the old Mission-to-Presidio trail stood the San Souci roadhouse, a refuge from the wind beside a lake that may have washed away in one night.
story:
Where Fulton meets Divisadero today, early travellers found a roadhouse. Historian Joel Pomerantz found a building at this spot on an 1853 map by City Surveyor Clement Humphreys. It stood on the city line of the time, now Divisadero Street, beside the dotted trail from the Mission to the Presidio [1]. It was the San Souci roadhouse, a refuge from the wind in sandy, hard country [1].

The best-known description comes from journalist Edward Morphy, writing around 1919: "probably the best known landmark of Divisadero street in the pioneer days was the old San Souci roadhouse which stood on the east side of a pretty little lake that then filled the space from Fulton to about midway between Hayes and Fell streets" [2]. Morphy said the lake broke its sandy banks in the very wet winter of 1861-62 and mostly drained away down the valley. Pomerantz points out that the lake rests on Morphy's word alone, and that parts of the flood story don't add up [2].

Much altered, the roadhouse survived until the 1920s [1]. Historian Joe Pecora counts it among the neighbourhood's lost landmarks [3]. Pomerantz found a reference crediting the roadhouse as the source of the name San Souci Valley, used for the Lower Haight and Panhandle area until about the 1920s [1].

title: The fort that never fired a shot
place: Fort Point, 999 Marine Drive
hook: Engineers blasted a 90-foot cliff down to 15 feet to build it. It was the Pacific's only fort of its kind, and it never fired in anger.
story: In 1853 the Army Corps of Engineers began the fort that would be the cornerstone of San Francisco Bay's defences [1]. The guns of the day had short range, so the lowest tier of cannon had to sit almost at the waterline, where cannonballs could skip across the water into enemy ships. To get the fort that low, the engineers blasted the 90-foot cliff where the Spanish castillo had stood down to just 15 feet above the sea [1]. The result had three tiers of vaulted gun rooms, walls seven feet thick and more guns on the roof. There were more than 30 forts like it on the East Coast and just this one in the West [1]. Its first 55 guns were mounted in 1861, when the Civil War began. As many as 500 men lived there, the enlisted men 24 to a casemate, and they gathered driftwood to eke out their coal [1]. It never fired in defence [1]. The Civil War had already shown that rifled artillery could smash brick forts like Fort Sumter [1]. The fort was even renamed Fort Winfield Scott in 1882, then went back to Fort Point in 1886 [2].

title: Two cottages older than the city's streets
place: Tanforan Cottages, 214 and 220 Dolores St
hook: Half a block from the mission stand two little redwood houses that may date from 1853. Nobody can quite prove it.
story: At 214 and 220 Dolores Street stand two plain frame cottages with modest Classical Revival fronts. They are probably the oldest houses in the Mission District [1][2]. Tradition says 214 went up a little before 1853 and its near twin at 220 soon after. They sat on land from an 1836 Mexican grant to Francisco Guerrero [1][2]. The architectural historians Roger Olmsted and T. H. Watkins were sceptical. The first date anyone could actually prove, they noted, is 1866, when Revilo Wells, owner of 214, had water piped in [2]. The houses take their name from the family of Toribio Tanforan, who lived in them from 1896 to 1945. A small carriage house behind 220 still held a Tanforan carriage as late as 1940 [2]. Their large gardens kept specimens of turn-of-the-century San Francisco taste in plants [2]. The city made them landmarks #67 and #68 in 1975 [3]. Since 1995, 220 Dolores has housed people living with HIV or AIDS who had been homeless [2].

title: Warm blood, ten cents a cup
place: Butchers' Reserve, Brannan Street near Ninth, on old Mission Creek
hook: Slaughterhouses on Brannan Street dumped their waste through trap doors for the tide to carry off. Local boys sold the blood to hospital patients.
story: In 1853 a group of factory owners asked the Board of Aldermen for an industrial zone "so remote from the inhabited part of the city" that nobody could call it a nuisance [1]. They were slaughterhouse operators, and they wanted land near Ninth and Brannan streets, on the banks of Mission Creek. The city agreed, and the area became the "Butchers' Reserve" [1]. They picked the spot for the tide, which came in from Mission Bay twice a day and washed away the offal they swept through trap doors in the floor [1]. Years later the South of Market Boys, an old-timers' club, remembered supplying patients at the French hospital with "healthy, warm animal blood, at 10 cents a cup, from the slaughterhouses on Mission Creek" [1]. The butchers stayed on Brannan between Sixth and Ninth streets until the city pushed them south to Islais Creek. Nancy Olmsted's history of Mission Bay dates that move to an 1870 ordinance [1]. Other accounts date it to an 1868 ban on slaughtering in the city, which created the Butchertown district in today's Bayview [2].

title: A London crescent in the sand
place: South Park, between Second and Third streets
hook: An Englishman tried to plant a slice of Georgian London in Gold Rush San Francisco, complete with a private oval garden and no saloons allowed.
story: George Gordon, a British immigrant who made money in lumber, wharves, an iron foundry and California's first successful sugar refinery, began buying lots here in 1852 [1][2]. His plan was to recreate one of London's elegant squares or crescents a mile from the rowdy business district, free of saloons, gambling halls and warehouses [1]. Architect George H. Goddard laid it out and building began in 1854 [1]. The houses were brick dressed in stucco to look like stone, with parlours above and English-style basements for kitchens and servants [1]. At the centre lay a private oval garden, 550 feet long, fenced in iron; a windmill pumped water for the homes [1][2]. The depression of 1855–57 slowed sales, but through the 1850s and 1860s bankers, politicians and society families moved in, riding an omnibus downtown [1]. Then warehouses crept closer and the Second Street cut of 1869 sank land values. By the 1870s the rich had left for Nob Hill and working families took their place; by the 1890s South Park was home to Japanese hotels and shops, and a settlement house opened at No. 15 in 1895 [1][2].

title: A Mormon farmer names the streets
place: Elizabeth and Noe streets, in the heart of Horner's Addition
hook: Elizabeth Street is named after a pioneer's wife and Jersey Street after his home state. Many of Noe Valley's street names came from one man's life.
story:
John Meirs Horner came to Yerba Buena in 1846 on the ship Brooklyn with Sam Brannan's party of Mormons. He became one of California's most successful early farmers [1]. In 1853 or 1854 (sources differ) he bought a large part of Noé's rancho [1][2]. He later wrote that they paid $285,000 for 5,250 acres and staked out 1,050 of them in streets, blocks and lots. The tract was called Horner's Addition [2].

He probably named many of its east-west streets. His own names became John (now 22nd) and Horner (23rd). Elizabeth was named for his wife and Jersey for his home state. Temple, Navy, Army, Vale, Dale and Grove later became 25th, 26th, Cesar Chavez, 28th, 29th and 30th [2]. On 29 January 1854 Caroline Barnes Crosby, who lived with the Horners, walked the hills to see "br Horners new purchase" and the adobe "where the spaniard resides." She called it "a most beautiful and romantic place" [2].

But the hills were steep and hard to reach, and few lots sold. Horner lost his fortune in the Panic of 1857 and had to sell his land [1][3].

title: Orphans, refugees and a teachers' college
place: Former San Francisco Orphan Asylum block (Haight, Buchanan, Hermann and Laguna streets)
hook: For $100, a group of women bought two remote blocks for their orphans. The site went on to shelter 1906 refugees and a teachers' college.
story: The San Francisco Orphan Asylum Society was founded in 1851 by women who met at the home of the Reverend Albert Williams, to care for siblings orphaned by cholera on the way to California. By 1852 it had outgrown its first home [1]. For $100 its managers bought two blocks bounded by Haight, Buchanan, Hermann and Laguna. The land was then thought remote, far beyond the city limits [1]. On March 22, 1854, the children moved into a two-storey stone dormitory, with stone hauled free by the Spring Valley Water Company [1]. It grew to about 300 children, and donors included Levi Strauss, Adolph Sutro and Lillie Coit. Local legend says Haight and Waller streets are named for two of its board members [1]. The 1906 earthquake damaged the building but did not destroy it, and refugees camped on the slopes nearby [1]. The Society had leased the southern half of its land to the state for the San Francisco State Normal School, which lost its Powell Street building and all its records in the fire. Within ten days, president Frederic Burk had found a new site 'on upper Market Street'. Classes resumed that June, making it the first public school in the city to reopen [2][1]. The orphans left in 1919, and the state bought the property [1].

title: Son, Observe the Time and Fly From Evil
place: Old St. Mary's Church, 660 California Street at Grant
hook: California's first cathedral was built on stone cut in China — and its clock tower still scolds passers-by.
story: Bishop Joseph Alemany laid the cornerstone of St. Mary's at California and Dupont (now Grant) on July 17, 1853, and the church was dedicated on Christmas Day, 1854 [1]. It was the first church built as a Roman Catholic cathedral in California [2]. It was a truly Pacific building: the landmark report notes that its stone foundations were cut to order in China, while the bricks came from New England [2]. A 200-foot spire was planned but never built, leaving a 90-foot tower [2]. When the clock was completed in 1857, a stern line from Ecclesiasticus was fixed beneath it: 'Son, observe the time and fly from evil' [3]. The church stood on the edge of Chinatown, facing the commercial city in one direction and Chinatown in the other, as the city's landmark report puts it [2]. The cathedral moved to Van Ness Avenue in 1891. The 1906 fire gutted Old St. Mary's, but it was rebuilt and reopened in 1909 [2].

title: Ten-pins, boats and a duel's rendezvous
place: Lake House roadhouse, east shore of Lake Merced (approximate)
hook: The lake's first roadhouse promised sailing, quoits and the finest dinner in California. In 1859 it was where a senator's duel party gathered.
story: The earliest pleasure resort at Lake Merced was humble: a one-story shanty with a kitchen and a bar, which de Haro's son-in-law Charles Brown moved in 1853 to the point where the lake's two big arms met [1]. In early 1854 P. L. White leased and enlarged it, aiming, one paper said, to give San Franciscans "a resort second to none of the kind in the Atlantic States" [1]. The Daily Alta promised visitors a lake, a boat, ten-pins, quoits and a swing, plus "the finest dinner that is possible to provide in California" [1]. In practice the crowd was mostly single men, "sports" and "fast drivers" out to race and drink [1]. In September 1859 the parties of Senator David Broderick and former Chief Justice David Terry met at the Lake House to choose their dueling ground; the articles of the duel named a farm adjoining the Lake House ranch [1][2]. Broderick was fatally shot at a ravine just across today's county line [2][3]. The old Lake House later ended up downtown, moved to Mission Street near 2nd, then to 7th and Bryant [1].

title: The Ocean House, respectable and not
place: Site of the Ocean House, now Lowell High School, 1101 Eucalyptus Dr
hook: Where Lowell High students now study stood a towered roadhouse that one newspaper called "an assignation house on a large scale."
story: In 1854 Joseph W. Leavitt opened the Ocean House beside one of the Green brothers' ranches on the old Ocean Road north of the lake [1]. For its place and era it was grand: dining rooms, parlors and a billiard saloon, open second-floor balconies looking out over the lake and ocean, and an enclosed view tower on top. Around it stood cottages, stabling for a hundred horses and even a bowling alley [1]. It advertised itself to families, wealthy parties and "invalids desiring to derive the benefit of the sea air," but its regulars were mostly men looking for a good time. When swindlers or robbers vanished from downtown, the police often found them drinking here [1]. In 1857 the Daily Globe called it "an assignation house on a large scale," with servants trained to "favor infamous enterprises" [1]. From 1865 a racetrack stood across the road [1][2]. The Ocean House burned in the early 1880s; Carleton Watkins photographed it around 1870, and its site is roughly where Lowell High School stands today [1].

title: The house that sailed round the Horn
place: Stanyan House, 2006 Bush St at Buchanan
hook: Five years into the Gold Rush, a New England house arrived by ship and was set down beside a toll road. It is still here.
story:
When this modest house went up at Bush and Buchanan in 1854, Bush Street was still a toll road and the Gold Rush was only five years old [1]. Many prefabricated houses were shipped to San Francisco from New England in the Gold Rush years. This "Boston House" is one of the few that has been positively identified as having come around Cape Horn [1].

Its first occupant was Charles Stanyan, who later sat on the city's Board of Supervisors from 1866 to 1869 and served on the committee that chose the site for Golden Gate Park [2]. Stanyan Street, which runs along the park's eastern edge, carries his name [2]. The house stayed in the Stanyan family for more than a hundred years [1], and it is the oldest surviving house in this part of the city.

The city made it Landmark No. 66 [3]. It is still a private home, a little wooden survivor of the frontier town, standing among the Victorians that came later.

title: Thirty Children in the Middle of Nowhere
place: Haight and Laguna streets (south side, the former asylum grounds)
hook: In 1854 a group of San Francisco women moved thirty orphans into a stone building among the sandhills, two blocks they had bought for $100.
story:
In 1851 several San Francisco women, most of them wives of Protestant clergymen, formed the San Francisco Orphan Asylum Society to care for children whose parents had died in an epidemic [1]. They soon needed a permanent home. Their own history describes the land they found as "far beyond the city limits and basically in the middle of nowhere" [2]. They bought two blocks bounded by today's Laguna, Hermann, Buchanan and Haight streets for $100 [2][3].

They raised building money by going door to door and still had to borrow $5,000 [2]. The masonry dormitory went up in 1853-54, from stone quarried on nearby Mint Hill [3][4]. It opened on March 22, 1854, and about thirty children and staff moved in [1][2]. 
The asylum took in more than 3,500 children in its first fifty years, and at its peak housed as many as 300 [1]. By the 1890s the children went to local public schools [2]. The building was damaged in 1906, and in 1919 the children moved out [2]. The site later became a state teachers' college, then the UC Berkeley Extension campus at 55 Laguna [3][4].

title: A Jesuit school in shifting sand
place: Market Street between Fourth and Fifth (site of the first St. Ignatius church and college)
hook: The archbishop pointed at an empty patch of dunes on the map. The Jesuits built there anyway, and their one-room school became USF and St. Ignatius Prep.
story: In spring 1855 the Jesuit Anthony Maraschi asked Bishop Joseph Alemany where in San Francisco he should build. By one account Alemany pointed his pen at a spot on the map. By another he swept his hand toward the empty land and said "any place over there!" [1]. Market Street then stopped at Third. Beyond it lay dunes, and Maraschi's lot sat in a hollow between two sand hills called St. Ann's Valley. Each time he visited, it looked different [1]. He bought Lot 127, on Market between Fourth and Fifth, from Thomas O. Larkin. Paul Totah's history gives the price as both $11,000 and $11,500. It was paid with a French loan at 1.5 percent a month, which pushed the Jesuits' debt to $26,000 [1]. Maraschi is reported to have said, "Here, in time, will be the heart of a great city" [1]. The plain $4,000 church opened on July 15, 1855, and the school on October 15 [1][2]. In 1880 the college moved to Hayes Street and Van Ness Avenue. It became the University of San Francisco and St. Ignatius College Preparatory [2][3].

title: A square saved in 1855
place: Hamilton Square, west of Steiner between Geary & Post
hook: Before the Western Addition had houses it had a plan, and that plan set aside eleven public squares. One of them is still green here.
story: In the early 1850s San Francisco ended at Larkin Street. The young city claimed the land beyond, as far as Divisadero and eventually the ocean, and the district between Larkin and Divisadero north of Market became the Western Addition [1][2]. The Van Ness Ordinance of 1855–56 extended the downtown street grid across the district and reserved land for public use, including eleven public squares [1]. Hamilton Square, just west of Steiner Street, is the one closest to Japantown [1]. Houses soon followed. The city's population grew by more than 160 percent in the 1860s, from 56,802 to 149,473, and by the turn of the century builders had covered the new blocks with Italianate, Stick and Queen Anne homes [1]. Nearby on Geary near Scott, Hamilton Junior High, built in 1875 and demolished in 1930, had a student body that Jerry Flamm described as a mix of white, Black and Japanese children [3].

title: The governor's grove on Sunnydale
place: Church of the Visitacion and parish school, Sunnydale Avenue (former Burnett estate)
hook: California's first governor built a country home here. Later its trees sheltered one of the city's first motels, until bulldozers took them in 1964.
story: Peter H. Burnett was elected governor of California in 1849, before California was even a state, and he resigned abruptly in 1851 [3]. In Oregon, years earlier, he had proposed a law expelling free Black people and flogging those who stayed. The state library's own biography of him records that fact [3]. In the mid-1850s, according to the Visitacion Valley History Project's account, Burnett built a large home on Sunnydale Avenue near where the Church of the Visitacion stands today [2]. SF Heritage describes the property as a six-acre estate [1]. Local tradition says famous visitors planted trees there, including one by President McKinley and another by Admiral Dewey [2]. Later the grounds held the San Francisco Auto Camp. The Grapevine calls it the city's first motel, and Heritage more cautiously calls it 'one of the city's first' [1][2]. It had 40 cabins, room for tents, and space for up to 300 cars in a garden-like grove [2]. In 1964 the camp and the Burnett house were torn down to build the new church and parish school, and about 200 trees went with them [2]. Burnett himself died in San Francisco in 1895 [3].

title: A Lone Cottonwood Marked the Water
place: Alamo Square (Hayes, Steiner, Fulton and Scott streets)
hook: Before the Painted Ladies, before streets, the hilltop was a trailside watering hole marked by a single tree. That tree gave Alamo Square its name.
story:
Long before anyone called it a square, the hill at the centre of this map was Alamo Hill. According to the San Francisco Parks Alliance, in the early 1800s a lone cottonwood on the hill marked a watering hole on the horseback trail between Mission Dolores and the Presidio [1]. Álamo is Spanish for poplar. Hoodline's history says the name most likely came from poplar trees on the land, and calls the hill a stopping point on the trail [2].

The Gold Rush city soon spread toward the hill. In 1856 Mayor James Van Ness set aside 12.7 acres around the watering hole and named it Alamo Square, and the state legislature confirmed it as a public park the following year [1][3]. City records from 1857 describe the reservation as "Alamo, bounded by Hayes, Steiner, Fulton and Scott streets", the same four streets that frame the park today [2].

For decades the reservation stayed what Hoodline calls "little more than a rocky knoll", far from the city's edge [2]. The cottonwood is long gone, but the Spanish name for it has stuck to the hill, the park and the whole neighbourhood.

title: A factory you had to walk
place: Tubbs Cordage rope walk, 22nd and Iowa streets
hook: For a century, men walked the length of a shed more than a thousand feet long, twisting rope for the ships and mines of the Pacific.
story: In the 1850s rope was made on foot. Brothers Alfred and Hiram Tubbs set up the San Francisco Cordage Manufactory on the empty south shore of Potrero Point. Its heart was a rope walk: a shed 35 feet wide and 1,000 feet long, running southeast from what is now 22nd and Iowa streets down to a wharf on the bay [1]. Skilled workers walked the length of it, twisting hemp and abaca yarn into rope. A 1964 history remembers men walking four or five blocks to make one continuous rope [2]. The walk was later stretched to somewhere between 1,400 and 1,500 feet, depending on the source, and it passed under Kentucky (now Third) Street to reach piers in the bay [1][3]. Sources give the start date as 1856 or 1857 [1]. In 1893 the Morning Call marvelled at the fireproof brick buildings, the 500-horsepower engine and the fibre shipped in from the Philippines and Yucatán. It boasted that all 250 workers were "white", which says a lot about the era [1]. Tubbs rope went as far as Mexico, Peru, China and Japan. The plant closed in 1962 and a Muni bus yard took its place in 1978 [1]. A row of oddly angled buildings between Third and Tennessee streets still follows the rope walk's diagonal line [3].

title: Fort Gunnybags and the vigilantes of 1856
place: Fort Gunnybags, Sacramento Street between Front and Davis
hook: After an editor was shot on Montgomery Street, thousands of armed citizens fortified a warehouse with sandbags and cannon and ran the city from inside it.
story: On May 14, 1856, James Casey, editor of the Sunday Times, shot his rival James King of William, editor of the Evening Bulletin, at Montgomery and Commercial streets [2]. Within two days 2,600 men had joined a revived Committee of Vigilance, organised into companies of 100 [2]. They made their headquarters on the south side of Sacramento Street between Front and Davis, walling it with sandbags; San Franciscans called it Fort Gunnybags, and guards and an alarm bell stood on its roof [1]. Inside were assembly halls, a kitchen, an armoury, an infirmary and prison cells [3]. The vigilantes seized Casey from the county jail, and on May 22, as bells tolled the end of King's funeral, they hanged him, together with Charles Cora, at the fort [1][2]. Four men were executed in 1856; the boxer James 'Yankee' Sullivan also died by his own hand in a vigilante cell [3]. One writer notes the committees gave detainees something like trials and released some [2]; others remember them as an armed, extralegal takeover of city government.

title: Graves the vigilantes filled
place: Mission Dolores cemetery, 16th and Dolores
hook: "Let no man point to my grave as that of an assassin," James Casey begged from the gallows. His grave is still there, among the roses at Mission Dolores.
story: In May 1856 Supervisor James P. Casey shot the editor James King of William, who had revealed that Casey once served time in Sing Sing. Thousands of armed citizens then formed the Committee of Vigilance and took over the city [1]. On May 22 they hanged Casey and the gambler Charles Cora from the windows of their headquarters, while crowds filled the streets below. Before the drop Casey cried out: "Let no man exult over me, or point to my grave as that of an assassin… I have an aged mother in the Atlantic States, and I hope that she will never hear how I died" [2]. He was buried at Mission Dolores on May 23 [3]. Days later the vigilantes' dead included the boxer James "Yankee" Sullivan. He had guarded the rigged ballot box that put Casey in office, and he was found in his cell with a slit wrist after confessing. Rumours of murder followed for years. He was buried here on May 31 [3]. His headstone asks God to "destroy mine enemies" [3]. In 1916 Belle Cora was moved here to lie beside Charles under one stone [4].

title: Haight Street Was Named for a Woman
place: Haight Street at Laguna
hook: Plaques credit a banker or a governor. The only first-hand account says Haight and Waller streets honoured two women who ran the orphan asylum.
story:
Ask who Haight Street is named for and you may hear a banker, Henry W. Haight, or a governor, Henry H. Haight. A mural and a plaque in the Haight-Ashbury name one man each [1]. Local historian Angus MacFarlane argues that both are wrong.

Weltha Ann Buell Haight arrived in San Francisco on December 6, 1852. Within months she was on the board and the building committee of the Protestant Orphan Asylum, alongside its founding leader, Elizabeth Waller [1][2]. The asylum's two blocks were first mapped on a paper street plan. When the Western Addition was resurveyed in 1855-56, those blocks ended up bounded by a new Haight Street to the north, with a new Waller Street running through them [2].

The only first-hand explanation comes from Weltha herself, in a pamphlet dated May 1, 1900. Once the land had been surveyed, she wrote, "out of compliment to two of the Managers, Waller street and Haight street were named" [1][2]. In 1928 a Chronicle writer heard the same story from the asylum's secretary and brushed it aside, suggesting the streets were more likely named for the women's husbands [1]. That version is the one that stuck. MacFarlane notes there is no record that Henry Haight gave the land [2].

title: Kidnapped over a bundle of land papers
place: Green family lands north of Lake Merced, west of 19th Avenue
hook: Alfred Green said he had pueblo papers that could void the land claims of powerful men. The Vigilance Committee dragged him from his bed.
story: In 1852 Alfred Green and several of his seven brothers settled north of Lake Merced, just west of today's 19th Avenue, claiming land by settler's preemption through a deal with de Haro's son-in-law [1]. Alfred had come west with Stevenson's New York Volunteers, served as a city alderman and married a Californian woman, Dolores Leyoreita [1]. The Greens were litigious and cantankerous, and defended their farm against rival claimants for years; one account says they built a metal-lined fort to hold it [1][2]. In 1856 Alfred claimed to hold old pueblo papers that would invalidate the titles of many powerful San Franciscans. The Vigilance Committee abducted him from his bed and imprisoned him [1]. He was released after promising to hand over the papers, which he said were hidden in a mine, and came home to a ransacked house and a mother and wife who had feared he'd been hanged. When he later produced papers for a ransom in coin, a deputy sheriff and constable grabbed at the bag outside the bank, and all parties walked to the sheriff's office clutching it [1]. Alfred went into exile in Mexico, returned, and died in San Francisco in 1899 [1].

title: Streets Drawn on Sand
place: Linden Street, Hayes Valley
hook: In 1856 three commissioners drew a grid across empty dunes west of Larkin Street. Their plan created the Western Addition, and its odd tree-named alleys.
story:
In the early 1850s the land west of Larkin Street was dunes, scrub and conflicting land claims. The Van Ness Ordinance of 1855 settled those claims largely in favour of squatters. Anyone in actual possession of land on or before January 1, 1855 got title. A new map then set out the streets and reserved lots for parks, schools and hospitals [1].

On November 12, 1855, the city council named Horace Hawes, Michael Hayes and Charles Gough to "lay off the streets in the Western Addition" [2]. They reported on April 21, 1856, having made "a patient and thorough examination of the land" [2]. Only four street names from earlier, unofficial surveys survived into the new era, Webster, Laguna, Haight and Hays, and three of those were moved to new lines [2].

The southern Western Addition came out with a quirk you can still walk through. Many blocks are cut in half by narrow east-west streets named for plants, such as Ivy, Linden, Rose and Hickory [3]. That created "through blocks" whose lots, often 25 feet by 120, front two streets. Builders put a house at each end, stretched one building between both frontages, or put stables at the back [3]. Linden Street is one of those alleys.

title: The county clerk who named a valley
place: Hayes Street between Van Ness Avenue and Franklin Street
hook: Hayes Valley is named for a Gold Rush county clerk whose brother helped name the streets and who also held the franchise for the West Coast's first railway.
story: Before there was a Hayes Valley there was Colonel Thomas Hayes, San Francisco's county clerk from 1853 to 1856. He held a large tract of land out here in the Western Addition, then the city's western fringe. The Van Ness Ordinance confirmed his claim, and his own house stood on Hayes Street between Van Ness and Franklin [1]. In 1856 a three-man committee named the streets of the new district. One of its members was Hayes's brother Michael, who, according to the Museum of the City of San Francisco, 'probably was instrumental' in giving this street the family name [1]. Hayes also held the franchise, granted by the state Legislature, for the Market Street Railway. It was developed by François Pioche, a Paris-born importer and banker, and it became the first railway on the Pacific Coast [2]. The company was founded in 1857. Market Street was graded, and three years later the first car rolled out toward 16th and Valencia streets, pulled by steam 'dummies' and later by horses [2]. Hayes's house is long gone. Its block is now part of the Civic Center's performing-arts district, but his name runs west across the whole neighbourhood.

title: The saloon where nobody swept the cobwebs
place: Cobweb Palace site, 2200 Powell St (now a post office)
hook: Parrots swore in four languages, bears ate the leftovers, and the spiders were strictly protected.
story: In 1856 Abe Warner opened a saloon at the foot of Meiggs' Wharf, on the northeast corner of Francisco and Powell [1]. He loved spiders and would not let anyone clear their webs, so curtains of cobweb hung from the rafters and the place became known as the Cobweb Palace [1][2]. Sailors paid him in curios, and the dusty walls filled up with scrimshaw, Alaskan totem poles, Japanese Noh masks and South Seas war clubs [1]. Scrimshawed walrus tusks carved by N. S. Finney, which old photographs show behind Warner's bar, are now at Mystic Seaport in Connecticut [2]. Monkeys, parrots, a fox and the occasional bear or kangaroo lived on the premises [1][2]. A parrot called Warner Grandfather would squawk "I'll have a rum and gum. What'll you have?" [1]. On Sundays families came out for free chowder, cracked Dungeness crab and French bread, which makes this an early seed of Fisherman's Wharf dining [1]. Accounts disagree on how it ended. City Guides says Warner retired in 1897 at about 80, while other accounts say he sold the bar in 1893 and died in 1896 [1][3]. Landfill has since moved the shoreline well away, and the site is now a post office at 2200 Powell [1].

title: Who was Haight Street named for?
place: Haight Street between Belvedere and Clayton
hook: Guidebooks credit a banker, a governor or a judge. One researcher found a woman's 1900 pamphlet pointing somewhere else.
story: The street that gave the Haight its name has a disputed namesake. The usual candidates are banker Henry W. Haight, his nephew Governor Henry H. Haight, and Fletcher Haight, a lawyer and later a judge. In 1916 the city's Municipal Record named Fletcher, without giving a reason [1]. Researcher Angus MacFarlane dug deeper. He found an 1851 map that already showed a "Haight Street", and argues that neither Henry had been in town long enough to be honoured. He thinks it more likely honoured an earlier arrival, Samuel W. Haight [2]. The street we know dates from the Western Addition survey that followed the 1855 Van Ness Ordinance [3]. Here MacFarlane's key witness is Weltha Haight, the banker's wife, who helped run the Protestant Orphan Asylum for decades. In a pamphlet dated May 1, 1900, she recalled that her husband, a city official, had the surrounding streets surveyed, "and out of compliment to two of the Managers [of the Asylum], Waller Street and Haight Street were named." Waller honoured co-founder Elizabeth Waller. Weltha died on February 7, 1906 [3]. Wikipedia now follows MacFarlane, but his is one researcher's case, not settled fact [4].

title: The eight-sided house of gravel
place: Feusier Octagon House, 1067 Green St
hook: A New York phrenologist promised that eight walls would make you healthier. On a remote Russian Hill summit, someone believed him, and built the house that still stands.
story: In the 1850s a craze swept America, launched by Orson Squire Fowler, a New York phrenologist who linked a person's well-being to the shape of their home. His book promised that an octagon would let sunlight into every room [1]. San Francisco had at least five octagon houses, and all but one stood on or near Russian Hill [1]. The Feusier Octagon on Green Street was built, as Fowler prescribed, of a mixture of lime or cement, gravel and clay, with no wooden skin [2]. No one knows exactly when. The National Register nomination estimates 1857 or 1858 and notes one claim of 1852 [2], while a later survey puts it about 1859, since it is missing from an 1859 map based on 1857 data [3]. At the time this hilltop was countryside, far from downtown and hard to reach [3]. Louis Feusier, a merchant in produce, mining, salmon canning and wine, owned it by 1875. He added the mansard third storey and the octagonal cupola [1]. In 1906 the outbuildings were dynamited, but residents who refused the order to leave saved the main house [1][3]. The family kept it until 1954 [1].

title: A duelling senator comes to Lone Mountain
place: Former Laurel Hill (Lone Mountain) Cemetery, around Euclid Ave & Collins St
hook: California's anti-slavery senator was shot at Lake Merced by the state's former chief justice, then buried under a state monument in the sand hills that are now Laurel Heights.
story:
In 1853 a group of investors bought 54 sandy acres bounded by today's Presidio Avenue, California Street, Geary Boulevard and Parker Avenue, and opened Lone Mountain Cemetery in 1854 [1][2]. Six years later it received its most famous body.

On 13 September 1859 Senator David C. Broderick, leader of California's Free Soil Democrats, met David S. Terry, a former chief justice of the state Supreme Court who favoured slavery, for a duel at Lake Merced. Broderick's hair-trigger pistol went off early, into the ground, and Terry shot him in the right lung. He died three days later [3]. A judge recalling the case in 1936 quoted his deathbed words: "They killed me because I was opposed to the extension of slavery and the corruption of justice" [4]. The California Police Gazette mourned "a fallen hero" [4].

Broderick was buried under a monument put up by the state. He remains the only sitting U.S. senator killed in a duel [3]. In 1942, when the cemetery was cleared, his remains were moved to Cypress Lawn in Colma [3].

title: A reservoir to water the Gold Rush
place: Francisco Reservoir (now Francisco Park), Bay St between Hyde and Larkin
hook: Before Hetch Hetchy, North Beach drank water carried along the cliffs of the Golden Gate in a wooden flume and pumped up to a basin on Russian Hill.
story: Gold Rush San Francisco had no running water to speak of. In 1857 John Bensley's San Francisco Water Company built the city's first permanent supply: a redwood flume that carried fresh water from Lobos Creek near the Golden Gate, along the shore, to a small pump station on the beach at Black Point Cove. From there, pumps pushed it up to reservoirs on Russian Hill [1]. The largest was the Francisco Reservoir on the slope between Hyde and Larkin, which held about 2.5 million gallons [2]. Sources disagree on when it was built. A local historian dates it to 1861 [2], while the park's own history says 1859 and calls it the first large reservoir in San Francisco [3]. They also differ on where the water came from: Lobos Creek in one account [1], Mountain Lake in another [3]. A reservoir keeper lived in a house at the corner of Hyde and Bay, which stood until 1950 [2]. The basin supplied the crowded northeast of the city, near the port where the Gold Rush arrived [3]. Long after it was retired, neighbours fought for decades to turn the site into today's Francisco Park [2].

title: A senator dies at Black Point
place: Haskell House (Quarters 3), Franklin Street, Upper Fort Mason
hook: Shot in a duel at Lake Merced, California's anti-slavery senator was carried to a friend's house on this bluff. He lasted three days.
story: In the 1850s, developers quietly built five handsome private houses on unused Army land at Black Point, and a colony of bankers, merchants and writers moved in. Its residents were openly hostile to slavery and secession [1][2]. Among them was a developer named Haskell (Park Service publications give his first name as both Leonidas and Leonard) [1][2]. Their political hero was David Broderick, a self-made man and U.S. senator who opposed the spread of slavery [1]. In 1859, after Broderick answered insults from California Supreme Court Justice David S. Terry, who championed slavery's expansion, Terry challenged him to a duel [1][3]. They met at Lake Merced on September 13. Broderick's hair-trigger pistol fired early, into the ground; Terry's shot hit him in the lung [3]. Friends rushed him to Haskell's house at Black Point, where he died three days later, reportedly saying: 'They killed me because I am opposed to the extension of slavery and a corrupt administration' [1]. At the funeral, Edward Baker called his death 'a political necessity, poorly veiled beneath the guise of a private quarrel' [3]. Haskell's house still stands as Quarters 3, one of the three oldest buildings at Fort Mason [1].

title: Lots for Sixteen Dollars Apiece
place: Near Oak and Webster streets
hook: When Hayes first sold his valley, a 25-foot lot cost sixteen dollars. A banker nicknamed Big John bought a stack of them and built a farm-like estate.
story:
Thomas Hayes surveyed and subdivided his tract in three rounds, in 1859, 1860 and 1861 [1][2]. At first he sold whole blocks to speculators, who waited for demand to catch up [1]. The prices look unreal now. A 1928 Chronicle history said that "cabin lots of 25-foot frontage were sold by Hayes at $16 each", even after the city limits had moved out past them [3].

One early buyer was "Big John" Sullivan, president of the Hibernia Loan and Savings Society. He bought a number of 25-foot lots at $16 apiece [1][2]. Near Oak and Webster streets, at the western edge of the Hayes tract, he built a large frame house with extensive gardens, a stable and a henhouse [1]. Mayor James Van Ness also built himself a villa somewhere in Hayes Valley [1][2]. Sullivan's house is long gone.

The streets were laid out but mostly ungraded and unpaved; an 1860s lithograph shows how raw it was [2]. The valley filled in quickly anyway. By 1869 the U.S. Coast Survey map showed its core built up along Hayes Street, reaching about a block north to Grove and south to Fell [1].

title: The Captain Who Carried Dutch Charley Away
place: Pierce and McAllister streets
hook: In 1856 tugboat captain Charles Goodall carried the banished Dutch Charley Duane out to an exile ship. Goodall later built a mansion on this corner.
story:
In June 1856 San Francisco's Vigilance Committee banished Charles "Dutch Charley" Duane. The man who carried him from the wharf to the steamer Golden Age was Charles Goodall, master of the steam tug Hercules [1]. Duane did not forget it. Duane later sued Goodall for damages, first asking $25,000 and later $2,000. In 1862, according to the Daily Alta California, Judge Hoffman ruled that the tug itself was not liable, so any judgment could only fall on Goodall personally [1].

Goodall did well for himself. He founded the Pacific Coast Steamship Company, whose ships called at ports from Alaska to San Diego [1]. His home stood at Pierce and McAllister streets, a block or two east of the land Duane squatted on. A 2017 Planning Department report dates the Goodall mansion to 1859 [2]. Accounts of his estate in 1899 place the "home place" on the west side of Pierce between Fulton and McAllister, and list a large improved lot on the southeast corner of Pierce and McAllister [1].

The mansion is gone. In 1950 Third Baptist Church, founded in 1852, bought the corner and built its present church there in 1952 [2]. Historian Joe Pecora counts the Goodall Mansion among the neighbourhood's lost landmarks [3].

title: The Chinese fishing village below Rincon Hill
place: Old South Beach shoreline, southern foot of Rincon Hill
hook: Before landfill buried South Beach, Chinese fishermen kept a small village on the shore under the mansions of Rincon Hill.
story: In the 1850s the bay still lapped the foot of Rincon Hill, whose name means 'inside corner' in Spanish, and the cove reached as far as today's First Street [1]. While the rich built houses on the crest for the views, a small Chinese fishing village sat on the shore below [1]. A painting by Matilda F. Mott, now at the California Historical Society, shows the village at the southern foot of the hill around 1859 [2]. Chinese fishermen worked the bay in redwood boats, staking long lines of triangular nets in the mudflats to catch shrimp on the tide, and they came to dominate the region's shrimp trade [2]. The Rincon village didn't last. It disappeared along with South Beach itself when the shoreline was filled in the late 1860s [1]. Chinese life here carried on in other forms: excavations for Rincon Center turned up evidence of 1880s Chinese laundries and small supply stores serving boarding-house residents and dockworkers, and some of the finds are on display in the building [1]. Chinese shrimp camps later flourished at Hunters Point and on other shores around the bay [2].

title: A Steam Train Against the Sand
place: Hayes Street between Octavia and Laguna
hook: On July 4, 1860, steam trains began running out Market Street toward Hayes Valley. Blowing sand beat the engines, and horses took over.
story:
Thomas Hayes knew his lots would only sell if people could reach them. In 1857 he got a franchise from the state legislature for a steam railroad along Market Street, with a spur six blocks out Hayes Street to his pleasure garden, Hayes Park [1][2]. It followed roughly the route of today's 21-Hayes bus [1].

The Market Street line opened with steam dummies on July 4, 1860, running from Third and Kearny out Market Street toward the Mission [3]. Planners say the Hayes line was completed the same year [1][2]. The dunes fought back from the start. Drifting sand covered the tracks, and the operators planted windbreaks of brush and scrub oak [1]. Grit still wore out the engines. After public complaints about the steam dummies, the company switched to horses on March 6, 1867 [1][3].

In a 1948 Examiner column, Dick Nolan said the old-timers "thought Hayes' newfangled contraption was downright effeminate" and would rather walk or ride [4]. Hayes ran into money trouble and lost the franchise, and the line became part of the Market Street Railway [2][4]. It had done its job, though. Planners say the investment paid off, and building took off in Hayes Valley during the 1860s [1][2].

title: California's first woolen mill
place: Pioneer Woolen Mills site (now Ghirardelli Square), Beach and Larkin
hook: Long before chocolate, the brick buildings above Aquatic Park held a smoking woolen mill staffed almost entirely by Chinese workers, until a racist campaign helped close it.
story: In the late 1850s, while the water company was building its pump house on the beach at Black Point Cove, the firm of Heynemann, Pick and Company put up a large complex of wood and brick next door. It housed California's first woolen mill [1]. A photograph from about 1860 shows black smoke rising from the Pioneer Woolen Mills below Russian Hill [2]. In 1863 the mill moved into a new brick building [1]. The cove became the city's industrial fringe. In 1867 Thomas Henry Selby built a large smelter on its eastern shore, and the shoreline in front of the mill was filled to extend it into the bay [1]. The mill relied almost entirely on Chinese workers. According to the National Park Service historian James Delgado, it closed in 1889, 'victim of intense competition from eastern mills and racist anti-Chinese agitators' who had campaigned against that workforce [1]. The empty buildings did not stay empty. The D. Ghirardelli Company bought them in the 1890s. Delgado gives 1894 [1], the city landmark record 1893 [3].

title: Jessie Frémont's salon on the bluff
place: Site of Porter's Lodge, north end of Franklin Street, Upper Fort Mason
hook: For a brief moment before the Civil War, the city's liveliest conversation happened in a cottage at the cliff's edge. Then the Army took it and knocked it down.
story: Jessie Benton Frémont was the daughter of Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton and the wife of the explorer John C. Frémont. In the Park Service's words, she was bright, courageous and ambitious at a time when those qualities were discouraged in women [1]. In 1860 the Frémonts moved to Black Point and set their house and gardens on the bluff [1]. The cottage, nicknamed Porter's Lodge, became a centre of San Francisco's intellectual life. Jessie invited writers, spiritual leaders and artists for lively conversation, and both Frémonts were Free-Soilers who lobbied against slavery [1]. The idyll was short. When the Civil War began, John was called to serve the Union and the family moved east [1]. In 1863 the government seized the property without payment, by President Lincoln's executive order [2]. The Army evicted Black Point's civilians and tore down the Frémonts' home to make room for new gun batteries [1]. The family pursued compensation for more than a century. At least 24 congressional committees voted to pay Frémont, and his descendants were still in federal court in 1968. Their lawsuit said he had paid $42,000 for 13.5 acres in the mid-1850s [2].

title: Summer girls at the Willows
place: The Willows resort site, 18th Street between Mission and Valencia
hook: A creek, a stand of willows, bowling alleys and an emu: the Mission's first great pleasure garden drew Mark Twain, then drowned.
story: San Francisco had no public parks in its early years, so people paid to visit private "pleasure gardens" [2]. One of the first was the Willows, set in a creek ravine between Mission and Valencia and 17th and 19th streets [1][2]. Willow trees fed by a stream from Twin Peaks gave it its name [2]. There was a dance platform, athletic fields, rides, rifle shooting, a winter skating pond and a small menagerie that included an emu [1][2]. The French banker François Pioche took it over around 1859 or 1860, and in 1860 opened a steam railway from Battery and Market out Valencia to the gates. The fare was 10 cents [2][3]. On a Sunday in August 1861, the silver man John Robinson found cars running every 15 minutes, "crowded with happy faces" [3]. Mark Twain went in 1863 or 1864 and later sighed over "summer girls and summer dresses, and summer scenes at 'The Willows'" [2]. The ravine was its undoing. Sources disagree on the details: one says a flood in 1861 closed it for good, another that the record rains of 1862 swamped it and it reopened but never recovered [2][3]. Pioche took his own life in 1872 [2].

title: The cemetery under Dolores Park
place: Former Home of Peace cemetery, Dolores Park near 18th St
hook: For three decades the city's Jews buried their dead where picnickers now lounge. The last grave held out, and it blocked the land sale.
story: In 1860 Congregation Emanu-El and the Eureka Benevolent Society bought the northern block of today's Dolores Park for a cemetery they called Home of Peace. Congregation Sherith Israel took the southern block for its Hills of Eternity [1]. Home of Peace was consecrated on July 25, 1860. The crowd struggled to get there because the only tramway to the Mission had just opened [1]. By 1867 each cemetery held about 300 graves [1]. As the city grew around them, neighbours blamed the graves for sickness. The foul smell more likely came from stagnant pools nearby [1]. In 1888 the supervisors ordered the cemeteries closed. Jewish leaders protested that they were being singled out, since Catholic burials were still allowed [1]. The congregations bought new land in Colma. From July 1892 nearly a thousand bodies were carted down the Mission road in express wagons [1][2]. One plot stayed behind: Augusta Neustadt and her two husbands, under a tall stone shaft, which kept the land from being sold [1]. Part of the old cemetery land north of 18th Street went to the new Mission High School, finished in 1898 [1][3].

title: The church whose walls outlasted the fire
place: St. Francis of Assisi Church, 610 Vallejo St
hook: In a Gold Rush town full of every nation, this parish preached in Latin, Spanish, Italian, French, Chinese and German.
story: St. Francis of Assisi on Vallejo Street is one of California's earliest churches outside the Spanish missions [1]. Its Norman Gothic building, with twin towers, was dedicated as a parish church on 17 March 1860 [1][2]. That was a time when North Beach's 'Latin Quarter' at the foot of Telegraph Hill was full of French, Italian, Mexican, Spanish and Portuguese families [3]. The parish reflected the Gold Rush crowd around it. Early sermons were given in Latin, Spanish, Italian, French, Chinese and German [1]. As the Italians spread down from Telegraph Hill into North Beach, St. Francis became one of the anchors of what turned into Little Italy [3]. In 1906 the fire gutted the interior, but the towers and outer walls survived. The parish built a new church inside the old shell and rededicated it on 2 March 1919 [2]. It was the city's fifth designated landmark, and in 1999 it was named the National Shrine of Saint Francis of Assisi, honouring the saint San Francisco is named after [1][2].

title: A letter to future ages
place: McElroy Octagon House, 2645 Gough Street at Union
hook: In 1953 an electrician rewiring an eight-sided house found a tin can hidden by the stairs. Inside was a letter the builder had written in 1861.
story: In 1848 the phrenologist Orson Squire Fowler published a book claiming that an eight-sided house enclosed more space with less material and was lighter, warmer in winter and cooler in summer than a square one. Several thousand octagon houses followed across North America [1]. William C. McElroy, a wood miller, and his wife Harriet Shober bought a lot on Gough Street in 1859 and built their octagon in 1860 and 1861 [2]. By the early 1950s it stood vacant and neglected, and the National Society of the Colonial Dames of America in California bought it, moved it across the street to the corner of Gough and Union, and restored it [2][3]. Nobody knew much about the house then, and one newspaper filled the gap with a ghost story: every November 24, something shrieked on the 20th stair [3]. Then, in March 1953, an electrician working on the renovation found a round tin canister hidden near the stairs to the cupola [3]. It held newspaper clippings, an ambrotype photograph of the family, and a letter McElroy wrote on July 14, 1861, confirming that the house was their 'privet Residence' [3]. The photo shows their daughter Emma at about nine. It is the only known record of what she looked like [4].

title: How Cow Hollow got its name
place: Hatman dairy block, Union, Filbert, Franklin and Gough
hook: A man once paid in octagonal gold coins bought this block for $500 in 1861 and filled it with cows. Thirty dairies later, the valley had a new name.
story: George William Hatman and his wife came around the Horn and arrived in 1853 [1]. His first job was driving a white mule at a brickyard, and one week's wages came as an octagon-shaped $50 gold piece. Potatoes were so expensive that $2.50 worth fit in his coat pocket. That gave him an idea: he leased land near today's Gough and Green and planted a vegetable garden [1]. In 1861 he paid $500 for the block now bounded by Union, Filbert, Franklin and Gough and started a dairy with 60 cows [1]. By the early 1870s there were at least 30 dairies between Van Ness Avenue and the Presidio, some with 200 cows, and San Franciscans stopped calling the valley Spring Valley and started calling it Cow Hollow [1]. The cows' days were numbered. Touring the hollow with a reporter, city health officer Dr. Keeney pointed out sick cows, cows fattened on brewery waste and stagnant drinking pools, and said the Board of Health would recommend moving them outside city limits [2]. The date is fuzzy: Hatman's son Bill, born on the dairy in 1867, remembered the cows leaving in the 1880s, while FoundSF dates Keeney's tour to about 1900 [1][2].

title: How Union Square got its name
place: Union Square
hook: A dune set aside for a park became a rallying ground for the Union, and in April 1865 fourteen thousand mourners marched here for Lincoln.
story: The square began as a windswept sand hill with chaparral, set aside as public land on early surveys and deeded to the city in 1850 by John Geary, the first mayor under American rule [1][2]. Through the 1850s it was mostly a dump, a squatters' camp and a sandy ball field; one writer suggests the phrase 'sand-lot baseball' may have started here [1]. During the Civil War it took its name from the pro-Union rallies held on it, often led by the Unitarian minister Thomas Starr King, whose church faced the square [1][2]. The rallies ended with grief: on April 20, 1865, fourteen thousand people marched past buildings draped in black to hear a memorial address for President Lincoln, given by King's successor Horatio Stebbins [1]. During the war years the Mechanics' Institute also held its industrial fairs in a wooden pavilion on the square; a larger one built in 1868 was said to seat 8,000 [1]. The square's war memory returned in 1903, when President Theodore Roosevelt dedicated the Dewey Monument to the U.S. Navy's victory at Manila Bay [1][2].

title: Streets Drawn Before Anyone Climbed the Hill
place: Howth St, east slope of Merced Heights (San Miguel City tract)
hook: In 1862 a surveyor drew 'San Miguel City' across a steep, empty ridge. Some of his lines took the better part of a century to become real streets.
story: In June 1862 George Black surveyed and filed the map for 'San Miguel City,' the first subdivision in the future OMI, on the northeast slope of Merced Heights beside the coming San Francisco-San Jose railroad [1][2]. Hopes ran high: that April the Evening Bulletin reported farmers ploughing wildflower patches on the San Miguel and Merced ranches in anticipation of the line [2]. Buyers did not follow. The steam train cost about three times a city streetcar fare, and the ridge had no water, sewers or gas [1][2]. San Miguel City saw no building until the first decade of the 20th century, and photos from as late as 1907 show much of it still under cultivation [2]. Today's Howth and Tara Streets survive from Black's plan [1]. In 1893 Easton, Eldridge & Co. filed 'Columbia Heights' on the east-facing slope along Lakeview Avenue [1]. In the 1910s and 1920s both tracts filled with modest homes on Howth, Tara, Josiah, Margaret, Majestic and Caine, many housing motormen, conductors and maintenance workers from the transit yards near Balboa Park [2]. Even so, a city photographer recorded Caine Avenue as a dirt street in January 1923 [1].

title: The houses that turned their backs
place: Funston Avenue officers' houses at the old Alameda entrance
hook: Civil War officers' homes on Funston Avenue once faced the parade ground. In 1878 the Army moved their front porches to the back to impress visitors from the city.
story: The Civil War set off the Presidio's first big building boom since the United States took it over. The post grew from a scatter of adobes and temporary wooden buildings into an Army post that could hold more than 1,500 officers and men [1]. Among the new buildings was a row of houses on what is now Funston Avenue. They were built for officers and their families and faced west, toward the new parade ground [2]. Then appearances started to count. From the 1860s until 1895 the official way in from San Francisco was the Alameda, halfway down Funston, where cannonballs lined the road as decorative curbs and sentries stood guard [3]. In 1878 the Army moved each house's front porch to the back, turning the whole row around so it would look better to visitors arriving along the Alameda [2]. White picket fences, street lamps and gardens followed in the mid-1880s, and later bay windows, gables and dormers [2]. Four large Victorian houses still mark the old entrance where Presidio Boulevard meets Funston Avenue [3].

title: A Presbyterian College on a Country Hill
place: University Mound, site of the 1863 college building (today 350 University Street)
hook: Long before it was a neighbourhood, the Portola's hill was a would-be campus. The college failed, but the name 'University Mound' outlived it by 160 years.
story: In 1863 the Presbyterians put up a big three-storey wooden building on a lonely rise far south of the city. It housed University Mound College, a boarding-school branch of the church's downtown City College, and it never really prospered [1]. From 1869 to 1871 the same building was the University Mound Institute and Boarding School for Boys, and then that closed too [1]. The ambition stuck even though the schools didn't. There had been plans for a city university on the hill, and the streets that grew up around it were named after colleges and universities: Harvard, Oxford, Cambridge, Yale, Amherst, Princeton and Dartmouth [1]. In 1884 trustees spending part of James Lick's fortune bought the old college with 25 acres and turned it into a home for elderly women [1][2]. The wooden building lasted until 1932, when architect Martin J. Rist replaced it with the red-brick building that still stands at 350 University Street [1][2]. By 1905 the name was so well established that Daniel Burnham's city plan proposed a 218-acre 'University Mound Park' on the heights next door [3].

title: A Toll Road, a Roadhouse and a Rope
place: Cliff House, 1090 Point Lobos Ave
hook: On July 4, 1863, a plain clapboard bar opened on the cliff. Three years later a woman walked a tightrope from it to Seal Rocks.
story: The Cliff House was born as a real-estate play. Speculator Charles C. Butler built it alongside the new Point Lobos Toll Road, backed by State Senator John P. Buckley, an officer of the road company [1]. It opened on July 4, 1863, with the well-known host Captain Junius G. Foster in charge. Despite being called a hotel, it served only food and drink, and the real draw was the view of the sea lions on the rocks below [1]. Omnibuses left Kearny and Clay streets for the seals at 50 cents a ride, and drivers paid a toll near today's Masonic Avenue [2]. Early-morning carriage rides out for breakfast became the fashion; Mark Twain made the trip in 1864 and wrote a grumpy, funny account [1]. When the view wasn't enough, Foster booked balloon ascensions and acrobats. On June 24, 1866, Miss Rosa Celeste walked a 400-foot rope from the cliff to Seal Rocks, 100 feet above the surf and without guide wires, while five thousand people watched [1]. Presidents Grant and Hayes later came to dine [1].

title: A college built on gold dust
place: Site of St. Mary's College, College Avenue at Mission Street
hook: The college now in Moraga began on a windswept Bernal slope, paid for partly with gold dust from Sierra miners.
story:
Archbishop Joseph Alemany wanted an affordable college for the children of miners, mechanics and farmers. The cornerstone was laid on 3 August 1862 [1]. He bought 60 acres of the old Bernal rancho from Jesus Bernal for $1,600 [2]. To pay for the building he sent the Irish priest James Croke on a two-year fundraising trip to farmers, merchants and Sierra gold miners. Croke came back with cash and gold dust worth $37,166.50 [3]. According to a lecture published by the college, one early donor was the celebrated Mary Ellen Pleasant [4].

St. Mary's College opened in 1863 as a college for boys. It struggled, and in 1868 nine mostly Irish Christian Brothers sailed from New York to take it over. It awarded its first bachelor's degrees in 1872 [3]. An 1875 photograph shows the walled campus facing Mission Road, with two baseball diamonds beside it [3]. In 1889 the college left its "cold, windswept campus" for Oakland, and later moved to Moraga [2][3]. The Bernal site became a parish and then a truck farm [2]. The south-west corner of Bernal is still called College Hill, and a 1962 marker stands at the west end of College Avenue [2].

title: Lake Geneva, a spring that fed Islais Creek
place: Block bounded by Geneva, Niagara, Delano and Cayuga avenues (approximate site of 'Lake Geneva')
hook: An 1863 map shows a spring-fed 'Lake Geneva' near today's Cayuga Avenue. It was one source of a creek that ran all the way to the bay.
story: Before the house lots, this corner of the city had its own lake. A spring-fed pond marked as 'Lake Geneva' on some maps sat roughly on the block now bounded by Geneva, Niagara, Delano and Cayuga avenues. The city's 1863 'West End Map #1' is one of those maps [1]. The pond was one of the sources of Islais Creek, which ran east through the valley and emptied into a wide tidal estuary at today's Islais Creek Channel [1]. According to stories passed down by local historians, travellers on the old road stopped at the spring to water their animals, although no written record from the colonial era confirms this [1]. The creek did not survive the city. Its valley was put into culverts and covered by San Jose Avenue and Alemany Boulevard, and later by Interstate 280 [2]. People still point to what is left. FoundSF notes that the headwaters of one branch of Islais Creek run somewhere deep beneath nearby Cayuga Park, under the BART tracks [3].

title: The first train left from 25th Street
place: Valencia Street station site, 25th and Valencia Streets
hook: Four hundred passengers, two locomotives and a speech about angels: the Peninsula railroad began at a depot in the Mission, not downtown.
story: The railroad that grew into today's Peninsula line began in the Mission. At about 10:30 on the morning of October 17, 1863, the first San Francisco and San Jose Railroad excursion left the Mission station, near 25th and Valencia. Two locomotives pulled six passenger cars, two baggage cars and a freight car, carrying about 400 people to the end of the line at Mayfield [1][2]. The company had been one of the first railroads to hire Chinese labourers [1]. Its hardest job was the cut through Bernal Hill, blasted in 1862 with "heavy and continuous assaults of powder" [1]. The line reached San Jose on January 16, 1864, and turned an eight-hour trip by steamboat and stagecoach into about three and a half hours [1]. The Valencia Street depot got a proper station building in 1866. It stayed a stop as the tracks were pushed closer to downtown, until most regular service ended in 1903 [2]. The tracks cut diagonally across the neighbourhood, crossing Mission Street between 24th and 25th. After the line was abandoned, the right of way became housing and, in one strip, the little park called Juri Commons [3].

title: Two blocks of middle-class time travel
place: Liberty Street between Valencia and Guerrero (Liberty Street Historic District)
hook: Gilders, Mint workers, box-makers and a judge built side by side on Liberty Street, leaving every Victorian style in one short walk.
story: Liberty Street sits on the eastern edge of the old Rancho San Miguel, which José de Jesús Noé received in 1845. He sold it in 1854 to John M. Horner, who laid out "Horner's Addition" and sold it block by block. Horner's 1863 map shows just one building here [1]. The oldest house on the National Register's list is the Marshall Doane House at 45 Liberty, dated 1863. Beside it is the Siamese Twin House of 1879 at 20-26 Liberty [1]. Over the next half-century, 51 houses went up on the two blocks between Valencia and Guerrero, in every style of the day: early Italianate, Stick, Eastlake, Queen Anne and Classical Revival [1]. No famous architects worked here, and only thirteen of the houses have known designers [1]. The owners were solidly middle class: foremen, attorneys, two U.S. Mint employees, two gilders, carriage makers, sailors and the partners in a box factory [1]. Around the corner, coal-yard partner Marsden Kershaw built his house at 845 Guerrero in 1871, one of the district's earliest [2]. Liberty Street still keeps more of that 19th-century feeling than almost any street in the city [3].

title: A racetrack built on a marsh
place: Former Bay View Park racecourse, around Yosemite Slough
hook: The Bayview got its name from a horse track built on tidal marsh, apparently because the soggy ground was thought to put a spring in the horses' step.
story: In the 1860s the mining millionaire George Hearst and other investors built Bay View Park, a racetrack with a hotel and stables, on a low tidal marsh south of the Hunters Point peninsula [1]. The 1864 city directory described it: 'The ground is reclaimed and protected from the tide by a breakwater or bulkhead. A large and spacious hotel, with stables and outhouses attached, has been added.' It also mentioned 'a beautiful shell road' about three miles long, expected to cost around $30,000 [1]. Historians think the shells were most likely dug from nearby Ohlone shellmounds [1]. The site was not chosen to sell real estate. Its springy marsh was thought to make the horses faster, and an 1869 drawing shows Yosemite Slough still running through the middle of the oval [1]. Weekend crowds rode out from the city, as they did to other tracks at the edge of town. The track did not last. By the early 1880s the hotel had burned, the tides had broken through the dikes, and by the 1883 Coast Survey map the course was gone [1]. Only its name survived. 'Bay View' spread to the flats and then to the whole district [1], and decades later land offered to the city was still described as the old racetrack site [2].

title: Colonel Hayes's Pleasure Garden
place: Near Hayes and Laguna streets
hook: To sell lots in a sandy hollow, Tom Hayes built a day-trip resort with a concert hall, gymnasium, shooting gallery and bar.
story:
Thomas Hayes was an Irish-born politician who sailed for San Francisco in January 1849 with two of his brothers. He got a 160-acre tract through a preemption deed, in effect a squatter's claim, and the Van Ness Ordinance confirmed it in 1855 [1]. A 1928 Chronicle writer called him "a rather picturesque but shrewd figure in early San Francisco politics and in state military affairs" [2].

Farming failed in the fog, wind and sand, so Hayes started selling his land for homes instead [1][3]. To bring buyers out, he opened what planners describe as a "come-on" attraction: Hayes Park, near today's Hayes and Laguna streets, with a picnic ground, restaurant and bar [3]. Sources give different opening dates. The city's context statement says around 1856, and other accounts say the early 1860s [1].

By 1864 the San Francisco Directory was advertising Hayes' Park, Pavilion and Garden as a "suburban resort" with a garden, concert hall, gymnasium and shooting gallery [2]. Townspeople made a day or half-day trip of it. A photograph of Hayes Valley taken that year shows the semicircular pavilion in the distance, with the Protestant Orphan Asylum in one corner [2].

title: Lakeville, a suburb only on maps
place: East side of Lake Merced (projected 'Lakeville' tract)
hook: In 1864 a speculator carved the east shore of Lake Merced into suburban lots. For twenty years 'Lakeville' existed only on maps.
story: By the 1860s San Francisco speculators were eyeing every open acre, and in 1864 land auctioneer John Middleton tried to sell lots of 160 by 200 feet on the eastern side of Lake Merced for a new suburb he called "Lakeville" [1]. It was a colossal failure, in a district so remote that even its roadhouses struggled against the distance, the weather and competition from resorts closer to town [1]. Lakeville never got beyond paper, yet it kept appearing on maps of the city for the next twenty years; George Goddard's 1869 map shows the projected suburb on the east shore alongside the Lake House, Ocean House and racetrack [1]. By 1875, after land schemes, roadhouses and racing had all come and gone, the best business around the lake turned out to be growing potatoes [1]. The east shore stayed farmland until the twentieth century, when the Spring Valley Water Company began selling its holdings and developers took options on the cultivated fields [2]. Large-scale housing finally reached the east shore with Parkmerced, which opened in 1952 [3].

title: Steam trains and a lonely Elkton stop
place: Site of Southern Pacific's Elkton station, just south of Ocean Avenue beside today's Balboa Park BART
hook: Long before BART, trains stopped here, at a quiet station called Elkton that served cabbage farmers and a reform school.
story: The first railroad from San Francisco to San Jose came through here in the early 1860s. Wikipedia gives October 1863 for the start of service through the city, and the historic context statement says the San Jose line was complete in 1864 [1][2]. The single track ran out of the Mission, through the Bernal Cut, and south along what is now the I-280 corridor [1]. Farmers were already ploughing wild iris meadows in 1862 because they expected the railroad to arrive [1]. There was a stop called Elkton about 300 feet south of Ocean Avenue, close to where BART's Balboa Park station is now [2]. It handled mostly farm freight, but it also served the Industrial School on the hill [2]. The railroad did less for the area than people had hoped. In 1884 a one-way ticket from Fourth and Townsend to Ocean View cost 15 cents, three times a cable car fare, and farmers kept driving their wagons to market [1]. After Southern Pacific opened its Bayshore Cutoff in 1907, this line was left with a few local trains [2]. Its right-of-way later became the route of the freeway and BART.

title: Sunday picnics among the Masonic tombs
place: Former Masonic Cemetery, now USF's lower campus
hook: Before Golden Gate Park, San Franciscans went for their Sunday air among the tombs. USF's campus still turns up the occasional casket.
story: The cemeteries around Lone Mountain were meant for the living as much as the dead. Lone Mountain Cemetery, opened in 1854, was modelled on the grand garden cemeteries of the East, a sign that the raw young city could match the country's great metropolises [1]. The Masons laid out their own lavishly landscaped cemetery for members here, opened in 1864 [1][2]. Sources disagree on its size: 38 acres in one account, 30 in another [1][3]. Families made Sunday outings of it, because surveying for Golden Gate Park did not begin until August 1870 [2]. Once the park opened, it took over the cemeteries' role as a place to stroll, and the neighbours began asking for the graves to go [1]. The Masonic Cemetery closed in 1931, and about 19,900 bodies were moved to Woodlawn Cemetery in Colma [3]. Its land became the lower campus of the University of San Francisco. Not every trace left. In 2011 construction workers digging for USF's new science centre uncovered 25 mostly empty caskets, and a skull tumbled out of a shovel [3].

title: Tar Flat and the 200-foot shot tower
place: First and Howard streets (gas works and Selby Shot Tower)
hook: At First and Howard a gasworks dumped tar into the bay and a 200-foot tower rained molten lead. Mothers brought coughing children to breathe the fumes.
story: East of First Street, the land being filled in from the bay became San Francisco's first industrial zone, with foundries, machine shops and boiler works [1]. Its landmark was a 200-foot tower raised in 1864 at First and Howard by the Selby Smelting and Lead Company for making bullets and shot; it worked until the 1906 earthquake [1]. Across the corner stood the Donahue brothers' gas works, which distilled coal and brought gas lighting to the city in early 1854 [2]. The early technology was crude, and the sludge was dumped into the open water at Fremont Street [2]. It killed the shellfish, and the smell gave the neighbourhood its name, Tar Flat [2]. Workers' families on nearby Mission Street lived in the thick of it, and some mothers carried sick children into the plant, believing the fumes would cure whooping cough [2]. The gas company absorbed its rivals and in 1905 re-incorporated as Pacific Gas and Electric [2]. Tar Flat came back in the 1980s: a layer of still-hazardous tar three to five feet thick stopped work on a new tower at Beale and Howard until it was removed [2].

title: The Union's preacher, buried at Geary
place: Sarcophagus of Thomas Starr King, First Unitarian Church, 1187 Franklin Street at Geary
hook: One of the few graves San Francisco never moved belongs to the preacher who campaigned for the Union and raised a fortune for wounded soldiers.
story: Thomas Starr King came west in 1860 to lead First Unitarian, then a congregation deep in debt on Stockton Street. He cleared the debt and raised money for a larger church at 133 Geary Street near Union Square, finished by January 1864 [1]. When the Civil War began he toured California speaking for the Union and campaigned with his friend Leland Stanford. Lincoln allegedly credited him with keeping California in the Union [1]. He also raised more than $1.5 million for the U.S. Sanitary Commission. His plaque calls it the forerunner of the American Red Cross [1][2]. Worn out by constant travel, he died of diphtheria and pneumonia on 4 March 1864, aged 39. Around 20,000 people attended his funeral, and Bret Harte gave a eulogy [1]. He was entombed in a sarcophagus beside the church. In 1889 the congregation moved to Percy & Hamilton's rough granite Romanesque church at Franklin and Geary, and the tomb moved with it [1][3]. Most of the city's burials were later removed, but his sarcophagus still sits in the corner of the lot near O'Farrell Street [1].

title: The railroad that cut the valley diagonally
place: Dolores Street at 27th Street, where the Southern Pacific bridge crossed
hook: Wonder why some Noe Valley houses are shaped like slices of pie? A steam railroad ran diagonally through the neighbourhood for nearly 80 years.
story:
In January 1864 the first train on the San Francisco–San Jose line left the city. It blew smoke across open cattle land on its way south. The route followed the flattest ground it could find. It ran down Harrison Street, angled west across the Mission, and curved southwest near today's Cesar Chavez and Dolores. Then it cut diagonally across lower Noe Valley to Duncan Street and ran south to 30th [1].

Photos show the line's bridge over Dolores at 27th Street as late as 1929. Another bridge is visible behind houses at 29th and Dolores around 1902 [2]. After the 1906 earthquake, a photographer on Valley Street near Dolores caught St. Paul's rising behind the old railroad bridge [3].

The line lost importance in 1907, when a new bayshore route opened on filled marshland. It became a branch line and finally faded out in 1942 [1]. The city grew around the tracks, and you can still trace the route today. Look for the odd triangular houses built to fit the right-of-way along its old path [1].

title: A mile of timber over the bay
place: Long Bridge landing, Third (Kentucky) and Mariposa streets
hook: To reach the Potrero you once needed a boat. Then the city built a bridge a mile long straight across Mission Bay's mudflats.
story: Before 1865, getting to the Potrero meant a slow trip around the edge of Mission Bay or a boat from the foot of Third Street [1]. Then the city built a bridge straight across the water. The first pilings went in off Steamboat Point in February 1865, and by 1867 the timber trestle had reached land near today's Mariposa Street [2]. It was about a mile long, and people called it Long Bridge or the Mission Bay Bridge [1]. Taking the road on south along Kentucky Street (now Third) meant blasting through a ridge of serpentine rock that joined Potrero Point to the hill. More than 100,000 cubic yards of rock were removed, the first big reshaping of Potrero Hill [2]. Within months, horsecars of the Potrero and Bayview Railroad were running across, linking downtown with Potrero Point for the first time [2]. The bridge was also a place for fun. Hobbs Wharf, off the bridge, was a favourite spot for Sunday smelt fishing, where hundreds of rented bamboo poles stuck out a yard apart [2]. Land speculation came next, and factories and workers' cottages followed [3]. Once the railroads filled in Mission Bay in the early 1900s, the bridge was closed [3].

title: Long Bridge: a causeway across the bay
place: Third Street, along the route of the vanished Long Bridge
hook: Third Street was once a wooden bridge over open water, crowded on Sundays with smelt fishermen, rowers and thirsty day-trippers.
story: In February 1865 pile drivers began hammering a causeway into Mission Bay. Long Bridge ran out along the line of Fourth Street, turned south near today's Third Street, and by 1867 reached the Potrero, later carrying horsecars all the way to the Bay View racetrack near Hunters Point [1][2]. It was sold as rapid transit for workers, but on Sundays it became the South of Market crowd's playground. Smelt fishing from the rails was so popular that elbow room was scarce. At Hobbs Wharf, off the bridge, hundreds of long bamboo poles, many rented from booths on the wharf, jutted out a yard apart [1]. Rowing clubs built boathouses on pilings, boats could be hired to row out to Mission Rock, and saltwater bathhouses stood right over the bay. James Gallandett and G.W. Purdy opened a Half-Way House beside the San Francisco Yacht Club's clubhouse [1][3]. The bridge also had a lasting effect. It sealed off most of the western bay, with only a narrow drawbridge for shallow scows at high tide, and the stagnant lagoon behind it was steadily filled in [1][2]. No trace survives, but Fourth and Third streets still follow its route [2].
