title: Five days watching the city burn
place: Summit of Buena Vista Park
hook: In April 1906 the city's oldest park became a grandstand for catastrophe, as crowds climbed Buena Vista to watch downtown burn for days.
story: The hilltop had been set aside in 1867 as Hill Park, among the first land reserved for San Francisco's park system, and renamed Buena Vista Park in 1894. John McLaren then forested its slopes, and schoolchildren planted seedlings on Arbor Day while Adolph Sutro was mayor [1]. In April 1906 the view that gave the park its name turned terrible. According to a history of the park by Jeanne Alexander, people gathered on the summit for five days to watch the fires spread after the earthquake [1]. Photographs collected on FoundSF show the blaze as seen from the park [2], and refugees walking up Baker Street toward it from the Panhandle [3]. The neighbourhood below survived. The National Register nomination for a building at Haight and Ashbury explains that the Haight-Ashbury had open land to build on and its infrastructure was intact. Much of its development, and much of its density, came after the earthquake and fire, as people who had lost their homes moved west [4]. The people who stood on this hill watching the old city burn were also looking at the reason their own neighbourhood was about to fill up.

title: Four Blocks for a Loaf
place: Fillmore Street between Turk and Eddy
hook: With cooking indoors banned until chimneys were checked, the breadline at Fillmore and Turk stretched four blocks.
story: At the end of the third day, Mayor Eugene Schmitz told everyone to put out their stoves. His proclamation warned "all citizens not to build fires in their homes until the chimneys have been inspected and repaired properly" [1]. Even families whose houses had survived now had no way to cook. Their pantries soon ran out, most goods in the shops had been seized, and depending on the district the ban on indoor fires lasted from a week to two or three months [2]. So the Western Addition queued. Officials took over the grocery stores still standing and handed out food. One breadline was set up at Fillmore and Turk, where "every person who stood in line was given a whole loaf." That line "was four blocks long all one afternoon" [1]. Milk shipped over from Oakland went to women and children [1]. A postcard from the time shows a breadline running east along Eddy Street from Fillmore, with a soldier patrolling beside it. The cataloguer notes some doubt about the exact spot [3]. Photographs from the Western Addition show families cooking in the street on wood-burning stoves [3].

title: Hayes Valley Fills Up
place: Hayes Street between Octavia and Laguna
hook: The houses west of Octavia survived the fire, and then filled with refugees. Big family homes turned into flats and backyards grew cottages.
story: West of Octavia, Hayes Valley came through the fire. It did not come through undamaged. The geologist H.O. Wood found cracked brick walls and fallen gables across the valley, and wrote that "most chimney stacks were broken" [1]. Brick-faced storefronts on Hayes Street collapsed onto the sidewalk [1]. The neighbourhood's biggest change came afterwards, as the burned-out moved in. Many refugees rented apartments or built new housing in Hayes Valley. Some owners moved away and turned their large single-family houses into apartments [1]. All over the Victorian districts just outside the fire line, Richard Walker notes, big old homes were quickly divided into flats [2]. Little was torn down. Instead, the 1913–15 Sanborn maps show large lots split up, flats built beside older houses, and cottages squeezed into back yards [1]. Hayes Valley had been middle-class, and it became increasingly working-class [1]. The same maps show the Jefferson Square Building, at the southwest corner of Golden Gate and Octavia, as headquarters of the San Francisco Socialist Party, and a Machinists' Hall on Oak Street [1].

title: Julia Morgan's clubhouse hosts the Supreme Court
place: Century Club of California, 1355 Franklin Street
hook: A women's club hired one of its own members, a young architect named Julia Morgan. After the fire, the state's highest court moved into the clubhouse.
story:
The Century Club of California was founded in 1888 as a private women's club [1]. Its early officers included Sarah B. Cooper, who founded the Golden Gate Kindergarten Association, a network of 50 kindergartens, served on the board of the Associated Charities and later turned to women's suffrage. She was the club's vice-president [2].

For its Franklin Street clubhouse, completed in 1905, the club chose one of its members, Julia Morgan [1]. She had recently returned from the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. In 1904 she became the first woman licensed as an architect in California and opened her San Francisco practice, so the clubhouse was one of her first commissions [1][3].

The clubhouse survived the earthquake and fire of April 1906. Afterwards it temporarily housed the California State Supreme Court [1]. Morgan's own office had burned [3]. She was then chosen to redesign the fire-gutted Fairmont Hotel because she had a rare knowledge of earthquake-resistant reinforced concrete [3].

title: Quake Refugees in a Cattle Corral
place: Felton Street near University Street, site of a probable surviving quake shack (1080 Felton)
hook: After the 1906 earthquake, one Portola family bedded down beside cattle headed for the slaughterhouses. A little shack on Felton Street may date from that time.
story: Hazel Laine came to the Portola as a baby in the wake of the 1906 earthquake. Her family camped in a corral next to cattle bound for the Butchertown slaughterhouses in the nearby Bayview [1]. She told her neighbours, the artists Kate Connell and Oscar Melara, about a Portola full of greenhouses and corrals. She also said her older brother later ran the local gas station and charged rum-runners extra during Prohibition [1]. Across the city, relief officials built 5,610 temporary cottages. By summer 1907 the tenants had to buy their cottages and move them to lots of their own, or be forcibly removed by park authorities [2]. The cottages were hauled off by horse-drawn cart, usually to hillsides that were still empty [2]. FoundSF's survey of survivors includes a small house at 1080 Felton Street in the Portola. The site admits, though, that some of the houses it lists may not really be quake shacks [2].

title: Refugee Tents Below the College on the Hill
place: Affiliated Colleges buildings, Parnassus Avenue (now UCSF)
hook: The 1906 fire wiped out the dental school downtown but never reached Parnassus. So the dentists moved up the hill and treated the refugees camped below.
story: Before April 18, 1906, the Affiliated Colleges stood on the city's outskirts. The earthquake did them only modest damage and the fire never came near. Suddenly they were close to a homeless population, with more than 40,000 people sheltering in Golden Gate Park just below [1][2]. Six days after the quake the university ended the academic year. Students were passed or failed without exams, and women students were urged to go home [2]. Downtown, the Dental Department's clinics in the Donohoe Building, recently fitted with new chairs and fountain cuspidors, were reduced to 'charred rubble.' Even so, the faculty rebuilt its records from what survived and recommended 24 students for graduation [2]. Dentistry moved up the hill and squeezed into the easternmost college building alongside Pharmacy. Its whole first floor was remodelled as a clinic with surgical and extracting rooms to meet the refugees' urgent dental needs [2]. The pharmacists objected to losing their lecture hall, and UC President Benjamin Ide Wheeler ruled for the dentists [2]. One building became a full hospital, a nursing school followed in 1907, and a new UC Hospital opened across Parnassus in 1917 [1].

title: Refugees fill the little valley
place: 207 Raymond Avenue at Rutland Street, a likely relocated earthquake shack
hook: The 1906 quake barely touched the valley, but it filled up with homeless San Franciscans. A little house on Raymond Avenue may be one of their relief cottages.
story: The April 18, 1906 earthquake did only minor damage in Visitacion Valley, but the fire downtown sent people south [1]. Refugees crowded into the small houses of relatives and friends, or lived in shacks until they could build new homes [1]. Residents later recalled that the local butcher shop served as the handout point for food and clothing [1]. Many of these newcomers went back to their old neighbourhoods within a few years. Others stayed, and building took off, which kept the local lumber yard busy [1]. Heritage notes that the rush out of the burned city helped start the valley's churches and small businesses, including the shops of Leland Avenue [2]. The Red Cross and relief committee built 5,610 temporary cottages citywide. By summer 1907 their tenants had to buy the cottages and haul them to their own lots or be evicted [3]. Chris Carlsson of FoundSF counts 207 Raymond Avenue at Rutland Street among the city's surviving 'quake shacks' [3]. FoundSF itself warns that some houses on its list still need more research, so treat this one as a strong candidate, not a proven case [3].

title: Refugees on the green hill
place: 'Nursing Settlement', Iowa and 19th streets
hook: Potrero Hill escaped the fire, and South of Market's homeless poured up its slopes. Local children envied the refugee kids so much that one pretended to be one.
story: Potrero Hill was spared by the 1906 earthquake and fire, and it filled up fast [3]. Residents long remembered the people of South of Market climbing the slopes with whatever they had managed to save: a bird on a woman's shoulder, a man carrying a single chair, another with a blanket. From the hill they watched the city burn [1]. Army surplus tents from the Spanish-American War went up between 19th and 22nd streets, from Indiana to Kentucky (now Third) [1]. Around Iowa and 19th streets grew what one resident remembered as the "Nursing Settlement", a refugee centre where nurses gave medical care. A Mrs. Sweitzer was in charge [1]. The refugee children there were the envy of the neighbourhood. One man remembered pretending to be a refugee so he could go and play [1]. Up at 18th and Pennsylvania, the Adams family's spring and well gave fresh water to the homeless [2]. The city later built small two-room refugee shacks all over the hill. Many survived for decades, easy to spot sitting at the back of their lots [1]. Plenty of refugees never left, among them Russian and Slovenian immigrants burned out of South of Market, and the hill's population changed for good [3].

title: Refugees who came for a week, then stayed
place: Chenery and Castro streets (site of the streetcar waiting house used as a shelter)
hook: After the 1906 fire, homeless families slept in a streetcar shelter and lined up at a shoe factory for bread. Many of them liked Glen Park enough to stay.
story:
On 21 April 1906, three days after the earthquake, the San Francisco Call announced that "the owner of Glen Park will care for the homeless on the grounds, where there are supplies and water" [1]. Tents went up around today's playground. Another camp filled the empty block where Glen Park School now stands [1][2]. The canyon camp never appeared on the Army's official list [1].

One neighbourhood history remembers that people freely opened their homes to refugees. The passenger waiting house at Castro and Chenery was turned into a shelter. At the old shoe factory people lined up for relief rations, bread one day and meat another [2]. By July shops had reopened, and families could go home once the militia had inspected their houses [2].

Many chose not to go back. They liked the village and noticed that its ground had held up well in the quake [2]. The real building boom in Glen Park came from these displaced families [1]. By October the Examiner was advertising Glen Park Terrace lots "from $500 upwards" at $10 a month [2]. Some families in Glen Park today are still descended from earthquake refugees [2].

title: Sixteen Thousand Refugees in Army Tents
place: Earthquake cottages behind the old Post Hospital, Lincoln Blvd & Funston Ave
hook: As the city burned, refugees streamed west to the Presidio, where the Army laid out a numbered grid of 3,000 tents with street corners and directories.
story: Within hours of the 5:12 a.m. shock on April 18, 1906, Presidio troops were in the city fighting fires and keeping order [2]. As the flames spread across the east side, homeless San Franciscans walked west toward Golden Gate Park and the Presidio. The Army eventually sheltered 20,000 people in military-style tent camps, 16,000 of them on the Presidio [1]. There were four camps on the post. The largest sat just east of the Army's General Hospital, and a separate, isolated camp held refugees from Chinatown [1]. Some 3,000 tents stood in a street grid, with numbers and corner directories. Children formed playgroups, and dining halls became the place to gather [1]. The Presidio camps were the first to close, in June 1906. Around the city, union carpenters built 5,300 small wooden cottages for people still without homes. Tenants paid $2 a month toward the $50 price, and once a cottage was paid off it had to be hauled away to a lot of its own. The last camp closed in June 1908 [1]. Two of those 'earthquake shacks' survive here, behind the old post hospital at Lincoln Boulevard and Funston Avenue [1].

title: Sold for a Bag of Gold
place: 294 Page Street (Charles Dietle House), at Laguna
hook: After the 1906 fire, a merchant who had lost his business bought this Stick-style house on Page Street. He paid with a bag of gold saved from the ruins.
story: Henry Geilfuss, who later designed the Westerfeld House, designed and built the Stick-style house at the corner of Page and Laguna for Charles Dietle [1][2]. The city's landmark records give the date as 1885, though the same NoeHill page also heads it "Built 1878" [1]. The house came through the 1906 earthquake and fire. Afterwards Dietle sold it to John DeMartini, who paid with a bag of gold he had rescued from his destroyed business [1][2]. It became San Francisco Landmark No. 48 in 1972 [2][3]. In 2006 it housed a law office, and its interior was later restored [2]. When it came up for sale in 2013 at $2,995,000, SocketSite worked the price out at about 2,034 troy ounces of gold [2]. Its Stick-Eastlake details and its ballroom are still there [4].

title: Tent city in brand-new Duboce Park
place: Duboce Park, at the foot of Potomac Street
hook: The park was barely four years old when 300 homeless San Franciscans pitched tents on its lawn. They stayed until February 1907.
story: Duboce Park was brand new in 1906. In 1900 the neighbourhood had elected Colonel Victor D. Duboce, a Spanish-American War veteran, to the Board of Supervisors. He pushed to turn an odd leftover piece of an old hospital reservation into a park, and he died before the plan was approved. The Board named the park for him, and it was finished by 1902 [1]. The earthquake left the surrounding blocks cracked but standing. Refugees from nearby streamed onto the lawn, and by July 1906 it was officially Relief Camp No. 19, with 300 people living in tents. Relief officials put redwood refugee shacks in parks across the city, but Camp 19 stayed a tent camp until it closed on February 8, 1907 [1]. Doris Bepler was ten and lived at 60 Portola Street, now Potomac, which runs into the park. Her family fled to the East Bay. When they came home, chimneys were still unsafe, so the neighbours cooked on grates and old stoves out in the street. "We girls were sure that we had the neatest and largest kitchen camp," she wrote in her nineties. Refugees still filled the park, and when a call went out for children's clothes, she tried to donate the dresses she disliked [2].

title: Tents and shacks on the old cemetery
place: Mission Park (now Mission Dolores Park)
hook: The city had bought the old Jewish cemetery for a park just a year before. In 1906 it filled with people who had lost everything.
story: In 1905 the city paid $291,350 for two blocks that had been the Jewish cemeteries of Congregations Sherith Israel and Emanu-El, planning a park called Mission Park [1]. Within a year, before it was finished, it became a refugee camp. One history puts the number of families who sheltered there in 1906 and 1907 at more than 1,600 [1]. First came tents. Later a camp of the city's standard wooden relief cottages opened on November 19, 1906, and stayed until October 22, 1907 [2]. Across 18th Street, the three-storey brick Mission High School survived the shaking and served as a neighbourhood shelter [3]. The camp's needs spilled into history in less obvious ways too. Refugees pulled trees, wooden grave markers and fences out of the old Mission Dolores cemetery nearby and burned them as firewood, and many of those markers were lost for good [4]. Camp life in the city ended in the summer of 1908. Some families kept their shacks as homes, and a few still stand in western San Francisco [1].

title: The 6 car climbs Masonic
place: Masonic Avenue at Frederick Street (route of the 6 streetcar)
hook: Seven weeks after the earthquake, a new streetcar line started up Masonic. It later carried a brass band to the 'streetcar to the stars.'
story: On June 10, 1906, less than two months after the disaster, United Railroads started a "Hayes and Masonic" streetcar line that ran up to 3rd Avenue and Parnassus [1]. It helped tie the growing Haight-Ashbury and the hills beyond it to downtown. In June 1912 the line was pushed up 9th Avenue to Pacheco Street. A longtime resident said neighbours had paid for the extension, and people called it the "streetcar to the stars." On opening day, two streetcars draped in bunting carried dignitaries and a band that played all the way from the Ferry Building to Sunset Heights, where about 4,000 people came to celebrate [1]. In February 1916 the cars were moved from Hayes Street to Haight Street, and the line became the 6 Haight and Masonic. It ran along Market, Haight, Masonic, Frederick, Clayton and Carl [1]. A 1928 photo shows track work at Ashbury and Frederick [2], and another shows the rails turning from Clayton onto Carl [3]. After the Sunset Tunnel opened, 6 cars shared Carl Street with the N Judah. Rail service ended on July 3, 1948 [1]. A 6 trolley bus still climbs Clayton [3].

title: The Chinatown That Refused to Move
place: 736 Commercial Street, Six Companies lot
hook: The ashes were still warm when City Hall decided Chinatown should be rebuilt somewhere else. Chinatown's merchants quietly decided otherwise.
story: When fire levelled Chinatown in April 1906, many officials saw an opportunity. A subcommittee of the Committee of Fifty set out to keep the Chinese from returning to their valuable site near downtown, and Hunters Point was floated as the new Chinatown [1]. Refugees were shunted from camp to camp; one site was abandoned after neighbours complained that 'the summer zephyrs would blow the odors of Chinatown into their front doors' [1]. Meanwhile, the Chronicle reported National Guard volunteers picking through the ruins for loot [2]. Nobody, it seemed, asked the Chinese where they wanted to live, though about 40 Chinese merchants owned roughly a third of the district's property [1]. They answered anyway. The secretary of the Six Companies announced that his association owned the lot at 736 Commercial Street, bought for $23,000, and would 'proceed at once with the erection of a nice building' [1]. Leaders then went to Oakland to talk about moving their trade across the bay [1]. Faced with losing Pacific commerce, and with Telegraph Hill residents protesting a fallback site, the subcommittee admitted defeat about three months after the quake [1]. Chinatown rebuilt where it had always been [2].

title: The Cigarmaker's Son Who Died Boxing
place: 335 Plymouth Ave (Gdovin family home)
hook: In February 1906 two young Ocean View cabinetmakers climbed into an unlicensed ring in Colma. Only one came home to Plymouth Avenue.
story: Alexander Gdovin, a cigarmaker who came from Austria in the late 1800s (the name was often shortened to 'Dovin'), and his wife Anna raised five children at 315 Plymouth Avenue, today numbered 335 [1]. The Ingleside and Ocean View of their day were known for roadhouses, gambling tracks and boxing camps, but many fights were staged just over the county line, where San Mateo law enforcement looked away [1][2]. On February 5, 1906, the couple's eldest son, 20-year-old Alex, fought another Ocean View cabinetmaker, 'Chiefy' Johnson, in an unlicensed bout at the Colma Athletic Club. He fell at the end of the third round, killed by a punch to the chest, and the crowd of some two hundred, who had paid fifty cents each, 'scattered in every direction' [1]. Everyone involved played innocent: the club's manager said he knew of no fight; the man who opened the hall claimed he just unlocked the door; the Colma constable sat ringside while his deputy refereed [1]. Johnson insisted they were only fighting 'to let the boys have some fun,' and turned himself in days later [1]. Anna Gdovin was summoned to the White House saloon, where she knelt weeping beside her son [1].

title: The Fire Chief's Beach Cottage
place: 1984 Great Highway, Fire Chief Dennis Sullivan's getaway cottage
hook: San Francisco's fire chief kept a wide-eaved getaway at Ocean Beach. When the 1906 earthquake struck, he was downtown instead.
story: Around 1900, San Francisco fire chief Dennis T. Sullivan used a wide-eaved cottage at what is now 1984 Great Highway as a getaway from the city. The cottage still stands, and a church uses it today [1]. Sullivan had joined the fire department at 25, after working as a blacksmith. As chief, in 1903 he proposed an emergency water supply for firefighting, fed from reservoirs on the city's high peaks [2]. He did not live to see it built. When the earthquake hit on the morning of April 18, 1906, Sullivan was in the chief's official quarters in a downtown fire station. His own quarters partly collapsed, or, in Wikipedia's version, a neighboring building fell onto the station, and Sullivan fell three stories [1][2]. His wife Margaret survived her injuries [2]. The chief lingered for days and died on April 22, leaving the department without its leader as fire swept the city [1][2]. Historian Woody LaBounty has wondered whether more of old San Francisco might have been saved if Sullivan had spent that night at his beach cottage [1]. The Auxiliary Water Supply System he had called for was begun in 1909 and finished in 1913, and it is still the backbone of the city's emergency water supply [2].

title: The Ham and Eggs Fire
place: 395 Hayes Street, at Gough
hook: A woman lit her stove to make breakfast after the earthquake. Her cracked chimney started the fire that burned City Hall and most of Hayes Valley.
story: The earthquake hit at 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906 [3]. Around nine o'clock, a woman in a house on the south side of Hayes Street, about 75 feet east of Gough, lit her stove to cook breakfast. The quake had cracked her chimney, and the house caught fire [1]. Tradition puts the kitchen at 395 Hayes, the corner building that housed a café in 2013 [2]. Every fire company was already busy. At Golden Gate Avenue and Buchanan another blaze burned five houses and kept much of the department tied up until ten [1]. Nobody could mount a proper fight, and Kennedy's 1908 study concluded that this one fire "may truthfully be said to have burned over more territory than any other single fire" [1]. It jumped Gough to the west and Franklin to the east. By about 1 p.m. it had reached the St. Nicholas Hotel on Market, and St. Ignatius Church and College at Van Ness and Hayes was burning. Embers set the roof of Mechanics' Pavilion alight [1]. Firemen found that the quake had broken the neighbourhood's water supply [2]. People called it the "ham and eggs fire" [1][2]. Before it was stopped it had destroyed City Hall and nearly everything east of Octavia [2][3].

title: The Hydrant That Saved St. Paulus
place: St. Paulus Lutheran Church, 999 Eddy St at Gough
hook: Crews were about to dynamite the German Lutheran church to stop the 1906 fire. Then the pastor asked them to try one more hydrant.
story: St. Paulus was the pioneer German Lutheran parish of its synod on the West Coast. Pastor Jacob M. Buehler organized the German Evangelical St. Paulus Congregation on May 15, 1867, and in 1872 the parish opened a German-American weekday school, the first Lutheran day school on the Pacific Coast [1]. Its carpenter-Gothic church at Eddy and Gough was dedicated on February 11, 1894. The architect, the Stuttgart-born Julius E. Krafft, seems to have had Chartres Cathedral in mind, and the tallest of its three redwood spires rose 55 meters [1]. In April 1906 the fire crept as close as Van Ness Avenue on one side and Golden Gate Avenue on the other. With the water mains broken, crews were dynamiting buildings to make firebreaks, and St. Paulus was on the list. Before the charges went off, Pastor G. A. Bernthal asked the workers to try the hydrant on the Eddy–Gough corner. It worked, and the church was saved [1]. In thanks the parish lent its lower rooms to the city as the First Reserve Hospital. Over two months, more than 3,000 injured people were hospitalized there and more than 10,000 were given first aid [1][2]. Services stayed German until 1920 [1][3]. The church survived a spire fire in 1940, but a fire on November 5, 1995 destroyed it [1][4].

title: The Most Irish Parish West of Chicago
place: Sacred Heart Church, Fillmore & Fell Streets (554 Fillmore St)
hook: Its first pastor was a Father James Flood, but not the silver millionaire. His parish at Fillmore and Fell came through 1906 without a scratch.
story: Sacred Heart was founded in 1885 to serve Catholics on the city's western edge. Its first pastor, Father James Flood, was no relation to the Comstock silver king of the same name. He began in makeshift quarters and lived in a rented flat at 710 Hayes Street [1]. Thomas J. Welsh's Romanesque church at Fillmore and Fell was finished in 1898 [1][2]. For more than three decades most of its parishioners were Irish Catholics, among them the Mahony and Fay families and the opera singer Maude Fay Symington. It was remembered as "the most Irish parish west of Chicago" [1]. The church came through the 1906 earthquake and fire unscathed. The parish school, then in the old Sutro mansion at Hayes and Fillmore, served as a temporary hospital and shelter [1][2]. In 1910 the parish unveiled three Carrara marble altars for its silver jubilee. The main one weighed 95 tons [3]. By the 1910s many Irish families were leaving the district, and Italian, Mexican, Guatemalan and Puerto Rican families joined the parish in the 1920s and '30s [1]. The Dominican Sisters, who taught about 500 pupils there in the early 1920s, had once lived in a "rat ridden shed." They finally got a proper convent in 1936 [1].

title: The Night the Fort Split Open
place: Fort Point, gorge barracks
hook: The quake left one half-asleep artilleryman trapped outside a barred window, and Fort Point's back wall pulled eight inches away from the rest of the fort.
story: On April 18, 1906, several dozen men of the Coast Artillery's 66th Company were asleep in Fort Point's gorge barracks when the ground began to shake [1]. They got out fast, then found one man missing. Going back, they heard him outside a window. Half awake, he had climbed out, found bars on the outside, and turned round to see the window had slammed shut behind him. He was only shaken and dirty [1]. The fort came off worse. A rock slide closed the road to the city. The footbridge from the lighthouse keepers' houses had collapsed. Worst of all, the whole gorge face had pulled away from the rest of the fort, leaving an eight-inch gap between the inner and outer walls [1]. Afraid of another shock, the soldiers formed a human chain to pass their belongings out. Then they climbed over the slide into the city and spent days fighting fires and helping with relief [1]. Engineers judged the south wall too costly to repair. The garrison moved to new barracks south of the point, and the fort was left to the weather and to vandals [1][2].

title: The Orphanage That Fed the Neighborhood
place: Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum, 600 Divisadero St at Hayes
hook: The earthquake wrecked its kitchen, so the superintendent grilled meat over a fire pit. The Jewish orphanage on Divisadero became a place where neighbors came to eat.
story: The Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum and Home Society was started in the early 1870s by B'nai B'rith and Temple Emanu-El [1][2]. In 1876 it settled permanently at 600 Divisadero, at the corner of Hayes. It cared for Jewish orphans and also for dependent elderly people [2][3]. When the 1906 earthquake destroyed the asylum's kitchen, Superintendent Henry Mauser grilled meat over a fire pit, and the orphanage became a place where neighbors came to be fed [3]. By the early twentieth century more than 200 people lived in the building, and it was aging badly [1]. Ideas about raising children without families were also changing. Reformers now favored a "cottage" plan of small family-style houses instead of big dormitories. One writer argued that "a boy or girl must be indeed incorrigible who cannot find rest and sweetness in the call of a robin or savor of the new cut grass" [1]. After years of debate, the trustees bought thirteen acres of Adolph Sutro's forest off Ocean Avenue. On June 13, 1921, under Dr. Samuel Langer, the children moved to the new Homewood Terrace [1][2]. Their old corner on Divisadero later became a Bank of Italy branch [3].

title: The Rink at Page and Fillmore
place: The Auditorium, Page Street between Fillmore and Steiner (SW corner of Page & Fillmore)
hook: Six months after the earthquake, an enormous skating rink with 6,000 electric lights opened on Page Street. It could hold 8,000 people.
story: While downtown was still rubble, the Western Addition was getting new places to go out. On November 2, 1906, the Auditorium opened at the southwest corner of Page and Fillmore. It ran the whole block along Page to Steiner [1][2]. It was built as a roller-skating rink, and a big one: the skating floor measured about 335 by 100 feet, and the building held 8,000 people [2]. The Call reported "6000 electric lights, arranged in festoons from the ceiling," with walls "paneled in Flemish oak," bevelled mirrors and painted landscapes [1]. People did more than skate there. The hall hosted boxing matches, basketball games, political rallies, dog shows, military balls, indoor carnivals, track meets and a poultry show [1]. There were also hospital benefits, St. Patrick's Day celebrations and roller polo [2]. Trouble came in 1913, when alcohol was apparently served to minors and the building lost its liquor licence [2]. On November 7, 1915, a huge fire destroyed the Auditorium, burned four neighbouring stores and killed a firefighter [1][2].

title: The Ticket Clerk Who Kept Ferries Running
place: Ferry Building, foot of Market Street
hook: With the south wall of the Ferry Building in the bay and the city burning behind him, Thomas Chase sold tickets and got the first boat out 20 minutes late.
story: Thomas Jefferson Chase, a telegrapher and ticket clerk, was walking to the early shift down First Street just after 5 a.m. on April 18, 1906, when the quake threw him flat. He watched power lines writhe "like reptiles" and cobblestones dance "like corn in a popper" [1]. Reaching the foot of Market, he found the Ferry Building's entire south wall had crashed through the driveway into the bay, but the boats were backing into their slips again. Chase and a captain decided to open: "We got the first boat out around 6:20, only 20 minutes late" [1]. As refugees poured in, he stopped selling long-distance train tickets and sold only ferry tickets to keep the crowds moving. Their abandoned bundles grew into a pile "like a hay stack" on the Embarcadero, and it later caught fire as buildings across the street went up [1]. Hose lines were run through the terminal until the heat drove the firemen back; the staff locked the cash in the vaults and opened the gates so the last of the crowd could reach the boats [1]. The 1898 building, with its tower modelled on Seville's Giralda, survived [2].

title: The Webster Street Shul
place: Congregation Keneseth Israel, 935 Webster St
hook: Its founders thought the Geary Street temple was not strict enough, so they built their own. On the High Holidays, crowds spilled onto the sidewalk.
story: Keneseth Israel was one of the Fillmore's two Orthodox synagogues. It was founded by religious immigrants who wanted to keep strictly to the practice of the Old Country. They had split away from the group that founded Beth Israel, the less Orthodox congregation on Geary Street [1]. The cornerstone of the Webster Street building was laid in 1903 [1]. After the 1906 earthquake and fire drove Jews out of South of Market, the synagogue found itself at the center of a growing Jewish district [1][2]. Neighbors called it the Webster Street Shul. Its sister congregation, Anshey Sfard, was known as the Golden Gate Avenue Shul, at 1140 Golden Gate [2][3]. On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, crowds gathered all day outside the district's three synagogues. Some came out for air between prayers, and plenty never went in at all. Some could not afford congregation membership. Others were nonbelievers who still wanted to "be counted" as Jews on the holiest days [1]. As families moved to the Richmond, the Sunset and the suburbs, the neighborhood's institutions followed. Anshey Sfard left in 1958, and Keneseth Israel left Webster Street in 1973 [3].

title: The arena that became a hospital, then burned
place: Mechanics' Pavilion site (now Bill Graham Civic Auditorium), Grove and Larkin streets
hook: On the morning of the earthquake, San Francisco's biggest arena filled with the injured and the dead. Within hours the fire came for it too.
story: Before 1906, the block at Grove and Larkin held the Mechanics' Pavilion, built in 1882 as the city's first major indoor arena, seating nearly 11,000 people [1]. When the earthquake of April 18, 1906 wrecked the Central Emergency Hospital in the basement of City Hall next door, the pavilion became a makeshift hospital and morgue [1]. Then a new danger appeared. A fire that broke out at Hayes and Gough streets, remembered as the "Ham and Eggs" fire, spread east through the Western Addition toward City Hall [2]. The Museum of the City of San Francisco's timeline says the injured were taken out from noon, some to Golden Gate Park, Children's Hospital and the Presidio, and that the pavilion caught fire at 1 p.m. [2]. FoundSF says the building was emptied the next morning and burned around 1 p.m. on April 19, so the sources disagree about the day [1]. Six years later the Mechanics' Institute sold the burned block to the city for $700,000 [1]. The Civic Auditorium went up on the site and opened in January 1915, the first Civic Center building to be finished [3].

title: The breakfast that burned Hayes Valley
place: South side of Hayes Street just east of Gough Street
hook: A woman cooked breakfast on a stove with an earthquake-cracked chimney. The fire that started there burned a church, a college and most of Hayes Valley east of Octavia.
story: At about 9 a.m. on April 18, 1906, in a house on the south side of Hayes Street about 75 feet east of Gough, a woman lit her stove to cook breakfast. The earthquake had damaged her chimney, and fire broke out [1]. With every fire company already busy, nobody could stop what became known as the 'ham and egg fire'. The historian Lawrence Kennedy judged that it 'burned over more territory than any other single fire' [1]. By about 1 p.m. it had reached the St. Nicholas Hotel at Market and Hayes. St. Ignatius Church and College at Van Ness and Hayes was burning, and flying embers set the roof of Mechanics' Pavilion alight [1]. The Jesuit church had been built in 1880 and could hold 4,000 worshippers. It was destroyed along with its college [2]. Through the night the fire spread west and north. Soldiers ordered the Lagan family out of their Haight Street home at 2 a.m. [3]. At about 5 a.m. on April 19, the fire was finally stopped along Octavia Street, 'assisted by neither wind, hills, or vacant lots', and Octavia became a permanent edge of the burned district [1]. At Market and Octavia, the 1894 Fallon Building is the only survivor of its row. The buildings to its east burned [4].

title: The earthquake that tipped over a liner
place: Union Iron Works drydock, Pier 70 waterfront
hook: The first ship ever lit by Edison bulbs was up on the shipyard's drydock when the 1906 earthquake hit. The shaking rolled her onto her side.
story: When the 1906 earthquake hit, the steamship Columbia was sitting in the Union Iron Works hydraulic drydock at Potrero Point, part way through a refit [1][2]. She was a famous ship. Built in 1880, she was the first ship to carry a dynamo powering electric lights, and the first commercial use of Thomas Edison's light bulbs outside his Menlo Park laboratory [2]. The quake knocked the iron-hulled liner off her supports. She rolled onto her starboard side and slammed into the dock, and her hull partly filled with water [1][2]. The ship could be saved: two months of temporary repairs got her floating again. The drydock, one of the yard's most useful features, was damaged beyond economic repair [1][2]. Columbia's bad luck continued. On her way to Hunters Point for permanent repairs, a steam pipe exploded and the crew abandoned ship. She finally went back into service in January 1907, and soon after was stuck in an ice pack on the Columbia River for four days [2]. Back at the shipyard, a photograph taken about six weeks after the earthquake shows tents for people left homeless by the disaster, pitched among the shops [3].

title: The hotel that sank three floors
place: Valencia Street between 18th and 19th
hook: At dawn on April 18, 1906, a four-storey Valencia Street hotel dropped into the ground until only its top floor was left above the street.
story:
The Valencia Street Hotel stood on made land: the block between 18th and 19th had been filled in over a gully that dropped more than 40 feet in half a block [1]. When the earthquake hit, people in the all-night coffee shop on the ground floor ran outside. From the street they watched the building 'simultaneously lurch forward and sink', until its fourth floor was the only one left above ground [1]. Two big water mains ran under Valencia, and when they burst the street flooded. A sinkhole later opened where the crowd had been standing [1][2]. Then the fire swept through [1].

Eight-year-old DeWitt Baldwin lived at 931 Dolores Street. That morning he ran across Valencia to watch a fire and saw 'a small old three-story hotel' with its first storey sunk into the earth [3]. Nobody agrees on how many died. The Burrito Justice essay passes on a reader's figure of at least 40 drowned [1]. A letter from a refugee a few days later claimed 103 of 106 guests were killed, but its own editor calls it a mix of first-hand observation and 'garbled reports' [4].

title: The little hydrant that saved the Mission
place: Golden Fire Hydrant, 20th & Church Streets
hook: With the city's water mains broken and the fire racing south, one squat hydrant at the top of Dolores Park kept flowing.
story: When the 1906 earthquake broke San Francisco's water mains, the fire that followed swept south toward the Mission with little to stop it. At the corner of 20th and Church Streets, beside what is now Dolores Park, one hydrant still had water. A plaque nearby records that although the mains were broken and dry on April 18, 1906, 'from this Greenberg hydrant on the following night there came a stream of water allowing the firemen to save the Mission District' [1]. Community accounts credit it with saving the houses between 20th and 22nd Streets, and one family history tells of neighbourhood men hauling a pump wagon up the hill again and again to fill its tanks from it [2]. Neither account can be checked hose by hose, but the hydrant has become the neighbourhood's emblem of that night. In the 1960s a dentist and historian, Doc Bulloch, started painting it gold every April 18 [1]. The ritual continues each anniversary, and in 2012 the organisers painted it silver by mistake in the pre-dawn dark, then repainted it gold the same morning [1]. After 1906 the city built an Auxiliary Water Supply System so that it would never again depend on one lucky pipe [1].

title: The milk drinkers of Carolina Street
place: First Russian Christian Molokan Church, 841 Carolina Street
hook: Russian religious dissenters came by way of Hawaii's cane fields. They built steam baths into the hillside and a prayer hall on Carolina Street.
story: In August 1906 a group of Russian Spiritual Christians, mostly Molokans with a few Pryguny ("Jumpers"), arrived in San Francisco from Hawaii. There they had refused to farm sugar cane. More came from Los Angeles, Russia and Manchuria [1]. Fewer than a thousand Molokans left Russia in the early 1900s, most between 1905 and 1912, fleeing persecution, and many ended up on and around Potrero Hill [2]. A 1964 study translated their name as "milk drinkers" [3]. Many men found jobs at Union Iron Works, and families built homes around Carolina, Rhode Island and De Haro streets and Southern Heights [3]. Even in the 1960s, Molokan women could be seen going to church in full-length skirts, heads covered with shawls. Bearded old men gathered at the top of De Haro Street cracking sunflower seeds [3]. Settlers used the hill's springs for private "bani" steam baths. The only sign of one from outside was a rusty stovepipe poking out of a hillside roof [3]. The community built its own two-storey prayer hall on Carolina Street, today the First Russian Christian Molokan Church at 841 Carolina. Sources date it to 1928, 1929 or "about 1930" [1][2][3].

title: The night the fire reached Franklin Street
place: Haas-Lilienthal House, 2007 Franklin St
hook: Soldiers dynamited the mansions of Van Ness Avenue to stop the fire. By dawn the flames had reached Franklin Street, and the Haas family's house survived.
story:
On the evening of 19 April 1906 the great fire reached Van Ness Avenue. On the orders of Colonel Charles Morris, army troops dynamited the mansions along the avenue to create a firebreak [1]. By 5 a.m. on 20 April the fire had burned as far as Franklin Street, then turned south [1]. The destruction largely stopped at Van Ness, and most of the Western Addition, including the new mansions of Pacific Heights, was left unburned [2].

One block west of Van Ness, on Franklin between Washington and Jackson, stood the Queen Anne house that architect Peter R. Schmidt had designed in 1886 for William Haas, a Bavarian-born wholesale grocer [3][4]. It survived the earthquake and the fire [4]. The Haas family's daughter Alice and her husband, Samuel Lilienthal, moved in in 1917, and Alice lived here until her death in 1972 [3].

In 1973 her heirs gave the house to the new Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage, now San Francisco Heritage [3][4]. Today SF Heritage looks after it, a grand Victorian that stood at the very edge of the 1906 fire.

title: The plan to banish Chinatown here
place: Hunters Point peninsula
hook: Days after the 1906 fire, city leaders drew up a plan to move all of Chinatown to the far edge of the city: here.
story: Chinatown was still smouldering when San Francisco's leaders saw an opportunity. Within six days of the 1906 fire, a committee including political boss Abe Ruef and ex-mayor James D. Phelan, bitter enemies united by anti-Chinese feeling, had adopted a plan to move the whole Chinese quarter to Hunters Point, then a remote edge of the city [1]. The idea was older than the quake: industrialist John Partridge had already proposed an "Oriental City" here, with Mayor Schmitz's support [1]. The Chronicle cheered a new Chinatown "far removed from the center of town" [2]. Nobody, it seemed, had asked the Chinese. They answered anyway. China's government sent word, through its diplomats, of the Empress Dowager's displeasure and vowed to rebuild its consulate on the old site [1]. Chinese leaders met Oakland's mayor and let it be known that Oakland, Portland and Seattle were courting them; about 40 Chinese merchants owned roughly a third of the old Chinatown land anyway [2]. Fearing the loss of the Asia trade, the city blinked. Within about three months the relocation subcommittee was discharged, and Chinatown was rebuilt where it had always stood [2].

title: The school Issei parents built in protest
place: Sano School site, 1761-65 Post Street
hook: San Francisco ordered 93 Japanese children into a segregated school. Their parents refused, opened their own classes on Post Street and started a diplomatic crisis.
story: On 11 October 1906 the Board of Education ordered the 93 Japanese students in its public schools to attend the segregated school it ran for Chinese children [1]. The Japanese community protested and alerted the press and officials in Japan, and Tokyo lodged a formal protest [1]. Here in the new Japantown, the city's historic context statement records, Issei parents set up the Sano School as a boycott measure, at 1761–65 Post Street [2]. The row became international. In his December 1906 message to Congress, Theodore Roosevelt called shutting Japanese children out of the public schools "a wicked absurdity" [1]. In January 1907 he invited the mayor and California officials to the White House. The city withdrew the order, and in return Roosevelt moved to cut Japanese immigration. That deal led to the 1907 Gentlemen's Agreement [1][2]. The Agreement still let wives and so-called picture brides come to join their husbands. Families grew, and with them this neighbourhood of Japanese schools, kindergartens and churches [2].

title: The well that watered 2,000 refugees
place: 70 Clipper Street, between Church and Dolores
hook: The earthquake broke the city's water mains. On Clipper Street, a teenager's family pumped their old backyard well 500 strokes a day for their neighbours.
story:
Frances Gibson was 19 and living at 70 Clipper Street with her Irish immigrant parents and several siblings when the earthquake hit at 5:13 a.m. by the family clock. "That sure was a corker!" her brother Tom said when the shaking stopped [1]. Mains laid around 1900 had brought running water to Noe Valley, and the quake broke them. The Gibsons still had a 40-foot well on an underground creek, and it kept working [1].

On 19 April people said Noe Valley would be dynamited if the fire reached 20th Street. The Powers brothers carted the family's belongings free of charge to the hill at 29th and Noe, and eleven of them slept on mattresses on the grass. The fire was stopped at 20th Street [1].

In the weeks that followed, refugees nearly doubled the neighbourhood's population. Soldiers camped on the 25th Street hill, and James Lick School became a food depot and emergency hospital [1]. Photographs show Valley Street residents living outdoors for days [2]. The Gibsons' well supplied more than 2,000 people. It took 500 strokes of the pump each day to keep the tank full [1].

title: The wine that saved Telegraph Hill
place: 1254-1256 Montgomery St, Telegraph Hill
hook: With no water left, the families on Telegraph Hill broke open their cellar casks and fought the 1906 fire with homemade wine.
story: The fire reached Telegraph Hill on April 20, 1906, the third day after the earthquake, after it had consumed downtown and swept through North Beach. Many residents ignored orders to leave. With the open ground of Pioneer Park as a firebreak, they poured homemade wine on the flames and spread wine-soaked sheets over shingle roofs to stop the blowing embers [1]. Writer Henry Anderson Lafler named the rescuers: a prizefighter, warehouse and lumberyard men, an old Irish woman who had saved a few buckets of water, and "the poor peasant Italian with a barrel of cheap wine in his cellar" who broke it open with an axe and fought "till he dropped" [1]. At 1254-1256 Montgomery, an 1860s rooming house, tenant Giovanni Doneri, his eldest son and neighbours kept the walls cool with burlap sacks soaked in wine from casks in the basement [2]. The crest and northeast slope became the largest of three islands of survivors in the burned city. Twenty-seven houses were left standing [1]. Fifty years later the new Telegraph Hill Dwellers stopped the same building being demolished for an 11-storey apartment block [2].

title: Three billion feet of lumber
place: E.K. Wood lumber yard, south bank of Mission Creek near Third Street
hook: After the fire, teamsters waited for hours on Channel Street for lumber, and a young clerk sat on a lumber pile writing home about it.
story: The fire of April 1906 stopped a few blocks short of the south waterfront, and the lumber yards on Mission Creek suddenly became the most important places in town [1]. William Kortum, a young man from Calistoga, was clerking at the E.K. Wood lumber yard on Channel Street. In a letter he described sitting on a high lumber pile in the midday sun, looking down on "the busiest place south of the channel, except for the Union Iron Works." Dozens of teamsters waited impatiently for one o'clock to load up. Some horse teams had already stood there for hours [1]. "On one morning we sell more lumber than in a week before the fire," he wrote. Payment was "a matter of lottery," but dealers reckoned three billion feet would be needed to rebuild the city [1]. Kortum planned to ask for a raise. The disaster also finished off the bay itself. Temporary rail lines brought rubble down to the last waters of Mission Bay, and the Southern Pacific loaded debris at its Mission Bay yard. By 1910 the bay was gone except for the channel [2][3].

title: Three miles of railroad fall into the sea
place: Coastal bluffs south of Lake Merced, Fort Funston
hook: On 18 April 1906 the new coast railroad's roadbed below Lake Merced was almost entirely wiped out by cliff landslides.
story: In 1906 the Ocean Shore Railroad was building a line from San Francisco down the coast toward Santa Cruz, and its grade ran south from Lake Merced along the coastal bluffs to Mussel Rock [1][2]. The earthquake of 18 April hit while the line was still under construction. The U.S. Geological Survey later noted that the grade between Lake Merced and Mussel Rock "was almost entirely destroyed for a distance of 3 mi" by rockfalls and dry sand flows along the cliffs [1]. It counted this among the worst hillside-landslide damage of the disaster: "3 mi (4.8 km) of the Ocean Shore Railroad was practically obliterated by landslides along the coastal bluffs south of San Francisco" [1]. Around the lake itself, lateral spreads and slumps damaged embankments and bridges [1]. The quake and the company's money troubles meant the railroad was never completed. It ran as two separate pieces, San Francisco to Tunitas Glen and Swanton to Santa Cruz, until it closed in 1920 [2]. The same bluffs slid again in the 1957 Daly City earthquake [1].

title: Twenty thousand escape by sea
place: Foot of Van Ness Avenue, Black Point Cove
hook: As the fire reached Van Ness, a small party of sailors on the beach at its northern end organised what sfmuseum.org calls the largest evacuation by sea in history.
story: On the evening of April 19, 1906, the fire reached Van Ness Avenue, and the army began dynamiting mansions along the street to make a firebreak [1]. The cruiser USS Chicago had arrived from San Diego at 6 p.m. that day [2]. With the city's telephone and telegraph systems destroyed, messages to the outside world went first through the Chicago's wireless [3]. The next day the waterfront at the foot of Van Ness, where the avenue meets Black Point Cove below Russian Hill, became an escape route. Sixteen enlisted men and two officers from the Chicago supervised the evacuation of 20,000 refugees fleeing the fire [1]. The Chicago and many other vessels carried them across the bay, many to Tiburon in Marin County [2]. The Museum of the City of San Francisco calls it the largest evacuation by sea in history, and probably as large as Dunkirk in the Second World War [1]. That is the museum's own comparison, not a precise count. By 5 a.m. on April 20 the fire had burned as far as Franklin Street, then tried to circle south [1].

title: Two decades in the 'Shirt Factory'
place: Hayes St & Shrader St, site of the post-1906 St. Ignatius College
hook: The 1906 fire burned the Jesuits out of Van Ness Avenue. Their 'temporary' wooden school near the park lasted more than twenty years.
story: In 1880 St. Ignatius College had moved into a grand new home at Hayes Street and Van Ness Avenue, where Davies Symphony Hall stands now [1]. It came through the shaking of April 18, 1906 with moderate damage, and then the fire that followed destroyed it [2]. The Jesuits moved west, to the corner of Hayes and Shrader streets near Golden Gate Park [1]. They put up a rambling wooden building in a hurry. It was meant to be temporary, and it came to be known as "the Shirt Factory" [2][3]. It served as the school for more than twenty years. The college moved up the hill to Fulton Street in 1927 [1]. The high school, which had just become a separate St. Ignatius High School, stayed in the Shirt Factory until 1929 and then moved to Stanyan Street [3]. There it stayed for forty years before moving to the Sunset District in 1969 as St. Ignatius College Preparatory [3]. Not bad for a school that began in 1855 as a one-room schoolhouse on Market Street [1].

title: Vaudeville under canvas at Post and Steiner
place: National Theatre site, NW corner of Post & Steiner
hook: Weeks after the city burned, the Graumans put a tent on a vacant lot and packed in thousands. Then they built the theatre around it without missing a show.
story: When the 1906 fire wiped out downtown's theatres, show business moved west to the parts of the city that had survived. On 28 May 1906 the National Tent Show Theatre opened on a vacant lot at the northwest corner of Post and Steiner, showing films and vaudeville. It was soon rebranded as Grauman's National [1]. Variety reported 2,400 people in the house that June [1]. In October 1906 the Examiner described a steel and iron building going up over the tent while three shows a day carried on, with 1,800 opera chairs planned [1]. The National was not alone. The Dreamland Rink behind it staged boxing by August 1906, and the Belascos' New Alcazar opened at Sutter and Steiner on 18 March 1907 [2][3]. Theatre historian Bill Counter warns that many Grauman legends conflict, including a hand-painted sign supposedly telling patrons that in another quake only the canvas would fall on them [1]. Some accounts, including Wikipedia's, put the first tent downtown on the site of the Graumans' old Unique Theatre. Counter says that was not the case [1][4].

title: Warehouses for a burned-out city
place: 101 Henry Adams Street (formerly Kansas Street)
hook: Two weeks after the fire, the railroads offered cheap land and instant steel sheds here to merchants who had lost everything downtown.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed San Francisco's wholesale district, and the railroads, the biggest landowners in this half-empty former marshland, moved quickly. On May 3, 1906, the Board of Trade's secretary, Martin Triest, announced that the Southern Pacific, Santa Fe and Western Pacific had all set aside land for displaced businesses [1]. The Western Pacific offered a tract bounded by Division, Kansas and 16th streets and San Bruno Avenue. For an extra five cents a square foot, the railroads would even put up temporary corrugated-steel buildings for tenants [1]. Speculators built too. On the block bounded by Alameda, Rhode Island, 15th and Kansas streets, the San Francisco Development Company raised three near-identical brick warehouses in 1906, designed by Meyers & Ward. They are known by the names of their occupants: the Bernhard Mattress Company/John Hoey, Pacific Implement and General Electric warehouses. All three, including this one at 101 Henry Adams, were still standing in 2009 [1]. The area was already being called the "New Wholesale District," and after 1906 much of the old waterfront warehouse trade moved south to be near Mission Bay's rail network [1][2]. Decades later, design showrooms gave the area its modern name, Showplace Square [1].

title: Watching the City Burn from Alamo Square
place: Alamo Square, near Steiner and Grove Streets
hook: On April 18, 1906, crowds climbed Alamo Square's hill, sat on the grass, and watched downtown San Francisco go up in smoke.
story: Alamo Square's hill looks east straight over the city, and on April 18, 1906 that made it a grandstand. Photographs taken that day show the lawn full of people sitting and watching smoke rise from downtown. Wagons loaded with refugees' belongings stand on Fulton Street below [1]. Another view, taken near Steiner and Grove, shows a crowd standing in the park looking east at the fire [1]. A century later, the Examiner still remembered the square as the place "where people gathered to watch downtown burn in 1906" [2]. They had a lot to watch. By about 1 p.m. the Hayes Valley fire had reached Market Street, and St. Ignatius Church and College at Van Ness and Hayes was burning [3]. A 1906 account called it "the greatest Jesuitical institution in the west" and put its cost at $2,000,000 [4]. The people on the hill were safe. The fire was stopped at Octavia Street, about half a mile east, at dawn the next day [3].

title: When Fillmore Street was downtown
place: Fillmore Street at Post
hook: With Market Street in ashes, City Hall, department stores and newspapers moved to Fillmore. Its boosters hung glowing iron arches over fourteen intersections.
story: The fire of April 1906 stopped at Van Ness Avenue, which left the Western Addition standing [1]. Almost overnight Fillmore Street became San Francisco's busiest shopping street [2]. The first streetcar to run after the disaster ran along Fillmore. City Hall, several department stores and newspapers set up on the street and the blocks around it [3]. The city's historic context statement says that in 1907 local boosters, hoping to keep Fillmore's new status, put up illuminated iron arches over fourteen intersections [3]. The arches can still be seen in photographs from around 1911 [1]. Nickelodeons followed. The Lyregraph, advertising "Moving and Talking Pictures", appears at 1730 Fillmore in the 1909 and 1911 city directories [4]. There was even a 1912 plan to tunnel under Fillmore to the Marina [1]. But once downtown was rebuilt, the offices and big stores went back. Fillmore settled into being a neighbourhood high street, and the old houses around it were divided up for the many families the fire had made homeless [1][3].

title: When Fillmore became downtown
place: Fillmore St at Bush St
hook: With downtown in ashes, City Hall and the big Market Street stores moved to Fillmore. For a few years a neighbourhood shopping street was the heart of the city.
story:
The 1906 fire stopped short of Fillmore Street. Within days of the earthquake, City Hall and most of the big Market Street department stores had moved into whatever space they could find along it [1]. The first streetcar to run again after the disaster ran on Fillmore [1].

Photographs from 1906 show Fillmore, looking north from Sutter to Bush, as the city's busiest shopping district [2]. Around the corner on Bush Street, between Fillmore and Steiner, families cooked in the street on wood-burning stoves [2]. Single-family Victorians nearby were turned into boarding houses, and the Western Addition quickly became a densely populated urban district [1][3].

The boom did not last. As downtown was rebuilt, the stores moved back [3]. In 1909 Fillmore merchants tried to keep their customers by hanging fourteen brightly lit arches over the street's intersections, and Fillmore was soon being called "the most highly illuminated thoroughfare in America" [1].

title: When the Portola Was 'Little Jerusalem'
place: San Bruno Avenue near Silver Avenue, the district's old main street
hook: After 1906, Eastern European Jews burned out of South of Market rebuilt their lives along San Bruno Avenue, far enough out that the district picked up a nickname.
story: The 1906 earthquake and fire wiped out the South of Market homes and institutions of San Francisco's Eastern European Jewish immigrants. Many of them moved west to the Fillmore-McAllister district, and many others moved south to the San Bruno Avenue district [1]. The valley was once nicknamed 'Little Jerusalem' [2]. Shopkeepers on San Bruno Avenue often lived with their families above their stores [2]. Artists researching the neighbourhood's past found records of a settlement house on San Bruno Avenue that welcomed new immigrants, and of two synagogues founded around the turn of the century [3]. Those who came were later interviewed. From 1976 to 1978 the Western Jewish History Center and the American Jewish Congress recorded the oral history project 'San Francisco Jews of Eastern European Origin, 1880-1940', with the San Bruno Avenue district as one of its focuses. The recordings are now held by the Magnes Collection at UC Berkeley [1]. Italian immigrants also settled here after the quake [4].

title: Where the Fire Stopped: Octavia Street
place: Octavia Street at Hayes Street
hook: For a full night the Hayes Valley fire crept west. At dawn on April 19, 1906, firemen held it at Octavia Street, and it never went further.
story: The Hayes Valley fire spent the afternoon and evening of April 18 working west from Gough. It reached Fell Street on the south and Golden Gate Avenue on the north [1]. One 1906 account described it spreading "like a sickle set to a field of grain" around the south end of the Western Addition, up to Oak and Fell along Octavia. There, the account went on, "one puny engine puffed a single stream of water upon the burning mass" [2]. At 12:30 a.m. on the 19th it reached Octavia between Golden Gate and McAllister [1]. Then it stopped. According to Kennedy's 1908 analysis, at five in the morning the fire "was finally stopped at the west along Octavia Street," and south of Fell half a block east of it. Firemen, "possibly assisted by some dynamiting," did it with no help from wind, hills or empty lots [1]. The line held for good [1][3]. City planners still use it: almost everything east of Octavia is post-1906, while Hayes Valley to the west keeps some of the oldest buildings in that part of the city [3]. Many of the Victorians west of Octavia today came through that night.

title: Whiskey for the Firemen, a Building Spared
place: Audiffred Building, 1-21 Mission Street
hook: As firemen dynamited the waterfront in 1906, a saloon keeper in this mansard-roofed building made them an offer they could not refuse. Or so the story goes.
story: Hippolite d'Audiffred put up his cast-iron, French mansard-roofed building at the foot of Mission Street in 1889, and it quickly became a waterfront hub [1][2]. The Sailors' Union of the Pacific rented rooms upstairs, and three saloons and a restaurant filled the ground floor [2]. In April 1906, as the fire swept east, firemen were blasting a firebreak between the burning city and the wharves where relief supplies were landing [2]. Legend says the barkeepers of the Bulkhead Saloon offered each firefighter two quarts of whiskey, plus a wagonload of wine, to save their block [1][2]. Tellings differ: another version offers a keg per fireman [2]. The city's own marker says only "whether the story, or some variation, is true," the Audiffred was the sole survivor on its block [1]. Along with the Ferry Building, it is one of just two central waterfront buildings that came through the earthquake and fire [1]. Its luck held: during the 1934 strike, longshore leader Harry Bridges had his office upstairs, and after a 1979 fire it was saved as City Landmark #7 [1][2].

title: Wireless Lifeline in the 1906 Disaster
place: Naval station on Yerba Buena Island (radio station and hospital)
hook: With San Francisco's telegraph wires down and the city burning, a small Navy radio station on Goat Island relayed its messages.
story:
In 1902 the Navy began setting up wireless stations at Mare Island and on Yerba Buena Island, among its first on the Pacific coast [1]. In January 1905 the Chronicle reported a "battle-ship at sea" talking with Goat Island, as the battleship Ohio's signals were picked up at a naval station on the island [2].

The real test came on 18 April 1906. The cruiser USS Chicago had left port the night before. Her operator picked up news of the earthquake at dawn, and by ten she was docked near the Ferry Building [3]. With Western Union and Postal Telegraph lines down, the Navy made the Chicago's weak set the city's outlet for priority messages. Stanley Hooper, a young officer who had worked a railroad telegraph key, ran the message office [3]. The Chicago's set could reach less than 100 miles, so the naval radio station on Yerba Buena Island worked full-time relaying traffic between the ship and Mare Island, where it went out by telegraph [3]. In about two weeks the Chicago handled over 1,000 messages [3]. The island itself was reported undamaged, and quake victims who needed emergency care were sent to its hospital [4].

title: "A Greater San Francisco or Lesser Nagasaki?"
place: Post & Buchanan, heart of the new Nihonjin Machi
hook: In 1900 not one Japanese household lived here. Seven years later the Chronicle was warning of an "invasion." By 1910 this was the heart of Japanese San Francisco.
story: The 1900 census found no Japanese households in these blocks, which were then home to German, Irish and Jewish families [1]. The 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed the city's two Japanese enclaves, in Chinatown and along Jessie and Stevenson streets south of Market [1][2]. Refugees moved west, where some property owners of European descent were willing to rent to them. The newspaper Shin Sekai (New World) urged readers to settle for good, predicting that rents would fall once the ruined districts were rebuilt [1]. Not everyone welcomed them. On 24 March 1907 the San Francisco Chronicle ran an alarmist piece titled "A Greater San Francisco or Lesser Nagasaki – Which?" about the Japanese "invasion" of the Western Addition [1]. The community stayed anyway. By the 1910 census the core bounded by Bush, Geary, Webster and Laguna had more than 50 Japanese-owned businesses and most of the city's 4,700 Japanese residents [1]. There were pool halls, hotels and employment agencies for single men, and a kindergarten and midwives for new families. Yet the 1910 block book lists no Japanese property owners at all [1].

title: A boss's cafe, then Sally Rand's Music Box
place: Blanco's / The Music Box, now Great American Music Hall, 859 O'Farrell Street
hook: The ornate hall on O'Farrell was built for a man called "the Blind Boss." In the Depression, a famous fan dancer made it her nightclub.
story: Soon after the fire, a restaurant with a lavish interior rose at 859 O'Farrell Street. The National Register dates the building to 1906 and names its first owner as Christopher A. Buckley, "the Blind Boss." It operated as Blanco's Cafe until 1923 [1]. It was a local example of the French restaurant with rooms upstairs, the kind that gave the Uptown Tenderloin its racy reputation [1]. Other accounts say it opened in 1907 and took its name from a notorious Barbary Coast brothel [3]. Its best-known tenant came in the Depression. Sally Rand, who became famous for her fan dance at Chicago's 1933-34 world's fair, turned the hall into her nightclub, the Music Box. She had come to San Francisco ahead of the 1939 Treasure Island fair, where she ran the "Nude Ranch" [2]. The National Register dates the Music Box to 1939-1946, and other accounts say she took over in 1936 [1][3]. The Museum of the City notes that the interior still looks much as it did when she danced there [2].

title: A burned-out palace, rescued by Julia Morgan
place: Fairmont Hotel, 950 Mason Street
hook: The Fairmont's new owners had held the deed for twelve days when the fire came. A year later, a young woman architect opened its doors.
story: Senator James Fair's daughters, Tessie and Virginia, built the Fairmont in his memory on the summit lot where he had planned his own mansion, hiring the architects James and Merritt Reid. Shortly before it was finished they sold it to the brothers Herbert and Hartland Law. The sale closed on April 6, 1906, twelve days before the earthquake [1]. The fire left the hotel little more than a shell: the interior burned badly, though the outer walls could be saved. Some experts doubted it could be rescued at all [2]. Every other residence on the summit burned except the Flood mansion across the street [1]. Herbert Law first hired the New York architect Stanford White, who was shot dead a few weeks later. The job then went to Julia Morgan, the first woman to graduate from the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, who had been practising in the Bay Area for about two years [1][2]. Under her supervision the Fairmont opened on April 18, 1907, a year to the day after the disaster, though some sources give April 16 [1]. In 1908 Tessie Fair Oelrichs took the hotel back from the Laws [1].

title: Bloody Tuesday at the Turk Street Car Barn
place: Turk & Fillmore car barn (yard on Turk behind the powerhouse)
hook: A year after the fire, strikebreakers with pistols drove streetcars out of the Turk and Fillmore barn. The shooting that followed became known as 'Bloody Tuesday.'
story: The earthquake gave United Railroads president Patrick Calhoun his chance. He had long wanted to turn his Market Street cable lines into overhead-wire trolleys, and after the disaster he got a permit. He was accused of bribing the entire Board of Supervisors to do it. A 22-month trial ended in a hung jury [1]. In May 1907 more than 1,500 carmen voted to strike for $3 for an eight-hour day [2]. The company brought in professional strikebreakers who could run streetcars and handle guns [2]. At 3:25 p.m. on Tuesday, May 7, six cars pulled out of the Turk and Fillmore barn. Each carried two company inspectors and four of James Farley's strikebreakers wearing pistols [1]. When the crowd threw rocks and bricks, Farley's men opened fire [1]. Strikers captured one car and brought it back, and it crashed into the barn gate. The men inside, thinking they were under attack, started shooting [2]. Accounts of the toll differ. The city's transit chronology says two men were killed and more than twenty wounded [2]. Market Street Railway counts a dead chauffeur and two fatally wounded strikers [1]. The brick powerhouse is still standing [1].

title: Butcher, Baker and Post Office by the Sea
place: 1460 48th Avenue, former Quality Market ('Bruecker's'), opened 1907
hook: Miles of dunes from the city, the Oceanside's first shops had to be everything at once. One grocery from 1907 still has its worn wooden floorboards.
story: At the start of the 1900s, miles of dunes and bad roads cut the beach settlement of Oceanside off from the rest of the city, so its first merchants had to sell a bit of everything [1]. John Brumund opened a saloon on the Great Highway in 1898 for weekend bicyclists. He ended up selling groceries, hardware, paint and crockery, and by the 1910s his store at La Playa and Irving also served as a real estate office, post office and social hall [1]. Around 1903 A.E. Harnish opened a general store at 4314–16 Judah Street selling tea, bread, notions and beer, plus wines and liquors 'for medical use,' and served lunches to Sunday beachgoers [1]. The neighborhood's first school, founded in 1903, met beneath a grocery store on 48th Avenue [2]. A grocery opened at 1460 48th Avenue in 1907. Charles and Henry Bruecker ran it for many years, and although it was officially the Quality Market, locals called it Bruecker's. Its 1925 ads offered 'stall-fed' meats, fish on Friday and two deliveries a day, rain or shine [1]. Neighbors ran a tab until payday, and Jake the butcher handed kids a free slice of bologna [1]. Down the block, Harry D. Rupp gave his butcher shop at 1446 48th Avenue the neighborhood's name: the Oceanside Market [2].

title: Fourteen Arches of Light
place: Fillmore Street at Fulton (southern end of the arches)
hook: To show that Fillmore was now a great city street, its merchants hung fourteen glowing iron arches over it. The arches stayed up until 1943.
story: Fillmore's merchants wanted their temporary boom to last. In one writer's words, the street had gone "from a row of suburban delicatessen and cigar shops to the main artery of a great city" [1]. In April 1907 the Fillmore Street Improvement Association asked the Board of Supervisors to let it build arches. That year Butte Engineering and Electric put up fourteen double iron arches from Sacramento Street down to Fulton. Each one crossed 32 feet above the pavement and carried 120 electric lights [1]. The first was lit at Pine on September 9, 1907, and the whole run on November 27, in time for holiday shopping. The contract was for $7,500 and costs reached $11,000, though boosters claimed $50,000 [1]. At Christmas the bulbs were changed to red and green [1]. In July 1908 a Call reporter, Gibson Adams, spent an evening on Fillmore and paid a quarter at a second-floor dance hall "where ladies of divers nationalities graciously waltzed with me without the formality of names" [1]. People often remember the arches as decorations for the 1915 Exposition, but they are older than that [1][2]. In June 1943 they were taken down for wartime scrap [1][2].

title: Freja Hall, the Swedes' home on Market
place: Swedish-American Hall, 2168-2174 Market Street
hook: When Upper Market was 'Little Scandinavia', the Swedes built a lodge so finely crafted that it still ranks among California's best Arts and Crafts interiors.
story: By 1910 the blocks around Upper Market and Mission Dolores were home to so many Danes, Norwegians, Swedes and Finns that the area was nicknamed Little Scandinavia [2]. Lutheran services there were held in five languages [3]. In 1907, as the city rebuilt after the earthquake, the Swedish community put up its own meeting hall on Market Street. Its architect was August Nordin, who had also designed New Era Hall down the street [1]. He gave each lodge room its own character. The grandest, Freja Hall, has ornate finishes and soaring truss work that the city's landmark report ranks among the finest Arts and Crafts work in California [1]. The report calls the hall the most significant surviving building of the city's Swedish community [1]. It has been changed remarkably little: apart from the storefronts, the rooms are much as Nordin built them [1]. The basement bar, Cafe du Nord, traces its business at the address back to 1907 [1]. The building became a city landmark and in 2019 was listed on the National Register of Historic Places [1].

title: Granny Clampett grew up on 'Sullivan Alley'
place: Arlington Street between Charles and Miguel streets (site of the Noblitt home, demolished c.1930)
hook: Before she was pipe-smoking Granny on 'The Beverly Hillbillies', Irene Noblitt was a Fairmount schoolgirl who won $3 for singing 'Pretty Baby' very loudly.
story:
In 1907 James Noblitt bought a lot on Arlington Street. He was a North Carolina army veteran who now worked as a watchman for the federal Chinese Bureau. He moved his wife Katie and their daughter Jessie Irene into a small one-bedroom house at 39 Arlington. Behind it the ground dropped steeply to the Bernal Cut, where Southern Pacific trains rumbled past day and night [1]. The street was full of the Sullivans' eleven children, and neighbours called it "Sullivan Alley." Irene went to Fairmount Grammar School at Chenery and Randall [1].

Her father died in 1913. At 11, Irene won $3 singing "Pretty Baby" in an amateur contest at the Valencia Theater [1][2]. She told the story later: "The manager told me I wouldn't get hit with the garbage if I sang loud enough... I've been singing loud ever since" [1]. At 15 she left with a touring stock company [1].

She went on to vaudeville with her husband Tim Ryan, then to radio with Bob Hope. From 1962 to 1971 she played Daisy May "Granny" Moses on The Beverly Hillbillies, a role that earned two Emmy nominations [2]. The house on Arlington was probably torn down around 1930, when the Bernal Cut was widened [1].

title: Houdini and His Rival on Ellis Street
place: Orpheum Theatre (1631 Ellis St) and Princess Theatre (1671 Ellis St), near Fillmore
hook: In 1907 the Orpheum, burned out of downtown, reopened on Ellis near Fillmore. Houdini topped the bill while a rival escape artist played next door.
story: The Orpheum vaudeville circuit lost its O'Farrell Street theatre in April 1906 [1]. While downtown was rebuilt, it opened a new Orpheum at 1631 Ellis, near Fillmore, in March 1907. The architects were O'Brien and Werner, and the house had about 1,750 seats [1][2]. On August 31, 1907, Sam Loverich opened the Princess right next door at 1671 Ellis [2]. That September Harry Houdini played the Orpheum. By then he had moved past handcuffs, and he was billed as "Houdini in New Sensations." The feature that week was a challenge to escape from a box built by employees of the Emporium department store [3]. For his last week, the Princess booked George W. Brindamour, advertised as "King of All Handcuff Kings" [3]. Variety expected a fight. Instead it reported, under the headline "Jail Breakers at Peace," that each man went about his business "as though oblivious of the other's existence" [3]. In April 1909 the Orpheum moved back downtown, and the Ellis Street house became the Garrick [1][2]. Both theatres later became churches and were demolished in the 1970s during Fillmore redevelopment [2].

title: Post office, potatoes, then candy
place: 708 Clement St at 8th Ave
hook: One Clement Street building went from post office to potato market to a sweet shop selling 'candy with a college education'.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, people moved into the Inner Richmond quickly, and the district needed a bigger post office. The building at 708 Clement Street went up in 1907 as branch post office Station M. Wagons unloaded mail on the Eighth Avenue side, and customers came in from Clement [1]. By August 1912 the neighbourhood had outgrown it again, and a bigger brick Station M opened at Tenth Avenue and Clement [1]. In 1918 former saloonkeeper John C. Jacobs opened the Pioneer Potato Market here, selling onions, potatoes, fruit and vegetables [1]. From 1921 to 1923 it was part of James O'Brien's candy factory, with a shop on the Clement Street side. O'Brien later moved to 506 Clement, the future home of Green Apple Books [1]. Then Ernest Wilson, a Stanford graduate who called his sweets 'the candy with a college education', opened a 'Confectaurant' here. It served ices, sodas, pastries and tea [1]. The vaulted ceiling probably dates from the O'Brien or Wilson years. Since 1984 it has been the Clement Street Bar & Grill [1].
