title: Refugee Shacks Hiding on Niantic
place: 30 Niantic Ave
hook: After 1906, relief-camp cottages were hauled to Ocean View's empty lots. In 2003 historians found two of them serving as the second floor of a Niantic home.
story: The 1906 earthquake and fire pushed thousands of working-class San Franciscans to the city's edges, and the OMI boomed: between 1900 and 1910 the Ingleside's population rose from 473 to 2,412 and Ocean View's from 1,039 to 1,853 [1]. Some newcomers brought their houses. An unknown number of refugee cottages from the relief camps were hauled here and joined together as starter homes on empty lots; examples survive at 74 Lobos, 233 Broad and 254 Montana Streets [1]. After the camps closed, entrepreneurial landowners rented out clusters of shacks along Niantic Avenue and in Daly City's Hillcrest, and when those settlements broke up the cottages were moved yet again [1]. On March 23, 2003, shack expert Jane Cryan and Woody LaBounty followed a tip to 30 Niantic, expecting a garden shed. Instead they looked up at the second storey of Tom and Maureen Ginella's house: two 'Type A' shacks joined end to end, with original park-green paint showing where they met [2]. Inside were early floorboards and cove ceilings. Rather than demolish them, the Ginellas were building a modern floor underneath, and the city's official count of surviving shacks rose to 21 [2].

title: Refugees, Horses and a Self-Made 'Mayor'
place: A. B. Frank real estate office, 4607 Mission Street
hook: The 1906 fire burned out the old city. Fields at the southern edge became the new one, and one real-estate man set up shop to sell it.
story: Decades after its streets were mapped, much of the Excelsior was still farm fields. The earthquake and fire of 1906 changed that, as burned-out San Franciscans moved to the outer districts [1]. The Cronin family was one of them. Jeremiah Cronin, an Irish immigrant with a team of horses, found plenty of rebuilding work. The fire had taken the family home, and his son Joe was born in October 1906 while they were living with Jeremiah's sister. Early in 1907 they moved into a new house in the Excelsior [2]. That same year real estate broker Ambrose B. Frank opened an office at 4607 Mission Street. He considered himself a pioneer and a key figure in the district's post-quake growth. By the 1930s, the Examiner reported, his neighbours hailed him as 'the mayor of the district' [1]. Promoters in the 1910s also tried out a softer name for the area, 'Green Valley.' It survived for a while in businesses like the Green Valley Macaroni Factory at 4736 Mission [1]. Joe Cronin grew up to be a Hall of Fame shortstop.

title: Survived the Quake, Lost to a Wire
place: Cliff House, 1090 Point Lobos Ave
hook: In 1906, rumours said Sutro's castle had slid into the sea. It hadn't. Seventeen months later, electricians did what the earthquake couldn't.
story: Adolph Sutro's turreted Cliff House opened in 1896, a wooden 'French chateau' with marble floors, electric lights, an elevator and twenty private dining rooms [2]. It survived the 1906 earthquake, but rumours that it had fallen into the ocean spread fast [1]. The building really was lost the next year. On September 7, 1907, while it was closed for remodelling, former proprietor James Wilkins was touring the work when he saw smoke rising through a floor where electricians had been working. He raised the alarm, got caught in the fire himself and had to be rescued [1]. The Examiner called the blaze 'something sent from the unknown to hold the human mind in awe and wonderment' [1]. Not everyone mourned: a letter to The Argonaut asked whether a score of readers had not said 'Thank Heaven!' [2]. Sutro's daughter Emma Sutro Merritt rebuilt in the post-quake spirit, with a modest fireproof building of steel-reinforced concrete that opened in 1909 and still stands [3].

title: The Cabin Boy's Blue Hillside
place: Sea Cliff hillside above Baker Beach
hook: In 1907 a teenage cabin boy saw a slope blue with lupins outside the Golden Gate. By 1938 he was a captain making his home there.
story: In 1907 W. O. Kohlmeister, a 17-year-old cabin boy, sailed in through the Golden Gate aboard the clipper Glory of the Seas. On his right, just outside the Presidio, he saw a treeless, empty hillside that was blue with lupins [1]. The ship was an old Donald McKay clipper that by then was working the Pacific coast, and she sailed to Callao in 1907–08 [2]. In 1938 a newspaper series on the city's districts caught up with him. He was now Captain Kohlmeister of the Dollar liner President Lincoln, and he was making his home on that same slope, which had become Sea Cliff [1]. The article said old-timers remembered the place mostly for Sunday balloon ascensions and parachute jumps. A railway had staged them to sell tickets on its steam train out to Baker Beach. Houses, the paper said, only began going up in 1916 [1]. It also named a less romantic landmark. A Richmond District sewer emptied at the shore and had made Baker Beach unfit for recreation, and the paper promised it would soon be rerouted to a plant in Golden Gate Park [1].

title: The Streetcars That Crushed the Sewer
place: Mission Street, San Mateo interurban (40-line) route
hook: The heaviest streetcars in San Francisco rolled down Mission Street, until the city found they were crushing the brick sewer underneath.
story: In 1902 the United Railroads took over the city's first electric railway and sent its San Mateo interurban, the famous 40-line, straight down the busy Mission Street corridor [1][2]. After the 1906 earthquake, URR president Patrick Calhoun wanted fast, luxurious cars to compete with the Southern Pacific's new Bayshore line. He bought sixteen ornate interurbans that the Philadelphia & Western had rejected. They were the largest electric vehicles San Francisco had seen: 52 feet long and 75,640 pounds, which earned them the nickname 'Big Subs' [1]. Mission Street gave them trouble from the start. Soon after they arrived in January 1907 they were pulled from service because they kept derailing, since their wheel flanges were too high for the rails, and they needed new wheels [1]. The end came from below the road. In 1922 the city's Water Department found that the cars' weight was crushing the lightly built brick sewer beneath the ties and threatened to sue. The Big Subs were withdrawn in 1923, and the last one was dismantled and burned in 1935 [1]. The 40-line itself, by the 1920s the Market Street Railway's most profitable route, ran until 1949 [1].

title: The hotel that announced the comeback
place: Cadillac Hotel, 366-394 Eddy Street at Leavenworth
hook: A poultry-and-whiskey man rebuilt on the lot where his wooden house had burned. Its dining room later became a boxing gym.
story: The earthquake and fire left almost nothing standing in the Uptown Tenderloin, and most rebuilding there was slow [1]. The Cadillac Hotel at Eddy and Leavenworth was one of the few big early exceptions. It was finished in 1907 by Andrew A. Louderback, who had made his money in poultry, game and distilling, on the same lot where his wooden house had stood until 1906 [1]. Randy Shaw writes that it was built to show the city was coming back, with a front desk where guests checked their furs [2]. The National Register counts 170 rooms and Shaw says 180 [1][2]. In 1924 the dining room became a boxing ring [1]. From 1924 to 1935 it was Taussig & Ryan's Gym, and later it was Newman's [2]. By local legend, Billy Newman helped a young Cassius Clay, the future Muhammad Ali, with gym time and a loan after the 1960 Olympics [2]. Longtime San Francisco political leader John Burton remembered the Cadillac of the early 1950s as part of an all-night Tenderloin where you could place a bet in nearly any restaurant [2].

title: The house jacked up for shops
place: 557 Ashbury St / 1500-1512 Haight St (northwest corner of Haight and Ashbury)
hook: The most photographed corner of the hippie Haight began as a quiet house that its owner lifted into the air after 1906 to fit in shops underneath.
story: In 1903 the financial agent Richard P. Doolan built a two-storey Colonial Revival house at Haight and Ashbury. It was designed by Frank T. Doolan, probably his brother, who worked as a draftsman [1]. After the earthquake and fire, Doolan guessed that Haight Street from Masonic to Stanyan would soon be all shops as the city moved west. So in 1907 he had the house raised and storefronts built beneath it, also designed by Frank [1][2]. The shops tell a neighbourhood story. The first business on the corner was the Gold Bar saloon, which closed when Prohibition began. Later, Holcombe Jewelers held the corner from 1931 until 1988, run by M. D. Holcombe and then his son Alex. Alex had flown as a crewmember on a World War II mission that served as a decoy for the Enola Gay. 1508 Haight was a barbershop in 1907, and Jimmy Shoe Shine worked at 1504 for 45 years [1]. By 1953 the house upstairs had been split into eight units, probably during the wartime housing shortage [1]. The street names lettered on the building later made it the backdrop for countless hippie-era photographs. It became city Landmark No. 253 [2].

title: The wooden ballpark at 15th and Valencia
place: Recreation Park site, now Valencia Gardens, Valencia and 15th
hook: The 1906 fire burned the Seals out of their ballpark. They rebuilt in the Mission, in a cramped wooden park where a right-field home run needed only 284 feet.
story:
The fire of 1906 destroyed the San Francisco Seals' ballpark South of Market, and they spent a spell playing in Oakland [1]. In 1907 they came home to a new Recreation Park, which filled the block between 14th, 15th, Valencia and Guerrero [1][2]. It held 15,000 people in wooden stands: a small lower deck sheltered under a big upper deck that was open to the sun [1]. The Oakland Oaks played most of their home games there too until 1913. The Chicago White Sox held spring training there in 1909 and 1910 [1].

In 1914 the Seals tried a new park, Ewing Field, near the Richmond District. The season was a fog-bound fiasco and they came straight back [1]. Even after the club knocked down buildings on 15th Street to enlarge the park in 1917, right field was just 284 feet down the line [1]. From 1926 a second team, the Mission Reds, shared the grounds. In 1931 both teams moved to the new concrete Seals Stadium at 16th and Bryant [1][2]. San Francisco State used the old field for football as Roberts Field. It was sold to the Housing Authority in 1940, and the block became Valencia Gardens [1].

title: Three Earthquake Shacks Become One Home
place: 1227 24th Avenue (City Landmark No. 171), between Lincoln Way and Irving Street
hook: Built as temporary shelter after the 1906 disaster, three little green cottages were hauled out to the dunes of 24th Avenue. Today they are a city landmark.
story: After the 1906 earthquake and fire, the relief effort put up about 5,610 small cottages in parks and squares across the city. The average one measured 10 by 14 feet, with two or three rooms and a gas connection [1]. Park superintendent John McLaren insisted they be painted park-bench green, and union carpenters built them from redwood, fir and cedar shingles [2]. As the camps closed in 1907, families bought shacks for $100 or less, and more than 5,000 were carted away. Often two or three were joined into one house, and many went to the sand hills of the Richmond and Sunset [2]. By the summer of 1908 the public lands were clear [1]. At 1227 24th Avenue, three shacks were joined to make the main house. The Western Neighborhoods Project credits the job to real estate developer Sol Getz [1][2]. In the early 1980s the tenant, Jane Cryan, found out what her odd little rental really was and led a campaign to save the city's surviving shacks. A Planning Commission resolution in February 1984 backed making it City Landmark No. 171 [1][2]. Four shacks on Kirkham Street near the beach were less lucky: they had to be moved to a temporary spot at the zoo in 2005 [3].

title: Two refugee shacks become a home
place: 43 Carver Street
hook: A Polish couple burned out in 1906 joined two relief cottages together on Carver Street. Their daughter lived to see the centennial.
story:
Theodore and Domicella Ferenz were Polish immigrants who lived on 11th Street until the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed the area. They became the first occupants of what is now 43 Carver Street, on Bernal's east slope. The house is made of two "Type B" relief cottages, each 14 by 18 feet, joined together [1]. Theodore built the hall that links the two shacks and later put in plumbing at the back. At first the family used an outhouse in the yard. That outhouse and the chicken coops were still standing when the house was sold in 1973 [1].

Their daughter, Helene Critler, remembered going down to the cellar to fill the oil lamps, and catching rainwater in buckets in the leaky hall between the shacks. She died in April 2006, just after the quake's centennial [1]. The earthquake-cottage expert Jane Cryan confirmed 43 Carver as a genuine shack. It is one of more than a dozen on the hill, which the Bernal Heights History Project calls the largest surviving group in the city [2]. That spring about 150 people began a centennial walking tour at the house [1].

title: Where Ansel Adams Learned to Look
place: 129 24th Avenue (Adams family home)
hook: The dunes, creek and cliffs outside this wooden house were the first wild landscape the photographer ever knew. The house itself nearly slid into a sinkhole.
story: Ansel Adams grew up at 129 24th Avenue, in a house built among the sand dunes above the Golden Gate [1]. Accounts differ on when the family moved in. SFGATE says the house was finished in 1903 and that Adams broke his nose there in a 1906 aftershock. The Wikipedia biography, which draws on his biographer Mary Street Alinder, says the family moved there in 1907 [1][3]. Everyone agrees on the nose. The four-year-old was thrown against a garden wall, and it stayed crooked for the rest of his life [2][3]. He was a restless, often sickly boy with few friends. He spent his days in the dunes, following Lobos Creek down to Baker Beach and exploring the cliffs toward Lands End. The Sierra Club counts those rambles as the start of the love of nature that later drove his photography [2][3]. The house had one more close call. In the December 1995 storm, a sinkhole opened next door and left it on the edge of a new cliff, but it survived [4].

title: 113 years behind the same counter
place: Teddy's Market (originally Peterson's grocery), 296–298 Teddy Avenue
hook: Charley and Petra Peterson opened a corner grocery in 1908. The building has held a store ever since.
story: In 1908, as families who fled the 1906 fire settled in the valley, Charley A. and Petra C. Peterson built a wood-frame store at the corner of Teddy Avenue and Delta Street and opened a grocery [1]. The 1909 city directory lists Charles Peterson living above the shop at 296 Teddy [1]. It was one of dozens of corner markets in the valley then [1]. A 1920s photograph shows a family posed outside the 'C.A.P. Grocery' [1]. Streets were sandy in summer and muddy in winter, and the local grocery ran its own delivery service [2]. The Petersons owned the store until the mid-1930s. Joseph and Mary Cimino later ran it as Teddy Grocery [1]. Tina Ballestrasse grew up across the street and was sent there almost daily for fresh bread. She remembered the snow of 1962, when neighbourhood children begged cardboard boxes from the store to use as sleds [1]. Mrs. Torres ran it as Teddy's Market from 1982 to 2018 [1]. In 2021, 113 years after the Petersons opened, the building was still a store. SF Heritage has proposed it for the city's Legacy Business Registry [1].

title: A Men's Club, a Women's Club, an Ode
place: Williams Store / Williams Hall, 2201 Taraval Street at 32nd Avenue (now Gene's Liquors)
hook: The hall above the Parkside's first store hosted dances, classes and suffrage speakers. The men's improvement club still kept women out until 1935, so women formed their own.
story: In 1908 Eugene Williams opened the Parkside's first store and grocery at 2201 Taraval Street, on the corner of 32nd Avenue [1]. The room upstairs, known as Williams Hall or Parkside Hall, was the neighborhood's auditorium and gym. It hosted dances, costume parties, classes and talent shows, and the monthly meetings of the Parkside District Improvement Club [1]. The club invited speakers on women's suffrage, yet it admitted only men until 1935 [1]. Shut out, Parkside women started their own organization in September 1908, the Parkside Women's Improvement Club, 'to advance interest among the women residents of this district in literature, education, social affairs and current events' [1]. Before long it was in citywide politics, protesting saloon permits at Ocean Beach. In 1910 the Bulletin reported that the club was planning a march on the mayor's home. The march never happened, and the article reportedly split the club between activists and members who didn't want to be 'dragged into political discussions' [1]. Mrs. F.W. Alsing, wife of the men's club's first treasurer, cheered the district on in her 'Ode to Parkside,' printed in the Sunset Journal in October 1911. Once the Twin Peaks tunnel was finished, she promised, 'They will all go home for dinner / Every day at noon' [2]. The Williams building still stands as Gene's Liquors [1].

title: A Painting Saved, a House on the Dunes
place: 1 25th Avenue, on the bluff above Baker Beach
hook: In 1906 Helen Brown cut a William Keith landscape from its frame to save it. By 1908 it hung in a new house on an empty bluff.
story: When the 1906 earthquake struck, the Brown family's house on Van Ness Avenue stayed standing, but its furniture, china and portraits lay smashed on the floor. As the fire came closer and houses along the avenue were dynamited, Helen Hillyer Brown loaded their belongings into a Victoria carriage [1]. Over the fireplace hung a landscape that the painter William Keith had given the couple as a wedding present. It was too heavy to carry, so she cut the canvas from its frame, rolled it up and took it with her [1]. Her husband, the physician Philip King Brown, lost his downtown office to the fire and took over an empty house to care for the injured [1]. In 1908 the family moved into a new home at One 25th Avenue, which Florence Holub called the first residence on the Sea Cliff bluff [1][2]. Their daughter Phoebe, who went on to become an architect, remembered "nothing else there but sand dunes, lupine and rabbits" [2]. She lived there until her death in 1990 [1]. The house later belonged to Sharon Stone and Phil Bronstein, and in 2022 it went on sale for $39 million [1][2].

title: A Railroad's Hospital Beside the Panhandle
place: 1400 Fell Street (Fell, Baker, Hayes and Lyon)
hook: When the 1906 fire destroyed its hospital, the Southern Pacific built a grand new one on the Panhandle, for railroad workers only.
story: The Southern Pacific's 1898 hospital at 14th and Mission Streets burned in the 1906 fire, and that same year the railroad bought an entire block facing the Panhandle, said to be one of the largest property deals after the disaster [1]. Daniel J. Patterson, an architect in SP's Maintenance of Way Department, designed the Neo-Classical hospital, annex and powerhouse, built from 1907-08 [1]. The location was deliberate: planners of the day wanted hospitals in pleasant residential districts, where fresh air and sunlight along the Panhandle would help convalescents [1]. The railroad had begun opening hospitals for its employees in 1868, which the National Register nomination calls the first in the world reserved for railroad workers; this was the flagship, paid for by employee dues and company money [1]. It formally opened on July 15, 1909 with 450 beds [2]. In 1911 Collis P. Huntington's widow and nephew gave Huntington Social Hall as his memorial [1]. Renamed Harkness Community Hospital in 1968, it closed in 1974, apparently bankrupt [1]. The failure halted an expansion plan and left the city's only intact early-1900s hospital complex. Mercy Housing converted it in 1982-83 into 158 senior apartments [2], and it became city Landmark No. 192 in 1989 [3].

title: A Saloon Hotel for Men Between Jobs
place: Hotel Utah, 500 Fourth Street at Bryant
hook: In 1913, forty thousand seasonal workers were wintering in San Francisco's cheap hotels. The Hotel Utah at Fourth and Bryant was built for men like them.
story: After the 1906 fire, South of Market was rebuilt with fewer family flats and more cheap hotels, saloons, pawnshops and missions for single working men [2]. The Hotel Utah, a four-story Edwardian saloon and hotel at Fourth and Bryant, went up in 1908 to house seasonal workers employed in nearby factories [1][3]. Its tenants belonged to a floating army. In December 1913 a survey of the city's ten- and fifteen-cent lodging houses counted 40,000 seasonal laborers "lying up" for the winter on stakes averaging about thirty dollars. Loggers and miners tended to stay between Third and Sixth streets, sailors and dockworkers farther east [2]. By the 1930s the saloon was a hangout for gamblers, madams and longshoremen [1]. After World War II owner Al Opatz renamed it Al's Transbay Tavern [1], and by the 1950s, the San Francisco Chronicle later wrote, its ornate wooden barback, imported from Belgium, served customers including Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe [3]. Almost all the neighboring residential hotels were razed in the 1940s and 1950s, but the Utah survived, and in 2018 it became a city landmark [1][3].

title: A firehouse built for downhill horses
place: Engine House No. 31, 1088 Green St
hook: After the 1906 fire destroyed half the city's firehouses, a new one went up on the ridge of Russian Hill, placed so its horses could gallop downhill in any direction.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed 22 of San Francisco's 44 firehouses [1]. In October 1907 the city hired Newton J. Tharp as City Architect, at $4,000 a year, to rebuild its lost public buildings [1]. Tharp had once designed a cover for The Lark, the little literary magazine of 1890s Russian Hill [1]. His Engine House No. 31 on Green Street, finished in 1908, is the only Craftsman or Tudor Revival firehouse known to have been built in San Francisco. Its style suits the fine houses of the neighbouring 'Paris Block' [1][2]. The site was chosen with horses in mind: from the ridgetop the team could race downhill to a fire in any direction [1]. The horse era soon ended. On July 11, 1912, a motor fire engine beat a horse-drawn one in a test race, and the city committed to buying only motor engines [1]. Tharp did not see it. He died of pneumonia on a business trip to New York after only 18 months in the job, and his obituary praised him for putting 'his duty toward his city' ahead of his own health [1].

title: A reform school's farm becomes Balboa Park
place: Balboa Park, San Jose and Ocean avenues (east half of the old House of Refuge lot)
hook: Before it had ball fields, Balboa Park was farmland worked by boys held at San Francisco's troubled juvenile reformatory.
story: In 1854 San Francisco bought 100 acres from John Horner where the San Jose Road met the Ocean House Road. The plan was a 'House of Refuge' for neglected and delinquent children. The context statement gives the price as $15,000 and the Western Neighborhoods Project gives $10,000 [1][2]. The Industrial School opened in 1859 on the higher western end, where City College's football field is now [1][2]. The eastern flats, today's Balboa Park, were described as 'fine arable land', and the inmates grew crops there for the school [1]. In 1872 officials refused to build a jail on this ground because 'the land there is the best' [1]. The school had scandals from the start, and in 1885 a grand jury declared that 'failure is written over it everywhere' [1]. It closed in the early 1890s [1][2]. On July 22, 1908, the city handed the lot to the Park Department, apart from the jail, the reservoirs and a firehouse. It became the city's second-largest park [1]. Hundreds of people came to its dedication on October 9, 1910, including 22 improvement clubs, and the day was marked with footraces and baseball [1].

title: A synagogue built not to be noticed
place: Congregation B'nai David, 3535 19th Street
hook: On 19th Street, Orthodox immigrants from Eastern Europe built a deliberately modest synagogue with northern California's first mikvah. Worshippers came from as far away as Nevada.
story:
Between about 1880 and 1910 a new wave of Jewish immigrants reached San Francisco from Russia, Poland and Romania. Most were Orthodox, unlike the established Reform congregations, and they started their own congregation in the Mission, B'nai David [1]. It first met near 16th and Mission. After the 1906 fire it built this temple on 19th Street between Guerrero and Valencia [1].

The building is stucco and tile over a wood frame and makes no fuss. It has been called 'recessive protective architecture', designed not to draw attention after centuries of persecution [1]. Inside was the first mikvah, or ritual bath, in northern California, and Orthodox Jews travelled from as far as Nevada to use it [1]. It was never a big community. In a district of Irish and German churches, B'nai David was the only synagogue, and a late-1930s survey found just 8 percent of the city's Jews living in the Mission [2]. The congregation shrank as members moved away. Accounts differ on when it closed: one source says regular services had stopped by about 1960, while a cantor's son recalls them running until 1978 [1]. The building became apartments in 1981 [1].

title: A temple finished twice
place: Site of Congregation Beth Israel's Geary Street Temple, 1839 Geary Boulevard
hook: The new synagogue was meant to open for the Jewish New Year of 1906. The earthquake came first.
story:
Congregation Beth Israel was founded in 1860. It worshipped on Sutter and Mission streets, then built synagogues on Turk Street in 1879 and on Geary near Octavia in 1891 [1][2]. In December 1905 it laid the cornerstone of a third temple at 1839 Geary. William Curlett designed it in a 'Byzantine style' to seat 1,600 at a cost of about $120,000, and it was due to open for the New Year beginning 19 September 1906 [2]. The earthquake of 18 April struck while it was still unfinished and badly damaged it [2][3]. The congregation rebuilt and dedicated the temple in 1908 [1][3]. Rabbi Meyer Solomon Levy led it until 1916, and Cantor Joseph Rabinowitz sang there from 1891 to 1943 [1].

The fire also sent Jewish families from South of Market into the Fillmore [4]. Jerry Flamm, writing about the 1920s Fillmore, described crowds outside the neighbourhood's three synagogues all day on the High Holidays. Some people could not afford membership. Others were non-believers who still wanted to 'be counted' [4]. Around the corner at 1740 O'Farrell, the Labor Lyceum's basement rooms were home to the Workmen's Circle and the Socialist Party [4]. A post office now stands on the temple's site [3].

title: Battleships too big for Mare Island
place: Hunters Point dry docks (later Hunters Point Naval Shipyard)
hook: When Teddy Roosevelt's Great White Fleet limped into San Francisco in 1908, the Navy's own yard was too shallow. A private dry dock at Hunters Point saved face.
story: In May 1908 the Great White Fleet, the battleships Theodore Roosevelt sent around the globe, steamed into San Francisco Bay needing repairs. There was a problem: the water at the Navy's own Mare Island yard was too shallow for the deep-draft battleships [1][2]. So the fleet turned to the private San Francisco Dry Dock Company at Hunters Point [1]. Accounts of the job differ. The district's historic context statement names two battleships, the Maine and the Alabama, serviced there [1]; the shipyard's own lore, retold in a 2025 exhibit, claims 23 ships repaired in 28 days, a record workers boasted of for decades [2]. Either way, the Navy noticed. That same year Charles M. Schwab, for Bethlehem Steel, bought the dry dock company for $1,875,000, taking over what was then the largest ship-repair plant on the West Coast [1]. The Navy would covet Hunters Point for three more decades before finally buying it in 1939 [1][2].

title: Brown's Opera House, the great survivor
place: Victoria Theatre, 2961 16th Street
hook: San Francisco's oldest working theatre began as a vaudeville house built by a governor's grandfather, and survived by reinventing itself again and again.
story:
In 1908 Edmund Joseph Brown opened a vaudeville house on 16th Street near Capp. He was the grandfather of Governor Jerry Brown [1]. Brown's Opera House showed vaudeville and early motion pictures [2]. At its peak the district had around 15,000 theatre seats, second only to mid-Market Street [3].

The little theatre got through by changing with the times. In the Depression it became the 16th Street Theater. It showed second-run films at half price and gave out Depression glassware to bring people in [1]. In the 1940s and 1950s, as Spanish-speaking families settled in the Mission, it became El Teatro Victoria and showed films in Spanish [1][2]. In the 1960s it turned to burlesque as the Follies, with Tempest Storm and Blaze Starr on stage [1]. Renamed the Victoria after a restoration, it is now the oldest operating theatre in San Francisco. Whoopi Goldberg performed her one-woman show here in 1984 [2].

title: Candles in the Rafters, Rabbits in the Streets
place: Parkside Realty Co. cottages, 2500 block of 28th Avenue (club's first meeting was at 26th Ave & Taraval)
hook: The Parkside began as 62 little cottages strung across the dunes. Their owners met by candlelight in an empty sales office and set about demanding a city.
story: In early 1908 the Parkside Realty Company built its first 62 cottages. They wound from 26th Avenue and Ulloa southwest along the old Central Ocean Road to 32nd Avenue and Vicente, in groups of three to seven facing each other across unpaved streets [1]. Each was about 800 square feet, with two bedrooms and one bath, and buyers could pick from six facades, among them Italianate, Spanish and Dutch Colonial [1]. The pioneer H.H. Dobbin, Sr. remembered walking home from the streetcar 'in utter darkness,' with 'scarcely any mark by which one street could be distinguished from another' [1][2]. That autumn residents met in the company's bare sales office at 26th Avenue and T (Taraval) Street. The only light came from candles stuck in the rafters, and people shielded them with their hats from the wind blowing in through broken windows [1]. Out of that meeting came the Parkside District Improvement Club. Within eighteen months it had won streetlights, telephones, mail delivery and a volunteer fire brigade of 25 men. The brigade got a donated firehouse near 28th Avenue and Ulloa, a hose reel, and a 100-pound brass alarm bell [1]. In 1910 the company said 59 of the 62 cottages had sold. A 2007 survey found all but one still standing, most of them raised over garages [1].

title: Five-cent flickers on Raymond Avenue
place: Former nickelodeon, 135 Raymond Avenue
hook: The valley's first movie house had tin walls, a player piano and a blue mercury lamp to pull people in. Today it is someone's home.
story: The valley's first cinema was a nickelodeon on Raymond Avenue, where 'flickers' cost five cents [2]. Its walls were fireproof sheet metal embossed with designs. A player piano played inside, and a blue mercury lamp out front drew crowds on show nights. Amateur Night was a big attraction [1][2]. Local historians place it at 135 Raymond Avenue, a 1908 wood-frame building that is now a private house just east of Hans Schiller Plaza [1]. There was more to do in town. Clubs held whist parties, dances and minstrel shows at the Bay Shore Hall on Leland, the Fireman's Hall on Wilde and the Alpine Hall on Raymond [2]. Film crews came too. Alma Taylor, born in 1911, remembered watching the Swedish-born star Anna Q. Nilsson filming at the Bay Shore Hotel corner. Alma called the film 'Ten Nights in a Bar Room', but researchers think it was more likely 1924's 'Half-A-Dollar Bill' [1]. In 1926 the 350-seat Bayshore Theatre opened near Leland. Locals nicknamed it the 'Flea House', and it ran double bills and 'dish night' until October 1957 [1].

title: Genoese Gardens and the Artesian Water War
place: Alemany Blvd near Sagamore St (former truck farms)
hook: Ocean View's Italian truck farmers hauled vegetables downtown by wagon before dawn, and in 1908 were fined for watering them from their own wells.
story: From the early Gold Rush on, the sandy valleys of southern San Francisco were checkered with vegetable farms, and most farmers were Italian immigrants from Genoa [1]. Whole families and hired hands worked small plots watered by windmill-pumped wells and fertilised with horse manure, then loaded horse-drawn wagons in the early morning for a drive of several hours to the Colombo Market, a produce exchange founded in 1876 at Davis and Front Streets [1]. The 1880 census listed Ocean View farmers and dairymen such as Patrick Breen and John Bauer, with Frank Lagomarsino and others along the Ocean House Road; most were of Italian, Irish or German descent [1]. As the city grew, water became a battleground. In 1904 the Spring Valley Water Company ejected tenant gardeners, claiming their fertiliser runoff polluted the city's supply, and in October 1908 the San Francisco Call reported that an Ocean View improvement club had denounced a court for fining vegetable growers who used artesian water [1]. The farms hung on anyway: a 1910s photograph at the future site of Alemany Boulevard near Sagamore shows a cow grazing, and a 1920s view catches a buyer at a roadside vegetable stand on Junipero Serra Boulevard [2][3].

title: Julia Morgan's quiet Presidio Heights houses
place: 3377 Pacific Avenue (Julia Morgan, 1908)
hook: Better known for Hearst Castle, the first woman admitted to study architecture at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts also designed a string of houses along the Presidio's edge.
story:
Julia Morgan studied engineering at Berkeley, where Bernard Maybeck taught her architectural design and urged her to go to the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris. With his help she became the first woman formally admitted to it [1]. After the 1906 earthquake her first major job was repairing the badly damaged Fairmont Hotel, which reopened on the quake's first anniversary [2].

The rebuilding city also needed houses, and Morgan designed many in Presidio Heights. FoundSF lists 306 Laurel Street (1906), 3377 Pacific Avenue and 3531 Clay Street (both 1908), 36 Presidio Terrace (1911) and 3630 Jackson Street (1917) [2]. Her 700-plus buildings included many Arts and Crafts houses, and she was especially popular with women clients [2].

Her houses here sit among work by Maybeck, Willis Polk and Ernest Coxhead. NoeHill calls the 3200 and 3300 blocks of Pacific Avenue, along the Presidio wall, the city's finest collection of Shingle Style houses [3]. Maybeck built a townhouse for Samuel Goslinsky at 3233 Pacific in 1909. Polk had remodelled 3203 Pacific in 1892 [1][4]. Few streets in the city show so many of these architects' work within a few steps.

title: Korean Patriots Confront Japan's American Advocate
place: Ferry Building plaza, foot of Market Street
hook: In March 1908 two Korean immigrants confronted the same man at the ferry landing. One gun jammed; the other did not.
story: Durham Stevens, an American diplomat working for Japan's colonial administration in Korea, arrived in San Francisco in March 1908 and told a San Francisco paper that ordinary Koreans were benefiting from Japanese rule [1][2]. The city's small Korean community, fewer than 2,000 people on the whole mainland, most of them recent arrivals, was furious [1]. Two local associations met and demanded he retract; on March 22 four men confronted him at his hotel and a scuffle broke out [2]. The next day, March 23, Jeon Myeong-un met Stevens at the waterfront as he headed for the Oakland ferry. His handkerchief-wrapped revolver would not fire, so he clubbed Stevens with it. Jang In-hwan, there on his own errand, fired into the struggle, hitting Stevens twice in the back and wounding Jeon too [2][3]. Stevens died two days later. Jang was convicted of second-degree murder; charges against Jeon were dropped for lack of evidence [2][3]. Money for the defence came from Koreans in Korea, Japan, Siberia, Manchuria, Mexico and the US, and in Korea the two men are remembered as patriots [1][2].

title: Look Tin Eli Dreams Up a Pagoda City
place: Grant Avenue (then Dupont Street) bazaar blocks
hook: The pagoda rooftops tourists photograph today were not in old Chinatown at all. A Mendocino-born merchant invented them, on purpose, after the fire.
story: Look Tin Eli was born in Mendocino County, yet officials barred him from re-entering the country after a trip abroad. His court case, In re Look Tin Sing, became one of the earliest rulings that a person born in the United States is a citizen regardless of ancestry [1]. After 1906 he became the public face of Chinatown's rebuilding. As general manager of the Sing Chong Bazaar, he sold the city on a new 'Oriental City' of 'veritable fairy palaces' [1]. With fellow businessman Wong G. Yow he worked with white architects, favouring tourist-friendly flourishes, including pagoda-style buildings that had not existed before the fire [2]. In 1908 he also stared down the police chief over a fireworks permit for Chinese New Year. 'It is part of the Chinese religion to set off fireworks as the old year closes,' he told the Chronicle, adding that treaty rights protected their worship [2]. He went on to help found the Canton Bank of San Francisco [1]. The ending was darker: pursued by gangs, he slipped out of the city in 1919, boarding his ship to China from a tugboat for fear of assassination on the dock [2].

title: Murder at the Acropolis Oyster Stand
place: Site of the Acropolis Chophouse (now Lands End Lookout), Point Lobos Ave
hook: Manuel Varvare served oysters from a recycled world's-fair kiosk above the baths. After he reported a robbery, the robber came back.
story: Around 1898 Manuel Varvare (his name is also spelled Varvaris and Vavare) opened the Acropolis Oyster Stand in a kiosk that Adolph Sutro had bought from the 1894 Midwinter Fair and set up on Cliff Avenue, today's Point Lobos Avenue [1]. It grew lean-tos for a kitchen, a dining room and a stand-up oyster bar, and Varvare slept in a small room at the back [1]. Business was poor after Sutro died and the nearby Merrie Way rides shut, and he twice tried to sell [1][2]. In February 1905 three soldiers refused to pay and attacked him with knives and a club [1]. On February 7, 1908, an armed robber took $87, wrote down Varvare's name, and warned he would kill him if he went to the police. Varvare reported it anyway [1]. The Call said the robber returned on a Friday night, struck him with a .45 revolver and fractured his skull. Varvare died at French Hospital on March 7, 1908; the police admitted they had no clue to the killer [1]. His fruit-stand neighbour, Nicholas Antipa, took over. The city demolished the stands in 1922 when it widened the road [1].

title: The Banker's Windmill Against the Water Monopoly
place: Murphy Windmill, near Lincoln Way and 47th Avenue
hook: When it first turned its sails in 1908, the park's south windmill was billed as the largest in the world, built to beat a private water company.
story: The Dutch Windmill of 1902 proved so popular that the Park Commission wanted a second one. Banker Samuel G. Murphy offered $20,000, and on June 7, 1907, commissioners voted to name it after him [1]. The goal was practical: pumping well water for irrigation so the park did not have to pay the Spring Valley Water Company's steep rates [1][2]. Donations poured in with strings attached: the Pacific Lumber Company gave two 114-foot spars, each cut from a single log; Louis Sloss gave the copper dome; and former commissioner W.J. Dingee gave concrete, while the mill was clad in slate from quarries he largely controlled [1]. On April 11, 1908, Mayor Taylor, John McLaren and the commissioners watched its sails turn for the first time, feeding a new reservoir named for commission president William Metson [1]. It even starred in Charlie Chaplin's 1915 film The Jitney Elopement [1]. Electric pumps soon made it redundant, and in 1944 a spar rotted so badly it had to be removed [1]. (One WNP article dates Murphy's gift to 1905 [3].)

title: The Bosworth Street banner that led America's marchers
place: Bosworth Street near Hamerton Avenue (site of Johanna Pinther's home at 1006 Bosworth, demolished)
hook: A Glen Park woman embroidered the banner that went at the head of what local historians argue was the first suffrage march in the United States.
story:
On 27 August 1908, women of the California Equal Suffrage Association lined up behind a silk banner and marched through Oakland to the state Republican convention. The banner carried the state coat of arms, embroidered by Johanna Pinther of Glen Park [1]. The Call described nearly 200 women marching in pairs, the line almost a block long, "with their yellow ribbons flying bravely" [1]. Next day the Chronicle printed a photo of them on its front page: Pinther, her step-daughter-in-law Jeanette carrying the banner, and Lillian Harris Coffin [1].

The Republicans turned them down flat. Their only offer was the vote on school questions, and the women wanted all or nothing [1]. The Glen Park Neighborhoods History Project argues that this was the first suffrage march in the US. Maude Malone's attempt in New York that February had been stopped by the police. Some historians still count Malone's as the first [1].

Back home, Pinther founded the Glen Park Outdoor Art League that same year, a women's club that pushed for city services while its members pressed for the vote [2][3]. Her house at 1006 Bosworth was torn down in the 1960s when the street was widened [3].

title: The Mission House Built From Its Own Rubble
place: Donaldina Cameron House, 920 Sacramento Street
hook: Firemen blew it up in 1906 trying to stop the flames. Its superintendent rebuilt it with the same bricks, and some say with hidden passages below.
story: Since 1873 the Presbyterian mission house at 920 Sacramento Street had taken in Chinese girls and women escaping prostitution, sweatshops and forced domestic service [1]. Its superintendent, the New Zealander Donaldina Cameron, led night-time rescue raids with police carrying axes and sledgehammers. The tongs called her Fahn Quai, 'white devil'; the girls called her Lo Mo, translated by some as 'old mother' and by others as 'little mother' [1][2]. By one estimate she rescued and educated around 3,000 girls [2]. As Chinatown burned in April 1906, firemen dynamited the mission house in a failed attempt to make a firebreak [1]. It rose again on the same spot in 1908, built with bricks salvaged from the original and designed by Julia Morgan [1]. The home was raided by brothel owners, and sometimes by police hunting 'illegal aliens', so according to one account Cameron made sure the new basement had hidden passages where the girls could hide [2]. She kept defending Chinese immigrants until she retired in 1934 [1]. The building is still Cameron House, a social service centre for Asian communities [1].

title: The library that moved seven times
place: 653 Chenery Street (branch library 1970-2007, now Bird & Beckett Books and Records)
hook: Glen Park's library started as a shelf in a dry-goods store. Over the next century it moved again and again, pushed out by freeway plans and a BART station.
story:
In 1908 forty Glen Park women founded the Glen Park Outdoor Art League. Its second president, Ada Parker Stillings, was herself a refugee of the 1906 disaster. She led the push for a library, and that September "Delivery Station F" opened inside Mary Bridget Mullally Hamilton's dry-goods store on Diamond Street [1].

Then the moves began. It went to Bosworth and Diamond in 1914, next door in 1918, and in 1927 it became a full branch at 700 Bosworth [1]. In 1964 that building was knocked down to widen Bosworth, part of the freeway plans that threatened Glen Canyon. The library went back to Diamond Street, until BART bought the block in 1968 and it had to move once more [1].

In 1970 Glen Park native William "Bill" Tietz and his wife Val gave the city their land at 653 Chenery Street. They turned the family's old hardware store into a library, and it stayed there for 37 years. The building is now Bird & Beckett Books and Records [1]. On 13 October 2007 the branch moved into the first building the city had ever owned for it, at 2825 Diamond Street [1]. Gum Tree Girl Zoanne Nordstrom had backed the new building and the housing that came with it [2].

title: Two Cable Cars and a Horsecar, Upstairs
place: Lower Great Highway near Moraga Street (private home; exact address withheld)
hook: From the street it looks like an ordinary beach house. Upstairs, passenger benches, slatted ceilings and a sliding horsecar door survive from Carville.
story: Most of Carville's streetcar houses vanished. Some were shingled over, some burned, some were torn down. One is known to survive, on the Lower Great Highway near Moraga Street [1][2]. It was built for Minnie Collins, a notary public and photojournalist, out of two streetcars and a horse car [2]. Researcher James Heisterkamp later found permits showing that she had the cars set on a frame in 1908, and that they were probably raised to make a second story in 1921 [1]. The San Francisco News profiled Mrs. Collins and her house in 1947 [1]. Heisterkamp, a San Francisco State student, tracked the house down in 1994. He walked 47th Avenue, 48th Avenue and the Great Highway asking strangers about cable cars, until a young man pushing a bicycle pointed him to the house next door [1]. Inside, the front door opens into a room made of two cable cars placed side by side with their inner walls taken out. One wall still has the cars' wooden benches under the original tongue-and-groove ceiling. The bedroom and bath fill an intact horse car, with a sliding panel door between them [1]. Filmmaker Scott Anderson bought the house in the 1990s and told his tenant not to put any new nails in the walls [1].

title: 'Julius Caesar' Today at the Gem
place: Former Gem Theatre, 2542 San Bruno Avenue
hook: When the Portola was still mostly cattle and greenhouses, a storefront picture house on San Bruno Avenue hung out the bunting for 'Julius Caesar'.
story: The Portola was still mostly farmland in the early 1900s. Cattle grazed on its hills and its few streets were unpaved. Along San Bruno Avenue, though, a line of businesses was growing, and their owners often lived upstairs [1]. One of them was the Gem Theatre at 2542 San Bruno Avenue, between Felton and Burrows. A photograph from about 1909 shows it decorated with flags and bunting, with a sign that reads 'Special To-Day Julius Caesar' and children waiting at the door [2]. The collection that holds the photograph dates the Gem to 1909-1910, and notes that the building was still standing in 2018 [2]. A generation later the district had grown enough to support a bigger house, the Avenue Theatre, a block south, where children paid a dime for Saturday matinees in the 1920s [3].

title: A Nob Hill Doorway Beside a Lake
place: Portals of the Past, Lloyd Lake
hook: Six marble columns on the edge of Lloyd Lake are all that survived of a railroad boss's Nob Hill mansion.
story: Alban N. Towne, longtime president and general manager of the Southern Pacific, built his mansion at 1101 California Street in 1891 to designs by Arthur Page Brown. He enjoyed it only briefly, dying of a heart attack in 1895; his widow Caroline stayed on until the fire of 1906 consumed everything but the marble portico [1][2]. Arnold Genthe photographed the empty doorway by moonlight, later writing that the picture 'brought out its classic beauty', and Willard Worden's images of it framing the ruined City Hall helped make it an icon [1][3]. In 1909 Caroline Towne donated the portico in her husband's memory. Park historian Christopher Pollock credits Senator James D. Phelan with leading the move and architect Edgar A. Mathews with choosing the site [1]. The nickname came from a line found by poet Charles Kellogg Field: 'This is the portal of the past — from now on, once more forward' [1]. Set at the water's edge, it works like the follies of English landscape gardens: a ruin placed to be reflected in a lake [2].

title: Dynamite under cover of the Fourth
place: Gray Brothers quarry, east face of Telegraph Hill near Lombard & Montgomery
hook: Court orders couldn't stop the Gray Brothers blasting Telegraph Hill away. So in 1909 they timed the dynamite to the holiday fireworks.
story: For about twenty years George and Harry Gray blasted and crushed rock from the east face of Telegraph Hill for ship ballast and roadbeds. Their explosions undermined and destroyed houses on Vallejo, Green, Union, Calhoun, Montgomery and Greenwich streets [1]. Irish and Italian residents sometimes answered with barrages of rocks. The brothers ignored court orders or paid their way around them [2]. A campaign led by Alice Griffith and the Telegraph Hill Neighborhood Association got blasting permits revoked in 1903, but the quarry kept going [2]. In 1909, despite another court order, the Grays set off a blast on the Fourth of July, timed to be drowned out by the Presidio's celebration guns (or the fireworks, in another telling). Falling rock gave them away, and angry neighbours chased the crew off [1][2]. The end came from inside the business. Sicilian quarry worker Joseph Lococo, unpaid for months, shot and killed George Gray. Sources date it to 1914 or 1915, and one says the sum owed was just $17.50 [1][2]. Lococo was acquitted and the blasting stopped. The raw cliffs it left behind are still sending rock slides down on Lombard Street and Broadway [1].

title: Fire in the Keepers' Gothic House
place: Light station keepers' quarters, Hillcrest Rd
hook: A keeper heard timbers crackling above his kitchen. A passing Navy tug blew its whistle, and the island's sailor boys came running.
story:
Uphill from the lighthouse stands a Victorian Gothic house with steep cross-gables and a sweeping veranda. It was built as a duplex for the keeper's and assistant keeper's families, and it is one of only two such keepers' houses left in California [1]. On the afternoon of 17 July 1909, Assistant Keeper John Kofod was sitting in his kitchen when he heard burning timber and saw the roof and eaves above him on fire [2]. He alerted his wife and daughter and Keeper Herbert Luff's family downstairs. Aboard the approaching Navy tug Vigilant, Captain Lockyer saw the flames and sounded his whistle, which brought men running from the Naval Training Station. They dragged a hose from the tug's engines up the hill and fought the fire for an hour. The roof and several upper rooms were lost [2].

The house carried on. Kofod's daughter Anna married Walter Fanning, a radioman at the island's naval station, and their son was born in the dwelling [2]. On New Year's Eve, Kofod would take his grandchildren down to give three blasts on the fog whistle. The passing ferries answered [2]. Today a senior Coast Guard officer lives in the house [1].

title: How Irving, Judah, Kirkham and Lawton Won
place: Irving Street at 9th Avenue
hook: Why do four un-Spanish names break the alphabet of Spanish explorers south of the park? Blame a furious 1909 revolt over 'Spanish Town.'
story: Until 1909 the streets south of the park had letters: H, I, J, K, L and on. A commission appointed by Mayor Taylor was asked to end the city's street-name confusion, and the Post Office estimated that 500 letters a day went astray [1]. It proposed giving every numbered avenue and lettered street in the Richmond and Sunset an alphabetical Spanish name. First Avenue would become Arguello, Third Avenue Coronado, and so on [1][2]. On November 15 the supervisors voted 12 to 5 in favour, and the western districts erupted. Speakers warned that the avenues would be mocked as 'Spanish Town,' and the Richmond Banner denounced a 'miserable surrender of American names' [1]. After mass protest the commission gave the avenues their numbers back. The Sunset Improvement Club then asked for the names of Americans 'that reflect glory and luster upon our civilization' [1]. H Street became Lincoln Way. I, J, K and L became Irving (after Washington Irving), Judah (after railroad engineer Theodore Judah), and Kirkham and Lawton (both army generals). Irving and Judah were borrowed from a list meant for Bayview [1][2]. After L the fight ran out, and Moraga, Noriega and Ortega stayed Spanish [2].

title: Maybeck's Tudor wedding gift, braced for quakes
place: Roos House, 3500 Jackson Street at Locust Street
hook: Three years after 1906, a theatre magnate gave his daughter a half-timbered dream house, secretly braced with piles and bolts. A later earthquake cost it its garden.
story:
In 1909, nineteen-year-old Elizabeth Meyerfeld married Leon Roos of the Roos Brothers clothing firm. Her father Morris Meyerfeld, a partner in the Orpheum theatre circuit, asked Bernard Maybeck to design a house for the couple as a wedding present [1][2]. Elizabeth had travelled Europe with her father looking for talent, and she wanted something theatrical. Maybeck mixed Tudor half-timbering with Gothic details. At about 9,000 square feet it is the largest house he designed for a San Francisco client [1][2].

The house was built just three years after the 1906 earthquake and fire. Maybeck and Leon Roos cared a great deal about seismic safety. It stands on wooden piles driven into the hillside, unusual for a house. Maybeck's engineer, Herman Kower, worked out the loads on the basement columns and showed exactly how they were to be bolted to the foundation and tied to the floor above. The decoration hides all of this [2].

Earthquakes shaped the house again eight decades later. After the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, the back of the lot, once Maybeck's formal vegetable garden, was sold to pay for repairs [2]. When the house joined the National Register in 2009, its owner was Jane Roos LeRoux [2].

title: Nine Children Above the Grocery
place: 118 Sagamore St (Pesce's Market)
hook: Paul and Marie Pesce left Genoa in 1903, opened a grocery across from the train station in 1909, and raised nine children in the flat upstairs.
story: Ocean View's early farmers were mostly Italian immigrants from Genoa, working vegetable plots in the valleys below Merced Heights [2]. Paul and Marie Pesce came to San Francisco from Genoa in 1903, and in 1909 opened a grocery at 118 Sagamore Street, just across from the Southern Pacific station, the centre of a small community still isolated from the rest of the city [1]. The family lived in the flat over the store, where they raised all nine of their children, and every one of them worked in the shop at some point [1]. It sat at the old village crossroads; a 1926 city photograph of Sagamore shows a meat market, a couple of barber shops and 'Blue Ribbon' ice cream signs nearby [3]. Pesce's outlasted the station, the plaza fountain and the steam trains. When the OMI News profiled it in 1977, son Elmer, 68, still made the deliveries, bought the produce and lived upstairs, and a third-generation Pesce studying at San Francisco State said she learned more in the store than at school: 'This is life' [1]. Known for large Italian sandwiches and gooey pastries at the checkout, Pesce's Market closed in the 1980s [1].

title: Operators Who Knew Every Name
place: Chinese Telephone Exchange, 743 Washington Street
hook: Callers never gave a number. They asked for a person by name, and the operators, who memorised about 1,500 of them, put them straight through.
story: The pagoda at 743 Washington Street was built in 1909 as the second Chinese Telephone Exchange on the site [1]. Sources disagree about when Chinatown's phone service began, giving 1887 or 1898 [2][3]. What made it famous was the switchboard. Callers asked for people, not numbers. In 1901 the Examiner marvelled that the operators had nearly 1,500 names to remember, along with where each person lived, and warned that the work 'would drive an American operator insane' [1]. The first operators were men. Women became the chief operators in 1906, and the Examiner claimed they were preferred for their good tempers [2]. Operators had to handle the district's many languages and dialects, and more than 13,000 calls a day. The switchboard doubled as a job exchange: employers phoned in work and the operators knew whom to connect [2]. In 1943 the exchange's thirty workers joined the Telephone Traffic Employees Organization Local 120, fought their seven-day schedule and won $5,000 in back pay and overtime [2]. Dial phones ended the exchange in the 1940s [2]. Long before, the site had housed Sam Brannan's California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper [1].

title: Palou Avenue, because Paine was an 'infidel'
place: All Hallows Church, 1715 Oakdale Ave (by Palou Ave)
hook: Palou Avenue was meant to honour Thomas Paine. Then the parish priest of All Hallows stood up and objected.
story: In 1909 San Francisco set out to end decades of misdelivered mail by renaming the Bayview's numbered "avenues, South" [1]. The Street Names Commission picked a roster of American heroes, arranged alphabetically, and proposed Thomas Paine for Sixteenth Avenue South [1][2]. Father O'Sullivan of All Hallows parish exploded. "He was an infidel, and in South San Francisco we are all Christians," the Examiner quoted him [1]. A local improvement club suggested hiding Paine's name on some "out-of-the-way avenue on the hillside where nobody lived"; the commission refused to use it at all [1]. The priests also vetoed Belfast and Cromwell as insults to Irish Catholics, who O'Sullivan said made up three-quarters of the district, and objected to Wallace, a "Scotch hero" [1][2]. He vowed locals would keep using the old numbers anyway. At the final vote on 21 December 1909, the commission placated him: Sixteenth Avenue became Palou, after the Franciscan padre, while Carroll (for the only Catholic signer of the Declaration of Independence) and Bancroft replaced Cromwell and Belfast [1]. Those names, from Arthur to Yosemite, are still on the street signs [2].

title: The Arctic Sloop Parked on the Sand
place: Site of the Gjøa and Amundsen monument, north of the Beach Chalet
hook: The first ship ever to sail the Northwest Passage spent 63 years in Golden Gate Park, guarded by a live-in caretaker and a barking seal.
story: Roald Amundsen's 69-foot sloop Gjøa finished the first voyage through the Northwest Passage in San Francisco in October 1906. Amundsen, to the dismay of the Norwegian community planning a grand welcome, slipped into the Bay Area by train ahead of his boat [1]. The Gjøa then languished at Mare Island until the Norwegian consul asked the Park Commission to take her [1]. On July 6, 1909, some 5,000 people watched her dragged by cables up onto Ocean Beach; some hung wet stockings on the cables. The Call predicted she would stand 'until her mighty timbers rot. That will be 200 years or more' [1]. Souvenir hunters carved initials into her hull, so the city fenced her, hired a caretaker who lived aboard (he appears in the 1910 census), and installed a fur seal in a tank that, the Call promised, would 'bark its bullet shaped head off' at pirates [1]. In 1929 a Norwegian granite shaft honouring Amundsen was added [2]. The sloop went home to Norway in 1972 [3].

title: The Chutes Come to Fillmore Street
place: Chutes Park, block of Fillmore, Turk, Webster & Eddy (entrance near 1226 Fillmore)
hook: In 1909 San Francisco's famous water-chute amusement park moved to Fillmore Street. Two years later a fire that began in a barber shop destroyed it.
story: After 1906 Fillmore had the crowds, and a showman moved in. On March 8, 1909, Irving Ackerman, son of the original Chutes owner, took a 13-year lease on the old Coney Island amusement park. It filled the block bounded by Fillmore, Webster, Eddy and Turk [1]. He spent $250,000 moving and enlarging the Chutes, and the new park opened on July 14, 1909 [1]. It had the famous water chute, a merry-go-round, a Circle Swing, a "Dante's Inferno" labyrinth, a human roulette wheel, a dance pavilion and an outdoor movie screen. There were daredevils, an elephant named Mike, a flea circus, and boxing exhibitions that included heavyweight champion Jack Johnson [1]. A fireproof Chutes Theatre opened on December 31, 1909 [2]. Some time after midnight on May 29, 1911, fire broke out in the Bondy brothers' barber shop. It killed three people, injured seven and wrecked most of the park [1]. The concrete theatre survived [1][2]. Ackerman did not rebuild the park. The theatre, turned to face Fillmore Street, reopened in 1915 as the Lyric under Ackerman and Harris [2].

title: The Richmond Refuses to Become Spanish Town
place: Cabrillo Street (formerly C Street)
hook: In 1909 the city voted to rename every numbered avenue in Spanish, from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond revolted within a week.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, the Post Office struggled with two sets of numbered streets. In 1909 a city commission proposed replacing the Richmond and Sunset's numbered avenues with Spanish names in alphabetical order, running from Arguello to Zamorano and then on to Spanish saints beyond 26th Avenue [1][2]. On November 15 the Board of Supervisors approved the changes 12 to 5 [1]. The avenues were furious. Speakers mocked the 'unpronounceable' names and the Richmond Banner warned the districts would be called 'the Spanish Town of San Francisco' [2]. The Richmond had the city's oldest continuously operating improvement club, and it mobilised fast [1][2]. At a packed Saturday meeting on November 20, the commission backed down. The Examiner claimed thirty-five thousand residents had 'arose en masse' [2]. The avenues kept their numbers; only First Avenue (Arguello) and 49th Avenue (La Playa, 'the beach') changed [2]. The Richmond's lettered streets went through several drafts before settling on explorers after all: A, B and C streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: The brownstone that outlived the fire
place: Pacific-Union Club (Flood Mansion), 1000 California Street
hook: Every wooden palace on Nob Hill burned in 1906. The one real stone mansion survived as a scorched shell, and a gentlemen's club moved in.
story: When the silver king James Clair Flood built his Nob Hill mansion in the 1880s, he had brownstone cut in Connecticut and shipped around Cape Horn. His neighbours' palaces were wood, painted to look like stone [1]. The difference showed on April 19, 1906, when the fire reached the house. It destroyed the interior, but the stone shell stood [1]. Flood's unmarried daughter Cora, who had lived there until that year, sold the scorched building to the Pacific-Union Club in 1909 [1]. The club held an architectural competition. Albert Pissis, a member, won with a grand white stone building that would have made Nob Hill "a second Acropolis". It began to look too expensive, and the commission went to Willis Polk, the only contender who wanted to keep what was left of the mansion [1]. NoeHill says William Bourn, who sat on the building committee, secured the job for Polk [2]. In 1910 Polk added semicircular wings and a third floor, using brownstone from the same Connecticut quarry, and fitted out five dining rooms, a swimming pool and a squash court [1]. By the time of the mansion's 1960s landmark nomination, women had been allowed inside only once, for the 1952 Centennial Ball [1].

title: The busiest, smelliest creek on the waterfront
place: Mission Creek channel between Third and Fourth streets
hook: Sailors said two gulps of Mission Creek would kill you. It turned white lead paint black overnight, and ships still came in droves.
story: Fred Klebingat arrived on the south waterfront in 1909, a 20-year-old German seaman working as a donkeyman, running the steam winch on the schooner Annie E. Smale. He never forgot Mission Creek. "It was an open sewer, a cesspool," he recalled. Great gas bubbles broke the surface, men said you would not last two minutes if you fell in, and the water "would turn white lead paint black in one night" [1][2]. It was also, in his words, "the busiest place on the San Francisco waterfront." Steam schooners, sailing vessels and hay scows lined both banks, from Pope & Talbot's lumber yard to the hay wharf opposite, leaving barely room to tow a ship down the middle. Sailors had their own blunt name for it [1]. Scow schooners brought hay from as far as Sacramento and Milpitas to feed the city's horses. They were tied three abreast and tacked out through the crush. Once a runaway scow's bowsprit came straight through Klebingat's porthole and backed out again [1]. Idle seamen haunted the wharves hoping for a berth. As Klebingat put it, it was "not what you knew, but WHO you knew" [1].

title: The nuns' hospital that fled the fire
place: St. Mary's Hospital (now UCSF Health), 450 Stanyan St / 2200 Hayes St
hook: Eight Irish nuns started it in 1857. After the 1906 fire burned it out, St. Mary's rebuilt at the edge of Golden Gate Park.
story: The Sisters of Mercy reached San Francisco on December 8, 1854. There were eight of them, led by 25-year-old Mother Mary Baptist Russell, who had nursed cholera victims in Ireland [1]. They had been booked on the steamer Arctic, which was lost with everyone aboard, but it was overbooked, so they sailed on another ship [1]. Within a year they were nursing the city through a cholera outbreak. When the county would not repay what they had spent running the county hospital, the sisters opened their own St. Mary's Hospital in 1857 [1]. Sources differ on its first site: one says a Stockton Street building, another Rincon Hill at First and Bryant [1][2]. After the 1906 fire the hospital worked from temporary quarters at 2344 Sutter Street. By 1909 it had settled at 2200 Hayes Street, between Shrader and Stanyan [2]. From 1951 its nursing graduates earned bachelor's degrees from USF next door. A new building replaced the old one in 1972 at 450 Stanyan Street [2]. It is the oldest continuously operating hospital in San Francisco, and it joined UCSF in 2024, when it stopped being a Catholic hospital [1][2].

title: The reservoir built because the city burned
place: Twin Peaks Reservoir ('Summit Reservoir'), off Twin Peaks Boulevard
hook: Near the top of Twin Peaks, 10.5 million gallons of water are kept only for fighting fires. It was the city's answer to 1906.
story:
The 1906 earthquake broke the city's water mains, and San Franciscans blamed the failed water system for the destruction. Insurance rates soared, and in some areas coverage could not be had at any price [1]. Fire Department chief engineer Dennis T. Sullivan had proposed a separate firefighting water system back in 1903. In 1908 City Engineer Marsden Manson studied 250 cities around the world to design one [1]. Construction ran from 1909 to 1913 [1].

The Twin Peaks Reservoir is the backbone of what is now called the Emergency Firefighting Water System. It holds 10.5 million gallons in a tank built of six-inch reinforced-concrete slabs, set at 758 feet [1]. The tank is split in two, so a broken pipe can drain only half of it. The white fire hydrants with black tops, west of Twin Peaks, draw on it [1]. In a big fire downtown, commanders can bring the reservoir online by radio, which raises the pressure in the mains to 328 pounds per square inch [1]. A city photograph captioned "Twin Peaks Reservoir. General view of work" records its construction [1].

title: The revolt against 'Spanish Town'
place: Arguello Boulevard (formerly First Avenue) at Clement St
hook: In 1909 the city tried to swap the numbered avenues for Spanish names from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond fought back, and a pirate joke helped end it.
story: In November 1909 a Street Naming Commission, trying to sort out mail muddled after the quake, proposed replacing every numbered avenue in the Richmond and Sunset with Spanish names in alphabetical order: Arguello, then Coronado, De Soto and on to Zamorano for 26th Avenue. Spanish saints would follow after that [1]. The Board of Supervisors approved it 12 to 5. Speakers from the Avenues called the names 'unpronounceable', and some said the city was 'selling out' to the Spain the country had just beaten in the Philippines. They said the district would be mocked as 'Spanish Town' [1]. The Richmond's improvement club organised petitions, and the commission backed down at a meeting in Richmond Hall on November 20 [1]. At one hearing a lawyer objected to naming First Avenue 'St. Francis Boulevard' because St. Francis Drake had been 'one of the very worst pirates'. The chairman reminded him that St. Francis of Assisi was a priest, and the room broke into laughter [1]. The numbered avenues stayed, but First Avenue became Arguello, and the lettered streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: A Diva Sings Free at Lotta's Fountain
place: Lotta's Fountain, Market, Kearny & Geary
hook: Blocked by a lawsuit, soprano Luisa Tetrazzini vowed to sing in the street if she had to. On Christmas Eve 1910, she did.
story: Luisa Tetrazzini had made her American debut at San Francisco's Tivoli in 1905 and gone on to conquer New York and London [1]. When impresario Oscar Hammerstein served her with an injunction in November 1910, she told reporters: "I will sing in San Francisco... If necessary, I will sing in the streets. I will sing at Lotta's Fountain" [1]. A judge let her tour go on, and she kept the promise anyway. On Christmas Eve 1910 a stage went up beside Lotta Crabtree's 1875 fountain, opposite the Chronicle's offices [1][2]. With no amplification, a crowd variously reported as up to 250,000 filled Market Street to Union Square; the historian who retold the story urges caution about the number [1]. Office workers hung telephone receivers out of windows so families at home could listen. Tetrazzini, in a gown sewn with 3,000 rhinestones, sang just two pieces, "The Last Rose of Summer" and the waltz from Romeo and Juliet. Men wept; she called the city "my home" [1]. In 1912 a plaque honouring the concert was placed on the fountain [1][2].

title: A Mayor's Fist at Sheridan School
place: 431 Capitol Ave (Sheridan School)
hook: At the cornerstone ceremony for Ocean View's new school in 1910, a speaker swore he would rather his right hand palsy than stay silent.
story: Ocean View's improvement clubs had long petitioned the city for services, a public school among them [1]. On February 20, 1910, a large crowd gathered at Capitol Avenue and Lobos Street for the cornerstone-laying of Sheridan Primary School [1][2]. Pupils sang 'America,' the Columbia Park boys' band played, and a speaker, likely Mayor P.H. McCarthy, raised his fist against the school board appointed by his predecessor: 'I would rather that my good right hand would palsy than fail to lift it against a subtle scheme to do redhot politics in the schools' [2]. The day also honoured the district's pioneers. Among the neighbourhood's 'honored settlers' at the dedication was Elias Wolfe, the roadhouse keeper who had helped start the area's first school decades earlier [1]. Sheridan opened to students in 1911 with special classrooms for 'manual training and domestic science' and one designated for 'delinquent pupils' [2]. A new building replaced it in 1975, yet the banner displayed onstage in 1910 is still shown at the school, and two buildings visible behind the 1910 crowd still stand [2].

title: A parish born in a 24th Street workshop
place: St. Philip the Apostle Church, 725 Diamond Street
hook: Upper Noe Valley's Catholics were tired of climbing hills and crossing creeks to get to Mass. So they started a church in an old workshop.
story:
In 1910 upper Noe Valley was a working-class, largely Irish neighbourhood with wooden sidewalks on 24th Street. It had no Catholic church of its own [1]. Every choice meant a long walk. Most Holy Redeemer was over the steep hill at 18th and Diamond. St. James was more than a mile downhill at 23rd and Guerrero. St. Paul's, at Church and 29th, was also about a mile from Diamond Street. "You had to cross three creeks to get to church," as one longtime parishioner puts it [1].

Archbishop Patrick Riordan approved a new parish, and the job of starting it went to Father John Cullen from County Cavan, Ireland. The first chapel was a converted workshop at 4296 24th Street. Cullen lived in a rented upper flat a few doors away, at 4262, for nearly two years [1].

The congregation soon outgrew the workshop. It opened a church on Elizabeth Street in 1914, then raised $71,000 for a Romanesque church at Diamond and Elizabeth, where the first Mass was held in 1925 [1]. Mae Silver's history notes that the Irish were the largest group in Noe and Eureka valleys from the start [2].

title: A secret airship in the racetrack gully
place: Former Ingleside Racetrack grounds, Ingleside Terraces (Urbano Drive area)
hook: Guards chased gawkers away while an inventor built an 8,000-pound flying machine on the abandoned Ingleside Racetrack, planning to fly it to Paris.
story: After the horses left, the empty Ingleside Racetrack had an odd tenant. In a gully out of sight of Ocean Avenue, Willis Grant Murray was building a $100,000 airship paid for by wealthy investors [1]. In December 1910 he gave a San Francisco Call reporter a long interview. The paper found the machine 'hardly nameable': part biplane, part dirigible, part helicopter, with three car engines driving 14-foot propellers, a deck for five crew and ten passengers, and aluminium boats for skids [1]. Murray planned to fly six days and nights without landing, cross the continent and perhaps go on to Paris. He called ordinary aeroplanes 'a plaything beside it' [1]. Then he hired watchmen to chase off the curious. By February 1912 Joseph Leonard's crews were grading the old track for Ingleside Terraces around him [1][2]. Murray was still trying to get the 176-foot machine off the ground, but high winds kept ripping its hydrogen bags and damaging the frame. The airship never flew, and Murray died in 1919 [1].

title: Before the Fillmore, the Majestic
place: Majestic Hall (later the Fillmore Auditorium), Geary & Fillmore
hook: The hall where Hendrix and the Dead later played began as a mother-and-daughters venture, and it kept a colour line for more than forty years.
story: Decades before the psychedelic posters, the corner of Geary and Fillmore held a dance hall built by women. According to the city's Japantown historic context statement, Emma Gates Butler and her daughters built the Majestic Hall at the southwest corner in 1910. It was designed by the well-known architects James W. and Merritt Reid, who in 1911 also designed a five-storey building across Fillmore Street [1]. Other accounts give 1912 and describe the first tenant as the Majestic Hall and Academy of Dancing [2]. It was part of the entertainment boom that followed the 1906 quake, when Fillmore Street briefly became the city's downtown [1]. For a neighbourhood that was fast becoming one of the most mixed in the West, the Majestic kept a colour line. The same report notes that it was segregated until the 1950s [1]. The building went on to become the Ambassador Dance Hall in 1936 and a roller rink from 1939 to 1952. In 1954 the Black promoter Charles Sullivan took the lease, renamed it the Fillmore Auditorium and opened its doors to everyone [2].

title: Gymnasts, then Norwegians, on 18th Street
place: Mission Turn Hall (now the Women's Building), 3543 18th Street
hook: Long before its famous murals, the Women's Building was a German gymnastics hall, and after that a Norwegian lodge called Dovre Hall.
story:
Around 1900 the Irish and Germans were the Mission's biggest immigrant groups, and the Mission Turn Verein, a German gymnastics club, already had a hall on 18th Street near Valencia [1]. In 1910 architect August Reinhold Denke designed the Turners a new four-storey home at 3543 18th Street in the Mission Revival style [2][3].

For 25 years Mission Turn Hall was open to the whole mixed district. It ran after-school classes for children and put on a monthly exhibition followed by a social and a dance. It hosted weddings, receptions and parties [2]. The Native Sons and Daughters of the Golden West were tenants for fifty years [2]. In 1935 the Sons of Norway and the Daughters of Norway bought the building and renamed it Dovre Hall, after a mountain range in Norway [2][3]. It kept that name until 1978, when the San Francisco Women's Center bought it. It has been the Women's Building ever since [2][3].

title: Opening night at the Haight Theater
place: Haight Theater, 1700 Haight St at Cole St
hook: The mayor gave a speech and every one of its 1,310 seats sold. For half a century, kids spent whole Saturdays here for twenty cents.
story: On March 8, 1910, the Haight Theater opened at the northwest corner of Haight and Cole. It had one screen and 1,310 seats. The Ashbury Club sold out the first night, and Mayor Patrick Henry McCarthy gave a speech. The building cost $33,000. It showed films and vaudeville, with a system of lines and pulleys for shifting backdrops quickly, and the Haight orchestra often played live with the double features [1]. John Molloy grew up nearby. His father had pitched for the Hollywood Stars in 1926, and later gardened for Golden Gate Park's John McLaren and then drove for him. As a preteen, Molloy's favourite weekend treat was spending the whole day at the Haight Theater. Admission was 20 cents, and the 50 cents his father gave him covered everything else. His mother shopped on Haight Street, and at the GallenCamps shoe store he liked to use the X-ray machine to watch the bones of his feet wiggle [2]. By the 1950s, the suburbs and television were emptying neighbourhood movie houses [1]. The Haight closed as a cinema in 1964, after more than fifty years [3].
