title: The Bomb at Steuart and Market
place: Steuart Street just south of Market
hook: A suitcase bomb killed ten at a pro-war parade. The city convicted a labour organiser, though a photo placed him a mile away.
story: On Saturday, July 22, 1916, the Chamber of Commerce staged a huge Preparedness Day parade, reportedly with 51,329 marchers and 52 bands, to rally support for entering the war in Europe [1]. At 2:06 p.m., about half an hour in, a bomb hidden in a suitcase exploded on the west side of Steuart Street just south of Market, killing ten bystanders and wounding forty, the worst terrorist act in the city's history [1][2]. Suspicion fell at once on radical labour. Tom Mooney, a militant organiser, and Warren Billings were convicted on testimony later shown to be false, and a detective with long ties to utilities had coached witnesses [2]. A photograph taken at 2:01 p.m. showed Tom and Rena Mooney on the roof of the Eilers Building at 975 Market, a mile away; prosecutors had it but never showed it at trial [2]. Mooney was sentenced to death. After pressure from President Wilson his sentence was commuted to life, and Governor Culbert Olson pardoned him in January 1939. Sources differ on Billings: one says he was pardoned too, another that he was freed in 1942 [1][2]. The bomber was never identified [1].

title: The Rooftop Photo That Proved an Alibi
place: Eilers Building, 975 Market Street (between Fifth and Sixth)
hook: At 2:01 p.m. a photographer caught Tom and Rena Mooney on a Market Street rooftop. Minutes later a bomb exploded a mile away, and Mooney was blamed.
story: On July 22, 1916, business leaders staged a huge Preparedness Day parade up Market Street to drum up support for entering the European war. At 2:06 p.m. a bomb exploded near Steuart Street, killing ten people and critically injuring 40 more [1]. District Attorney Charles Fickert charged militant labor organizer Tom Mooney, his wife Rena, Warren Billings and two others [1][3]. Yet a photograph by Wade Hamilton places Tom and Rena on the roof of the Eilers Building at 975 Market, between Fifth and Sixth streets, at 2:01 p.m., when prosecutors claimed they were planting the bomb a mile east [1]. A Market Street clock linked to the photographs is now preserved in Vallejo as the "Alibi Clock" [2]. Mooney was convicted anyway and sentenced to hang; Billings got life, and Rena was acquitted [2][3]. After protests around the world, Governor William Stephens commuted Mooney's sentence to life in 1918, and he became one of America's most famous political prisoners [2]. Governor Culbert Olson finally pardoned him in 1939, after more than two decades behind bars [1][2].

title: Guns on the dunes: Fort Funston
place: Fort Funston (former Lake Merced Military Reservation)
hook: The Army bought these dunes in 1900 and left them empty for seventeen years. World War I brought mortars from the Presidio.
story: In December 1900 the federal government acquired about 45 acres of the sandy ridge between Lake Merced and the Pacific as the Lake Merced Military Reservation [1][2]. The Army had sued the Spring Valley Water Company for the land and paid $42,162 [3]. The plan was two mortar batteries, but nothing was built [1][2]. When the United States entered World War I in 1917, construction finally began. Battery Howe got four 12-inch mortars and Battery Bruff two 5-inch guns, both taken from older batteries at Fort Winfield Scott by the Presidio [1][2]. That year the reservation was expanded by about 150 acres to the south, and wooden buildings went up for the garrison [1]. It was renamed for Major General Frederick Funston, who died in 1917. He had commanded the Army troops in San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake [1][3]. Peace came quickly: Battery Bruff was disarmed in 1920, and the fort sat largely inactive until 1936 [1][3].

title: Strikebreakers and the door to nowhere
place: Geneva Car Barn yard side, 2301 San Jose Avenue (the second-storey 'door to nowhere')
hook: High on the Geneva Car Barn's yard wall is a door that opens onto a sheer drop. It dates from a streetcar strike in 1917.
story: On the night of August 11, 1917, a hundred platform men walked off their United Railroads streetcars near Market and Valencia. They were demanding union recognition, $3.50 a day and an eight-hour day [1]. More than 1,600 of the company's roughly 1,800 workers soon joined them, and the city saw daily marches, mob attacks on cars and armed company men [1]. United Railroads brought in hundreds of strikebreakers and housed them in its carbarns, including 75 at the Geneva barn [1]. At Geneva, the company turned a second-floor window into a doorway and built a temporary wooden stairway down to the rail yard. Strikebreakers could sleep in the office building, then go down and start the streetcars without being seen by the strikers outside [2][3]. The company waited the strikers out, and the walkout was defeated by late November [1]. The stairway is gone, but the doorway is still there on the eastern wall, opening onto a drop to the yard below. It is known as the 'door to nowhere' [2].

title: Tallest Man in San Francisco, at 5'4"
place: San Francisco National Cemetery, Officers' Section
hook: The general who ran the city in the days after the 1906 fire came back to the Presidio in 1917, and the whole city stopped for two minutes.
story: Frederick Funston stood less than five and a half feet tall, but he loomed large over San Francisco [1]. On April 18, 1906, his superior was at a daughter's wedding in Chicago, so Funston had command at the Presidio. He called out the troops, took charge of relief and had buildings dynamited for firebreaks [2]. Critics said he overstepped his authority. His shoot-looters orders led to innocent people being shot, and his dynamiting often started new fires [3]. He went on to Veracruz and the Mexican border and was in line to lead American troops to France. Then, on February 19, 1917, he died of a heart attack in a San Antonio hotel, aged 51 [2]. San Francisco brought him home. Funston lay in state at the Alamo and then under the City Hall rotunda, the first person given that honour there. Presidio cannon fired a thirteen-gun salute and the city stopped for two minutes [2]. He was buried in full dress uniform in the Officers' Section, Section 68, Grave 3 [2][4]. The command he was expected to take went to his former subordinate, John J. Pershing [3].

title: The streetcar that cuts through the park
place: J-Church right-of-way, west edge of Mission Dolores Park
hook: Church Street was too steep for a streetcar, so in 1917 Muni sent its trains off the road, through Dolores Park and behind people's backyards.
story: Riders on the J-Church notice it at once: heading south, the train leaves Church Street at 18th, runs along the west edge of Dolores Park, then weaves through private land around Liberty and 21st before rejoining Church at 22nd [1]. The detour exists because of the hill. When Bion J. Arnold planned the young Municipal Railway in 1912, he faced the steep climb over Dolores Heights. One of his ideas was a tunnel for cars and streetcars under the line of Chattanooga Street. That was one of at least fifteen proposals. The supervisors chose the cheaper private right-of-way around the steepest part of the hill [1]. Track-laying in the park was under way by May 1916 [1]. On August 11, 1917, Mayor 'Sunny Jim' Rolph drove the first car himself, as he liked to do, after being handed a union motorman's cap, card and button [1]. The grade through the park is still 9 percent, the steepest in the Muni Metro system [1]. That hill also saved the line. After the Second World War, when the city turned streetcar routes into bus routes, Church Street proved too steep, and the J kept its rails [1][2].

title: When the Barbary Coast moved uptown
place: Mason Street near Eddy (Poodle Dog Restaurant and Hotel, 111 Mason, c. 1910)
hook: A French restaurant with a discreet back driveway. Each time police closed the Barbary Coast, its trade moved a few blocks west.
story: Prostitution was one of the first businesses to return to the Uptown Tenderloin after the fire. By autumn 1906 the District Attorney was already trying to shut it down [1]. By 1910 the Poodle Dog Restaurant and Hotel stood at 111 Mason Street, with dining downstairs, rooms upstairs, and a discreet driveway to a "female boarding house" at the back [1]. A WPA writer in the 1930s remembered Mason Street as the "White Way," lit by cabarets, the Poodle Dog and Billy Lyons' saloon, "the Bucket of Blood" [2]. The same account quotes madam Tessie Wall, who refused to move to San Mateo: "Why I'd rather be an electric light pole on Powell Street than own all of the county" [2]. Reformers kept pushing vice out of the Barbary Coast, and it kept landing here. Police ordered the Coast's dance halls closed in 1913. When the Red Light Abatement Act was finally enforced on February 14, 1917, prostitutes scattered, "especially" to the Uptown Tenderloin [1]. After another crackdown in 1921, "many of the clubs followed the parlors into the Tenderloin" [1].

title: Yiddish Lectures in a Painted Lady
place: 1057 Steiner St (now the Chateau Tivoli), at Golden Gate Ave
hook: A shipping magnate's colorful Victorian became a home for young Jewish immigrant women. Later it became a hall for Yiddish writers and radicals.
story: The colorful Victorian at the corner of Steiner and Golden Gate was built in 1892 for the shipping magnate Daniel B. Jackson [1]. After 1906, as the Jewish Fillmore filled in around it, the house took on two new lives. In 1917 it became the Emanu-El Sisterhood's Residence for Single Jewish Women [1][2][3]. The Sisterhood had been founded in 1894 by women of Temple Emanu-El. It offered job help and clubs for working girls, and the Steiner Street house was meant to ease newly arrived Eastern European immigrants into American life [1][4]. The residence stayed until 1923, when the Sisterhood moved into a new building designed by Julia Morgan on Page Street [2][3]. In 1929 the house became the Yiddish Cultural Center [2][3]. It was the district's hub for secular Jewish life: classes in Yiddish language and literature, and lectures by prominent Yiddish writers from around the world. It was, the New Fillmore notes, "also a center of radical politics" [1]. The center lasted into the 1960s [3]. The house, now the Chateau Tivoli, is one of the few buildings of the Jewish Fillmore still standing [1].

title: A new church rises beside the adobe
place: Mission Dolores Basilica, 16th & Dolores Streets
hook: The 1791 adobe came through the earthquake, but the big brick church beside it did not. What replaced it became the West's first basilica.
story: In 1876, for the mission's centennial, a large red-brick church was built next to the 1791 adobe at 16th and Dolores [1]. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it, and it was torn down. The adobe, also damaged, survived [1][2]. Firefighters kept the flames from both buildings by dynamiting the convent and School of Notre Dame across the street [2]. For years the parish worshipped in a hastily built wooden church behind the old mission [1]. The cornerstone of a new church was laid on September 7, 1913. America's entry into the First World War slowed the work, and the church was finished in 1918 and dedicated at Christmas [1][2]. In 1917, architect Willis Polk quietly strengthened the adobe with concrete-covered steel beams and roof trusses, an early earthquake retrofit [1]. In 1924 part of the old cemetery became a parking lot and schoolyard for parishioners who now came by car [1]. In 1926 the plain new church was redone with ornate Churrigueresque detail inspired by San Diego's 1915 exposition [1]. In 1952 Pope Pius XII made it a minor basilica, the first west of the Mississippi [1][2].

title: Eight destroyers in one day
place: Bethlehem Steel Administration Building, 20th and Illinois streets
hook: On July 4, 1918, the shipyard launched eight warships in one day. That same summer, the last of Irish Hill's saloons and cottages were torn down.
story: In 1905 Charles M. Schwab stood on the steps of the Union Iron Works office on 20th Street as the only bidder at an auction, and bought the whole yard for Bethlehem Steel for $1 million [2]. By 1918, with America in the First World War, the yard was working flat out. According to the Dogpatch historic district study, it employed 10,000 people, and with Bethlehem's other Bay Area yards it made up the largest shipbuilding complex in the world [1]. In 1918 alone it built 18 submarines, ten of them for Britain, and 66 destroyers [1]. On July 4, 1918, eight destroyers went down the ways in a single day [1][2]. A new administration building had been finished in 1917 on the northeast corner of 20th and Illinois, and it still stands [1][3]. The boom finished off the neighbourhood next door. Bethlehem bought the Irish Hill lots on 20th Street for a new concrete foundry. Photographs from May 1918 show a saloon, a French laundry and another saloon facing Illinois Street, months away from demolition [3]. Accounts differ on the foundry's date and cost, and one says it was never built at all. What was left of Irish Hill became a parking lot next to a rocky stump [1][3].

title: Holed through, off by an eighth
place: West portal of the Twin Peaks Tunnel, West Portal Avenue at Ulloa Street
hook: Drillers boring from opposite sides of Twin Peaks met almost perfectly. Ten months later Mayor Rolph drove the first streetcar out of the hill here.
story: Digging on the Twin Peaks Tunnel began on December 11, 1914, at three sites, including this western portal near Ulloa Street [1]. It cost lives. In July 1915 inspector Ernest Dunden slipped onto live wires at the west portal and was killed, and in February 1917 a delayed dynamite cap killed several more [1]. In August 1916, 90 feet down, workers found a petrified redwood trunk [1]. On April 5, 1917 came the drillers' shout of 'Holed through!' The two bores met out of line by just an eighth of an inch [1]. Four supervisors raced to be first through the gap, and Joseph Lahaney won with his suit covered in mud. On February 3, 1918, Mayor James Rolph drove the first official streetcar through the 2.27-mile bore himself. It stopped at Laguna Honda (now Forest Hill) station, some 70 feet below ground, and came out here to a huge crowd [1][2][3]. The next Sunday more than 21,000 people rode out just to look. The tunnel opened the west side to settlement [1].

title: Miss Friedman's forty-one years
place: Visitacion Valley Community Center, Raymond Avenue near Bayshore Boulevard
hook: A schoolteacher took charge of a new community centre in 1918 and ran it for 41 years. Local men built its gym by hand.
story: The valley's first school opened in September 1896. After a court session it was decided to keep the Spanish 'Visitacion' in its name, but the new sign arrived reading 'Visitation' [1][2]. One of its early teachers was Florence Friedman. In 1918 she left the classroom to become the first director of the new Visitacion Valley Community Center, and she led it for 41 years until she retired in 1959 [1][2]. Old newspaper clippings reprinted by the neighbourhood paper show how it grew [3]. A friend of the Center donated materials for a gymnasium and men's clubroom, on condition that the valley's men supply the labour. One clipping counted about 6,000 hours of work needed, a quota of eight hours for every man [3]. Architect Dorothy Wormser donated plans for a clubhouse on Raymond Avenue between Alpha Street and San Bruno Avenue, the road now called Bayshore Boulevard. It was to have a gym, an auditorium, a clinic and a domestic science room [3]. Women and girls who had never used a needle took dressmaking and millinery classes there [3]. Friedman lived in the valley until her death in 1984 [2].

title: Praying in masks on Van Ness
place: Site of the second St. Mary's Cathedral, Van Ness Avenue at O'Farrell Street (NW corner)
hook: In the autumn of 1918 San Francisco made masks the law, and worshippers gathered outdoors at the cathedral on Van Ness.
story:
Archbishop Patrick Riordan bought the corner of Van Ness Avenue and O'Farrell Street in 1883. He broke ground in 1885 and dedicated the new St. Mary's Cathedral in January 1891 [1]. Twenty-seven years later it faced a different kind of emergency.

The city's first case of Spanish flu was diagnosed on 23 September 1918 [2]. From 18 October the Board of Health closed theatres, schools and lodge meetings. According to the University of Michigan's influenza archive, it did not close churches but advised that services stop or be held in the open air [3]. A local account says churches were ordered shut, so the sources disagree [2]. From 25 October a city ordinance required everyone in public to wear a mask. On 27 October alone, police arrested 110 people for not wearing one [3].

A photograph from 1918 shows an outdoor service at the cathedral, with some worshippers in influenza masks [2]. By the time the epidemic ended in early 1919, the city had recorded almost 45,000 cases and more than 3,000 deaths [2]. The cathedral burned in 1962 and was replaced by the present cathedral on Cathedral Hill, completed in 1970 [1].

title: Tent City and Influenza, 1918
place: Camp Paul Jones site, Lighthouse Reservation slopes
hook: World War I crammed 13,000 men onto a hilly island built for 500. Then the flu came, and the caskets went out by launch.
story:
When America entered World War I, Yerba Buena Island's training station exploded. It reached a peak of 13,000 men on an island with maybe 150 usable acres [1][2]. Rows of canvas tents on wooden floors spread across the slopes [2]. The Lighthouse Service gave up 1.5 acres of its reservation, where the Navy carved Camp Paul Jones into the hillside. By 1919 it had 806 tents, and a separate detention camp had 384 more [2].

In 1918 influenza swept the Bay Area and the island was quarantined for weeks. A young boat orderly who ferried caskets to San Francisco remembered that "funerals seemed an almost daily occurrence, sometimes with six to nine caskets". The first coffin of the day rode on a field gun and the rest followed on a truck [2]. Every recruit spent three weeks isolated in a hilltop tent camp. A separate camp for meningitis patients stood on the northwest point, next to the cemetery [2]. The crowding convinced the Navy to move training to San Diego. On 31 July 1923 the Goat Island station was officially closed, and only a "receiving ship" stayed behind [1][2].

title: The Tyrrels, Fairmount's first Black family
place: Poole-Bell House, 196-198 Laidley Street at Fairmount Street
hook: Myths about the Laidley Street mansion claim Mary Ellen Pleasant and a trapdoor. The true story is a Guyanese-born City Hall clerk and his family.
story:
For decades the gothic house at Laidley and Fairmount was said to belong to Mary Ellen Pleasant, with a trapdoor for disposing of unwanted guests. Researchers have shown that Pleasant never lived there [1][2]. The house was built for the attorney John P. Poole, dated to 1887 by one researcher. His widow Annie sold it in 1906 to Teresa Bell, who had once shared a mansion with Pleasant [1][2].

In 1918 Bell moved out and rented the house to Bertram and Frances Tyrrel. They were the first African American family in the Glen Park-Fairmount district, and in the 1930 and 1940 censuses they were the only one [3]. Bertram, born in 1867 in Demerara, British Guiana, had served in the US Navy. He was one of 28 workers fired in 1896 when white unions pushed the Palace Hotel to get rid of its Black staff. He later rose from messenger to clerk at the Board of Public Works, an unusual promotion for a Black man then [3]. Frances was the daughter of Black pioneers who had come to California in the 1850s. She was Grand Secretary of her Eastern Star chapter [3]. They rented the house until 1921 and stayed in the district for three decades, finally settling on Chenery Street [3]. Bertram died in 1946 [3].

title: Under the mountain in seven minutes
place: Twin Peaks Tunnel east portal, Market & Castro Streets
hook: From a hole at the top of Market Street, crews dug more than two miles under Twin Peaks, opening up the whole southwest of the city.
story: By 1910, neighbourhood improvement clubs were holding conventions to push for a streetcar tunnel under Twin Peaks. They argued that thousands of acres of empty land on the far side would fill with homes [1]. The city hired Chicago consultant Bion J. Arnold. The property owners who stood to gain agreed to pay through assessment districts, with the undeveloped west side carrying most of the cost [1][2]. Digging began in December 1914, with the eastern end cut open from the top of Market Street near Castro [1][2]. The soft ground there meant the first blocks were built as concrete boxes in an open trench, one box for each track, with a small underground station at Eureka Street [2]. The work was deadly. An inspector was electrocuted in 1915, and several men died when a delayed dynamite charge went off in February 1917 [1]. On February 3, 1918, Mayor James Rolph took the controls of Muni car No. 117 for the first passenger run [2]. Contemporary reports called it the longest streetcar tunnel in the world, about 12,000 feet from end to end [3]. The trip took seven minutes, and new neighbourhoods such as West Portal, Forest Hill and St. Francis Wood grew up at the far end [2][4].

title: Willis Polk's Wall of Glass
place: Hallidie Building, 130 Sutter Street
hook: Decades before glass towers took over downtown, a seven-storey building on Sutter Street hung its whole face in glass.
story: Architect Willis Polk designed a modest seven-storey office block at 130 Sutter Street whose street front was not masonry at all but a sheer sheet of glass hung in front of the structure: a curtain wall [1][2]. It is often called one of the first glass curtain walls in the country, though a 1909 clothing building in Kansas City came earlier, and even the opening year is disputed: guidebooks give 1917 or 1918 [1][2]. The building was named for Andrew Smith Hallidie, the cable car pioneer, and Polk softened the glass with ornate iron fire escapes and sheet-metal cornices [2]. In 1971, when a bank was thinking of replacing it with a much taller tower, the Board of Supervisors made it City Landmark #37, and it was added to the National Register the same year [1][2]. The technique Polk tried here would come to dominate commercial architecture later in the century [1]. A two-year restoration finished in 2013, and the local chapter of the American Institute of Architects now occupies its ground floor [2].

title: Constantinople Cafe and Greek Town's Third Street
place: Greek Town, Third Street between Folsom and Harrison
hook: A century ago the cafes on Third Street were named Smyrna, Athens and Constantinople. This was Greek Town, until a bridge pushed it aside.
story: A city photograph from January 23, 1919, captures a row of Greek businesses on Third Street between Folsom and Harrison: Patris Photo Studio, the Constantinople Cafe, the Acropolis Bar and Grill and Apollo Bros. Cigars. Around 1920 the Athens Restaurant & Oyster House and the Smyrna Cafe stood nearby [1]. Greeks began arriving in San Francisco in the 1880s but came in far greater numbers after 1906, when workers were needed to rebuild the city. The 100 through 400 blocks of Third Street and adjoining side streets were overwhelmingly Greek-owned, according to Jim Lucas of the Greek Historical Society [1]. The Greek consulate sat at Mission and Third, the Greek American Hall at Second and Harrison, and the first Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church at 345 Seventh Street [1]. Community life was not always calm: in July 1908 a quarrel over parish elections and money turned violent at Holy Trinity, and a breakaway faction built its own church on Rincon Hill before the two sides reconciled in December 1909 [2]. Building the Bay Bridge in the 1930s displaced many Greeks, who moved their businesses elsewhere in the city [1][2].

title: Forest Hill's residents take over their suburb
place: Forest Hill Clubhouse (Bernard Maybeck), 381 Magellan Avenue
hook: Fed up with their developer's shoddy streets, Forest Hill's homeowners took over the whole tract in 1918. Then came a clubhouse by Bernard Maybeck.
story: Newell-Murdoch sold Forest Hill as 'sylvan solitude' carved from Sutro's forest. They hired landscape architect Mark Daniels, who gave it a grand staircase on Dewey Boulevard, and advertised every Saturday in the city papers [1]. They also cut down most of the trees they were selling, and they wrote strict rules about the design of homes and the race of the people who could live in them [1]. The first house was finished in February 1914. In October 1912 the company had given the city 21 lots for the Laguna Honda tunnel station, betting on a quick commute [1][2]. When the tunnel opened in 1918, war had stalled sales, and homeowners were fed up with streets and utilities that did not meet city standards. They formed the Forest Hill Association and took over the entire tract from the developer [1]. In 1919 the neighbourhood got a community clubhouse at 381 Magellan, designed by the renowned Bernard Maybeck [1][3]. A 1968 Junior League guide called its high, heavily beamed interior 'Maybeck at his best' [3].

title: The Pilot Who Never Came Back
place: Crissy Field historic airfield buildings, Mason St
hook: Major Dana Crissy took off from the Presidio in a coast-to-coast race in 1919. He died the first day out, and the new airfield took his name.
story: Dana Crissy started out as a Presidio coast artilleryman fascinated by flying. By 1917 he had transferred to the Signal Corps' Aviation Section, and he rose to major and commander of Mather Field in Sacramento [1]. In October 1919 a new airfield at the Presidio hosted the Army's first Transcontinental Reliability and Endurance Test. Sixty-one planes took part, 46 flying west from Long Island and 15 flying east from here [1]. Only nine finished. Crissy and his observer, Sgt. 1st Class V. Thomas, were killed on the first day, trying to land their de Havilland DH-4 near Salt Lake City [1]. Wikipedia gives the date of the crash as October 8 [3]. His friend Col. Henry 'Hap' Arnold asked that the new field be named for him [1]. The Army accepted Crissy Field on June 24, 1921. The 91st Observation Squadron arrived that August [3]. Its pilots watched artillery practice, took aerial photographs and supported the Air Mail, and they flew the first aerial forest-fire patrols in the West [2]. Crissy is buried in the Presidio's national cemetery, in grave 98-5 of the Officers' Section [1].

title: Cowboys on Third Street
place: Butchertown, around Third Street and Evans Avenue
hook: In the 1920s, streetcars on Third Street sometimes had to stop while cowboys drove cattle across the tracks to the slaughterhouses.
story: Well into the 20th century, the Bayview's northern corner was Butchertown, the city's wholesale butchers' reservation since 1868 [1]. Its big slaughterhouses, Miller & Lux, James Allan and Son, H. Moffatt and J. G. Johnson, stood on pilings over Islais Creek so the tides could carry off the offal, and cowboys drove cattle from the railroad stockyards to the killing floors [1]. Riding the No. 16 streetcar down Third Street in the 1920s, Ruth Eshow Upton remembered halting "to let cowboys drive their livestock to the slaughter houses," and never forgot the cattle's bloodshot eyes and sad moans [2]. Neighbours were not always charmed: in 1917 federal health officials ordered the "hog hotels" cleaned out before the Navy would consider moving in [3]. Yet Butchertown was also a close-knit village of French, Italian, Maltese and Irish families who lived side by side, and many kept vegetable gardens, chickens, rabbits and even goats to stretch Depression-era wages [1]. The last slaughterhouse did not close until 1971 [1].

title: Kites, feuds and a fatal shot
place: Bernal Hill, between the Cortland and Precita sides
hook: In 1920 a feud between boys from the north and south sides of the hill grew into gang fights of 300. Then someone was shot.
story:
Bernal lore tells of a rivalry between the north and south sides of the hill. In February 1920 it turned deadly. Police said gang fights between the Cortland Avenue and Precita Avenue crowds, involving as many as 300 men and boys, went on for several days [1]. In one brawl, 20-year-old Louis Coppo of Andover Street was shot dead by 15-year-old James Byne of Rutledge Street [1]. The Chronicle's headline called him a "Boy Bystander" [2].

Fifteen-year-old Philip Ragone of Bessie Street explained it to the Chronicle: "These boys always come on our side of the hill and break our kites and spoil our games. The feud among us has been going on three years" [1]. The city sent a special squad of uniformed officers "instructed to use their clubs freely." Some residents asked for something else: a clubhouse and outdoor sports for the hill's young people [1]. That June, residents met to found the Bernal Community Council. By July it had won the neighbourhood a health centre [2].

title: A Palace Poured Over the Paupers
place: California Palace of the Legion of Honor, 100 34th Ave
hook: When the cornerstone of the Legion went down in 1921, the cemetery beneath it turned out not to have gone anywhere.
story: On February 19, 1921, with Mayor James Rolph as master of ceremonies, the cornerstone was laid for Alma and Adolph Spreckels' copy of the French pavilion from the 1915 exposition [1]. The site was spectacular, a bluff above the Golden Gate. It was also the old City Cemetery, which the city had ordered emptied into Colma in 1909 [2]. Hundreds of burials came up during construction [2]. 'The workers were uncovering a couple dozen coffins a day right where the museum was going to go,' said retired park ranger John Martini. He recalled an exposé at the time: the dead were bulldozed aside into a mass grave, and people picked through exposed graves for jewelry [3]. Architect George Applegarth built with the latest ideas: 21-inch hollow-tile walls to hold an even temperature, and 7,000 cubic yards of concrete [1][4]. The past came up again in the 1990s. Excavation for a new underground wing found hundreds more graves, about 780 by one count, and more are likely still buried beneath the museum [2][3].

title: A home when the YWCA said no
place: Madame C.J. Walker Home for Girls, 2066 Pine St
hook: Barred from the YWCA, Black women arriving in San Francisco found rooms, jobs and a Christmas street party at an Italianate house on Pine Street.
story:
In 1921 this Italianate house of 1878-79 on Pine Street became the Madame C.J. Walker Home for Girls. It was named after the cosmetics entrepreneur often described as the first African American woman to become a millionaire [1][2]. The home was opened by Irene Bell Ruggles, president of the California State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs, with financial support from Third Baptist Church [2].

It met a real need. Black women new to the city were not eligible to use the YWCA's services, and although the Chinese and Japanese communities had their own YWCA branches by the 1910s, there was no branch for Black women in San Francisco [1][2]. "There being no colored YWCA in the city," an account from around 1920 said, "the Home must perform to some extent the duties of a 'Y'" [1]. Single women found lodgings and job referrals here. The social hall and large kitchen, with a basement hall added in 1926, hosted community gatherings [1][2]. Every Christmas "the block is roped off so that the children may safely enjoy the games dancing and music" [1].

The home ran until 1972 and became city Landmark No. 211 in 1999 [2].

title: An orphanage of cottages on Ocean Avenue
place: Site of Homewood Terrace, north side of Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone
hook: San Francisco's Jewish orphanage left its big Divisadero Street asylum for a village of cottages at the edge of Sutro's forest.
story: The Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum and Home Society was founded in 1872, when, in its own words, the city's Jewish community took up 'its historic obligation to provide shelter and care for children who knew the tragedy of parent loss'. From 1876 it ran a large home at 600 Divisadero Street [1]. Under Dr. Samuel Langer it tried a different approach. On October 3, 1920, the asylum's Anspacher Band played at the dedication of a new campus on Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone, and on June 13, 1921 the children moved in [1]. Renamed Homewood Terrace, it housed children in small cottages rather than a single institution. The organisation later claimed these were the first cottage-style child-care facilities in the United States [1]. An aerial photograph shows the campus beside Sutro's forest [1]. During the Second World War it took in children brought from the Holocaust in Europe. In 1965 it moved the children to family-style homes in the Richmond District, and houses and shops now cover the Ocean Avenue site [1][2].

title: Filipino Seamen Buy a House on South Park
place: Gran Oriente Filipino Hotel, 106 South Park
hook: Barred from buying property directly, Filipino sailors joined the Freemasons, and with $6,000 bought a home that still shelters their community.
story: South Park's oval, once ringed by wealthy families who later decamped to Nob Hill, had become a working neighbourhood by the early twentieth century [2]. It was one of the city's largest Japanese American enclaves, with Japanese-run hostels, hotels, baths and shops sandwiched between the waterfront and the railroad terminus; the Madrid Hotel at 22 South Park was once the Eimoto Hotel [2]. After the 1906 fire the blocks were rebuilt with warehouses, workshops and hotels, drawing longshoremen and immigrants from many countries [2]. In 1921 a group of Filipino immigrants working as seamen and merchant mariners bought a three-storey house on the park and named it the Gran Oriente Filipino Hotel, after a fraternity in the Philippines [1]. Because Filipinos were not allowed to buy property directly, a couple of dozen men joined the Freemasons and formed their own chapter so it could hold the title [1]. The 24-room hotel became a meeting place for Filipinos working in the city and the Central Valley, and the group later bought an apartment building and a lodge nearby [1]. Bought with a $6,000 investment, the property was later worth millions, but by the late 1990s the fraternity still refused to sell, and elderly Filipino men, many of them World War II veterans, still lived there in low-cost rooms [1].

title: From Nickel Rides to Playland
place: Chutes at the Beach / Playland site, Great Highway between Balboa and Fulton
hook: A carousel, a candy stand and a water chute grew into Playland at the Beach, taken over by two brothers who had learned showmanship in Melbourne.
story: In 1883 the Park and Ocean Railroad began bringing nickel-fare crowds to a terminus near today's La Playa and Balboa, where waffle stands, shooting galleries and carnival games soon gathered [1]. In the 1910s Charles Looff installed a carousel, and candy-stand operator John Friedle teamed up with Looff's son Arthur to build a real amusement park [1]. Sources differ on dates: the Western Neighborhoods Project says Chutes at the Beach opened in 1921 with the Big Dipper coaster following in 1922, while FoundSF puts the carousel building at 1912 and both rides at 1922 [1][2]. Admission was free [1]. Among the concessionaires was George K. Whitney, who with his brother Leo had run a shooting gallery in Melbourne, Australia, during World War I and developed a quick-finish photo process [3]. George opened a shooting gallery at the Chutes in the early 1920s and began buying up other leases [1][3]. In 1928 the Whitney brothers bought much of Friedle's investment and renamed the park Playland at the Beach [1]. 'Playland is a nickel and dime business,' George liked to say [3].

title: German spoken at the Tell House
place: Sickles Avenue beside the old Ocean View station (site of the Tell House, demolished for I-280)
hook: Beside the Ocean View tracks stood a boarding house and bar where German was spoken and some lodgers had served in the Kaiser's army.
story: The Tell House stood on Sickles Avenue next to the Ocean View railroad station. It served both as a place to worship and as a place to drink [1][2]. According to Marsha Fontes's history of Ocean View, Catholics heard Mass upstairs over the Tell House bar every Sunday from 1872 until a small church, St. Michael's, was built on Broad Street in 1899 [2]. In the 1920s, Ray Muther told historians in 2008, it was a 'cupping house', meaning a place to drink, and a boarding house for Swiss and German immigrants [1]. German was the house language, and some of the lodgers had served in the Kaiser's army. The bar and dining room opened on weekends [1]. Muther's relative Theodore Houser bought the building in 1921, and Muther's father lived there in 1928 [1]. The house was believed to have been a stage-wagon stop. A back room with stained-glass windows may once have been the waiting room [1]. The Tell House was demolished along with Wolfe's and the Diamond Saloon when Interstate 280 came through [1].

title: Miss Hodgens' Prize Dahlias
place: 26th Avenue at Lake Street (Sea Cliff Dahlia Gardens)
hook: While Sea Cliff's lots were still waiting for houses, a woman on 26th Avenue was breeding dahlias as big as dinner plates and winning prizes across California.
story: In the early 1920s Miss Aimee Hodgens ran the Sea Cliff Dahlia Gardens on Twenty-sixth Avenue, "between Lake and California Sts.", as her 1921 catalogue put it. Later catalogues simply said "at Lake Street" [1][3]. She sold tubers by mail and guaranteed every one "true to name". Her growing advice suited the neighbourhood's dune soil: lay the tuber nearly flat and cover it with six inches of sandy earth [1]. She also bred her own varieties. The 1921 catalogue opens with Priscilla, "an immense white shading to pink" that "attracted great attention" at every show, and it lists her Haida and Glorianna [1]. By 1923 she was also selling a canary-yellow dahlia named Suffragette and Elena Eyre, which had taken the top award at the Dahlia Society of California's trial gardens in Berkeley. She had also won a specially designed cup for six English cactus blooms [2]. Her 1925 catalogue listed a long run of prizes from shows in 1924, among them "Best Dahlia in the Show" and "Largest Dahlia in the Show" [3].

title: One Church for Nine Congregations
place: 1345 Ocean Ave (Ingleside Presbyterian Church)
hook: The builder of Ingleside Terraces designed a church for every Protestant faith on Ocean Avenue, and its director chose a boys' gym over a pipe organ.
story: The congregation that became Ingleside Presbyterian was organised in 1907 [3], and it began as a Sunday school for earthquake refugees in the basement of the Robinson Apartments at Faxon and DeMontfort avenues [1]. After its wood-framed church burned in 1920, Joseph A. Leonard, developer of Ingleside Terraces across Ocean Avenue, donated land and designed and built the 'Ingleside Community Church' at 1345 Ocean, intended to house all the area's Protestant denominations [1][2]. Ground was broken on September 16, 1921. The Western Neighborhoods Project says it was completed in 1923 at a cost of $65,000; other accounts date the building to 1922 [2][3]. It hosted nine congregations, including Methodists, Baptists, Episcopalians and Presbyterians [2]. When funds ran short, a newspaper reported, religious director Rev. Albert E. Kelly had to choose between gymnasium equipment and a pipe organ, and 'yielded to the little fellows,' who got their parallel bars, Indian clubs, dumbbells and rings [2]. The gym mattered again decades later: Rev. Roland Gordon took the pastorate in 1978 partly because of it, and covered its walls with images of African American achievers [2][3]. The church became a city landmark in 2016 [3].

title: The 'Gaudí' that Gaudí never designed
place: Chambord Apartments, 1298 Sacramento Street at Jones
hook: People have long credited this billowing, wedding-cake apartment house to Barcelona's Antoni Gaudí. In fact it was designed by a San Francisco architect.
story: Built in 1921 at Sacramento and Jones, the Chambord is a five-story apartment house of poured concrete. Its balconies bulge outward, following the oval living rooms inside [1]. The building's National Register nomination compares it to a wedding cake, and the city's landmarks board called it "a first-rate architectural enigma which intrigues the casual passer-by and confounds the architectural historian" [1][2]. It has often been attributed to Antoni Gaudí. The real designer was James Francis Dunn, a San Francisco architect with a taste for Art Nouveau [1][3]. The developer, James Witt Dougherty, was the grandson of an Alameda County pioneer landholder. He moved into the top-floor unit with his parents, and other family members took several of the apartments below [1]. That top floor was originally one apartment arranged around an open, octagonal garden room [1]. In 1926 the building was sold to Herbert E. Law, who also owned the Fairmont Hotel, and that year the garden room was walled in [1]. The city's landmark report suggests the Chambord may have set off the 1920s wave of luxury apartment houses nearby [2]. Its ornament was stripped in the 1960s and recreated in a 1982–83 restoration [1].

title: The farm family's drugstore library
place: Visitacion Valley Pharmacy, 100 Leland Avenue
hook: The Rossis went from vegetable farmers to druggists. For years their Leland Avenue pharmacy shelf was the valley's only library.
story: Members of the Rossi family came to the valley just after the Civil War, and John Rossi joined them in 1880 [2]. By hand labour they turned their acres into large vegetable gardens, and later hired farmhands [2]. Their land was part of the first section of the valley divided into house lots in the early 1900s [1][2]. Then the family moved into shopkeeping. Building permits show the Rossi brothers owned the two-story drugstore-and-residence at 100 Leland Avenue by 1921. That year they had it jacked up to pour a new concrete foundation [1]. Sales records show Virginio and Theodore Rossi buying the property in November 1924 [1]. Virginio ran the Visitacion Valley Pharmacy until 1970, when his daughter took over [1][2]. The family owned and ran it for more than 70 years [1]. Long before the valley had a branch library, oral historians Mary Leotta Schwartz, Anna Stuart Johnson and Viola Cuccaro Rusca remembered a bookshelf in the pharmacy. People borrowed books and put them back when they were done, with no card and no fines [1]. The shop has changed owners, but it still sells medicine under the same name [1].

title: A Department Store Takes to the Air
place: Hale Brothers Department Store, 901 Market Street at Fifth
hook: In 1922 a Navy radio man talked the Hale brothers into putting a transmitter in their Market Street store. It grew into one of the West's great stations.
story: In 1921 Joe Martineau came home from Navy radio work and pitched an idea to Francis, Marshall and Reuben Hale, owners of the Hale Brothers department store at Fifth and Market: let him run an experimental broadcast transmitter in the store [1]. Built for just $2,400, KPO went on the air at 9 a.m. on April 17, 1922 [1][2]. At first it was a one-room, one-man operation on the sixth floor, with a piano, a phonograph and a "home-brew" transmitter. It broadcast one hour a day, and commercials were not allowed; programs, Reuben Hale recalled, had to suit "a mother with children in the home" [1]. The Hales soon saw radio's publicity value. In 1923 they spent $60,000 on a 500-watt station with a pipe organ and two 125-foot steel towers on the store's roof [1]. That summer KPO set up to carry President Harding's San Francisco speech in what was to be the first coast-to-coast broadcast, but Harding fell ill and died at the Palace Hotel before it aired [1]. The Chronicle bought half of KPO in 1925, it joined NBC in 1927, and it survives today as KNBR [2].

title: A home for the chief who never returned
place: Dennis T. Sullivan Memorial Fire Chief's Home, 870 Bush Street
hook: The 1906 earthquake sent a hotel's dome crashing through the fire chief's bedroom. As San Francisco burned for three days, its firefighters fought on without him.
story: On the morning of April 18, 1906, Chief Engineer Dennis T. Sullivan of the San Francisco Fire Department was at his quarters at 410 Bush Street. When the earthquake struck, brick chimneys and the dome of the neighbouring California Hotel crashed down through the firehouse [1]. Battalion Chief Walter Cook reported that the roof and upper floors fell right through to the cellar. As rescuers dug, a broken radiator sprayed Sullivan with steam and scalding water. He managed to walk out of the rubble and was rushed to hospital with a fractured skull and broken ribs. His wife Margaret was pulled out and taken into the hotel, where a doctor treated her. Sullivan lingered for four days and died at the Presidio's Army hospital [1]. A marker outside notes that his firefighters, left leaderless, fought the flames for three days and nights [2]. In 1922 the city finished a new official residence for its fire chiefs at 870 Bush Street, designed by John Reid Jr. It has ground-floor doors for fire vehicles and was named for Sullivan [3]. It has gone on housing the city's chiefs, and it is San Francisco Landmark No. 42 [1][3].

title: Driving onto the bay
place: Hyde Street Pier, 2905 Hyde St
hook: Before any bridge crossed the bay, drivers queued down Hyde Street to roll their cars onto ferries bound for Sausalito and Berkeley.
story: In the 1920s, driving to Marin or the East Bay meant taking a boat. The Golden Gate Ferry Company, incorporated in 1920, built a single ferry slip at the foot of Hyde Street, and the first auto ferry left for Sausalito on May 28, 1922 [1][2]. Demand kept growing. In 1927 the pier was extended several hundred feet and two more slips were added for a new Berkeley run, whose first boat sailed on June 16, 1927 [1]. The pier became part of U.S. Routes 101 and 40, so the highway, in effect, ran across the water [2]. The ferry company then joined forces with Southern Pacific's ferries. The National Park Service dates the merger to 1928, while other accounts give early 1929 [1][2]. The bridges ended it. The Bay Bridge opened in 1936 and the Golden Gate Bridge in 1937, ridership collapsed, and the last ferry left Hyde Street on July 25, 1938 [1]. The pier's later life began in the 1950s, when it was turned into a berth for historic ships. It is now the heart of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park [1].

title: Eight turns down a 27 percent hill
place: Lombard St between Hyde and Leavenworth
hook: The 'crookedest street in the world' was not built for tourists. Neighbours who wanted to drive home to a hill too steep for their new cars came up with it.
story: The block of Lombard Street between Hyde and Leavenworth began as a straight cobblestone street with a 27 percent grade [1]. By the 1920s the people who lived there wanted cars, but the hill was too steep for them. Because no car could reach the lots, they were worth less than those on neighbouring streets [1]. Carl Henry, an insurance and drug-company executive, is credited with first suggesting a curved roadway. He owned half the lots on the 1000 block and had planted a lily pond and rose gardens that he hoped to give to the city as a park. That plan failed after his death, when his widow sold the land to pay debts [1]. The owners took the idea to city engineer Clyde Healy, who designed the switchbacks [1]. The winding street was built in 1922 [2]. It was not the first such proposal. In 1905 engineer William Barclay Parsons had suggested turning the California Street hill into a winding driveway [1][2]. Lombard's version, with eight hairpin bends [3], is the one that got built.

title: Julia Morgan's Women's Residence, Then a Zen Temple
place: 300 Page Street, at Laguna
hook: Julia Morgan designed this brick residence for single Jewish working women. In 1969 it became the home of San Francisco Zen Center.
story: Women of Temple Emanu-El founded the Emanu-El Sisterhood for Personal Service in 1894. Rather than handing out money, they gave Eastern European Jewish immigrants food, education, training and help finding work [1]. From 1912 the Sisterhood rented houses for single women [2]. It then commissioned Julia Morgan, working with Dorothy Wormser, to design a permanent residence at Page and Laguna, which was finished in 1922 [1]. The brick building housed up to 60 women [1]. Its residents over the years included German women fleeing Europe in the 1930s and '40s, and in 1942-43 nearly all of them were war workers [1][2]. The Sisterhood also offered counselling, childcare and classes in its Institute for Practical Arts [2]. Renamed the Emanu-el Residence Club in 1955, it gradually lost residents, and in 1969 the board voted to close it [2]. That same year San Francisco Zen Center bought the building, and Shunryu Suzuki Roshi founded City Center there as a Soto Zen training centre open to the public [1][3]. It was the Zen community's second Jewish home. Suzuki's congregation, Sokoji, met in the former Bush Street synagogue that Congregation Ohabai Shalome built in 1895 [1][2].

title: Julia Morgan's house for the Molokans
place: Potrero Hill Neighborhood House, 953 De Haro Street
hook: It started when a pastor helped an injured shipyard worker. The result was a Julia Morgan community house at the top of De Haro Street that even got moved.
story: At first the Molokans of Potrero Hill kept to themselves. According to local historians Peter Linenthal and Abigail Johnston, things changed after a Molokan was hurt in an accident at Union Iron Works. Dr. William Parker, a lawyer and pastor of Olivet Presbyterian Church on Missouri Street, helped him get help from his employer [1]. After that the church ran Sunday school, a children's choir, and English and citizenship classes [1]. The small rented rooms soon filled up. In 1919 the Presbyterian Church, through a women's group called the California Synodical Society of Home Missions, hired architect Julia Morgan to design a permanent centre [2][3]. Her single-storey Arts and Crafts building at the top of De Haro Street opened on June 11, 1922. It had a lobby with a fireplace, an assembly hall, clubrooms, a kindergarten and a gym [3]. The Molokani learned English, machine sewing and other skills there [2]. Only two years later the building was moved to make way for the new diagonal Southern Heights Avenue. One account says it was shifted 90 feet, another that it was turned 90 degrees [3][4]. "The Nabe" became a city landmark in 1977 and still serves the hill [2][3].

title: Night school, six alarms, a human guideline
place: Mission High School, 3750 18th Street
hook: More than a thousand night students were in class when embers from a faulty flue set Mission High's roof alight in January 1922.
story: On the evening of Thursday, January 19, 1922, more than 1,000 students and teachers were at Mission High School for the Humboldt Evening High School night classes. Live embers from a faulty flue landed on the roof and set it alight [1]. When the lights failed, the principal and teachers formed a human 'guide line' to lead students out in the dark. Students left carrying typewriters, adding machines and lab specimens, and firemen had to stop some from going back in for more [1]. Two students trapped on the third floor were brought down by ladder [1]. The only serious injury was to Captain E. R. Doherty of Engine Company No. 11, who fell from a ladder and broke his leg. Boy Scouts linked arms to hold back the crowds and later received 'Fire Scout' badges from the fire chief [1]. Classes moved to Lowell High, to army tents and to temporary buildings in Mission Park across the street [1]. City Architect John Reid Jr. designed a new school in the ornate Spanish Baroque style known as Churrigueresque, with a 127-foot tower, and Mayor Rolph dedicated it on June 12, 1927 [1][2].

title: St. Paul of the Shipwreck, a Maltese home
place: Former St. Paul of the Shipwreck Church, 1515 Oakdale Ave
hook: By 1920 San Francisco had the fourth-largest Maltese community in America, and its heart was an old hall on Oakdale Avenue named for a shipwreck.
story: Few San Franciscans know that the Bayview was once a Mediterranean island's outpost. Maltese men came first, often for railroad work, then sent for their families; they settled among the slaughterhouses of Butchertown [1]. By 1920 San Francisco had the fourth-largest Maltese population in the United States [1], living side by side with French, Italian and Irish neighbours [2]. In 1914 the community welcomed the Reverend Andrew Azzopardi, who organised California's first Maltese Catholic parish. In 1915 the archbishop gave the congregation an 1874 hall at what is now 1515 Oakdale Avenue, and in 1922 it was consecrated as St. Paul of the Shipwreck, after the New Testament story of the apostle's shipwreck on Malta [1]. By the late 1920s the city's Maltese numbered an estimated 5,000. When the Maltese Club opened at 1789 Oakdale in 1930, crowds had to be turned away; it staged plays in Maltese and kept a traditional band [1]. In the late 1950s the congregation built a new St. Paul of the Shipwreck in the Bret Harte neighbourhood, and the old hall became Bayview Baptist Church [1].

title: The Church Pushed Uphill in Halves
place: Church of the Epiphany, Naples Street and Amazon Avenue
hook: When their little wooden church got too small, Excelsior parishioners cut it in two and rolled it up the hill on logs and barrels.
story: By 1911 there were enough German, Irish and Italian families in the Excelsior and Crocker-Amazon to need a church of their own; until then they had to walk to St. John's or St. Michael's for Mass. On January 21 that year Archbishop Patrick Riordan dedicated a wood-frame, shingle-roofed mission church, the Church of the Epiphany, at the southwest corner of Russia Avenue and Paris Street. It seated about 300 [1]. Accounts put the cost, lots included, at about $18,600 [1][2]. It became a parish in 1914. In 1922 the parish boundaries were redrawn, and the new pastor, Irish-born Father Patrick Ryan, faced a congregation too big for the building [1]. The archdiocese bought a whole block bounded by Naples, Vienna, Amazon and Italy for $24,011. Rather than build new, the parish sawed the old church in half. The two halves were set on logs and barrels, pushed up Russia Avenue and placed twenty-three feet apart on Naples Street, and new construction joined them. The enlarged church seated 480 [1][2]. The old building was moved once more, on rollers, when the present church was built (sources give 1950 or 1952), and ended its life as the parish gym [1].

title: The Excelsior Gets a Picture Palace
place: Excelsior (later Granada) Theatre, 4631 Mission Street
hook: In 1922 the Excelsior got its own movie house, named after the district. Nine years later it got a new name and a Spanish tower.
story: By the early 1920s the Excelsior was big enough to want its own movie palace. The Excelsior Amusement Company hired the architect G. Albert Lansburgh, and his plans appeared in Building and Engineering News in 1921 [1]. The theatre opened in 1922 at 4631 Mission Street, near Ocean Avenue, as the Excelsior [1][2]. It was not the only screen on the street. The Bell Theatre stood near Mission and Leo, and that same year it was a temporary church. The congregation of the Ocean Avenue Presbyterian Church worshipped there for three months while its new building, designed by Julia Morgan, was being finished [3]. In 1931 the Excelsior was renamed the Granada and given a $150,000 remodel with a tall Spanish-style tower. About a decade later it was remodelled again in sleek Streamline Moderne [2]. It closed in 1982 and is now a Goodwill store. Neighbourhood advocates want to put up a new vertical sign that says 'Excelsior' again [1][2].

title: The Marshal's Golden Shovel
place: Joffre and Foch cypresses, east side of the Legion of Honor
hook: On a rainy April day in 1922 the hero of the Marne dug into a building site on a former graveyard and planted a tree that still stands.
story: While the Legion of Honor was still a construction site, Alma Spreckels brought France's great generals to see it. First came Supreme Allied Commander Ferdinand Foch, and a few months later Marshal Joseph Joffre [1]. Joffre arrived on a state visit on April 7, 1922. In a rainy ceremony in Lincoln Park he was handed a gold shovel and planted a cypress by the construction site [2]. The city had never welcomed foreign figures so lavishly. Receptions and parades for the two marshals were the most elaborate it had ever staged for political visitors [3]. Each man planted a Monterey cypress. The trees and their plaques still stand on the east side of the palace [3]. The ties went further. Joffre later gave the museum the uniform he had worn at the Battle of the Marne, the turning point of 1914 [2]. Joffre and Foch, with Pétain, also signed Alma's Book of Gold of California's war dead when she took it to Paris [4]. Not everyone saw heroes. A FoundSF essayist argues that the war discredited 'the Fochs and Joffres who had the blood of millions on their hands' [1].

title: The Nassers' movie palace on Castro Street
place: Castro Theatre, 429 Castro Street
hook: In 1922 the Nasser family opened a Spanish Baroque movie palace by Timothy Pflueger, a few doors up from Castro Street's first little theatre.
story: The first Castro Theatre opened in 1910 in a modest building at 479 Castro Street, a few doors down the hill [1][2]. The Nasser family, descended from Lebanese immigrants, would become San Francisco's oldest movie-business family [2][3]. In the early 1920s they built something far grander. The new Castro opened on June 22, 1922, with an invitation-only screening of Paramount's Across the Continent, starring Wallace Reid, with Mayor James Rolph in the audience. The public came in the next day [1]. Its architect was Timothy L. Pflueger, and the city's landmark report calls it one of his major works and the first and finest big theatre the Nassers built [3]. California theatre builders of the 1920s loved the Spanish Colonial style, and the Castro was among the most ornate neighbourhood houses in the city [3]. The Art Deco marquee was added in 1937 [1]. Remarkably, apart from moving the screen for CinemaScope, the theatre was left almost unaltered, which the report calls 'a very rare phenomenon in the movie business' [3]. The old 1910 theatre became a shop and, since 1971, Cliff's Variety [1].

title: The Tanker That Old Sailors Took Over
place: Lyman Stewart wreck site, beside Helmet Rock below Lands End
hook: Rammed in the fog, an oil tanker was run onto the Lands End rocks. Then homeless old sailors moved aboard and sang shanties to passing streetcars.
story: On October 7, 1922, the Union Oil tanker Lyman Stewart was heading out through the Golden Gate in thickening fog and a strong current. The freighter Walter A. Luckenbach was coming in. Muffled horns warned neither ship in time [1]. The Luckenbach cut deep into the tanker's port bow. Captain Cloyd ordered his crew into the boats and stayed aboard to steer the sinking ship ashore. She tore her hull on the rocks of Lands End and stuck fast despite every salvage effort [1]. The hulk sat a few feet offshore and became a magnet for sightseers. Adventurous visitors waded out at low tide [2]. Just before Christmas 1923 the Chronicle reported that aging merchant sailors had taken over the abandoned ship. Hikers and passengers on the #1 streetcar could hear sea shanties drifting from the rusting hull [2]. The waves slowly broke her in two [1]. In 1937 her sister ship Frank H. Buck, also built at Union Iron Works, was wrecked in another fog collision and came to rest beside her [3]. At low tide the Stewart's engine block still shows in the surf just west of Helmet Rock [2].

title: The women who won back Glen Canyon
place: Glen Canyon Park Recreation Center, 70 Elk Street
hook: After the zoo closed, Glen Canyon became a private, bookings-only picnic ground. It took residents more than ten years of campaigning to get it back.
story:
When the zoo era ended, the Crocker Estate Company kept the south end of the canyon as a private picnic ground. People booked it by the week, and it had a baseball diamond and a dance hall locals called the Red Barn [1]. In the 1910s the National Guard even used the canyon for sham battles and set up a rifle range [1].

The Glen Park Improvement Association and, from 1908 to 1917, the women of the Glen Park Outdoor Art League campaigned for more than a decade to make it public again [2]. The city finally paid $10,000 a year from 1919 to 1921 and opened the Glen Park Playground in 1922 [2]. Carrie Bauer of Mizpah Street was the League's last president and fought hard for the deal. According to her descendants, when she died in 1932 her funeral procession drove once around the playground before heading to the cemetery [2].

The Red Barn burned down in 1932. WPA workers finished the present recreation center in 1938, designed by William G. Merchant, a protégé of Bernard Maybeck [1]. Up the canyon, Islais Creek still runs above ground through willow thickets, one of the last open creeks in the city [3].

title: A Lifesavers' House Moves to Cabrillo Street
place: 47th Ave and Cabrillo St
hook: The surfmen's motto was 'You have to go out. You don't have to come back.' One of their Victorian station buildings still stands as a Richmond house.
story: California's first lifesaving station opened in 1878 at Fulton Street and Great Highway, run by the U.S. Lifesaving Service. Its surfmen lived on site, ready to rescue crews from ships wrecked on Ocean Beach or the cliffs of Lands End. Their unofficial motto was grim: 'You have to go out. You don't have to come back' [1]. Crowds gathered to watch them drill. They fired lifelines from a small cannon to a fake ship's mast set in the sand, or rowed self-righting surfboats out past Seal Rocks, after horses hauled the boats across Great Highway on wheeled carts [1]. In 1914 the station became part of the new U.S. Coast Guard. In the 1920s the Coast Guard began replacing its aging Victorian buildings [1]. A former lifesaver, Carvel Torlakson, bought one of the 1870s buildings from the government for $75, moved it to a vacant lot at 47th Avenue and Cabrillo Street, set it on a new foundation and moved in [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project dates the move to 1923 [2]. When John Martini wrote about it in 2015, it was still there [1].

title: A Prodigy's House on Steiner Street
place: Menuhin family home, 1043 Steiner St
hook: A Hebrew teacher bought a hillside house with a double parlor that could seat sixty. His seven-year-old son, Yehudi, was about to astonish the concert world.
story: Moshe and Marutha Menuhin were Russian Jewish immigrants. They brought their son Yehudi to San Francisco when he was nine months old [1]. Moshe taught Hebrew and went on to run the Jewish Education Society [1][2]. He was also for a time principal of the Central Hebrew School at Grove and Buchanan, which hundreds of neighborhood children attended [3]. Yehudi began violin at five with Sigmund Anker, a teacher of young children. He then studied with Louis Persinger, concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony, and gave his first professional concert around 1923 at the Oakland Auditorium [1]. That autumn the family left 732 Hayes Street for a two-story wooden house at 1043 Steiner. Its double living room, divided by sliding doors, could seat about sixty guests for informal concerts, and there was a small practice room off the kitchen [4]. Moshe covered the $50-a-month mortgage partly by renting out garage spaces and upstairs rooms [4]. The children, Yehudi and his sisters Hephzibah and Yaltah, were taught at home [1]. Hephzibah, a gifted pianist, had been born in San Francisco in 1920 [2]. In 1927, at age ten, Yehudi played his Carnegie Hall debut and became a star overnight [1].

title: A car ad on the mountaintop
place: North-west face of Bernal Hill
hook: Before the Hollywood sign, Bernal Hill wore giant letters spelling MAXWELL, with real cars parked on the summit.
story:
In July 1923 aerial photographs caught a marketing stunt on Bernal Hill. Huge letters spelling MAXWELL were laid across the north-west face, and cars were parked on the summit to show off the car's climbing ability [1][3]. Terry Milne of the Bernal Heights History Project points out that this was the same year the "Hollywoodland" sign went up above Los Angeles [1]. Bernalwood noticed two "insane tilt-up automobile silhouettes" at the top as well [2].

The photos also show a hill still half wild. Grassland and dirt roads cover the slopes, many streets are not yet graded, and there is no road around the top yet. The north and south sides were still cut off from each other [1]. Below lay Bernal Park with its acacias, the old LeConte school of 1912 at Alabama and Norwich, and cleared ground for the new school built in 1924-25 [1]. The brand soon vanished: Maxwell was absorbed by Chrysler and dropped in 1925, which Bernalwood uses to date one aerial view to about 1924 [2]. The hill's two quarry scars on the south side are visible too [2].

title: A castle on the cliff edge
place: Julius' Castle, 302 Greenwich St
hook: An Italian restaurateur built himself a castle on a Telegraph Hill precipice, and then needed a turntable to turn his customers' cars around.
story: Building permit No. 114873, dated March 20, 1923, started one of San Francisco's oddest buildings. Julius Roz, an Italian restaurateur who had come to San Francisco in 1898, began a castle on a ledge of Telegraph Hill at the dead end of Montgomery Street [1][2]. The lot had held a grocery and then a family home that burned around 1918 [1]. Architect Louis (Luigi) Mastropasqua designed pointed arched windows and battlements in a mix of Gothic Revival and Arts and Crafts. It was a tribute to Layman's wooden castle, which had stood on the hill from 1882 to 1903 [1][2]. Roz is said to have bought the interior panelling from the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition. Food was being served by 1924 [1]. Montgomery Street was then barely a one-car dirt track, so in 1931 a turntable was installed at the dead end, and an employee spun cars around and parked them [1]. During Prohibition it was a speakeasy for well-off customers. From its windows diners watched the Bay Bridge rise, Treasure Island being dredged up from the bay for the 1939 fair, and the wartime fleet coming and going [1].

title: Everything Under the Sun at Eighth and Market
place: Crystal Palace Market site, Eighth and Market streets
hook: Sixty-five shops, a snake-handling soap salesman, a weeping horseradish man: for 36 years the Crystal Palace Market was San Francisco's giant indoor bazaar.
story: The four-acre lot at Eighth and Market had already hosted a mechanics' pavilion, a baseball park, a theater and, after 1906, the circus [1]. In 1922 brothers Oliver and Arthur Rosseau bought it, and in 1923 they opened the Crystal Palace Market, a steel-framed, skylit bazaar named for London's famous glass hall [1][2]. The gamble was that one huge market could replace the corner grocery. Its 65 shops included six butchers, three fish markets, four dairy stands selling 36,000 eggs a day, a pet shop, a record store and a stall that sold only honey. Three hundred people worked there, and shoppers could enter from 22 doors on five streets [1]. Clerks hollered over strolling minstrels and an organ grinder with his monkey. The Horseradish Man wept as he grated, and soap salesman Fred Wiedeman let snakes crawl over him before washing himself clean [1]. Novelist Gus Lee called it "the FAO Schwarz of the stomach" [1]. But families moved to the suburbs, and in August 1959 the market closed, to be demolished for Del Webb's 400-room TowneHouse motel [1][2].

title: Japanese America's newspaper on Ellis Street
place: 650 Ellis Street (Nichi Bei Shimbun offices, 1923-1937)
hook: From a plain apartment block on Ellis Street, an immigrant publisher reached 25,000 readers across the West and urged a generation to put down roots.
story: From 1923 to 1937, an influential Japanese-language newspaper was published from 650 Ellis Street, a 1916 apartment building with a stucco front [1]. It was the Nichi Bei Shimbun, run by Kyutaro Abiko [1][2]. Abiko was born in Niigata in 1865, arrived in San Francisco in 1885, and worked menial jobs while he studied, eventually attending UC Berkeley [2]. In 1899 he merged two small papers into the Nichi Bei. By 1910 it was the leading Japanese American paper, and by the 1920s it had San Francisco and Los Angeles editions and about 25,000 readers across the West [2]. Abiko used its pages to urge Issei laborers to settle permanently and raise families in America. He even bought land in Livingston, California, and founded the Yamato Colony for Japanese farmers [2]. After the 1924 Immigration Act shut out new Japanese immigrants, he turned toward the American-born Nisei. He added an English-language section and sponsored study tours to Japan [2]. Abiko died in 1936, and his widow Yona ran the paper until the forced removal of Japanese Americans closed it in 1942 [2].

title: Julia Morgan's church on Leland
place: St. James Presbyterian Church, 240 Leland Avenue
hook: A Sunday school started the year of the great fire. By 1923 its congregation worshipped in a church by Julia Morgan.
story: St. James Presbyterian Church began as a Sunday school in 1906, the year of the earthquake and fire [1]. Displaced San Franciscans were then pouring into the valley [2]. By 1908 the congregation had formed with 69 original members [1]. Their first church on Leland Avenue dated from 1906 [2][3]. In 1923 it was replaced by a new building designed by the celebrated architect Julia Morgan [1][2]. She drew another Presbyterian church on Ocean Avenue around the same time [1]. Its most eye-catching feature was not Morgan's idea. A stained glass window, showing a figure sowing a field apparently among palm trees, is said to have come from a church in the Sierra foothills after the building went up. Heritage treats this as a story rather than proven fact [1]. The church also had a gymnasium where valley youngsters played basketball [3]. In 2021 the valley still had no designated city landmarks. SF Heritage listed St. James as one of three obvious candidates, noting that 'just about anything' by Morgan is landmark-worthy [1].

title: The Easter crosses that kept burning down
place: Summit of Mount Davidson, site of the Easter sunrise crosses
hook: Five thousand people climbed the city's highest hill for an Easter dawn in 1923. Over the next six years, two of the crosses they raised burned down.
story: In 1918 the land developer A. S. Baldwin cut footpaths to the top of Mount Davidson 'for the pleasure of the public' [1]. One hiker, James Decatur, was so moved by the wooded climb and the view from the Pacific to Mount Diablo that he asked Baldwin's permission to hold an Easter sunrise service up there [2]. On April 1, 1923, about 5,000 people gathered at a 40-foot wooden cross built by Adolph Anderson, and Dean J. Wilmer Gresham of Grace Cathedral led the service [1][3]. The crowds kept coming, and so did the fires. An 87-foot cross built in 1924 burned in December 1925. Its replacement, nearly 100 feet tall and lit every night of Easter week, burned in December 1928 [1][3]. In 1929 an 80-foot cross of wood and stucco outlined in electric lights went up [1]. Historian Jacquie Proctor notes that the cross also helped Baldwin bring buyers out to his new homes on the slopes [2]. A permanent 103-foot concrete cross followed in 1934 [3].

title: The Summit of the Great Sand Drift
place: Grand View Park, Golden Gate Heights (14th Ave & Moraga St)
hook: Sand once blew in from Ocean Beach and climbed this hill. In 1923 the city saved an acre of its summit, and the dune plants are still there.
story: The rocky top of Grand View Park is, in Harold Gilliam's words, 'the highest point in the great sand drift' that blew in from Ocean Beach over thousands of years. The sand climbed some 700 feet here and flowed around outcrops of dark red chert and volcanic greenstone [1]. The 1869 U.S. Coast Survey map simply marks a hill of 673 feet [2]. In 1923 an acre or so at the summit was dedicated as city park land [1]. Park superintendent John McLaren planted the Monterey cypresses and eucalyptus on top, and photographs show Grand View Peak being graded in the late 1920s [1]. The sandy openings still hold a rare survival of native dune scrub: dune tansy, the rare Franciscan wallflower and beach strawberry [1]. The rest of the hill nearly disappeared. In 1952 the city sold the surrounding lots for unpaid taxes, and in the 1960s bulldozers cut into the south side. After Gilliam's 1967 Chronicle column, the city bought the lots back in the mid-1970s 'for much more than what they had sold them for' [1].

title: A Dancer, a Thinker and a Thunder Pedal
place: Rodin gallery and courtyard, Legion of Honor
hook: The laundry girl from the dunes met a Paris dance star, and through her Rodin. Then an organ with 4,500 pipes arrived.
story: Alma de Bretteville grew up poor, the daughter of Danish immigrants on a sandy farm at the city's edge. She left school at 14 to deliver laundry to the mansions of the rich [1]. By 1914 she was Mrs. Adolph Spreckels and in Paris, where at a dinner at Ciro's she met Loie Fuller, the Illinois-born dancer whose 'Serpentine Dance' had made her famous [1]. Fuller introduced her to Auguste Rodin and bought bronzes for her. The first thirteen had their San Francisco debut at the 1915 exposition [1]. One of the earliest was The Thinker, a cast made around 1904 by Rodin's founder Alexis Rudier and bought through Fuller. It became one of the more than seventy Rodins Alma gave the Legion, and it still sits in the Court of Honor [2][4]. The palace got a voice too. In 1924 Adolph's brother, John D. Spreckels, gave a Skinner organ built in Boston. Its 4,500 pipes run from half an inch to 32 feet, hidden behind a cloth apse painted to look like marble. It even has a thunder pedal [3].

title: A Palace for 3,600 Lost Sons
place: Court of Honor, California Palace of the Legion of Honor
hook: On Armistice Day 1924 the Spreckels' marble memorial opened. Its most moving treasure was a parchment book of names made for the Gold Star mothers.
story: In January 1920 Adolph Spreckels told the park commissioners that he and his wife wanted to give their native city a memorial 'to our brave boys who gave their lives' in the Great War, which would also be a home for art [1]. Before the building was finished, the American Legion held a convention ceremony in its Court of Honor. The guests included Gold Star mothers who had lost sons in France, seated with amputee, blind and shell-shocked veterans [2]. That scene probably inspired Alma Spreckels' Book of Gold. Military records were searched for the names and hometowns of the roughly 3,600 Californians who had died. A calligrapher inscribed them on parchment under the title Our Sons 1914–1918, work that took eight years. Marshals Foch, Joffre and Pétain signed it in Paris, and General Pershing signed the title page beneath the single word 'Mothers!' [2]. Adolph died on June 28, 1924, before the opening. The city still had to vote on accepting the gift, and on November 4 it did, by a margin of 73,500 [3]. On the morning of November 11, Armistice Day, the palace was dedicated [3]. France's Albert Tirman announced that Alma had been awarded the Cross of the Legion of Honor [4].

title: A neighbourhood shaped like a bell
place: St. Mary's Park, Agnon Avenue and Justin Drive
hook: From above, the streets of St. Mary's Park trace a giant bell, a tribute to the college that once stood there.
story:
After St. Mary's College left for Oakland in 1889, its Bernal campus became a parish and then a truck farm growing fruit and vegetables for the city [1]. In 1924 the land was surveyed and opened for building. The developers hired Mark Daniels, the architect behind the residential parks of Sea Cliff and Forest Hill [1]. As a nod to the college, Daniels laid the curving streets out in the shape of a bell. Justin, Agnon and Genebern were named after teaching brothers at the college, and the new tract was called St. Mary's Park [1]. The residents' club today describes the bell as a nod to the college's belfry. It says the neighbourhood's eight landscaped islands, including the College Medians and Benton Island, are what put the "park" in its name [2].

The bell shows up clearly from the air. It appears on the huge wooden scale model of San Francisco built in 1940 from 1938 aerial photographs [1]. Soon after the first families moved in, the city set aside 13 acres to the east for a recreation ground. It paid $87,500 for ten of them, and the Archdiocese donated the rest [1].

title: Houses Moved for the Bayshore Boulevard
place: Boutwell Street near Silver Avenue, a block later erased for the freeway
hook: In 1924 a city photographer went house by house along the Portola's eastern edge, recording homes about to be moved or knocked down for a new highway.
story: In January and February 1924 Department of Public Works photographer Horace Chaffee walked the planned route of the Bayshore Boulevard. On Boutwell Street between Silver and Augusta he photographed the houses at 235, 243, 247 and 253 Boutwell. They were demolished or moved for the boulevard, and that block of Boutwell later disappeared completely under the US 101 freeway [1]. South of there, at Paul Avenue, all of Ware Street was demolished [2]. Ruth Eshow Upton grew up just outside the Portola. She remembered the day her street, Le Conte Avenue, was torn up: the road split it in two and the eastern block disappeared, along with the ditch where children collected watercress and pollywogs [3]. On June 6, 1926, the doctor on his way to deliver her baby brother at home got his car stuck in the construction mud [3]. When the highway opened, the Eshow children ran across it four times a day to reach school instead of using a smelly underpass [4].
