title: Where the Giants first played in the West
place: Seals Stadium site, 16th and Bryant (now Potrero Center)
hook: Men begged for $3-a-day jobs building it. Joe DiMaggio hit in 61 straight games here. Then, in April 1958, major-league baseball arrived on the West Coast at 16th and Bryant.
story:
Seals Stadium opened on April 7, 1931, at the height of the Depression. Seals president 'Doc' Strub said workers jumped onto the running boards of his car to beg for a job at $3 a day [1]. The stadium had no roof, since fans liked the Mission sun, and some years a live seal lived in a tank under the grandstand [1]. Dorothy Bryant remembered it as one of the few entertainments her neighbourhood could afford, where 'local boys like Joe Dimaggio played' [2]. In 1933, playing for the Seals, DiMaggio hit safely in 61 straight games [1]. In 1950 the fans staged a 'Peanut Revolt' after peanut sales were stopped [1].

On April 15, 1958 the relocated Giants played the first major-league game on the West Coast here, beating the Los Angeles Dodgers 8–0 [1]. Pitcher Johnny Antonelli was less charmed by the wind: 'Worst ballpark in America' [1]. After the last game on September 20, 1959, the stadium was knocked down that November. Its light towers and many of its seats went to Tacoma. A shopping centre now covers the site [1][3].

title: A Spanish Gothic college crowns Lone Mountain
place: Lone Mountain campus (former San Francisco College for Women), 2800 Turk Blvd
hook: In 1930 the last cross came down from Lone Mountain's summit. Two years later the Religious of the Sacred Heart began building a women's college there.
story: The last of the wooden crosses that had topped Lone Mountain was torn down in 1930 [1]. In 1932 construction began at the top of the hill on a Spanish Gothic building for the San Francisco College for Women [1]. It was run by the Religious of the Sacred Heart, and it had begun as Sacred Heart Academy in Menlo Park in 1898 [2][3]. From Turk Street, three flights of garden stairs modelled on Rome's Spanish Steps climb to the main building [1][2]. In 1958 the Chronicle wrote that the hill gave "the impression ... of a place remote and apart from the city around it," and ran a photo of a nun in full habit on the roof, looking out at the Golden Gate Bridge [2]. The 1960s undermined all of that. In 1969 the school admitted men and renamed itself Lone Mountain College, but by then enrolment and alumnae giving were falling [2]. In 1978 the University of San Francisco, the Jesuit school down the hill, bought the 23-acre campus for $5.8 million [2]. The college's former chapel now houses USF's admissions office [2].

title: A cornerstone laid in the snow
place: Jewish Community Center of San Francisco, 3200 California Street at Presidio Avenue
hook: On the coldest day San Francisco had ever recorded, the governor laid the first stone of a Jewish centre that soon welcomed refugees from Hitler's Europe.
story:
On 11 December 1932 the city recorded its coldest temperature ever, 27 degrees, and snow was falling. That day Governor James Rolph Jr., Mayor Angelo Rossi and Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel laid the cornerstone of the Jewish Community Center at 3200 California Street [1]. Arthur Brown Jr. designed it with Hyman and Appleton in a Mediterranean style with Art Deco touches [1].

The centre traced its roots to the Young Men's Hebrew Association of the 1870s. Sources give the founding year as either 1874 or 1877 [1][2]. Louis Blumenthal ran it from the mid-1920s until his death in 1959, and Emma Loewy Blumenthal was associate director for 39 years [1][2]. By 1936, one in ten Jews in the San Francisco area was a member [1].

In 1938 refugees from Germany, Austria, Poland, Spain and Czechoslovakia began arriving. The centre gave them free membership and classes in English and citizenship [1][2]. In the war years it ran civil defence and Red Cross courses and childcare for mothers in war industries [1]. Radio host John Rothmann remembered that the city's first Holocaust commemorations were held here [1].

title: A war memorial that sings
place: War Memorial Opera House, 301 Van Ness Avenue
hook: A court ruling blocked San Francisco's opera house until a returning major had an idea: build it as a memorial to the war dead.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed San Francisco's theatres and opera houses. In 1911 and 1912 the Musical Association tried to build a new hall, but the state Supreme Court ruled that the city could not give land for what was essentially a private building [1]. The group met again in April 1918. That November Major Charles H. Kendrick came home from the First World War with an idea: combine the hall with a memorial to the war's veterans [1]. The Association bought land on Van Ness Avenue, where St. Ignatius Church and College had stood before 1906 [1]. Arthur Brown Jr. and G. Albert Lansburgh designed twin buildings, an Opera House and a Veterans Building, facing City Hall [1]. Foundation work began on January 28, 1931, and the cornerstones were laid on Armistice Day that year [1][2]. The Opera House opened on October 15, 1932, in the depths of the Depression, with Puccini's Tosca. Gaetano Merola conducted and Claudia Muzio sang the title role [1][2]. The nine performances sold out, and three more were added [2]. According to the city's landmark report, it was the first municipally owned opera house in the world [1].

title: Julia Morgan's YWCA for Chinatown's Women
place: Chinese YWCA (now Chinese Historical Society of America), 965 Clay Street
hook: Chinatown's women commissioned Julia Morgan, and she gave them a building that blends Chinese and Tuscan styles and hides its true size.
story: The first Chinese YWCA in America was organised in San Francisco in 1916 [1]. By the early 1930s its members wanted a proper home. The YWCA's women's governing committee commissioned Julia Morgan, who had designed the rebuilt Cameron House mission nearby, to design and build it [2][4]. The building opened in 1932 [2]. Morgan mixed traditional Chinese and Tuscan elements, and from the Clay Street side the building is much larger than its modest Powell Street face suggests [3]. For half a century it was a social centre for Chinese American women, offering dance lessons, cultural programmes, cooking classes and youth activities [1]. By the 1980s it was out of date and fell short of building codes. Faced with the cost of retrofitting, the city handed it to the Chinese Historical Society of America [1], which opened its museum and learning centre there in 2001 [2]. The Powell Street portion now holds ninety-seven subsidised apartments for low-income elderly and disabled residents [3].

title: Skippers, Pirates, Bulldogs and Carlos Santana
place: James Lick Middle School, 1220 Noe Street
hook: An ivory Art Deco school rose on Noe Street in 1932. Its hallways have seen home-ec circle skirts, Beatles-haircut expulsions and a future guitar legend.
story: The big ivory-coloured Art Deco building at 1220 Noe Street was finished in 1932. A James Lick school had been on the site since at least the 1890s, when a grammar school stood at 25th and Castro, on what is now the upper yard [1]. The school is named for James Lick, the piano builder and land baron who was the richest man in California when he died in 1876 [1]. Alumni remember it well. Rose Shuck, a student in the late 1950s, still sang the Skippers' school song decades later. She remembered girls being kept out of shop class and made to sew circle skirts, and a 1956 earthquake that knocked a projector off a table mid-film [1]. Joe Cepeda, there in the early 1960s, recalled the first two boys who turned up with Beatles haircuts. Both were sent straight home with letters for their parents [1]. The most famous graduate is Carlos Santana, who lived in the Mission, finished at James Lick and left Mission High in 1965 [2]. When the building turned 75 in 2007, he came back to open the Santana Peace Garden at the front entrance [1]. The team names, by the way, went from Skippers in the 1950s to Pirates by the 1980s and Bulldogs in the 1990s [1].

title: The Henry Ford of Housing's Front Door
place: Doelger Building, 320 Judah St
hook: A $4,000 Art Deco office on Judah Street was mission control for the man who covered the Sunset's dunes with houses, two a day.
story: In January 1932 Henry Doelger, a builder who had quit school after eighth grade, hired architect Charles O. Clausen to design a headquarters at 320 Judah Street. It cost $4,000: a bold Art Deco front with miniature model houses displayed in cases beside the entrance [1]. It needed to be bold. From here Doelger ran the firm that the city's landmark report calls the largest home builder in the United States from 1934 to 1941, averaging two houses a day and employing 500 people. He borrowed Henry Ford's assembly-line methods, with specialised crews moving from house to house [1]. The office grew with the business: a raised roof and a neon 'Henry Doelger Homes' sign in 1936, and a Streamline Moderne wing in 1940 [1]. The same report doesn't flatter him. His childhood hotdog stand in Golden Gate Park reportedly fronted for homemade liquor, and by the late 1930s his Doelgerville deeds barred anyone but white buyers [1]. A longtime Inner Sunset pharmacist heard the rumour that Doelger kept his Prohibition liquor in a building at 9th and Irving [2]. His brother Frank ran a real estate office a few blocks away on Irving [3]. The building became a city landmark in 2013 [1].

title: The Rosy Dome Above Judah Street
place: St. Anne of the Sunset Church, 850 Judah St
hook: The 1906 quake flattened the Sunset's little wooden parish church. The domed church that replaced it in 1932 still anchors a parish that now prays in Cantonese too.
story: St. Anne's parish was founded in 1904. Its first church, a small wooden building, fell in the 1906 earthquake. Work on a new church began in 1930 and ended in 1932, when Archbishop John J. Mitty dedicated a Romanesque Revival building with a huge dome, two uneven towers and seats for 750. The frieze over the entrance, carved by Sister Justina Niemierski, tells the whole story of salvation [1]. For decades it was the landmark of the Inner Sunset. Photos of the streetcar graveyard a block north, around 1940, show the church and school behind the rows of dead cars, and one view of the yard was probably taken from the church itself [2]. Frank Dunnigan remembers his family going to the parish festival and the July novena to St. Anne. When he was at St. Ignatius in the late 1960s, more than half the students came from four Sunset parishes, St. Anne's among them [3]. The novena has run every year since 1908 [1]. The parish has changed along with the neighbourhood: Sunday's noon Mass is now in Chinese, and the parish runs a Chinese School [4].

title: Turrets and Tudors on 34th Avenue
place: Oliver Rousseau houses, 34th Avenue between Kirkham and Lawton streets
hook: In the middle of the Depression, one builder gave a plain row of Sunset houses Spanish turrets, Parisian balconies and patios open to the sky.
story: In the early 1930s Oliver M. Rousseau, a builder, developer and sometime architect, gave the plain Sunset some storybook streets. His biggest cluster is more than 100 mostly attached houses on 33rd to 36th Avenues between Kirkham and Lawton. Walking down 34th you pass a plum-colored Parisian facade, a Spanish castle with a tiled turret and solid half-timbered Tudors [1]. The houses are 27 feet wide instead of the usual 25. Inside, many have a patio open to the sky at the center of the plan, a living room set two steps down, and bathrooms tiled in combinations like green and peach [1]. Rousseau was a trained architect. He built mostly in the central Sunset, and added extras such as hand-painted designs on kitchen walls. With his brother he later formed the Rousseau Brothers and built well beyond the Sunset [2]. His houses were aimed at working and lower-middle-class buyers who loved the architect-designed homes of St. Francis Wood but couldn't afford them. "The owners of Rousseau homes were always a little bit snotty because their homes were of better quality," local historian Lorri Ungaretti told the Chronicle [1]. Architectural sleuth Gary Goss warned that many "Rousseau-style" houses were really built by his imitators, Henry Doelger among them [1].

title: A Beach Named for an Exclusionist
place: China Beach (formerly James D. Phelan State Beach)
hook: For more than forty years, a cove named for Chinese fishermen carried the name of one of California's loudest campaigners against Asian immigration.
story: In 1933 the State of California bought the little cove below Sea Cliff and turned it into a public beach. According to the Parks Conservancy, former mayor James D. Phelan helped make the purchase happen, and the beach was named after him. For decades it was known as James D. Phelan State Beach [1][3]. The Conservancy does not explain how he helped, and Phelan had in fact died at his Saratoga estate, Villa Montalvo, in 1930 [2]. He had been a reforming mayor from 1897 and a U.S. senator from 1915 [2]. He was also, the Densho Encyclopedia notes, a leader of California's anti-Japanese movement. In 1920 he ran for re-election under the slogan "Keep California White" [2]. He had backed Chinese exclusion as well [1]. So a cove that locals had named for Chinese fishermen was renamed for one of exclusion's champions. The state held the beach until 1976, when it passed to the federal Golden Gate National Recreation Area [1].

title: Golden Gate's engineer builds a drawbridge first
place: Lefty O'Doul Bridge (Third Street Bridge), Mission Creek
hook: Four years before the Golden Gate Bridge opened, its chief engineer designed a humbler span that still tilts skyward for boats on Mission Creek.
story: The old Third Street crossing over Mission Creek shut to traffic in November 1931, and on May 12, 1933, Mayor Angelo Rossi opened its replacement: a bascule bridge designed by Joseph Strauss, chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge [1]. It cost $640,000 and carried pedestrians, cars and streetcars; tracks for the State Belt Railroad's steam trains were planned for later [1]. City photographs from its first days show the leaf raised as the freighter SS Talamanca slipped out behind a tugboat [2]. Great concrete counterweights still swing the deck up. In 1980 the city renamed it for baseball player Lefty O'Doul, and it was seismically retrofitted in 1999 before the ballpark rose beside it [1]. Hollywood loved it: it appears in three Dirty Harry films and in the James Bond movie A View to a Kill (1985), where Bond drives a fire truck over the opening bridge [1]. Today it is the gateway to McCovey Cove, and it still rises to let boats through [2].

title: The tavern that welcomed everyone first
place: Jack's Tavern, 1931 Sutter Street (later the Boom Boom Room, 1601 Fillmore)
hook: Years before the Fillmore was called the Harlem of the West, a Sutter Street bar opened its doors to Black drinkers and never really closed them.
story: According to Fillmore jazz historians Elizabeth Pepin and Lewis Watts, Jack's Tavern opened in 1933 at 1931 Sutter Street, one of the first nightclubs in the neighbourhood to cater to African Americans, and, by The New Fillmore's account, the first live-music club that welcomed Black patrons in what became the wartime Fillmore jazz district [1][2]. Over the decades it was also called Jack's of Sutter and the New Jack's Lounge. In 1988 it moved to 1601 Fillmore, beside the Geary bridge [2]. A young bartender there, Alexander Andreas, met John Lee Hooker in 1990 and ended up carrying the bluesman's guitar case to his Bay Area shows. When Andreas later took over the lease, he renamed the bar after Hooker's song "Boom Boom"; after Hooker's manager objected to the legal risk, Hooker lent his name and likeness but invested nothing [2]. His red leather booth was still kept empty for him years after his death in 2002 [1]. Brass plaques on the bar honour old regulars such as Trumpet, a Jack's bartender whose trumpet case, Andreas says, held loaded dice [1]. In 2020 the pandemic-shuttered club appealed for emergency funds to survive [3].

title: Bloody Thursday at Steuart and Mission
place: Steuart and Mission streets
hook: On July 5, 1934, police fired into striking longshoremen at the foot of Rincon Hill. Within days, the whole city stopped work.
story: By July 1934 West Coast longshoremen had been on strike for nearly two months, and shipowners, backed by Mayor Rossi and the police, decided to "open the port" [1]. On July 5, police charged 2,000 pickets at Pier 38, then spent the afternoon trying to drive about 5,000 strikers off Rincon Hill, which overlooked the Belt Line Railway. Tear gas and "vomit gas" filled the streets, and salesmen from competing firms handed out free samples to the police [1]. Strikers answered with bricks and railroad spikes. Police bullets killed Howard Sperry and Nicholas Bordoise, and more than a hundred people were hurt [1]. Accounts differ on details: a sidewalk marker names Gene Olsen among those who fell, and one essay blames National Guardsmen rather than police [2][3]. The corner of Steuart and Mission was covered in flowers and chalked: "Two men killed here, murdered by police" [1]. Strike leader Harry Bridges's office in the Audiffred Building overlooked the spot [2]. Within days, tens of thousands marched in silence down Market Street behind the coffins, and a general strike shut the city for four days [4].

title: Coit Tower's murals locked away
place: Coit Tower, 1 Telegraph Hill Blvd
hook: In the summer of the 1934 waterfront strike, the city padlocked its brand-new tower. The danger was inside: a hammer and sickle painted on the wall.
story: Lillie Hitchcock Coit died in 1929 and left money to beautify the city she loved. Arthur Brown Jr.'s concrete tower on Telegraph Hill was dedicated on October 8, 1933 [1]. Its walls became the pilot project of the Public Works of Art Project, the New Deal's first relief program for artists. About twenty-five painters, paid roughly $25 to $45 a week, began frescoes of California life in January 1934 [1][3]. Several put their politics into the plaster. Victor Arnautoff painted left-wing papers on a newsstand. John Langley Howard painted miners holding the Western Worker. Bernard Zakheim painted a man pulling Marx's Capital from a library shelf [2]. Then the waterfront strike broke out at the foot of the hill, and the press whipped up fears of communist agitation. The Parks Commission cancelled the July 7 opening and locked the tower [1][2]. Most of the murals survived. Clifford Wight's hammer and sickle, part of a panel showing America's range of political systems, did not. It was chipped out, along with the Western Worker banner, and the tower opened on October 12, 1934 [1][2].

title: Tearing Down a Jail to Build a College
place: City College Ocean Campus athletic fields (site of the Ingleside Jail)
hook: Before City College, this hillside held the Ingleside Jail, where prisoners were packed two to a cell barely six feet long.
story:
From 1874 the County Sheriff's House of Correction Number Three stood on the slope above Ocean Avenue [1]. One account calls it "a real hellhole" and says prisoners were squeezed in pairs into cells 6 feet long, 4 feet 7 inches wide and 6 feet 6 inches high [1].

On July 8, 1934, the Ingleside Jail closed. A photograph from that day shows prison buses pulling away while a guard with a rifle watches, as inmates were moved under heavy guard to a new county jail at San Bruno [2]. Then the Depression's public-works crews moved in. Photographs from about 1934–35 show Works Progress Administration workers grading the land on which the jail had stood [1]. Groundbreaking for the new junior college near the old jail site followed in 1937 [3]. The jail grounds are now the college's athletic fields [1].

Writing in 1994, a time of prison-building and campus budget cuts, the writer "Dr. Weirde" called it "nice to remember a time when it worked the other way around" [1].

title: The President Lights the Cross by Telegraph
place: Mount Davidson Cross, summit of Mount Davidson Park
hook: Three wooden crosses on the city's highest hill burned down. The fourth, made of concrete, was switched on from the White House.
story:
Easter sunrise services began on Mount Davidson in 1923 at a 40-foot wooden cross, and 5,000 people came despite the rain [1]. The crosses that followed kept burning down: one in 1925, another in 1928, and a third in 1931 [2]. For a permanent monument, architect George Kelham and engineer Henry Brunnier, who were helping shape the downtown skyline, designed a 103-foot shaft built from 750 cubic yards of concrete and 30 tons of steel, with its foundation sunk 16 feet into solid rock [1]. A time capsule containing a transcript of earlier ownership deeds went into the base [2].

Madie Brown, the park's founder, then wrote to Franklin D. Roosevelt: "I have dared to dream that you would press a button in Washington, D.C., which in turn would light for the first time this giant cross." [1] On March 24, 1934, the president pressed a telegraph key and the cross lit up at 7:30 p.m. in front of a crowd of 50,000 [1][2]. Brown's letter praised him for bringing light "to many a darkened American home" [1]. It came two days after Roosevelt had persuaded the longshoremen's union to postpone a strike, months before the great waterfront and general strikes of 1934 [1][2].

title: The day they tried to open the port
place: Pier 38, The Embarcadero
hook: On July 3, 1934, police ringed Pier 38 with freight cars and ran trucks through a gauntlet of strikers. Two days later came Bloody Thursday.
story: By July 1934 the West Coast waterfront strike was two months old and shipowners were losing, by one estimate, $100,000 a day. With the backing of Mayor Rossi and the police, the employers' Industrial Association decided to 'open the port' [1]. At noon on July 3 they started at Pier 38. Freight cars of the state-owned Belt Line Railway were drawn into a barricade around the pier, and a lane of police cars formed a corridor to a warehouse. Trucks rolled through it with cargo while, outside the lane, police attacked strikers with clubs, guns and tear gas; strikers answered with bricks and railroad spikes. The fighting lasted all afternoon [1]. After a July 4 truce, police charged some 2,000 pickets at Pier 38 on July 5, and the battle spread up Rincon Hill into what became known as Bloody Thursday [1]. Longshoremen's grievances went back years: star-gang pay had dropped to about $10.46 a week, and men were hired by humiliating daily shape-ups [2]. After a general strike and federal arbitration, union hiring halls became a reality that autumn [2].

title: Two Houses a Day in Doelger City
place: 41st Avenue between Kirkham and Lawton streets, in the tract Henry Doelger advertised as "Doelger City"
hook: For seven years the biggest homebuilder in America worked the Sunset's sand dunes, finishing two stucco houses a day. His famous origin story may have been a fib.
story: Between 1934 and 1941 Henry Doelger was the largest homebuilder in the United States. His firm employed 500 people and finished an average of two houses a day, most of them one story of living space over a street-level garage [2]. Over his career he put up about 11,000 buildings in San Francisco, mostly in the Sunset. In 1946 the Chronicle called him "the poor man's Frank Lloyd Wright" [2]. In newspaper ads he gave the area roughly between 27th and 39th Avenues, from Kirkham to Quintara, a proud name: "Doelger City" [1]. Each house sat on a 25-by-120-foot lot. Historian Woody LaBounty describes standing on 41st Avenue between Kirkham and Lawton, looking at stucco fronts in razor-straight lines. The strips of lawn the first buyers got in the 1930s had nearly all been paved over [1]. Critics called the houses ticky-tacky, but Doelger framed them in redwood and they have lasted. Federal Housing Administration loans let middle-income families afford them [1]. Doelger liked to say he started out running a hot dog stand at 7th Avenue and Lincoln Way. A granddaughter of his brother John tells it differently: the brothers sold bathtub gin and homemade beer at a tamale stand in Golden Gate Park, and Henry put the earnings into land bought from artichoke farmers [1].

title: Bread ovens under a terra-cotta crown
place: Royal Baking Company building, 4769-4773 Mission St
hook: In 1935 a macaroni feud and a North Beach bakery ended up sharing one odd building. Its Dutch ovens are still baking.
story: In 1935 the real estate man Ambrose B. Frank, whom his neighbours called 'the mayor of the district', put up a 'new modern type' building at 4769-4773 Mission Street [1]. It has two fronts: a Storybook-style cottage and an Art Deco façade in green and yellow terra-cotta, topped by a three-pointed parapet [1]. The first tenant was Gaetano Ferrigno, who had just left the Golden Grain Macaroni Company after a bitter split with his relatives. He opened the rival Sorrento Macaroni Company here [1]. The Royal Baking Company came next, moving from Filbert Street in North Beach. In October 1935 two large double-brick Dutch ovens were installed, and they are still in use [1][2]. In 1982 Sara Monroy bought the bakery from its Italian owners. Her husband Isaac, a baker from Guanajuato, Mexico, took it over after her death in 1996 and renamed it New Royal Bakery [2]. The Storybook front is now a Salvadoran pupuseria, and a Last Supper mural sits above the bakery door [3]. In June 2020 the Board of Supervisors unanimously approved its path to City Landmark status [4].

title: The Atom Mural the WPA Found Too Radical
place: Woods Hall Annex, 218 Buchanan Street
hook: Reuben Kadish wanted to paint the splitting of the atom on a college stairway. What he painted instead was a shattered egg.
story: Woods Hall Annex, completed in 1935, was the last building on the Teachers College campus and the only one built by the WPA [1]. On the second-floor landing of its main stair, muralist Reuben Kadish painted 'A Dissertation on Alchemy', six panels of figures and symbols about alchemy and science [1]. The nomination dates it to 1935, while a later account gives 1937 [1][3]. At the centre, a huge shattered egg releases a stylised spiral. Kadish had originally planned to show the splitting of the atom, an idea WPA officials considered too radical, and the egg may be an abstract reworking of it [1]. He had studied with the Mexican muralist David Siqueiros, and the influence shows [1]. The campus was one of the city's busiest centres of WPA art. At least five murals were made here by Kadish, Jack Moxom, Hebe Stackpole, Maxine Albro and John Gerrity [1]. Most are gone. Albro's marble mosaic over the Haight and Buchanan entrance to Woods Hall has been removed or covered, and Gerrity's canvas panels have probably been taken down [1][2]. Kadish's mural and Moxom's winged fresco angel in Richardson Hall survive [1]. The mural was restored after graffiti damage in 2013, and the old campus now houses an apartment complex called Alchemy [3].

title: The city's first foreign-film cinema
place: Clay Theatre, 2261 Fillmore Street
hook: A Fillmore nickelodeon became San Francisco's first foreign-film house, then a midnight-movie shrine. Several of the best stories about it turned out to be untrue.
story: The little cinema at 2261 Fillmore opened in 1913 as the Regent, showing Mary Pickford films. In 1935 it reopened as the Clay-International. The city's historic review later confirmed that it was San Francisco's first theatre dedicated to foreign films, and a major art-house screen until the late 1980s [1]. Later it became a midnight-movie institution, known for The Rocky Horror Picture Show and The Room [2]. In 1985 it even hosted the world premiere of the western spoof Lust in the Dust, with Divine in attendance [2]. The landmark review also punctured some local legends. The Clay did not open in 1910, and it did not show San Francisco's first midnight movie with Pink Flamingos in 1972, a claim John Waters himself had repeated. Pink Flamingos reached the Clay in 1974 [1]. Landmark Theatres ran the cinema from 1991 [2]. It showed its last film on January 26, 2020: a midnight Rocky Horror [1]. In April 2022 the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to make it a landmark [1]. In 2025 venture capitalist Neil Mehta, who had been buying up Fillmore Street properties, announced plans to reopen it as a 200-seat repertory cinema [3].

title: Baby-buggy racers on Carolina Street
place: Carolina Street between 19th and Mariposa
hook: In July 1936 thousands lined a steep Potrero Hill block to watch a hundred kids hurtle downhill in homemade racers, towards a rope net for anyone whose brakes failed.
story:
On July 31, 1936, San Francisco held its first All-American Soap Box Derby, billed as "the greatest amateur racing event in the world", on Carolina Street between 19th and Mariposa [1]. Thousands of spectators and a hundred young racers turned out. The 900-foot course ran past the Pioneer & Queen Lily Soap factory at 18th Street, today's Pioneer Square, and ended at a rope net that caught drivers whose brakes gave out [1][2].

The cars had no engines and were built at home. Kids scavenged baby-buggy wheels from a South of Market dump nicknamed The Crematory. Some racers were named for girlfriends, others "The Tear Drop" and "Green Dragon". Girls weren't welcomed as racers until 1971 [1].

The winner was 15-year-old Russel Scott of San Rafael. He covered the course in 25.1 seconds and won a trip to the national finals at Derby Downs in Akron, Ohio [1]. The photographer John Gutmann, who had fled Nazi Germany and went on to build San Francisco State's creative photography programme, recorded the day [1]. The Hill hasn't lost its taste for downhill mischief: every Easter, big-wheel riders race down the twisting block of Vermont Street [1].

title: Helen Brooks's Garden on Poppy Hill
place: Brooks Park, Shields & Ramsell Streets
hook: In 1936 a stationer and his wife bought a windswept hilltop "because it was out in the country", then spent thirty years turning it into a wild garden.
story: In 1936 Jesse and Helen Brooks bought the peak of the westernmost hill of Merced Heights "because it was out in the country." Helen's architect brother helped design a crafty, brick-trimmed house facing the views, and Jesse ran a stationery store on Irving Street [1]. Locals called the summit Kite Hill, Poppy Hill or Pansy Hill. The rest of the ridge was a place for wildflower-picking parties among the rocky outcrops [1][2]. Helen gardened "from noon until night", her daughter Winifred recalled. She kept the native plants and added vegetables, trees and a beehive. She composted, wove her children's clothes on a loom and taught local kids to garden, while chickens, ducks and even a fawn roamed the lot [1]. Winifred watched postwar houses swallow the slopes: "It was sad seeing all these beautiful fields of wildflowers disappearing" [1]. When the couple decided to retire in the mid-1960s, the city wanted the land as a park but bid below other offers. After threats of eminent domain it paid $70,000 in 1966 [1]. (Another account dates the city's purchase to 1978 [3].) Several dozen native plant species still grow on the hilltop's outcrops [3].

title: Labaudt's San Francisco on the Chalet Walls
place: Beach Chalet, 1000 Great Highway
hook: For two years a fashion designer painted San Francisco onto wet plaster by the sea, about two square feet a day.
story: Willis Polk's Beach Chalet, his last design, opened in June 1925 with a changing room for bathers downstairs and a restaurant seating 200 upstairs [1][2]. In 1936 and 1937, funded by the WPA's Federal Art Project, fashion designer and muralist Lucien Labaudt covered about 1,500 square feet of the ground floor in frescoes, working on wet plaster roughly two square feet a day [1]. He said he painted them so 'people without an understanding of art may recognize and enjoy the subject' [1]. The walls show 1930s San Francisco: the Embarcadero, Fisherman's Wharf, Chinatown, the park [3]. There are real faces too: John McLaren on a bench, and sculptor Benny Bufano on horseback [4]. Primo Caredio's mosaics include an Indian aiming an arrow toward the men's room, and Michael von Meyer carved an octopus newel post for the stairs [1]. In World War II the Army made the chalet a coastal defense headquarters. From 1947 the Veterans of Foreign Wars ran a bar there, and in the 1950s beach gangs were among its regulars [1].

title: The hilltop mansion that blocked a park
place: Hilltop of Lafayette Park, site of the Holladay mansion
hook: For seventy years a lawyer's private mansion sat at the top of a public park. The Depression finally cleared it away.
story: Samuel Wirt Holladay was a lawyer who, as city attorney from 1860 to 1863, had defended San Francisco's claims to public land. Then he challenged the city's claim to this hill under the 1855 Van Ness Ordinance [1]. He fenced six parcels between Gough and Octavia, dug a well in 1869 and built an Italianate mansion with a water tower. By one account Bret Harte, Mark Twain and Leland Stanford visited [1]. The legal fight lasted seventy years, mostly in Holladay's favour. The empty house later grew eerie with neglect [1]. Developer Louis Lurie bought it in the 1920s and pushed to run Clay Street through the park to reach an apartment building he planned. Neighbours and Park Commissioners led by Herbert Fleishhacker fought him off, and in 1935 he sold the land to the city [1]. Between 1936 and 1938 WPA crews put in more than 100,000 hours of work. They demolished the mansion and water tower but kept the estate's old paths and stairs, and made the spot where the house stood into a play area for mothers and small children [1]. One private building survived: the St. Regis apartments on Gough Street, still the only privately owned building in a San Francisco public park [2].

title: The world's tallest bore
place: Yerba Buena Tunnel, Bay Bridge, Yerba Buena Island
hook: Bay Bridge traffic runs straight through a rocky island in the middle of the bay, in a tunnel once billed as the tallest in the world.
story:
When the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge opened to cars at 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, November 12, 1936, its two halves met on Yerba Buena Island. Traffic passed through a tunnel cut through the island's rock [1]. With a diameter of 58 feet, the double-deck Yerba Buena Tunnel was billed as the tallest bore in the world [1]. The bridge cost $79.5 million, including the rail lines on its lower deck [1].

The trains did not last. When the Key System gave up the interurban service, a 1958 rebuild turned each deck into a one-way road. As part of that work, the lower deck was lowered 16 inches through the tunnel [1].

The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the eastern span, closing the bridge for a month, and led to its complete replacement. The new span was due to be finished in 2013 [2]. Its approach runs over the oldest building on the island, an 1891 Army torpedo storehouse by the concrete pioneer Ernest Ransome [3]. A roadside panel nearby credits an unlikely prophet of the bridge, the Emperor Norton, who once decreed that the bay be bridged [4][1].

title: Where the most beautiful women were men
place: Finocchio's, 506 Broadway
hook: It began when a tipsy customer at a Prohibition speakeasy got up and sang exactly like Sophie Tucker. Joe Finocchio saw his future.
story: In the late 1920s Joe Finocchio ran a speakeasy on Stockton Street. One night a well-oiled customer got up and sang in a voice exactly like Sophie Tucker's, and the crowd loved it [1]. In June 1936 the Finocchios opened a bigger club at 506 Broadway, upstairs from what became Enrico's. The draw was female impersonators, and much of the audience was straight [1][2]. The police were not charmed. In July 1936 Joe was arrested for "keeping a disorderly house and selling liquor after 2 a.m." A Chronicle reporter noted the raid took place at 1:45 a.m. [1]. Joe promised to "run it like a regular theater", and he did. Performers had to arrive and leave dressed as men and were not to mingle with customers. According to Harry Hay, it was Joe's wife Marjorie who really drove the business [2]. Gray Line tour buses unloaded tourists night after night. Bob Hope and Tallulah Bankhead came to watch, and Lucien Phelps did his Sophie Tucker act there for 27 years [1][2]. The club lasted 63 years and closed on November 27, 1999, after a rent rise. Lawrence Ferlinghetti's verdict: "What a drag" [1].

title: A Concrete Horse for the Horseshoe Pitchers
place: Horseshoe Courts, Mount Lick, northeast corner of the park
hook: Up a slope in the park's northeast corner, a giant concrete horse keeps watch over sixteen horseshoe pits built with Depression relief labour.
story: Horseshoe pitchers were reportedly playing on the side of Mount Lick, in the park's northeast corner, by 1922 [1]. In the Depression the site was rebuilt, and according to a history of the WPA in San Francisco, the courts there were 'entirely the result' of the Works Progress Administration [2]. The mortared rock walls probably date from those 1930s projects [1]. There are sixteen courts [1]. At the end of them, on the hillside, is a large concrete horse in bas-relief, made in 1937 by Jesse 'Vet' Anderson of the Horseshoe Club [1]. The courts were part of a wider building boom. The WPA regraded and resurfaced thirteen miles of park roads, cleared ground for the arboretum and built the Police Stables from scratch, one of seventy parks and recreation projects on a December 1939 citywide list [2]. The National Register counts the courts and the horse among the park's historic features [1].

title: A school with no barriers
place: Sunshine School, 2728 Bryant Street
hook: Decades before the ADA, the Mission got the West's first public school built for disabled children, with a barrier-free ground floor and a therapeutic pool.
story:
The San Francisco Rotary Club helped start the California Society for Crippled Children in 1926. A year later the state passed the California Crippled Children Act, which provided services for disabled children [1]. Rotary founded the Sunshine School, and the city's School Department later took it over [1]. Between 1935 and 1937 the Public Works Administration gave it a building of its own on Bryant Street, in the Spanish Colonial Revival style with Moorish and Art Deco touches [1][2].

It was the first purpose-built public 'orthopedic' school west of the Rockies [2]. The ground floor had no barriers, anticipating the federal accessibility laws of 1968 and 1990 by decades [2]. Children with physical disabilities studied downstairs, where they had a therapeutic pool and a specially designed gym. Children with chronic or acute illnesses recovered upstairs in open-air rooms and ate meals cooked at nearby San Francisco General Hospital [2]. The school ran this way until the 1970s, when disability-rights groups won the right for these children to attend mainstream schools [2]. The city made it a landmark in 2019 [1].

title: Collision in the Fog, and the Ship's Dog
place: Lands End Trail shipwreck overlook
hook: An oil tanker and a luxury liner met head-on in the fog. The tanker ended up on the rocks below Lands End, beside its sister ship.
story: On 6 March 1937 the tanker Frank H. Buck was coming in through the Golden Gate with oil from Ventura, bound for Martinez [1]. In thick fog it ran head-on into the President Coolidge, one of the two largest American passenger liners of the day. The warning signals were heard too late [1]. The liner came away with a crushed bow. The tanker was fatally holed. The Coast Guard and the San Francisco Police got all of her crew off, and the ship's dog too [1]. The Buck came to rest on the rocks off Lands End, beside its sister ship the Lyman A. Stewart. That tanker had been wrecked at the same spot after its own fog collision in 1922 [1][2]. In 1938 both hulks were dynamited in a clean-up of the wrecks littering the harbour approach [1][2]. Some of the Buck still refused to leave. From the trail overlook at low tide you can still see its engine and sternpost next to the Stewart's engine block [1][2].

title: Fourteen stools and a sawdust floor
place: Original Joe's, 144 Taylor Street
hook: A Croatian immigrant opened a Depression-era counter on Taylor Street. It grew into the place where, its owner said, politicians and prostitutes ate side by side.
story: In 1937 Ante "Tony" Rodin, a Croatian immigrant, and a couple of partners opened a lunch counter on the ground floor of a 1910 Taylor Street hotel [2][3]. At first Original Joe's had 14 bar stools and a floor covered in sawdust [2]. Diners watched the cooks work in the open kitchen. As business grew, the owners took over the space next door for a dining room and then added a full bar. The restaurant eventually seated 140 [2][3]. Its best-known dish was Joe's Special, a hash of scrambled eggs and ground beef, served with portions big enough for a family [2]. The waiters wore tuxedos, but the clientele was mixed. In 2007 owner Duggan, one of the Rodin grandchildren who ran it, put it this way: "We have everyone from the head politician to the head prostitute in here, and we love them all" [2]. The neon blade sign reading "Original Joes. Fine Italian Food" is listed in the historic district survey [1]. A fire in the flue closed the Taylor Street restaurant in 2007, and the family reopened in North Beach [2][3].

title: Grading the Haight for the bankers
place: Page Street near Clayton (HOLC area D2, north of Haight Street)
hook: Federal appraisers colored the Haight yellow and the blocks near the Panhandle red, warning of a 'possible threat' from 'inharmonious racial elements' who weren't even there.
story: In 1937 the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation mapped San Francisco and graded each neighbourhood by how risky it was for mortgage lenders [2]. Most of the Haight between Golden Gate Park and Buena Vista Park became area C13, "Definitely Declining." The appraisers found it fully built up, 75 percent owner-occupied, and home to skilled workers, small business owners and white-collar workers earning $1,800 to $4,000 a year. They noted "no racial concentrations" and called any change "remote." Even so, most lenders would lend there only "upon a very restricted basis" [1]. The blocks around the Panhandle, reaching down to Haight Street, became D2, graded "Hazardous." This was an area of flats and small apartment houses over stores, with old mansions now owned by small business owners and artisans. The appraisers wrote: "On account of age there is a possible threat of an infiltration of inharmonious racial elements. However, no concentrations exist at the present time." Several lenders said they would not consider loans on single-family homes there at all [3]. Maps like these, drawn to guide mortgage lending, marked the Haight and the Western Addition in red [2].

title: Stilts, Skates and 50,000 Hot Dogs
place: Golden Gate Bridge toll plaza
hook: Before any car crossed, the bridge belonged to walkers. By 6 a.m. on May 27, 1937, about 18,000 people were waiting at the turnstiles.
story: The Golden Gate Bridge opened with a Pedestrian Day. On May 27, 1937, the roadway was open only to people on foot, from dawn to dusk. By 6 a.m. an estimated 18,000 were waiting to cross. About 15,000 an hour went through the turnstiles, each paying 25 cents, and hot-dog stands may have sold as many as 50,000 [1]. People raced to be first at everything. They ran, roller-skated, tap-danced, rode unicycles, played harmonicas and tubas, pushed baby carriages and walked on stilts. The Chronicle recorded some winners. Florentine Calegeri, a houseman from the Palace Hotel, was the first across and back on stilts. Sisters Carmen and Minnie Perez of Bush Street were the first on roller skates. And 11-year-old Anna Marie Anderson was the first girl lost on the bridge, and found again [1]. News reports put the day's crowd as high as 200,000 [1][2]. Down at Crissy Field, parade floats passed a 'Span of Gold' reviewing stand, and Strauss read his poem 'At last, the mighty task is done' [1]. The next day, President Roosevelt pressed a telegraph key in the White House and opened the bridge to cars [1][2].

title: The Arch That Saved Fort Point
place: Fort Point arch, Golden Gate Bridge south anchorage
hook: The bridge plans called for demolishing the old brick fort. Then its chief engineer walked through the empty casemates and changed his mind.
story: Fort Point stood exactly where the Golden Gate Bridge's southern anchorage was meant to go, so the fort, it seemed, would have to be demolished [1]. Before work began, chief engineer Joseph Strauss toured the empty fort and changed both his mind and his design. In a 1937 memo to the bridge board he wrote: 'While the old fort has no military value now, it remains nevertheless a fine example of the mason's art… it should be preserved and restored as a national monument' [1]. He designed a steel arch in the southern anchorage to span the fort. Construction of the arch and the San Francisco approach viaduct began on July 21, 1936 [2]. During construction the fort's casemates became workspace for hundreds of workers, and the second-tier gun rooms served as their cafeteria [1]. Not everything survived. A small counterscarp gallery and a separate ten-gun battery on the hill were demolished. The Fort Point lighthouse's beam was hidden by the rising steel, and in 1934 it was replaced by a light at the base of the south tower [1]. The brick fort still sits under the arch today [3].

title: The Last Greek Café on the Cliff
place: Louis' Restaurant, 902 Point Lobos Avenue
hook: A Greek boy who landed in San Francisco at eleven opened a diner above Sutro Baths in 1937. His family flipped burgers there for 83 years.
story: In the early 1900s the road above the Cliff House was crammed with little cafés, and, as Tom Hontalas later put it, 'for some reason, the little cafes were all run by Greek immigrants' [1]. His grandfather Louis had arrived from Greece in 1906, aged 11, and worked at his older brother's Cliff Cafe before opening his own place, Louis', in 1937 [1]. The diner hung on the cliff edge overlooking the Sutro Baths; when the baths burned in 1966, eight-year-old Tom was brought up the hill by his aunt to watch the flames [1]. The land later became part of a national park, and the family's lease became the problem. When the Park Service talked of closing Louis' in 1992, Hontalas ran a postcard campaign and found that two-thirds of his customers were locals [1]. In 2010, on a year-to-year lease and facing a federally required bidding process, supporters gathered nearly 5,000 petition signatures and the Board of Supervisors passed a resolution backing the family; they won a new ten-year lease [2][3]. Louis' finally closed during the pandemic in 2020, months before its Greek-American neighbours at the Cliff House [1].

title: The Net That Made the Halfway-to-Hell Club
place: Golden Gate Bridge south tower and Fort Point wharf
hook: Hard hats, sauerkraut juice for hangovers and a $130,000 rope net: the Golden Gate Bridge's chief engineer tried to break the rule of one death per million dollars.
story: Bridge builders of the day expected about one death for every million dollars spent. Chief engineer Joseph Strauss set out to beat that, and fired any man caught stunting on the job [1]. Workers had to wear 'Bullard' hard hats, adapted from a local manufacturer's mining helmet. They also got glare-free goggles, wind cream, diets meant to prevent dizziness, and sauerkraut juice 'cures' for hangovers. Doctors staffed a field hospital near the wharf at Fort Point [1]. Beneath the roadway hung a $130,000 net of manila rope that stretched from pylon to pylon. It caught 19 men, who became known as the 'Halfway-to-Hell Club' [1]. It could not save everyone. Kermit Moore, the first to die, was killed on October 21, 1936 [1]; the Presidio Trust's account says he was struck by falling equipment [2]. On February 17, 1937, a section of scaffold tore through the net and ten men fell to their deaths: O.A. Anderson, Chris Andersen, William Bass, Orrill Desper, Fred Dümmatzen, Terence Hallinan, Eldridge Hillen, Charles Lindros, Jack Norman and Louis Russell [1]. A plaque at the south end of the west sidewalk honours them [1].

title: The Proudly Named Park Bums
place: Big Rec ball grounds, opposite Seventh Avenue
hook: Wear a proper baseball uniform to Big Rec and the Park Bums would send you off the field as a dandy.
story: Pickup baseball at the Big Rec grounds began in the 1890s [1][2], and by 1937 its regulars had a name they refused to give up: the Park Bums. That July Chronicle writer Will Connolly profiled them, drawing on veteran player Anson Orr, a window trimmer who had joined in 1910 [1]. The first Bums, Orr said, were 'perpetually unemployed citizens' who took a break from avoiding work by choosing sides [1]. Later, men with jobs could play on Sundays. There was no roster and no officers. A newcomer turned up with glove and spikes every Sunday and waited on the sidelines, sometimes for weeks, until someone was missing [1]. Old trousers were compulsory. Anyone in a full uniform was banished as a 'fop and dandy', and 'Old Jeff' played third base for 25 years in corduroys, a vest and a derby hat [1]. One attempt to organize the club drew just four members to a Sunset real estate office [1]. Alumni included big-leaguers such as Joe Cronin and Mark Koenig [1].

title: The money fortress on Clinton Mound
place: United States Mint, 155 Hermann Street
hook: After 1906, refugees camped on this rocky hill. Since 1937 it has held a working U.S. Mint that almost nobody is allowed to visit.
story: The rocky rise above Market and Duboce was once known as Clinton Mound. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, refugees camped on its slopes [1]. In 1937 the federal government built the third home of the San Francisco Mint on the hill. The branch had opened in 1854 to serve the Gold Rush mines [2]. Designed by Gilbert Stanley Underwood in a stripped classical style, the building at 155 Hermann Street replaced the 1874 'Old Mint' on Fifth Street, which had saved the nation's gold reserves from the 1906 fire [2][3]. Since then its history has been oddly stop-start. From 1955, circulating coinage was suspended for 13 years, and from 1962 to 1988 the building was officially only an 'assay office' [2]. Since 1975 it has struck almost nothing but proof coins for collectors, apart from Susan B. Anthony dollars and some cents, many marked with a small 'S' [2]. Visitors are admitted only as a rare exception. For the Mint's 50th anniversary in May 1987, a limited number of people got a tour, advertised in the Chronicle with reservations required [2]. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988 [2][3].

title: A WPA Fresco History of Medicine
place: Toland Hall, UC Hall, UCSF Parnassus campus
hook: A Warsaw-born upholsterer who studied with Diego Rivera painted California's medical history on a UCSF lecture hall, Black midwife and plague panic included.
story: Bernard Zakheim came to San Francisco from Warsaw in 1920 and worked as an upholsterer and furniture maker. He visited Diego Rivera in Mexico in 1930 and went on to paint at Coit Tower [1]. In 1935 he started two fresco projects at the medical school on Parnassus. The larger one was ten panels called The History of Medicine in California, painted on the walls of Toland Hall with Works Progress Administration money and dated 1938 [1]. Many faces in the panels belonged to people on the medical school staff in 1936 [1]. It is not a tidy story of progress. The panels set superstition against science and show officials declaring bubonic plague around 1900. They also show Biddy Mason, a formerly enslaved woman who became a midwife and nurse, treating a malaria patient beside a white doctor [2]. UC Hall was seismically unsafe and slated for demolition. In 2021 UCSF hired conservators to remove the curved frescoes, scanned them in 3D and formed a task force, including Mason's descendants and Zakheim's family, to find them a new public home [3].

title: A Widow's Gift of Free Music
place: Concert Meadow, Sigmund Stern Grove, 19th Ave & Sloat Blvd
hook: Rosalie Stern bought a boozy old roadhouse gully for $50,000, gave it away, and insisted the music there always be free. Nearly ninety summers later, it still is.
story: In 1931 Rosalie Meyer Stern, widow of civic leader Sigmund Stern, used a memorial fund she had set up in his name to buy the Trocadero Inn and twelve surrounding acres from the aging George W. Green for $50,000. She gave the land to the city on one condition: it was to be used only for recreation. The gully's steep, wooded sides made a natural amphitheater, which was a big reason she chose it, and she wanted music at its heart [2]. The grove was dedicated on June 4, 1932, and the San Francisco Symphony played the first concert there on June 19 [1]. In 1938 Stern founded the Stern Grove Festival Association. Its first summer concert, on July 10, 1938, was played by the Bay Region Symphony of the Federal Music Project, a New Deal orchestra, and was followed by eleven more Sunday programs through September 25 [1]. It never charged admission. The family kept it going: her daughter Elise Stern Haas took over in 1956, then granddaughter Rhoda Goldman, then great-grandson Douglas Goldman. Ansel Adams photographed the 25th-anniversary crowd in 1963, and the Preservation Hall Jazz Band played nearly every year from 1969 to 1999 [1].

title: A sculptor rescues the Albion Castle
place: Albion Brewery ('Albion Castle'), 881 Innes Ave
hook: Prohibition killed a Norman-style stone brewery above India Basin. A sculptor bought the ruin and rebuilt it, stone by stone, from old photographs.
story: Above India Basin stands a Norman-style stone brewery built in 1870 by English immigrant John Hamlin Burnell to brew English ales with water from springs beneath the hill [1][2]. Ale was stored in tunnels cut 200 to 300 feet into the hillside [1]. After Burnell died in 1890, his widow and relatives kept it going until 1919, when her death and Prohibition ended brewing for good [1]. The buildings fell into ruin [2]. Then a sculptor, Adrien Voisin, bought the property. Sources disagree on when: the city's 1973 landmark report says 1938, while NoeHill's landmark summary says 1933 [1][2]. Working from old photographs and drawings, Voisin restored the stonework of the main building, with its three-story tower, and lived and worked there [1]; a stone plaque commemorates a 1939 restoration [1]. The springs still had value: the Mountain Springs Water Company bought the water rights from Voisin and, in 1964, the building itself, letting him stay for life [1]. The castle became San Francisco Landmark No. 60 [2].

title: Filling Rice Bowls for a Nation at War
place: Chinatown streets, Rice Bowl parade and party
hook: Three hundred thousand people crowded into Chinatown for a party that raised more money for starving Chinese civilians than any other city in America.
story: When Japan's war on China brought mass hunger in the late 1930s, Chinese communities across the U.S. raised relief money. San Francisco's answer was the Rice Bowl. The first, on June 17, 1938, was part of a national effort in more than 700 cities [1]. The Chronicle promised 'not a mere gathering of the well-to-do about a banquet table — but rather a unified community project', with Chinese bands and two Chinese opera companies performing in the streets [1]. By the next morning 300,000 people had come, and San Francisco's $55,000 topped all 700 cities [1]. Later Rice Bowls brought floats, dragon dances and banners [2]. The 1940 festival added a mock 'kangaroo court', where columnist Herb Caen broadcast on the radio from the jail [1]. Accounts of the totals differ: the Chronicle reports more than $80,000 in 1940 and $100,000 in 1941 [1], while historian K. Scott Wong, as cited on FoundSF, puts one four-day party at $93,000 [2]. The same community boycotted Japanese silk and picketed docks where ships bound for Japan were loading [2].

title: Methuselah Arrives by Steamship
place: Steinhart Aquarium, California Academy of Sciences, Music Concourse
hook: In 1938 an Australian lungfish moved into the Steinhart Aquarium. She is still there, and possibly the oldest aquarium fish on Earth.
story: After the 1906 fire destroyed its Market Street museum, the California Academy of Sciences moved to Golden Gate Park, dedicating a new museum on the Music Concourse in 1916 [1][2]. Steinhart Aquarium opened beside it on September 29, 1923 [2][3]. In 1938 an Australian lungfish arrived by sea. She was named Methuselah [3][4]. Lungfish breathe with both lungs and gills and are thought to be an evolutionary link between fish and amphibians [4]. In 1947 the Chronicle described them as creatures 'with green scales looking like fresh artichoke leaves' and a possible 'missing link' [4]. When the previous record-holder, a lungfish named Granddad at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, died in 2017 aged 95, Methuselah was left as the oldest known aquarium fish. By 2022 she was thought to be about 90 [4]. Her keepers describe a mellow 'underwater puppy' who enjoys belly rubs and will only eat figs when they are fresh and in season [4].

title: The Women Who Struck the Dollar Store
place: Strike meeting site, 720 Washington Street
hook: Chinatown's garment workers had been shut out of unions for generations. In 1938 more than a hundred of them walked out, and won.
story: In the 1930s the garment trade was Chinatown's largest employer, with low pay, long hours and poor light and ventilation [1]. Unions had long treated Chinese workers as 'unfair competition' [1]. That changed at the National Dollar Stores factory, owned by Joe Shoong. With help from organiser Jennie Matyas, workers formed Local 341 of the Chinese Ladies' Garment Workers' Union in November 1937 [2]. A union election on January 24, 1938, went their way, and an agreement followed the next day. Two weeks later the company announced it had sold the factory to its own foreman and manager, a move the workers saw as a ploy to break the union [2]. At 8 a.m. on February 26, 1938, they struck, picketing the factory and three National Dollar stores. White retail clerks refused to cross the lines and the stores closed for two weeks [2]. Strikers met at 720 Washington Street [1]. The strike lasted 13 weeks [3] and ended with a closed union shop, a 5% raise and a 40-hour week [1]. One striker recalled: 'The strike was the best thing that ever happened. It changed our lives' [2].

title: The neighbourhood flea pit that went international
place: Larkin Theatre (later the Century), 816 Larkin Street
hook: Ten-cent features changed every night. Then a new operator filled the little Larkin with films from abroad, and San Franciscans came across town to see them.
story: The Larkin opened in June 1914, the work of an entrepreneur named Joy B. Rothschild, and closed within weeks [1]. In early 1916 Charles and William Goodwin reopened it with new ventilation and a Wurlitzer organ. They changed the feature every night and charged 10 cents, so for $3 a month a regular could see thirty studio pictures [1]. Film historian Jack Tillmany calls it a "little known neighborhood flea pit" until 1938 [1]. That year Herbert Rosener, who had filled the Clay on Fillmore Street with imported, subtitled films, took over the Larkin and brought the same policy [1]. In January 1942 the Australian war film "40,000 Horsemen" premiered at the Larkin and the Clay on the same day [1]. After the war, audiences tired of films censored by Hollywood's Production Code came for foreign ones, and "Diabolique" ran 24 weeks [1]. The building is listed as a contributor to the Uptown Tenderloin Historic District. It is the Tenderloin's only surviving early movie theatre, though it later turned to adult films [1][2].

title: Two Women Paint Noah's Ark
place: Mother's Building, San Francisco Zoo
hook: Two artists who came to sketch the animals spent four and a half years painting the flood's aftermath across the walls of a mothers' lounge.
story: Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker gave $50,000 for a Mother's Building in memory of their own mother, and it opened in 1925 beside the giant Fleishhacker Pool as a refuge for mothers and small children [1][2][3]. In the Depression, two San Francisco artists who had been sketching animals at the zoo, Helen Forbes and Dorothy Puccinelli, won New Deal support to decorate it [2][3]. Given free choice of subject, they picked Noah's Ark, after the waters recede [2][3]. Working in egg tempera for four and a half years, they finished in 1938 [3]. Elephants, white pelicans and donkeys make their way across the drying land while Noah stands among deer, a theme of renewal for a city in hard times [3]. Hoodline has described them as the largest set of egg tempera murals in the West [3]. Advocates note that every mural here was painted by women, unlike Coit Tower [3]. Moisture from fog and sea has damaged the walls, and the building has long been closed to the public while supporters push for restoration [2][3].

title: A marble mansion given to the nuns
place: Flood Mansion, Convent of the Sacred Heart, 2222 Broadway
hook: In 1939 a widow gave away her marble mansion with its Golden Gate view. Within a year, 97 schoolgirls and 25 nuns had moved in.
story: In June 1939 the Society of the Sacred Heart learned that Maud Lee Flood wanted to give them her family home: a marble mansion on the Broadway ridge that looked out over the Bay and the newly finished Golden Gate Bridge [1]. Her husband had died and her children had grown up and left, and she wanted the house to have a purpose. So she handed it over to Reverend Mother Eleanor Deming [1]. The family drawing room became a chapel. At the start of 1940 about 25 nuns, seven lay teachers and 97 students moved in [1]. Mrs. Flood wrote that she was pleased the house of "happy and unforgettable memories" had become "a house of learning, refinement, and peace" [1]. The war changed the school too: many families wanted their sons and daughters in one school, so boys joined the lower grades [1]. When the Grant mansion next door came up for sale, the nuns had already slipped religious medals onto its grounds through the latticework. The family sold it to them for $150,000. The school gives 1950 as the year, while NoeHill says 1948 [1][2]. In 1956 the Society bought Hammond House on the other side, and Stuart Hall for Boys opened there with 42 boys [1].

title: A quarter to peek at the Nude Ranch
place: The Gayway, north end of the fairgrounds
hook: The fair borrowed Botticelli's Venus from Italy. For six months, a sideshow of cowgirls in G-strings outsold it.
story:
At the north end of the island, beside a 12,000-car parking lot, lay the Gayway, a 40-acre fun zone of thrill rides and shows [1]. Its sideshows included 82 little people in cowboy costumes and a racetrack where monkeys drove cars. The one everybody remembered was Sally Rand's Nude Ranch [2].

For a quarter, visitors could peek through glass panels at 20 'cowgirls' wearing only G-strings and boots as they tossed horseshoes, swung lariats and played badminton [2]. The museum's account adds pistol belts and donkeys [3]. About 65,000 people packed in during the first week. Meanwhile, most other Gayway shows lost money; about two-thirds of them went broke [2].

The fair also showed a celebrated collection of European masterpieces. When, after six months, the art exhibit finally took in more than the Nude Ranch, the exposition put out a press release about it [2].

Rand herself, the fan dancer who became famous at 1930s world's fairs, did not perform on the island. She owned the Music Box Theater on O'Farrell Street, which is still there today as the Great American Music Hall [4].

title: Chinatown builds China's pavilion
place: Chinese Village, Golden Gate International Exposition (approximate site)
hook: Invaded by Japan, China couldn't come to the fair. So San Francisco's Chinese community built its own village, complete with opera.
story:
The 1939 fair billed itself as a 'Pageant of the Pacific', but one great Pacific nation was missing. China, exhausted by the Japanese invasion, did not take part. Instead, Chinese residents of San Francisco built and ran a Chinese Village [1]. It was a pointed contrast. Japan had put up an expensive, elaborate pavilion, and historians later concluded its purpose was to project 'harmony' and deflect attention from Japan's atrocities in Asia [1].

The Chinese Village was designed by the landscape architect Mark Daniels, who had a long interest in Chinese garden design [2]. Performers from San Francisco's Chinatown staged classical Chinese opera there, and a photograph in the Bancroft Library shows the Village's opera troupe [3]. The Works Progress Administration's 1938 guide to the fair listed a 'Chinese City' among the showplaces planned for the Gayway fun zone [4].

The fair's gateway to China outlasted the peace. After Pearl Harbor, anti-Japanese feeling in the city ran so high that there was a serious proposal to turn Golden Gate Park's Japanese Tea Garden into a hamburger stand. Daniels wrote to the Examiner urging that it become a 'Chinese Tea Garden' instead [2].

title: Give 'Em the Pools!
place: Anglers' Lodge and Fly Casting Pools, west of the Polo Field
hook: Some members of this fishing club have never set foot in San Francisco. They join for the WPA casting pools, some of the finest anywhere.
story: The fly casters began with a small lodge and dock at Stow Lake. When they outgrew it, John McLaren himself picked a new site west of the Polo Field [1]. During the Depression, Works Progress Administration crews built a rustic lodge with fish-carved shutters overlooking concrete casting pools 450 feet by 185 feet [1][2]. Getting them wasn't easy. Club member Ralph Keating recalled 'real bumps in the road' until Herbert Fleishhacker settled a civic meeting by declaring: 'They are performing a public service. Give 'em the pools!' [1]. Keating also remembered meeting McLaren at Stow Lake as a ten-year-old [1]. The WPA handed the finished facility to the Park Commission on a Sunday afternoon in March 1939, and it has barely changed since [1]. Members still honour an old agreement to coach any novice who asks [1]. The records disagree on some dates: the National Register gives the lodge as 1936 and the club's founding as 1890, while the WPA history says 1894 [1][2].

title: Gutters paved with forgotten gravestones
place: Paths on the western and northern slopes of Buena Vista Park
hook: Look down at the rain gutters beside Buena Vista's paths. Some of the marble still carries names and dates carved for people buried long ago.
story: San Francisco ordered its cemeteries emptied in 1914, and the removals dragged on through the 1940s. Headstones went to Colma, though the remains were not always moved with them. Unclaimed stones were recycled into sea walls, landfill and park gutters [4]. In Buena Vista Park, Depression relief crews built retaining walls and drainage ditches out of broken marble slabs, and in places the inscriptions can still be read [1]. Clyde Healy's December 1939 report on the Works Progress Administration lists improvements to Buena Vista among its 70 park projects [2]. Sources disagree about where the stones came from. One points to the Odd Fellows Cemetery, cleared in the early 1930s [2]. The Encyclopedia of San Francisco says tombstones from Laurel Hill were broken up for the park's gutters once removal there was complete [3]. Others say only "Lone Mountain cemeteries" [1]. The hill was almost lost to development as well. In 1950 Supervisor Chester MacPhee proposed selling parts of the park, calling it "unused, unsightly" and in need of a policeman at all times. The Board tabled the idea indefinitely [1].

title: Last drinks at Weepers' Corner
place: Top of the Mark, Mark Hopkins Hotel, 999 California Street
hook: Pacific-bound servicemen toasted their last night of liberty nineteen floors up. As their ships slipped out the Golden Gate, the women they left behind gathered at one window.
story: The Mark Hopkins Hotel opened on December 4, 1926, on the site of the railroad magnate Mark Hopkins' mansion, which burned in 1906 [1][2]. In 1939 the owner, George D. Smith, turned the 11-room penthouse on the 19th floor into a glass-walled cocktail lounge with a 360-degree view. NoeHill credits the design to Timothy Pflueger and dates it to 1936 [2][3]. The hotel's own history says Smith doubted anyone would ride 19 floors just for a drink. But the Top of the Mark was an instant hit when it opened on May 11, 1939, the year the Golden Gate International Exposition lit up Treasure Island [3]. According to the Chronicle columnist Herb Caen, the name came from Smith's friends. When Smith said he didn't know what to call the top of The Mark, they told him he had just named it [3]. During the Second World War it was a favourite last stop for Pacific-bound servicemen. Squadrons left a bottle with the bartender, and returning men signed the label and drank for free. Whoever finished the bottle bought the next one [2][3]. As the ships left the Golden Gate, wives and sweethearts gathered in the northwest corner to watch, and it became known as "Weepers' Corner" [3].

title: Mona's, where girls could be boys
place: Mona's 440 Club, 440 Broadway
hook: Waitresses in tuxedos, Gladys Bentley in a top hat, and a teenage Johnny Mathis learning his stagecraft: the story of San Francisco's first famous lesbian bar.
story: Mona Sargent and her husband Jimmie opened a bar at 451 Union Street soon after Prohibition ended. They moved to 140 Columbus in 1936, then to 440 Broadway. FoundSF dates that last move to 1939, and other accounts are earlier [1][2]. They had imagined a sawdust-floored bohemian hangout for writers and artists. Instead it became a club where women in men's clothes waited tables and sang [2]. Mona's is often called San Francisco's first lesbian bar. It advertised itself as the place "where girls can be boys", and its male impersonators became local celebrities [2]. The 440 had actually been opened by Charlie Murray, who brought Mona in as a partner. Men often had to front for lesbian-run bars [1]. Blues singer Gladys Bentley, famous for performing in a tuxedo and top hat, played there in the 1940s [1][2]. In the mid-1950s singer Ann Dee took over and renamed it Ann's 440. In 1955 she hired a 19-year-old Johnny Mathis two weeks into his professional career and coached his stage presence [1][3]. Mona went on with a new club, Mona's Candle Light, at 473 Broadway from 1948 to 1957 [1].

title: Motel Row on the Road to the Bridge
place: Marina Motel, 2576 Lombard Street
hook: Why does a stretch of a San Francisco street look like a 1940s highway town? Blame the Golden Gate Bridge, and one retired man's hunch.
story: Before the Golden Gate Bridge, Lombard Street through the Marina was a quiet two-lane road [1]. Once the bridge was planned as the longest suspension span in the world, Lombard became its main approach, and after the bridge opened in 1937 drivers poured through [1][2]. One man saw what was coming. Heidi Detjen says her grandfather, the son of a Gold Rush miner, came out of retirement after visiting a motor court. In 1939 he opened the Marina Motel at Lombard and Broderick, the first motor lodge on the street [1]. Motor lodges let guests park right outside their own door, which suited a country that had fallen for the car [1]. The city then widened Lombard to six lanes. To do it, buildings on the south side of the street were torn down, leaving empty lots, and that's when all these other motels appeared, Detjen says [1]. In the early days, she recalls, drivers came off the bridge and went from motel to motel looking for the best rate. The strip of roadside motels is still there today [1][2]. So is the Marina Motel, now run by the third generation of the same family, with the fourth getting involved [1].

title: Relief crews and ten thousand trees
place: Brazil Avenue entrance, start of the WPA view drive
hook: In the Depression, federal relief workers carved roads, bridle trails and a scenic drive into bare hills, and planted a forest.
story: The Depression finally brought workers to McLaren Park's empty hills. Money and labour from the Works Progress Administration built a scenic 'view drive' in the 1930s. It started at Brazil Avenue and ended just east of the twin water tanks off today's Mansell Street. The WPA also built equestrian trails on the south slopes [1]. The McLaren Park Collaborative's timeline says that by 1939 WPA workers had finished a long network of footpaths, hiking, fire and bridle trails, plus culverts, roads and the view drive. They had also planted more than 10,000 eucalyptus, cypress and pine trees [2]. For a while the park had a stable and riders on its trails. That didn't last. By 1983 the city's planners noted that horseback riding was no longer allowed, because without separate trails nobody could keep horses out of areas the public used [1]. The park's plant life has changed since. In 2004 a park worker told the Chronicle that invasive plants like eucalyptus, pampas grass, fennel and French broom worried him far more than human intruders [3].

title: San Francisco's first international airport
place: Hall of Transportation (Building 2), 300 California Ave
hook: For a few short years, passengers walked out of a Treasure Island hangar, down to a floating dock, and flew off across the Pacific.
story:
Treasure Island was built to be an airport. With federal aid, three permanent buildings went up alongside the fair: an administration building meant to be the terminal and two steel-and-concrete hangars, each 335 feet long and 78 feet high, that spent 1939 full of borrowed art [1][2]. This one, now Building 2, housed the fair's Hall of Transportation [2].

Pan American Airways moved its Clipper flying boats here from Alameda in 1938, making Treasure Island San Francisco's first international airport, the only time the island served its planned purpose [3]. During the fair, passengers and crew walked from Building 2 to a floating dock and boarded aircraft that took off and landed on the water of Clipper Cove [3]. It was luxury travel: the trip to Manila took five days, hopping between islands with overnight hotel stops, and a one-way ticket cost about $2,000 in 1935 [3].

War ended the dream. The airport was never built [2]. By 1943, Pan Am-operated 'Coronado' transports were loading wartime cargo at the Clipper Cove dock, and by the war's end the flying boats were obsolete [3].

title: The Avenue Club's Organist and All-American
place: The Ave Bar, 1607 Ocean Avenue
hook: A 1922 Ocean Avenue storefront went from fix-it shop to shoe repair to bar, run for a while by a Fox Theatre organist and later by an All-American football star.
story: The building at 1607 Ocean Avenue, near Capitol, dates from 1922. Its first known tenant was Crown Electrical and Plumbing, and from 1934 it housed Louis Nessier's Balboa Shoe Repair [1]. In 1938 it began selling alcohol as Horgan & Fex liquors. It first appears as the Avenue Club in 1939, ten years earlier than the date on its Legacy Business listing [1]. From 1944 Audrey and Mel Hertz ran it. Mel had been a popular theatre organist and in 1933 was house organist at the Fox Theatre on Market Street. He was declared bankrupt in 1932 [1]. In 1949 the bar passed to Johnny Schiechl, a Balboa High graduate named All-American center at Santa Clara for the 1939 season. He played for the Steelers, Lions and Bears, and for the 49ers in 1947. After a divorce and a nervous breakdown in 1950, he reportedly sold his share to his partner, Bob Wells [1]. In 1959 the owners, Jim and Hallie Emmett, made the papers when their Dalmatian Debbie, a "bar stool regular", went missing. She was found [1]. The bar entered the city's Legacy Business Registry in 2017 [1]. City records list The Ave Bar at the address under one owner from 2006 to 2024 [2].

title: The Mansion the WPA Tore Down
place: Sutro Heights Park, site of the Sutro residence and parapet
hook: Adolph Sutro's daughter lived on in his crumbling clifftop estate until 1938. Within months of her death, New Deal crews knocked the house down.
story: Sutro Heights passed to the city in 1920 on condition that it be 'forever held and maintained as a free public resort or park,' but Adolph Sutro's daughter, Dr. Emma Sutro Merritt, kept the right to live there [1]. Upkeep dwindled; in 1935 the San Francisco Garden Club found cypresses 'under the spell of some enchantment' and statues 'moss grown' [1]. Emma died in residence in 1938, while Works Progress Administration crews were already shoring up the western slope with artificial concrete cliffs [1]. The WPA then demolished the decaying house, the remains of the conservatory, the entrance gates and fences and the structures on the parapet, spending $90,994 on the 'improvements' [1]. Historian John Martini calls it an 'ill-advised WPA clean up'; Sutro's two Belgian lion statues, by Guillaume Geefs, survived at the vanished gate for another forty years [2]. During the Second World War the park was closed for security because it stood so close to Fort Miley, and concrete range-finding stations were built beside the parapet [1]. After 1977 the National Park Service retired the weather-worn lions to storage and installed cast copies [2].

title: The Palace for the People, padlocked
place: Aquatic Park Bathhouse (Maritime Museum), 900 Beach St
hook: The WPA built San Francisco a shining ship-shaped bathhouse for everyone. Days after it opened, the public was shown the door.
story: Between 1936 and 1939 the Works Progress Administration built a Streamline Moderne bathhouse on Black Point Cove, designed by William Mooser III to evoke a ship at port. It had lockers for 3,000 swimmers and showers switched on by photoelectric "eyes" [1]. Hilaire Hiler, just back from Paris, painted the lost continents of Atlantis and Mu across the lobby. Sargent Claude Johnson, the first Black artist on the West Coast to win national fame, carved the green slate frieze and designed the veranda mosaics [1][2]. At the dedication on January 22, 1939, the Chronicle called it "A Palace for the People." But just before opening, the city had leased it to Gordon Brothers Concessions, and it became the Aquatic Park Casino, an exclusive nightclub. Up went signs reading "Private – Keep Out," and schoolboys eating sack lunches on the veranda were ordered to leave [1]. Beniamino Bufano hauled his animal statues down to the beach: "I would rather have kids playing over my statues than to have drunks stumbling over them." Johnson walked away, and his mosaic is still unfinished. By the end of 1940 the concessionaires had been ousted amid lawsuits and the doors were padlocked [1].
