title: The Swing Mikado's two-week run
place: Golden Gate International Exposition fairgrounds (central Treasure Island)
hook: An all-Black, swing-era Gilbert and Sullivan hit the island running. Two weeks later, politics shut it down.
story:
Among the fair's liveliest shows was The Swing Mikado, a production of the New Deal's Federal Theatre Project. It moved Gilbert and Sullivan's story from feudal Japan to a make-believe South Pacific island and set it to swing music with an all-Black cast [1][2]. It had played Chicago and New York before arriving on Treasure Island in 1939 [2].

It did not last. Political attacks on progressive New Deal programmes closed the show after only two weeks on the island [2]. It then did very well at the Geary Theater in San Francisco and toured the Western states. A few days after its sudden closure, Benny Goodman, 'the King of Swing', started a sold-out residency at the fair [2].

Black music kept a place on the island. A three-day 'Negro Music Festival' traced African American music from ancient Africa to swing [1]. When the fair closed in 1940, the ASCAP festival's afternoon concert included works by the Black composer William Grant Still. That evening W. C. Handy, 'the Father of the Blues', played 'St. Louis Blues'. Years later he remembered it as 'the greatest program of all-American music ever staged' [2].

title: The goddess the Navy tore down
place: Site of the Court of Pacifica (today's Mersea restaurant parking lot)
hook: An 80-foot goddess of the Pacific once ruled this corner of the island. She did not survive the war; some of her stone companions did.
story:
The fair's theme, Pacific Unity, found its grandest expression in the Court of Pacifica, designed under Timothy Pflueger [1]. Presiding over it stood Ralph Stackpole's 80-foot 'Pacifica', the fair's goddess of the western ocean, conceived as a composite of peoples of the Pacific Rim [1][2]. At her feet the three-tiered Fountain of Western Waters was ringed by twenty oversized sculptures of Pacific peoples, dancing, making music, working and sleeping. Chronicle critic Alfred Frankenstein thought them the finest sculpture made for the fair [1].

Pacifica herself was demolished when the Navy took over the island for the war [2]. The fountain figures, cast in stone rather than the usual plaster, were built to last. Accounts of how many survive vary: the museum's sculpture exhibit says ten are in storage and four are lost, while six restored figures have stood flanking the doors of Building One [1][3]. The court itself lay where the Mersea restaurant's parking lot is now [3]. In 2013 an Oakland engineer, William Chamberlain, was raising money to build a new Pacifica, estimating the cost at up to $2 million [2].

title: Thirty-five thousand pioneers evicted to Colma
place: Iris Avenue, Laurel Heights (houses built on the former Laurel Hill Cemetery)
hook: The city's 'silent city' of senators and founders held out for decades against Richmond District boosters. Then its tombstones ended up in park gutters and Marina breakwaters.
story:
By 1900, when the city stopped new burials, Laurel Hill held some of San Francisco's most famous dead, including the cable car pioneer Andrew Hallidie and several U.S. senators [1][2]. It had also become an obstacle. The Richmond Banner campaigned for almost twenty years to remove the cemeteries that blocked the way west. "This district of ours, beyond the land of the dead, wants to be firmly united to the rest of San Francisco," one editorial said in 1924 [1].

In 1914 the Board of Supervisors ordered all bodies out of the city. The Calvary, Masonic and Odd Fellows cemeteries gave in, but Laurel Hill's association held out until 1937, when the supervisors demanded that it be emptied at once [3]. Campaigners for a Pioneer Memorial Park lost [2]. Between 1939 and 1941 about 35,000 bodies were reburied, most at Cypress Lawn in Colma. NoeHill puts the number buried at 38,000 [1][2].

The headstones were not wasted. Some became sculptors' blocks, gutters in Buena Vista Park and breakwaters along the Marina shore [2]. Houses, flats and small apartment buildings rose on the slopes in the 1940s and 1950s [4].

title: A Zoo Poured in Concrete
place: San Francisco Zoo, Sloat Boulevard
hook: Depression-era builders wanted a zoo that could never burn. Decades later, renovators found concrete poured seven feet deep under the elephants.
story: Banker and parks commissioner Herbert Fleishhacker founded the zoo in 1929, and it carried his name until 1941, when at his suggestion it became the San Francisco Zoological Gardens [1][2]. Its first director, George Bistany, was an animal importer who got the job after delivering many of the first animals [1]. The zoo was largely built in the 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project, under zoologist Edmund Heller [1]. The rules were simple: it had to be fireproof, permanent and cheap to maintain, built only of reinforced concrete, with nothing blocking the view of the animals [1]. By 1940, at a cost of about $3.5 million, it had ten structures, including the Pachyderm and Lion Houses, an aviary, bear grottos and Monkey Island, with barless pits that were then considered innovative [1]. Monkey Island was demolished in 1995 [2]. Generations of west-side kids remember the Lion House at feeding time, when "hungry lions lunging for a dozen or so raw pot roasts" held them spellbound [3].

title: A dentist's vow, rung in 44 bells
place: Grace Cathedral, Singing (north) Tower, 1100 California Street
hook: In 1875 a lonely young immigrant knelt in a church with no bell tower and promised it chimes. Sixty-five years later, his bells rang out over Nob Hill.
story: When Nathaniel T. Coulson arrived in San Francisco in 1875, he found his way to Grace Church, which had no bell tower. As he knelt there, he later said, a thought came to him: "If ever I will have the money, this church will have its chimes" [1]. Coulson was a British-born dentist and realtor, and a Methodist. He spent his life savings on that promise, and in his last years he lived on a dollar a day [1]. His gift was a carillon of 44 bronze bells, cast by Gillett & Johnston in Croydon, England, in 1938, with a six-ton hour bell. He also paid for the "Singing Tower" to house them in Lewis Hobart's Gothic cathedral, which was then still being built [1][2]. One small bell is named Sympathy after Abigail Santo, a Sunday school organist in Cornwall. When other children refused to sit near the orphaned Coulson, he had seen her cry [1]. The tower wasn't finished in time, so the bells first rang at the Tower of the Sun during the 1939–40 exposition on Treasure Island. They rang from Nob Hill for the first time on Christmas Eve 1940 and were dedicated in 1943. At first they chimed every hour through the night, until neighbours who couldn't sleep complained [1].

title: Cottages for Children Fleeing Europe
place: Former Homewood Terrace campus, Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone
hook: On Ocean Avenue, a Jewish orphanage replaced dormitories with cottages. During the Second World War it took in children who had escaped the Holocaust.
story:
In 1921 the Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum, founded in 1872, left its building on Divisadero Street for a new campus on Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone, and renamed itself Homewood Terrace [1][2]. Led by Dr. Samuel Langer, it housed children in a campus of cottages. Its own 1972 centennial history calls these "the first cottage type child care facilities in the United States" [1].

The same history says the agency grew most under director Benjamin Bonaparte, and that "during World War II, Homewood Terrace provided for many children brought from the European Holocaust." [1] Many alumni went on to careers in the professions and business, it adds [1].

In 1965, as fewer children needed institutional care, director Ralph Ross moved the children into seven ordinary houses in the Richmond District, where they lived with house counsellors [1]. The Ocean Avenue cottages took years to be torn down, and homes and shops now cover the site [1]. The agency merged with Jewish Family Service in 1977 to form today's Jewish Family and Children's Services [2].

title: Diego Rivera paints in public
place: Palace of Fine and Decorative Arts (Building 3), 600 California Ave
hook: In 1940, fairgoers could watch Diego Rivera paint Hitler, Frida Kahlo and a Detroit stamping press in wet plaster.
story:
In the fair's second season, organizers turned the Palace of Fine and Decorative Arts into a working studio called Art in Action. Sculptors, weavers, printmakers and potters worked while visitors watched [1]. At its centre was Diego Rivera [2]. The architect Timothy Pflueger, his friend and patron, had brought him back to San Francisco to paint a fresco in ten sections in front of the public. It was meant to go afterwards to a library Pflueger was designing for the new junior college [2][3].

The result is 22 feet high and 74 feet long [3]. Rivera called it The Marriage of the Artistic Expression of the North and of the South on this Continent; it is better known as Pan American Unity [3]. It includes Frida Kahlo, Charlie Chaplin and Paulette Goddard in The Great Dictator, and Hitler, Stalin and Mussolini in a war cloud. At its centre is a figure that merges an Aztec earth goddess with a Ford stamping press [2].

Then war intervened, Pflueger died in 1946 and the library was never built. The crated panels waited until 1961, when they were installed in a City College theatre lobby [2][3].

title: Hearing Lions from 34th Avenue
place: Van Dyke family home, 1727 34th Avenue
hook: A dentist's son skied the dunes on barrel staves and fell asleep to lions roaring at the zoo. Later he rode some of the biggest waves on Earth.
story: In 1940 Fred Van Dyke's parents paid $6,000 for a new Henry Doelger house at 1727 34th Avenue. Only five houses stood on the block, and nothing but sand dunes lay between them and the beach. From the windows they could see Marin, the ocean and Lake Merced [1]. Fred, born in 1929 to a downtown dentist, said the neighborhood was like a ghost town at certain times of day. At night he could hear the surf, and the lions and elephants at the Fleishhacker Zoo. By day he saw rabbits, raccoons, hawks, snakes and now and then a deer [1]. He and his friends skied the dunes between 22nd and 30th Avenues on redwood barrel staves tied to their feet, an idea they got from a movie. After big windstorms, families were "sanded in" and sometimes waited three or four days for bulldozers to dig out their street. Getting groceries meant a walk through the dunes to 43rd Avenue [1]. Van Dyke learned to bodysurf on San Francisco beaches and first stood up on a board in 1950. In the mid-1950s he became one of the first California surfers to move permanently to Hawaii's North Shore and ride its giant winter waves [2].

title: Soccer got him out of a Nazi camp
place: Negoesco Stadium, USF (near Stanyan St & Golden Gate Ave)
hook: At 15 he punched a German soldier and was sent to a labour camp. Soccer with the guards helped him escape, and he became USF's legendary coach.
story: Steve Negoesco was born in New Jersey, the son of a sea captain, and was sent to Romania as a boy to live with an aunt and uncle [1][2]. At 15, after the Nazi occupation began, he beat up a German soldier who had hit him on his own street. The soldier said "Come with me" [1]. Negoesco packed two soccer balls first and his clothes second. He was sent to a camp at Immendorf in Germany, where prisoners rolled bomb casings between factory buildings on one meal a day, and his weight fell from 155 to 135 pounds [1]. The prisoners started playing soccer, and the young guards joined in. One guard told him that if he were going to run, he would go on a Friday, when the camp commander visited his girlfriend. Negoesco and three others left that Friday and made it by train to Vienna [1]. He played fullback for USF in the late 1940s and early 1950s, took over the soccer program in 1962 and coached it until 2000. His teams won national titles in 1966, 1975, 1976 and 1980 [2]. In 1982 the university named this field after him [2].

title: The Pontiac Dealer Who Lost to a Firehouse
place: Former Sunset Service / Mohawk station, SE corner 16th Ave & Irving St
hook: A brick gas station at 16th and Irving pumped gas, sold Pontiacs, and then lost a showroom lot to City Hall by eminent domain.
story: In 1926 Charles Kleinclaus opened a gas station on the southeast corner of 16th Avenue and Irving Street. The 1930 city directory lists him at the 'Sunset Service Station' [1]. To make room for it, the family moved its house around the corner onto 16th Avenue. His grandson Jack Goldsworthy grew up pumping gas and fixing flats there, and he remembered customers by their cars: a Hupmobile he kept going, a creamery owner's Buick convertible, the Furlong sisters' Roadmaster [1]. Pumps and tyres, Jack said, 'just wasn't enough'. So the family took on a small Pontiac agency. General Motors wanted a real showroom, so they bought the vacant lot across the street. Before the carpenters arrived, a man from City Hall said the city needed the corner for a firehouse. The city took the lot by eminent domain, and the car business ended [1]. The little brick office outlived all of them. Columnist Frank Dunnigan called it one of the city's last truly old gas stations and thought it dated from around World War I, earlier than the family's account [2]. Jack lived next door until he died in 2012, aged 86 [1].

title: The city's first public housing
place: Holly Courts, 100 Appleton Ave
hook: The architect of City Hall and Coit Tower also drew San Francisco's very first public housing, on a quiet slope beside Holly Park.
story:
San Francisco set up its housing authority in 1938, using money from the new federal Housing Act of 1937. Of the first projects it started, the most prominent was Holly Courts, on the southern slope of Bernal Heights between Holly Park and Mission Street [1]. The architect was Arthur Brown Jr., the man behind City Hall and Coit Tower. His plan put 118 homes facing the street, wrapped around inner courtyards and play spaces [1][2]. A photo from March 1940 shows it still under construction [1].

Like other early projects, it was meant for the 'deserving poor' of the Depression, who were mostly white. The city's housing projects stayed officially segregated until the NAACP won Banks v. San Francisco Housing Authority, which led to desegregation in 1954 [1]. Decades later the residents were running things themselves. Karen Huggins, president of the Holly Courts Resident Council, helped write the city's 2011 community-policing ordinance and pushed for broken lights and gates to be fixed. She told reluctant neighbours to get involved: 'You'll learn' [3]. In 2015 Mayor Ed Lee toured units in need of repair with Resident Board president Deborah Gibson [2].

title: Twelve Years of Lobbying for Lincoln High
place: Abraham Lincoln High School, 2162 24th Avenue
hook: Sunset teenagers once paid two streetcar fares to reach a high school across town. Their parents spent twelve years fighting for one of their own in the dunes.
story: Before 1940, teenagers from the fast-growing Sunset and Parkside had to ride across town to Commerce High in the Civic Center or Poly High by Kezar Stadium. In 1927 the Parkside District Improvement Club began campaigning for a local high school named for Abraham Lincoln [1]. "About 3000 children from our district right now have to pay two fares to get to the high schools they are compelled to attend," activist Ray Schiller told the Chronicle, "and the cars are so crowded they can't get on them" [1]. The city finally put an education bond on the ballot in 1938. Voters passed it after the club lobbied for it [1][2]. Lincoln was dedicated on September 22, 1940: a four-story concrete building by Fred H. Meyer, Martin Rist and Timothy Pflueger [1][2]. Tight budgets kept out the kind of elaborate frieze Pflueger had given Washington High [2]. It opened with 50 classrooms, and "temporary" bungalows stood in the upper yard for more than 50 years. The school song begins "High on a hilltop, 'Mid sand and sea" [1]. After Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968, teachers Jackie Andersen and Yvonne Golden used the money raised for a memorial to buy his portrait for the library. It still hangs on the same wall [1].

title: Two hundred men, then the women
place: Italian American Social Club, 25 Russia Ave
hook: Founded in a Naples Street basement, this Art Deco club stayed men-only for nearly a century, though women had been running it for decades.
story: The club began in 1928 in the basement of a member's home on Naples Street. After a merger with the Alfieri Club in 1938, the members voted to build a hall of their own [1]. It was dedicated in 1940 just off Mission Street. Along its roofline runs Art Deco ornament in green, white and red, the colours of the Italian flag [1][2]. The members played cards, pool and bocce, and later the hall hosted wedding banquets and dinner dances [2]. Membership was a badge of honour. According to its current manager, the club once took only 200 members, all of whom had to be '100 percent Italian', and kept a waiting list [3]. That manager, Julie Clima, took over in 2005 as the first woman in the job. Her grandfather opened Joe's Fish Grotto up the street in 1946 [3]. As the old families moved to the Peninsula the waiting list disappeared, and in 2025 the club finally admitted women. About 30 joined in the first year [3]. It was added to the city's Legacy Business Registry in 2021 [2].

title: Where San Francisco's Streetcars Went to Die
place: Former Market Street Railway 'Boneyard', Lincoln Way to Irving, Funston to 14th Ave
hook: For a few years a whole block beside Golden Gate Park was filled with dead streetcars, and one boy spent hours at their controls.
story: Around 1940 the whole block between Lincoln Way and Irving Street, from Funston to 14th Avenue, held rows of dead streetcars. Rail fan Val Golding called it 'a streetcar graveyard.' The Market Street Railway parked retired cars there in the open, where they rotted fast. A small shed handled the few 6, 7 and 17 runs sent out from the yard, which also staged the extra cars for football crowds at nearby Kezar Stadium [1]. Some of the most exotic cars in the fleet ended up there: second-hand cars from Williamsport and East St. Louis, and the five all-steel St. Louis 'Sedan' cars, the company's most modern. They stayed until 1941, when they went to be scrapped. As the company switched to buses, the tracks filled with the old cars it no longer needed [1]. Golding, still under his teens, went in and 'played motorman'. Most of the controls, he recalled, 'could be operated with a wrench' [1]. He also remembered the 7-line cars racing empty down Lincoln Way late at night [2]. Two large apartment buildings and a grocery store later replaced the yard [1]. Frank Dunnigan remembers the Park & Shop at Funston and its 'modern' apartments facing the park [3].

title: Where the Catholic dead gave way to shoppers
place: Geary Blvd & Masonic Ave (2675 Geary, former Calvary Cemetery corner)
hook: The big-box store at Geary and Masonic sits on the city's old Catholic burial ground, which held out longer than almost any other.
story: Calvary, the Catholic cemetery, was the giant of the Lone Mountain group. The archdiocese received 49 acres for it in 1860 [1], and by the time it left it held about 55,000 bodies [1][2]. The Church resisted removal, believing that the dead deserved a permanent home [2]. Its lawyer argued that selling the land would not even cover the cost of moving the graves. As a compromise, the archbishop offered to let the city cut roads through the cemetery so traffic could flow between the western neighbourhoods and downtown [1]. Once the city set its 1937 deadline, Calvary quickly gave in [1]. By 1940 its dead had been sent to Holy Cross Cemetery in Colma [2]. A photograph from June 26, 1946 shows the corner of Geary and Masonic scraped bare [3]. Housing, Kaiser's hospital and a big Sears store went up on the old burial ground [3]. Today the retail building at 2675 Geary is a Target, one of two in the city that stand on former cemeteries [2].

title: 18,500 workers, round the clock
place: Bethlehem Steel San Francisco Yard gate, 20th and Illinois Streets
hook: In May 1941 machinists picketed the shipyard gate at 20th and Illinois. Within months the same yard was running around the clock, building destroyers and patching up battleships.
story:
The old Union Iron Works at the foot of Potrero Hill had been Bethlehem Steel's shipyard since 1905 [1]. Through the 1930s its workers, many of whom lived in Dogpatch, went on strike for higher wages. A photograph from May 12, 1941 shows striking machinists outside the plant at 20th and Illinois Streets [1].

Once the US entered the war, the disputes were set aside. The yard employed 18,500 people on round-the-clock shifts [1]. Its slipways turned out Atlanta-class cruisers and dozens of destroyers, including Benson- and Fletcher-class ships [2]. Repair crews overhauled the aircraft carrier Essex and the battleships California, Maryland, Mississippi, Nevada and Pennsylvania [1].

The work remade the neighbourhood. Recruiters brought in Dust Bowl migrants from Oklahoma and Texas, African Americans from Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas, and Mexican workers. With no materials or land for new housing, families doubled and tripled up in Dogpatch's old flats and cottages [1]. By the 1950 census the Potrero Hill tract had 568 African American residents, almost all of them in Dogpatch or the Potrero View defense housing [1]. Shipbuilding ended with the war, and the yard fell back on repairs [2].

title: A Merry-Go-Round Retired From the Fair
place: Carousel, Koret Children's Quarter
hook: The park's carousel spent decades in Los Angeles and a season at a world's fair before it came to Golden Gate Park in 1941.
story: The carousel in the Children's Quarter was built in 1914 (some records say 1912) by the Herschell-Spillman Company of North Tonawanda, New York. It first ran in Lincoln Park in Los Angeles, then at the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island. The city bought it and installed it in Golden Gate Park in 1941 [1]. It joined a playground that had been there since about 1888, next to the sandstone Sharon Building, a Richardsonian Romanesque canteen for mothers and children that was badly damaged in 1906 and rebuilt to its original plans [1]. Pat French Swendsen remembered the scramble at the end of each ride, with children rushing for their favourite animals and 'barely three seconds' to climb off, the tall giraffes that didn't move, and the chariots that were 'a choice of last resort' for mothers with toddlers [2]. She also recalled elephant rides at two for a nickel and grizzly bears kept in pits near the playground [2]. The carousel was fully restored in 1984 [1].

title: A Seals pitcher from Mizpah Street
place: Mizpah Street, home of the Dunn family from 1924
hook: George Dunn grew up a block from Glen Canyon's ball field and pitched for the Seals. He died aboard the USS West Virginia on 7 December 1941.
story:
The Dunn family moved to Mizpah Street in 1924, one block from Glen Canyon. Their son George was born in 1917 [1]. He grew into a pitcher who could hit, and the Examiner wrote in 1936 that "this boy wins most of his games and does what most chuckers are not expected to do, pummel that horsehide" [1]. He trained with the San Francisco Seals. In 1938 he was at their Hanford camp when Joe DiMaggio turned up to get in shape. In 1939 he tried out in front of manager Lefty O'Doul [1]. In 1940 the Glen Park Athletic Club hired him to revive neighbourhood baseball on the canyon's field [1].

That November he joined the Navy. He trained as a radioman and was posted to the battleship USS West Virginia at Pearl Harbor. On 7 December 1941 torpedoes and bombs hit the ship, and Dunn was among more than 200 men killed on board. His body was found only months later, when the ship was raised [1]. In October 1947 his remains came home under the Golden Gate Bridge among 2,967 fallen service members, and he was buried at Golden Gate National Cemetery [1]. His signature survives in a Mizpah neighbour's school autograph book, dated May 1931 [1].

title: A Secret School in a Hangar
place: Building 640, Crissy Field (MIS Historic Learning Center)
hook: Five weeks before Pearl Harbor, sixty soldiers sat on orange crates in an old Crissy Field hangar and began to learn the Army's Japanese.
story: In 1941, as relations with Japan fell apart, the Army found it had hardly anyone who could read military Japanese. Officials grudgingly budgeted $2,000 for a language school under Lt. Col. John Weckerling [1]. The school's own survey found that of 3,700 Nisei (American-born children of Japanese immigrants), only about three percent were accomplished linguists [1]. Classes began on November 1, 1941, in Building 640, a small, abandoned hangar on Crissy Field [1][2][3]. It served as office, classroom and barracks all at once. Orange crates stood in for desks and chairs, and students worked from mimeographed sheets. The first class had 60 students: 58 Nisei and two white soldiers [1]. Head instructor John Aiso drove them hard. Lessons ran ten hours a day, and some students kept studying after 'lights out' by flashlight under their blankets, or in the latrine, the only room lit at night [1]. Forty-five graduated in May 1942 [1]. By then the Army was forcing their families out of the West Coast, and the school soon moved to Minnesota [1][2]. Its graduates served as translators and interpreters across the Pacific [1][2]. The hangar is now the MIS Historic Learning Center [2].

title: A Spanish Monastery in Crates
place: Monastery stones, San Francisco Botanical Garden (Strybing Arboretum)
hook: William Randolph Hearst bought a 12th-century Spanish monastery, shipped it to San Francisco, then sold it to the city for a token sum.
story: In 1930 William Randolph Hearst paid $97,000 for Santa María de Óvila, a Cistercian monastery near the Tagus River in Spain, planning to rebuild it as part of a vast new castle at Wyntoon [1]. Julia Morgan oversaw a year of dismantling. The numbered stones crossed the Atlantic on eleven freighters and then sat in the Haslett Warehouse for ten years at $1,000 a month [1]. As his money ran out, Hearst gave up. In August 1941 his friend Herbert Fleishhacker persuaded him to sell the stones to the city for $25,000, meant to be reassembled in Golden Gate Park as a museum of medieval art [1][2]. Soon after the crates arrived in the park, a fire burned them, damaging stones and their markings. A second fire in 1958 did more damage, and the museum was never built [1]. Gardeners reused the stones in walls around the botanical garden and the Tea Garden [1]. In 1994 museum trustees released many of the stones on indefinite loan to a Cistercian abbey at Vina, where the chapter house has been rebuilt [1].

title: Hillside homes for wartime shipbuilders
place: Potrero Terrace and Annex, south slope (around 25th and Connecticut)
hook: Potrero Terrace opened in 1941 on terraces cut into the south slope. Its first homes went to shipyard families, and at first not one went to a Black family.
story:
When the San Francisco Housing Authority opened Potrero Terrace in 1941, its 469 units made it one of the city's first public housing projects [1]. Builders cut "benches" into the steep south slope, and the new streets followed the land rather than the city grid, which set the project apart from its neighbours [2]. Most of the first residents worked in the shipyards [2]. Of the Authority's first five projects, only Westside Courts in the Western Addition housed African Americans. Potrero Terrace, like the other three, had no Black tenants [1].

That changed after the war. In 1955 the Authority added Potrero Annex: 137 more units in 23 buildings, on land it described as "marginal land which perhaps otherwise would have laid undeveloped for many years" [2]. Over the decades its residents, some 1,300 at a time, included O.J. Simpson and the actor Danny Glover [2][3]. But unemployment rose and the complex's reputation sank. In 2017 BRIDGE Housing put violent crime there at five times the city average [2]. Under the city's HOPE SF rebuild, the first new building, at 1101 Connecticut, was finished in 2019. Excavators began tearing down the Annex in 2026 [2].

title: Hitler's captain on Jackson Street
place: Whittier Mansion, 2090 Jackson Street
hook: In the spring of 1941 a sandstone mansion on Jackson Street became Nazi Germany's San Francisco consulate. Its consul had been Hitler's commanding officer in the First World War.
story: William Franklin Whittier's Arizona sandstone mansion was built between 1894 and 1896 [2]. In April 1941 it passed in quick steps from the family to a title company, then to Herman Loeper on April 28, then to "Das Deutsches Reich" the next day [1]. The Chronicle later reported that the price was $44,000 [3]. The consul general was Fritz Wiedemann, whom a 1937 Chronicle headline had called "Hitler's War Captain" [3]. According to the federal architectural survey, he entertained elegantly while carrying out secret Nazi business, including trying to pressure German-Americans into "serving the party" [1]. Staff piled filing cabinets in the old dining room, and his family lived on the third floor [3]. In July 1941 he was ordered to leave. A stove near the furnace is thought to have been used to burn documents [1]. After a false start via Japan, the consular party flew to New York and sailed home via Portugal [1][3]. The US government seized the house, which stood shut through the war. In March 1950 it was auctioned [1]. It later housed Mortimer Adler's Institute for Philosophical Research and, from 1956, the California Historical Society [2].

title: Sunnydale: garden homes for war workers
place: Sunnydale housing, Sunnydale Ave south of McLaren Park
hook: Built on a hillside in the shadow of the Cow Palace as the country geared up for war, Sunnydale became San Francisco's biggest public housing project.
story: Three years after San Francisco created its Housing Authority in 1938 [2], a new kind of neighbourhood rose on the valley's western slopes. Sunnydale, designed by the architects Roller and Stringham, was built in 1941 to house war workers [1]; a 2005 Chronicle history gives 1942 and notes it became home to many returning servicemen [3]. It spread over about 50 acres: 767 single-storey units of one to four bedrooms, strung along long, winding streets south of McLaren Park [1]. The thinking of the era favoured shared lawns, laundries and play spaces. "Everything should be open, shared, so children could play," is how architect Gita Dev summed up that philosophy in the 1990s [1]. The housing was meant to be temporary, but residents stayed for decades [2]. By 2008 an estimated 1,633 people lived in what had become the city's largest housing project, known to locals as "The Dale" [2]. Its long, slow decline, and the fight over what should replace it, would shape the valley for the rest of the century.

title: The Hospital Emptied by Pearl Harbor
place: San Francisco VA Medical Center, 4150 Clement Street (Fort Miley)
hook: Four days after Pearl Harbor, 300 veterans were moved out of their brand-new hospital. Its neighbours were big guns, and the Army expected bombers.
story: In 1932 the Army handed 29 acres of Fort Miley to the Veterans Administration. Barracks, stables, a mess hall and the officers' club came down, and a 21-building complex went up for $1.25 million in the Mayan Deco style of the day, meant to look strong, permanent and efficient [1]. It opened on Armistice Day, 11 November 1934, with 25 staff doctors and 340 beds, 12 of them for women [2]. The site had one drawback. It sat in the middle of a coastal fort. When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the Army brought Fort Miley's old batteries back into service, and on 11 December 1941, fearing an air raid on San Francisco, the hospital sent away its 300 patients [2]. For the rest of the war the empty wards stood on alert, ringed by mobile guns [2]. Patients were only allowed back in 1946 [2]. The complex has been expanded several times since. A modernization programme started in 1963, and a $35 million seismic upgrade was finished in 2008 [1]. Western Neighborhoods Project notes it now serves more than 310,000 veterans across Northern California [3].

title: The last Chinese shrimp camps
place: Hunters Point shoreline (former shrimp camps, now shipyard)
hook: Bay shrimp were once so cheap that restaurants gave them away free. They came from Chinese camps at Hunters Point, until the Navy arrived.
story: For decades the southeastern tip of San Francisco belonged partly to Chinese shrimp fishermen. After a 1915 state rule confined their bag nets to the bay south of Yerba Buena Island, most Chinese shrimpers worked from docks at Hunters Point [1]. When a 1919 law forced them to sell half their catch fresh, they priced it so low that many San Francisco restaurants served bay shrimp as a free appetizer [1]. Bayview families drove out on Sundays to buy bags of freshly cooked shrimp from the fishermen [2]. The catch peaked after 1900 at 3.4 million pounds in 1935, when more than 99 percent of California's shrimp came from the bay [1]. The 1940 census counted 136 residents of "other races" in the district, most probably these fishermen [3]. Then war came. Japan's invasion of China had already disrupted exports, and in 1941 the Navy evicted most of the remaining shrimpers to expand the shipyard [1]; its condemnations initially displaced 86 homes and 23 businesses on the peninsula [3]. By about 1960 the last Hunters Point shrimp camp was gone [1].

title: The lock factory that went to war
place: Schlage Lock Co. Old Office, Bayshore Blvd at Leland Ave
hook: The push-button doorknob lock was perfected here. During the Second World War, the same Bayshore factory turned out bomb fuses and shell casings.
story: For most of the 20th century, the valley ran on Schlage time. The lock company built a 12-acre complex of factory, warehouse and office buildings on Bayshore Boulevard, its administration building designed by William P. Day in 1926 [1]. Schlage perfected and popularised the push-button lock, the little button in the centre of a doorknob [1]. During the Second World War the plant switched to war work: shell casings, bomb tail fuses, aircraft parts and proximity fuses [1]. By the 1970s it employed 1,600 people, making it the largest manufacturer in San Francisco [1]. Neighbours remember the rhythm. When the factory whistle blew at 4:30, scores of workers walked home up the hill to Little Hollywood in a slow blue-collar wave, the realtor Cathy Saunders, who grew up there, told The Frisc [2]. "Schlage Lock was one of those famous San Francisco names, like Levi's and Ghirardelli Chocolate," local historian Edie Epps said in 2014 [3]. Like those names, it left: the plant closed in 1999 [3]. When the factory was demolished in 2009, only the original office building was kept [4].

title: Two-Thirds of an Army Sailed From Here
place: Fort Mason piers (San Francisco Port of Embarkation)
hook: For many soldiers of the Pacific war, these three piers were the last American ground they stood on, and the first they touched coming home.
story: Lower Fort Mason's three wharves and Mission Revival warehouses were built from 1912 as an Army supply port, with a rail tunnel under the hill feeding tracks right onto the piers [1]. After Pearl Harbor they became the nerve centre of the San Francisco Port of Embarkation. The first convoy sent to rebuild Hawaii's military bases sailed from here [2]. Over 45 months of war, 1,647,174 passengers and 23,589,472 measured tons of cargo moved through the port into the Pacific. That was two-thirds of all troops sent to the Pacific and more than half of all Army cargo shipped from West Coast ports. The busiest month was August 1945, when 93,986 people sailed [1]. (Fort Mason Center's own history gives a bigger figure, 2.5 million soldiers [2]; the NPS numbers above come from Army records.) Liberty ships lined the piers, packed for the voyage out, and the same ships brought soldiers home [3]. The piers stayed busy through the Korean War, until embarkation moved to Oakland in 1962 [3]. One serviceman remembered steaming in through the fog in 1956 as a band on the pier played 'California, Here I Come!': 'There was not a dry eye on board' [1].

title: 'The island is ours, and that's final'
place: Naval Station Treasure Island (former fairgrounds)
hook: San Francisco built an island for an airport. In April 1942 the Navy simply took it, and offered $44,801.
story:
The Navy moved onto the island under a lease after the fair closed. On April 17, 1942, it stopped negotiating and seized the island outright [1]. The Navy filed a 'declaration of taking' rather than condemnation proceedings, a federal judge signed it shortly afterwards, and the Navy offered the city $44,801 for its improvements. The island had cost $7,874,318.01, and the city had put in $3,691,000. Utilities Manager Cahill had hoped for $500,000, and there were rumours the Navy might offer a check for $1 [1]. The city was eventually compensated with $10 million in airport improvements [2].

The lease had been 'for the duration of the war and for five years thereafter'. Fifty-five years later the Navy was still there [2]. Exhibit palaces became barracks, and the fair's food hall became a mess hall that served more than 7,000 men an hour. From 1941 to 1945, about 4.5 million servicemen and women passed through the 'Gateway to the Pacific' [2]. In 1942 the first eighteen WAVES arrived; at the peak, 800 women worked in fifteen different duties. At the war's end the base also held more than 1,300 German prisoners of war [2].

title: A Sea of Ooze on Foerster Street
place: 700 block of Foerster Street, between Teresita Blvd and Los Palmos Drive
hook: After two weeks of storms, a builder's embankment gave way above Foerster Street. The mud flipped a house and buried a cook in her kitchen.
story:
Mount Davidson's slopes had already given trouble. In February 1936, carpenter John Mickelson's house at 625 Foerster Street slid onto the sidewalk on a pile of mud, and he moved it up the street to what is now 750 Foerster [1].

Six years later it was much worse. Contractors had been moving earth to build new homes on the winding streets above. On February 6, 1942, after two weeks of storms, mud from a Bella Vista Way embankment broke loose and roared downhill "in a lava-like sea of ooze" [1]. It hit first at 375 Kenyon Avenue, a dirt lane roughly where Los Palmos Drive runs today. Dora Kammer, a 62-year-old cook, was in the kitchen when the house was almost flipped over. Her brother-in-law, steamfitter Thomas Hill, was pinned by timbers and pushed out a window [1]. Hill died two days later. Rescuers needed five days to recover Kammer's body [1].

The mud pushed 775 and 777 Foerster into the middle of the roadway, and a woman and her five-year-old walked out unhurt [1]. City photographers recorded Foerster Street buried between Teresita and Los Palmos that same day [2]. Number 785, swamped but still standing, remains today [1].

title: Detained on Silver Avenue
place: Silver Avenue, Portola (wartime detention centre; exact site not given in sources)
hook: When fire gutted Angel Island's immigration station in 1940, detainees came to the mainland. During the war, Italian 'enemy aliens' were held on Silver Avenue.
story: In 1940 fire destroyed the administration building and women's quarters at the Angel Island Immigration Station, and its roughly 200 detainees were moved to a facility on the San Francisco mainland [1]. Portola artists Kate Connell and Oscar Melara write that a neighbourhood landmark built in the 1920s became the city's Immigration and Naturalization Service station in the early 1940s, where Asians and Italians, and briefly the longshore leader Harry Bridges, were held; they note this "unsavory" chapter is "kept under wraps" [2]. Historian Deanna Paoli Gumina adds that during the war, Italian aliens picked up around San Francisco were held in a temporary detention centre on Silver Avenue and at an Immigration Service facility at Sharp Park in Pacifica; some were then taken by train under armed guard to Fort Missoula, Montana [3]. One was Nereo Francesconi, an anti-fascist announcer on Italian radio whose "misunderstood devilish wit" got him taken away in handcuffs by the FBI in front of his screaming wife and children [3]. On Columbus Day, 12 October 1942, Attorney General Francis Biddle announced that Italians would no longer be treated as enemy aliens [3].

title: Dime matinees and wartime newsreels at the Noe
place: Former Noe Theater, north side of 24th Street between Noe and Castro (approx. 3982 24th St)
hook: Kids queued for ninety minutes for a ten-cent double bill. Then the Second World War arrived on the screen, and the theatre joined the war effort.
story: In the 1930s and '40s, Saturday in Noe Valley meant the Noe Theater on 24th Street. Fred Lossman, born on Jersey Street in 1934, remembered kids arriving an hour and a half before the box office opened just to be near the front of the line [1]. A child's ticket cost a dime. Once it went up to 11 cents, and Lossman had to run home for a penny and came back to find himself last in line [1]. For that you got a double feature, a cartoon, a newsreel and a serial such as Flash Gordon. The tough boys up in the balcony flicked lit cigarette butts down onto the main floor, so the dark looked full of 'fireflies' [1]. The Second World War changed the Noe. It ran bond drives and scrap-metal drives, and even the children sat and watched the war unfold in the newsreels [1]. In 1943 Cyril Saunders opened a soda fountain across the street and named it the X from Noe. Herb Gaines bought it in 1945 and renamed it Herb's Fine Foods in 1953, as customers began staying home to watch TV. The theatre itself closed a few years later [2].

title: Enemy aliens on Fisherman's Wharf
place: Fisherman's Wharf, Jefferson St near Taylor
hook: While their sons served in the war, Italian fishermen who had worked this wharf for decades were banned from it. One was Joe DiMaggio's father.
story: Fisherman's Wharf was a community of mostly Italian families, and many of its fishermen had lived here for decades without becoming citizens [1]. Italy declared war on the United States in December 1941. Italian nationals became "enemy aliens". They had to register, carry photo ID and hand in cameras and short-wave radios, and they fell under curfews and travel limits. The rules were enforced more strictly around San Francisco than in Los Angeles [2]. Exclusion zones along the coast cost Italian fishermen and longshoremen their jobs [2]. About 1,400 San Francisco Italians were forbidden to fish, non-citizens could not come within 14 blocks of the wharf, and 650 Italian-owned boats were taken by the Navy [1]. Dominic DiMaggio later told the U.S. Senate that he came home from the war to find his parents classed as enemy aliens: "My father was forbidden from fishing or even visiting his friends at the wharf." He was sure it changed his father [1]. After protests, Attorney General Francis Biddle announced on Columbus Day 1942 that from October 19 Italian residents would no longer be classed as enemy aliens [2]. The ban had lasted less than a year [1].

title: Guarding the Pacific from a bathhouse
place: Aquatic Park and Hyde Street Pier
hook: The padlocked party palace got a new tenant in wartime: the Army command charged with defending the whole Pacific Coast from air attack.
story: After its nightclub fiasco, the Aquatic Park Bathhouse sat padlocked, opening briefly in 1941 to show Alma Spreckels' historic ship models [1]. Then came the war. The city leased Aquatic Park to the U.S. Army, and soldiers of the 216th Coast Artillery moved into the building meant for swimmers. Later it became headquarters of the Fourth Anti-Aircraft Command, responsible for defending the Pacific Coast [1]. Next door, the Army also took over Hyde Street Pier. Its car ferries had stopped running in July 1938, killed off by the new Bay and Golden Gate bridges. Now the empty slips held military vessels, including leased ferryboats and riverboats that carried troops to the Army's Port of Embarkation piers at Fort Mason [2]. When the war ended in 1945 the military handed the bathhouse back to the city. Peacetime brought gentler tenants. In 1947 the San Francisco Senior Center leased the ground floor, and the park service calls it the oldest private non-profit senior center in the United States. In 1948 the Marine Reserve even staged a mock amphibious landing on the beach [1].

title: Hands on Hearts at Raphael Weill School
place: Raphael Weill School (now Rosa Parks Elementary), 1501 O'Farrell St
hook: On April 20, 1942, Dorothea Lange photographed Japanese American children reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. Within weeks, the government had taken them away.
story: Raphael Weill School on O'Farrell Street served most of the children of the Japanese American community. Its student body reflected one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the West, and Dorothea Lange called the area "the so-called international district" [1]. In the spring of 1942 Lange was photographing the removal ordered under Executive Order 9066 for the War Relocation Authority. Between April 16 and 20 she photographed the school [2][3]. Her caption for one frame read: "Pals at Raphael Weill Public School... Yuichi Sumi (left), of Japanese ancestry, and Tommy Wong of Chinese descent, on one of the last days before evacuation" [3]. On April 20 she photographed a flag-pledge ceremony [3]. Two seven-year-olds in plaid coats stood in the front row, hands over their hearts. Hideno Nakamoto and Yoko Itashiki were soon sent to the Tanforan Assembly Center in San Bruno and then to the camp at Topaz, Utah [4]. The pictures were taken nine days after the first wave of more than 600 Japanese Americans had been removed from the city [2]. By the end of May every Japanese American family in San Francisco was gone [2].

title: Lieutenant Reagan's Desk at Fort Mason
place: Building 201, upper Fort Mason
hook: The future president's war took him no farther than a San Francisco office. Decades later, his memory of it grew a lot more dramatic.
story: When the Army called Ronald Reagan to active duty in April 1942, Warner Bros. had already won him deferments so he could finish Kings Row. He reported for duty with severe near-sightedness [3]. His first posting was here at Fort Mason, headquarters of the San Francisco Port of Embarkation, as a liaison officer [3]. The state military museum notes that a young lieutenant named Ronald Reagan served under the port commander, Maj. Gen. Frederick Gilbreath [2]. FoundSF places him in Building 201, tracking down shipments that had gone astray [1]. The job did not last. The liaison post let him transfer to the Army Air Forces, and he spent the rest of the war in Culver City working on training and morale films [3]. He left the Army as a captain in December 1945 without ever going overseas [1][3]. That is why a story he told later caused such a stir. As FoundSF recounts, citing Salon, in 1983 President Reagan told Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Shamir that his Army film unit had filmed the Nazi camps as they were liberated. In fact he had spent the whole war in the United States [1]. Building 201 now houses the national park's headquarters.

title: Orders Signed Here Emptied the West Coast
place: Western Defense Command headquarters, Main Post
hook: From his Presidio headquarters, Gen. John DeWitt issued 108 orders that removed every Japanese American family from the West Coast, neighbourhood by neighbourhood.
story: Lt. Gen. John L. DeWitt commanded the Fourth Army and the Western Defense Command from the Presidio [1][2]. After Pearl Harbor he swung back and forth. In late December 1941 he told a colleague that 'an American citizen, after all, is an American citizen' [2]. By January 1942 he was telling officials he had 'no confidence' in the loyalty even of American-born Japanese [2]. Pressed by Washington officials and by California politicians including Attorney General Earl Warren, he came to back mass removal. President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on February 19, 1942 [2]. From late March to August, DeWitt's command issued 108 Civilian Exclusion Orders. Each one was posted on telephone poles and buildings and gave Japanese Americans in a district a week to register, sell what they could, and report with only what they could carry [3]. The Census Bureau illegally gave the command confidential data to map where Japanese Americans lived [3]. By August 18, 1942, all Japanese Americans outside the camps had been forced from the West Coast [3]. At the same moment, Nisei soldiers were studying at the Army's secret language school on Crissy Field, a short walk away [1].

title: Six Greyhound Buses on O'Farrell Street
place: Raphael Weill School (now Rosa Parks Elementary), 1501 O'Farrell St
hook: On the morning of May 20, 1942, the last 274 Japanese Americans in San Francisco boarded buses outside a neighborhood school. "There were tears," the Chronicle reported.
story: On December 7, 1941, about 5,280 people of Japanese ancestry lived in San Francisco [1]. Executive Order 9066, signed in February 1942, let the Army clear them out, citizens and non-citizens alike [2]. Each exclusion order gave families only days to register at a Civil Control Station, which offered to arrange the "leasing, sale, storage or other disposition" of homes, businesses, cars and household goods [3]. The first groups left in April from control stations at 1701 and 2020 Van Ness Avenue [4]. The city's Japanese Americans reported to sites including Kinmon Gakuen on Bush Street, the YMCA on Buchanan and Raphael Weill School [2]. The last were cleared on May 20. That morning, reported the Chronicle, "at the Raphael Weill School on O'Farrell Street, they started their ride to Tanforan" in six Greyhound buses, watched by military police. "There were tears – but not from the Japanese. They came from those who stayed behind – old friends, old employers, old neighbors" [1]. By noon all 274 were at the San Bruno racetrack [1]. That night, the paper said, Japanese town was empty, its windows "plastered with 'To Lease' signs" [1]. Most San Franciscans were later sent on to Topaz, Utah, and many stayed there until 1945 [2].

title: Sixteen-Inch Guns Above the Surf
place: Battery Davis, Fort Funston
hook: The Army's secret weapon at Fort Funston could fire more than 25 miles out to sea. Today hang gliders float past its concrete casemates.
story: Battery Davis was begun in 1936 as part of the Harbor Defenses of San Francisco, the southern partner of Battery Townsley across the Golden Gate [1]. It held two 16-inch Navy guns, which arrived by rail from Mare Island in 1937 [2]. The National Park Service calls the 16-inch gun the Army's "secret weapon", able to shoot more than 25 miles into the Pacific [1]. After Pearl Harbor, soldiers worked 24-hour shifts in concrete lookouts, scanning sea and sky, and used listening devices to pick up the vibrations of ships or planes offshore [1]. The war swelled Fort Funston with 86 temporary barracks and other buildings [1]. The Japanese invasion never came [3]. By war's end the batteries were outdated and most of the post was torn down [1]. Nike missiles stood here from 1956 to 1963, and the land later went to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area [2]. Today the battery is a backdrop for hang gliders riding the cliff winds [3].

title: The Family Who Lost Their Garden
place: Japanese Tea Garden, Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive
hook: For almost half a century the Hagiwaras lived inside the Japanese Tea Garden. In 1942 they were sent to a racetrack and never allowed back.
story: Makoto Hagiwara turned the 1894 Midwinter Fair's Japanese village into a permanent garden, expanding it to about five acres and building a family home there in 1909. He kept improving the garden until he died in 1925 [1][2][4]. His daughter Takano and her children carried on [3]. In 1942 the family was among roughly 120,000 Japanese Americans forced from their homes [2]. Tanako Hagiwara was four when they left their 17-room house in the garden, first for Tanforan racetrack in San Bruno and then for the Topaz camp. She later remembered 'barbed-wire fences and sage brush' [1]. Months after they left, the house was torn down and replaced with a European-style sunken garden [1]. The garden was renamed the 'Oriental Tea Garden' and lost several buildings [1][3]. After the war the family was not allowed to return, and many of their treasures were removed [2]. Reconciliation came slowly: in 1945 the Gump family gave a bronze Buddha cast in 1790, after vandals destroyed the garden's wooden one [4].

title: Where Jerry Garcia's story began
place: 121 Amazon Ave
hook: Before the Grateful Dead, before the missing fingertip, a baby named Jerome Garcia came home to a Mediterranean-style house on Amazon Avenue.
story: Jerome John Garcia was born in the Excelsior District on August 1, 1942. He spent his earliest years at 121 Amazon Avenue, a Mediterranean Revival house built in 1930 between London and Paris Streets [1][2]. At four he lost two-thirds of his right middle finger when his brother Tiff, splitting wood, cut it off [2]. In 1947 his father drowned on a fishing trip, and the family moved less than a mile to his grandparents' house at 87 Harrington Street [1][2]. He lived there with his grandparents, Tillie and William Clifford, for about five years and went to Monroe Elementary School [2]. Harrington is a tiny one-block street between Alemany Boulevard and Mission Street, and the yellow house has become a pilgrimage site for Deadheads [4]. The neighbourhood has kept him close. The city put plaques on both childhood homes, unveiled in October 2016 during Sunday Streets in the Excelsior [3]. In April 2025 supervisors voted to add the name 'Jerry Garcia Street' to Harrington Street [4].

title: California's first farmers market
place: Alemany Farmers Market, 100 Alemany Blvd
hook: Opened in the middle of the Second World War, the 'People's Market' on Alemany Boulevard was once the only farmers market in California.
story:
On Saturdays the lot at 100 Alemany Boulevard, on Bernal Heights' southeastern edge, fills with farm stands. The city says that when the market opened in 1943 it was the first and only farmers market in California, and that it helped start the state's whole farmers market movement [1]. Locals call it 'the People's Market'. Today up to 90 small family farms and food businesses sell there, many of them part of the market for generations [2]. It is run in partnership with the city's Real Estate Division, and in February 2026 the nonprofit Foodwise took over as operator [1][2].

The market has had its own characters. For more than 15 years Jackie Jones, a Bernal neighbour, played 1920s jazz tunes on a washboard guitar at Alemany, with a wooden tap-dancing cat keeping time. In 2014, aged 88, she was stuck at home after a bad fall. Neighbours raised money for her care so she could get back to her Saturday spot [3].

title: Fifteen to a Room: The Wartime Fillmore
place: Fillmore Street between McAllister and O'Farrell
hook: In one decade San Francisco's Black population grew about tenfold, as shipyard workers from Texas and Louisiana crowded into the flats along Fillmore Street.
story: In 1940 San Francisco had 4,806 African American residents. By 1950 it had 43,460, an increase of about 900 percent [1]. They came from Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and across the South for work at Hunters Point Naval Shipyard and Marinship in Sausalito. Racial covenants and prejudice closed off many neighborhoods to them, so many settled in the Fillmore [1][2]. By 1950 about 15,000 lived in the Western Addition [2]. Conditions were grim. A 1944 survey by the San Francisco Reporter found war workers "crowded 9, 10, and 15 to a single room with only one window" [1]. Sociologist Charles S. Johnson reported that neighborhood groups and merchants were working to "restrict the area of living for Negro families to the present boundaries of the Fillmore district" [1]. Newcomers spread south along Fillmore and Webster toward Hayes Valley [3]. An eight-block stretch of Fillmore, from Sutter down to McAllister, had already become the main street of Black San Francisco [1]. The newcomers' churches, clubs and shops would soon earn the district a new nickname: the Harlem of the West [1].

title: Guns That Arrived After the War
place: Battery Chester and Battery 243, West Fort Miley
hook: Fort Miley's 12-inch guns had been written off as obsolete. Then Pearl Harbor happened. Its newest guns weren't mounted until three years after the war ended.
story: By 1937 the Army had decided that 12-inch batteries like Battery Chester at Fort Miley should be abandoned, and the fort's guns were decommissioned [1][2]. Then came Pearl Harbor. Chester's 12-inch guns were put back into service and guarded the approaches to the Golden Gate [1]. Once the Allies started winning in the Pacific in 1943, the danger of an attack on San Francisco seemed so remote that the Army ordered the guns salvaged [1]. Nearby, a new emplacement called Battery 243 was completed in 1944 for two 6-inch rapid-fire guns behind steel shields. Its job was to cover the submarine minefields outside the Gate [1]. Oddly, its guns weren't mounted until 1948, when most other coast guns had already been scrapped. The National Park Service calls it one of the last phases of traditional coastal defence [1]. NPS says Fort Miley's last guns left in 1950 [2]. The concrete gun pads still overlook Ocean Beach, and families now use Battery Chester as a picnic area [2].

title: Rustin, Mattachine and the empty YWCA
place: Japanese YWCA / Issei Women's Building, 1830 Sutter Street
hook: When Japantown's women were sent to camps, their building became a Quaker hub where Bayard Rustin taught nonviolence and America's first homophile group met in public.
story: After Executive Order 9066 removed everyone of Japanese ancestry from the neighbourhood, the San Francisco YWCA leased the Issei women's building at 1830 Sutter Street to the American Friends Service Committee, the Quaker relief group, from 1942 to 1959. It became the Friends Center [1]. The Quakers helped Japanese immigrants facing travel and work restrictions and relocated Nisei college students to schools in the Midwest and East [1]. In 1943 a San Francisco chapter of the Committee on Racial Equality (CORE) formed here [1][2]. The same year Bayard Rustin, a gay Black pacifist who would later organise the 1963 March on Washington, led a seven-week course here and visited Manzanar [1][2]. In May 1954 the building hosted the first annual convention of the Mattachine Society, the pioneering homophile organisation founded in Los Angeles in 1950 by Harry Hay and others [1][2]. The National Park Service now lists the building for its ties to Issei women, the Black civil rights movement and LGB history alike [1].

title: The Statue He Hid Under Blankets
place: John McLaren statue, John McLaren Memorial Rhododendron Dell
hook: The man who built Golden Gate Park hated statues so much that he hid the one made of him.
story: John McLaren spent 53 years as keeper of Golden Gate Park and loathed statues, which he called 'stookies' [1]. He couldn't stop donors installing bronze generals and poets, so he planted shrubbery around them until they vanished; some of the park's lushest groves exist to hide monuments he disliked [1]. When a friend insisted on having a statue of McLaren himself made, he hid it under blankets at the park stables, and it was only found after he died [1]. He was loved anyway. When he reached the mandatory retirement age of 70, the city changed the charter so he could stay in the job for life, and he died in 1943 aged 96 [1]. By then he had begun a new 25-acre rhododendron dell east of the Music Concourse, planted with rhododendrons, which grow in abundance in his native Scotland, to replace the first dell lost to Kezar Stadium. After his death it became the John McLaren Memorial Rhododendron Dell, and the National Register dates his statue there to 1944 [2]. He stands at ground level, holding a pine cone [1].

title: The cottage on Castro Street that never was
place: Castro Street History Walk plaque near 564 Castro Street
hook: 'For as long as I could remember, the small cottage on Castro Street had been home.' The line made Castro Street famous. It wasn't quite true.
story: In 1943 Kathryn Forbes published Mama's Bank Account, a book of warm stories about a Norwegian immigrant mother holding her family together in a 'small cottage on Castro Street' [1]. It became the Broadway play I Remember Mama in 1944, an RKO film with Irene Dunne in 1948, and the CBS series Mama, which ran from 1949 to 1957 [1][2]. Forbes was the pen name of Kathryn Anderson McLean, born in 1908. Her book drew mostly on the life of her Norwegian-born grandmother [1][2]. Did the cottage exist? A search of old city directories found that the Andersons never lived on Castro Street. They lived nearby at 132 and 134 Hancock Street, where Kathryn was born, and then at 22 Diamond Street by 1909, before moving to the Western Addition [1]. Even the 'Castro Creamery' where Papa washes bottles in the book does not show up in the directories [1]. None of the adaptations kept the Castro setting either. The TV family lived on Steiner Street [1]. Still, the book first put Castro Street on the national map, and a 2014 sidewalk plaque now honours it [1].

title: The surrealist who walked out of Balboa
place: Balboa High School, 1000 Cayuga Avenue
hook: At 15, an Excelsior kid had poems in a New York surrealist magazine and André Breton's blessing. So he quit Balboa High.
story: Philip Lamantia was born in San Francisco in 1927, the only child of Sicilian immigrants, and grew up in the Excelsior. As a boy he worked in the old Embarcadero produce market, where his father was a produce broker [1][2]. He was writing poems by middle school. Then he saw paintings by Miró and Dalí at the San Francisco Museum of Art and started reading André Breton, the leader of the Surrealists [1][2]. In 1943, aged 15, he had poems published in View, a New York magazine that leaned towards Surrealism. Breton called him "a voice that rises once in a hundred years" [1]. Soon afterwards Lamantia dropped out of Balboa High School on Cayuga Avenue and moved to New York. There he worked as an assistant editor at View and met Marcel Duchamp, Max Ernst and Yves Tanguy [1][2]. He came home and joined Kenneth Rexroth's circle [2]. In October 1955 he was one of the five poets on the bill at the Six Gallery reading where Allen Ginsberg first read 'Howl' [1]. Lawrence Ferlinghetti later said it was Lamantia who turned Ginsberg on to Surrealist writing [1].

title: A City in a City for Renters
place: Parkmerced garden apartments, Font Boulevard
hook: A New York insurance giant laid out a renters' utopia on an old golf course, with streets named after Anza's colonists and courtyards meant for highballs.
story: Having ridden out the Depression, the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company decided rental housing was a steadier bet. After Parkchester in the Bronx and Park La Brea in Los Angeles, in 1941 it bought almost 200 acres beside Lake Merced from the Spring Valley Water Company [1]. Met Life promised that only 18 percent of the land would be built on; the rest would be gardens and play fields [1]. Architects Leonard Schultze and Associates brought in landscape architect Thomas Dolliver Church, and they drew pie-shaped blocks radiating from Juan Bautista Circle, with avenues named for members of the 1775–76 Anza expedition [1][2]. War rationing forced a switch from steel to wood frame, but the first tenants moved into Font Boulevard garden apartments in early 1944, paying $52 to $84.50 a month [1]. A 1949 permit added eleven thirteen-story towers, the tallest buildings west of Twin Peaks [1]. One reviewer, Mark Daniels, praised the private front terraces where tenants could "serve a highball (if they dare)", though he noted the planners "had to omit provision for nudists" [1].

title: A Geneva Avenue snapshot for the troops
place: Former Amazon (Apollo) Theatre, 965 Geneva Ave
hook: In December 1944 a dozen mothers asked a newspaper for one picture: their own street corner, to mail to sons overseas.
story: The Amazon Theatre opened on Geneva Avenue on September 14, 1928, with 963 seats. It was built by the Reid Brothers a block and a half east of Mission Street [1]. In December 1944 a newspaper printed a view of Geneva Avenue running into Mission Street, with the Amazon showing 'Wing and a Prayer.' The caption spoke directly to 'you fellows' in uniform: at least a dozen mothers of servicemen had asked for the picture so they could send it to their sons [1]. After the war the theatre stayed a family place. In September 1953 it offered a $1-per-family night, and Mr. and Mrs. John Fabela of 1128 Geneva arrived with all 15 of their children [1]. The Amazon was renamed the Apollo in 1969 [1]. In the 1970s it began showing Filipino films, and one Crocker-Amazon kid remembered a marquee that stayed unchanged for months [2][3]. It closed in 1983, later served as a church, and was gutted for a Walgreens with housing above [1].

title: Eighteen years of fighting over the map
place: Eastern hilltop of the main ridge, toward Bowdoin and Ervine streets
hook: Convents, reservoirs and a housing project nibbled the park away. In 1944 city planners invoked Central Park to stop the shrinking.
story: By November 1944 the city had spent about $720,000 to buy 222 acres. The argument over how big McLaren Park should be had been going on 'almost continuously for the past eighteen years' [1]. Land inside the original 550-acre outline had already gone to other uses: the Good Shepherd convent and school, the Lick Home, two city reservoirs, Crocker Amazon Playground and the Sunnydale public housing project [1]. That year the supervisors proposed shrinking the park to about 271 acres. The Planning Commission argued for 413. Builders avoided slopes this steep anyway, it said [1]. Its report made a grand comparison, claiming that in 1905 there had been a plan to split New York's Central Park into building lots until the public protested. It recommended native plants, with the East Bay's Tilden Park as a model, and said the sunny southeast could attract tourists [1]. It also asked for the eastern ridge to reach Bowdoin and Ervine streets, so houses would not block 'some of the best views of the city and the Bay' [1]. In 1946 the supervisors settled on 318 acres [2].

title: Fifty sailors on trial for mutiny
place: Yerba Buena Island, site of the 1944 Port Chicago court-martial
hook: After an explosion killed 320 men, fifty Black sailors refused to go back to loading bombs. The Navy tried them for mutiny here.
story:
On July 17, 1944, an explosion at the Port Chicago Naval Magazine near Concord killed 320 sailors and civilians, 202 of them African American [1]. The men had loaded munitions with poor training and under pressure for speed [1]. On August 9, when survivors were ordered back to the same work with no changes, 258 Black sailors refused. Fifty were charged with mutiny [1].

Their court-martial was held on Yerba Buena Island, part of Naval Station Treasure Island [2]. It ran from September 14 to October 24, 1944 [1]. Lt. Gerald E. Veltmann led the defence, and Thurgood Marshall of the NAACP advised and drew national attention to the case [1]. All fifty were convicted and sentenced to 15 years in prison and dishonourable discharges [3]. The outcry helped push the Navy, and later the whole military, toward desegregation [1][2].

In 1999, President Clinton pardoned one of the men, Freddie Meeks [1]. On July 17, 2024, the 80th anniversary of the disaster, Navy Secretary Carlos Del Toro exonerated all the Port Chicago sailors [3]. A permanent monument to the Port Chicago 50, fully open to the public, now stands in Panorama Park on this island [4].

title: From seven Black residents to thousands
place: Hunters Point ridge war workers' housing
hook: In 1940 the census found seven African American residents in the whole district. By 1945 a third of the shipyard's 18,000 workers were Black.
story: In 1940 the two census tracts covering Bayview-Hunters Point held 14,011 people, including just seven African Americans [1]. Then the Navy took over the dry docks and needed workers by the thousand. Recruiters, railroad men and word of mouth drew migrants west from Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Arkansas and Oklahoma [2]. At its peak the shipyard employed between 17,000 and 18,500 people [2]; by August 1945, Black workers were more than a third of its 18,235-strong workforce [1]. Landlords turned many away, so federal and city housing authorities threw up 4,000 family apartments and 7,500 dormitory units on the ridge [1]. The yard itself was no utopia: a 1943 photograph shows a cafeteria that was not integrated [2]. But newcomers built fast. Women such as Katherine Newlin, Ruth Spriggs and Lucy Cupp Pickens made the cotton grommets that kept submarines watertight [3], a shipyard softball team, the Honey Bees, played in the city league against teams like Coca-Cola and Southern Pacific [4], and in 1944 residents founded the Crispus Attucks Club, named for the Black patriot killed in the Boston Massacre [2].

title: A society swimming pool becomes a lagoon
place: Tonga Room, Fairmont Hotel (terrace level, Powell Street side)
hook: The Fairmont's 1929 indoor swimming pool never really went away. In 1945 a Hollywood set designer turned it into a tropical lagoon, complete with indoor rainstorms.
story: In 1929 the Fairmont's owner, George D. Smith, added an indoor pool, the Fairmont Terrace Plunge, designed by Lewis Hobart. Building it enclosed the terrace level along the hotel's east side [1]. The 75-foot pool became a magnet for well-heeled locals and celebrities [2]. In 1945, the year Benjamin Swig and J.D. Weiler bought control of the hotel, Mel Melvin, then MGM's leading set director, was hired to turn the Plunge into the Tonga Room. He made the pool the central lagoon of a new bar and restaurant [1][2]. Apart from a late-1960s update and a 2008 restoration, it has changed little, and it still feels like a film set [2]. Musicians play on a floating barge, fake thunderstorms send "rain" into the lagoon every half hour, and the dance floor is made from planks salvaged from a lumber schooner [2]. In 2009 the hotel's owners floated a redevelopment that put the bar at risk. Fans responded by packing it, with lines out the door for months, and the plans stalled for the time being [2]. Anthony Bourdain later joked that it was "the greatest place in the history of the world" [2].

title: America's Busiest Hospital for the Pacific War
place: Letterman General Hospital (today's Letterman Digital Arts Center)
hook: In 1945 alone, more than 73,000 patients came through Letterman, many of them straight off hospital trains from Okinawa and Iwo Jima.
story: The Army built its pavilion-style General Hospital here between 1899 and 1902. In 1911 it was renamed for Jonathan Letterman, the Civil War medical director of the Army of the Potomac [1][4]. By 1918 it was the Army's largest general hospital. In 1918 and 1919 it cared for more than 18,000 soldiers home from World War I, including the badly wounded and psychiatric cases. Its doctors developed orthopedic devices such as the 'Letterman Leg' and helped pioneer physical therapy [1]. Dora Thompson, who had led the hospital's nurses through the 1906 earthquake, went on to head the Army Nurse Corps in World War I. She returned as Letterman's chief nurse in 1922 [3]. World War II made Letterman the most important hospital for sick and wounded soldiers from the Pacific. In 1945 alone it received more than 73,000 patients [2]. At times entire trains of wounded arrived from the battles of Okinawa and Iwo Jima [4]. Near the end of the war a small stockade held Italian and German prisoners, who worked at the hospital [2]. Today the Letterman Digital Arts Center stands on the site [2].

title: Big Five bargaining in a hotel penthouse
place: Fairmont Hotel penthouse, 950 Mason Street
hook: In spring 1945 the shape of the United Nations was hammered out, night after night, in a Nob Hill penthouse whose resident was asked to move out.
story: From April 25 to June 25, 1945, San Francisco hosted the United Nations Conference on International Organization. Seven hotels housed delegates, and the Fairmont became the base for the United States, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Belgium, South Africa, Saudi Arabia and Norway [1]. Secretary of State Edward Stettinius, who chaired the US delegation, took the penthouse, which had been added in 1927. Its resident, Maude Flood, agreed to move out temporarily at the State Department's request [1]. It became the room where the Big Five, the United States, Britain, France, the Soviet Union and China, met before and after consulting the other nations. "Tonight," Stettinius wrote to President Truman on June 1, "a big five meeting is scheduled at 9 in my apartment." The next day he reported progress on voting procedures, amendments and the nomination of a Secretary-General [1]. Popular accounts often say the Charter was signed at the Fairmont [2]. It wasn't. It was negotiated during the conference and signed the day after it closed by fifty nations in the Herbst Theater auditorium of the Veterans Building [1].

title: Fifty nations sign on Van Ness
place: Veterans Building and Herbst Theatre, 401 Van Ness Avenue
hook: In the spring of 1945 the world came to Van Ness Avenue. Delegates of fifty nations spent two months there writing the United Nations Charter.
story: From April 25 to June 26, 1945, while the Second World War was still being fought, delegates of fifty nations met in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. There were 850 delegates, 3,500 people once advisers and staff were counted, and more than 2,500 press, radio and newsreel reporters and observers [1]. The twin War Memorial buildings on Van Ness were the conference's home. According to the UN, the Charter was adopted unanimously in the Opera House on June 25. The next day it was signed in the auditorium of the Veterans Building, now the Herbst Theatre [1]. The War Memorial's own history agrees, with President Truman and other dignitaries signing on the Veterans Auditorium stage [2]. The city's 1974 landmark resolution, however, puts the signing 'on the great stage of the Opera House' [3]. Six years later the Opera House hosted another ending. On September 8, 1951, the peace treaty with Japan was signed on its stage. The War Memorial calls the broadcast America's first live coast-to-coast television broadcast [2].

title: From Topaz camp to Hunters Point
place: Former war workers' housing, Hunters Point
hook: As the war ended, some Japanese American families released from the Topaz internment camp found their first San Francisco homes in the shipyard's barracks.
story: When Japanese Americans were finally allowed back to the West Coast, many had no homes to return to. Their old neighbourhood around Post and Fillmore had filled with war workers, and housing was desperately short [1][2]. Hunters Point offered an unlikely refuge. As the war wound down, many white shipyard workers left the district's segregated war housing for private homes, a choice most Black workers were denied [1]. Some of the freed-up units went to 340 Japanese Americans just released from the internment camp at Topaz, the Chronicle reported in October 1945; more followed, and their children were bused to schools across the Bayview [1]. By November about 26,000 people lived in the district's war housing projects, 42 percent of them Black [1]. It made for a remarkable mix of newcomers. In the book Making Home from War, one elderly Nisei who was sent with his family to live in Hunters Point recalled running away in fear as a child when he first saw a large Black man on the street, and offered a poignant apology that had troubled him all his life [2].

title: Orson Welles names a theatre for Dorie Miller
place: Former Theater Number Three (Basilone Theater), 680 Avenue I
hook: On a December night in 1945, Orson Welles went on national radio from a Treasure Island movie theatre to honour three fallen heroes.
story:
On December 9, 1945, ABC radio broadcast a half-hour programme from the Navy's Training and Distribution Center on Treasure Island. Orson Welles hosted. The occasion was the renaming of the base's three movie theatres, until then known simply as Theater Number One, Two and Three, for three naval heroes killed in action [1][2].

Theater Number Three, where the broadcast took place, was named for Marine Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone, a Medal of Honor recipient at Guadalcanal who was killed on the first day at Iwo Jima. Theater Two honoured Lt. Cmdr. Edward 'Butch' O'Hare [1]. Theater One was named for Doris 'Dorie' Miller, a Navy cook who became the first African American to receive the Navy Cross for his actions at Pearl Harbor. He was lost with the USS Liscome Bay in 1943 [1].

The programme linked in the families. Basilone's father spoke from New York, O'Hare's mother from St. Louis and Miller's parents from Waco, Texas. Welles, who had edited the script by hand in pencil, said he hoped Miller's life and death would help enlighten others [1]. A recording survives as a 'Dorris Miller Tribute' [2].

title: The Preacher Who Ran for City Hall
place: Third Baptist Church, 1399 McAllister Street
hook: Two decades before San Francisco seated a Black supervisor, a Baptist pastor ran three times, and in 1951 he won 36,000 votes.
story: Frederick Douglas Haynes was born in Talcott, West Virginia, in 1899 and orphaned as a child. He took the pulpit of Third Baptist in 1932, when, a 1953 profile said, most members were unemployed and "often the Sunday offering did not exceed thirty dollars" [1]. By his death in 1971 the church had more than 3,000 members [1]. In 1945 Haynes became the first African American to run for the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and he ran again in 1947 and 1951 [1]. One campaign flyer read: "I have pledged myself to fight to my dying day to wipe out discrimination against minority races in the economical, political, and social life of our city, state, and nation" [1]. He never won, but his 36,000 votes in 1951, backed by the Union Labor Party, the CIO Council and the Fillmore Democratic Club, showed white politicians that Black voters counted [1][3]. The city context statement names him among the ministers who served as the community's main liaisons with the white power structure [2]. Terry Francois became the first Black supervisor in 1964, and in 1972 Haynes's widow, Charlie Mae, won a seat on the school board [1].
