title: Blabbermouth Night at The Place
place: The Place, 1546 Grant Ave
hook: While the rest of America watched Gunsmoke, upper Grant Avenue climbed into a box and ranted, with a bottle of champagne for the best speech.
story: From 1955 to 1959 a small storefront bar at 1546 Grant Avenue was a centre of Beat San Francisco. The Place was run by two former Black Mountain College students, Knute Stiles and Leo Krikorian [1]. Its walls showed work by Jay DeFeo, Wally Hedrick and Robert LaVigne. Krikorian later said Ginsberg tried out Howl there before it was published, Kerouac was "there all the time", and a 19-year-old Richard Brautigan was a regular [1]. Once On the Road came out, hitchhikers arrived from all over with their luggage, and he let them leave it there [1]. Its most famous event was Blabbermouth Night. Each week speakers climbed into a loft called the Blabberbox and talked about anything they liked. The best got a free bottle of champagne [1]. On April 15, 1957, one speaker proposed a pipe up Coit Tower that would shoot a 1,000-foot beer geyser every hour. Another proposed passport controls to "save North Beach for the Bohemians" [1]. Italian neighbours complained about the noise. By one account, audiences started snapping their fingers instead of cheering. In 1959 the poets were thrown out anyway for making too much noise [1].

title: Fifty Cents to Fly Over Sutro Baths
place: Sky Tram route over the Sutro Baths basin, Cliff House to Point Lobos
hook: For eleven years a little cable car dangled over the surf between the Cliff House and Point Lobos. Its own family called it a big mistake.
story: George K. Whitney, the showman who a Chronicle columnist said owned 'all of San Francisco west of Sutro Park,' announced an aerial tram in 1954 [1]. It opened on 2 May 1955 and ran roughly 1,000 feet from the Cliff House across the Sutro Baths basin to Point Lobos, with the Chronicle's Joe Rosenthal, the Iwo Jima photographer, shooting opening day [1]. Fifty cents bought a seat in a car of 20, all facing west toward Seal Rock; unusually, the motor rode in the car itself rather than pulling it from a terminal [1]. An operator travelled along to calm passengers startled when spray hit the windows above the rusting wreck of the freighter Ohioan in the cove below [1]. Columnist Terence O'Flaherty called it 'a kind of funicular conspiracy to further invade the private lives of the sunbathers on Seal Rock' [1]. Whitney's son was blunter: built by the Roebling company rather than bought off the shelf, the tram was too small to carry enough riders and 'couldn't generate enough revenue to pay for itself' [2]. It stopped running in 1966, the year the baths beneath it burned [1][3].

title: The Freeway That Would Have Crossed 9th Avenue
place: 9th Avenue at Lincoln Way, planned Western Freeway entry to Golden Gate Park
hook: 1950s planners drew an eight-lane freeway up through the Inner Sunset and into Golden Gate Park. Sunset families packed a school auditorium to stop it.
story: San Francisco's 1955 Trafficways Plan included a Western Freeway, roughly a straight line from the airport to the Golden Gate Bridge. Columnist Frank Dunnigan traced its route: eight lanes up the west side, a tunnel beneath the streets of Golden Gate Heights, back to the surface near the Forest Hill Muni station, then through the Inner Sunset. It would have entered Golden Gate Park around 9th Avenue, wiping out the Hall of Flowers and cutting through the Rose Garden [1]. A mid-1950s photo in FoundSF's archive marks a proposed freeway running up 7th Avenue into the park, and the plans drew an interchange for the Inner Sunset [2]. For Sale signs went up. One cold December night in 1955, several hundred residents, rallied by St. Cecilia's pastor Monsignor Harold Collins, filled a public meeting at Lincoln High School [1]. Across the city, more than 30,000 people signed petitions at meetings in the Sunset and other threatened neighbourhoods. In 1959 the Board of Supervisors voted to cancel 75 percent of the planned freeway routes [3]. The 'Freeway Revolt' had won, and 7th and 9th Avenues kept their houses and shops.

title: The Navy lab that wanted the 49ers
place: Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory, Hunters Point Naval Shipyard
hook: In 1955 a Navy scientist at Hunters Point arranged to inject San Francisco 49ers with radioactive chromium, to learn who might survive a nuclear war.
story: After the 1946 Bikini atomic tests, 79 contaminated ships from Operation Crossroads came to Hunters Point to be scrubbed, and the Navy created a research lab to study the problem, officially the Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory from 1948 [1]. In 1955 it moved into Building 815, a six-story, windowless concrete block built as a bomb shelter; that year the lab used 30,000 test animals [1]. Its radiological medical director, Capt. Albert Behnke Jr., had another idea. He theorised that elite athletes might be best suited to "rescue and survival" after an atomic attack [2]. In letters to 49ers team physician William O'Grady and general manager Lou Spadia, he proposed "special examinations": an injection of radioactive chromium and a drink of water laced with tritium [2]. A Berkeley collaborator wrote on 10 January 1955 that Behnke had "completed arrangements" for the players [2]. No final report has surfaced, but in 1994 a former lab scientist, Ed Alpen, said he was in the room when the 49ers were examined [2]. Reporters later counted at least 24 studies exposing humans to radiation there between 1946 and 1963 [2].

title: The Night 'Howl' Was First Heard
place: Former Six Gallery, 3119 Fillmore Street
hook: In a small gallery on Fillmore near Union, a young poet opened with 'I saw the best minds of my generation' and left the stage in tears.
story: On October 7, 1955, Allen Ginsberg was living on Milvia Street in Berkeley, with Jack Kerouac as his houseguest. The two took a bus into the city and got a ride from Lawrence Ferlinghetti, in his Aston Martin, to the Six Gallery at 3119 Fillmore [1]. The gallery doubled as a performance space. Kenneth Rexroth was host, and the reading began around 8 p.m. with Philip Lamantia, then Philip Whalen and Michael McClure [1]. After a short break Ginsberg started a poem he had finished only days before: 'I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness' [1][2]. Kerouac sat at the side of the low stage with a jug of wine and shouted 'Go!' at the end of lines. The crowd, under a hundred people by the Chronicle's count, joined in and burst into applause at the end. Ginsberg left the stage in tears, and Gary Snyder had the bad luck to follow him [1]. Ferlinghetti's City Lights published 'Howl' in 1956. It survived an obscenity trial in 1957 and sold nearly a million copies [1]. In 2005 the city laid a bronze plaque outside the old gallery, then a furniture store [2].

title: The Nobody Who Beat Ben Hogan
place: Olympic Club Lake Course
hook: Ben Hogan was congratulated on a record fifth U.S. Open. Then a municipal-course pro from Iowa birdied two of the last four holes.
story: In June 1955 the U.S. Open came to the Lake Course at the Olympic Club [1][2]. Ben Hogan, already a four-time champion, finished at 287 and appeared to have won a record fifth Open [1]. But Jack Fleck, 32, a municipal-course pro from Davenport, Iowa, in his first full year on tour, made two birdies on the last four holes to tie him [1]. Fleck forced the playoff by sinking an eight-foot birdie putt on the 18th [2]. There were only seven rounds under par all week, and Fleck shot three of them [1]. In the 18-hole playoff Hogan never led. He trailed by three after ten holes, fought back to one behind at the final tee, then his foot slipped and he drove into deep rough far to the left. It took him three strokes to get back to the fairway [1]. Fleck shot 69 to Hogan's 72 [1]. Adding to the sting, Fleck was reportedly playing clubs made by Hogan's own company [2]. Hogan never won another major [2].

title: The Village That Fought the Planners
place: West Portal Station, West Portal Avenue at Ulloa Street
hook: West Portal's homeowners stopped a freeway tunnel under Forest Hill and kept their shopping street from being dug up. They could not save the old tunnel gate.
story:
After the war, highway engineers drew a "Western Freeway" running north along Junipero Serra Boulevard from today's I-280. North of Sloat it would swing northeast and tunnel under Forest Hill to meet a Crosstown Freeway coming out of Glen Canyon, and many homes stood in its path [1]. On December 2, 1955, neighbourhood clubs including the West Portal Home Owners Association challenged the state Division of Highways at a meeting at Lincoln High School [1]. The fight fed the city's freeway revolt. In 1959 the Board of Supervisors cancelled most planned routes, and a 1961 vote went against the Western Freeway [1][2].

The next threat came from rail. BART's planners wanted to dig up West Portal Avenue and run the streetcars underground all the way to Sloat. Merchants who had watched Market Street torn up for BART construction defeated the idea [1].

The neighbourhood lost one fight. The original tunnel entrance, an imposing Beaux-Arts portal, was demolished in 1976 for the Muni Metro station. It had been found eligible for the National Register, but local merchants called it an eyesore. The new station cost $8.5 million, more than twice the cost of the entire 1918 tunnel [1].

title: The picture window where lesbians danced
place: Lyon-Martin House, 649-651 Duncan Street
hook: Two women bought a hillside cottage for the view in 1955. Months later a phone call in the living room started America's first lesbian organisation.
story: Del Martin wanted a view. In 1955 she and Phyllis Lyon, who had moved in together on Valentine's Day 1953, ignored a 'do not disturb occupants' sign and knocked on the door of a small house on Duncan Street. The owners asked $11,000. The couple offered $10,000, and Lyon's stash of war bonds covered the down payment [1]. They had few lesbian friends. That September, Lyon was vacuuming the living room when a woman called to ask whether they would help start an organisation for lesbians. 'OF COURSE,' she said [1]. That group became the Daughters of Bilitis, the first lesbian-rights organisation in the United States. Its early meetings and dance parties were held in the house, and some guests worried that neighbours could see women dancing together through the huge picture window [1]. Back then a car on Duncan Street was an event, the couple said: 'We would run to the window' [2]. On February 12, 2004, they were the first same-sex couple married at City Hall [3]. In 2008 they married again, legally, after a lawsuit they had joined. Martin died that August [1][3]. In 2021 city planners recommended the house become a city landmark, for its significance from 1955 to 2020 [1].

title: A car jack from Fillmore Street
place: Former Stanford hospital campus, Clay Street near Webster
hook: The first medical linear accelerator in the Western Hemisphere saved a small boy's sight in a Pacific Heights hospital, with help from a jack borrowed from a local garage.
story: In the 1950s Stanford's medical school still stood on Clay Street, next to the old Lane Hospital [3]. Its radiology chief, Henry Kaplan, heard at cocktail parties about the atom smasher that physicists on the Palo Alto campus were building. He and physicist Edward Ginzton turned it into a cancer-treatment machine. It was the first medical linear accelerator in the Western Hemisphere, installed at Stanford-Lane Hospital in San Francisco [1]. In January 1956 it treated its first patient, a boy with a tumour, a retinoblastoma, in his one remaining eye. Stanford's 2007 account says he was two, while a faculty memorial of Kaplan says he was a seven-month-old baby [1][2]. The lead shielding needed a steady mount. Kaplan remembered "the puzzled look on the face of the garage owner down on Fillmore Street" when he asked to borrow a heavy-duty car jack. It held a block of lead with a pinhole, lined up day after day for six weeks with the tumour while missing the lens and cornea [1]. The boy kept his sight [1]. The machine treated patients for 16 years before going to the Smithsonian in 1972 [1]. Kaplan also pushed, over strong opposition, to move the medical school out of San Francisco to the Palo Alto campus [2].

place: Raphael Weill (now Rosa Parks) Elementary School, 1501 O'Farrell Street
hook: When Western Addition A-1 cleared 108 acres, the plan said to demolish every building except a YMCA and two public schools. This school was one of them.
story: The Board of Supervisors approved the Western Addition A-1 redevelopment plan on May 28, 1956 [1]. Its 108 acres ran from Post Street south to Eddy and O'Farrell, and from Franklin west to Broderick. The plan called for demolishing every building except the Buchanan Street YMCA and two public schools: Raphael Weill Elementary, here at 1501 O'Farrell, and Benjamin Franklin (now Gateway High) on Scott Street [2]. Geary, a block north, was widened into an expressway [1]. Clearing the land displaced 1,350 households and 358 businesses, and a relocation office opened in the YMCA in February 1958 [1]. The area's population went from 6,112 before the project to 3,724 after it [2]. The Agency's final relocation report in 1963 claimed that "two out of three of the residents moved into standard housing" [1]. The longshoremen's union saw it differently, calling it "disgraceful that the Redevelopment Agency cannot even find two-thirds of the former residents of A-1" [3]. Most of the work was finished by March 1973 [1]. The school survived and became Rosa Parks Elementary, where the activist Mary Rogers later volunteered as a parent [4].

title: Gene Walker and the aging barracks
place: Hunters View, Middle Point Road
hook: A decade after the war, families still lived in 'temporary' barracks with iceboxes instead of refrigerators. A neighbourhood activist made the city pay attention.
story: The war workers' housing on Hunters Point ridge was never meant to last. A decade on, many Black families who had come for shipyard jobs still lived there. Espanola Jackson, whose family moved in during the late 1940s, remembered no refrigerators: "the iceman came," and people built boxes outside their windows so food would not spoil at night [1]. There was also community: Texas-born neighbours kept Juneteenth with barbecues and guitar-picking elders [1]. In 1953 the San Francisco Housing Authority took formal ownership of the overcrowded, deteriorating units [1]. Activist Gene K. Walker organised the Hunters Point Project Committee to demand repairs and a community centre, even asking for $12,000 to buy the old South San Francisco Opera House as a recreation hall; that bid failed, but it drew citywide attention [1]. In 1954 the committee pressed the Housing Authority to fix conditions, and in response it tore down most of the barracks on the ridge and built Hunters View, 55 no-frills buildings with bay views [1]. The context statement dates it to 1956; other accounts say 1957 [1][2]. Residents greeted it with enthusiasm [1].

title: Papa Gianni's first cappuccino
place: Caffe Trieste, 601 Vallejo St
hook: A window washer from Istria who had wanted to sing opera opened a little espresso bar at Grant and Vallejo, and taught San Francisco to drink cappuccino.
story: Giovanni Giotta grew up in Rovigno d'Istria, a fishing town that was then Italian, and studied opera as a young man. He arrived in San Francisco with his family in 1951 with nothing [1][2]. "We had nothing, no place to stay, no bread to eat," he recalled. Priests at Saints Peter and Paul found the family a home and found him a job washing windows [1]. He missed the coffeehouses of Trieste. In 1956 he took over the small Piccola Cafe at 601 Vallejo and renamed it Caffe Trieste. It is described as the first espresso house on the West Coast [1][2]. At first, he said, "It was all Italian people. But I got the American people to like cappuccino" [2]. Beat writers soon outnumbered the Italians, crossing the few blocks from City Lights. On its 50th anniversary cappuccino was sold at the 1956 price of 30 cents, and espresso at 25 [2]. Francis Ford Coppola later wrote much of The Godfather at a table along the back wall. For decades the Giotta family and guests have broken into opera there, with an accordion, on Saturdays [2][3].

title: The Confession Program's Paper Families
place: Family association halls, Waverly Place
hook: The government offered Chinatown's 'paper sons' a way to come clean. One confession could expose hundreds of villagers.
story: Under the exclusion laws, many Chinese entered the United States as 'paper sons', claiming descent from citizens whose birth records had supposedly burned in 1906 [1][2]. Jim Fong arrived in 1929 at seventeen after studying a 200-page coaching book on his 'paper' village and family. He passed three weeks of interrogation, then worked his way up from dishwasher to manager at a Chinatown restaurant [2]. In the 1950s, anti-communist fervour turned that history into a threat. In 1956 a federal grand jury began investigating immigration fraud, and Chinatown's family associations were told to hand over all their records within twenty-four hours [3]. The next year a 'confession program' invited people to admit false identities and adjust their status [3]. Law professor Bill Ong Hing notes that nothing in the law actually changed; many who confessed were deported, and only about 10,000 Chinese in San Francisco came forward [1]. Confessions could implicate whole networks: when twenty men surnamed Huey from one Toisan village confessed, they implicated 300 to 400 fellow villagers [3]. In 1966 Jim Fong gave up his false citizenship and took back his real name, Quock [2].

title: The Night the B-Geary Stopped
place: Geary Boulevard at 10th Avenue
hook: America's first big-city public transit began on Geary. In 1956 a new mayor broke a promise, and the Richmond was told light rail would come back soon.
story: On 28 December 1912 Mayor James Rolph opened the Municipal Railway's first lines, both on Geary: the A turned left at Tenth Avenue for Golden Gate Park, while the B ran on to the ocean [1]. It was the first big-city publicly owned transit system in America [2]. The Geary lines became Muni's busiest; the B alone needed more than 50 streetcars at rush hour [2]. After the war Muni tore out streetcars across the city, and almost every Richmond route became a bus in 1948 and 1949, but the B and C still rattled along Geary [1]. Plans for a BART subway through the Richmond gave some officials a reason to pull the tracks [1]. George Christopher, running for mayor in 1955, promised the B would stay until rapid transit plans were final; within his first year he reversed himself [1]. On 29 December 1956 the last passenger streetcar ran on Geary [2]. The 38 bus that replaced it has been Muni's busiest line ever since [2]. BART never came. As historian Jack Tillmany put it decades later, the promised light rail was 'still in the future' [1].

title: The Scenic Boulevard the Cliffs Swallowed
place: Former El Camino del Mar roadbed, west of the Legion of Honor
hook: The city built a grand coastal drive from the Marina to Ocean Beach. Wartime closed part of it, and landslides finished it off.
story: El Camino del Mar was planned in the 1910s as a scenic boulevard linking the Harbor View district (today's Marina) with Ocean Beach. In 1924 it was pushed through Lincoln Park to Sutro Heights [1]. The ground had other plans. The first damaging landslide hit in 1928, and repairs went on for decades with mixed results [1]. When World War II began, the road was closed for military safety. It was repaired and reopened to the public in 1951 [1]. An NPS photograph from 1947 shows workers putting up signs warning walkers of landslide danger [2]. Then slides in 1955 and again in 1956 persuaded the city to stop repairing it until a permanent fix could be found. None ever was [1]. Engineering studies came and went. Today only fragments of the old roadway survive, as an easy walking trail from Lincoln Park to Lands End with sweeping views [1]. The same unstable bluffs killed the Lands End streetcar line and still strand the occasional hiker [2].

title: The high-calorie Coit Tower
place: La Grande Tank, McLaren Park
hook: Everyone on I-280 has seen the Tiffany-blue tower above the Excelsior. Hardly anyone knows its name, or that it once improved the neighbours' TV reception.
story: In 1956 the city built a water tank on a hilltop at the northwestern edge of McLaren Park, just above La Grande Avenue. The 350,000-gallon steel tank stored pumped water to keep up the pressure for about 400 homes on the slopes below [1]. Neighbours found the design sleek and modern. It also happened to improve their TV reception [1]. The San Francisco Call-Bulletin said McLaren Park now had 'a monument that is as utilitarian as it is esthetic... a kind of high-calorie Coit Tower' [1]. The tower is painted a striking Tiffany blue, and Google Maps simply calls it 'The Blue Water Tower' [1][2]. When the Public Utilities Commission gave it a seismic overhaul in the 2000s, some locals pushed for something grander and 'not blue.' 'People either love it or hate it,' said park booster Linda Litehiser. The commission kept it plain and paid instead for upgrades to Philosopher's Way, a 2.7-mile trail with 14 'musing' stations [2]. SF Heritage puts the cost of the work, completed in 2008, at almost $7 million [1].

title: An office park naps on the cemetery hill
place: 3333 California Street (former Fireman's Fund headquarters, later UCSF Laurel Heights)
hook: The old cemetery hilltop was saved for a high school. Instead an insurer built a long, low headquarters, likened to a downtown tower taking a nap on the grass.
story:
When Laurel Hill Cemetery was cleared, the summit on Presidio Avenue between California and Bush streets was kept back for the future Lowell High School [1][2]. The plans changed. The land was rezoned for commercial use, and in 1953 the city sold it to the Fireman's Fund Insurance Company [1][2].

Fireman's Fund built a four-storey office complex and moved in in 1957 [1][2]. It was the new suburban-style corporate campus, spread flat across landscaped grounds rather than stacked downtown. NoeHill's Alvis Hendley called it "sort of a Crown Zellerbach building taking a nap on the grass" [2]. By the 1980s the site covered 10 acres, with a 354,000-square-foot main building and a 13,000-square-foot annex [3].

In 1985 the insurer left for the suburbs [2]. That February the University of California Regents bought the building, then called the Presidio Corporate Center, to ease crowding at UCSF's Parnassus campus [3]. The move started one of the city's longest neighbourhood fights. The spot is also California Historical Landmark #760, the site of Laurel Hill Cemetery, though by the time of Hendley's later visit the plaque had gone [2].

title: Sinatra's nightclub in a sugar palace
place: Spreckels Mansion, 2080 Washington Street
hook: In Pal Joey the limestone palace of sugar heir Adolph Spreckels played Frank Sinatra's nightclub. The real owner was a former artist's model from the sand dunes.
story: In the 1957 film Pal Joey, the French Baroque mansion at 2080 Washington Street played Chez Joey, Frank Sinatra's nightclub [1]. George Applegarth designed it in 1912 for sugar heir Adolph Spreckels and his wife Alma de Bretteville [1]. Alma was born in the Sunset District to poor Danish immigrants and modelled for local artists. Robert Aitken used her as the model for the figure on top of the Dewey Monument in Union Square [1]. She married Adolph in 1908. He died in 1924, and she stayed on in the house [1]. It became her base for charity work. During the Second World War its huge garage served as a recycling centre and air-raid shelter. A thrift shop that raised money for the Legion of Honor, the museum she founded, ran there until 1978 [2]. In old age Alma kept to herself at home and was rumoured to swim naked [2]. She died of pneumonia in 1968 and left the house to her two daughters [1]. It was split into four units until novelist Danielle Steel bought it and made it a single home again [2]. Today a towering hedge hides the facade, which Chronicle critic John King called "comically off-putting" [3].

title: A Burnt Cross on Cedro Avenue
place: 90 Cedro Avenue, Ingleside Terraces
hook: The city's first Black deputy district attorney bought a showpiece house in a covenanted neighbourhood. One morning his small daughter ran straight into a burnt cross.
story:
Ingleside Terraces was laid out with racial covenants that limited sales to white buyers. The courts later struck them down [1]. Cecil Poole, who had become San Francisco's first Black deputy district attorney in 1949 [2], still struggled to buy a house there. With a VA loan in hand, he would phone about a listing and arrive to be told it had been sold. His daughter Patti said the family got 90 Cedro Avenue only because the owner, who was being transferred to Los Angeles, sold it to them himself [3]. The fourteen-room house had been built by the tract's developer, Joseph Leonard [3].

In 1958 someone burned a cross on the lawn [1]. Patti, then about five, found it while racing her father to the garage on the way to school: "I did that one day and ran smack into a burnt cross." [3] Her mother had smelled burning the night before. The family stayed. "They got over it, though," Patti said of the neighbours. "They had to. We weren't going anywhere." [3]

In 1961 Poole became San Francisco's first Black U.S. Attorney, and in 1979 he was appointed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals [2].

title: A Pulpit for Du Bois and Robeson
place: Third Baptist Church, 1399 McAllister Street
hook: When other San Francisco venues would not have Paul Robeson, a church at McAllister and Pierce did. W.E.B. Du Bois came too.
story: Under Rev. F.D. Haynes, Third Baptist became a stage for nationally known Black figures, intellectuals and artists [1]. Du Bois and his wife, the author Shirley Graham Du Bois, chose the church for their West Coast lectures and for Du Bois's 90th birthday celebration; a 1958 photograph shows him addressing the congregation [1]. Dr. Carlton Goodlett, publisher of the Sun-Reporter and a trustee of the church, stayed in close touch with Paul and Eslanda Robeson, and was largely responsible for bringing Robeson to Third Baptist for a concert when all other venues were closed to him [2]. Josephine Baker also appeared there, and a 1958 program advertised Mahalia Jackson [1]. That year Haynes and his church hosted the National Baptist Convention, more than 25,000 Baptists [1]. In the spring of 1960 Haynes invited Martin Luther King Jr. and Ralph Abernathy to a citywide mass meeting on the treatment of minority youth in San Francisco's schools [1]. Others who used its pulpit included Adam Clayton Powell and King himself [3].

title: Carlotta's Portrait, Gallery 6
place: Legion of Honor, 100 34th Avenue
hook: Visitors still ask the Legion to show them the Portrait of Carlotta. It never belonged to the museum, and nobody knows where it went.
story: In Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo (1958), James Stewart's detective Scotty Ferguson trails Kim Novak's Madeleine to the Legion of Honor. She sits on a bench in Gallery 6 and stares at the Portrait of Carlotta, a 19th-century San Franciscan who looks strikingly like her [1]. The film uses three exterior and three interior scenes at the Legion, mostly the rotunda and Gallery 6. Real works from the collection hang in the background, including Largillière's Portrait of a Gentleman (1710), which the museum says can still be seen in Gallery 7 [1]. Madeleine drives her green 1957 Jaguar right up to the entrance. At the time a gravel road ran in front of the building [1]. The famous painting was a prop. It was made by the abstract expressionist John Ferren, Hitchcock's artistic adviser, and taken away when filming wrapped [1]. It reportedly vanished soon after the film was finished [1][2]. Vera Miles, who was first cast as Madeleine, had sat for an early version before she withdrew [2]. Visitors still turn up at the museum asking where Carlotta is [1].

title: Cleopatra Played Here for 56 Weeks
place: Alexandria Theatre, 5400 Geary Boulevard at 18th Avenue
hook: In 1958 the Richmond's Egyptian-style movie palace went big-time with reserved-seat epics. The neighbourhood lost its local cinema, and gained a parking nightmare.
story: The Levin brothers opened the Alexandria in 1923 with an Egyptian theme by the Reid Brothers; a 1941 remodel gave it a Moderne look [1][2]. On 1 July 1958, with South Pacific, it became a first-run, reserved-seat 'roadshow' house: numbered seats, tickets bought in advance, like a live theatre [1]. The runs were enormous. South Pacific played 48 weeks, Cleopatra 56 and Oliver! 43, film historian Jack Tillmany recorded [1]. He called the policy 'a mixed blessing.' Crowds poured in from all over the city, but locals who had counted on a weekly change of programme drifted to the Four Star and the Balboa, and hundreds of cars descended on Geary looking for parking [1]. The actor Richard Egan reportedly ushered here in the 1940s [1]. United Artists split it into three screens in 1976 [1][2]. It closed on 16 February 2004, a week after being sold to investors; about 100 people saw the final 4 pm showing of Miracle in the 600-plus-seat main house [1][2]. The building then stood empty for years, collecting graffiti and break-ins [2].

title: Herb Caen Coins 'Beatnik' at Fifth and Mission
place: San Francisco Chronicle Building, 901 Mission Street at Fifth
hook: Six months after Sputnik, a Chronicle columnist stuck a Russian-sounding suffix onto the Beat Generation. The word escaped his column and never came back.
story: In 1950, unhappy with his paycheck, Herb Caen left the San Francisco Chronicle for the rival Examiner. In 1958 he came back, at a salary of $38,000 [1]. Once again writing for the paper in its 1924 Gothic-style tower at Fifth and Mission [4], he filled his April 2, 1958 column with his usual three-dot items. One reported that Look magazine, preparing a picture spread on the city's Beat Generation, "hosted a party in a No. Beach house for 50 Beatniks, and by the time word got around the sour grapevine, over 250 bearded cats and kits were on hand, slopping up Mike Cowles' free booze. They're only Beat, y'know, when it comes to work" [2]. The item is traditionally credited as the birth of "beatnik," Beat plus the suffix "-nik," which was in vogue thanks to Sputnik [3]. The mocking label spread nationwide. Jack Kerouac, who said he meant "beat" to suggest "beatific," later complained that pundits including Caen had twisted it, and told a reporter, "I'm not a beatnik. I'm a Catholic" [3]. In the same column Caen quoted a salesman praising the new Bayshore Freeway: "It gets me to the traffic jams so much FASTER" [2].

title: Hitchcock's Forgotten Fort
place: Fort Point seawall
hook: Boarded up and stripped by fishermen, Fort Point made the perfect lonely backdrop for Kim Novak's plunge into the bay in Vertigo.
story: In World War II, Fort Point's barbette tier briefly held four quick-firing guns, 'Battery Point', which guarded the minefields and the anti-submarine net strung across the Golden Gate in 1942 [1]. After the war the Army had little time or money for the old fort. Visitors found the sallyport doors locked and the lowest gun openings plugged with cinderblocks. The seawall railings had rusted away, and generations of fishermen had dug the lead sheathing out from between the granite blocks to use as sinkers [1]. Hollywood liked it that way. In Dark Passage (1947), Humphrey Bogart's opponent falls from the bluff above the fort. In Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo (1958), Kim Novak's character throws herself into the bay here [2]. Real preservation came a year later. In 1959 a group of retired military officers and civilian engineers formed the Fort Point Museum Association to push for the fort to become a historic site. Their effort paid off on October 16, 1970, when Fort Point National Historic Site was created [1].

title: Hitchcock's invented grave at Mission Dolores
place: Mission Dolores cemetery, 3321 16th Street
hook: In Vertigo, Kim Novak stands at the grave of Carlotta Valdes. The grave was never real, and neither was the cemetery quite as you see it.
story: In Alfred Hitchcock's 1958 film Vertigo, James Stewart's detective Scottie follows Madeleine, played by Kim Novak, to the small cemetery beside Mission Dolores. There she stands at the grave of Carlotta Valdes, a woman said to have died in 1857 [1]. Carlotta never existed. The headstone was a studio prop that the crew left at the mission, and the mission later removed it as disrespectful to the dead [1]. By then Mission Dolores was one of the few cemeteries left in San Francisco. Most burial grounds had been moved out of the city by 1912 [1]. The real graveyard holds Ohlone people, Spanish and Mexican families and Gold Rush-era Irish immigrants [2][3]. Visitors today often say it looks different from the film. The film-makers superimposed more elaborate grave markers during production [3]. The garden that looked so mysterious on screen had its own losses. In 1906, refugees camped nearby burned many of its wooden grave markers and fences as firewood [3]. The adobe church beside it, finished in 1791, is San Francisco's oldest intact building [3].

title: Hitchcock's two Nob Hill addresses
place: Empire Hotel (later York Hotel), 940 Sutter Street
hook: In Vertigo, Kim Novak lives on Nob Hill twice: as elegant Madeleine at the summit, and as shop girl Judy in a neon-signed hotel down the slope on Sutter Street.
story: Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo (1958) gives Kim Novak's character two addresses a few blocks apart. Madeleine Elster, the doubly fictional woman Scottie is hired to follow, lives in the Brocklebank Apartments on the summit, a building designed by Weeks & Day [2]. In real life the Brocklebank was home to the Chronicle columnist Herb Caen, who rode the Powell Street cable car to work [2]. Judy Barton, a sales clerk at Magnin's, is the woman Scottie spots on the street. She leads him along Sutter Street, past a beauty salon at 916 and a tailor and cleaners at 920, and into the Empire Hotel at 940 Sutter, between Leavenworth and Hyde [1]. He watches from across the street as she opens her window beside the letter P of the hotel's vertical sign. Reel SF's frame-by-frame reading puts the window at today's room 401 [1]. Her room scenes were shot on a studio set based on 401's layout, but Hitchcock flipped it so the door is on the left [1]. The Empire later became the York Hotel. By the time Reel SF wrote about it, the hotel had been renamed the Hotel Vertigo and played the film on a loop behind the check-in desk [1].

title: Scottie's door on Lombard Street
place: 900 Lombard St at Jones
hook: Hitchcock chose a brick-chimneyed corner house for James Stewart's hero and painted its door red. Half a century of fans later, the owner walled it off.
story: In Alfred Hitchcock's "Vertigo" (1958), James Stewart's detective Scottie pulls Madeleine out of the Bay and brings her home to Russian Hill. The exterior of his home was filmed at 900 Lombard Street, at the corner of Jones, one steep block below the famous crooked street [1][2]. The interiors were shot on a studio sound stage [1]. Hitchcock wanted Coit Tower in the window view, saying in a later interview that it was "because it's a phallic symbol." The front door was painted red for filming [1]. For more than 50 years the house looked much as it did on screen, and the Vertigo fans kept coming [1]. In 2012 the owner, apparently tired of film pilgrims knocking on his door, built a wall across the entrance, added a parapet along the roofline and plastered over the red brick chimney [1][2]. Film-location sleuth CitySleuth mourned the change: "Unique to eunuch ... grand to bland." [1] From the corner you can still line up the view toward Coit Tower, though a newer apartment building now hides the spires of Saints Peter and Paul Church [1].

title: Soil from 58 counties on Nob Hill
place: California Masonic Memorial Temple, 1111 California Street
hook: When California's Masons outgrew their Van Ness temple, they built a modernist hall on Nob Hill and filled a planter with earth from every county in the state.
story: Fraternal orders boomed after the Second World War. Between 1946 and 1953 the number of Masons in California nearly doubled, to 225,000 [1]. Their 1913 temple at 25 Van Ness couldn't keep up. From 1952 the annual meeting moved to the Civic Auditorium, and an arson fire that January did more than $100,000 in damage [1]. In 1953 a search committee whose tongue-in-cheek motto was "make haste slowly" settled on the southwest corner of California and Taylor. At the time it held a gas station and a four-story apartment building, across from the unfinished Grace Cathedral [1]. Every member was asked to give "one day's wages", about $9, and each giver's name went into an open book [1]. At the groundbreaking on October 27, 1955, Grand Master Henry C. Clausen poured corn, oil and wine onto the ground. Strikes slowed the work, and on May 9, 1956, a cave-in buried two workers. One died; the other, Kenneth Archer, was rescued after three hours [1]. Albert Roller's modernist temple was finished in spring 1958, and the San Francisco Symphony gave the first concert on April 19 [1][2]. Beneath Emile Norman's memorial frieze, a planter holds soil from all 58 California counties and every Hawaiian island [1].

title: Downtown's First Glass Box Turns Its Back
place: Crown Zellerbach Building, 1 Bush Street
hook: The first big downtown building in thirty years was a gleaming glass tower in its own plaza. Its front door faced away from Market Street.
story: For three decades after the Crash of 1929, almost nothing significant rose in downtown San Francisco. That changed in 1959, when the paper giant Crown Zellerbach, born of San Franciscan Isadore Zellerbach's 1924 company and a 1928 merger, finished its 20-storey headquarters at 1 Bush Street [1][2]. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it was the city's first International Style glass tower, built soon after the Lever House and Seagram Building in New York [1][2]. It was also the first to stand apart in a private plaza, an idea later copied across downtown with mixed results [1]. Wide steel girders spanned the whole floor without interior columns, ushering in, as one guide puts it, the Age of Cubicles [1]. Market Street was in decline, so the architects put the main entrance on Bush Street and turned the tower's back to the city's main boulevard [1][2]. The site had its own history: here, in 1898, Charles Fey invented the three-reel Liberty Bell slot machine in his workshop, now marked by a state plaque [1]. Crown Zellerbach itself was swallowed in a hostile takeover in the mid-1980s [1][2].

title: Poems on the Bagel Shop window
place: Co-Existence Bagel Shop, Grant Ave & Green St
hook: The Beats hanged a policeman in effigy on Grant Avenue. Then Bob Kaufman taped a poem to a shop window comparing the officer to Hitler.
story: By 1959 the Police Department had a two-man "beatnik patrol" on upper Grant Avenue. Officer William Bigarani made it his mission to keep North Beach in line. Critics said that meant pretext arrests and the occasional beating [1]. His favourite target was Bob Kaufman, a Black poet from New Orleans and former merchant seaman who co-founded the magazine Beatitude that year [1][2]. By one account, Kaufman was arrested on disorderly charges 39 times [2]. In August 1959 the Beats hanged Bigarani in effigy from a telephone pole outside the Co-Existence Bagel Shop at Grant and Green. Police tore it down within minutes [1]. Days later Kaufman and William Margolis pasted poems on the shop window. Kaufman's imagined a bored Hitler moving to San Francisco and becoming "an ordinary policeman, dedicated... to stamping out Beatniks" [1]. Bigarani tore them down at 2 a.m. The Associated Press made it national news. The ACLU called it "a clear violation of freedom of speech", and a lawyer advised the poets to post copies all over North Beach [1]. Kaufman went looking for another confrontation and remarked, "You can never find a policeman when you want one" [1].

title: Sam Jordan, the Mayor of Butchertown
place: Sam Jordan's Bar, 4004 Third St
hook: A Navy veteran and prizefighter took over a Third Street saloon in 1959, put his own name on it, and made it the Bayview's living room.
story: Sam Jordan came to San Francisco straight out of the Navy after World War II. For a decade he worked as a longshoreman, boxed in the Golden Gloves and tried a string of small businesses [1]. As a light-heavyweight he won the championship diamond belt in 1948 [2]. In 1959 he bought the old bar at 4004 Third Street, a working-class saloon site for decades, renovated it and reopened it as Sam Jordan's Tavern [1]. There was a reason he put his own name over the door, one columnist noted [2]. Many of the old white-owned businesses along Third Street did not always welcome the district's growing Black population, and pioneers like Jordan opened places of their own [3]. His bar became a gathering spot for Black working people, hosting scholarship drives, nights for local musicians, businessmen's lunches and political strategy sessions [1]. In 1963 Jordan became the first African American to run for mayor of San Francisco [1]. He lived there from 1959 until he retired in 1995, and by his death in 2003 he was known as the Mayor of Butchertown [1].

title: The B-men and the banana gang
place: China Basin Building rail siding, Mission Creek
hook: New longshoremen got the dirtiest job on the waterfront: carrying green banana stalks off United Fruit ships on Mission Creek, nine hours a ship.
story: From 1947 to 1959 the longshore union's books were closed; there were more men than jobs. When they reopened in 1959, somewhere between 600 and 800 newcomers were added, among them Al Ohta [1]. The new 'B' men were handed the Mission Creek banana boats, because it was dirty, strenuous work [1]. Green bananas were stowed on their stalks in the hatches. One gang fed them onto a conveyor that brought them up out of the hold; the dock gang walked each stalk from the belt to chilled refrigerator cars on the siding beside the China Basin Building. Nobody wanted the end of the belt, where the fruit fell off [1]. A ship took nine hours, at $2.85 an hour, with time-and-a-half after six hours [1]. The banana gangs were known for drinking and a crap game so big that wives complained and the company shut it down. Ohta recalled a story that when a man died at a nearby bar, his buddies laid him in a boxcar so his widow could collect benefits for a death on the job [1]. In 1934 the building, which stands on filled bay, had served as the Southern Pacific wholesale grocers' warehouse [1][2].

title: The Freeway That Stopped at Broadway
place: Embarcadero at Broadway, end of the Embarcadero Freeway
hook: In 1959 a double-decker freeway opened along the waterfront. The same year, 30,000 San Franciscans signed petitions that made sure it went no further.
story: Postwar planners drew freeways across San Francisco, and in the 1950s the state began a double-decked Embarcadero Freeway meant to link the Bay Bridge with the Golden Gate Bridge [1][2]. Its first section, from the bridge approach near First Street north to Broadway, opened on February 5, 1959 [2]. It walled off the Ferry Building and left older waterfront buildings in shadow [3][4]. Opposition had been growing in neighbourhoods from Telegraph Hill to the Sunset and the Haight. In January 1959, after neighbourhood groups delivered petitions with 30,000 signatures, the Board of Supervisors voted to cancel seven of ten planned freeways, including the rest of the Embarcadero route [1][2]. Preservationists call it the first time any government body voted to stop freeways [1]. The Embarcadero Freeway stopped just past Broadway, and for decades a stub hung in the air where it was supposed to continue [1]. The "freeway revolt" became a founding moment for the city's environmental movement, and after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the structure it came down in 1991 [1][4].

title: The fight over Twin Peaks' eastern slope
place: Vista Francisco apartments, Gardenside Drive
hook: A late-night rezoning, campaign cash and a builder who boasted he'd never sold to a Black buyer. How the Peaks' east face became apartments.
story:
On October 19, 1959, San Francisco's supervisors were approving a new zoning map for the whole city. They added last-minute amendments, and one of them rezoned about 21 acres of the Gellert brothers' land on the east face of Twin Peaks for apartments. It passed 6-4 [1]. Two days later the News-Call Bulletin reported that the Gellerts' Standard Building Company had given campaign money to five of the six "yes" voters [1]. Supervisor Charles Ertola admitted taking "maybe $200" and insisted it hadn't swayed him [1].

Jack Morrison, soon a supervisor himself, called the project "the rape of Twin Peaks." He proposed that the city buy the land back for a park [1]. The parks department balked at the $6 million price. At the hearing, Carl Gellert said "Some day, these people will thank me" over a chorus of boos [1]. The Catholic Interracial Council sent the Board a letter quoting Gellert: "I have never sold a house to a Negro ... I don't think there will be any change in this policy" [1]. On December 17, 1962, the Board approved the subdivision 8-3 [1]. Today about 4,000 people live in the Vista Francisco apartments [1]. The same company had built Midtown Terrace on the other side of the hill [2].

title: The freeway Hayes Valley finally beat
place: Octavia Boulevard at Market Street
hook: Planners called the neighbourhood blighted and ran a double-decker freeway through it. After an earthquake and three ballot fights, a boulevard replaced it.
story: In the mid-1950s, city planners called Hayes Valley blighted and in need of 'social surgery'. By 1959 the elevated Central Freeway had been built through it as far as Turk Street [1]. The wealthier neighbourhoods to the north, active in the freeway revolts, blocked its extension, so the freeway emptied its traffic onto Hayes Valley's streets. By the late 1960s more than 150,000 vehicles a day came through, and by the 1970s the freeway's shadow was notorious for drug dealing and prostitution [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake shut the freeway. The damaged stretch north of Fell Street was torn down, which opened Hayes Street to the sky and helped its shops revive [1]. Then came three ballot measures, in 1997, 1998 and 1999. In 1997, Proposition H, backed by west-side and merchant groups, passed with 53 percent to rebuild the freeway, shocking residents and City Hall alike [2]. The fight went on. The final compromise ended the freeway just south of Market Street and replaced the rest with a tree-lined boulevard along Octavia. It opened after an 11 a.m. ribbon-cutting at Octavia and Market on September 9, 2005 [3]. 'Half the city wanted the freeway restored, and half wanted it torn down,' a Caltrans spokesman said [3].

title: Zen in a former synagogue
place: Bush Street Temple (Sokoji), 1881 Bush Street
hook: A Venetian-Gothic synagogue became a Japanese Zen temple, and then the place where Americans first sat zazen with Shunryu Suzuki.
story: In 1895 Congregation Ohabai Shalome, meaning "Lovers of Peace", consecrated a redwood synagogue at 1881 Bush Street. Its facade had Venetian tracery modelled on the Ca' d'Oro or the Doge's Palace [1]. As membership shrank, the building was sold in 1934 to Teruro Kasuga, one of about twenty followers of the Zen priest Hosen Isobe [1]. The Soto Mission was incorporated in 1939. During the Second World War its Japanese American congregation was sent to internment camps, and a Christian group used the building [1]. By the 1950s the Mission had grown to 250 people [1]. In 1959 Shunryu Suzuki arrived from Japan as chief priest. He had no grand plan: he sat zazen every morning in the temple, alone, until American students began to join him [3]. The former synagogue became the place where Westerners first sat with Suzuki, and the first home of the San Francisco Zen Center, until the Center bought 300 Page Street in 1969 [2]. The Redevelopment Agency bought the building in 1973, and the Soto Mission moved to Laguna Street [1]. The old temple is now part of the Kokoro assisted-living centre [1].

title: A Congregation Rebuilds on Golden Gate
place: First A.M.E. Zion Church, 2159 Golden Gate Avenue
hook: Its old church on Geary stood inside A-1. The congregation rebuilt out west for $130,000, and its pastor later sat on the Redevelopment Commission.
story: From 1912 the A.M.E. Zion congregation worshipped at 1669 Geary Street, at Webster [1]. That corner lay inside what became the A-1 project area, bounded by Post, Franklin, Eddy and O'Farrell, and Broderick [1]. The old church was torn down in the late 1950s. In 1960 the congregation rebuilt here at 2159 Golden Gate Avenue, in a building designed by the architect Robert Batchelor that cost about $130,000 [1]. The Assessor's roll still gives 1960 as its year of construction [2]. Other Black churches were making similar moves. After the war, older congregations were either full or too far from where their members now lived, and their pastors moved them to the Western Addition. Third Baptist built at 1399 McAllister in 1952, and Bethel A.M.E. settled on Laguna Street [1]. By 1960 more than a third of San Francisco's African Americans lived in the Western Addition [1]. The church also kept a voice in how the district was rebuilt. Its pastor, Parree Porter, joined the Redevelopment Commission, taking the seat of Hannibal Williams, who resigned in 1978 after calling his fellow commissioners "white liberal zookeepers" [3].

title: Fire hoses on the City Hall stairs
place: San Francisco City Hall rotunda, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl
hook: Students sang 'We Shall Not Be Moved' outside a Red-hunting hearing. Police answered with fire hoses, and a decade of protest was born on a marble staircase.
story: In May 1960 the House Un-American Activities Committee came to City Hall to question suspected Communists, including union leaders and teachers. On Friday, May 13, it let mostly its own supporters into the hearing. Students from Bay Area campuses sat down outside the chamber, chanting and singing 'We Shall Not Be Moved' [1]. Then, without warning, police turned fire hoses on them. The protesters held on at the top of the rotunda staircase 'like trees in a hurricane', the Chronicle reported, until they were washed down the marble steps while officers swung clubs [1]. 'If you know what water and marble is like, it's like glass,' recalled Becky Jenkins, then a 23-year-old San Francisco State student [1][2]. Sixty-four people were arrested. Charges against all but one were dropped, and he was acquitted [1][2]. The next day longshoremen from the ILWU joined a much bigger crowd outside [2]. HUAC's film 'Operation Abolition' blamed Communists, but on television the soaked demonstrators looked like college kids [1]. Veterans of 'Black Friday' later said it led straight to Berkeley's Free Speech Movement [1].

title: Osaka's Gift for a Samurai Voyage
place: Kanrin Maru Monument, El Camino del Mar at 34th Avenue
hook: A granite stone above the Golden Gate marks the arrival of the first Japanese ship to cross the Pacific. Its captain had never tasted ice cream.
story: On 17 March 1860 the Kanrin Maru sailed through the Golden Gate, the first Japanese ship ever to cross the Pacific. Japan had been closed to the outside world for more than 200 years, and only one of her crew had ever sailed out of sight of land [1]. San Franciscans stared at samurai topknots and paired swords. The visitors were amazed that the governor travelled without retainers and that men treated women as equals [1]. Captain Katsu Kaishu, later one of the architects of Japan's navy, said of the ice cream he was served: 'I have never tasted such a wonderful thing in my life' [1]. A hundred years later, on 17 May 1960, San Francisco's sister city Osaka presented this monument overlooking the Gate. It marks the centennial of diplomatic relations and a 'sincere desire to further strengthen the ties of friendship' [2]. The granite-and-bronze monument is part of the city's civic art collection [3]. It came just fifteen years after the war. As the Chronicle's Carl Nolte put it, relations 'did not live up to the early promise, as World War II proved' [1].

title: The Longshoremen's Answer: St. Francis Square
place: St. Francis Square Cooperative, Quickstep Lane (south of O'Farrell between Laguna and Buchanan)
hook: On land the bulldozers had emptied, a dockworkers' pension fund built a co-op where a three-bedroom share cost $610 and a family of any colour could buy in.
story: In 1960 the Redevelopment Agency set aside three blocks of cleared A-1 land for moderate-income garden apartments [1]. Lou Goldblatt, secretary-treasurer of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), wanted the union's growing pension fund put to work: "I thought there was no reason why that money shouldn't be used to build some low-cost housing" [1]. The ILWU-PMA trustees set up a Longshore Redevelopment Corporation. Architects Marquis & Stoller and landscape architect Lawrence Halprin designed 299 apartments in twelve three-story buildings arranged around shared courtyards, built in 1962–63 with a 3-1/8 percent federally subsidized mortgage [2]. A share cost $410 for a one-bedroom and $610 for a three-bedroom, and monthly payments ran from $84 to $140 [1]. The sales office advertised the Square as "open to all." In 1964 a new resident, Josephine Solomon, wrote to the Chronicle about "our marvelous, mixed-up collection of white, brown, and yellow children playing together" [3]. The co-op paid off its HUD mortgage in 2004 [2]. The city has not yet designated it a landmark, but SF Planning lists it as a proposed one [4].

title: The box Disneyland came in
place: Jack Tar Hotel (later Cathedral Hill Hotel), 1101 Van Ness Avenue at Geary
hook: It promised 'the world's most modern hotel', with a rooftop ice rink and drive-up rooms. San Franciscans called it Texas' idea of Los Angeles.
story: The Planning Commission approved it in under five minutes in 1958, and in spring 1960 the Jack Tar opened on a whole block of Van Ness between Geary and Post. Its owners hailed 'the world's most modern hotel'. It had 403 rooms, a 450-car garage and a 12-storey office block, and it was the first new hotel in the city in 30 years and the first with air conditioning [1]. Guests could drive almost to their doors, watch closed-circuit TV, swim, or skate on the roof [1]. San Franciscans hated its bright modernist skin. They called it 'the box Disneyland came in', 'the Wurlitzer Hilton' and 'Texas' idea of what Los Angeles looks like' [1]. The hotel was part of a chain named for the old slang for a sailor, and it had its moment on film in Coppola's The Conversation [1]. Renamed the Cathedral Hill Hotel in 1982, it burned the next year: two people died and 37 were hurt, and Mayor Dianne Feinstein called it 'total devastation' [1]. It was rebuilt, closed for good in 2009, and was briefly taken over by Occupy protesters before the wreckers arrived [1][2].

title: The eight-lane trench through the Fillmore
place: Geary Boulevard underpass at Fillmore Street
hook: In 1960 the city tore up Geary Boulevard and sank it into a trench. Neighbours say it became a wall between two communities.
story: Before the 1960s, Geary was an ordinary street where the Black Fillmore and Japanese American Nihonmachi met. Then the Redevelopment Agency's A-1 project arrived. Carol Cuenod writes that families and businesses were removed by eminent domain and whole blocks bulldozed, and that the first job in the cleared zone was to widen Geary into an eight-lane expressway, with tunnels under Fillmore Street and Presidio/Masonic, to rush traffic out to the Richmond [2]. Gary Kamiya dates the start to 1960, when 'Geary Boulevard was demolished and work began on the enormous Geary Expressway' [1]. For years the cleared land lay empty, and the displaced scattered [2]. Kamiya calls the result 'an ugly gash', built partly to carry shoppers to department stores on Masonic that no longer exist, and 'a Berlin Wall separating blacks and Japanese Americans' [1]. Redevelopment chief Justin Herman had warned that without housing for the poor, urban renewal would rightly be condemned as 'a land-grab for the rich' [1]. By 1967 residents had formed the Western Addition Community Organization to picket the agency and block bulldozers [1]. The dip that still carries traffic under Fillmore Street is part of that expressway [1][2].

title: A Saint's Tomb Beneath Geary Boulevard
place: Holy Virgin Cathedral (Joy of All Who Sorrow), 6210 Geary Boulevard
hook: The archbishop who led 5,000 refugees out of Shanghai built these golden domes on Geary. He now lies in the crypt as a saint.
story: When the communists took power in China in 1949, Archbishop John Maximovitch led the exodus of his Russian flock from Shanghai, helping some 5,000 refugees to a camp on the Philippine island of Tubabao while he lobbied in Washington for a change in the law to let them into the United States [1]. Assigned to the city in 1962, he found a community divided, but brought enough peace for its new cathedral, dedicated to the Joy of All Who Sorrow icon, to be finished [1]. Ground was broken on Geary Boulevard on 25 June 1961 [2]. The parish says the cathedral was completed in St. John's lifetime and consecrated in 1977; a 2010 Chronicle story gives 1974 for its completion [2][3]. He died on a visit to Seattle on 2 July 1966 and was laid to rest in a crypt chapel beneath the altar [1]. On 2 July 1994 the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia glorified him as a saint in this cathedral [1][2]. The domes still anchor what Carl Nolte called 'a neighborhood of Russian restaurants and shops' [3].

title: Diego Rivera's Mural Waits Twenty Years
place: Diego Rivera Theatre lobby, City College Ocean Campus
hook: Rivera painted his largest single mural for a college library that was never built. For two decades it sat in crates at the college.
story:
In 1940, during the second season of the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island, Diego Rivera painted a fresco 22 feet high and 74 feet long while fairgoers watched [1]. Its full title is "The Marriage of the Artistic Expression of the North and of the South on this Continent" [1]. It mixes Quetzalcoatl with an auto-plant stamping machine, and Chaplin's "Great Dictator" with Hitler, Stalin and Mussolini [2]. Rivera also painted three self-portraits and a portrait of Frida Kahlo into it [1].

The mural was meant for a new library at San Francisco Junior College designed by Timothy Pflueger, Rivera's patron [1]. The war stopped the library from being built, and its panels were crated and stored first on the fairgrounds and then at the college [1]. In the Red-baiting 1950s Rivera, a Communist, was shunned, and the fresco was still in storage when he died in 1957 [2]. Then Pflueger's younger brother Milton proposed putting it in the lobby of the campus theatre he was designing, and in 1961 it finally went on view [1][2]. On loan to SFMOMA until January 2024, it drew some 600,000 viewers. A dedicated Diego Rivera Performing Arts Center is now under construction on campus [3].

title: Jazz Moves West to Divisadero
place: Divisadero and McAllister streets (site of The Playpen)
hook: In the 1960s a string of small jazz rooms opened on Divisadero, where Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery and Ike and Tina Turner played.
story: In 1961 Joseph "Bunny" Simon, a former clerk at the Melrose Record Shop, opened his first club at Divisadero and McAllister. It became known as The Playpen [1]. In a neighborhood torn apart by redevelopment, it was a place where everyone in the Fillmore could gather. Neighbors lined up around the block to drink and dance to the jukebox, and teenagers were let in with chaperones on Sunday afternoons [1]. Upstairs, Redd Foxx, Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery, Sly and the Family Stone and Ike and Tina Turner performed [1]. Simon liked to tell how young Willie Brown opened a campaign office across the street in the early 1960s, and blamed losing the election partly on volunteers who spent their days in the club [1]. Others followed. The Both/And opened at 350 Divisadero in 1965, where Dexter Gordon and Archie Shepp made live records, and in 1967 Herman Warren opened the Half Note in a former coffee shop, with Thelonious Monk among its players [2]. The clubs were friendly rivals: each fielded a softball team, and the losers drank at the winners' bar [2].

title: Lenny Bruce Busted at the Jazz Workshop
place: Jazz Workshop (site), 473 Broadway
hook: Police sat in the audience waiting for one dirty word. Lenny Bruce gave them plenty, and a North Beach jury ended up defending his right to say it.
story: In early October 1961 the comedian Lenny Bruce played a two-night run at the Jazz Workshop, a North Beach club at 473 Broadway [1][3]. He arrived trailing trouble: a week earlier he had been arrested in Philadelphia on a narcotics charge, and on his first night he ridiculed the Philadelphia police. A newspaper wrote up the show, and on the second night San Francisco officers sat in the audience listening for anything they could call obscene [1][2]. Bruce obliged. He mocked the city's policing of gay bars, repeated a word no newspaper would print, and played on the double meaning of "to come." Police booked him at the end of the set [1][2]. His lawyer, the First Amendment attorney Albert Bendich, told the jury that Bruce belonged to the tradition of Aristophanes and Jonathan Swift. Jazz critics and literature professors testified, jurors listened to a tape of the whole performance, and they acquitted him [2]. The verdict widened the room for free speech on stage, but it also marked the start of Bruce's decline. Arrests followed in Los Angeles, Chicago and New York, and he died in 1966 [1][2].

title: Merced Heights Bets on Integration
place: Ramsell Street, Merced Heights
hook: Realtors told white owners to "get out while you can." One Merced Heights neighbourhood group answered with street sweeps, coffee and a bet on living together.
story: After World War II builders covered the empty Merced Heights ridge with stucco homes, and much of this new housing was sold to African-American families [1]. Unlike the residence parks nearby, the area had no racial covenants, and it became one of the few places in San Francisco where Black families could buy [2]. In 1950 African-Americans made up 5% of the Ingleside, Merced Heights and Ocean View census tracts. By 1970 they were 62% [2]. A 1961 Council for Civic Unity study called the OMI "a higher class Negro district" [1]. The change was not only natural. Genevieve Jefferson of Ramsell Street told the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights in 1967 that estate agents "swooped down on white people with offers to relocate" and urged her "to get out while you can" [1]. Jefferson belonged to the Merced Heights Neighborhood Association, formed in October 1961. Alongside cleanup days and lobbying for buses, it promoted integration. Realtor Julius T. Johnson hoped the races would "sit down over a beer or a cup of coffee and talk things out" [1]. In 1963 an assistant state labor commissioner called Merced Heights a model of integration [2]. Not every memory is so gentle. Longtime resident Ray Wilson recalled hearing that a Black newcomer was shot with buckshot [3].

title: Nine holes on the park's rough edge
place: Gleneagles Golf Course, 2100 Sunnydale Avenue
hook: The 1926 dream was 18 holes. What San Francisco got was a nine-hole course, a money-loser that was once the scene of a robbery on the third green.
story: The 1926 dream of an 18-hole course shrank to nine holes. Gleneagles was completed in 1961 on 60 acres along Sunnydale Avenue, on the park's south side [1]. By 1983 the city's master plan admitted that the course had lost money for years while its greens and fairways declined. New managers were fixing it up. If it ever became a liability, planners suggested, it could be turned into lawns for picnics and play [1]. The Chronicle later described the course as bordering the 'violence-prone' Sunnydale housing project. In 1995 three gunmen robbed three golfers on the third green [2]. In 2013 John King pointed out that Sunnydale's residents, on the park's southern slopes, could reach few of its facilities apart from the golf course, 'not the most logical fit' [3]. That same year, according to a park group's timeline, the course's operator signed a nine-year lease extension and started a pre-apprentice gardener program with Local 261 [4].

title: Polk Street becomes the gay main street
place: Former Town Squire, 1318 Polk St
hook: Before the Castro, there was Polk. A mod clothing shop and a record store opened by gay couples turned a street of candy stores into San Francisco's first gay neighbourhood.
story:
In the 1950s Polk Street below Nob Hill was lined with "mom and pop" shops: news stands, shoe repairers, candy stores. "It wasn't a magnet," recalled Randall Wallace, but it was "the cruisiest street in the city" [1]. Around 1960 a gay couple, August Territo and Terry Popek, opened the Town Squire, a trendy men's clothing store, at 1318 Polk [2]. (Sources differ on whether it opened in 1960 or 1961 [1][3].) In May 1961 Wallace and his partner opened Gramaphone Records nearby in a derelict old market, betting that society-page customers from Nob Hill and Pacific Heights would follow [1][2].

"Then the bars began," Wallace said. "It just began to multiply, and it was the place to be on the weekends and the weeknights" [1]. The city's historic context statement calls Polk San Francisco's first modern gay neighbourhood [3]. By 1966 there were at least 26 gay bars and businesses in Polk Gulch, and it was the first time the city's gay business owners formed an above-ground, upscale commercial bloc [1]. A bartender from the Suzy-Q on Polk became the first president of the Tavern Guild, the country's first gay business association, and in 1971 a gay magazine called Polk "the gayest street in San Francisco" [3].

title: The Hill's ladies versus the freeway
place: Pennsylvania Avenue above Interstate 280
hook: In 1961 Potrero Hill women presented the mayor with their own freeway plan while others marched outside. The freeway came anyway, and then the hillside began to slip.
story:
In April 1961 San Francisco supervisors approved a $40 million freeway to link the Southern Freeway at Evans with the Embarcadero, "nestled into the East slope of Potrero on Iowa Street" [1]. Residents remembered what the James Lick Freeway, Highway 101, had done fourteen blocks away. They fought to save the 64 properties in its path, 34 of them homes [1]. While some women presented an alternative plan to the mayor, others marched outside with anti-freeway signs. The mayor said he was impressed but had to be guided by the experts [1]. The Hill's activist women were everywhere; the press nicknamed two of them the "Gold Dust Twins" [1].

The freeway, now Interstate 280, cut off the flats to the east, which more and more people began calling Dogpatch. Residents forced out were paid well below market prices [2]. The damage outlasted construction. When the state built a big retaining wall, the ground settled under houses about 40 feet above the freeway on Pennsylvania. In May 1970 the damaged homes were auctioned off as-is. Repairs and $100 a day to bus St. Teresa's pupils were set to double the cost of the job. "This fiasco might have been avoided," the Hill's chroniclers wrote, "if they had only listened." [1]

title: The Pitcher the Wind Blew Off the Mound
place: Candlestick Park (site), Candlestick Point
hook: At the 1961 All-Star Game a gust at Candlestick made a slight Giants reliever sway. The legend that followed took on a life of its own.
story: Candlestick Park opened on 12 April 1960, built on landfill at Candlestick Point [3]. The next summer it hosted the first of two 1961 All-Star Games. The day was unusually hot and several fans collapsed, until the park's notorious wind picked up in the eighth inning [2]. Giants reliever Stu Miller threw famously slow junk pitches. He was listed at 5-foot-11, though people who stood next to him put him closer to 5-foot-8 [2]. He came in during the ninth with the National League ahead 3–2 [2]. As he set to pitch, a gust hit him. "My whole body waved," he recalled, and the umpire called a balk that moved the runners up and helped the American League tie the game [2][1]. The next day's headline read "Miller Blown Off Mound," and the tale kept growing. Don Zimmer remembered him going backward "and he just kept going" [1]. But the game wasn't televised, and the radio call, later dug up by a researcher, never mentioned the wind [1]. Miller said he had only swayed "2 or 3 inches", and he was also the winning pitcher once Willie Mays scored [1]. "I guess that's better than 'Stu Who?'" he said in 2007. "I'd rather be remembered for something." [1]

title: The red house of the sedition trial
place: Near 24th and Kansas Streets, base of Potrero Hill
hook: When the federal sedition case against a Potrero Hill couple finally fell apart in 1961, they painted their Victorian barn red and threw a party for 150.
story:
John W. "Bill" Powell and his wife Sylvia had published the China Monthly Review in Shanghai. In April 1956, back in San Francisco, a federal grand jury indicted them and associate editor Julian Schuman for sedition. The most damaging charge was that they had reported Chinese claims that the US used germ warfare in the Korean War [1]. Shut out of newspaper work, the Powells bought, rebuilt and resold old houses, starting with one on Potrero Hill [1].

Their son Tom remembers a three-room cottage on Carolina Street under the water tower, then the "house with 47 steps" on Rhode Island Street. By 1959 they were in a corner Victorian at the foot of the hill, kitty-corner from the Dutch Boy paint factory at 24th and Kansas [2]. At the old Starr King school, Sylvia had Tom sit out A-bomb drills in the principal's office. Nobody, she said, could survive a bomb in that basement [2].

The 1959 trial ended in a mistrial, and in 1961 Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy dropped the last charges [1]. Bill finished painting the house barn red. Every wooden house then was white, Tom recalls. Sylvia threw a party for about 150 professors, lawyers, union members, journalists and artists, with drums, torches and an oak cask of red wine [2].

title: The song first sung on Nob Hill
place: Fairmont Hotel (Venetian Room), 950 Mason St
hook: A ballad two homesick New Yorkers wrote about San Francisco got its first public airing in a Fairmont supper club, and the city never let it go.
story:
In December 1961 Tony Bennett stepped onto the stage of the Venetian Room, the Fairmont Hotel's supper club, and sang "I Left My Heart in San Francisco" in public for the very first time [1][2]. Released on record the following year, the 1962 ballad became either the city's ultimate ode or its most overplayed cliché, depending on whom you ask [1].

The bond lasted six decades. When Mayor Dianne Feinstein passed the hat to save the crumbling cable cars in the early 1980s, Bennett was among the stars who lent their names [3]. In June 2018 the city renamed the block of Mason Street in front of the Fairmont "Tony Bennett Way." A stuntman dressed as the singer rappelled down the hotel's facade to open the party, and then the real Bennett, aged 91, took the stage: "It's so beautiful. The sun is out and it's San Francisco at its best right now," he said [2].

On 25 April 2020, with the city sheltering from COVID-19, residents were invited to sing the song together from windows and balconies at noon as a salute to health workers, and Bennett released a fresh rendition for them to sing along to [1].

title: Who Rolled the First Mission Burrito?
place: El Faro, 2399 Folsom St at 20th
hook: Some firemen wanted sandwiches. The grocer had none. The next day he had something else, wrapped in three overlapping tortillas.
story: Febronio Ontiveros and his wife opened a corner grocery, El Faro ("the lighthouse"), at 2399 Folsom Street on September 25, 1961 [1]. The next day, by Ontiveros's account, firemen from a station down the street came in wanting sandwiches. He had none, so he returned ready with burritos [1]. Large tortillas were not sold commercially then, so he overlapped three six-inch ones and charged a dollar [1]. The title is contested. At Mi Rancho market on 20th Street, a woman named Juanita Villalobos served burritos from around 1965; its manager conceded, "He had 'em before we did" [1]. On Valencia Street, Raul Duran of La Cumbre dates his first burrito to September 29, 1969, "because it was my wife's birthday" [2]. In 1972 he and his wife Micaela turned their meat market into a taqueria, and he says the new thing was the style of service: "Taquerias were new. No one had anything like that" [2]. By 1993, SF Weekly estimated the Mission was eating about 25,000 burritos a day [1].

title: Fire in the tunnel under the hill
place: 19th and Arkansas Streets, above the old Western Pacific tunnel
hook: In summer 1962 a fire burned inside a railroad tunnel under Potrero Hill. As its timbers gave way, the ground sank beneath houses at 19th and Arkansas.
story:
Western Pacific trains ran through a tunnel under the north side of Potrero Hill, coming out near Mariposa and Carolina Streets [1]. At the end of June 1962 the tunnel caught fire. Photographs from June 30 and July 1 show the scene at Texas and Sierra, Missouri and Sierra, 23rd and Pennsylvania, and at the tunnel's north mouth [1]. The fire weakened the tunnel's wooden supports and it collapsed [2].

The Hill's own history records homes at Arkansas and 19th collapsing, and houses on Missouri between 20th and 22nd cracking and settling [3]. The dates don't agree. That timeline puts the Arkansas Street collapse in July 1962. Another dates it to July 1960, with a separate Missouri Street collapse in 1962 [4]. A photo caption also shows a hole at Arkansas and 19th in July 1960 [1].

The city plugged both ends of the tunnel with concrete and the railroad abandoned it. The city demanded $781,000 and settled with Western Pacific for $700,000 in 1964 [1]. The slope above stayed empty for thirty years. After a neighbourhood fight to keep it as open space, lofts were built where the tunnel had caved in [2].

title: The night the Van Ness cathedral burned
place: Site of the second St. Mary's Cathedral, Van Ness Avenue at O'Farrell Street (1001 Van Ness)
hook: For 71 years a red-brick Gothic cathedral climbed steep stairs at Van Ness and O'Farrell. On a September night in 1962 it went up in flames.
story: In May 1887 Catholics laid the cornerstone of San Francisco's second cathedral at the corner of Van Ness Avenue and O'Farrell Street, and after four years of building it was dedicated in January 1891 [1]. It was a red-brick Gothic Revival church with steep front stairs and a rose window [1]. Nearly two decades later, on 18 April 1906, firefighters trying to stop the post-earthquake fire set off dynamite a block away at O'Farrell and Van Ness [3]. On the evening of 7 September 1962, a huge fire destroyed the cathedral [1][2]. Archbishop Joseph McGucken first wanted to rebuild right there, in 'a modern, contemporary design, but not what most people call modernistic' [1]. Instead the corner was judged too small. After tense negotiations and land trades, the archdiocese got a new hilltop site at Gough and Geary, and KRON-TV got the old cathedral corner for its offices and studios [1]. A 1959 photograph looking up O'Farrell from Van Ness shows the brick cathedral with St. Mark's Lutheran on the hill behind it [3]. That is one of the last views of the corner before it became a TV station.

title: The tower that promised beauty
place: Microwave tower, Bernal Heights summit
hook: In 1962 a newspaper called Bernal Hill ugly and promised that a phone company relay tower would make it beautiful.
story:
On May 31, 1962, the News-Call Bulletin ran the headline 'Ugly Hill to Be Beautified'. Pacific Telephone had paid $90,000 for just over an acre on the 430-foot summit of Bernal Heights. It planned a $2 million, 400-circuit microwave relay station there, one link in a nationwide chain [1]. City planner Ruth Joffe worked with the company to curve the access road and the building's roof to follow the hill. Her idea of making the antenna a free-form sculpture was 'reluctantly abandoned as not feasible'. The company promised trees, wild lilac and manzanita. It also promised to use its excavated rock to cover a scar left by 30 years of city quarrying, and it promised no fences [1].

A neighbour's history dates the finished tower to 1962, inside a minimal chain-link fence [2]. Greta Van Praag of Prospect Avenue led a campaign to plant pines that would soften its outline [2]. The neighbourhood blog Bernalwood nicknames it 'Sutrito Tower', though Sutro Tower did not exist for its first decade [1]. Some residents still wish it gone. A few, one neighbour wrote, call it Bernal's Eiffel Tower [2].

title: A ferry pier becomes a harbor of ghosts
place: Hyde Street Pier, foot of Hyde St
hook: A movie 'pirate ship' rusting in Sausalito, a museum founder with a passion for sail, and a dead ferry pier: together they made a floating museum.
story: Hyde Street Pier opened in 1922 as a car-ferry landing for Sausalito, and the last ferry left on July 25, 1938 [1]. It came back to life thanks to Karl Kortum, a maritime historian who loved the age of sail. In 1951 he founded the San Francisco Maritime Museum in the empty upper floors of the Aquatic Park Bathhouse [2]. In 1954 the museum, led by Kortum and Alma Spreckels, paid $25,000 for the Pacific Queen, a rusting square-rigger in Sausalito. She had been launched in Scotland in 1886 as Balclutha, sailed 17 times around Cape Horn, and later appeared in Mutiny on the Bounty and toured the coast as a "pirate ship." Local people gave cash, materials and labor to restore her and her original name [3]. Their efforts led to a state historical monument in September 1957. The state leased the pier in 1961, rebuilt it in 1962 and 1963, and opened the Maritime State Historical Park on October 5, 1963. In 1988 it became part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park, and the park still docks its historic fleet at the pier [1].
