title: Longshoremen build a garden in the rubble
place: St. Francis Square Cooperative, Geary to O'Farrell between Laguna and Webster
hook: Redevelopment had flattened the blocks. A dockworkers' pension fund bet it could build the West Coast's first racially integrated housing co-op there.
story: By 1960, bulldozed land around Geary had sat empty for years, while developers planned luxury towers on a hill newly renamed 'Cathedral Hill' [1]. Lou Goldblatt, secretary-treasurer of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, had another idea. 'There was no reason why the pension funds... should just be laying around being invested in high grade securities,' he recalled, when the money could 'build some low-cost housing' [1]. Justin Herman of the Redevelopment Agency offered three blocks for moderate-income garden apartments. The ILWU-PMA pension fund, shared by the union and the shipowners' Pacific Maritime Association, sponsored the project [1]. Built in 1962 and 1963, St. Francis Square had to fit what working families could pay: a $410 to $610 share, then $84 to $140 a month, with utilities and taxes included [1]. Two streets were closed to make a superblock. Twelve three-storey buildings by Marquis & Stoller surround three shared gardens by landscape architect Lawrence Halprin, designed around Jane Jacobs' 'eyes on the street' [2]. The Cultural Landscape Foundation calls it the first racially integrated housing cooperative on the West Coast [2]. At the 1963 dedication Harry Bridges credited Goldblatt as 'the man with the imagination and drive' [1].

title: The Castro's first gay bar
place: Missouri Mule, 2348 Market St
hook: Before rainbow flags, the Castro was an Irish-Catholic parish emptying out for the suburbs. Then a tavern on Market Street got a new owner and a piano singer.
story: In the 1950s and 1960s, Eureka Valley was a working-class, largely Irish-Catholic district whose families were leaving their Victorians for new houses in the Sunset, the Peninsula, Marin and the East Bay [1]. The empty flats and cheap rents left space for something new. In 1963 John Burgoa took over the Missouri Mule at 2348 Market Street, a tavern that had run as a straight bar under the same name for more than a decade, and it became what historians count as the Castro's first gay bar [1][2]. Burgoa ran it until 1973. Its star was a 'campy' singer called Vivacious Vivian, who played honky-tonk piano while, in one recollection, 'all order of gay men gathered round' [1]. Others soon followed: the Honey Bucket at 4146 18th Street, The Mistake at 3988 18th, and restaurants like Burke's Corner House [1]. Public historian Gerard Koskovich describes the whole area as a 'declining working-class neighborhood' that was already turning into a gay enclave. By the early 1970s, he says, it 'was becoming very clearly marked as a gay neighborhood' [2].

title: The Mayor of Butchertown Runs for Mayor
place: Sam Jordan's Bar, 4004 Third Street
hook: A Navy veteran and Golden Gloves boxer turned a Third Street tavern into Bayview's living room, then became the first African American to run for mayor of San Francisco.
story: Sam Jordan came to San Francisco from Texas after serving in the Navy in World War II. He spent about ten years as a longshoreman and boxed in the Golden Gloves, where he won as a light-heavyweight [1][2]. In 1959 he bought the old tavern at 4004–4006 Third Street, fixed it up and reopened it as Sam Jordan's Tavern [1]. It quickly became the gathering place of Bayview's Black working class, with scholarship drives, nights for local musicians, businessmen's lunches and political strategy sessions [1]. In 1963 Jordan became the first African American to run for mayor of San Francisco. He ran on equality, civil rights and workers' rights and finished fourth of eight [1][2]. Neighbours called him the "Mayor of Butchertown," after the district's old slaughterhouse trade. He wasn't sure he deserved it: "What good is it to be called a leader if you can't get people to do for themselves?" [3]. He lived at the bar until he retired in 1995 and died in 2003, and the building became City Landmark No. 263 [1]. His children kept it going through a TV makeover and heavy debt. In 2019 they announced it would close, with a last-call block party that November [2].

title: The Sun-Reporter's Upstairs Room on Turk
place: 1366 Turk Street (site of Dr. Goodlett's office and the Sun-Reporter)
hook: A doctor who won a newspaper in a poker game moved it to Turk Street, where Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali and future mayors came upstairs.
story: Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett came to San Francisco in 1945 and opened a medical practice. He soon invested with the dentist Daniel Collins in the Reporter, a Black paper founded in the Fillmore during the war [1]. The paper's longtime editor, Thomas Fleming, later told the story of how they got a second paper, the Sun: its white owner lost about $2,500 to Goodlett at poker one night and offered him the Sun for $1,500 [2]. The two papers became the Sun-Reporter, with the motto "That no good cause shall lack a champion, and that evil shall not thrive unopposed" [2]. The sources disagree on some early dates. In 1963 Goodlett moved both his medical office and the paper to his new building at 1366 Turk Street [1][2]. Its upstairs Community Room became a hub: Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, Dick Gregory and the Black Panthers came through, and politicians from Willie Brown to George Moscone stopped by for advice [2]. Goodlett also led the local NAACP and in 1966 ran for governor, finishing third in the Democratic primary [1][2]. He died in 1997. The Turk Street building is gone [1].

title: The freeway that became a bike path
place: Mansell Street through McLaren Park
hook: Ever wondered why Mansell Street is so absurdly wide? It was meant to be a crosstown parkway that never came.
story: Mansell Street is suspiciously wide. In 1951 a redevelopment study proposed a seven-and-a-half-mile 'John McLaren Parkway' from Lake Merced to Bayview Park, running along Mansell [1]. Only one section was built, a four-lane divided road through the park from Brazil Avenue east toward San Bruno Avenue. It was finished in 1963 [1][2]. Then Interstate 280 was built and the crosstown route was dropped. The 1983 master plan bluntly called the leftover road 'an unneeded anachronism' [1]. For decades it cut the park in half. The Chronicle noted in 2004 that most San Franciscans knew the park mainly as a shortcut to Candlestick Park, and a visiting class spotted fresh skid marks from drivers using Mansell as a speedway [3]. In 2013 the Recreation and Park Commission approved a plan to close one side of the median to cars and give it to people walking and cycling. The other side would carry one lane of traffic each way, including Muni's 29-Sunset [4]. The rebuilt road reopened in February 2017 [2].

title: The pastor who took down the cross
place: Glide Memorial Church, 330 Ellis St at Taylor
hook: When Cecil Williams arrived, Glide's congregation was down to a handful. He opened the doors to addicts, sex workers and gay runaways, and it grew into a phenomenon.
story: In 1962 Glide Memorial, a well-endowed Methodist church at Ellis and Taylor, hired the Rev. Lewis Durham to rethink its mission. Durham brought in young clergy, among them Cecil Williams, the grandson of a slave from segregated San Angelo, Texas, who arrived in 1963 [1][2]. Randy Shaw, who wrote a history of the neighbourhood, says the congregation was 'almost down to the single digits' [2]. Williams rebuilt it by becoming a fierce advocate for civil rights and, most controversially then, for gay and transgender people at a time when police were arresting them in bars [2]. Glide's pastors worked with sex workers, runaways, hippies and addicts. In the early 1970s an activist said: 'You knew where the women's movement was: it was at Glide church at 7:30' [1]. Williams took the crucifix out of the sanctuary. A 1995 Chronicle profile dates this to 1965, while other accounts say 1967 [3]. Sunday services, with a gospel choir and jazz band, became joyous celebrations [2][3]. In 1980 Glide started a free meals programme serving three hot meals a day [2]. Williams stepped down as pastor in 2000 and died in 2024, aged 94 [2].

title: A model-yacht pond that wanted to be marsh
place: McNab Lake, beside Louis Sutter Playground
hook: The lake was built for toy sailboats with state money. Nature, and the state's accountants, have had opinions ever since.
story: McNab Lake, in the park's northeast corner next to Louis Sutter Playground, was built in 1964 as a basin for model yachts. The State of California paid for it [1][2]. It was designed as part of the hillside's natural drainage. Water from the slope ran in through gaps in the concrete walkway around its edge, and when the lake filled, the overflow drained into pipes heading east [1]. By 1983 the city's planners admitted it went stagnant in the dry season and looked ugly whenever it was drained to clear out weeds and rushes. They suggested paving the bottom but ruled out filling it in. One reason: the state would want its construction money back [1]. In 2013 the Chronicle's John King reported that its water still regularly turned dark with algae and silt, because the reclaimed former marsh had been badly designed in the 1960s [3]. The wildlife doesn't seem to mind. That year Chronicle photographers caught a double-crested cormorant fishing and ducks swimming and foraging on the lake [3].

title: Fifty Men Lift a Dome Form
place: Palace of Fine Arts rotunda
hook: The beloved 1915 'ruin' was falling down for real. So San Francisco knocked it flat and built it again in concrete, sometimes by sheer muscle.
story: Bernard Maybeck's Palace of Fine Arts was meant to last one season. It was a wood frame covered in 'staff', a mix of plaster and burlap-like fibre [2]. In the decades after the 1915 fair it held eighteen lighted tennis courts (1934 to 1942), wartime trucks and jeeps, phone books and even a temporary fire headquarters. By the 1950s the fake ruin was a real one [2]. In 1964 it was demolished, with only the steel of the exhibit hall left standing, and rebuilt in poured-in-place concrete. A plate in the rotunda credits B.F. Modglin of MacDonald & Kahn for the work of 1964 to 1967 [2]. Construction worker Eric Johnson remembered the day his crew had to move a huge dome form that weighed many tons. No forklift could carry it safely, so fifty men in dusty white overalls lifted it by hand while their foreman, Howard, called out orders [1]. Johnson said getting it moving was like 'shoving an elephant into her stall'. For a moment they felt 'like being gods, or dreamers in unison', until the form swung wide at a doorway and nearly crushed them [1]. The steel dome was up by December 1966 [1].

title: Full carts, no sale: the Lucky shop-in
place: Former Lucky supermarket, 1201 Gough Street near Geary
hook: Demonstrators filled their carts, waited at the till, then changed their minds. After a few days of it, the supermarket agreed to hire.
story: In February 1964 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) put picket lines outside Lucky supermarkets. CORE had fought the chain over jobs for Black workers as far back as 1948, and an agreement the summer before had produced no new hires [1]. A week later CORE began something cleverer, the 'shop-in' [1]. A San Francisco Public Library photograph places one at the Lucky store at 1201 Gough Street, near Geary [2]. Everything the demonstrators did was legal. They piled their carts high, reached the checkout, and changed their minds, leaving cashiers with ringing registers and counters full of unwanted groceries [1]. Managers could not tell real customers from protesters, and real customers did not want to wait while every item went back on the shelves [1]. Jo Freeman, who took part in the Bay Area campaigns that year, writes that after a few days Mayor John Shelley brokered a deal: Lucky's parent company promised to hire at least sixty Black workers, and the shop-in ended [1]. The same week, pickets appeared outside the Sheraton-Palace Hotel. The 1964 season of Bay Area civil rights sit-ins had begun [1].

title: Railroad, freeway, then BART in one valley
place: I-280 cut beside Balboa Park station, Ocean to Geneva avenues
hook: The trench where BART now runs past Balboa Park began as an 1860s railroad. In 1964 engineers squeezed a freeway into it, then left room for trains.
story: The valley that runs southwest across the Outer Mission has always carried traffic. In 1964, the state's engineering magazine explained that the new Route 82 'Southern' Freeway, now I-280, followed the natural corridor of Alemany Boulevard and San Jose Avenue. For almost two-thirds of its length it used the old Southern Pacific 'Main Line' of the 1860s [1]. Sources disagree on when passenger trains stopped running: the state gave 1907, while a later account says about 1922 [1][2]. The state adopted the route in 1956. Its four miles cost $24 million to build and another $18 million to buy land [1]. The key section ran through Balboa Park and across a corner of City College. It included pedestrian ramps down from the Ocean Avenue overpass so express-bus riders on the freeway could change to local buses, and a crib wall 35 feet high and 450 feet long to keep the Cayuga Playground from eroding [1]. The engineers also worked with the new Bay Area Rapid Transit District, whose tracks would 'enter the freeway right-of-way' [1]. BART's Balboa Park station opened in November 1973 [2][3].

title: Saving the chocolate factory from a tower
place: Ghirardelli Square, 900 North Point St
hook: A high-rise had just swallowed the pasta factory next door. The chocolate works looked like the next to go, until a shipping heir intervened.
story: In the early 1960s, Ghirardelli's chocolate making moved out to San Leandro [2]. Just to the west, the Fontana Towers had gone up on the site of the old brick Fontana pasta factory, and there was talk of tearing down the chocolate works for another modernist high-rise [1]. In 1962 William M. Roth and his mother, Lurline Matson Roth, bought the property to stop it being demolished for apartments [3]. Roth hired landscape architect Lawrence Halprin and the firm Wurster, Bernardi & Emmons. They kept the old brick buildings, some dating from the 19th-century Pioneer Woolen Mill, and added new modernist elements, turning the complex into shops and restaurants [1][3]. The square opened on November 29, 1964 [2]. It is often called the first major adaptive reuse project in the United States [3]. Its owners say it became a model for places like Boston's Faneuil Hall Marketplace and Baltimore's Harborplace [2]. The idea spread quickly. A few blocks east, Leonard Martin turned the old Del Monte cannery, idle since 1937, into The Cannery [1]. In 1982 the complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places [2].

title: Sitting in on Auto Row
place: Van Ness Avenue 'Auto Row' at O'Farrell Street
hook: In spring 1964 hundreds of people were arrested in Van Ness car showrooms, all over one question: who got to sell the Cadillacs?
story: By the 1920s, Van Ness Avenue was San Francisco's Auto Row. There was a Don Lee Cadillac showroom at O'Farrell, and dealers lined the avenue [2]. In 1964 it became a civil rights battleground over who could work in those showrooms [2]. On 14 March, 107 people were arrested in front of the Cadillac agency [1]. The dealers insisted in a published 'Declaration of Policy' that they already hired fairly. The NAACP asked them to commit to '16 to 30 percent employment of minority group persons' in future openings [1]. When they refused, sit-ins resumed on 11 April and 226 were arrested [1]. Jo Freeman, one of those arrested, writes that the Auto Row protesters were older and far more often Black than those at the Sheraton-Palace sit-ins, though newspapers called them 'predominantly white' [1]. The Lincoln-Mercury dealer hit hardest settled on 17 April [1]. On Saturday 18 April thousands massed on Auto Row ready to go in again, and a sit-in was called off at the last minute when both sides made pledges to the Mayor's Interim Committee on Human Relations [1]. A 1964 photograph shows the crowd cheering the settlement [2].

title: The Freeway That Never Ate the Panhandle
place: Western end of the Panhandle, near Shrader St
hook: State engineers wanted to pave 60 percent of the Panhandle and tunnel under Golden Gate Park. A folk singer, a poet and one deciding vote stopped them.
story: In the early 1960s the state's plan was blunt: extend the Central Freeway up the Oak and Fell corridor, slice away about 60 percent of the Panhandle, tunnel under the north edge of Golden Gate Park and emerge on Park Presidio toward the Golden Gate Bridge [1]. On May 17, 1964, protesters rallied at the park's Polo Grounds, where Malvina Reynolds sang her anti-freeway ballad "Cement Octopus" ("Old John McLaren won't take this lying down") and poet Kenneth Rexroth spoke [1]. Supervisors received a 15,000-signature petition, 20,000 letters and telegrams and opposition from 77 community groups. On October 13, 1964, they rejected the park freeway 6-5; Terry Francois cast the deciding vote with a six-page, point-by-point rebuttal [1]. Mayor Jack Shelley, a former union man, wanted the freeway, and in 1966 the plan came back [2]. It died for good on March 21, 1966, again 6-5 [1]. Henry Heller, a key Panhandle defender, was photographed in 1966 watching a youth plant a tree there [3]. The Haight-Ashbury Neighborhood Council traces its origins to it. A small memorial near Shrader honours activist Sue Bierman [1].

title: The Freeway That Never Crossed the Panhandle
place: The Panhandle, between Fell and Oak Streets
hook: The state wanted to run an interstate through the Panhandle, the park's oldest planting ground. A folk singer, a rally and three 6-5 votes stopped it.
story: The block-wide Panhandle between Fell and Oak was Golden Gate Park's first testing ground. Activist Calvin Welch described it as John McLaren's arboretum, where every tree and bush was planted first to see whether it would survive, which is why it has the park's oldest trees and 21 kinds of eucalyptus [1]. By the 1950s, state highway planners wanted a freeway here, carrying traffic from the Central Freeway through Hayes Valley, partly sunk into the Panhandle, and under Golden Gate Park to link up with Highway 1 at 14th Avenue and Fulton [2]. Supervisors turned down versions 8-3 in 1956 and 6-5 in 1962 [2][3]. On May 17, 1964 the Citizens Committee to Save Golden Gate Park held a rally at the park's Polo Grounds, where folk singer Malvina Reynolds sang 'Cement Octopus' [2]. That October the board rejected the route 6-5 again [3]. The state came back with the plan, and some $250 million in federal interstate money was at stake [2]. On March 21, 1966, the supervisors voted 6-5 against both the Panhandle and Golden Gate freeways [2][3]. In 1966 Reynolds was photographed singing to protesters in the Panhandle itself [1]. The route was taken out of the state highway system in 1972 [3].

title: The Leather Bar That Made Life Magazine
place: Site of the Tool Box bar, 399 Fourth Street at Harrison
hook: In 1964 a national magazine opened its story on gay America with a photo of a South of Market leather bar and its giant mural.
story: When the Tool Box opened at Fourth and Harrison in 1962, South of Market was a district in limbo, its future tied up in redevelopment fights and its streets empty after dark. That emptiness gave gay men a kind of privacy, and the Tool Box became the neighbourhood's first leather bar and a magnet for leathermen from near and far [1][2]. Its walls carried an enormous mural by the gay artist Chuck Arnett. In June 1964 Life magazine ran "Homosexuality in America" and gave the bar and its mural a two-page spread. It was believed to be the first time a photograph of a gay bar with its patrons visible had appeared in the national mass media [1]. The Chronicle columnist Herb Caen joked that some of the "young fellers" there wore an "S" or "M" on their shirt pockets [1]. The publicity helped cast San Francisco as the nation's gay capital. It also helped draw a generation of new arrivals [2]. The bar did not survive redevelopment. It closed in 1971 and was demolished that same year. City planners now note that whatever lies under the site could still tell us more about it [1].

title: The Night the Condor Went Topless
place: Condor Club, 300 Columbus Ave at Broadway
hook: A cocktail waitress, a white piano lowered from the ceiling, and a daring swimsuit. One June night on Broadway set off a nationwide craze.
story: On June 19, 1964, Carol Doda, a 26-year-old former cocktail waitress who sang and go-go danced at the Condor Club, went on stage in a "monokini", the designer Rudi Gernreich's topless swimsuit. The club's publicist, Davey Rosenberg, had handed it to her with the words "Try this in the act" [1]. Her entrance was already pure theatre: she danced on top of a white grand piano as it was lowered from the ceiling [1][3]. Less than a month later, delegates to the Republican convention that nominated Barry Goldwater were slipping away from the Cow Palace to see her [1]. Police arrested her some months later, but she was acquitted on community standards, and the ruling let bare-breasted dancing spread [1][3]. At the peak, as many as 28 North Beach clubs had topless acts [2]. The Condor's topless era ended with a grand finale on New Year's Eve 1987. In 1991 a new owner announced that the club's 40-foot sign of Doda, complete with blinking nipples, would come down [2]. In 2022 the city added the Condor to its Legacy Business Registry [3].

title: The first class and its buried tube
place: Former Woodrow Wilson High School, now Burton High, 400 Mansell Street
hook: Woodrow Wilson High's first graduates sealed a time capsule in 1964. Fifty years later it held a senior-ball programme, and memories of fistfights.
story: Woodrow Wilson High School on Mansell Street, brand new and the first high school on the city's southeast side, graduated its first class in 1964 [1][2]. A few months after the Beatles appeared on "The Ed Sullivan Show," those seniors filled a metal tube and buried it beneath a "1964" plaque [1]. It was a tense start. Blue-collar white students mixed with Black students from Hunters Point, and there were fistfights; to build a common bond the students chose the Warriors as mascot, to the dismay of teachers who knew Woodrow Wilson was a pacifist, recalled math teacher Mary Jane Mikuriya [1]. Twenty years later a 1984 consent decree between the NAACP and the city created Phillip and Sala Burton Academic High School, named for the two former congressmembers; it began in Silver Terrace and later moved onto the Wilson site [2]. On 2 April 2015 a crew broke through the concrete. Inside was nothing about civil rights or the Cold War, just a class photo, the student newspaper and the senior-ball programme, themed "Non Dimenticar," Italian for "never forget," tickets $5 [1]. Mikuriya, 80, stood again at the spot where she had heard President Kennedy was dead [1].

title: Dr. King fills Grace Cathedral
place: Grace Cathedral, 1100 California St
hook: Weeks after Selma, Martin Luther King Jr. preached on Nob Hill to a crowd so vast the fire marshal shut the doors and offering baskets went outside.
story:
Grace Cathedral was consecrated in November 1964 after decades of construction [1]. To celebrate, the controversial Bishop James Pike, who had marched at Selma, invited Martin Luther King Jr. to preach, and on 28 March 1965, the fourth Sunday of Lent, King came [2][4].

Crowds surged around the cathedral from early morning. By 10 a.m. it was packed, and Grace had never seen so many people, most of them African American. About 5,000 filled the nave, steps, plaza and parking lot; not until the memorial service after 11 September 2001 would a crowd that size gather there again [2]. King was slipped in through a rear door among bodyguards.

Dean Julian Bartlett later recalled the fire marshal shutting the doors before 10:30, plainclothes police stationed in front of and behind the pulpit, and a moment of panic when he spotted a figure on the catwalk above the unfinished vaulting. It turned out to be a seminarian taking photographs. When the crowd outside heard over loudspeakers that the collection was being taken, they shouted for their own offering takers, and ushers waded out with baskets [2]. The same day King was also due at the KRON studios for an episode of Meet the Press [3].

title: Duke Ellington swings the cathedral
place: Grace Cathedral nave, California & Taylor Sts
hook: Ellington called it the most important thing he ever did. Some in the pews thought a saxophone had no business in an Episcopal nave.
story:
As part of a year-long Festival of Grace marking the cathedral's completion, Dean C. Julian Bartlett, a jazz lover from New Orleans, met Duke Ellington in North Beach and commissioned an extended sacred work [1]. Ellington later wrote that he saw it as "an exceptional opportunity": now he could say openly "what I have been saying to myself on my knees" [1].

The Concert of Sacred Music premiered at Grace in September 1965 before an overflow crowd of about 2,500 and was filmed by the young public station KQED with Chronicle jazz critic Ralph Gleason [1]. The phrase "In the Beginning God" ran through the evening; Bunny Briggs tap-danced to "David Danced Before the Lord With All His Might"; and Esther Marrow, who had only ever sung in church, sang "Come Sunday." Her nerves were matched by Ellington's: his white suit arrived without its trousers [1].

It was near-scandalous at the time. A Chronicle review said the band left many "discomfited, nervous or edgy" at a sax piercing the nave, and a cathedral staffer says priests organising a jazz mass by Vince Guaraldi that same festival year got death threats [1]. The cathedral's archivist pairs the concert with Dr. King's visit as the signature events of 1965 [2]. Ellington called it "the most important thing I've ever done" [1].

title: Eichler's twin towers on the hill
place: Geneva Towers site, 1001 Sunnydale Ave
hook: Joseph Eichler's twin 20-storey towers were meant for middle-income tenants. They could be seen for miles from Highway 101.
story: In the 1960s the developer Joseph Eichler built something unusual for Visitacion Valley: twin 20-storey towers at 1001 Sunnydale Avenue [1][2]. Geneva Towers was planned as private housing for middle-income tenants, including workers at the airport [1][2]. Vice President Hubert Humphrey paid a visit [1]. Sources give opening dates from 1964 to 1967 [1][2], and counts of 576 or 585 apartments [1][2]. At first, the columnist Lee Hubbard wrote, the buildings held a mix of doctors, lawyers and people of all incomes [3]. They were the only high-rises south of downtown you could see for miles from Highway 101; for him, a glimpse of the two white towers meant he was almost home [3]. But the towers failed to draw enough middle-income renters, so the owners took low-income tenants whose rent was subsidised by the federal government [2]. By 1976 the complex was entirely Section 8 housing [1]. The owners collected $200,000 a month in federal rent subsidies while the buildings fell apart [2]. Even so, many residents loved the place. "It was a great place to live," said Vernon Long, who lived there from 1970 to 1981 [2].

title: Gonzo's Birthplace Had a Parnassus Address
place: 318 Parnassus Ave
hook: Before he was famous, Hunter S. Thompson wrote letters from a flat on Parnassus Avenue while riding with the Hells Angels for his first book.
story: In 1964 Hunter S. Thompson was a struggling journalist. He moved with his wife Sandy and their baby son Juan from Glen Ellen to 318 Parnassus Avenue, near Golden Gate Park [2]. By October 1964 his letters carried that address [1]. It was from this flat that he wrote to Carey McWilliams, editor of The Nation [1]. His essay on the motorcycle gangs for The Nation became the seed of a book [3]. Thompson spent more than a year riding with the San Francisco and Oakland Hells Angels, and a motorcycle history describes Angels coming and going from Hunter and Sandy's Parnassus apartment [4]. The project nearly cost him his teeth. On a Labor Day run near Mendocino, several Angels beat him after he objected to one of them beating his wife and his dog [3]. The result was his first book, Hell's Angels (1966). SF Weekly argues that this immersive, first-person style became what the world later called Gonzo [3]. The building's neighbourhood is described differently depending on who's writing: 'Haight-Ashbury' in his letters' editors' notes, 'near Golden Gate Park' in his son's memoir [1][2].

title: Last frigates, BART's tube, and alien pods
place: Pier 70 shipyard, east end of 20th Street
hook: The yard that built warships for three wars launched its last two in the 1960s, helped make BART's tube under the bay, then served as a set for alien pods.
story:
The last ships built at Pier 70 were two Navy frigates, the Bradley and the Garcia, between 1962 and 1965 [1]. The yard also won a huge job: 57 steel sections for BART's tunnel under the bay between Oakland and San Francisco [1]. After that it mostly repaired other people's ships [1][2].

Decline followed. In 1978 Philip Kaufman filmed scenes for his remake of Invasion of the Body Snatchers in the yard's Building 6. There Donald Sutherland and Brooke Adams discover a warehouse being used to incubate pods [3]. The ownership story after that is tangled. Wikipedia says the city bought the Bethlehem site for one dollar in 1982 [2]. A 2005 report says Todd Industries bought the shipyards that year, broke its lease with the Port in 1987 as it faced bankruptcy, and that San Francisco Drydock later bought the dry-dock facilities from the Port for $1 [1].

By 2005 a few hundred workers were still repairing ships in one corner of the pier. One was the machinist Juan Ramirez, 77, who had worked on the waterfront for 35 years and said he had no plans to retire [1].

title: Light shows upstairs at Geary and Fillmore
place: Fillmore Auditorium, 1805 Geary Boulevard
hook: A Mime Troupe benefit in a Black promoter's dance hall turned a brick ballroom into the world capital of psychedelic rock, for just two and a half years.
story: On 10 December 1965, the San Francisco Mime Troupe held its second Appeal Party at the Fillmore Auditorium. A band that had just renamed itself from the Warlocks debuted there as the Grateful Dead, alongside Jefferson Airplane and the John Handy Quintet [1]. The venue was operated by Charles Sullivan, a Black concert promoter with a nightlife empire in the Fillmore district [2]. The young man behind the benefits, Bill Graham, stayed on: by February 1966 'Bill Graham presented' Jefferson Airplane at 1805 Geary [1]. That August, days after Sullivan was found shot dead in a killing that was never solved, a young, mostly white crowd queued upstairs for Sam the Sham [2]. Graham ran the Fillmore for about two and a half years, and 'the Fillmore Sound' came to mean the San Francisco Sound [2]. Historian Rickey Vincent notes how the story is usually told as if the Fillmore began in 1966. Longtime resident Danny Duncan put it plainly: 'African Americans — we used the Fillmore Auditorium before Bill Graham took it' [2]. Graham died in a helicopter crash before the hall reopened in 1994. The Fillmore still hands out his apples [2].

title: Love and prescriptions behind the counter
place: Central Drug Store, 4494 Mission St at Santa Rosa Ave
hook: Three couples met behind the counter of this corner drugstore, and one young comic-book buyer grew up to be Jerry Garcia.
story: For more than a century a drugstore stood at Mission Street and Santa Rosa Avenue. SF Heritage dates it to 1910, and Mission Local calls it 116 years old when it closed [1][2]. Around 1950 it got a sleek Vitrolite sign with 'Central Drug Store' in neon [1]. Young Jerry Garcia bought comic books here [1]. In the 1940s, when the store still had a soda fountain and sold roasted nuts by the half-pound, a clerk and a pharmacist-in-training fell in love behind the counter. They were Jerry Tonelli's parents, and they married in 1947 [2]. In 1965 his father, Dino, bought the store from the Divencenzis. Two more couples later met working there [2]. Jerry Tonelli started in the family shop in 1978, and his teenage photo still hung behind the counter captioned 'The delivery boy' [3]. Staff sometimes delivered medicine for free, and customers who missed closing time could collect it at the Round Table Pizza across the street [3]. Tonelli retired and closed the store on July 15, 2025 [3].

title: The Ballroom in the Basement
place: 1090 Page Street (the Albin rooming house)
hook: Under a shabby Page Street rooming house lay an old ballroom with a proscenium arch. The jam sessions held there helped give birth to San Francisco rock.
story: In the mid-1960s, 1090 Page Street was a Victorian rooming house. Rod Albin managed it from 1964 and let his brother Peter and other San Francisco State students take over rooms and the basement [4]. Down there, the band later wrote, was "the ghost of a beautiful old ballroom complete with proscenium arch that was a perfect rehearsal and dance space" [1]. Chet Helms organised dances and jam sessions in that rosewood-panelled room. The Chronicle's Joel Selvin wrote that musicians who played there went on to form Quicksilver Messenger Service, the Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company [2]. Peter Albin, who had started out wanting to write songs for children, formed Big Brother with Sam Andrew. They were joined by guitarist James Gurley and drummer Dave Getz, a cook and art instructor who "simply asked for the job" [1]. For about six months the band worked on its sound underground. It made its public debut on January 22, 1966, at Ken Kesey's Trips Festival [1]. Janis Joplin later rehearsed with the band at what Hoodline called the "Albin House" [3]. Selvin reported in 2009 that the old house had been torn down long ago [2].

title: The Margarita Born at 23rd and Geary
place: Tommy's Mexican Restaurant, 5929 Geary Boulevard
hook: A Yucatecan guest worker opened a family restaurant in the fog in 1965. His son's tweak to the margarita is now an international standard.
story: Tomás 'Tommy' Bermejo came north from Oxkutzcab in the Yucatán on a guest worker programme, and in 1965 he and his wife Elmy opened a restaurant on Geary serving the food of their home region [1][2]. Behind him came a brother, six cousins, 20 nieces and nephews and many acquaintances; a 2002 profile said he gave dozens of newcomers occasional jobs and an informal safety net [1]. Tommy's did not get a liquor licence until 1972, their son Julio recalled, and at first its bar looked like any other [2]. In the late 1980s Julio began visiting tequila distilleries. Around 1989 or 1990 he started sweetening margaritas with agave nectar instead of orange liqueur, so that 'it tastes of the base spirit' [2]. It was so expensive then that he cut it with simple syrup [2]. Bartenders he met while travelling with President Vicente Fox's tequila delegation to Europe in 2001 spread the recipe, and in 2008 the International Bartenders Association adopted the Tommy's Margarita, its first drink named after a single bar [2][3]. Tomás died in 2011, leaving Julio to carry on what the blog called the Bay Area's tequila mecca [1].

title: Three mothers stop a freeway
place: Gum Tree Girls Trail (Alms Road), Glen Canyon Park
hook: "Like hell you'll build a freeway!" A surveyor's stakes set off five years of fighting City Hall, and in the end the Gum Tree Girls won.
story:
The 1948 freeway plan included a "Circumferential Expressway" that would have crossed Glen Park on a viaduct, running beside Bosworth and O'Shaughnessy and hanging 60 feet above the canyon [1]. Local woman Minnie Straub Baxter helped beat the first version in 1958. She packed 500 residents into Glen Park School and took her case to Sacramento [1].

In 1965 Zoanne Nordstrom and Joan Seiwald saw a surveyor putting in stakes on Bosworth. When he explained what they were for, Nordstrom told him, "Like hell you'll build a freeway!" [2]. With Geri Arkush they started the Save Glen Park Committee on 19 October 1965 [1]. City Engineer Clifford Geertz dismissed them as the "Gum Tree Girls," after the eucalyptus that would have been cut down [1]. "It wasn't a compliment," Seiwald recalled. "We were beating them, one of the world's greatest sins" [2]. Their children kept pulling the surveyors' flags off the trees [1].

The supervisors voted to stop the work and repair the canyon, and in 1970 they killed the O'Shaughnessy widening for good [1]. In 2014 the Recreation and Park Department renamed the canyon's main path, Alms Road, the Gum Tree Girls Trail [1].

title: A Chicago Wurlitzer for silent-film nights
place: Avenue Theatre, 2650 San Bruno Avenue
hook: In 1966 a neighbourhood movie house on San Bruno Avenue became a shrine to silent film, with a 16-rank theatre organ brought from Chicago.
story: In the mid-1960s the Lyric Photoplay Film Society, led by Edward Millington Stout III, took over the Avenue [1][2]. In 1966 it installed a three-manual, 16-rank Wurlitzer that had first played in the State Lake Theatre in Chicago, and on 7 October 1966 organist Tom Hazelton opened it by accompanying the silent "The Lost World" [1][3]. The Avenue became a destination with an eclectic diet of foreign films, 3-D revivals and, above all, silents with live organ [1]. A surviving calendar, probably from the late 1970s or early '80s, lists "Son of the Sheikh" and "Speedy" beside "The Gay Divorcee" [2]. Lyn Larsen was staff organist in 1967 and 1968; Bob Vaughn took over in 1968 and played until the end, and the American Theatre Organ Society featured the organ at its 1975 and 1983 national conventions [1]. A 1983 TV news report on theatre organs caught the Friday-night silents and the marquee lit up [3]. But crime in the area kept patrons away, and the Avenue closed on 22 December 1984 amid financial trouble [1]. The organ went into storage; a later owner wrote that he had it trucked to Florida in 2005 for restoration [3].

title: A cup of coffee starts a riot
place: Site of Gene Compton's Cafeteria, 101 Taylor St at Turk
hook: Three years before Stonewall, trans women at an all-night Tenderloin cafeteria fought back against police. For decades almost nobody remembered it happened.
story: Gene Compton's cafeteria at Turk and Taylor was open all night, and in the 1960s it was a haven for drag queens, trans women and young hustlers who spent hours over cheap coffee. Management often called the police to clear them out. Officers arrested people for 'female impersonation' [1]. On an August night in 1966, an officer grabbed a queen and she threw her coffee in his face. The cafeteria 'erupted', historian Susan Stryker says. Sugar shakers went through the windows, heavy purses swung at police, a patrol car was trashed and a newsstand burned [1][3]. 'We just got tired of it,' Amanda St. Jaymes later said. 'We wanted our rights' [1]. The riot made no newspapers, and the exact date has never been found [2]. The only written record that survived was a short piece by activist Raymond Broshears in the program for the city's first Pride parade in 1972 [1]. Stryker pieced the story back together from archives and interviews for her 2005 documentary 'Screaming Queens' [2]. In 2021, photos of a 1970 hotel fire turned up on Facebook showing Compton's sign in the background, one of the few known pictures of its exterior [3].

title: Admiral Nimitz's house on the hill
place: Quarters 1 (Nimitz House), 1 Whiting Way, Yerba Buena Island
hook: The admiral who commanded the Pacific Fleet in the Second World War died in a columned house on a hill above the Bay Bridge.
story:
Long before there was a Treasure Island, the Navy had a training station on Yerba Buena Island, then called Goat Island. In 1898 President McKinley set aside a 'goodly portion' of the island for it. In 1900 the first barracks and the commander's house were finished [1]. For years it was the Navy's only training station on the West Coast, usually with four to five hundred trainees [1].

Quarters 1, the commander's house, is a Classical Revival wood-frame house of 5,886 square feet. It has Ionic columns, a lawn that sweeps down the hill and formal gardens set into the slope behind [2]. The training station moved to San Diego in 1923, but the senior officers' houses survived [1].

The house is best known for Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet in World War II. According to the National Register summary, he had full use of Quarters 1 from 1946 and died there in 1966, although his main home was in the East Bay [2]. Roadside panels in front of the house now tell his story [3].

title: Four Shots, Then Five Days of Fury
place: Third Street and Palou Avenue
hook: On a sweltering September afternoon in 1966, a police officer shot a fleeing Black teenager. Within hours Third Street was in uproar, and the National Guard soon followed.
story: The afternoon of 27 September 1966 was unusually hot. Patrolman Alvin Johnson pulled up to a car he suspected was stolen, and three Black teenagers ran. He chased two of them toward Navy Road. As 16-year-old Matthew "Peanut" Johnson ran down a hill near a housing project, the officer fired four shots. One hit the unarmed boy in the heart [1]. (One account gives Matthew's age as 17 [2].) By late afternoon an angry crowd had gathered at Third Street and Palou Avenue. At a War on Poverty job centre there, people demanded to know whether the officer would be charged with murder [1]. That night bottles and rocks flew and stores along Third Street were looted [1]. The next day police, saying they had been fired on, poured hundreds of rounds into the Bayview Community Center, which was then housed in the Opera House. More than 60 unarmed youths were huddled inside, and no weapons were found on anyone who came out [3][2]. Governor Pat Brown sent in the National Guard, and troops patrolled Bayview and the Fillmore until 1 October [2]. In the end 457 people were arrested and 161 injured [3]. Matthew Johnson was the only person killed that week. The officer was never arrested [3].

title: Hayes Street's Gay Main Street
place: 488 Hayes Street (David's House / Marlena's)
hook: Long before the boutiques came, a few blocks of Hayes Street held a gay thrift shop, a drag bar, a gay weekly newspaper and a street fair.
story: In the 1960s the Society for Individual Rights, San Francisco's leading gay-rights group, ran the Sirporium on Hayes Street [1][2]. It was a thrift shop that sold items donated by members and used the money to pay for community events [1]. Sources disagree on the address: the city's LGBTQ context statement gives 515 Hayes, while the neighbourhood association gives 525 [1][2]. In the 1970s Dottie's Stardust Lounge, a gay bar, stood at the corner of Hayes and Laguna [2]. In 1984 David's House opened at 488 Hayes, next to David's Garden Cafe. It became the Overpass in 1986 and Marlena's in 1990, a bar remembered for its welcome to older gay men [2]. Next door, from 1983 to 1992, 500 Hayes housed the offices of the San Francisco Sentinel [2]. Founded in the early 1970s, the Sentinel was one of the city's first commercially successful gay weeklies and stopped weekly publication in 1995 [1]. From 1981 to 1990, during the worst years of AIDS, the Lily Street Fair filled a four-block alley nearby [2]. Around the corner at 320 Fell Street, the photographer Daniel Nicoletta ran a studio from 1990 to 2000, where he hosted salons, fundraisers and memorial services [2].

title: Mary Rogers, WACO and the Bulldozers
place: Western Addition A-2 project area (centred near Fillmore and Turk)
hook: She had a ninth-grade education and twelve children. She lay down in front of bulldozers, and she helped take the federal government to court.
story: Mary Helen Rogers moved to San Francisco from Texas in 1965, just as the Redevelopment Agency was razing whole blocks of the Western Addition [1]. In March 1966 she and Hannibal Williams took the lead in organizing the Western Addition Community Organization, known as WACO. It brought together churches and tenants, including many residents of St. Francis Square [2]. Rogers had a ninth-grade education, but she became an expert in housing law, and on at least one occasion she lay down in front of the bulldozers [1]. On December 15, 1967, WACO sued the federal housing secretary to stop funding for A-2 [3]. HUD's own staff had found a shortfall of 689 units of relocation housing [3]. In December 1968 Judge Sweigert held that HUD's approval of the relocation plan was "completely arbitrary and without basis in fact" and blocked the Agency from forcibly displacing residents until it produced a plan for decent, safe and sanitary housing [3]. The injunction was lifted in March 1969, after HUD approved a revised plan [4]. Rogers kept fighting for forty years, until her death in 2006 [1].

title: Stew through the Free Frame of Reference
place: The Panhandle near Ashbury Street
hook: To get a free bowl of stew in the Panhandle, you first had to step through a giant yellow picture frame.
story: The Diggers took their name from 17th-century English radicals and set out to live as if money were already obsolete [1][2]. From 1966 they served free food in the Panhandle every day at four o'clock, a stew made from donated meat and vegetables for about 100 people [2]. Before you got a bowl you had to step through an oversized yellow wooden frame, the Free Frame of Reference [1][2]. The Digger women did most of the actual work. They cooked soup in steel milk cans using packing-house meat and unsellable produce from the wholesale markets, and baked small loaves in empty coffee cans [1]. The journalist Naomi Wolf was brought along as a child and remembered prostitutes, schoolkids and professors waiting quietly together under the eucalyptus [1]. The group's division of labour has since been criticised as sexist: men promoted and took credit while women collected, cooked and served [2]. They also ran free stores and crash pads, including an apartment at 1775 Haight rented for runaways [1]. By the end of 1967, worn out by the crowds, they had left for rural communes [1][3].

title: The Day LSD Became Illegal
place: The Panhandle at Masonic Avenue and Fell Street
hook: The day California outlawed LSD, the Haight threw a party on the Panhandle, with the Grateful Dead and Big Brother playing, dogs in psychedelic gear and Kesey's bus.
story: On October 6, 1966, the day a new California law against LSD took effect, the editors of the San Francisco Oracle staged a "Love Pageant Rally" on the Panhandle [1]. Contemporary newspaper accounts put the gathering at the corner of Masonic and Fell, with a traffic jam building along Masonic [2]. Estimates of the crowd ranged from about 500 in one contemporary report to between 1,000 and 3,000 in later retellings [1][2]. The Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company played. Ken Kesey's multicoloured bus turned up, carrying "long-haired children" and dogs outfitted in "psychedelic gear" [2]. Afterwards, organiser Michael Bowen told Richard Alpert, "People are sure hungry for some communicating," and that remark helped inspire the Human Be-In a few months later [1]. The rally was the first of five Grateful Dead appearances in the Panhandle over eight months [4]. Other bands also played free in the grassy strip between Fell and Oak. The most famous was Jimi Hendrix, who played on Jefferson Airplane's flatbed truck one Sunday in June 1967, farther west near Cole Street [3]. On March 8, 2026, musicians revived the flatbed tradition for an estimated 5,000 people. The generator powering the amplifiers ran out of fuel in the middle of "Wharf Rat" [4].

title: The Fire That Saved the Wrecking Crew
place: Sutro Baths ruins, below Point Lobos Avenue
hook: By 1966 Adolph Sutro's glass bathing palace had become an ice rink, then a demolition site. Then, one June night, it burned.
story: Attendance at Sutro Baths slid through the 1920s and 1930s as the coastal railway closed, the Depression bit and new state health rules demanded costly repairs; in 1937 part of the building became an ice rink [1]. In 1952 George Whitney bought it, closed the pools and turned the complex into skating and a museum of his 'collection of collections' [1][2]. In 1964 Whitney's mother sold control to developer Robert Fraser, who planned a 200-unit apartment complex [1]. In June 1966, with demolition already under way, fire burned the structure to its foundations, and thousands came to watch [1]. Tom Hontalas, eight, watched from the diner above with his aunt and siblings [3]. George Whitney Jr. later called it 'a very fortuitous fire for the wrecking company' [2]. Public feeling after the blaze may have hindered the apartment plan, and the Park Service bought the site in 1973 [1]. The concrete shell is still there, a ruin Park Service planning meetings often chose to leave as it was [1][3].

title: The Steel Wedding Cake Loses Its Top
place: Mile Rock Beach, looking out to Mile Rocks Lighthouse
hook: For sixty years, keepers lived on a wave-swept rock in plain sight of the city. One keeper's wife sent him flashlight greetings from Lands End.
story: Offshore from Mile Rock Beach, the Mile Rocks lighthouse was built after the 1901 wreck of the City of Rio de Janeiro, the worst shipwreck in San Francisco's history [1]. Locals called its tiered steel tower the 'steel wedding cake' [2]. For more than 60 years a small crew lived there in cramped quarters for days at a time, cut off from a city they could see [1]. It was a 'stag station' with no room for families. One keeper's wife walked the family dog out to Lands End in the evenings and flashed a greeting to her husband with a flashlight [3]. In the 1960s the Coast Guard decided to automate the light. Supervisor William Blake and the Conference of California Historical Societies protested [3]. The keepers were removed on 18 August 1965. For $110,000 contractors cut off the lantern and the top two tiers and built a helicopter pad [3]. The Maritime Museum wanted the top 40 feet for display at the foot of Hyde Street, but saving it would have cost $87,000 more, so the living quarters were scrapped [3]. NPS dates the automation to 1966 [1].

title: Thirty-Three Minutes in a Cage
place: Candlestick Park (site), second base
hook: On 29 August 1966 the Beatles played Candlestick Park privately knowing it was their last concert. Their press officer taped it, until the cassette ran out.
story: Worn down by riots, death threats and screaming that drowned out their amplifiers, the Beatles came to Candlestick Park on 29 August 1966 for the last date of their U.S. tour [1]. Only about 25,000 of the stadium's 42,500 seats sold, at $4.50 to $6.50 each [1]. When their bus arrived, the gates were locked [1]. Just before showtime Paul McCartney quietly asked press officer Tony Barrow to tape the show on his cassette recorder, which had never happened before [1]. At 9:27 p.m. the four ran from the Giants' dugout to a stage built over second base. It was fenced in chain-link, with an armoured car idling behind it in case they needed a quick getaway [1]. They played 11 songs in 33 minutes. Between songs they set their cameras on timers and photographed themselves with their backs to the crowd. "We knew: 'This is it,'" George Harrison said [1]. They closed with Little Richard's "Long Tall Sally," and Barrow's 30-minute tape ran out before the song ended [1]. The Beatles never toured again. Nearly 48 years later, Paul McCartney came back to play the last scheduled event at the stadium [2].

title: When Fillmore Street Went Quiet
place: Fillmore Street at Eddy
hook: The "Harlem of the West" had clubs, barbershops and banks. After A-2, the stretch of Fillmore down to Turk stayed empty lots for decades.
story: A-2 was far bigger than A-1. It covered 60 blocks and 277 acres surrounding the first project, and the Board of Supervisors approved it on October 15, 1964 [1]. Work did not start until May 1966, because HUD would not pay for projects while Proposition 14, the state measure that barred anti-discrimination laws in housing, was in force [1]. Then the clearance came. Of 180 Black-owned businesses operating in A-2, only 48 were successfully relocated, and the other 132 went out of business [2]. Fillmore Street between Pine and Turk, famous in the 1950s as the "Harlem of the West," was left as barren lots for decades [2]. City officials later put the toll of Western Addition redevelopment at 883 businesses shut and 4,729 households forced out [3]. A co-op historian wrote that through the 1980s, the commercial life of lower Fillmore came to one Safeway and a few fast-food chains [4]. Willie Brown, looking back years later, said: "The black businesses, which had been viable, wonderful, and productive, were totally destroyed. The entertainment world for African Americans virtually ceased to exist in San Francisco" [2].

title: A Beatle Borrows a Guitar
place: Hippie Hill, near Sharon Meadow
hook: In August 1967 a Beatle walked up Haight Street unrecognised, borrowed a busker's guitar on Hippie Hill, and set off a stampede.
story: On August 8, 1967, George Harrison, then 24, walked along Haight Street with his wife Pattie Boyd and Beatles press officer Derek Taylor. At first nobody noticed him [1]. At Hippie Hill, the slope where congas and drum circles had gathered since the mid-1960s [2], they found a young man playing to about 20 long-haired listeners. Harrison asked to borrow the guitar and began to play. Then a young woman shouted, "That's George Harrison!" Chronicle reporter David Swanston wrote that "hippies clambered down hills, dropped from trees and sprang from behind bushes." After about ten more minutes Harrison called out, "Let's go for a walk," and led a growing crowd back down Haight, strumming as he went. Asked what he thought of the neighbourhood, he answered, "Wow, if it's all like this, it's too much" [1]. In private he was less charmed. A biographer quotes him calling the scene's young people "hideous, spotty little teenagers," and gives a harsher account of the day that differs from the Chronicle's [1]. Hippie Hill still hosts weekend drum circles [3].

title: A Gathering of the Tribes
place: Polo Field, Golden Gate Park
hook: On a January Saturday, 20,000 to 30,000 people packed the Polo Field and Timothy Leary told them to turn on, tune in, drop out.
story: The Human Be-In of January 14, 1967, was billed on the cover of the San Francisco Oracle as "A Gathering of the Tribes" [1]. Its organizers, artist Michael Bowen and poet Allen Cohen, wanted to bring together two feuding camps: Berkeley's anti-war activists and the Haight's psychedelic dropouts [2]. The trigger was California's ban on LSD, which took effect on October 6, 1966. That same day, Bowen and Cohen had held a smaller Love Pageant Rally in the Panhandle [2]. At the Polo Field, Timothy Leary made his first San Francisco appearance and set the tone with "Turn on, tune in, drop out." Allen Ginsberg chanted mantras. Gary Snyder, Michael McClure, Lenore Kandel, Lawrence Ferlinghetti, Dick Gregory and Jerry Rubin also took the stage [1]. Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead, Big Brother and Quicksilver played. The Hells Angels looked after lost children, and 'underground chemist' Owsley Stanley supplied his White Lightning LSD plus 75 twenty-pound turkeys for the Diggers to hand out [1]. Estimates of the crowd ranged from 20,000 to 30,000. The national coverage helped draw thousands more young people to the Haight that summer [1][3].

title: A Whole Year of Just Two Movies
place: Balboa Theatre, 3630 Balboa Street at 38th Avenue
hook: From Christmas 1966 to Christmas 1967, the Balboa showed only The Sound of Music and Doctor Zhivago. Nobody seemed to mind.
story: Samuel Levin opened the New Balboa on 27 February 1926, promising entertainment 'worthy of family patronage' [1]. For decades it changed programmes two or three times a week, but by the 1960s films ran longer [1]. On 25 December 1966 the Balboa opened the first neighbourhood run of The Sound of Music at 'popular prices,' straight after its 92-week roadshow on Market Street [1]. On 24 May 1967 it swapped to Doctor Zhivago, fresh from 66 weeks at the Orpheum, and kept it for 30 weeks until 19 December [1]. 'For one entire year, they only played two separate films,' historian Jack Tillmany noted [1]. Like its Richmond rivals the Balboa split into two screens in 1978 [1]. In February 2001 the Levin family, facing megaplex competition, asked Landmark Theatres co-founder Gary Meyer to run it rather than close. 'I just can't let another old theater close,' he said [1]. In 2011 the San Francisco Neighborhood Theater Foundation took a lease through 2024, and the Balboa's marquee stayed lit [1][2].

title: A funeral for the hippie
place: Summit of Buena Vista Park
hook: At dawn one October morning the Haight carried a coffin up Buena Vista hill and set fire to the word "hippie".
story: By autumn 1967 the Haight was overwhelmed by runaways, tourists and the press, and police had raided the Grateful Dead's house on October 2 [1]. Two days later Ron Thelin, who ran the Psychedelic Shop with his brother Jay (it had opened on Haight Street in January 1966 and was often called the first head shop), announced a funeral [1][3]. At dawn on October 6 more than a hundred people set off from the now-closed shop, with more joining as they went. They carried a pine coffin marked "Hippie, devoted son of mass media" and filled with beads and shaved-off beards. A medieval bugle played "Taps" [1][2]. The march went east along Haight into Buena Vista Park and up to the crest. There, in silence, they lit a fire and burned papers reading "hippie" and "freebie" along with copies of the Chronicle and the Berkeley Barb [1]. Back on Haight Street, organisers handed out brooms: "You got to clean house when you have a funeral" [1]. One organiser later explained the message: don't come here, bring the revolution home [2][3].

title: A house where runaways could phone home
place: 1 Broderick Street (original Huckleberry House)
hook: In 1967 running away was an offence for minors. One Victorian at Haight and Broderick offered teenagers a counsellor instead of a cell.
story: Thousands of teenagers came to the Haight in 1967, and for those under 18 running away was a status offence. Police could enter a crash pad without a warrant if they suspected a minor was inside, and most hippie households would not risk taking them in [1]. The Diggers asked for help, and Glide's Methodist ministers answered. Huckleberry House opened at 1 Broderick Street on June 18, 1967, run by Rev. Larry Beggs and social worker Barbara Brachman with 25 volunteers, four of them clinical psychologists [1]. Overnight stays needed parental consent, so staff acted as go-betweens. Sometimes they drew up written contracts in which a teen promised to keep parents informed and the parents agreed to allow a little more freedom [1]. One boy said he "had to come all the way here to find someone to listen to me" [1]. The model helped pave the way for the federal Runaway Youth Act of 1974 [1]. Huckleberry moved to Page Street in 1981 and describes itself as the oldest program for runaway and homeless youth in the country [1][2].

title: Charlie Manson's summer on Cole Street
place: 636 Cole Street
hook: Before the murders, Charles Manson was a paroled ex-con dancing at Grateful Dead shows and collecting followers a few doors from Haight Street.
story: Charles Manson was released from federal prison on March 21, 1967, aged 32. He had spent more than half his life in institutions [2]. Within weeks he was in Berkeley, and then, with his probation officer's permission, in the Haight [2]. That officer, criminologist Roger Smith, also worked at the Haight Ashbury Free Medical Clinic, which Manson and his growing group of mostly young women began to visit [2]. FoundSF places his Haight pad at 636 Cole Street, near Haight [1]. In his own later account he panhandled, hustled pot and LSD for small-time dealers, and busked on guitar. He also described losing himself on the dance floor at a Grateful Dead show and collapsing, then waking the next morning in a room full of strangers [1]. Mixing Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land, the Bible, Scientology and the Beatles into a message of free love, he gathered followers there [2]. Before the summer was over they left in a converted school bus for Southern California [2]. A few years later his followers killed Sharon Tate and Rosemary LaBianca [1].

title: Janis Lived Next Door
place: 122 Lyon Street
hook: Tour guides have pointed at four different Lyon Street houses as Janis Joplin's. Her driver's license points to just one of them.
story: During the Summer of Love, Janis Joplin lived in a small flat on Lyon Street, across from the Panhandle. The Chronicle later wrote that she walked her dog around the neighbourhood and browsed the shops on Haight Street [3]. Her exact address has been muddled ever since. In 1999 a nonprofit announced a new 20-bed rehab centre for drug-addicted mothers at 124 Lyon and said it was Joplin's old house. Media as far away as England repeated the claim. Then experts produced a copy of her 1960s driver's license, which gave her address as 122 Lyon, the house next door [1]. According to local lore, she had lived in any of four houses on the block [1]. "It just shows how mythological the whole thing is," said Country Joe McDonald, her boyfriend at the time, who had lived with her there for "three somewhat fuzzy months" [1]. Her roommate, the clothing designer Linda Gravenites, said they loved the flat but it had only one bedroom, so in 1968 they moved to Noe Street [1][2]. The confusion never quite ended. A 2009 Chronicle guide listed the apartment as 112 Lyon, No. 3 [3]. In 2014 the six-unit Queen Anne at 122 Lyon went on the market for $1.7 million [2].

title: One psychedelic month on outer Mission
place: Former Rock Garden club, 4742 Mission St
hook: In spring 1967 the Grateful Dead played a week in Jerry Garcia's old neighbourhood, and his mother came to watch.
story: In the 1950s 4742 Mission Street was an Italian bocce club [1]. In March 1967 the North Beach club owner Dave Rapkin turned it into the Rock Garden, a psychedelic venue meant to compete with the Fillmore and the Avalon [2]. It printed diamond-shaped posters, and the engineer Charlie Butten built bass speakers right into the stage [2]. The opening bill was Love with Big Brother and the Holding Company. From March 28 to April 2 the Grateful Dead played a week there, a few blocks from where Jerry Garcia grew up. His brother Tiff helped get the room ready, and their mother, who still lived nearby, saw her son perform for the first time in years [1][2]. Steve Miller and Buffalo Springfield followed. But the club served liquor, which kept out underage hippies, and it was a long ride from the Haight. Within about a month it went back to Latin dance music [2]. As 'The Ghetto' it later helped launch San Francisco Latin rock bands such as the Aliens and the Prophets, with Samoan bouncers on the door [1][2].

title: Philosophy Shelves in Grandma's Bedroom
place: Green Apple Books, 506 Clement Street at 6th Avenue
hook: A visitor walked into Green Apple Books and found the bedroom she slept in as a girl in the 1930s. It is now, probably, the philosophy section.
story: Before it held books, the building at Sixth and Clement was a family home: Hippolyte Cuneo, a foreman at the Joshua Hendy Machine Works, moved here with his wife and six children around 1895 [2]. A storefront was later pushed out in front of the house, and in the late 1940s the shopfront was shared by Ed's Togs menswear and Coliseum Furs [2]. In 1967 Richard Savoy opened Green Apple Books in a 750-square-foot space [1][3]. The store kept growing while other bookshops folded, adding a mezzanine, a second floor and its neighbour, Revolver Records [1][4]. Savoy, who ran it for almost 40 years, eventually offered the business to three employees, including Pete Mulvihill, a former temp earning $8 an hour; an owner-financed plan let them buy it over ten years, completing in 2008 [1]. In 2017, as the store turned fifty, Cuneo's granddaughter Jean Portello came back and found the bedroom she had slept in during the 1930s, upstairs in what historian Woody LaBounty believes is now the Philosophy section [2].

title: Sixty Years to Close One Road
place: JFK Promenade near the Conservatory of Flowers
hook: The park's main road got its Kennedy name and its first car-free Sunday on the same day in 1967. Making it car-free for good took 55 more years.
story: On April 2, 1967, the Recreation and Park Commission shut the park's Main Drive to cars for its first 'People's Day in the Park,' and renamed it John F. Kennedy Drive that same day [1]. Chronicle columnist Ron Fimrite, cycling through the tunnels, wondered what downtown would be like without cars [1]. Sundays became a roller-skating party. In 1979 skaters formed the Golden Gate Park Skate Patrol to fight a proposed skating ban, and in 1989 the city smoothed a patch at Sixth Avenue, the 'Skatin' Place,' largely thanks to its leader David Miles Jr. [1]. For decades the de Young and the Academy of Sciences fought longer closures, saying they cost them visitors [1]. Then the pandemic arrived. In April 2020 Mayor London Breed closed the 1.5-mile stretch every day. In April 2022 supervisors voted 7-4 to keep it closed after a 12-hour meeting [1]. That November voters rejected Proposition I, which would have reopened the road, by 61 percent, and passed Proposition J to keep it car-free [2]. Renamed JFK Promenade, it has logged millions of visits since 2020 [1].

title: The Many Lives of 628 Divisadero
place: 628 Divisadero Street (The Independent)
hook: Jazz, punk, Nirvana, lesbian dance nights, turntablists: behind one plain red front on Divisadero, the city's music changed about every ten years.
story: "Supposedly, Thelonious Monk played here back when this was a hot jazz strip," Justice League owner Michael O'Connor told the Chronicle in 1998. He wanted to put up a plaque listing every club the room had been [2]. Accounts disagree on the 1960s name. The Bay Guardian called it the Half Note, a jazz club with a house band that included George Duke and a young Al Jarreau [1]. The Chronicle named the Both/And as a past tenant, where Janis Joplin first heard Big Mama Thornton sing "Ball and Chain" [2]. In the early 1980s it was the VIS Club, playing punk, new wave and experimental music. By the late 1980s it had become the Kennel Club, where Nirvana opened for Tad [1][2]. The DJ Page Hodel's roving club The Box drew hundreds of gay men and lesbians to monthly dances there [3]. After the short-lived Crash Palace failed, O'Connor opened the Justice League around 1997. The artist Barry McGee ("Twist") painted its murals, and the club hosted drum-and-bass, hip-hop and house nights [2]. In February 2004 it reopened as The Independent, a 500-capacity room. "The night we opened, the fire department [was] signing everything off while the band was sound-checking," recalled owner Allen Scott [1].

title: The Promise Printed on a Certificate
place: 1800 block of Ellis Street
hook: Displaced families were given a certificate promising they could come back. On this one block of Ellis Street, the city's list of affected addresses runs to 99 entries.
story: When the Agency took a house, it handed the head of household a certificate promising preference for housing built later. In 2008 an Agency spokesman admitted, "there wasn't a lot of housing built for a long time" [1]. A state law passed in 1969 made that priority a legal requirement, and the Agency's Certificate of Preference Program carried it out [2]. By 2023, the Public Press reported, city agencies had issued almost 7,000 certificates since the program began in 1967, and only 1,483 had ever been used [3]. Many of them, reporters found, were never honoured [3]. Today the city publishes the addresses of displaced households, with no names attached. The Western Addition A-2 list has 4,792 entries. The 1800 block of Ellis Street alone accounts for 99 of them, spread across 52 street numbers, and many list a flat, a floor or a basement [4]. Under a 2021 state law, descendants became eligible as well, and in January 2022 the city began issuing certificates to the children and grandchildren of people who lost their homes [3]. Investigators working with a city partner have tracked down eligible families as far away as Texas, the Carolinas and Georgia [3].

title: The Refugee Rabbi Who Talked to Germany
place: Temple Emanu-El, 2 Lake Street at Arguello
hook: He fled the Nazis as a teenager. Decades later, from Emanu-El's great domed pulpit, he asked American Jews whether it was time to speak to Germany again.
story: In 1967 Temple Emanu-El, San Francisco's largest synagogue, installed a senior rabbi with an unusual biography [1]. Joseph Asher was born in Germany into a long line of rabbis; the New York Times counted seven generations [1]. Accounts differ on when he got out: the Times said his family fled in 1936, while his son Raphael remembered his father as 'a refugee from Germany in 1938' [1][2]. His son described 'a very exciting but episodic life' in England, Australia, Cincinnati, upstate New York, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina before San Francisco [2]. In the South he became known for civil rights work [2]. On a 1964 return trip to Germany he concluded that schools were trying to instil 'a sense of atonement' but offered 'a negative and incomplete approach' [1]. At his urging, in 1966 the Union of American Hebrew Congregations sent rabbis to West Germany to teach Germans about Jews [1]. He led Emanu-El under its dome at Lake and Arguello until 1986 [1]. In 1989 West Germany awarded him the Grand Cross of Merit; he died of cancer the following year, aged 69 [1].

title: The clinic where health care was free
place: 558 Clayton Street
hook: On its first day, a second-floor flat on Clayton Street treated about 250 young people who had nowhere else to go.
story: In 1967 David Smith was a young UCSF researcher studying how drugs affect the mind. Walking home through the Haight, he kept seeing flower children in the middle of bad LSD trips [1]. The neighbourhood's established hospitals would not treat them. By one activist's account, nearby St. Mary's had a standing policy of refusing drug overdoses [2]. On June 7, 1967, Smith opened a small second-floor clinic at 558 Clayton Street [3][4]. According to his account, more than 250 patients came on the first day, including over 40 with venereal disease and 15 with hepatitis. Years later he remembered it as "like 300 people" [1][3]. His malpractice insurance was cancelled, and he said he broke the law several times a day by treating drug users without calling the police [1][3]. His motto was that health care is a right, not a privilege [1]. The clinic became the first of more than 600 free clinics opened across the US over the following decade [4]. It merged into HealthRIGHT 360 in 2011–12, and the original site closed in July 2019 after years of losses as the neighbourhood gentrified [3][4].

title: The day the Dead got busted
place: 710 Ashbury Street
hook: Police carried away a pound of pot and two Grateful Dead members. Then the band did something it would never do again: it held a political press conference.
story: In 1966–68, 710 Ashbury was the Grateful Dead's communal home. Bob Weir recalled that people came in through his front window "with fair regularity" [1][2]. On October 2, 1967, city and state narcotics officers raided the house and found about a pound of marijuana and some hashish. They arrested Weir, then 19, Ron "Pigpen" McKernan, and several friends on felony charges. The Chronicle's front page ran "The Grateful Dead: Rock Band Busted" [1]. The same day, police raided four other Haight homes [1]. The band's lawyers ran the Haight Ashbury Legal Organization from the ground floor of the same building and were not arrested [1]. Instead of keeping quiet, the Dead read out a statement at a press conference in the house attacking California's marijuana laws. Their lawyer complained that if they had lived on Russian Hill, they wouldn't have been busted [1]. In June 1968 everyone pleaded guilty to reduced misdemeanours, and most paid $100 fines [1]. It was the last time the band took a public political stand, and they soon left the Haight [1].

title: When Haight Street stopped the buses
place: Haight and Ashbury Streets
hook: First the tour buses came to gawk. Then the crowds grew so thick the buses couldn't move, and the hippies decided they wanted the street for a park.
story: On April 6, 1967, Gray Line launched its "Hippie Hop" bus tour, billed as "the only foreign tour in the domestic U.S." Guides handed out a glossary of hippie slang to passengers peering through the windows [1]. It was short-lived. By mid-May the sidewalks were so jammed that buses could not get through, and Gray Line cancelled the tour [1]. The neighbourhood organiser Calvin Welch later recalled that many early hippies resented cars and buses on Haight Street. "They weren't going anywhere, they'd arrived" [2]. From 1968, he said, there were "mill-ins": thousands of people filled the street between Baker and Stanyan, skipping rope and chanting "We want a park!" until the traffic stopped [2]. Mayor Joseph Alioto answered with police. Welch described almost a month of daily clashes and said CS gas was used [2]. In his telling, the confrontation turned the Haight's long-time residents and newcomers into allies against City Hall's plans for the district. That alliance led to a later rezoning that held development to the density already there [2].

title: A pagoda from a sister city
place: Peace Pagoda, Japantown Peace Plaza, Post and Buchanan
hook: Osaka paid for a concrete pagoda as a symbol of lasting friendship. Sixty years into the sister-city pact, Osaka walked away over a statue.
story: San Francisco and Osaka became sister cities in 1957 [1]. When Japan Center opened in 1968, a five-tiered concrete stupa stood at the heart of its plaza. It was designed by Yoshiro Taniguchi, the Japanese architect who had designed the Crown Prince's palace [1][2]. Unlike the rest of the complex, the pagoda was paid for largely by donations from Osaka, and it was given to San Francisco as a symbol of friendship and peace between Japan and the United States [2]. On 8 September 2007, for the 50th anniversary of the pact, the block of Buchanan Street across Post was renamed Osaka Way [1][3]. The friendship did not last. In 2018 Osaka ended the 60-year relationship after Mayor Ed Lee accepted a memorial statue honouring the "comfort women" of World War II [1]. The pagoda still stands, and in 2025 the plaza around it was being rebuilt [3].

title: Bullet Holes, Opera and Ruth Williams
place: Bayview Opera House, 4705 Third Street
hook: Police shot up Bayview's 1888 opera house during the 1966 uprising. A playwright and activist, with a young Danny Glover on its stage, helped bring it back to life.
story: The South San Francisco Opera House at Third Street and Newcomb Avenue was built in 1888 for a Masonic lodge, to a design by Henry Geilfuss [1]. By the 1960s it had been reduced to a warehouse. The Bayview Neighborhood Community Center moved in in 1965, and during the 1966 uprising police fired into the building [1]. Community leader Ruth Williams raised money to hire the Black architect Harry Overstreet to repair the damage [1]. In May 1968 Western Opera Theatre staged "The Barber of Seville" and "La Bohème" there, probably the first operas the building ever hosted [1]. That same year a young Danny Glover did improv on its stage, and longshoremen screened movies for neighbourhood kids [1]. In October 1968 it became City Landmark No. 8 [1]. Williams was a Southern University graduate who had come west with her husband and six sons. She founded the Bayview Repertory Theater Company, wrote and acted in 37 plays, and produced the first Miss Black San Francisco pageants in 1977–79 [2]. On 7 December 1995 the supervisors renamed the building the Bayview Opera House Ruth Williams Memorial Theater [3].

title: Lili Knits: Prom Dresses on Ocean Avenue
place: Lili Knits, 1500 block of Ocean Avenue
hook: An Italian dressmaker who, her daughter says, made Carol Doda's first topless swimsuit moved her business to Ocean Avenue. For decades it dressed the Bay Area's proms.
story: Rita Rivera Doyle, born Pozzi, told an interviewer in 2003 that her mother had worked in the clothing trade since she was a little girl in Italy [1]. In San Francisco her mother first worked for a manufacturer, then ran her own business on Townsend Street, and her clothes sold at I. Magnin, Saks Fifth Avenue, City of Paris and Livingston's. In Rita's telling, her mother also "made the first topless swimsuit for Carol Doda" [1]. After buying a house in the Ingleside, her mother moved the business to Ocean Avenue. Rita thought that was in 1968, though she was not sure [1]. For more than 30 years Lili Knits made prom dresses, formal wear and pep squad uniforms for customers across the Bay Area [2]. Rita remembered people warning her mother away from the neighbourhood, and a warm welcome on opening day. "As soon as African American families moved in, people moved out. What is that about?" [2]. She missed Betty's Hamburger, where truck drivers came for Tuesday meatloaf and Friday fish, and was blunt about the street's future: "It will never be West Portal" [2]. A city business registration lists Lili Knit at 1556 Ocean Avenue from 2005 [3].

title: Ruth Asawa's schoolyard of clay
place: Alvarado Elementary School, 625 Douglass Street
hook: A sculptor who learned to draw in an internment camp opened an art workshop at her children's school. It became a model for 50 more.
story: Ruth Asawa learned to draw in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during the Second World War, and went on to become famous for her looped-wire sculptures [2]. In 1960 she and her husband, architect Albert Lanier, moved to Noe Valley [1]. In 1968 she started an arts programme at Alvarado Elementary, the public school her children attended [3]. She co-founded the Alvarado Arts Workshop with art historian Sally Woodbridge, and it became a model for arts programmes at 50 other San Francisco schools [1]. Her son Paul Lanier was 10 in 1968. He helped make a boy holding a red balloon for a 30-by-15-foot mosaic mural that still anchors the schoolyard [3]. Thirty years later Paul, now a ceramic artist, led the design of a second mural: 1,200 sculpted tiles forming a tree full of birds and insects. His own kindergarten daughter helped make it. Three generations of Asawa-Laniers were at its unveiling on Eureka Street in May 2000 [3]. By then Alvarado was the only public school in the city with a full-time artist-in-residence working in his own ceramics studio [3]. Asawa died at home in 2013, aged 87 [2].
