title: Santana's jam sessions above Precita Park
place: 205 Mullen Ave
hook: Carlos Santana lived in a cottage on Mullen Avenue and played free Sunday concerts in the park below.
story:
The Mission District usually gets the credit for Carlos Santana, but Bernal Heights neighbours say he commuted to the Mission from their hill [1]. Longtime resident Peter Wiley pointed Bernalwood to the house: a cottage on the north side of Mullen Avenue, just east of the Franconia steps [1]. That is 205 Mullen, where Santana lived in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Later some members of Journey lived there too, a band founded by musicians who had started out with Santana [2].

Santana has called Precita Park 'where it all started' [3]. Orlando Galvez was six years old and living on Folsom Street at the time. He remembers weekend jam sessions that turned the park into an amphitheatre. 'Oye Como Va' always got the party started. Hippies, Black Panthers and neighbourhood Chicanos with their sparkling lowriders gathered around the playground. Buckets of Kentucky Fried Chicken sat among clouds of marijuana smoke [3]. In 2016 the two-bedroom house was listed at $975,000. A blog lamented that a San Francisco 'starter home' now cost nearly a million dollars [2].

title: The Church That Built a Co-op
place: Bethel A.M.E. Church, 916 Laguna Street (corner of Golden Gate Avenue)
hook: As A-2 flattened the blocks around it, San Francisco's oldest Black congregation stayed put, built a new sanctuary, and sponsored 382 co-op homes next door.
story: Bethel A.M.E. traces its roots to a meeting house dedicated in 1852 as the pioneer Black congregation of San Francisco. By its own history, it moved to 916 Laguna Street on January 21, 1945 [1]. The church stood inside the part of A-2 that was cleared most completely. Between Ellis, Gough, Fulton and Webster, an area that had held about 2,500 Victorian-era houses was clear-cut entirely, and most of the replacement housing was two- and three-story townhouses built from the late 1960s into the early 1970s [2]. Bethel stayed and rebuilt. Under the Rev. J. Austell Hall it put up a new sanctuary and education building (1968–72 by the church's count, 1969–73 by the city's) and started a credit union in 1969 [1][2]. Hall also wanted housing, so the church sponsored Freedom West, which became the largest cooperative in the Western Addition [3]. It has 382 co-op units on about 11 acres bounded by Golden Gate, Gough, Fulton and Laguna, and the church stands at its corner [4]. Bethel went on to run Fellowship Manor for seniors, and later Prince Hall Apartments, Laurel Gardens and Thomas Paine Square [1]. A current plan, Freedom West 2.0, proposes to rebuild all 382 units [4].

title: The Longest Student Strike
place: 19th and Holloway avenues, SF State
hook: At 19th and Holloway, a linguist-turned-president climbed onto a strikers' sound truck to rip out the speaker wires, and a crowd snatched his tam o'shanter.
story: On November 6, 1968, the Black Students Union and the Third World Liberation Front called a strike at San Francisco State College, demanding a larger Black Studies program and the reinstatement of suspended instructor George Murray [1]. Their demands included Black, Asian American, American Indian and La Raza Studies departments within a College of Ethnic Studies [2]. After weeks of clashes the campus closed, and on November 26 President Robert Smith resigned [1]. English professor S. I. Hayakawa became acting president [1]. When the campus reopened on December 2, strikers parked a sound truck at the corner of 19th and Holloway. Hayakawa climbed on and tried to disconnect the speakers, and someone in the crowd pulled off his tam o'shanter [1]. In January about 350 teachers joined the picket lines [1]. An agreement on the fifteen demands was signed on March 20, 1969, and the strike ended the next day [1]. The result was the country's first College of Ethnic Studies [2].

title: The Rainbow House on Steiner Street
place: 908 Steiner Street, between Fulton and McAllister
hook: A redevelopment official told Maija Peeples-Bright to paint her Victorian beige. She painted it every colour she could find instead, with a fibreglass alligator in the window.
story: Contractor P. O. Chandler built 908 Steiner in 1888 for Niels Iverson, a Danish immigrant who had sailed round Cape Horn in 1848. SF Heritage gives the builder as R. O. Chandler [1][2]. By the 1960s the house had spent years as a St. Anthony Dining Room shelter for homeless men [1]. Then the artist Maija Peeples-Bright and her husband David Zack bought it for $17,000, with $5,000 from her father [1]. When a city redevelopment agent suggested beige, she said no. "I liked color. I decided to paint it multiple colors," she recalled. She used marine enamel, and passers-by sometimes climbed the scaffold to help [1]. She added a peacock head in a gable and a 10-foot Nile alligator in an upper window [1][2]. A 1968 Chronicle story described an exterior "painted in five different psychedelic hues" [3]. The Saturday Evening Post and Progressive Architecture wrote it up too, and the house became a stop for tourists [1][2]. Artists of the Funk movement gathered there. A later owner called it the city's first "Painted Lady" [1].

title: The World Trade Center architect's Japantown mall
place: Japan Center malls, Post Street between Laguna and Fillmore
hook: The man drawing the Twin Towers was also designing Japantown's mall at the same time, and he insisted he had no idea how to make it look Japanese.
story: The Japanese Cultural and Trade Center, bounded by Laguna, Geary, Fillmore and Post, was built from 1965 and dedicated in March 1968 [1]. It was partly funded by Japanese corporations, and Kintetsu ran its shopping centres [1][2]. Its architect was Minoru Yamasaki, working with local firm Van Bourg-Nakamura, during the same years he was designing New York's World Trade Center [1]. Yamasaki was uneasy with the brief. When Redevelopment Agency chief Justin Herman urged him to make the hotel rooms as authentically Japanese as possible, he replied: "I really do not know enough about Japanese detailing to feel adequate in this respect" [1]. The boxy buildings use concrete panels and wood meant to suggest shoji screens, and Yamasaki felt the finished project was not what he had envisioned [1]. The complex had a human cost: according to preservation architect Bridget Maley, it displaced more than 50 businesses and about 1,500 residents in a neighbourhood already emptied once by the wartime removal of its Japanese American families [1].

title: The mermaids that beat the modernist
place: Ruth Asawa fountain, Ghirardelli Square plaza
hook: The square's famous landscape architect wanted a sleek metal shaft. Ruth Asawa gave him nursing mermaids and amphibians, and the city took her side.
story: As Ghirardelli Square neared completion, sculptor Ruth Asawa was commissioned to make a fountain for its courtyard. She made a cast-bronze fountain of mermaids and sea creatures, installed in 1968 and titled Andrea [2]. FoundSF calls it the "Mermaids" fountain [1]. Lawrence Halprin, the square's landscape architect, hated it. He attacked it as too representational and out of keeping with the plaza, and he had wanted a 15-foot metal shaft instead. The fight spilled into the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial pages, and Halprin lost [1]. Local residents, especially women, rallied to keep the sculpture [2]. Historian Alison Isenberg argues the fountain was an early skirmish of second-wave feminism, disguised as a charming piece for families. "In 1968 San Franciscans saw relatively unprecedented scenes in Ghirardelli Square," she writes: "breast-feeding, a lesbian family, an amphibian orgy, possibly mermaid vaginas." [1] In her reading, a dispute about artistic style turned into a public argument about gender, sexuality and who shapes urban space.

title: Twenty-Seven Prisoners Sat Down and Sang
place: Presidio stockade, Building 1213, Fort Winfield Scott
hook: A guard shot a disturbed young prisoner in the back. Three days later, 27 soldiers sat on the stockade lawn and the Army charged them with mutiny.
story: In 1968 the Presidio stockade was packed with AWOL soldiers. Peter Barnes wrote that Building 1213 held up to 120 prisoners when the Army's own limit was 88. Another account says the jail was built for 56 and held 115 [1][2]. One inmate counted 33 suicide attempts by 21 men between May and October [1]. On 11 October, Private Richard 'Rusty' Bunch, a troubled young man from Dayton, Ohio, was on a shotgun work detail. He asked his guard, 'If I run, will you shoot me?' The guard answered, 'You'll have to run to find out.' Bunch skipped away and was killed by a shotgun blast to the back. Officials called it justifiable homicide [1]. On the morning of 14 October, 27 of the 123 prisoners sat down on the grass and sang 'We Shall Overcome'. They read out demands that included an end to shotgun details, the removal of racist guards and a chance to tell the press about Bunch [1]. Firemen called in to hose them down refused [2]. The 27 were charged with mutiny, a capital offence. The first man sentenced got 15 years, but after public outcry all were released within about 18 months [2]. Sixth Army commander Stanley Larsen later explained: 'We thought the revolution was starting, and we were trying to crush it' [2].

title: A Blacklisted Physicist's Museum of Curiosity
place: Former Exploratorium, Palace of Fine Arts exhibit hall, 3601 Lyon Street
hook: Frank Oppenheimer helped build the atomic bomb, lost his career to McCarthyism, raised cattle, then filled an empty exhibition hall with things you were told to touch.
story: Frank Oppenheimer had worked with his brother J. Robert on the Manhattan Project. After a brief youthful embrace of communism he was blacklisted from research and teaching in the McCarthy era, and ended up a cattle rancher in small-town Colorado [1]. He drifted back into teaching at a local high school. There he swapped the textbook for hands-on tools and materials, which became his trademark [1]. A National Science Foundation grant let him build about a hundred experiment models, and a 1965 Guggenheim tour of European science museums sharpened the idea [2]. In 1969, aged 57, he took over the 'cavernous, and very empty' exhibit hall behind the Palace of Fine Arts [1]. The Exploratorium opened in August 1969 [2]. Oppenheimer put the exhibit workshop in full view, believing visitors should know 'the way a shop smells when you burn the wood in a saw' [2]. He worked alongside the artists and builders who made the exhibits, and ran the museum until just before his death in 1985 [1]. The Exploratorium stayed in the Marina for more than four decades, then moved to Pier 15 on the Embarcadero in April 2013 [1][2].

title: A Killer's Cipher Mailed to Fifth and Mission
place: San Francisco Chronicle Building, 901 Mission Street at Fifth
hook: A letter in November 1969 brought 340 strange symbols to the Chronicle's newsroom. It took 51 years and three strangers on three continents to read them.
story: Since the 1920s the San Francisco Chronicle had been made at 901 Mission Street, at the corner of Fifth and Mission [1]. In the autumn of 1969 that newsroom became the killer's chosen mailbox. A letter that reached the paper in November 1969 held a cryptogram of 340 characters, and the paper ran a story on it on November 12 [2]. An earlier cipher, sent in pieces to the Chronicle, the Examiner and the Vallejo Times-Herald, had been cracked by a Salinas schoolteacher and his wife. The "340" held out for five decades [2]. In December 2020 it finally gave way to Virginia web designer David Oranchak, Australian mathematician Sam Blake and Belgian warehouse operator Jarl Van Eycke. They had tested around 650,000 ways of reading the symbols over eight months [2]. The text runs diagonally down the page and gives no name. It begins: "I hope you are having lots of fun in trying to catch me." It also says "that wasnt me on the TV show", an apparent reference to a caller on KGO's AM San Francisco in October 1969. The FBI confirmed that private citizens had solved the cipher. The case remains open [2].

title: Bethel A.M.E. Leaves Chinatown for Laguna
place: Bethel A.M.E. Church, 916 Laguna Street
hook: After most of a century on Powell Street in Chinatown, a pioneer Black congregation followed its people west, then helped house them.
story: Bethel A.M.E. was one of San Francisco's three pioneer African American churches. Since the nineteenth century it had worshipped at 1207 Powell Street in Chinatown [1]. After the war the old downtown churches were full, and far from where the city's fast-growing Black population now lived. One by one their pastors moved to the Western Addition [1]. In the late 1950s Bethel bought an old, disused church building on Laguna Street. When that grew too cramped, the congregation replaced it with a new church, which it moved into in 1969 [1][2]. Like Third Baptist and A.M.E. Zion, the new building rejected traditional church architecture in favor of strong, simple geometric shapes and plain walls [2]. Bethel then became a builder. During the Western Addition A-2 redevelopment it partnered with the Redevelopment Agency on affordable housing [2]. It sponsored Freedom West, the area's largest co-op, spread over four blocks at the church's corner, and also operates Laurel Gardens, Prince Hall Apartments, Thomas Paine Square and Fellowship Manor [3].

title: Los Siete and the Storefront on 24th
place: Los Siete Defense Committee, 24th St near South Van Ness Ave
hook: After a police officer died on May 1, 1969, seven young Latinos from the Mission were charged with murder. Their defenders built a clinic, a breakfast programme and a newspaper.
story: On May 1, 1969, two plainclothes officers stopped a group of young men carrying a television into a house on Alvarado Street [1]. In the struggle, Officer Joe Brodnik was killed by a shot from his partner Paul McGoran's gun [1]. Police flooded the house with tear gas while helicopters circled; Francisco FloresLanda, then seventeen, watched them from Dolores Park [1][2]. Seven young men, mostly Central American and some linked to the Mission Rebels youth group, were charged with murder and defended by the lawyer Charles Garry [1]. The defence argued McGoran drew his gun and shot Brodnik in the struggle [1]. The trial began in late June 1970 and ended in acquittals; FoundSF reports six were tried and a seventh had fled [1][3]. Near 24th and South Van Ness, the Los Siete Defense Committee ran a free breakfast programme, the Basta Ya! newspaper and Centro de Salud [1]. It also ran a Valencia Street restaurant selling a Coke, hamburger and fries for a dollar [2].

title: Panther Breakfasts and an FBI Plant
place: Sacred Heart Church basement hall, 554 Fillmore Street
hook: A Catholic parish fed up to 100 children a day with the Black Panthers. Then the FBI planted hate-filled coloring books in its basement.
story: Father Eugene Boyle became pastor of Sacred Heart in 1968, having already marched with Cesar Chavez from Delano to Sacramento in 1966 [1][2]. In 1969 the Black Panther Party, which had approached most of the churches in the area, came to Sacred Heart. They 'finally came to us on a lark,' Boyle recalled [1]. The parish opened its basement hall and kitchen, and the Breakfast Program for Children began there on March 10, 1969, feeding 75 to 100 local children a day, many of them pupils at the parish school [1]. Police and the FBI took notice. That year San Francisco police told the McClellan Senate investigations committee that Boyle was letting the Panthers hand out coloring books that showed police as pigs [1]. The Panthers had printed a few but never distributed them. In 1975 the Church Committee revealed that the FBI had planted the books in the church basement as part of its campaign against the party [1]. The episode cost the program liberal support, but it carried on [1]. The parish also hosted anti-war and SF State student activists, and on September 21, 1970 Boyle said Mass there for the United Farm Workers' lettuce boycott, whose San Francisco campaign started at Sacred Heart [1][3].

title: The Mitchell Brothers' 'Carnegie Hall'
place: Mitchell Brothers O'Farrell Theatre, 895 O'Farrell St
hook: Two film-school brothers opened a porn theatre on the Fourth of July, beat the city in court over and over, and ended in a Marin County shooting.
story: Jim and Artie Mitchell got their start in San Francisco State's film department, then opened their theatre at 895 O'Farrell Street on July 4, 1969 [1]. Police raided it again and again, but prosecutors struggled to win convictions [1]. The brothers were involved in nearly 200 obscenity lawsuits, and their wins helped set legal precedents far beyond the city [2]. In 1972 they spent $60,000 on 'Behind the Green Door'. Just before release, their star Marilyn Chambers told them her face would soon be on Ivory soap boxes nationwide. The publicity made it a smash, and it went on to earn over $50 million [1][2]. After a 1980 vice raid, the brothers put Mayor Dianne Feinstein's phone number on their marquee under 'For a Good Time Call…' [2]. Hunter S. Thompson dubbed the club the 'Carnegie Hall' of sex in America [1][2]. The story turned dark on February 27, 1991, when Jim shot Artie dead at Artie's Corte Madera home. Jim was convicted of voluntary manslaughter [1][2]. The theatre survived him but not the pandemic, closing for good in 2020 [2].

title: Where American Beauty was recorded
place: Wally Heider Studios (now Hyde Street Studios), 245 Hyde St
hook: Behind a plain door in a former film warehouse, the Grateful Dead, CSNY and Creedence cut classics. A drunk Grace Slick warned the night receptionist not to wake her.
story: In 1969 Los Angeles engineer Wally Heider leased 245 Hyde Street, a building 20th Century Fox had used to store film, and built what is generally considered the Bay Area's first high-tech recording studio [1]. Unusually, it gave musicians almost complete creative control [1]. 'It was ground zero,' engineer Stephen Barncard said. 'San Francisco for years had been waiting for a full-fledged professional studio' [2]. Here the Grateful Dead recorded 'American Beauty', Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young made 'Déjà Vu', and Creedence Clearwater Revival cut 'Cosmo's Factory' [1]. Jefferson Airplane, Santana, Van Morrison and Herbie Hancock worked here too [1][2]. In 1974 Susie Foot, 28, was the studio's gopher, guarding the front desk at night. Grace Slick wandered out of a Jefferson Starship session and told her: 'My name's Grace, and I drink a lot. If you see me passed out on the couch, don't wake me up' [1]. Foot rose to first engineer by the time Heider's closed in 1980 [1]. Under Michael Ward it reopened as Hyde Street Studios, where Tupac Shakur, Green Day and Cake recorded. A sidewalk plaque now marks the spot [1][3].

title: Lawrence Halprin's fountain for the elders
place: Jewish Home (SF Campus for Jewish Living), 302 Silver Ave
hook: Behind a fence on Silver Avenue, a master landscape architect built cascading concrete waterfalls for the residents of a home founded in 1891.
story: The Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum and Home Society was incorporated in 1871 to care for orphans and 'aged and infirm Israelites.' In 1891 it opened a two-storey wooden Victorian home on Silver Avenue for twelve residents [1]. In 1923 that building was replaced by a brick Georgian Revival home designed by Samuel Lightner Hyman [1]. In 1969 the architect Howard A. Friedman added a Brutalist tower, Annex A, now the Goodman Building. A year later Lawrence Halprin designed the courtyard it encloses [1][2]. His fountain is a set of overlapping concrete planes. Water streams over them into a shallow sunken pool, and they form a kind of stage for a mother-and-child sculpture by the Israeli artist Ursula Malbin. Around it are lawn, a curving concrete seat wall, pines and pollarded sycamores [2]. The Cultural Landscape Foundation notes that Halprin was himself Jewish and was serving that same year on the Jerusalem Committee, which reviewed that city's master plan [2]. The almost 9-acre campus is still a senior home [1].

title: Miz Maxwell at the top of De Haro
place: Potrero Hill Neighborhood House, 953 De Haro Street
hook: No estate agent would sell her a house on Potrero Hill. Twenty years later Enola Maxwell was running its Julia Morgan community centre, and she ran it for three decades.
story:
Enola Maxwell left Baton Rouge in 1948 with her two children to join her mother, who had found work in a San Francisco laundry [1]. The two women lived in a housing project at 18th and Missouri, where Maxwell's daughter Sophie was born in 1950. Maxwell saved her wages as a housekeeper for a down payment, but no real estate agent would sell them a house on Potrero Hill. They bought on Harrison Street in the Mission instead [1].

In 1963 she travelled to Washington to hear Martin Luther King Jr. She became the first female lay minister in the Presbyterian Church while earning her living as a postal clerk [1][2]. Then the church put her in charge of the Neighborhood House on De Haro Street, a Julia Morgan building from 1922. It was then used almost entirely by white residents, in a fast-changing neighbourhood [1]. Accounts date her appointment to 1970, 1971 or early 1972, when the Potrero View reported the board had "wrangled" with her supporters [1][2][3].

She ran "the Nabe" until her death in 2003, known for her striking hats. By then it offered a Head Start programme, a theatre, job training for teenagers and drug-diversion counselling [1]. In 2001 Potrero Hill Middle School was renamed after her. Sophie Maxwell became a city supervisor [1][2].

title: The Fort the Bridge Refused to Destroy
place: Fort Point, beneath the Golden Gate Bridge
hook: The fort never fired a shot in anger. It was nearly flattened for the bridge, then saved by retired officers who spent eleven years lobbying to keep it.
story: Fort Point was built between 1853 and 1861 to guard the Golden Gate at the height of the Gold Rush. It was the only 'Third System' masonry fort ever built west of the Mississippi. Its guns never fired at an enemy [1]. By the 1930s it was obsolete, and early plans for the Golden Gate Bridge called for knocking it down. Chief Engineer Joseph Strauss saw its architectural value and designed a special arch so the roadway could leap over the fort [1]. Interest in preserving it rose and fell for decades. Then in 1959 a group of retired military officers and civilian engineers founded the Fort Point Museum Association [2]. With the Sixth Army's blessing, they cleaned up the interior and put up safety barricades. They held open houses, led school groups and civic groups on tours, and opened the sallyport doors on weekends to more and more visitors. The members knew the public had to be able to get inside before it would back a new historic park [2]. In 1968 local congressmen introduced bills to make the fort a national historic site. On 16 October 1970, President Richard Nixon signed the final bill into law, and Fort Point National Historic Site was born [1][2].

title: The Galería That Brought Frida to the Bay
place: Galería de la Raza, 24th St at Bryant
hook: SFMOMA turned down a Frida Kahlo show. So a Chicano gallery on 24th Street put one on itself, years before the rest of the country caught Frida fever.
story: René Yañez came to the Bay Area after army service in North Carolina, where a lieutenant spotted his sketches and had him use art as therapy with shell-shocked soldiers [1]. In 1970 he co-founded the Galería de la Raza, which later spent decades at 24th and Bryant [1][2]. The Galería invited the public in to critique the art, and it invented traditions: a simple altar it set up for Día de los Muertos in 1971 sparked the neighbourhood's procession and displays [1]. In 1977, after SFMOMA declined his pitch for a travelling Kahlo exhibition, Yañez curated a retrospective of her work at the Galería, the first in the Bay Area [1]. Friends called him the Padrino of the Mission [1]. In 2018 the Galería left its longtime building. In January 2019 the Historic Preservation Commission voted unanimously to begin landmarking it anyway, over the owner's objections; his attorney said "The Galería is now gone, though" [2].

title: The Old Men Who Stopped the Bulldozers
place: Yerba Buena Gardens (former residential hotels of South of Market)
hook: The redevelopment chief called them skid row bums. A retired union organiser, 80 years old, took the city to federal court and won.
story: Before Yerba Buena Gardens, these blocks were a neighbourhood of cheap residential hotels, home to poor and elderly people, many of them retired seamen and trade unionists, whose rents averaged less than $40 a month [1]. From 1967 the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency began clearing them for a convention centre; by mid-1969 it owned 44% of the land [1]. Agency director M. Justin Herman reportedly called the residents "nothing but a bunch of skid row bums." George Woolf, an 80-year-old former Alaska cannery union president who had lost his front teeth in the 1934 General Strike, answered: "I'm not a bum and I resent being discredited and discounted" [1]. With co-chair Peter Mendelsohn, a merchant seaman of 40 years, he led Tenants and Owners in Opposition to Redevelopment (TOOR) [1]. In 1970 federal judge Stanley Weigel halted the huge project until an adequate relocation plan existed [2]. The eventual decree required 1,500 to 1,800 replacement homes, with residents holding four hotels as "hostages" until they were built, though few of the original tenants were ever properly rehoused [1]. TOOR's offshoot, TODCO, went on to become a major builder of affordable housing South of Market [1].

title: "We Potrero Hill boys got to stick together"
place: 18th and Missouri Streets (298 Missouri)
hook: Dirty Harry grew up here, on screen at least. A cat burglar, Ant-Man and one of Charlize Theron's characters have all lived at the same photogenic corner: 18th and Missouri.
story:
Hollywood keeps casting Potrero Hill. In Don Siegel's Dirty Harry (1971), the Black doctor treating Clint Eastwood's Harry Callahan, who grew up on the Hill, tells him: "It's okay. We Potrero Hill boys, we got to stick together." [1] Scorpio's second victim is found on a hillside lot at Texas and Sierra Streets, where the Sierra Heights condominiums stand now [1]. Three years earlier, parts of the car chase in Bullitt were shot on the Hill, at Kansas and 20th and at Rhode Island and 20th [1][2].

The corner of 18th and Missouri often gets the call. Whoopi Goldberg's cat burglar lived there in Burglar (1987). In Sweet November (2001), Charlize Theron's Sara Deever lived at 298 Missouri and ate with Keanu Reeves at Farley's coffee shop, while the now-vanished Daily Scoop ice cream parlour was dressed up as a produce stand [1]. In Ant-Man and the Wasp (2018), Paul Rudd's foot goes through the painted fence on 18th Street [1].

The television detective Lt. Mike Stone, played by Karl Malden, lived at 768 De Haro in The Streets of San Francisco (1972–77), which filmed all over the Hill [1][2]. Along the way, the View notes, the films have recorded the neighbourhood's many changes [1].

title: A concrete sail rises on Cathedral Hill
place: Cathedral of St. Mary of the Assumption, 1111 Gough Street
hook: Critics mocked the first designs as a camel mating a donkey. What rose on Cathedral Hill instead was a 190-foot concrete sail.
story: When the archdiocese named three local architects for its new cathedral in April 1963, the Chronicle later recalled, the reaction was a stunned 'Who?' [1]. Critic Allen Temko fumed that McSweeney's name could not be linked to 'a single significant piece of modern architecture'. The editor of the liturgical magazine Worship said an early scheme looked like 'the effort of a camel and a donkey to mate' [1]. Archbishop McGucken brought in MIT dean Pietro Belluschi and the Roman engineer Pier Luigi Nervi [1][2]. Ground was broken in August 1965 and the building was blessed on 5 May 1971 [2]. It sits on a Redevelopment Agency site bounded by Gough, Geary, Ellis and Cleary Court. Before the first concrete was even poured, the archbishop was picketed and the project was attacked as 'an affront to the poor' [1]. The roof is made of hyperbolic paraboloids rising from a square to a cross, crowned by a 55-foot gold cross [1][3]. Critics said it copied Kenzo Tange's cathedral in Tokyo [1]. Nervi called it 'the first cathedral truly of our time' [2]. In 2007 local architects named it one of San Francisco's 25 best buildings [3].

title: A shotgun through the station window
place: Ingleside Police Station, 1 Sgt. John V. Young Lane, Balboa Park
hook: On August 29, 1971, gunmen burst into the Ingleside police station and killed a desk sergeant. The case stayed open for almost forty years.
story: The Ingleside Police Station, a Spanish-style stucco building with big arched doorways and a terracotta tile roof, first opened in 1910 [3]. On August 29, 1971, at least three men burst in, and one of them fired a shotgun through an opening in the bulletproof glass window [1]. Sergeant John V. Young, 51, was killed, and a civilian clerk was wounded [1]. The case stayed open for decades. In 1975 three men arrested in New Orleans were charged, but a judge dismissed the charges after finding that police there had tortured them [1]. In January 2007, eight men described by prosecutors as former members of the Black Liberation Army, a violent offshoot of the Black Panther Party, were arrested. All of them denied involvement and called the evidence coerced and fabricated [1]. In 2009 the case ended in pleas and dismissals. Herman Bell pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter and Anthony Bottom pleaded no contest to conspiracy. Charges against four others were dropped [2]. The station was renovated in 1991, and its address now carries the sergeant's name [3].

title: Koko, the Fireworks Child
place: Children's Zoo, San Francisco Zoo
hook: A gorilla born at the zoo on the Fourth of July learned her first signs from a Stanford graduate student in the Children's Zoo.
story: On July 4, 1971, a western lowland gorilla was born at the San Francisco Zoo and named Hanabi-ko, Japanese for "fireworks child" [1][2]. The world would know her as Koko. Stanford doctoral student Francine Patterson began teaching her sign language in 1972 [1]. Until June 1973 the lessons took place at the Children's Zoo exhibit, before Patterson and her partner Ronald Cohn moved the sessions to a trailer and then took Koko to Stanford [2]. Patterson and Cohn founded The Gorilla Foundation, and in 1979 Koko moved with them to the Santa Cruz Mountains [1]. According to the foundation, she came to use more than 1,000 signs and understand about 2,000 spoken English words [1]. National Geographic put her on its cover in October 1978 with a photo she took of herself in a mirror [1]. Scientists argued over whether she was really using language, and critics objected to her lifelong confinement [1][2]. She died in her sleep in June 2018, aged 46 [1].

title: The Pool Lifeguards Patrolled by Rowboat
place: Former Fleishhacker Pool site, now zoo parking
hook: The world's largest swimming tank held six million gallons of seawater. A 1971 storm broke one pipe, and the zoo wanted a parking lot.
story: Fleishhacker Pool opened on April 23, 1925: 1,000 feet long, 150 feet wide, filled with six million gallons of seawater and patrolled by up to two dozen lifeguards, some in rowboats [1]. Swimmer Ann Curtis set world records in it [1]. It was supposedly heated to seventy degrees, but everyone remembers the cold [1]. By the 1950s editorials called it a white elephant [1]. In January 1971 a storm damaged the outflow pipe to the ocean and the water became contaminated. The city tried fresh water for the first time and got algae instead [1]. The zoo campaigned to bury the pool. Director Saul Kitchener said that "its day has passed," and most of the land was earmarked for a parking lot [1]. A 1977 ballot measure to spend about a million dollars restoring it failed, and bulldozers began filling the pit in 1981 [1]. Old lifeguard Billy Nichols once asked Herbert Fleishhacker why he had built it so big. Fleishhacker told him to swim the length and back, then asked whether anyone had got in his way. "That's why I did it" [1].

title: The Potrero View follows its nose
place: Former Safeway Coffee Plant, 1501 Mariposa Street (at Arkansas)
hook: In August 1971 a new neighbourhood paper went hunting for the source of Potrero Hill's "smell spells". The spice factory blamed the coffee plant across the street.
story:
The Potrero View began in 1970 as "Hills and Dales", a newsletter that five neighbours typed on stencils and ran off on St. Teresa's church mimeograph. It first appeared under its new name on August 1, 1970 [1]. A year later it took on one of the Hill's oldest complaints: the smell [1][2].

The View reported that the last great "Smell Spell", in spring 1970, had brought more than 400 calls to the air pollution district, from as far away as Telegraph Hill [2]. Then the reporters went to see the culprits. A worker at Pacific Rendering, where whale and animal parts were cooked down, said: "They pay me $16,000 a year so I don't give a damn what it smells like." [2]

On the north slope, Pioneer Soap at 18th and Carolina gave off "a very musky smell". Mr. Markman of First Spice Mixing, at Arkansas and Mariposa, said: "If you really want a strong odor, go across the street to the coffee factory." That was the Safeway coffee plant at 1501 Mariposa, blamed for the smell of burned coffee almost every day [2]. The View later reported the plant would cut the odour by 1972, after 29 residents petitioned [1].

title: A bordello becomes a jazz jewel box
place: Great American Music Hall, 859 O'Farrell St
hook: Built for a blind political boss's pleasure palace, nearly lost, it was reborn in 1972. Duke Ellington got his own shower. The Grateful Dead brought live crickets.
story: 859 O'Farrell opened in 1907 as Blanco's, a lavish cafe of gilded mirrors and frescoes. By mid-century it had passed through Sally Rand's cabaret, a Moose lodge and a restaurant whose owner vanished amid a tax investigation, after which the building was sold at an IRS auction. It was in such decline that it nearly came down [1][2]. In 1972 Tom Bradshaw bought it, restored it and renamed it the Great American Music Hall [2]. It started as a jazz room. Sarah Vaughan, Bill Evans and Duke Ellington played here, and Ellington had a dressing room and shower built in the basement for his 1970s residencies. Carmen McRae and Sonny Rollins recorded live albums on its stage [1]. In February 1974 Journey debuted here with drummer Aynsley Dunbar [1]. The Grateful Dead recorded 'One From the Vault' at an invitation-only show in 1975 [1][2]. According to the hall's general manager, they wanted to open with the sound of crickets and brought in live ones. It was too dark and cold for the crickets to chirp, so the band used a tape, and crickets roamed the building for ages [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta quake shook loose a long-papered-over secret door to the hotel next door [1].

title: Balmy Alley: Garage Doors Become Galleries
place: Balmy Alley, between 24th and 25th Sts
hook: Two young Chicanas borrowed house paint from the neighbours and painted a garage door. Men laughed. A decade later the whole alley was shouting about Central America.
story: In 1972 Patricia Rodriguez and Graciela Carrillo, who shared a building at 54 Balmy Alley, asked a neighbour if they could paint the garage door across the way [1]. There were no proper mural paints, so they used outdoor house paint from neighbours and bartered for bright colours [1]. Men teased them, and some women began a rival mural to prove anyone could do it, but never finished it [1]. Ralph Maradiaga of the Galería de la Raza backed them and suggested the name that stuck: Mujeres Muralistas [1]. The group wanted to prove that women could paint big outdoor walls, something the Mexican mural movement had not shown [1]. In the 1980s Ray Patlán and Rodriguez co-founded PLACA, a volunteer effort that filled the alley with murals supporting Central American resistance and opposing US intervention; Patlán guided some 40 artists, and residents later called him the Mayor of Balmy Alley [2]. In 2014 Miranda Bergman and O'Brien Thiele were back on scaffolding restoring their 1984 panel, the last complete PLACA mural in the alley [3].

title: Co-ops Built on the Square's Formula
place: Loren Miller Homes, 937 McAllister Street
hook: Once St. Francis Square showed that a pension fund could house working families, Black union leaders used the same formula to build co-ops in A-2.
story: In 1964, while A-2 was still being planned, the ILWU and its architects sent Mayor Shelley a proposal. Build first on vacant land, it said, and move no family until low- and moderate-income housing was ready for them in the Western Addition. Keep costs down with cheap land, low-interest loans, tax breaks and sponsors willing to forgo profit. "Basically," one co-op historian wrote, "it was the formula which made St. Francis Square possible" [1]. The union's plan also gave current residents first priority as new housing was finished, and the ILWU helped local African American groups build their own co-ops modeled on the Square [2]. Three of them are nearby: Loren Miller Homes here at 937 McAllister, Ammel Park at 656 Grove, and Martin Luther King–Marcus Garvey Square at 1680 Eddy [2]. Loren Miller Homes and Amel Park (the spelling varies between sources) were sponsored by the Labor Assembly for Community Action, a group led by Black ILWU leaders including Bill Chester and Leroy King [1]. The Assessor's roll dates the Loren Miller Homes building to 1972 [3]. In 1981 Leroy King became a commissioner of the Redevelopment Agency [4].

title: Four cars down the park steps
place: Alta Plaza Park stairs, Clay Street at Pierce
hook: Alta Plaza's grand stairway, built in 1905, still has scars from a 1972 Barbra Streisand comedy that never had permission to drive cars down it.
story: Alta Plaza was set aside as a public square under the 1855 Van Ness Ordinance, though the city didn't hold clear title until 1888 [2]. By July 1905 the Parks Department, under John McLaren, had built four flights of terrace steps up its steep southern side. A few months later, on the morning of April 18, 1906, residents stood on the hill and watched the city burn [2]. The stairway's best-known moment came in 1972. In Peter Bogdanovich's screwball comedy What's Up, Doc?, Barbra Streisand and Ryan O'Neal's characters flee through the city in a stolen Volkswagen Beetle, and the chase takes a shortcut straight down the Alta Plaza steps [1]. The stunt, with four cars crashing down the stairs, wasn't authorised, and it left permanent damage that can still be seen today [1]. Legend has it that it made the city change its film-permit rules, but SFGATE presents that only as legend [1]. The film was a huge hit, earning $66 million on a $4 million budget [1].

title: Laughing Sal's Last Labor Day
place: Site of Playland-at-the-Beach, 48th Avenue and Cabrillo Street
hook: For three decades a cackling mechanical woman gave children nightmares at Ocean Beach. On 4 September 1972, the laughing stopped.
story: Playland-at-the-Beach grew to more than three blocks along the Great Highway: the Big Dipper, the Diving Bell, Topsy's Roost, and a Fun House with long wooden slides and a spinning turntable [1]. Over its entrance, from the 1940s, swayed Laughing Sal, a papier-mâché giant with red curls, freckles, a gap-toothed grin and a recorded cackle heard all along the midway [1]. Playland was also the birthplace of the It's-It ice cream sandwich [1][2]. After George Whitney died in 1958 and the Big Dipper came down, the park grew faded and seedy as families headed for the suburbs [2]. Developers bought it, and it closed for good on Labor Day, 4 September 1972 [2]. Herb Caen wrote a farewell column, 'We'll Never Go There Anymore' [1]. An auction scattered the rides; the Looff carousel went to Long Beach and came back in 1998 to Yerba Buena Gardens [1][3]. The main Sal went to the Santa Cruz Boardwalk, and condominiums and a Safeway rose on the site [1][2]. In 1996 artist Ray Beldner put up five perforated steel silhouettes nearby, Sal among them [1].

title: Pool tables where the Rialto's seats were
place: Billiard Palacade (former Rialto Theatre), 5179 Mission Street at Rolph Street
hook: Just south of Geneva, a 1910s movie house has been a pool hall for more than half a century. Its bar still looks like the old ticket counter.
story: The Rialto Theatre opened at Mission and Rolph Street in the 1910s, designed by Marc T. Jorgensen in a Spanish Moorish style. One researcher dates the opening to about May 1, 1916, while others say 1918 [1]. It did not last long as a cinema. After the bigger Amazon Theatre opened around the corner on Geneva Avenue in 1928, the Rialto soon closed [1]. The building found its long-term use in 1972, when it became the Billiard Palacade, a large pool hall and diner [2]. By 2011, one visitor noted that it had been a pool hall far longer than it had ever been a theatre, and that its interior details were better preserved than most in the city. The bar still looked like an old ticket counter. An older Salvadoran woman told the building's history while she wrapped beers in napkin 'koozies' for the regulars under the soft pool lights [3]. In 2023, a writer riding the 14R Mission bus noticed the old movie palace, freshly painted blue and orange. He saw it as part of a Mission Street where evangelical churches sing in Spanish and shops wire money to Latin America and the Philippines. It was a neighbourhood once mostly Italian and Irish and now largely Asian and Latino [2].

title: Saving the Granite Lady From the Wrecking Ball
place: Old U.S. Mint, 88 Fifth Street at Mission
hook: In the 1960s people argued about tearing down the Old Mint for a high-rise. Instead, visitors were soon striking their own medals on its 1869 press.
story: After coining stopped in 1937, the Old Mint at Fifth and Mission became a federal office building. By 1968 it was empty. Through the 1960s it sat at the centre of a fight between people who wanted it demolished for a high-rise and people who wanted the landmark restored [1]. The preservationists won. In spring 1972 the General Services Administration handed the building to the Bureau of the Mint, and restoration began. When it reopened in spring 1973, it was the first public building to open under a new federal law allowing surplus historic buildings to be adapted for new uses [1]. National Park Service specialists studied flakes of old paint under a microscope to recover the original colours. The basement vaults and front rooms became a free museum with a $1 million gold bar on display and an 1869 press where visitors could strike their own souvenir medals. Mint Director Mary Brooks announced the restoration complete in November 1976 [1]. Its later story is shakier. By 2015 an 11-year city effort to make it a history museum had collapsed. The unreinforced masonry needed about $60 million in repairs, and it was being reborn as an events space [2].

title: The Army Base That Became a Commons
place: Great Meadow, Fort Mason (Phillip Burton statue)
hook: When the Army moved out, developers drew up plans for Fort Mason's bluffs and piers. Instead the whole place became a park, with gardens, theatres and a meadow.
story: In 1962 the Army moved its embarkation work to Oakland and declared lower Fort Mason surplus. The post was formally closed in 1966, and in 1968 the piers were handed to the Maritime Administration as a storage yard [1]. A SPUR newsletter of June 1970 showed a development proposed for the site [2]. Then, Fort Mason Center says, the 1969 Indian occupation of Alcatraz turned public attention to the Bay's empty federal lands [2]. In 1972 Congressman Phillip Burton fought off rival development plans and passed HR 9498, creating the 78,000-acre Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Fort Mason included. President Nixon signed it [1][2]. The Park Service could not run the old warehouses itself, so it looked for a partner that would be a 'pioneer in the imaginative use of urban national parklands'. A new Fort Mason Foundation spent months repairing the run-down buildings and opened the campus to the public on January 1, 1977 [2]. Neighbours had been growing vegetables at the Fort Mason Community Garden since 1976 [3]. Today a statue of Burton, 'legislative architect' of the recreation area, stands in the Great Meadow on land that might have been built over [3].

title: The Tenants Who Sued Over a 'White Ghetto'
place: Parkmerced towers near Juan Bautista Circle
hook: Two Parkmerced tenants, one Black and one white, argued that segregation hurt everyone. The U.S. Supreme Court agreed with them unanimously.
story: By the late 1960s Parkmerced, home to about 8,200 people, was overwhelmingly white in a city that was fast diversifying [1]. Two tenants filed complaints under the new Civil Rights Act of 1968. According to the Supreme Court, one was Black and one white [2]. They alleged that the owner had kept nonwhite applicants out by making it known they would not be welcome, manipulating the waiting list, delaying applications and using discriminatory standards [2]. Their injury, they said, was that they had lost the social benefits of living in an integrated community, missed business and professional advantages, and been stigmatized as residents of a "white ghetto" [2]. The Western Neighborhoods Project tells the story through Paul Trafficante, a white New Yorker who had come west after the war [1]. Could people who were not turned away themselves still sue? In Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life, decided December 7, 1972, Justice William O. Douglas wrote for the Court that they could [2]. Met Life settled and opened its apartments to all races, and Trafficante lived at Parkmerced until his death in 2001 [1].

title: The bar that took down its curtains
place: Twin Peaks Tavern, 401 Castro St
hook: Gay bars hid behind painted windows. Two women bought a dive on Castro and Market and did the unthinkable: they let the street look in.
story: Until 1971 the Twin Peaks Tavern was, in MaryEllen Cunha's words, 'a dive Irish bar' that served neighbourhood men and visiting seamen. Its windows were papered over from inside and painted on the outside. One old patron remembered that this way 'wives couldn't see their husbands drinking in here' [1]. Cunha had worked in Peggy Forster's liquor store at Valencia and 16th. State records show her licence at Twin Peaks was issued on October 11, 1972 [1]. The two women, known to regulars as 'The Girls', tore out the suspended ceiling, redid the room as a fern bar and put in full-length plate glass. 'People were used to being in windowless bars, but I didn't like it! … We wanted to look out!' Cunha recalled [1]. It is thought to be the first gay bar in America with open plate-glass windows. That kind of visibility still had limits: the house rule was no touching or kissing [2]. Cunha and Forster ran the bar until 2003, when they sold it to two of their bartenders. The city made it Landmark No. 264 in 2013 [1][3].

title: The temple at 1859 Geary
place: Peoples Temple, 1859 Geary Boulevard (now a post office)
hook: An old Masonic temple beside the Fillmore became the headquarters of San Francisco's most politically powerful church, until Jonestown.
story: In September 1972, Peoples Temple paid $125,000 for 1859 Geary Boulevard. The building had been a Scottish Rite Masonic temple and, briefly, a skills and education centre [1]. Jim Jones' church had been renting Benjamin Franklin Junior High at Geary and Scott for Sunday services. Over the next four years it moved its headquarters here from Redwood Valley [2]. Its preaching drew on the Black church tradition and appealed to working-class white and African American members, and the temple became known as the place to go if you wanted something done [2]. Assembly Speaker Willie Brown said that in a tight race you could 'forget it without Jones' [2]. In January 1977 the temple sent some 2,000 people to the protest against evictions at the International Hotel [3]. But from 1977 about a thousand members moved to the settlement in Guyana [2]. There, on 18 November 1978, Congressman Leo Ryan and members of his party were shot at an airstrip, and some 900 people died in the settlement [3]. The Geary building was later ravaged by an earthquake and demolished. A post office now stands on the site [3][4].

title: A brutalist station like a Romanesque church
place: Glen Park BART Station, Diamond and Bosworth streets
hook: Ernest Born designed BART's lettering and gave this station a marble mural with almost no right angles. Many people call it the most beautiful stop on the system.
story:
BART bought the block at Diamond and Bosworth in 1968, over residents' protests, and knocked down its buildings, the branch library among them [1]. Glen Park station opened on 5 November 1973 [2]. It was designed by architect Ernest Born with the firm Corlett & Spackman. Born was also an illustrator, and he designed the lettering for all of BART's original signs [2][3].

The station is built in the concrete brutalist style of BART's early stations, but it feels calmer than the rest. Architectural Record admired its 60-foot-high volume, with daylight from skylights pouring down to the lower platform, "an extraordinary sight in a subway" [2]. Born hung a "utility beam" over the platform edge to carry the lights and speakers. He also designed the marble mural in the concourse, about 100 pieces, few if any cut at right angles [2][3]. BART director Tom Radulovich wrote in 2009 that the dark walls and great arches make it feel "like a Romanesque church" [3]. The mural appears in the 2006 film The Pursuit of Happyness. In 2019 the Glen Park Association nominated the station for the National Register of Historic Places [2].

title: A bus barn plopped on Dogpatch
place: Muni yard, 22nd and Indiana Streets (former Tubbs Cordage site)
hook: In 1973 the city planned a Muni yard in the middle of Dogpatch, a community of 500 then said to have 95 percent unemployment. One resident's objection still stings.
story:
For about a century, Tubbs Cordage made rope along 22nd Street between Minnesota and Indiana. Its rope walk was a shed more than 1,000 feet long, running toward a wharf on the bay [1][2]. Tubbs closed its San Francisco plant in 1962 [1]. In 1971 the city bought three blocks at 22nd and Indiana for bus storage and repair shops [3].

The Potrero View's coverage shows the neighbourhood's name taking hold. In January 1972 the paper called the area "Dog Patch". In February it apologised to people near the proposed car barn, saying they were "a concerned and active part of the Potrero Hill" and nothing like Li'l Abner's comic-strip town [4]. By 1973 the Dogpatch Community Development Association and Youth Council faced eviction, with the barn "Plopped on Dogpatch". The View described Dogpatch as a community of 500 with 95 percent unemployment [4]. At one meeting resident James Holley shouted: "You're gonna put a cable car barn in the middle of Dogpatch when Muni doesn't have one black repairman." [4]

The yard went ahead. The View later noted that Muni's workforce changed colour too [4]. In 1978 the last Tubbs buildings came down to make way for the Muni bus yard [1].

title: A camera shop becomes a headquarters
place: Castro Camera, 573-575 Castro St
hook: Angry that a developer had ruined his film, Harvey Milk opened his own camera store. It became the front office of a political revolution.
story: Harvey Milk was a keen amateur photographer. After a lab ruined a roll of his film, he and his partner Scott Smith spent their last $1,000 opening a camera shop in an 1894 Victorian storefront on Castro Street [1]. The city's landmark report dates the shop to 1973. Some accounts say 1972 [1][2]. The building had once held hardware stores, a plumber and a tinsmith. Now it filled up with new arrivals looking for friends, work and a place to belong. Milk even made the shop an official polling station [1]. Castro Camera was the headquarters for all four of his campaigns, and from 1975 to 1978 he lived in the flat upstairs [2]. It was here that photographer Daniel Nicoletta, future campaign manager Anne Kronenberg and activist Cleve Jones first met him [1]. His fourth campaign put him on the Board of Supervisors in 1977. It changed San Francisco politics: for the first time, openly gay candidates were widely accepted in an American city [2]. Since Milk's assassination in 1978, his memorial march has often set off from this doorway every year [1].

title: A future mayor shot on Wisconsin Street
place: 900 block of Wisconsin Street
hook: On December 13, 1973, Art Agnos left a meeting on a clinic for Potrero Hill's public housing and was shot twice in the chest. Fifteen years later he was mayor.
story:
On the evening of December 13, 1973, Art Agnos, then 35, attended a meeting at Potrero Hill's largely Black public housing project about building a publicly funded health clinic [1][3]. After he left, on the 900 block of Wisconsin Street, he was shot twice in the chest at point-blank range [1][2]. The bullets travelled downward, which saved his life. By his own account he lost a year to recovery [1]. Less than ninety minutes later, Marietta DiGirolamo was shot on Divisadero Street [3].

Agnos had survived an attack by the "Zebra" killers, named after the police radio band assigned to the case. Between October 1973 and April 1974 they killed at least fifteen white people and wounded eight others [3]. During the manhunt, police stopped and searched young Black men, and the NAACP and ACLU sued over it [3]. Four men were convicted and sentenced to life after a trial that ran from March 1975 to March 1976 [2][3].

Accounts differ on what Agnos was doing then: a social worker, an aide to Assemblyman Leo McCarthy, or a member of the state Commission on Aging [1][2][3]. He was mayor from 1988 to 1992 [2]. A stretch of Connecticut Street near his Potrero Hill home now carries his name [4].

title: BART's Dream of Towers Over Mission Street
place: 24th St Mission BART plaza, Mission St at 24th
hook: The 1966 plan had 13-storey towers, sunken plazas, moving sidewalks and a "miniature vehicle service". What the Mission got was a plain plaza and a long escalator.
story: In May 1966 Okamoto/Liskamm, architects and urban designers, sketched what the Mission's 16th and 24th Street BART stations could become: office and apartment towers of at least 13 floors, parking structures, elevated walkways, moving sidewalks and even a "miniature vehicle service" [1]. A nod to the neighbourhood came in drawings of stalls selling piñatas and tacos [1]. Historian Lindsey Passenger Wieck notes the plans mostly served commuters and newcomers, and says they were never built partly because Mission residents persuaded the Board of Supervisors to drop them [1]. The stations that opened for regular service in November 1973 had plazas of about 1,000 square feet, 700-foot-long underground platforms, cast-concrete sculptures by the British artist William Mitchell, and Mayan-style tile inlays [1]. The fear of displacement remained. In April 1970 the radical paper Basta Ya! warned that realtors were replacing family flats with apartments for single people and childless couples, and protesters demonstrated against BART at 20th and Mission [2].

title: Church Starts at Six A.M.
place: The EndUp, 401 Sixth Street at Harrison
hook: A former 22-room hotel became the dance floor where San Francisco went after the other clubs closed. On Sundays, the doors opened at dawn.
story: In November 1973 Al Hanken opened the EndUp in an old 22-room hotel at Sixth and Harrison. It was a companion to his nearby gay country-western bar, the Roundup. The new club had a transparent light-up dance floor and a quadraphonic sound system, and it was built for the disco craze [1]. Far from the Castro, the club needed gimmicks, so it ran a Sunday jockey-shorts contest with a $150 prize. The crowds were so big that the scuffed floor had to be replaced [1]. In 1979 the EndUp began opening at 6 a.m. on Sundays so dancers could carry on after the all-night Trocadero Transfer closed. DJ Steve Fabus played this "Church" party from dawn until 2 p.m. [1]. City planners count the EndUp, with the Trocadero, among the key gay discos South of Market [2]. The club's staying power was tested in 1999. Police Captain Dennis Martel of Southern Station put it at the top of his list of clubs to close and even shut it for a month [1][3]. Nightlife supporters formed the San Francisco Late Night Coalition, Martel was moved to airport duty, and in 2003 the city created an Entertainment Commission to oversee permits [3].

title: Cut, Paste, and the Birth of Biotech
place: Herbert Boyer's laboratory, UCSF Parnassus campus
hook: A molecular scissor found in a UCSF lab, late-night sandwiches in Hawaii, and a ten-minute meeting that ran three hours helped launch the biotech industry.
story: Herbert Boyer joined UCSF in 1966. His UCSF lab had found an enzyme called EcoRI, which cuts DNA leaving staggered, 'sticky' ends that can latch onto any other piece cut the same way [1]. In November 1972 Boyer and Stanley Cohen of Stanford were both at a plasmid conference in Hawaii. Over late-night sandwiches they agreed to work together [1]. For months plasmids travelled between the two labs. Stanford's went to San Francisco to be cut with EcoRI, and the pieces went back to be joined and put into E. coli. In spring 1973 it worked: bacteria carried and copied a plasmid spliced together in a test tube, passing it to their offspring. Paul Berg had first spliced DNA in 1971; this made it copy itself inside living cells [1]. In 1976 Robert Swanson, a 29-year-old venture capitalist, called Boyer and asked for a meeting. Boyer gave him ten minutes, and they talked for three hours. By the end, according to the company, Genentech was born [2]. In fall 1977, before Genentech had facilities of its own, Boyer's UCSF group and City of Hope chemists got bacteria to make a human hormone, somatostatin [1].

title: From quarry and dump to park
place: Bernal Heights Park, top of Folsom Street
hook: For decades the hilltop was quarried, used as a dump and torn up by motorbikes. In June 1973 neighbours celebrated its new life as a park with kites and bagpipes.
story:
Bernal Heights Boulevard was cut around the hill in 1935 as a Depression make-work project [1]. After that, the summit was city wasteland under the Department of Public Works. From the late 1940s, by one account, two quarries bit into the hilltop and supplied fill for the 101 freeway and Candlestick Park [1]. People dumped mattresses and car parts in the pits. Motorcycles carved tracks into the slopes, and at night the boulevard turned into a lovers' lane [1]. Jerry Schimmel, who moved to Prentiss Street in 1966, remembered calling Public Works so often about the dumping that staff asked whether he was one of the dumpers [1].

Neighbours pushed for a change. In 1972 the Recreation and Park Commission voted to take over the 26 acres and protect them from development. Residents agreed not to ask for improvements for several years because the department had no money for upkeep [2]. A handbill dated June 10, 1973 invited everyone to celebrate the transfer. The party had kites, balloons, clowns and bagpipes near the top of Folsom Street. Even Bernalwood admitted it could not be completely sure of the year [1][2].

title: The Victorian that joined the preservationists
place: Haas-Lilienthal House, 2007 Franklin Street
hook: When the last Haas daughter died, her children gave away the family's Queen Anne house to a group formed to fight the bulldozers.
story: William Haas, a Bavarian-born wholesale grocer, built this Queen Anne house on Franklin Street in 1886, to designs by Peter R. Schmidt [1]. It came through the 1906 earthquake and fire [2]. His youngest daughter Alice married Samuel Lilienthal, who led the family business and the Federation of Jewish Charities. They moved in in 1917 [1]. Samuel died in 1957. Alice stayed on in the house until her death in 1972 [1]. San Francisco had only recently seen whole neighbourhoods of the Western Addition flattened for "urban renewal". A new group, the Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage, had formed in 1971 to fight back, and it had rescued twelve threatened buildings in the largest house-moving project in the city's history [3]. In May 1973 Alice's three children gave the house to that group [1][2]. It became the group's headquarters and a house museum with docent-led tours, and in 2012 the National Trust named it a National Treasure [2].

title: The tripod the city loved to hate
place: Sutro Tower, Clarendon Heights
hook: Herb Caen feared it would 'stalk down the hill and attack the Golden Gate Bridge.' Instead it became the city's unofficial mascot.
story:
San Francisco's hills scattered TV signals and left reception patchy. In the 1960s the big stations wanted one tall tower for the whole Bay Area [1][2]. They considered San Bruno Mountain but judged it too close to the airport. They picked the old Sutro mansion site instead [1]. The project was approved in 1967, and few people noticed until it began to rise [2]. After years of hearings and lawsuits, construction of the $4 million tower started in 1971. It was designed by Albert C. Martin & Associates and put up by Kline Towers of South Carolina [1]. It stands 977 feet tall. Its three legs sit in 15 million pounds of cement and hold up 3.5 million pounds of steel [1]. The first stations went on the air on July 4, 1973 [1].

The reviews were brutal. Planning Director Allan Jacobs called it "pretty terrible, aesthetically, environmentally and from about every standpoint." Supervisor Dianne Feinstein called it "undoubtedly one of the worst structures, visually" she had seen. Herb Caen feared it would "stalk down the hill and attack the Golden Gate Bridge" [2][3]. Decades later the tower is widely accepted as a Bay Area icon and appears in local logos [3].

title: "I'm Tania" at the Hibernia Bank
place: Former Hibernia Bank, Sunset branch, 1450 Noriega Street at 22nd Avenue
hook: A security camera on Noriega Street turned a kidnapped newspaper heiress into America's most wanted revolutionary. It took just a few minutes on an April morning.
story: At 9:40 on the morning of April 15, 1974, members of the Symbionese Liberation Army held up the Sunset branch of the Hibernia Bank at 1450 Noriega Street. Five went inside while four waited outside, and they got away in two cars with $10,960 [2][3]. One of the gunmen caught on the bank's surveillance cameras was Patricia Hearst, granddaughter of William Randolph Hearst. Ten weeks earlier the SLA had dragged her, then 19, from a Berkeley apartment. On April 3 a tape had announced she'd joined them and taken the name Tania [1]. When a reporter took the footage to the Berkeley School for the Deaf, students read her lips: "I'm Tania. Up, up, up against the wall" [2]. Two men were shot. The SLA's own communiqué explained that one had jumped out the front door and the other ran toward the bank [2]. The FBI launched one of the largest manhunts in its history and caught Hearst in San Francisco on September 18, 1975. Despite her brainwashing defense, a jury convicted her [1]. By the 1990s the robbery site was an ordinary Bank of America branch [3].

title: A circus with no ringmaster, no elephants
place: 400 Missouri Street, near 19th
hook: In 1974 two Mime Troupe veterans started a one-ring circus on Potrero Hill. Everyone earned the same wage, clowns ran the show, and the animals were people in gorilla suits.
story:
Larry Pisoni and Peggy Snider, veterans of the San Francisco Mime Troupe, founded the Pickle Family Circus in 1974 [1][2]. The name was made up on the spot: after they passed a TV juggling audition, someone asked what they called themselves [2]. The company kept its offices and practice space at 400 Missouri Street, and many members lived nearby [1]. The family lived at Carolina and 22nd, and the troupe rehearsed at The Church, at Missouri and 19th [3].

It was a stripped-down circus: one ring, a five-piece jazz band, no ringmaster and no animals, except performers dancing the Charleston in gorilla suits. "We're somewhat lacking in the sequins department," Pisoni said [2]. Everyone earned the same wage and shared the offstage work. Three clowns ran the show: Pisoni as Lorenzo Pickle, Bill Irwin as Willy and Geoff Hoyle as Mr. Sniff. Federal CETA jobs money paid several of them in the 1970s [1].

The couple's son Lorenzo walked into the ring at two with his own silent clown act and signed a contract at six [3]. The circus went bankrupt in 1992. In 1984 two members had founded what is now the Circus Center, and at least seven Pickle performers went on to Cirque du Soleil [1].

title: Blum's cake survives in a grocery corner
place: Yasukochi's Sweet Stop, Super Mira Market, 1790 Sutter Street
hook: San Francisco's most famous birthday cake was born at a vanished Union Square pastry shop. It lives on in the corner of a Japantown grocery.
story: Moses and Hatsy Yasukochi both spent part of their childhoods in wartime internment camps. They married in 1964 and in 1974 opened the Sweet Stop, a small bakery inside what is now Super Mira Market at Sutter and Buchanan [1][2]. Earlier they had owned a bakery in San Leandro, where a baker named Tony, who had worked at Blum's on Union Square, shared the recipe for Blum's famous Coffee Crunch Cake. Moses mastered it, and the retired Blums gave him their blessing to use the name [1]. The cake became a fixture of San Francisco birthdays, holidays and weddings. Hatsy, called the "smile of the bakery," died in 2020, early in the Covid pandemic, after an illness with cancer [2]. Their grandson Kenji Yick, trained at the French Culinary Institute, kept the shop going with longtime employee Debbie Ishida. In 2023 the tiny counter was named a James Beard Award semifinalist for Outstanding Bakery [2].

title: Eavesdropping on Union Square at Lunchtime
place: Union Square
hook: Coppola's paranoid masterpiece opens high above Union Square, listening. The only footage its fired cameraman shot that survived is that famous opening.
story: Francis Ford Coppola began writing The Conversation in 1966 and finished it in 1970 [1]. He shot it in San Francisco, on location in Union Square and at his newly formed American Zoetrope studio, one of the first major directors of his generation to base a studio outside Los Angeles [1]. Gene Hackman plays Harry Caul, a surveillance expert hired to record a young couple as they circle the crowded square at lunchtime; stitching his three imperfect tapes together, he uncovers a sentence that convinces him they are in danger [2]. The shoot was fraught. Cinematographer Haskell Wexler clashed with Coppola and was replaced within weeks by Bill Butler, and all of Wexler's footage was reshot except that technically demanding Union Square sequence, the film's most memorable [1][2]. With Coppola busy on The Godfather Part II, editor Walter Murch shaped the film, and Murch later described the opening: a God's-eye view of "the soft, billowy sounds of the city at lunchtime," suddenly cut by digital racket as you realise you are hearing through a hidden recorder [2]. Released in 1974, it turned a sunny civic square into the setting for an American nightmare about being watched.

title: Houseboaters who beat City Hall
place: Mission Creek houseboat harbor, Channel Street
hook: The Port stapled eviction notices on every houseboat on Mission Creek. Two women got on the phone and played the TV stations against each other.
story: In 1960 the state moved a houseboat community from Islais Creek to 55 berths on Channel Street [1][2]. Ruth Huffaker, an electronics worker, and her welder husband Steve built their first houseboat there in 1962; she remembered jackrabbits, foxes, cobbled streets and men living in six-foot weeds [1]. In 1974, after a fire in sheds across the channel, a Port official told her he would tear the dock down on Monday and put the boats in storage. The next day eviction notices were stapled to every boat [1]. Sharon Skolnick, who lived on a wooden-pyramid houseboat called the Azteca, had her boss Rose Farrington call one TV station, then tell another that Channel 5 was on its way; Ruth told Channel 7 that Channel 4's camera had just arrived. The coverage embarrassed the Port, which shelved the eviction and built a new float. A local paper's headline: 'It's true, you can beat City Hall!' [1]. A 1976 agreement produced a lease and new berths, and in 1977 the Mission Creek Harbor Association took over the harbor [1]. In 2001 around 20 houseboats remained, home to artists, veterans, blue-collar workers and professionals [2].

title: Mammy Pleasant's eucalyptus trees
place: Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, SW corner of Bush and Octavia
hook: Her 30-room mansion is long gone. What remains of one of Gold Rush San Francisco's most powerful Black women is a row of old eucalyptus trees.
story: On March 21, 1974, San Francisco named a row of trees a Structure of Merit, a category the city had used only a handful of times [1]. They stand at the southwest corner of Octavia and Bush. The eucalyptus trees were planted when this was the site of Mary Ellen Pleasant's home, and a plaque in her memory stands among them [2]. Pleasant reached San Francisco around 1852, fleeing prosecution under the Fugitive Slave Law. She cooked for rich families and invested her wages, eventually owning laundries and boardinghouses and building a 30-room mansion at 1661 Octavia [3]. She is credited with giving $30,000 to John Brown before his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry [3]. FoundSF calls her an important western terminus of the Underground Railroad in the 1850s, and says she gained quiet power by placing servants in rich households [2]. Rumours followed her: newspapers and gossip painted her as a brothel keeper and claimed there was a voodoo altar in her basement [3]. Historian Lynn Hudson told the Chronicle she was a woman who "led the Underground Railroad like Harriet Tubman, and amassed a huge fortune, but is largely unknown" [3]. The city proclaimed Mary Ellen Pleasant Day in 2005 [3].

title: Ransom paid in groceries
place: China Basin Building, 185 Berry Street
hook: To free kidnapped Patty Hearst, her father ran a giant free-food program from this old banana warehouse. The volunteers ended up remaking city politics.
story: After the Symbionese Liberation Army kidnapped Patricia Hearst in February 1974, it demanded that the Hearst Corporation feed California's poor. The first distribution, on February 22, was chaos: panicked workers threw boxes off moving trucks into huge crowds and scores were hurt. Governor Ronald Reagan quipped, 'It's just too bad we can't have an epidemic of botulism' [1]. A community coalition led by the Western Addition Project Area Committee then took over and, from February 26 to the end of March, organised six distributions: more than 100,000 bags of groceries at some 16 sites in four counties [1]. The nerve centre was the huge China Basin Building. Scores of trucks came and went every hour, with Patty's father and brother there around the clock [1]. The building, raised in the 1920s as a banana-processing plant, had been painted a rich blue by then [2]. Volunteer Calvin Welch later argued that the coalition's organisers went on to register voters for George Moscone and to win district elections, giving birth to the neighbourhood movement [1].

title: The Beatles House on Precita
place: 191 Precita Ave
hook: A junior-high girl ran out of wall space in her bedroom, so she painted the Fab Four across the front of her family's house.
story:
In 1974 Jane Weems was in junior high and had already covered her bedroom walls with Yellow Submarine and a giant Elton John album cover. So she asked her parents whether she could paint the outside of the house at 191 Precita Avenue. They said yes [1]. She sketched the Beatles freehand in pencil on the parts she could reach. Then her mother rented a scaffold so she could finish the whole front, working slowly around school [1].

One neighbour who used to stop and 'watch me paint' and talk about the Beatles was Emily Harris of the Symbionese Liberation Army. She was then living secretly in a safe house down the street [1][2]. Later Weems played drums in the teenage punk band The Maggots, and she repainted the mural in 1982 [1]. For almost two decades the 'Beatles House' was a local landmark. Strangers rang the bell, the San Francisco Bay Guardian gave it an award, and the film Living on Tokyo Time used it as a rehearsal studio [1]. Today the mural is gone without a trace [1].

title: The Day the Shipyard Went Quiet
place: Hunters Point Naval Shipyard (Crisp Road)
hook: When the Navy closed Hunters Point Naval Shipyard in 1974, over 5,000 jobs went with it. Third Street shops held closing sales where a bedroom set sold for five dollars.
story: For three decades the shipyard had driven the local economy. By the mid-1950s it employed about 8,500 civilians, many of them Black workers recruited from the South during World War II [2]. The Navy deactivated it in 1974 [2]. A 1996 community history counted 5,060 workers who lost their jobs. The Navy found other posts for most of them, often at bases in Southern California or Washington State. Many locals stayed, though, and either joined the unemployed or retired early without savings [1]. The blow hit Third Street. "The community died when the shipyard left," activist Espanola Jackson recalled. "There was nothing. Everything that was here disappeared." She remembered stores so desperate to clear their stock that she bought a bedroom set for five dollars [1]. A private firm leased the yard from 1975 to 1985, hired few locals and was fined for environmental violations [1]. Also in 1974, resident Oscar James joined the push to end naval operations and raised alarms about radioactive waste. As a boy he had heard his father's shipyard friends talk about it while he hid under a table during "Friday Night Fights". City officials dismissed him [3]. In 1989 the EPA made the yard a Superfund site [2].

title: The Sewing Aunties Who Shook Chinatown
place: Jung Sai garment factory, 646 Washington St
hook: They were called 'goats and sheep'. In 1974, 135 garment workers from an Esprit-owned factory walked out, and Chinatown's own newspaper called it earth-shattering.
story: The Jung Sai factory at 646 Washington Street was one of Chinatown's biggest sewing plants, owned by Esprit de Corps, the fashionable maker of clothes for young people [1]. In Cantonese, Jung means Chinese and Sai means West, and the English name was "Great Chinese American", a picture of happy partnership [1]. To the women at the machines it meant something else: harassment, speed-ups, no breaks and low pay [1]. In 1974, 135 workers, almost all immigrant women plus two men, went on strike [1]. They rallied in Portsmouth Square and picketed for almost a year, through sixty-four arrests and court injunctions, drawing students and activists to their side [1]. On July 27, 1974, the Chinese Times ran an editorial saying these once-obedient "sewing factory aunties", once thought of as "subservient goats and sheep", were now shouting, clapping and carrying picket signs: a "shi po tian jing", an earth-shattering and heaven-startling event [1]. Historian Harvey Dong argues the strike became a turning point for Asian American activism in the Bay Area. Afterwards, locals heard the name Jung Sai and thought of resistance [1][2].

title: The merchants who wouldn't let them in
place: Castro Street between 18th and 19th
hook: The old merchants' group tried to block a licence for two gay antiques dealers. Harvey Milk answered by starting his own association and throwing a party.
story: In the early 1970s even gay men who had started their own Castro businesses were not welcome in the local Eureka Valley Merchants Association. In 1973 the association tried to block a business licence for two gay men who wanted to open an antiques store. Harvey Milk's response was to organise gay shop owners into a rival group, the Castro Village Association [1]. Milk was its first president. Working from his shop at 575 Castro, he used it to launch the first Castro Street Fair [2]. That fair drew about 5,000 people and brought a flood of dollars into local cash registers. Even the old-time merchants came round [1]. The planning department's own history gives two dates for the first fair, 1974 and 1975. The festival itself counts from October 1974 [1][3]. In 1977 fairgoers could pay to dunk Milk in a water tank outside Castro Camera, to raise money against the anti-gay Briggs Initiative [1]. The fair has become a fixture on the first Sunday in October [1].

title: Twelve Victorians Roll West
place: 33–35 Beideman Street, Beideman Place
hook: Over three stormy November weekends, a convoy of condemned Victorians crept a mile west through the Western Addition. Eight of them ended up on this narrow alley.
story: In late 1971 the new San Francisco Architectural Heritage group and the city's Landmarks Board picked out the best Victorians still standing in A-2 [1]. The Agency set aside 19 of them to sell for nominal sums, but 13 would have to be moved. Only two sold, and one was knocked down by mistake [1]. To buy time, Heritage entered minimum bids on the 12 that remained. The Agency got a $150,000 grant to cover moving costs, so a buyer needed only about $20,000 [1]. Over three weekends in November 1974 the houses moved west, most of them from the block where Opera Plaza now stands. Crews had to shift phone and power lines and Muni overhead wires along the way [1][2]. Eight of the houses ended up together along Beideman Place, the alley between Scott, Divisadero, Eddy and O'Farrell [1]. One of them, 736–738 Franklin, had been restored by 1977 and renumbered 33–35 Beideman Street [2]. The rescue was bittersweet. Some houses landed on lots where other Victorians had been demolished, and many low-income Black residents resented a rescue led, and bought into, mostly by white, upper-middle-class people [3]. About 2,500 other Victorians were demolished [3].
