title: A Rock Revolutionary with an Ocean View
place: Sea Cliff (Kantner's clifftop house; exact address not published in sources)
hook: He wrote anthems about the young and poor rising up against the Empire. He wrote many of them from one of the priciest clifftops in San Francisco.
story: Paul Kantner co-founded Jefferson Airplane. Like many of the San Francisco rock crowd, he left for Marin County as the 1960s ended and spent a short time in Bolinas in the early 1970s. When the Jefferson Starship era began, he moved back to the city and settled for many years in Sea Cliff [2]. The music writer Blair Jackson interviewed him six or seven times for the Bay Area magazine BAM in the mid-1970s, and he enjoyed the contradiction. Kantner, he wrote, "lived very comfortably in a beautiful house perched over the blue Pacific in the ritzy Sea Cliff neighborhood" while writing "stirring anthems about the poor and the young rising up together in rebellion against the status quo" [1]. Jackson did not call it hypocrisy. He noted that Kantner played hundreds of benefit shows, never put on rock-star airs, and turned up regularly at punk and new wave gigs, even though that crowd dismissed him as a dinosaur [1]. He later moved to North Beach and died in 2016 [1][2].

title: Bulldozers at the Redwood Conservatory
place: Sunnyside Conservatory, 236 Monterey Boulevard
hook: Neighbours got an inventor's Victorian plant house declared a city landmark. Then a cyclist rode past and saw heavy equipment tearing it down.
story:
In 1902 William Augustus Merralls, a British-born inventor of gold-mining machinery, built an octagonal redwood conservatory for his exotic plants on what is now Monterey Boulevard [1]. After him came Ernest Van Beckh, a con man from the "Big Five" mining-stock swindle. He bought the estate in 1919 and lived there until he died in 1951 [1].

In 1974 a new owner, Robert Anderson, began dividing up the lots with an eye to development. The newly formed Sunnyside Neighborhood Association fought back, and in 1975 the city designated the conservatory a landmark [1][2]. Anderson still managed to get a demolition permit. Neighbour Greg Gaar was cycling to City College when he saw machines at work: "I knew it was a registered historic landmark." [1] His calls to City Hall stopped the demolition, but part of the building had already been torn off and almost all the windows knocked out [1].

In 1980 the city bought the site with Open Space Fund money [1]. Neighbour Ted Kipping kept the trees alive. After Friends of Sunnyside Conservatory formed in 1999, another neighbour brought back the original rooftop spire, which he had kept in his garage for 30 years. It was too rotten to reuse, so builders copied it in copper [1].

title: Dylan, Brando and the School Budget
place: Kezar Stadium
hook: To save after-school sports, Bill Graham packed Kezar Stadium with Dylan, Neil Young, the Dead and a surprise Marlon Brando. Then the school board found the money anyway.
story: In early 1975 San Francisco's school district, short of money, planned to cut after-school sports and activities. Promoter Bill Graham read about it in a February 4 newspaper story. By February 19 he had signed up Jefferson Starship, Jerry Garcia, Carlos Santana, Joan Baez and others to play for free [1]. Herb Caen supplied the name: SNACK, Students Need Athletics, Culture and Kicks [2]. The day before the show, the school board announced it had 'found' $2.1 million through an accounting change, wiping out most of the shortfall. An angry Graham went ahead anyway [1]. On March 23 the gates of Kezar, the stadium the 49ers had left in 1971 [3], opened at 6 a.m. Seven to ten thousand fans had camped overnight on the lawn or in the park [1]. Across nine hours the crowd, put at more than 60,000, heard the Doobie Brothers, Tower of Power and the Dead, who, Graham joked, were given 30 minutes "and held themselves down to 40" [1]. Willie Mays spoke. Marlon Brando appeared unannounced. Neil Young closed the day with Bob Dylan and members of the Band [2].

title: Joggers arrested on Precita Avenue
place: 288 Precita Ave
hook: FBI agents in sandals and beads waited in a camper on Precita Avenue. When the couple from No. 288 came back from their run, they pounced.
story:
In 1975, during the hunt for the kidnapped heiress Patty Hearst, 288 Precita Avenue was one of two San Francisco safe houses used by the Symbionese Liberation Army [1][2]. The FBI's Charles Bates had both houses watched. Time magazine reported that four agents sat in a light green Ford LTD at the curb and three more waited in a yellow-and-white camper down the block. They wore sandals, beards and beads to blend in. Neighbours spotted the stakeout anyway, but nobody suspected the 'athletic and pleasant young couple' who had just moved in [1].

At 1:15 p.m. on a clear day in September, the couple jogged off towards Bernal Park. When they came back, agents burst out with pistols, a sawed-off shotgun and submachine guns. The woman ran and was caught within 20 feet. The man put his hands up 'like a little kid who had been caught doing something wrong' [1]. They were William and Emily Harris. Inside their flat agents found 40 pounds of black powder and a small arsenal. Less than two hours later Hearst was found at the other house, on Morse Street [1][2]. At her trial, Hearst testified that she had visited 288 Precita once [2].

title: Knock at 625 Morse Street
place: 625 Morse St
hook: The most hunted fugitive in America was hiding in a quiet Crocker-Amazon flat. An FBI agent and a city inspector climbed the stairs.
story: On September 18, 1975, the FBI was watching a postal box belonging to Kathleen Soliah. Messengers had been collecting its mail and taking it to two addresses: 288 Precita Avenue and 625 Morse Street, a concrete house with redwood facing [1]. Agents first arrested Bill and Emily Harris of the Symbionese Liberation Army on Precita. An hour and ten minutes later, FBI Special Agent Tom Padden and San Francisco Police Inspector Tim Casey climbed the stairs at Morse Street and pounded on the door [1][2]. Wendy Yoshimura opened it, and behind her stood Patty Hearst, the newspaper heiress kidnapped nineteen months earlier. 'Don't move or I'll blast your head off,' Padden said. Neither woman moved, though each had a .38 in her purse. Inside officers found a cat, dirty dishes, more guns and a two-foot marijuana plant [1]. At booking Hearst gave her occupation as 'urban guerrilla' [3]. A boy who grew up nearby later wrote that his neighbourhood was a good place to disappear [4].

title: The Corner House That Nearly Fell
place: 722 Steiner Street, at Grove
hook: The oldest and largest house on Postcard Row came through the 1906 quake and was later marked for demolition. In 1975 someone bought it for $65,000.
story: The corner house at 722 Steiner, the oldest of the Postcard Row group, was Matthew Kavanaugh's own home [1][2]. It came through the 1906 earthquake, but by the 1970s it was slated for demolition. It survived that threat too and was restored [2][3]. Michael Shannon bought it in 1975 for $65,000 [4]. By 2010 it was marketed as "The Shannon-Kavanaugh House", and it paid its way with movie and TV shoots, advertising, tours, weddings and parties [2]. It was listed that year at just under $4 million and then went through years of cuts, default and scheduled foreclosure auctions [3]. In 2014 it finally sold off-market for $3.1 million [1][4]. The new owners repainted it from its longtime spearmint green to a new palette [4]. When they listed it in 2022 at $5.75 million, the agents said it had also been home to José Sarria, the drag performer and activist who in 1961 became the first openly gay candidate for public office [1].

title: The railroad retreats to Fourth and King
place: San Francisco Caltrain station, 700 4th Street
hook: In 1975 Southern Pacific swapped its grand Mission Revival depot for a modest commuter shed one block away, then knocked the old one down.
story: Southern Pacific's Third and Townsend depot went up in 1914-15 for the Panama-Pacific Exposition. It was meant to be temporary until a grander terminal downtown, but it lasted six decades [1]. Designed by the railroad's own architectural bureau, the reinforced-concrete, Mission Revival station was one of the city's best examples of the style, and San Francisco was 'zero mile' for the whole SP system [1]. It sent commuter trains to San Jose and long-distance trains down the Coast Line to Los Angeles [1][3]. Freeways and the loss of long-distance passenger trains doomed it. Southern Pacific built a much smaller station at Fourth and King, which opened on June 21, 1975, and the old depot was demolished in 1975-76 [1][2]. The new terminal is still the northern end of Caltrain. Muni light rail arrived in 1998, and the station is the planned first-phase terminus for California High-Speed Rail. The Portal project would eventually carry trains underground to the Salesforce Transit Center [2].

title: When the blues came to the hills
place: McLaren Park amphitheatre (now Jerry Garcia Amphitheater), off John F. Shelley Drive
hook: Before it was Jerry Garcia's, the hillside theatre hosted the country's pioneering San Francisco Blues Festival for three summers.
story: McLaren Park's Greek-style amphitheatre sits in an eastern slope, out of the afternoon wind. It was the city's bet in the early 1970s that culture could bring people to its overlooked southeast [1]. Sources disagree on the date. A park group's chronology says construction finished in 1970, while the city's 1983 master plan says 1972 [2][3]. According to that chronology, the amphitheatre opened in 1971 with 700 seats and 'excellent acoustics', and the press said it added 'a new cultural dimension to San Francisco' [2]. From 1975 to 1977 it was home to the third, fourth and fifth San Francisco Blues Festivals [2]. Tom Mazzolini had started the festival in 1973 to celebrate the blues played in San Francisco, Richmond and Oakland in the 1940s and '50s. At the time the country had only a handful of blues festivals [4]. In 1978 the festival outgrew the hillside and moved to the Golden Gate Park band shell, and later to Kezar and Fort Mason [2]. The lighting and sound system built with the amphitheatre are long gone [1].

title: 'No Soviet Domination,' Said the President
place: Palace of Fine Arts Theatre
hook: In a Marina theatre in 1976, Gerald Ford made one of the most famous slips in the history of presidential debates, and then repeated it.
story: The second Ford–Carter debate, on October 6, 1976, was held before an audience in the Palace of Fine Arts Theatre [1][2]. The theatre had opened in the rebuilt exhibit hall only six years earlier [3]. Moderator Pauline Frederick of NPR noted that San Francisco had seen the signing of the United Nations Charter 31 years before, which made it a fitting place for a debate on foreign policy. She told viewers an estimated 100 million Americans were watching [1]. (Later estimates put the audience at about 64 million [2].) Asked about the Helsinki accords, President Ford declared: 'There is no Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and there never will be under a Ford administration' [1]. Max Frankel of the New York Times, one of the panel of questioners, gave him a chance to take it back. Ford instead said he did not believe the Yugoslavians, Romanians or Poles considered themselves dominated by the Soviet Union [1]. Jimmy Carter answered with a chuckle and invited Ford to convince Polish-, Czech- and Hungarian-Americans that their homelands did not live behind the Iron Curtain [1]. The line became the debate's most infamous moment [2].

title: A butterfly clinging to the summit
place: Grassy slope inside the hairpin south of South Twin Peak
hook: On the slope below the south peak, a thumbnail-sized blue butterfly survives in one of only a handful of places on Earth.
story:
The Mission blue butterfly was listed as federally endangered in 1976. It survives in only a few places around the Bay, and Twin Peaks is one of them [1]. Its caterpillars eat nothing but lupine. They feed, sleep through winter in the roots, and emerge as adults in April and May to sip nectar from coast buckwheat [2]. Sources disagree about where the first specimens came from. The Chronicle's 2004 garden column calls Twin Peaks the "type locality", the place where the species was first collected. Wikipedia says it was first collected in the Mission District in 1937 [1][2]. The strongest patch of its food plants grows on the grassy hill inside the road's hairpin turn south of the south peak [2].

The summit nearly lost them. By around 1980 cars, hikers and off-road motorbikes had torn up the hill, and weeds were moving in [2]. In the late 1980s the city hired the San Francisco Conservation Corps. The crews built footpaths with railroad-tie steps and set massive timber barriers at the trailheads to keep motorbikes out [2]. Volunteers filled in the ruts, pulled out broom and ice plant, and replanted lupine and bunchgrass [2].

title: Food for People, Not for Profit, on 9th
place: 9th Avenue between Irving and Judah (Inner Sunset Community Food Store; Arizmendi Bakery, 1331 9th Ave)
hook: A volunteer-run grocery collective opened on 9th Avenue in 1976, got evicted, kept moving, and left a co-op tradition that still sells hot baguettes.
story: In May 1976 the Inner Sunset Community Food Store opened in what one member called 'a funky store front on 9th Avenue near Golden Gate Park'. It grew out of the Bay Area's People's Food System under the slogan 'Food For People, Not For Profit' [1]. Volunteers organised and staffed it at first. Later a collective ran it, barely paid, as a steward for the neighbourhood. Around 1982 a landlord's eviction forced it several blocks west along Irving, where members turned a former plumbing shop into a store. Later it moved again, to 20th Avenue [1]. In 1994 a statewide survey found it stocked more kinds of organic produce than any store in California [1]. Rent hikes and bitter internal fights closed it in 1995, and a former member wrote a scathing post-mortem [1]. The cooperative idea came back to 9th Avenue anyway. In October 2000, with help from Berkeley's Cheese Board and the Arizmendi bakery in Oakland, worker-owners opened Arizmendi Bakery at 1331 9th Avenue [2]. It is named after a Basque labour organiser, and the only job it has is worker-owner [2].

title: Ruth Asawa's paper-flower fountains
place: Origami Fountains, Buchanan Mall (Osaka Way) between Post and Sutter
hook: A sculptor who spent her teens behind barbed wire gave Japantown two fountains shaped like folded paper, then had merchants' children help shape the benches.
story: Ruth Asawa was 16 in 1942 when FBI agents arrested her father and her family was forced off their farm in Norwalk and into camps [1]. She became one of the country's celebrated sculptors. When redevelopment turned a block of Buchanan Street into a pedestrian mall in 1975 and 1976, she designed its two Origami Fountains, meant to look like flowers of folded paper [1][2]. Planner Rai Okamoto designed the mall itself, with a torii-like gate at Sutter [3]. Asawa also designed the benches and got the children of the mall's merchants to help make relief panels of Japanese fairy tales and festivals, sculpted in dough and then cast in concrete [3]. The original steel fountains corroded and were removed, but after public outcry bronze replicas cast under Asawa's supervision returned in 1999 [2][3]. The water was switched off more than a decade before 2025. A 2016 estimate put repairs at $437,177, and the city planned renovation for 2026 to 2027 [2][3].

title: The Bookstore That Gave Lesbians Happy Endings
place: Old Wives Tales bookstore, 1009 Valencia St
hook: In the novels Carol Seajay grew up on, lesbians ended in suicide or conversion. So she skipped the last chapters, rode a motorcycle west and opened a bookstore.
story: Carol Seajay arrived from Michigan in December 1973, having read every lesbian novel she could find; none had a happy ending, so she simply never read the last chapter [1]. With $6,000 from a credit union and a $2,000 loan from her partner Paula Wallace's parents, the two opened Old Wives Tales on Halloween 1976 at 532 Valencia, directly below the Club for the Deaf, paying themselves $200 a month [1]. The shop later moved to larger premises at 1009 Valencia [1]. It sat in a remarkable corridor: Artemis Cafe, a women-only cafe; Osento, the city's only women's bathhouse; Amelia's dance bar, sister to Maud's in Cole Valley; and a feminist credit union lending to women-owned businesses [1][2]. Seajay also started the Feminist Bookstore News, whose first issue appeared in October 1976 [1]. "I would walk home at night and feel that it was the golden age of the world," she said [1]. Strife, debt and collective turmoil took their toll, and Old Wives Tales closed in 1995 [1][2].

title: The Cancer Gene Was Ours All Along
place: Bishop-Varmus laboratory, UCSF Parnassus campus
hook: Two UCSF virologists chasing a chicken cancer virus discovered that the gene behind it came from normal cells, including ours. Stockholm called in 1989.
story: J. Michael Bishop moved to UCSF in February 1968, turning down an East Coast offer because, he said, he would be 'genuinely needed in San Francisco' [2]. In 1970 a young physician named Harold Varmus arrived as his postdoc. The two soon worked as equals and shared lab space, staff and funding until 1984 [2][3]. Their target was src, the gene that lets Rous sarcoma virus turn chicken cells into tumour cells. Where did the virus get it? Experiments run mainly by Dominique Stehelin and Deborah Spector gave the answer [2]. In 1976 the team published a startling conclusion: src was not really a viral gene at all. It was a normal cellular gene, found across the animal kingdom, which the virus had picked up from a host and carried along [1]. Normal genes that control growth, it turned out, can become cancer genes when damaged. Researchers soon identified more than 40 of these oncogenes [1]. On 9 October 1989 Bishop and Varmus were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Varmus, meanwhile, had spent most of those years living in a Victorian house in the Haight [3].

title: The Corner Where Chinatown Spilled West
place: 8th Avenue and Balboa Street
hook: During the 1976 city strike, Chinese Muni drivers living at one Richmond corner quietly organised rides so elderly neighbours could still reach their doctors.
story: Steve Hong grew up at Eighth Avenue and Balboa in the 1970s, when it seemed every corner had a grocery, and three near his home were run by Chinese families [1]. Before 1965, he writes, most Chinese San Franciscans were confined to Chinatown; after immigration law changed, families moved out to the Richmond, and Clement Street became known as a 'New Chinatown' [1]. His corner held more than groceries. About 20 Chinese Muni operators worked in the whole city, and a handful lived on the south corners of Eighth and Balboa [1]. In spring 1976, city craft workers walked out and Muni drivers stopped running buses in solidarity [2]. Hong recalls that the Chinese drivers across the street organised and dispatched rides so seniors could reach their medical appointments; he believes those efforts were seeds of today's paratransit [1]. An apartment on the corner was a hangout for young Chinese activists who fought for housing and for the International Hotel, among them Fred Lau [1]. Lau had been admitted to the police academy in 1970 after Chinatown protested a height rule he missed by three-quarters of an inch; in 1996 he became the city's first Chinese American police chief [3].

title: The Cove Gets Its Name Back

hook: When the federal government took over Phelan Beach, it quickly gave the cove back its older name. Five years later a family added a stone to say why.
story: In 1976 the state beach below Sea Cliff passed to the federal government and became part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. The Parks Conservancy says it was "promptly renamed, once again, to China Beach", dropping the name of James D. Phelan, a champion of exclusion [1]. In 1981 Henry and Diana Chung gave a monument for the trailhead near the parking area at the end of Sea Cliff Avenue [1][3]. It is a stone carved with Chinese characters. Its English text says that since gold rush times the cove was a campsite for Chinese fishermen who worked in and around the Bay, and that their efforts to supply a young city "helped establish one of the area's most important industries and traditions" [1][3]. The Conservancy points out that every visitor walking down to the sand has to pass it, and says: "This is by design" [1]. The National Park Service still directs visitors to the monument to the fishermen and early residents who camped in the cove [2].

title: The ice rink that hosted rock's farewells
place: Winterland Ballroom site, 2000 Post Street at Steiner
hook: An old skating rink at Post and Steiner saw The Band's Last Waltz, the Sex Pistols' last show and an all-night Grateful Dead goodbye.
story: Winterland began in 1928 as the New Dreamland Auditorium, an ice rink that could be turned into an event hall [1]. Bill Graham started renting it in 1966, and after closing the Fillmore West in 1971 he ran it as a full-time concert hall holding 5,400 people [1]. On 25 November 1976 The Band played its farewell concert here, The Last Waltz, filmed by Martin Scorsese, with guests including Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, Neil Young and Eric Clapton [1]. Van Morrison sang "Tura Lura Lural" and "Caravan" [2]. On 14 January 1978 the Sex Pistols played their last show here [1]. Photographer Bob Minkin lost his wallet and tickets on arriving for the Grateful Dead's December 1977 run, then got new tickets from Winterland's office [3]. The Dead closed the building on New Year's Eve 1978 with a show of nearly six hours, broadcast on KSAN and KQED [1]. It was razed in 1985, and apartments now occupy the corner [1][3].

title: The real Barbary Lane
place: Macondray Lane, between Jones and Taylor
hook: A hidden, tree-shaded footpath with wooden stairs became 28 Barbary Lane, home of Mrs. Madrigal and the most beloved tenants in San Francisco fiction.
story: Macondray Lane is a pedestrian path on the southeastern side of Russian Hill, running between Leavenworth and Taylor streets. At the Taylor end, wooden steps drop down to the street, and the views reach to Alcatraz [1]. It is named for Frederick W. Macondray, a merchant who came to California in the 1850s, and it feels a world away from the city below [2]. In 1976 Armistead Maupin began "Tales of the City" as a daily serial in the San Francisco Chronicle [3]. Newcomer Mary Ann Singleton rents an apartment at 28 Barbary Lane from the eccentric, marijuana-growing landlady Anna Madrigal, who is later revealed to be a transgender woman [4]. Maupin followed a group of friends and lovers, gay and straight, through the 1970s and 80s. The series became one of the earliest works of fiction to confront the AIDS epidemic [3]. Readers long suspected Barbary Lane was Macondray Lane, and Maupin confirmed it in the 2017 documentary "The Untold Tales of Armistead Maupin" [1]. The lane was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988 [1].

title: A haunted hotel with a magic show
place: Chambers Mansion (the Mansions Hotel), 2220 Sacramento Street
hook: An adman bought a rundown Victorian with a gruesome legend, turned it into a haunted hotel with a magic show, and spent years fighting his neighbours.
story: The Chambers Mansion, a Queen Anne built in 1887, came with a gory legend. Chambers's two feuding nieces supposedly inherited it, and one was later found "cut almost in half". NoeHill notes that the story is an urban legend and that even basic facts about Chambers are hard to confirm [2]. In 1977 advertising man Bob Pritikin bought what was by then a rundown boardinghouse. He turned it into an eccentric 16-room hotel and made the most of its haunted reputation [1]. He put on a magic act, the "Pritikin Squished Eyeball Theater", and the Examiner reported that Barbra Streisand and Robin Williams stayed there for a time [3]. Chronicle photographers recorded Beniamino Bufano's grown children setting up his sculpture in 1978, and the demonologists Ed and Lorraine Warren in the billiard room in 1982 [1]. For years the hotel was also a neighbourhood polling place [1]. Not everyone was charmed. From 1979 to 1991 the Chronicle kept reporting on Pritikin's feud with the Pacific Heights Neighborhood Association [1]. The hotel was sold in 2000 and converted to housing [1].

title: Diana Ross Parts the Trocadero Crowd
place: Former Trocadero Transfer, 520 Fourth Street at Bryant
hook: Every week the DJ put 'Diana Ross +1' on the guest list and people laughed. Then one night she really walked in.
story: The Trocadero Transfer opened in 1977 in a 1930 warehouse at 520 Fourth Street. It was an after-hours gay disco that stayed open until 2000, when the building was remodelled into another club [1][2]. When the club won its all-night permit, DJ Steve Fabus remembers, it "ushered in a New York-style all-night party" held every weekend [3]. The room had good acoustics because television shows had once been produced there. Its lighting, run by Billy Langenheim, was taken as seriously as the music [3]. Bobby Viteritti, the main DJ in its peak years, won Billboard's national DJ of the Year award in 1979 and 1980. Dancers came from Los Angeles and Miami [3]. Viteritti used to put "Diana Ross +1" on the guest list every week as a joke. Then one night in 1978 she arrived. The crowd parted, and she climbed into the booth, kissed him and hit the turntable, silencing the sound system to huge cheers [3]. By 1982 AIDS had changed the dance floor. Local disco producer Patrick Cowley died that year aged 32, and the singer Sylvester died in 1988 [3].

title: Japantown fights its second uprooting
place: Nihonmachi (Japantown) blocks around Post and Buchanan
hook: Thirty-five years after the camps, Japantown's residents faced eviction again, and this time they occupied the buildings.
story: Before World War II, Nihonmachi covered about 20 blocks and was home to 95 percent of San Francisco's Japanese Americans [1]. By 1940 it had more than 200 Japanese American-owned businesses [2]. Many returned after the camps, only to find the neighbourhood targeted by the Redevelopment Agency's Western Addition projects, which leaders in both the Japanese American and African American communities opposed [2]. The first big change, the Japan Center, displaced more than 50 businesses and about 1,500 residents [2]. In 1977 residents formed Citizens Against Nihonmachi Eviction (C.A.N.E.) to fight the eviction of low-income tenants and small businesses [1]. The group brought thousands of people to protest at City Hall and against Kintetsu, and occupied several buildings slated for demolition, in the same spirit as the International Hotel tenants [1]. They lost. FoundSF's account says foreign-owned hotels and shops displaced hundreds of local Japanese American residents and businesses [1].

title: Leroy Looper saves the Cadillac Hotel
place: Cadillac Hotel, 380 Eddy St at Leavenworth
hook: A 180-room hotel had 40 tenants and a drug market out front. A former Harlem street kid bought it with no money down and pioneered a new kind of housing.
story: The Cadillac Hotel went up after the 1906 earthquake, a grand place where guests checked their furs at the front desk [1]. By the 1960s it was on the way down. One owner, a then-unknown Donald Fisher, before he founded the Gap, stripped much of its ornament [1]. In July 1977 it was sold, with no money down, to Leroy Looper, who ran the Reality House West drug-treatment programme [1][2]. The 180-room hotel had only 40 tenants. Looper planned to restore it and house people coming out of prison. The mostly elderly residents were wary, so he promised they could vote to end the halfway-house programme if they were unhappy. They never did [1]. The legendary manager Sarah Kearney swept the sidewalk daily and used her broom on anyone dealing drugs in front of the hotel [1]. Randy Shaw calls it the West Coast's first 'supportive housing', and its lobby became a meeting hall for neighbourhood organizing [1][2]. Reality House West was the first group to blaze the Tenderloin's nonprofit-housing trail [2]. Today the Tenderloin Museum occupies its corner at 398 Eddy [3].

title: Lightboxes Behind the Bar at the Utah
place: Hotel Utah Saloon, 500 Fourth Street at Bryant
hook: A 1908 workers' hotel beside the Bay Bridge ramps became a saloon stage for Robin Williams and Whoopi Goldberg, with lightboxes behind the bar for photographers checking their slides.
story: The Hotel Utah went up in 1908 at Fourth and Bryant as a saloon and rooms for working men. In the 1930s its bar took the name Transbay Café, after the new Bay Bridge ramps nearby. After 1945 it was Al Opatz's "Al's Trans-Bay", a blue-collar bar whose regulars included a duck-hunting club [1]. On March 18, 1977, film producer and screenwriter Paul Gaer turned Al's into the Hotel Utah Saloon [2]. He spread the bar into the two neighbouring storefronts and built a stage. Comedians and musicians including Robin Williams, Whoopi Goldberg, PJ Harvey and Guns N' Roses played there. Upstairs, rooms long used by drug dealers became homes for artists and musicians [1]. Photographers from a photo lab across the street drank there so often that the bar installed lightboxes so they could edit their work over a drink [1]. The Utah outlasted the dot-com boom too. "We saw them pull up in limos," owner Damian Samuel, who started as the doorman, said in 2007. "And we watched them drive off in U-Hauls" [2]. In 2018 the city's Historic Preservation Commission moved to make it an official landmark [1].

title: Precita Eyes paints the neighbourhood
place: Precita Eyes studio, 348 Precita Ave
hook: A mural workshop for the local library turned into one of the few community mural centres in the United States.
story:
Susan Cervantes came to San Francisco from Dallas in 1961 on a scholarship to the San Francisco Art Institute. She married the muralist Luis Cervantes, and they raised their family near Precita Park [2]. She wanted to brighten her neighbourhood. That led her to Las Mujeres Muralistas, the pioneering all-women mural collective, and to its idea of collaborative, accessible art [1][2].

Founded in 1977, the organisation grew out of a community workshop that designed and painted a mural called 'Masks of God, Soul of Man' for the Bernal Heights Library. Because it was a group effort, they signed it 'Precita Eyes Muralists', and that became the name of the organisation [1]. 'Precita' refers to Precita Valley and its old creek. The 'Eyes' are the ones we see with [1]. By its 30th anniversary in 2007, Precita Eyes had helped create more than 450 murals and was one of just five community mural groups in the nation [2]. It still runs youth and toddler classes from its studio at 348 Precita Avenue [3]. 'We pretty much stick with pencil and paper and paint,' Cervantes said [2].

title: Sami Sunchild paints the Red Vic
place: The Red Victorian, 1665 Haight Street
hook: Goldfish swam in a toilet tank, and the guest rooms had names like Flower Child. Later, a Banksy rat went up on the outside wall.
story: The building went up in 1904 as the Jefferson Hotel. In the Summer of Love it was the Jeffrey Haight, a free crash pad [1]. In 1977 the artist and activist Sami Sunchild bought it, painted the facade red and reopened it as the Red Victorian Bed, Breakfast & Art [1]. She gave the rooms themes such as the Flower Child, the Rainbow, the Redwoods and the Peacock suite. In one shared bathroom, goldfish swam in the toilet tank [1][2]. Downstairs were a Peace Cafe and a gift shop. From the 1990s she hosted Sunday-morning World Peace Conversations [1]. "The Red Vic is at the centre of the Haight, and the Haight is at the centre of the universe," she told a reporter at 81 [2]. In April 2010 Banksy sprayed a rat clutching a marker pen on the side of the building from a neighbouring roof [3]. Sunchild was about to paint over it when collector Brian Greif arranged to remove the siding, promising her he would never sell it. He later said one collector had offered him $700,000 [3]. Sunchild died in 2013, aged 87 [1].

title: The 'Radio City' of gay cinemas
place: Nob Hill Cinema, 729 Bush St
hook: Behind a plain stuccoed front on Bush Street, the old Club Hangover became a members-only gay film house with free coffee in the lobby.
story:
In the 1960s, when Nob Hill and Polk Street were centres of gay male life, the hilltop had its own after-dark geography. Police in the 1950s had already called Huntington Park "a major meeting spot," and one resident recalled hedges "taller than I am" that made it ideal for cruising [1].

Down the south slope at 729 Bush Street, the former Club Hangover became a members-only theatre and then, in the late 1960s, a gay porn cinema, the Nob Hill Cinema and Arcade [1]. In January 1977 Chronicle columnist John L. Wasserman went "trucking" there and reported a "tidy little theater" seating fewer than 100 that "serves free java in the lobby" and "has been called 'The Radio City Music Hall of gay porno theaters'" [1]. Behind it ran a dim 30-foot arcade of small rooms [1]. The city's LGBTQ context statement noted in 2015 that it was still in business [1].

The building itself hides in plain sight. It was designed by C. A. Meussdorffer to house a store, but its facade was later sheathed in stuccostone, leaving only the parapet original, so it counts as one of the few non-contributing buildings in the Lower Nob Hill Apartment Hotel District [2].

title: The Fab Mab and the Pope of Punk
place: Mabuhay Gardens, 443 Broadway
hook: A Filipino supper club became the loudest room in San Francisco, run by an emcee who insulted everyone and got his nose broken seven times.
story: Mabuhay Gardens at 443 Broadway was a Filipino restaurant before it became ground zero for San Francisco punk in the late 1970s and '80s [1]. Local bands like the Avengers, Dead Kennedys and the Nuns played its basement stage, and touring acts from Devo to the Cramps came through until it closed in 1987 [1]. Running the show was Dirk Dirksen, the self-styled "pope of punk," who baited crowds and bands alike, often with his little dog, Dummy, tucked under his arm [2]. He once told an audience to "show some intelligence and sophistication and not just accept any slop that's thrown in your trough" [2]. He reckoned his nose had been broken seven times. Every year he staged a mock torture of himself for his birthday, and one year he had himself burned at the stake [2]. Robin Williams described comedy hell as "opening for the Ramones at the Mabuhay Gardens" [2]. After the club closed, the building became a dinner theatre and events hall. In 2025, after the death of owner Francesca Valdez, neighbours and investors began raising money to buy it and bring back the Mab [1].

title: The Night 400 Police Emptied the I-Hotel
place: International Hotel, 848 Kearny St at Jackson
hook: For nine years, elderly Filipino and Chinese tenants, students and artists held a red-brick hotel against the Financial District. Then came 3 a.m. on August 4, 1977.
story: The International Hotel was a three-storey red-brick building at Kearny and Jackson, the heart of Manilatown, and its leftist politics earned the block the nickname the "Red Block" [1]. In autumn 1968 its owner, Milton Meyer and Company, began sending eviction notices; the plan was a parking lot. "To my mind, I was getting rid of a slum," said chairman Walter Shorenstein [1]. Some 150 elderly Filipino and Chinese tenants, many retired farmworkers and seamen, refused to go [2][1]. In March 1969 a suspicious fire on the top floor killed three tenants [2]. Students repaired burnt-out rooms, and the storefronts filled with the Asian Community Center, the Chinese Progressive Association, Everybody's Bookstore (the nation's first Asian American bookstore) and the Kearny Street Workshop, an artists' collective founded in 1972 [2][3]. The hotel was later sold to Four Seas Investment, which planned more commercial development [1]. At 3 a.m. on August 4, 1977, over 400 riot police, mounted patrols and fire ladder trucks cleared a 3,000-person human barricade, and the tenants were physically removed [2]. The artists were evicted too. Eighteen years later the site was, as one reporter put it, "still a hole in the ground" [3].

title: The Pharmacist Who Flyered the Whole Sunset
place: Former West Coast Pharmacy, SW corner 7th Ave & Irving St
hook: Leon Levy mailed get-well cards with every prescription, walked flyers door to door from Masonic to 19th, and got UCSF to send him Sunday customers.
story: Leon Levy came to the Inner Sunset in 1954 as a UCSF pharmacy student. He parked in Golden Gate Park and climbed the hill to class for exercise [1]. From 1959 to 1977 he filled prescriptions at the Reliable Rexall. It had taken over Furlong's dry goods store at 801 Irving, where the Furlong sisters (two or three, depending on who remembers) sold school uniforms and baby clothes and lived upstairs [1][2]. In 1977 the owner of West Coast Pharmacy, at 7th and Irving, offered Levy the business for the cost of its stock, and he took it [1]. He ran it his way. Every customer who filled a prescription got a mailed get-well card with a thank-you note inside. For six weeks he spent half an hour each morning walking flyers to doors from Masonic to 19th Avenue [1]. When the other pharmacies refused to take turns opening on Sundays, he went to UCSF's emergency room, and the hospital began sending patients down [1]. He also spent seven years petitioning for the parking lot on 7th Avenue [1]. Low HMO payments closed the shop in 1997. One customer followed him for over 30 years [1].

title: The college station that broke Metallica
place: KUSF, University of San Francisco, 2130 Fulton St
hook: For 34 years a student station on the hilltop played punk before almost anyone else. Then one January morning in 2011 it abruptly went silent.
story: KUSF started in 1963 as a campus AM station and moved to FM at 90.3 in 1977 [1]. Run mostly by students and volunteers, it became known far beyond the campus. It was among the first stations to play punk rock, and it gave early airtime to the B-52's and Metallica [1]. Then, at 10 a.m. on a Tuesday in January 2011, the station went off the air without warning. USF had sold the frequency for $3.75 million in a deal that moved the classical station KDFC to 90.3, and many of KUSF's staff and volunteers learned about it that same morning [2]. The more powerful of KDFC's new signals would come from a transmitter on a USF campus building [2]. Fans pushed back hard. A Save KUSF campaign gathered 7,200 members on Facebook and support from Yo La Tengo and the Kronos Quartet. On February 8, 2011, the Board of Supervisors voted 8-3 to oppose the sale [3]. KUSF never returned to the FM dial. It kept its call letters and survives as an online-only station broadcasting from the campus at 2130 Fulton Street [1][2].

title: The parish that learned to care
place: Most Holy Redeemer Church, 100 Diamond St
hook: In 1977 protesters chanted outside its doors. Ten years later its empty convent was taking in the dying.
story: Most Holy Redeemer was the parish church of old Irish-Catholic Eureka Valley, and at first it resisted the gay newcomers [1]. On June 7, 1977, 'Orange Tuesday', Florida voters had just repealed a gay-rights ordinance. Marchers left the Castro and stopped outside the church to chant 'Two, four, six, eight, separate the church and state' [1]. Things began to change in 1983. Archbishop John Quinn sent a new pastor, Fr. Tony McGuire, who brought the parish's mostly older women together with a handful of gay parishioners [2]. That same year gay members set up an outreach committee and ran a booth at the Castro Street Fair [1]. When AIDS came, parishioners drove sick neighbours to doctors and helped around their houses. The older women were central to this work, and Sister Cleta Harold helped lead the ministry [1][2]. In 1985 the Examiner described the congregation as 'mostly older people and younger gay men who—because of AIDS—were facing the same fears of disease and death' [1]. From 1986 the parish kept a scroll of members who had died of AIDS [2]. In 1987 its disused convent across the street opened as Coming Home Hospice, reportedly the nation's first AIDS hospice [1].

title: Toilets in the garden, dykes at the bar
place: Wild Side West, 424 Cortland Ave
hook: Neighbours greeted the lesbian bar with a rock and broken toilets through the windows. The owners planted flowers in the toilets.
story:
Pat Ramseyer and Nancy White opened their bar in Oakland in 1962. They named it after Walk on the Wild Side, a Barbara Stanwyck film about a lesbian madam, and at the time it was still illegal in California for a woman to tend bar [1][2]. In 1968 they moved to North Beach, near Broadway, where off-duty dancers from the strip clubs found a refuge behind a heavy leather curtain [1]. Then they moved one last time, carrying the actual bar and mirror, to an 1890s Italianate building at 424 Cortland Avenue. They lived there as well as ran the bar. Most accounts give 1977 for the move, though some say 1976 [1][2].

The welcome was rough. Less than two days after opening, someone threw a rock through the front window. Broken toilets came through another window. Pat and Nancy turned the toilets into planters in the back garden [1]. Pat also began leaving Halloween candy outside for trick-or-treaters, which grew into a Cortland Avenue tradition [1]. Tom Ammiano once joked that everyone who walked in became an 'honorary dyke' [1]. By 2021 it was called San Francisco's last remaining lesbian bar [2].

title: Twenty to Three at the Golden Dragon
place: Golden Dragon Restaurant, 822 Washington St
hook: At 2:40 a.m. on Labor Day weekend, masked gunmen came for a gang leader. He dove to the floor. Five bystanders died.
story: At 2:40 a.m. on Sunday, September 4, 1977, about 100 people were eating at the Golden Dragon on Washington Street [1]. Among them was 20-year-old Michael "Hot Dog" Louie, head of the Wah Ching gang [1]. A friend saw a man with a sawed-off shotgun run past the window and yelled "Man with a gun!" in Cantonese; Louie ducked as three gunmen in stocking masks burst in [1]. The shooting lasted about a minute. Five people died and eleven were wounded, and none of them had any link to the gangs [1][2]. The dead were Paul Wada, a 25-year-old law student at USF; his friend Denise Louie, 20, from Seattle; waiter Fong Wong, 48, a violinist and family man; and City College students Calvin Fong, 18, and Donald Kwan, 20 [1]. It was revenge by the Joe Boys for a Fourth of July gunfight over fireworks sales at the Ping Yuen projects [1][3]. Mayor George Moscone offered an unprecedented $100,000 reward, Chinatown business fell by half, and police formed a Gang Task Force [3]. The shooters were convicted, but the getaway driver was never caught [1]. The Chronicle called it the worst mass murder in the city's history [2].

title: Twenty-five days inside the Federal Building
place: Former Federal Building (HEW offices), 50 United Nations Plaza
hook: Disabled activists moved into a federal office and refused to leave. The Black Panthers brought dinner every night. They walked out with a civil-rights law.
story: Section 504 of the 1973 Rehabilitation Act banned discrimination against disabled people in federally funded programmes, but it could not take effect until the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare signed its rules. Four years later he still had not [1]. On April 5, 1977, after a rally in Civic Center, more than 100 people, many of them disabled, entered HEW's regional offices on the fourth floor of 50 United Nations Plaza and stayed [1][2]. Organizers Judy Heumann and Kitty Cone had spent years building alliances, and it showed [2]. Officials turned off the hot water and cut the phones down to a pair of pay phones [1]. Glide Memorial, Delancey Street and above all the Black Panther Party, which brought hot meals every day for fellow Panther Brad Lomax and the others, kept the sit-in fed [1][2]. Congressmen held a hearing inside, and Mayor Moscone brought in portable showers [1]. On April 28 Joseph Califano signed the regulations unchanged. Two days later the occupiers walked out together to champagne on UN Plaza [1]. It was the longest occupation of a federal building in US history. Accounts put it at 25 or 26 days [1][2].

title: A Pulitzer Written for a Warehouse Stage
place: Magic Theatre, Building D, Fort Mason Center
hook: Sam Shepard's darkest family play, Buried Child, had its world premiere in an old Army warehouse on the Marina waterfront, and went on to win the Pulitzer.
story: The Magic Theatre began in 1967, started by a group of Berkeley graduate students led by John Lion who had not planned to found a theatre [1]. It took its name from the magic theatre in Hermann Hesse's Steppenwolf [3]. In 1976 Lion heard about plans to turn a historic military base into an arts centre and moved the company across the bay, making it one of Fort Mason's first nonprofit residents [1][3]. It is still there, on the third floor of Building D, a Mission Revival warehouse built for the Army [1]. Sam Shepard had become playwright in residence in 1975 [3]. In 1978 the Magic staged the premiere of his Buried Child, a bleak comedy about a ruined Illinois farm family keeping a terrible secret. It won the 1979 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and Fort Mason Center counts more than 400 productions worldwide since [2]. More Shepard premieres followed here, including True West in 1980 and Fool for Love in 1983 [3]. The company also became a home for Beat poet Michael McClure, whose play The Beard had been raided by police [1].

title: El Rio: 'Your Dive' since 1978
place: El Rio, 3158 Mission St
hook: Two gay men who loved leather, motorcycles, salsa and Brazil built a patio bar where everyone was welcome, as long as they were welcoming back.
story:
In 1978 Malcolm Thornley and Robert Nett, a couple, opened a bar at 3158 Mission Street near Precita Avenue. The bar says it was built on 'neighborhood, community and dance' [1]. The two men loved leather, motorcycles, salsa, Brazil and tropical plants. They were gay, but they wanted the club open to everyone, 'as long as they were welcoming back' [1]. They were big music fans too, and they built a lush back patio with a stage for salsa, rock, country and pop [1].

The patio became the bar's heart. Bernalwood called El Rio 'a true Bernal Heights treasure' when the bar threw a free 35th birthday party in October 2013. The lineup had burlesque, a BBQ, cake, and a band that included the rock writer Ben Fong-Torres [2]. The bar is still queer-owned. It centres its queer and BIPOC family as well as neighbourhood nonprofits, teachers and trades workers, and it hosts more than 150 benefits a year [1]. Its own description: 'a patio for dancing, a community space for organizing, a friendly dive for canoodling' [1].

title: Pizza, then chorizo on the pizza
place: Little Joe's Pizza, 5006 Mission St
hook: An Italian pizzeria changed hands in 1978, and the new owners' Mexican pizza tells the neighbourhood's whole story.
story: In 1958 Joseph 'Little Joe' Russo, who had learned to make pizza at his father's North Beach pizzeria, opened Little Joe's at Mission Street and Persia Avenue. He served pizza, chicken parmesan and pasta [1]. Business was good enough that in 1972 he moved to a bigger space at 5006 Mission and took the neon sign with him [1]. By then the Excelsior was changing. Census figures for its main tract show Hispanic residents outnumbering Italians by 1960, and by 1970 the Hispanic population had nearly doubled [2]. In 1978 Alfredo and Gloria Rodriguez took over [1][2]. They kept the Italian dishes and added a Mexican pizza with refried beans, homemade chorizo and jalapeños. Later came a second menu of tacos, tamales and enchiladas from Gloria's recipes [1]. Alfredo, known as Fred, died in 1995. All three of his daughters met their husbands working there, and the family says the place, with its deep red wallpaper, has been home to four generations of Rodriguezes [1]. It joined the Legacy Business Registry in December 2017 [1].

title: Punk Night at the Club for the Deaf
place: The Deaf Club, 530 Valencia St
hook: You wrote your beer order on a slip of paper. The bands were deafening. And half the regulars, signing and grinning at the back, could not hear a note.
story: Daphne Hanrahan, manager of the band the Offs, went to La Cumbre for a burrito and spotted a "Hall for Rent" sign on a fire escape across Valencia Street [1]. Upstairs she found two men watching television with the sound off: this was the San Francisco Club for the Deaf. She wrote her request on paper and got a written reply; accounts of the price differ, from $50 a night to Hanrahan's remembered "OK & $250" [1]. The first show, on 9 December 1978, featured the Offs, the Mutants and On the Rag, for $2 [1]. There was barely a stage, no lights, and you scrawled your drink order for the bar; Penelope Houston recalled that nobody was carded [1]. Deaf members stayed on at their end of the hall, some resting their hands on tables to feel the music, and Winston Smith reckoned the sheer volume was what they could appreciate [1]. Police, noise complaints and neighbours' grievances forced repeated closures, and the club ended in autumn 1979 [1]. One night survives on record: the Dead Kennedys' set of March 1979, released in 2004 as Live at the Deaf Club [2].

title: Rev. Gordon's Gym Full of Faces
place: Ingleside Presbyterian Church, 1345 Ocean Avenue
hook: In 1978 a seminary student took over a four-member church that neighbours called the "pink elephant". His secret weapon was its old gymnasium.
story: Joseph Leonard, the developer of Ingleside Terraces, designed and built this church at Ocean and Granada. When it was completed in 1923 it housed nine Protestant congregations. Short of money, the religious director chose gym equipment for the boys over a pipe organ [1]. By 1978 the congregation was down to four members and facing closure, and neighbours called the building the "pink elephant" [2][3]. That year Roland Gordon, a former high school and college ballplayer from Gary, Indiana, began preaching there while at seminary [2]. He opened the gym and "the children came to me": kids of all races, mostly Black, who played in his church leagues, prayed before games and all got trophies at the season's banquet [2]. Starting with a photo of Muhammad Ali, Gordon pinned up pictures of African-American achievers. The collage, now called the Great Cloud of Witnesses, has spread floor to ceiling and down the halls, under a 1992 mural of African-American leaders [2][4]. In September 1986 he founded the Ingleside Community Center [3]. Standing up for the neighbourhood had a cost. When he backed a senior housing plan across Ocean Avenue in the 1990s, racial slurs were painted on the church [2].

title: The Book That Named the Painted Ladies
place: Postcard Row, 710–720 Steiner Street
hook: By the 1970s, San Francisco's Victorians were blooming into three, four and five colours. In 1978 a photographer and two writers gave the movement its name.
story: The colour revolution started with artists. SF Heritage credits the painter Butch Kardum with trying intense blues and greens on his own Italianate house in 1963. His neighbours hated it at first, but soon his whole block had been repainted just as brightly [1]. By the 1970s colour consultants such as Bob Buckter, known as "Dr. Color", were leaving their business cards on newly painted houses [1]. In 1978 Dutton published an 80-page book by the photographer Morley Baer and the writers Elizabeth Pomada and Michael Larsen. They called it Painted Ladies: San Francisco's Resplendent Victorians [2]. It celebrated how "San Francisco's Painted Ladies have enjoyed an astonishing renaissance" and covered the Western Addition, colour choices and restoration [2]. The name stuck. It came to mean a Victorian or Edwardian house painted in three or more colours to bring out its architectural details [3]. Pomada and Larsen went on to write six books in the series [4].

title: The Rent Strike That Lit Ping Yuen's Stairs
place: Ping Yuen public housing, Pacific Ave
hook: After a teenager was murdered on the stairs of her public-housing block, her neighbours stopped paying rent until the city fixed the lights.
story: Ping Yuen, the public housing blocks on Pacific Avenue near Stockton Street, was where Chinatown gangs sold illegal fireworks each summer [3]. In August 1978, 18-year-old tenant Julia Wong was sexually assaulted and murdered as she walked up the stairs to her apartment [1]. The papers made it a story about crime-ridden public housing. The tenants blamed dim lighting, a broken elevator and weak security, problems their association had been asking the San Francisco Housing Authority to fix for a long time [1]. So they went on rent strike. They met regularly, paid their rent into escrow and held together until the Authority brought in security guards, more bilingual staff and better lighting [1]. On February 26, 1979, the tenants threw a Unity Party and invited tenants from other projects [1]. Soon North Beach Place was threatening a strike of its own, and the Housing Authority's director worried about a rent-strike "syndrome" [1]. The organising lasted. In 1999, Ping Yuen tenants led by Chang Jok Lee noisily protested at Housing Authority headquarters over a new commissioner they feared would tear the project down [2].

title: A Campus Won in Exchange for Sewage
place: Southeast Community Facility, 1800 Oakdale Avenue
hook: When San Francisco sent most of its sewage to a Bayview plant, neighbourhood activists made the city pay with a community centre and a college campus next door.
story: Most of San Francisco's sewage is treated at the Southeast plant in Bayview–Hunters Point. A 2010 report put the share at 80 percent [3]. Activist Espanola Jackson fought the plant's placement there and put it bluntly: "Everybody's sh*t from all over San Francisco being dumped over here on us" [2]. When that fight was lost, residents bargained. According to the city utility, in 1979 the southeast neighbourhoods won a community centre at 1800 Oakdale Avenue as part of an agreement to offset the plant's effects [1]. The SFPUC credits six founding activists, "the Big 6": Alex Pitcher, Harold Madison, Ethel Garlington, Espanola Jackson, Shirley Jones and Elouise Westbrook [1]. The people who eulogized Jackson in 2016 counted it among her biggest wins, forcing the city to build a place for her people to get an education, now a City College campus beside the plant [2]. By 2015 the old building needed extensive repairs. Residents favoured rebuilding, and a new centre built with local-hire goals opened in 2022 at 1550 Evans Avenue. More than 98 of the workers who built it came from the 94124 zip code [1].

title: Esta Noche, Where Queer Latinos Came Home
place: Esta Noche, 3079 16th St
hook: Turned away from Castro bars, two gay Latino activists opened their own on 16th Street. For 35 years it offered drag, cumbia, AIDS outreach and belonging.
story: In 1979 Anthony Lopez and Manuel Quijano, members of the Gay Latino Alliance, opened a bar at 3079 16th Street [1]. Both had been refused entry to white gay bars in the Castro, and they met resistance from city officials when seeking permits [1]. Esta Noche became the city's first Latino gay bar: a place to speak Spanish, dance to cumbia and bachata, and watch drag [1]. Vivian Lopez, who came from Nicaragua at eleven, saw her first drag show there at about nineteen: "I said, when I dress up, that's what I want to look like" [1]. She met others who were transitioning and soon began hormone therapy herself [1]. During the AIDS epidemic the bar worked with the Stop AIDS Project to hand out more than 17,000 condoms, and performers such as Adela Vazquez raised money for people with HIV [1]. By 2014 the rent had risen from $360 in 1979 to nearly $7,000 a month [1]. A crowdfunding campaign fell short, and Esta Noche announced it would close, to be replaced by a cocktail lounge [2].

title: From cactus-shop café to Zuni
place: Zuni Café, 1658 Market Street
hook: Zuni began in a corner of a cactus shop, cooking on an espresso machine, a toaster oven and a Weber grill. Its roast chicken became famous.
story: In 1979 Billy West opened a little café in one corner of a triangular building on Market Street. Most of the building belonged to a cactus shop called Red Desert, and the café borrowed its Southwestern style. West cooked Southwest food with an espresso machine, a toaster oven and a Weber grill [1]. Through the 1980s he expanded it, made it a queer hot spot, and won praise from the British food writer Elizabeth David [1]. In 1987 he brought in Chez Panisse alumna Judy Rodgers as chef and partner [1]. As a teenage exchange student in France, Rodgers had lived with the Troisgros family, whose restaurant had three Michelin stars [2]. She insisted on a massive wood-fired brick oven long before other chefs took up the idea. From it came a roast chicken with bread salad that became the signature dish, alongside a benchmark Caesar salad [2][1]. Zuni won the James Beard Foundation's top restaurant award in 2003, and Rodgers won its chef's award a year later [2]. West died in 1994 of complications related to AIDS, and Rodgers died in 2013 [1]. When a new chef later took over the kitchen, some dishes, the chicken among them, could not be changed [1].

title: Steam beer in an old coffee plant
place: Anchor Brewing, 1705 Mariposa Street
hook: Fritz Maytag bet everything he owned on moving Anchor Brewing into a former coffee plant on Mariposa Street. It brewed there for 44 years, then closed with 60 days' notice.
story:
Fritz Maytag bought 51 percent of the failing Anchor Brewing in 1965 and the rest in 1969 [1]. To expand, he pledged all his personal assets. In August 1979 the brewery moved into the former Chase and Sanborn coffee plant on Mariposa Street, with bankruptcy looming. The new plant lost money in its first year before sales began to climb [2]. In 1993 Maytag opened a small distillery at the back, making Old Potrero rye [2].

Anchor could be a complicated neighbour. In 1990 Maytag put out a special "Potrero Commons Ale" to support residents fighting to keep a nearby hillside as open space. One of the group's founders later wrote that the promised proceeds from 648 cases never arrived [3].

Maytag sold the company in 2010, and Sapporo bought it in 2017. In 2019 the workers voted almost two to one to join the ILWU, which made Anchor the first unionised craft brewery in the US [1]. On July 12, 2023, Sapporo announced it would stop brewing and liquidate the business, giving employees 60 days' notice [1][4]. The workers tried to buy the brewery as a cooperative. In 2024 Chobani founder Hamdi Ulukaya bought it instead, promising to keep it in San Francisco [1].

title: The Santo Niño Comes to Tenth Street
place: St. Joseph's Church, 1401 Howard Street at Tenth
hook: An Irish parish church became the largest Filipino parish in America. Then an earthquake emptied it for decades.
story: St. Joseph's was founded in 1861 for the Irish families of South of Market. Its Romanesque Revival church at Tenth and Howard rose after its cornerstone was laid in 1913 [1]. By the 1960s and 70s the neighbourhood had changed. Filipinos who had first settled around South Park spread across the district, and old Irish parishes such as St. Joseph's and St. Patrick's became mostly Filipino [2]. By 1979 St. Joseph's was the largest Filipino parish in the United States. That April the parish enthroned an image of the Santo Niño de Cebu, the patron of the Philippines, in the church [1][2]. The Loma Prieta earthquake of October 17, 1989 damaged the church, parish hall and rectory. The Archdiocese closed the parish in the early 1990s, and the buildings stood empty for years. A photograph taken in 2003 still shows them vacant [1][2]. The church is a city landmark and is listed on the National Register [2]. In 2015 designer Ken Fulk bought a half interest in the deconsecrated building. After seismic work he reopened it in 2018 as an arts venue, Saint Joseph's Arts Society [1].

title: The night police stormed the Elephant Walk
place: Elephant Walk bar, 500 Castro St (18th & Castro)
hook: After City Hall burned, a squad of officers drove to 18th and Castro, smashed a bar's plate glass and started swinging clubs.
story: On May 21, 1979, Dan White was convicted only of manslaughter for killing Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone. Thousands marched from the Castro to City Hall, smashing windows and setting police cars on fire [1]. Hours later police cars carrying dozens of officers came to the Castro. Against orders, they went into the Elephant Walk at 18th and Castro, shattered its big plate-glass windows and beat the customers. Then they turned on people in the street [2]. Cleve Jones ran back to his apartment and started a phone tree: 50 neighbours, each of whom rang 10 more. Soon a crowd was shouting 'Go home' at the police [1]. The trouble lasted nearly two hours, until Police Chief Charles Gain arrived and ordered his officers out [2]. The next day would have been Milk's 49th birthday. The community went ahead with its planned party anyway. Volunteers trained as monitors at nearby Douglass Elementary, and first-aid posts were hidden in apartments and behind the Castro Theatre [1]. Between 10,000 and 20,000 people filled Castro and Market to dance. Gay leaders refused to apologise for the night before [1][2].

title: Zen Students Taught America to Eat Vegetables
place: Greens Restaurant, Building A, Fort Mason Center
hook: A candle has burned on a spice-shelf altar in this waterfront kitchen since opening day in 1979, when Zen Center students set out to change vegetarian cooking.
story: Greens opened on the bay at Fort Mason in 1979 as part of the San Francisco Zen Center, inspired by the food at Tassajara Zen Mountain Center. It was meant as a place where Buddhist practice and daily life could meet [1]. For years the only employees were Zen students. They meditated and got their day's work assignments at a small altar to Chenrezig, the Buddha of compassion, on a kitchen spice shelf. It has stayed lit since opening day [1]. Founding chef Deborah Madison had spent eighteen years as a Zen student. She set out to make sure no diner would miss meat, and put then-unfamiliar vegetables such as fingerling potatoes, golden beets and arugula on the menu [1]. Much of the produce came from Green Gulch Farm, a working Zen farm founded in 1972 [1]. Annie Somerville arrived in 1981, became executive chef three years later and was an early champion of farm-to-table cooking [1]. Zen Center carpenters built the dining room from twelve kinds of wood using Japanese joinery, without nails [1]. Fort Mason Center quotes the New York Times: Greens 'established vegetarian food as a cuisine in America' [2].

title: A subway stop named for Harvey
place: Castro Station and Harvey Milk Plaza, Market & Castro
hook: The streetcars had come out of the Twin Peaks Tunnel at this corner since 1918. In 1980 the city went underground, and Sylvester sang to launch it.
story: Streetcars had come out of the Twin Peaks Tunnel at Market and Castro since 1918. The Castro Station, dug as part of the BART-era Market Street subway, finally opened to Muni Metro riders on June 11, 1980 [1][2]. Architect Howard Grant wanted each of his stations to reflect its neighbourhood. Here he designed a diagonal stair, a sunken garden with a clerestory window, cedar benches and red-brick paving [1]. About two weeks before service began, a 'Metro Madness' party was held on the Van Ness platform as a benefit for the Harvey Milk Fund, with a shuttle from the Castro. The disco star Sylvester was the special guest [1]. The Board of Supervisors had named the plaza for Milk in 1979. It was only formally dedicated on September 15, 1985, during the Castro Street Fair [1]. On November 7, 1997, the 20th anniversary of Milk's election, a giant rainbow flag designed by Gilbert Baker was raised on a pole above the plaza. It has become a worldwide symbol of LGBTQ+ pride [1].

title: Couches, popcorn and Harold and Maude
place: Red Vic Movie House, 1727 Haight Street
hook: For 31 years a worker-owned cinema showed movies to people lounging on worn couches, and it ended the way it began, with Harold and Maude.
story: The Red Vic Movie House opened on July 25, 1980, in rented space inside the Red Victorian hotel at Haight and Belvedere [1][2]. It was run by a six-member employee-owned collective. At first there were 80 seats, and many of them were worn-out couches [1]. In 1991 it moved a block west to 1727 Haight, into the former Full Moon Saloon, and grew to 143 seats with a concession stand selling organic snacks [1]. In the 1980s it started annual screenings of "The Hippie Temptation", Harry Reasoner's shocked 1967 CBS report on the Summer of Love [2]. The collective outlasted most of its kind. The San Francisco Neighborhood Theater Foundation estimated that 25 to 30 neighbourhood cinemas had closed in the previous 30 years [1]. Home video, cable and streaming finally caught up with it. The Red Vic closed on its 31st anniversary, July 25, 2011, with a last showing of Harold and Maude [1].

title: Four lesbians buy a house
place: Richland Avenue near Andover Street
hook: Evicted from the Castro, four women pooled their money for a $135,000 building on Bernal's south slope and set off a quiet lesbian migration.
story:
In 1978 Molly Martin, an electrician, and the three other women in her lesbian collective were evicted from a Castro Victorian. They had no recourse, because rent control was still a few years away [1]. After a cramped spell near 29th and Mission, they decided to buy. Their list of needs was a garden for Ruth, a garage for Molly's electrical tools, and good transit [1]. They found a three-unit building on Richland Avenue, on the south side of Bernal Hill. The listing price was $135,000, which seemed impossible. They scraped together a down payment, wrote their own contracts, and took possession in 1980 [1].

Then they had to evict the tenants. 'We had been powerless tenants... and then we became agents of displacement,' Martin wrote [1]. Some neighbours left nasty notes on windshields and sprayed DYKES graffiti on the building. Years later one of them admitted, 'We were watching you' [1]. With each refinancing, the house helped other women buy homes, and the real estate industry later adopted tenancy-in-common as a way for unrelated people to buy [1]. Martin, who founded the group Tradeswomen, lived there for 37 years [1][2].

title: The Cole Valley café that made comedians
place: The Other Café, Carl and Cole Streets (100 Carl St)
hook: On a quiet Cole Valley corner, a small coffee house became a comedy club where Robin Williams, Whoopi Goldberg and Dana Carvey worked out their acts.
story: In the 1980s the Bay Area had nearly a dozen comedy nightclubs, five of them in San Francisco, and one of the most influential was a small coffee house at 100 Carl Street, on the corner of Cole [1][2]. The Other Café became a full-time comedy club run by Bob Ayres and Chip Romer, with Richard Snow as a silent partner [1][2]. It helped launch the careers of Robin Williams, Whoopi Goldberg and Dana Carvey [2]. San Francisco "was not a farm team," Williams recalled, "but an alternative to all that" [1]. Carvey said his Saturday Night Live character the Church Lady was developed at the Other Café, but added, "I can't take all the credit" [1]. The club lost its lease, moved to Emeryville and closed in 1992 [1]. In 2010 Ayres staged a 30th-anniversary reunion at the Palace of Fine Arts with about 30 comics from that era, which dates the club's start to around 1980 [1]. Today the corner is a crêpe restaurant [2].

title: The bookstore in Bop City's house
place: Marcus Books, 1712 Fillmore Street
hook: A drugstore, then a jazz club, then the nation's oldest Black bookstore: one lavender Victorian, rolled down the street to escape the bulldozers.
story: The Stick-Eastlake house at 1712 Fillmore was built around 1893 at 1686-1690 Post Street. There it housed the Nippon Drug Co. before the wartime removal, then Jimbo's Bop City [1][2]. In 1978, as the Redevelopment Agency cleared the Western Addition, it was one of a group of Victorians moved to Fillmore Street [1]. Activist Mary Ann Jones later recalled that her mother, Helen Jones, "laid down in front of this building the first time they tried to bulldoze it" [2]. In 1980 it became the home of Marcus Books, which San Francisco State professors Julian and Raye Richardson had started out of their print shop and named Marcus Books in 1960 [1][2][3]. The landmark report calls it a haven for Black intellectualism [1]. Visitors over the years included Malcolm X, James Baldwin, Rosa Parks and Toni Morrison [3]. After the building was sold at a bankruptcy sale in 2013, community leaders fought to buy it back [2]. They failed, and in 2014 the store, then the oldest Black-owned and Black-themed bookshop in the nation, was evicted [1].

title: The librarian's champion who wouldn't let it close
place: Noe Valley/Sally Brunn Branch Library, 451 Jersey Street
hook: Twice the city tried to close Noe Valley's Carnegie library. Twice a soft-spoken Hoffman Avenue neighbour stopped it, and now the building carries her name.
story: When Sally Brunn moved to Hoffman Avenue in the 1960s, the branch library on Jersey Street wasn't open on Saturdays and had no children's librarian. She set out to change that [2]. The city threatened to close the branch in 1980 and again in 1988. Both times Brunn led the fight to keep it open and to stop it being turned into a storehouse [1][2]. She also raised money for the community room and lobbied against cuts to the book budget [1]. 'Sally was always soft-spoken in her activism, but very effective,' her husband John said [1]. Brunn died of cancer in 1991. The following year the city, 'with a swiftness rarely seen in politics,' renamed the branch the Noe Valley-Sally Brunn Library [1]. A book fund in her name buys titles on grassroots organising, each marked with a bookplate by her friend and neighbour Ruth Asawa [1]. In 2008 the 1916 Carnegie building reopened after a $5.7 million seismic renovation, helped by more than $200,000 raised by neighbours. It won a Governor's Historic Preservation Award [3].

title: The neighbourhood that stopped the towers
place: Eastern edge of the Tenderloin near Mason and O'Farrell Sts
hook: Three hotel chains planned nearly 2,000 luxury rooms on the Tenderloin's edge. Tenants, seniors and VISTA volunteers answered by rewriting the zoning map.
story: By the late 1970s tourism was booming, and Tenderloin hotel owners worked out that a room renting for $180 a month could fetch $30 or $40 a night [1]. Blocked by rent laws from evicting long-term tenants, some turned down the heat, shut off elevators and pulled the chairs out of lobbies until people left [1]. Then, in summer 1980, Ramada, Hilton and Holiday Inn announced luxury high-rises that together would plant nearly 2,000 rooms on the neighbourhood's eastern edge [1]. The North of Market Planning Coalition, founded in 1978 and staffed by young VISTA organizers, fought back [1]. Joe Kaufman, a disabled poet recently priced out of the Haight, joined after seeing a sign in an Eddy Street laundromat. 'Here was a way to fight back,' he said [1]. Instead of fighting project by project, the coalition drew up its own zoning plan, with fewer bars, limits on commercial uses and height caps of mostly 80 feet, and persuaded the city to adopt most of it [2]. The rezoning became law in 1985. It shut the neighbourhood's core to high-rise development and kept land cheap enough for nonprofits to buy buildings [2][3].

title: Bobby McFerrin's first concert hall
place: Noe Valley Ministry, 1021 Sanchez Street
hook: A flutist bumped from a jazz club rented a Gothic church for Saturday nights. Within two months a singer who passed the hat was on its stage.
story: In 1980 flutist Larry Kassin's fusion band lost a Monday-night slot at Keystone Korner and faced a six-month wait for another. So he went looking for his own venue. 'I looked around at churches, figuring that they're nice rooms and not used on Saturday night,' he said [1]. The newly revived Noe Valley Ministry, in the Gothic former Lebanon Presbyterian Church at 1021 Sanchez, wanted community events. On February 8, 1981, Noe Valley Jazz presented its first show, the Bishop Norman Williams Quartet [2]. 'Two months later, we had Bobby McFerrin,' Kassin said. 'He was still playing little jazz clubs, passing the hat. This was his first concert hall' [2]. McFerrin lived on Valley Street and would walk down to try out new ideas [1]. Joan Baez, Bill Frisell, Ramblin' Jack Elliott and Warren Zevon played there too. Zevon's entourage asked for security and 10 pounds of carrots, and wanted the chairs removed so the audience would have to stand [2]. The Noe Valley Music Series ran at the church for 30 years before a renovation sent it to Turk Street in 2011 [2].

title: From midnight dump to padlocked tower
place: Wilde Reservoir Overlook, Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue
hook: An abandoned reservoir full of illegally dumped trash became a viewing tower with some of the best views in the city. Then someone locked the door.
story: At the southeast corner of Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue stood the heavy concrete walls of the old Wilde Reservoir. Once it had stored city water. After it was abandoned it became a spot for illegal late-night trash dumping [1]. City planners thought the site had perhaps the best view in the whole park. So in 1981 they kept the old walls as a viewing platform and built a reinforced-concrete tower in the middle. From the top you could see Twin Peaks, downtown, the East and South Bay and round to the Cow Palace [1]. The 1983 master plan says the tower is 35 feet high. The Chronicle's John King called it a 30-foot concrete tower built in the early 1980s with federal funds [1][2]. It didn't stay open. By 2013 neighbours said it had been padlocked for at least 15 years [2]. A tip if you ask for directions: locals pronounce Wilde Street 'Wild-E' [3].

title: The AIDS Clinic Before AIDS Had a Name
place: UCSF Kaposi's Sarcoma Clinic, Clinics Building, 400 Parnassus Ave
hook: In late 1981 UCSF opened a clinic for young gay men with a rare cancer. Its patients were already there before anyone was hired to run it.
story: In autumn 1981 doctors on Parnassus were seeing young gay men with Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer until then associated mainly with elderly men [2]. Dermatologist Marcus Conant was looking for money for a clinic. Oncologist John Ziegler wrote to the American Cancer Society in September, and the grant arrived that December [1]. Helen Schietinger, a newly graduated nurse, heard about the job coordinating 'a new clinic that was being developed for gay men that had cancer'. When she started in January 1982, doctors were already seeing patients, and it was 'totally chaotic' [1]. Resource lists pointed patients to the 'KS Clinic at UCSF, Clinics Bldg, 400 Parnassus' [1]. One early patient was Bobbi Campbell, a UCSF nurse whom Conant diagnosed in October 1981 [1][2]. Campbell began turning up at the clinic, saying, 'I want to meet the patients.' Some doctors found him 'a little off the wall', Schietinger recalled, but he was 'very, very serious'. It mattered, she said, for newly diagnosed men to see 'somebody that was functioning even though he had AIDS' [1]. Campbell went on to call himself the 'KS Poster Boy' in print and to help found the People With AIDS movement [2].

title: Mother Teresa takes an empty convent
place: Former St. Paul's convent, 312 29th Street near Church
hook: 'Give me a convent and I will send them,' the Nobel laureate told the archbishop. Noe Valley had one standing empty.
story: On June 4, 1982, after speaking at St. Mary's Cathedral, Mother Teresa came to Noe Valley to look over a vacant convent belonging to St. Paul's Parish at Church and 29th streets [1]. The winner of the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize was 72. Archbishop John R. Quinn had invited her to send sisters to San Francisco. Her answer, as Herb Caen reported it: 'Give me a convent and I will send them' [1]. The building at 312 29th Street had been built in 1920 for the parish school's teachers. It had since housed a community of priests, the Sisters of the Sacred Heart and even the United Farm Workers union [1]. On July 10 about 30 parishioners turned out to scrub it. The sisters, however, did not want comfort. Their order serves 'the poorest of the poor,' and they asked for every carpet, curtain and modern convenience to be taken out of the three-storey house [1][2]. In July it became a novitiate of her Missionaries of Charity, dedicated at a small Mass in the convent chapel. Mother Teresa, Quinn and the pastor, Father Kevin Gaffey, were there [1].

title: The 21 months without cable cars
place: Cable Car Barn & Powerhouse, 1201 Mason St
hook: The cable cars were worn out and accident-prone. Saving them took Mick Jagger, Pac-Man, Jefferson Starship and a gutted car barn on Nob Hill.
story:
By the late 1970s the cable car system was badly deteriorated, and an engineering study concluded it needed a complete rebuild [1]. The Chronicle put the bill at $60 million, and some San Franciscans argued the cars were relics that should go [2]. Mayor Dianne Feinstein passed the hat publicly. Two airlines gave $1 million each; Atari gave $1 million too, which meant Feinstein, then backing curbs on video arcades, posing beside a six-foot Pac-Man. Jefferson Starship raised $50,000 with a benefit concert, and in October 1981 Mick Jagger dropped by City Hall for a five-minute photo on a fake cable car on rubber wheels: "Once they're gone," he said, "you can't get them back" [2].

Service stopped in September 1982 (sources give the 21st or 22nd) [1][2]. Crews replaced track and cable channels under 69 city blocks. Here at Washington and Mason, the old car barn and powerhouse was almost entirely rebuilt inside its retained brick walls and chimney, with new motors, gearboxes and alarms [1]. Muni craftspeople repaired 37 cars. The California line reopened on 3 June 1984, the barn was dedicated the next day, and on 21 June a parade of cable cars climbed Powell Street behind the Marine Corps Band [1].
