title: An acre of pink, raised in the dark
place: East face of Twin Peaks below Christmas Tree Point, facing the Castro
hook: In 1995 a few friends crept up Twin Peaks at night to pin a Nazi-era symbol to the hillside, and turned it into a Pride tradition.
story:
In 1995 architect Patrick Carney and some friends wanted to add colour to Pride weekend. "There's a big blank canvas on Twin Peaks," he remembered thinking [1]. A friend suggested a rainbow flag, but the city already had plenty. Carney chose the pink triangle instead, because many people did not know where it came from [1][2]. In Nazi concentration camps, prisoners labelled homosexual had to wear a pink triangle badge [1][3]. "We put it up in the dark of night, just to have it appear, sort of anonymously," Carney said. "We didn't expect it to continue" [1]. That first installation went up without city permission [2].

It continued. The triangle grew several times over the years and now covers about an acre, facing the Castro and downtown [2]. For the 30th display in 2025, volunteers staked out borders of pink sailcloth 240 feet long. The next morning around 800 people filled the outline with 175 pink tarps [1]. In 2020, during the pandemic, it was built from pink LED lights instead [3]. Carney calls the pink triangle and the rainbow flag "the Yin and Yang of the gay rights movement" [1].

title: Keith Haring's last work
place: AIDS Interfaith Chapel, Grace Cathedral north tower
hook: Weeks before AIDS killed him, Keith Haring carved an altarpiece into wet clay without a single sketch. One casting now glows just inside Grace Cathedral's doors.
story:
Keith Haring finished The Life of Christ, a triptych drawn freehand into wet clay for casting in bronze and white gold, about two weeks before he died of AIDS in 1990. He never saw it cast [1]. In the centre panel a many-armed figure cradles the infant Jesus beneath a radiant heart; tears rain onto a jostling crowd, angels tumble at the sides [1][2].

On World AIDS Day, 1 December 1995, a casting was unveiled at Grace Cathedral as the heart of a new AIDS chapel [1]. The space, the ground floor of the north "Singing Tower," had been a storeroom, a classroom and briefly the gift shop; it was set aside in 1995 and dedicated in 2000 [2]. It sits just inside the entrance, so that people wary of the vast cathedral could come in "just a little way," as Vice Dean Frances Tornquist put it [2].

The chapel honours the 19,400 San Franciscans the archivist counted as lost to AIDS, alongside caregivers and volunteers, with symbols of many faiths on its piers and a section of the AIDS Memorial Quilt on the back wall. Quilt panels had hung here since 1992 [2]. The cathedral's own accounts credit both an anonymous donor and a group of major donors for the purchase [1][2].

title: The Day Army Street Became Cesar Chavez
place: St. Anthony's Church, Cesar Chavez St at Folsom
hook: A gust of wind unveiled the sign before the officials could. Neighbours waved petitions to change it back. Thirty-one years later, the name is in question again.
story: On March 31, 1995, about 250 people gathered in the parking lot of St. Anthony's Church to unveil the first of 100 signs renaming Army Street after the farmworker leader Cesar Chavez [1]. "Every day you look at that street sign, you should feel great," said Supervisor Susan Leal [1]. Supervisor Tom Ammiano called it "a reclaiming, not a renaming" [1]. A gust of wind blew the burlap off the sign before the official unveiling, while some residents circulated petitions to switch the name back [1]. Opponents, largely from Noe Valley, said they felt attached to the 140-year-old name, and they put a repeal on the November ballot. With Proposition 187's anti-immigrant politics in the air, it lost by a wide margin [2]. In March 2026, after allegations that Chavez had sexually abused young girls, politicians proposed stripping his name from streets and schools. Leal suggested any new name should honour the movement, "probably Dolores Huerta" [2].

title: The Night the Glass House Shattered
place: Conservatory of Flowers
hook: Gusts of more than 100 mph tore through the park in December 1995, smashing the Victorian greenhouse's glass and shutting it for seven years.
story: The Conservatory of Flowers had already survived two fires [2]. Its worst night came in the second week of December 1995. After torrential rains, gusts of more than 100 mph were reported on December 12 and brought down an estimated 1,000 trees across Golden Gate Park [2]. The Chronicle called the Conservatory the storm's worst casualty. Its glass was smashed and much of the interior lay open to the weather [2]. Accounts of the damage differ: SFist, citing the Chronicle, reports hundreds of broken panes, while Wikipedia says 30,000 were blown out and the dome shattered [1][2]. Wikipedia also says cold air and flying glass killed about 15 percent of the plants, and that a 112-year-old philodendron was one of the hardest to save [1]. The World Monuments Fund added the building to its 1996 watch list [1]. Repairs were first estimated at about $10 million, and the final bill came to $25 million, with support from the Richard & Rhoda Goldman Fund and a public fundraising campaign [1][2]. After seven years the Conservatory reopened in 2003 [2].

title: The Night the Hillside Swallowed a Mansion
place: 125 El Camino del Mar (still an empty lot)
hook: On a December night in 1995, a century-old brick sewer burst under 24th Avenue. By morning, TV cameras were watching a three-storey house fall into a canyon.
story: The storm of December 1995 dropped close to three inches of rain on San Francisco in less than a day. Under 24th Avenue, a six-foot brick sewer about a century old gave way in the early hours of December 11 [1][2]. The water ate the dune sand like "a water hose hitting a sand pile", said city engineer Todd Cockburn [1]. Soon after dawn, the empty 85-year-old house at 125 El Camino del Mar began to tilt. When it fell into the hole, a neighbour said, "it sounded like an avalanche" [1]. The pit grew to 40 feet deep and 250 feet wide. Around two dozen homes were evacuated, among them Ansel Adams's boyhood house, which was left teetering at the edge [2]. Neighbours and state Senator Quentin Kopp blamed the city's new Richmond Transport Tunnel project. Kopp said: "I do not hesitate to say I told you so." Cockburn replied that "the evidence has all washed away" [1]. Crews filled the hole with rubble from the demolished Embarcadero Freeway [3]. In 2024 the lot was still empty [2].

title: Where a buried creek begins
place: Yosemite Marsh, north end of McLaren Park
hook: A tiny eggplant-shaped marsh shelters one of the city's rarest insects, and in 2005 it was quietly silting to death.
story: In a quiet corner at the park's north end, a creek bubbles out of the hillside and tumbles into a small freshwater marsh shaped like an eggplant [1]. This is Yosemite Marsh, the start of a creek that once flowed to the bay and is now buried under homes and streets [2]. The city named it a 'significant natural resource area' in 1995 [1][2]. Rare species live here: the San Francisco forktail damselfly, with its iridescent blue-green body, and the flowering quillwort. Red-winged blackbirds nest in the cattails, and great blue herons hunt gophers in the meadow above [1]. Writing for FoundSF, Pete Holloran calls the marsh home to one of the damselfly's last populations [3]. By 2005, silt from the creek's collapsing banks was turning the marsh into a muddy pond. The city set aside $304,000 to save it. Engineers offered competing fixes, and so did Belles Yelda, a retired civil engineer in Friends of McLaren Park. The group's president, Franco Mancini, doubted any of them would work. 'Everyone is flying blind,' he said. 'It's like designing a building with blindfolds on' [1].

title: From Biker Bar to Brewpub
place: Beach Chalet, 1000 Great Highway
hook: Fifty Harleys out front and chairs flying through windows under priceless WPA frescoes: the Beach Chalet had a rough middle age before a student's business plan saved it.
story: Willis Polk's Spanish-style Beach Chalet opened on May 30, 1925 [2]. In 1936 and 1937 Lucien Labaudt covered its lobby with WPA frescoes of Depression-era San Francisco [2]. After the Army used the building in the Second World War, the city leased it to the Veterans of Foreign Wars for $50 a month [1]. For a time it was a rough bikers' bar, and hurled bottles damaged the frescoes and Moorish tiles. "I remember driving past here and seeing maybe 50 Harleys parked out front and chairs flying out the window," recalled Donna Ernstson of the Friends of Recreation & Parks [1]. The VFW left in 1979 after the city raised the rent to $500. The padlocked building drew feral cats and squatters who nearly burned it down [1]. Then Gar Truppelli cycled past on his mountain bike. As a San Francisco State senior in 1993, he wrote the business plan for a brewpub there, and he and his wife Lara won the 20-year lease against four other bidders [1]. After a $6.7 million restoration, which also restored the murals, the Beach Chalet Brewery and Restaurant opened on New Year's Eve 1996 [1][2].

title: The Alligator of Mountain Lake
place: Mountain Lake, southern edge of the Presidio
hook: In 1996 an abandoned pet alligator outwitted rangers, zookeepers, two rival newspapers and a hired Florida gator hunter for more than two months.
story: In the summer of 1996, a retired architect and birdwatcher, Dan Bushnell, 72, said he had twice seen an alligator with 'pop-up eyes' swimming in Mountain Lake [1]. It seemed to be a dumped pet, and it became a sensation. The Chronicle flew in a professional hunter from Florida. The rival Examiner sent its executive editor, Phil Bronstein, and a reporter in wetsuits to 'protect' the reptile, but police stopped them at the water's edge, citing a rule against swimming in the lake [2]. Examiner readers voted to name it 'Golden Gator', ahead of 'Van Nessie' and 'Presidio Domingo'. A Texas radio station played updates set to a rewritten 'Crocodile Rock' [2]. On 8 October, zoo associate curator John Aikin finally caught the 3-foot-2-inch male with a fishing pole and $1.47 worth of supermarket fish [2][3]. That December the zoo threw a farewell party, with a cake reading 'Best of luck', before flying him to a Louisiana preserve [3]. The gator was a sign of deeper trouble. Neighbours already complained that golf-course contaminants and litter were fouling the once-clear lake [1]. In November 2014 the Presidio Trust used a rotenone-based chemical to wipe out the invasive fish that had plagued it for years [4].

title: The Internet's Memory in an Army Building
place: Internet Archive, 116 Sheridan Avenue (Main Post)
hook: For years, the project trying to save a copy of the entire web worked out of an old Army building on the Presidio's Main Post.
story: Brewster Kahle's dream was what he called 'a Library of Alexandria for the internet'. In the 1990s he began sending out programs called crawlers to take snapshots of every page on the web [1]. The nonprofit he founded, the Internet Archive, described itself in 2002 as 'founded in 1996 and located in the Presidio of San Francisco'. Its mission was to build an 'Internet library' so that born-digital culture would not vanish into what computer scientist Danny Hillis called our 'digital dark age' [2]. It pointed out that many early films had been recycled for their silver, which captures the worry behind the whole project [2]. Its address was 116 Sheridan Avenue, a building on the Main Post of the former Army base. The Archive told visitors its Presidio facilities were open to the public on most Friday afternoons, and it recommended printing a map of the Presidio to find them [3]. Archived copies of that same contact page show the move: by 2010 the headquarters address had changed to 300 Funston Avenue, a former church in the Richmond District [3][1]. Many of the web pages the Archive saved are available to anyone through its Wayback Machine [1].

title: A Castro's house joins the gay center
place: Fallon Building and SF LGBT Center, 1800 Market Street
hook: The founders of San Francisco's gay community center planned to demolish an 1894 Victorian. Gay preservationists fought back. The house had been built by a member of the Castro family.
story: The Victorian at Market and Octavia was built in 1894 by Carmel Fallon, born into the prominent Californio Castro family [1]. She had married Thomas Fallon, a Bear Flag Revolt veteran and later mayor of San Jose. According to the landmark account, she caught him with the maid, divorced him, and invested her settlement in San Francisco real estate [1]. Her building is the only survivor of its row on this stretch of Market. The 1906 fire took the buildings to its east, and development later took those to the west [1]. In December 1996, leaders of a proposed gay and lesbian community center bought the site. In 1997 their board voted 'not to use' the battered house after the architects estimated that renovating it would cost $1.6 to $2.6 million [2]. A coalition of gay activists and preservationists rallied to save it and collected more than 1,000 signatures [2]. The Chronicle pointed out the irony: a gay center was about to demolish a house built by a Castro, a name that had come to symbolize the gay movement around the world [2]. The house survived. It became city Landmark No. 223, and it is now part of the San Francisco LGBT Community Center, which opened in March 2002 [1][3].

title: A naval base becomes a neighbourhood
place: Former Navy housing, Avenue H area, Treasure Island
hook: When the sailors left in 1997, their houses went partly to families climbing out of homelessness. 'Everybody you see in the world, you see on the island here.'
story:
Naval Station Treasure Island officially closed on September 30, 1997 [1]. San Francisco soon let civilians move into the old Navy housing. It set aside 375 units for vulnerable people, including those with a history of homelessness [1]. An organisation founded in 1994 to plan for them, the Treasure Island Homeless Development Initiative, now One Treasure Island, still runs food pantries, job training and services [1]. In 1998 the Department of Labor opened a Job Corps centre on 35 acres, and the Life Learning Academy charter high school opened [1].

It remains one of the city's poorest ZIP codes. About half of its more than 2,000 residents live below the poverty line [1]. In 2009 Mayor Gavin Newsom agreed a deal with the Navy that could be worth more than $105 million to transfer the island and remake it as a model of sustainable development [2]. Redevelopment plans call for 8,000 homes, including 2,173 below-market-rate or affordable units [1].

In oral histories, residents describe a close community. 'Everybody you see in the world, you see on the island here,' said Atta Pilram. Ishmael Wesley and his son Jahfari were the first father and son to graduate from the construction training programme [3].

title: From a Burned Hotel to Bayanihan House
place: Bayanihan House and Community Center (former Delta Hotel), Sixth and Mission streets
hook: A deadly fire gutted Sixth Street's most prominent hotel, home to Filipino veterans. The community turned the ruin into its headquarters.
story: In 1997 a fire killed one person and left the Delta Hotel in ruins. It was the most prominent building on the Sixth Street corridor [2], and many Filipino veterans of the Second World War had lived there [1]. Owner Dr. Mario Borja negotiated with the neighbourhood housing group TODCO to buy the site. Filipino American leaders already planned to open a centre for Central City immigrants there [1][2]. TODCO used Redevelopment Agency funds to buy the building. In 2003 it reopened as Bayanihan House, named for the Tagalog word for community spirit. It had 152 residential hotel rooms with kitchenettes [2]. In 2005 the Filipino-American Development Foundation opened the Bayanihan Community Center on the ground floor, serving immigrant families and seniors [1][2]. The building became the anchor of a wider fight. As the second tech boom pushed rents up, community groups said the neighbourhood's Filipino population had been cut in half in ten years. In 2016 the city recognised SOMA Pilipinas as its Filipino Cultural Heritage District, a move organisers described as a way to protect the community and its culture from displacement [1].

title: Records where the bowling pins fell
place: Amoeba Music, 1855 Haight Street
hook: Why is the world's most famous independent record store so wide? Because it used to be a bowling alley, and the "Bowling" sign is still on the roof.
story: Amoeba Music began on Telegraph Avenue in Berkeley in 1990. For about a year before its San Francisco opening, the owners stockpiled records for a second store at the Stanyan end of Haight Street [1]. When the doors opened on November 15, 1997, the line went around the block. "We had a huge, huge day," partner Joe Goldmark remembered [1]. The building was the former Park Bowl, a 24,000-square-foot bowling alley. That explains the long, wide sales floor, and the old "Bowling" marquee still stands on top [1][2]. The pin machines, Goldmark said, all ended up in Hong Kong and Taiwan [1]. Its 1990s rivals were Tower Records and Virgin Megastore. Goldmark credits Amoeba's survival to used stock: broke locals traded in old LPs for cash, and when vinyl came back those trade-ins paid off [1]. Elvis Costello, the Raconteurs and Lana Del Rey have played in-store [1]. It regularly stocks more than 100,000 CDs, records and cassettes [2].

title: The City Auctions Its Tallest Cross
place: Mount Davidson Cross (0.38-acre private parcel)
hook: Courts ruled that a city-owned cross broke the separation of church and state. The fix was an auction, and Armenian Americans won it for $26,000.
story:
In 1990 the American Civil Liberties Union, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and the American Jewish Congress sued the city over its ownership of the Mount Davidson cross, arguing that a religious symbol on public land was unconstitutional [1]. The federal courts agreed, and in 1997 the Supreme Court rejected the city's appeal [1].

The settlement put the cross itself up for auction. On July 21, 1997, a 0.38-acre parcel around the cross was sold to the highest bidder, the Council of Armenian American Organizations of Northern California, for $26,000 [1][2]. On November 4 voters approved the sale by a wide margin with Proposition F [2]. The council has kept the cross as a memorial to Armenians killed under Ottoman rule, and signs on the surrounding public parkland remind visitors of the separation of church and state [1].

Two members of American Atheists argued that the city had stacked the bidding to guarantee the cross would survive. The Supreme Court declined their appeal in April 2003, ending a 13-year legal fight [1]. The council's bronze genocide plaque was stolen in 2007 [2].

title: The Peep Show That Joined a Union
place: Lusty Lady, 1033 Kearny St
hook: Tired of hidden cameras and random firings, the dancers behind the glass on Kearny Street organized, won a contract, and later bought the business.
story: At the Lusty Lady, 1033 Kearny Street, dancers performed behind glass for customers who paid by the minute [1]. In 1996 they started organising, angry about arbitrary firings, pay cuts, and one-way windows that let customers secretly photograph and film them [1][2]. Management fought back with lawyers, propaganda and a two-day lockout, but the workers voted 57 to 15 to join Service Employees International Union Local 790, forming the Exotic Dancers Union [1][2]. In April 1997 about 100 strippers, bouncers, cashiers and janitors ratified a first contract: pay of $12 to $25 an hour, grievance procedures, a sick day, and the removal of the one-way mirrors [2]. "They're tough, and they don't like injustice," said union representative Stephanie Batey, as calls poured in from dancers in Texas, Kansas and Massachusetts [2]. When the owners announced in 2003 that they would close, the workers bought the business and ran it as a cooperative [1]. It lasted another decade. After the co-op missed a rent payment, the landlord would not negotiate, and the country's only unionised, dancer-run peep show closed on September 2, 2013, which was Labor Day [3].

title: The Pigeon Lady flies home to Estonia
place: 1329 Sanchez Street, near Cesar Chavez
hook: Hundreds of pigeons lined the wires waiting for Anna Muru. A court order stopped her feeding them, but her farewell party drew more people than birds.
story: For years Anna Muru made her rounds of Noe Valley streets dropping birdseed from her coat pockets, while hundreds of pigeons waited on the wires overhead [1][2]. Neighbours whose roofs were being slimed complained, and the Voice covered the feud from 1988 on [1]. In the fall of 1996 a group of mostly homeowners won a restraining order barring the 84-year-old from feeding birds on the street [1]. Her supporters saw something else. One neighbour traced her compulsion to the Second World War, when she had been a homeless, parentless, starving teenager in an Estonia overrun by Nazis and Soviets [1]. In the spring of 1997 she sold her dilapidated, feather-coated Victorian at 1329 Sanchez. It drew 17 bids and sold to an East Bay developer for $241,000, well above the asking price of $199,000 [1]. That money paid for her return to Estonia, which she had not seen in 50 years [1][2]. At a sidewalk farewell party on May 10 she danced to a swing band. 'They were right too in a way,' she admitted of her critics. 'I did get carried away with the birds.' She flew home on May 19 with her cat, Zsa Zsa [1].

title: 'We can do that': saving the egrets
place: Mission Creek Park, south bank of Mission Creek
hook: When developers planned to armour Mission Creek with broken concrete, houseboaters spent $30,000 of their own money on newspaper ads: 'Catellus must be stopped.'
story: Houseboaters and conservationists formed the Mission Creek Conservancy in 1983 and published Vanished Waters, a history of Mission Bay, in 1986 to prove the railyards were not a blank slate [1]. The 1991 development plan promised an eight-acre wetland, but it died when Catellus pulled out in 1995 [1]. In 1998 an environmental report revealed plans to line the creek's banks with rip-rap. The Conservancy bought third-page ads in the Examiner and Chronicle declaring 'Catellus must be stopped'. The $30,000 bill, its biggest expense ever, was paid by its board members [1]. Catellus's new vice president, Doug Gardner, called a meeting. Conservancy president Bob Isaacson told him they had 'charismatic shorebirds' and wanted to keep them. 'He looked me in the eye and said, “we can do that”,' Isaacson recalled, 'and for the next decade he was steadfast' [1]. Native plants were replanted along the banks. Residents now report herring runs, sea lions, bat rays, seals and even porpoises [1]. Mayor Willie Brown appointed houseboaters Jack Davis and Corinne Woods to the citizens' advisory committee [2].

title: Fifteen seconds to erase Geneva Towers
place: Former Geneva Towers site, now Kelloch and Velasco Mini Park and housing
hook: Police dodged bowling balls thrown from the balconies. Tenants held a candlelight vigil. Then 600 pounds of explosives brought the towers down.
story: By 1991 conditions at Geneva Towers were so bad that the federal housing department (HUD) took the complex over. It was the first time the agency had foreclosed on a property because it was unsafe [1]. "The post office would not deliver on site. Pizza parlors would not deliver," recalled former mayor Art Agnos [1]. Police approaching the towers braced for rocks, televisions and once a bowling ball thrown from the balconies [1]. Still, many tenants called it home. Days before the demolition, former residents held a candlelight vigil. "It was like a little, small community," said Lela Jones [1]. Marie Harrison, a former resident, argued that the towers' bad reputation was unfair to the people living there: "The stigma always fell on the tenants" [2]. At 2:30 p.m. on May 16, 1998, 600 pounds of explosives brought the two towers down in what the Chronicle called the biggest implosion California had seen [1]. Onlookers brought barbecue grills and kegs of beer [2]. HUD promised a 341-unit replacement complex [1]. Today the site holds the Kelloch and Velasco Mini Park, low-income housing and senior homes [1][3]. Former residents still gather for a reunion every Fourth of July weekend [3].

title: A Bridge Footing That Became a Marsh
place: Heron's Head Park (former Pier 98)
hook: Pier 98 was built from rubble for a bay crossing that never came. Shorebirds moved in first, and eventually the city gave up and made it a park.
story: In the 1970s trucks dumped fill on the Port's southern waterfront to build an industrial pier. Later it was planned as the footing for a new span across the bay [1]. Both plans fell through and years of arguing followed. Some people wanted all the fill taken out, but the port warned that removal would cost millions and leave a big hole in the shoreline [1]. Meanwhile birdwatchers noticed that as the loose fill settled, tidal pools were forming and migrating birds were arriving [1]. In 1998 crews cleared some 5,000 tons of debris and dug a winding channel to let the tides into a salt marsh. The 25-acre park, which looks like a heron's head from above, opened in 1999 [1]. Hunters Point schoolchildren planted native species, and by 2004 at least 68 native varieties grew there, next door to a working power plant and cargo pier [1]. In 2010 Literacy for Environmental Justice prepared to open its EcoCenter in the park. About 400 young people helped plan it. It was the first building in the city to run completely off the grid, and it treats its own wastewater on site [2].

title: A campus built on a patent fight
place: Genentech Hall, UCSF Mission Bay, 600 16th Street
hook: The first research building on UCSF's new Mission Bay campus was paid for partly by the company the university had sued over human growth hormone.
story: In 1990 the University of California sued Genentech, claiming the biotech pioneer's human growth hormone drug infringed a UC patent covering genetic material from UCSF labs [1][2]. A 1999 jury upheld the patent but deadlocked on infringement, and a second trial was set for January 2000 [1][2]. On November 19, 1999, the two sides settled instead. Genentech agreed to pay $150 million, plus $50 million toward the first biological sciences research building on Mission Bay, which the press release called 'a new 43-acre research and teaching campus'. The building would carry a name Genentech proposed [1]. The deal admitted no wrongdoing. Genentech chief Arthur Levinson, himself a former UCSF postdoc, said the company wanted to avoid 'another jury trial covering complex patent issues' [1]. Under UC patent policy, the three inventors and two collaborators were to share roughly $85 million [1]. The result was Genentech Hall, which was under construction by late 1999: the first building of a campus that would turn old railyards into a biomedical research district [3].

title: What a Drag: Finocchio's Final Bow
place: Finocchio's, 506 Broadway
hook: For 63 years tourists climbed the stairs above Broadway to see men in spangled gowns. Then the rent went up.
story: For 63 years, tourists and locals climbed to Finocchio's at 506 Broadway, above what became Enrico's cafe, to watch men in spangled gowns sing, dance and crack bawdy jokes [1][2]. Joe Finocchio, who had worked in his father's Prohibition speakeasy, got the idea at his own Stockton Street speakeasy when a tipsy customer did a dead-on Sophie Tucker. He moved the show to Broadway in 1936 and was promptly raided [1][2]. The emcee Carroll Wallace opened each show with: "In New York, Mr. Ziegfeld glorified the American girl ... Here at Finocchio's, we glorify the American boy" [2]. Headliners included Lucien Phelps, a Sophie Tucker specialist for 27 years, and the 6-foot-5 Don McLean, known on stage as Lori Shannon, who played Archie Bunker's drag queen friend on All in the Family [1]. Bob Hope and Tallulah Bankhead came, and Gray Line buses unloaded crowds night after night [1]. By 1999 the buses had stopped. When the landlord raised the rent from $4,000 to $6,000 a month, Eve Finocchio, who had run the club since Joe's death in 1986, announced it would close on November 27 [1]. Lawrence Ferlinghetti's three-word eulogy: "What a drag" [1].

title: A Bookstore Declared a Landmark
place: City Lights Bookstore, 261 Columbus Ave
hook: As dot-com money swept through San Francisco, the Beats' old bookstore got protection usually given to buildings, not businesses.
story: By 2000 the dot-com boom was sending rents soaring, and City Lights, the bookstore Lawrence Ferlinghetti had opened in 1953, was feeling it. Ferlinghetti said a computer company had tried to push the store out by making the building's owners a huge offer [2]. San Franciscans rallied behind the shop. In June 2000 a city advisory board unanimously backed landmark status for its 1907 building, which would make it hard to demolish [1]. The Daily Telegraph reported that this was the first time landmark status had been offered to a business rather than just a building, in recognition of its "cultural value" [2]. "Being recognized as a landmark is sort of a bulwark against the dumbing down of America," Ferlinghetti said [1]. His co-owner Nancy Peters warned, "The old San Francisco is under attack to the point where it's disappearing" [2]. It was a fitting fight for a store whose founder had been arrested in 1957 for selling Allen Ginsberg's "Howl" [1]. The city designated it Landmark No. 228 in 2001 [3]. The shop outlasted the boom, and Ferlinghetti marked his 100th birthday in March 2019 with a new novel [4].

title: A Real Library for Ocean View
place: Ocean View Branch Library, 345 Randolph Street
hook: For years Ocean View's library was one room with a glass storefront and a toilet too small for a child. In 2000 the neighbourhood finally got a real one.
story: Ocean View's was the 15th branch of the San Francisco Public Library. The first opened in 1903 on Broad Street near Capitol Avenue [1]. Dorothy Coakley remembered the later one-room branch at Broad and Plymouth. It had a glass storefront, a kitchen that doubled as reference room and community copy centre, and "a bathroom so small that even a single child had trouble fitting into it" [2]. Classes from Sheridan and Jose Ortega elementary schools, 30 children and a teacher at a time, packed in several times a week for stories, sharing the room with seniors, teenagers and merchants. Bassim Al-Abood of Fountains's Pizza was a favourite: he could fold paper animals and hand out pizza samples [2]. The branch held its last New Year's party just before 2000 [2]. Neighbourhood leaders including Lovie and Minnie Ward had fought for a new library [3]. The two-storey branch at 345 Randolph Street, designed by the city's Bureau of Architecture, opened on June 7, 2000. It cost $2.5 million, and private funds paid for its furniture and equipment. It was the first new branch building in San Francisco since 1969 [1].

title: A ballpark on the old warehouse wharf
place: Oracle Park, 24 Willie Mays Plaza
hook: The Giants' new park was the first major-league stadium built without public money since Dodger Stadium, and its brick arches echo the warehouse it replaced.

Ground was broken at China Basin on December 11, 1997, and the $357 million ballpark opened in 2000 as Pacific Bell Park [1][2]. It was the first big-league park built without public funds since Dodger Stadium in 1962, though the city gave a $10 million tax abatement and $80 million in infrastructure, including a Muni extension and a new I-280 ramp [1][2]. Before the Giants, stevedores and switch engines worked this wharf, moving cargo between freighters in China Basin and a warehouse on the site; the right-field wall's arched openings mimic that warehouse's windows [3]. The water beyond became McCovey Cove, named for the Giants' great first baseman [2][3]. The hated Dodgers swept the first three games played there [1]. The name changed to SBC, AT&T and then Oracle Park [2].

title: Give Us a Brake, Said Sea Cliff

hook: Sea Cliff neighbours fed up with speeding cars and tour buses put up their own traffic signs. City Hall cut them down within days.
story: By the late 1990s Sea Cliff's biggest complaint was traffic. In 1998 the newly formed Sea Cliff Residents' Association already had committees on tour buses, parking and the neighbourhood's stone pillars. John Schiffeler of the Sea Cliff Gazette called on residents to stand together against "this onslaught by the tour bus industry" [1]. In 2000, neighbours on West Clay Street got tired of waiting for the city and put up five homemade signs on Lake Street at 22nd and 24th Avenues. They read: "Give Us A Brake. Slow Down. Children at Play." [2] Days later, city traffic engineers came out and cut them down. The acting traffic director explained that such signs were illegal and that the state no longer allowed "children at play" warnings, because it believed they encouraged children to play in the street [2]. Supervisor Gavin Newsom had pushed for lower speed limits and speed humps. "I've ended up doing exactly the opposite of what I set out to do," he said [2]. The Chronicle added that lost tourists wandered past the homes of Robin Williams and Sharon Stone [2].

title: The neighbours who said no to Home Depot
place: Former Schlage Lock site, Bayshore Blvd at Leland Ave
hook: When the valley's biggest employer shut down, a big-box store wanted its land. Residents had other ideas, and they're still waiting to see them built.
story: Ingersoll-Rand, Schlage's owner, closed the Bayshore factory in 1999, ending more than 70 years of lock-making [1]. By 2000 Home Depot wanted to build a store on the empty site [1]. Neighbours fought it over traffic and other worries, and Supervisor Tom Ammiano sponsored legislation that blocked "big box" stores there [1]. Residents then drew up their own plan. A 2002 city-led community plan asked for a grocery store, open space and housing [1]. The site was polluted, though, and for years it was stuck in a lawsuit over contaminated groundwater. In 2008 Ingersoll-Rand settled and handed the 12.3 acres to the developer Universal Paragon [1]. In 2009 the factory buildings came down, all except the original office [2]. One resident noticed that, with the buildings gone, the shapes of San Bruno Mountain and McLaren Ridge could be seen again from Tunnel Avenue [2]. Building has been slow. In 2018 the site was still terraced dirt awaiting nearly 1,700 homes [3]. Russel Morine, who ran a coffee shop on Leland, had predicted in 2011: "I'm pretty sure something will happen … eventually" [4].

title: Where Five LaBountys Ate Thanksgiving
place: 139-141 11th Avenue near California Street
hook: A historian drove his brother past their childhood flat and found it stripped to the frame. Soon their old address no longer existed.
story: In the early 1970s Woody LaBounty's grandmother would walk him and his brother to catch the 21 Hayes at its terminus at Eighth and California, bound for the Emporium downtown [2]. Home was a basement flat at 139 11th Avenue, in a two-unit house that held nine people in 1975 [1]. In 1999 he saw the house listed for $689,000 [1]. A year or so later his brother visited from Seattle, and they drove by. The building had been stripped to its frame; they could see straight through where their apartment had been into a weedy backyard [1]. A woman got out of a car and said she owned it. 'It was a nice place to live,' LaBounty offered. 'Too small,' she replied [1]. When he returned months later, a double garage had replaced the ground-floor flat 'where five LaBountys had eaten Thanksgiving dinners' [1]. The address 139 no longer existed [1]. He guessed the rebuilt house held two or three people, with room for two cars [1]. His essay became a plea to value the ordinary Richmond and Sunset houses that no preservation society fights for [1].

title: A Banker's Free Banjo Festival
place: Hellman Hollow (formerly Speedway Meadow)
hook: A former Lehman Brothers president who took up banjo in his seventies paid for one of America's biggest music festivals and refused to let anyone sponsor it.
story: Warren Hellman had been president of Lehman Brothers at 39 and co-founded the private equity firm Hellman & Friedman [2]. On a ski trip in 2000 he told his friend Jonathan Nelson about his dream of a bluegrass festival in the park [1]. Booker Dawn Holliday warned him that if the bill featured only the music he loved, mainly Hazel Dickens and her songs about coal-mining strikes, "there will be about 13 people there" [1]. The first festival, in 2001, drew perhaps 13,000 people [1]. Hellman paid for it every year, turned down corporate sponsors and kept it free [2][3]. When Emmylou Harris played that first year with her non-bluegrass band, the name slowly shifted, and in 2004 it officially became Hardly Strictly Bluegrass [3]. Hellman got serious about the banjo after 70 and toured with his band, the Wronglers [1][2]. In 2011 more than 600,000 people came, to a meadow supervisors had just renamed for him [1]. He died that December at 77, having arranged for the festival to be funded for years after his death [1][2].

title: Fifteen pylons for the pink triangle
place: Pink Triangle Park, Market & 17th St
hook: A weedy scrap of city land above the Muni tunnel became America's first memorial to the gay victims of Nazi persecution.
story: Where Castro, Market and 17th Streets meet, there was once a city-owned scrap of land choked with weeds, vines and trash. In June 2001 neighbours from the Eureka Valley Promotion Association held a 'Big Dig' with a city public works crew. In October more than 20 volunteers came back to plant 40 rose bushes and 30 rosemary plants [1]. Artists Robert Bruce and Susan Martin designed the memorial. Bruce had been a founding member of STOP AIDS in 1982 [2]. It is a set of 15 granite pylons, each inlaid with a pink quartz triangle, arranged together into one larger triangle that points toward Harvey Milk Plaza [2]. The stone was cut in Minnesota. The memorial was dedicated on December 10, 2001, the anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights [1][3]. Some later accounts give its opening as 2003 [4]. It is called the first permanent, free-standing memorial in America to the gay men and lesbians persecuted by Nazi Germany [3][4]. The artists wanted visitors to remember the colours the camps assigned: pink triangles for gay men, black triangles for lesbians, yellow stars for Jews [2]. Visitors may take one quartz stone home [3].

title: From Needle Alley to Microbrew Alley
place: 500 block of Haight Street (Toronado, 547 Haight)
hook: At the turn of the millennium, the Chronicle called the Lower Haight the city's underground: beer bars, record shops, DJ nights and a dark bar lit by static.
story: "Lower Haight is to the underground what Upper Haight was 30 years ago," the Chronicle declared in 2001 [1]. The 500 block of Haight Street, once known as Needle Alley, had become Microbrew Alley. On one side was the Toronado, where owner David "Big Daddy" Keene kept a back room lined with hundreds of custom tap handles. Across the street, English fans at the Mad Dog in the Fog watched European football over pints at 6 a.m. [1]. Next door to the Toronado, Noc Noc was lit mostly by old TVs showing static [1]. The strip had five record stores, which supplied the records DJs wheeled into clubs on dollies [1]. At 460 Haight, Nickie's BBQ was one of the Bay Area's oldest destination dance clubs. It hosted Grateful Dead jams by Dark Star Dan on Mondays and Cheb I. Sabbah's global "Outer National Mix" on Tuesdays [1]. Nickie's went back to 1948, when it was Nicki's Barbecue. It was later a dancehall and a dive bar, and from 2007 an Irish sports bar [2]. In 2020 a longtime regular, Tom Mills, bought it. He said he and 20 or 30 other regulars thought of it as "the neighborhood's living room" [2].

title: Lantern on the Hill Finds a Keeper
place: Chinese Historical Society of America, former Chinatown YWCA, 965 Clay St
hook: Julia Morgan designed it with dragons on the floor and Chinese towers on the roof. After the 1989 earthquake it stood empty for years before historians moved in.
story: The Chinatown YWCA began in 1916 in an old saloon at Stockton and Sacramento [1]. For its new home on Clay Street, the YWCA hired Julia Morgan, who worked closely with a Chinese American committee [1]. Her 1932 building mixed Western and Chinese design: a courtyard with a koi pond, three Chinese-style towers, glazed tiles with Chinese motifs and a dragon painted on the corridor floor. It also kept white and Chinese American residents apart under one roof [1][2]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the building, and the YWCA could not afford to retrofit it, so it sold up [1]. The Chinese Historical Society of America, founded in 1963 by Thomas W. Chinn, C.H. Kwock, Chingwah Lee, H.K. Wong and Thomas W.S. Wu, had moved from a small donated building on Adler Place to Commercial Street and Broadway [1]. With help from Supervisor Tom Hsieh and Mayor Willie Brown it bought the building in 1996, and in 2001 it opened its museum there [1]. The building had sat unused for 14 years [2]. In 2004 the restoration of the "Lantern on the Hill" won a National Preservation Honor Award from the National Trust [2].

title: Let the Dog Out!
place: Doggie Diner head, Sloat Boulevard median at 45th Avenue
hook: The last grinning fiberglass dachshund survived a developer, a two-year fight and an April Fool's Day nosedive onto Sloat Boulevard. Then it became an official city landmark.
story: Doggie Diner ran from 1948 to 1986 and grew to about 30 hot dog stands. Each had a fiberglass dachshund head in a chef's hat and bow tie, sketched by billboard designer Harold Bachman in the early 1960s [1]. The last head in San Francisco stood on a pole above a former Doggie Diner on Sloat Boulevard that had become the Carousel restaurant. When the Sloat Garden Center, which owned the property, wanted to clear the site, fans gathered thousands of signatures and held eat-ins. Bill Griffith drew the fight into his Zippy the Pinhead strip. The city took ownership of the head after two years of campaigning [1]. Then, on April Fool's Day 2001, a windstorm blew it off its rusted pole and smashed its nose [1][2]. John Law remembers Ed Lee, then head of Public Works and later mayor, sweating at the scene in the cold ocean wind [1]. Public Works recast the snout from a head lent by Burning Man co-founder John Law. The Art Commission consulted Bachman to match the original candy-apple red [2]. On June 30, 2001, about 400 devotees chanted "Let the dog out!" as a crane lifted the hood [2]. It became a city landmark in 2006 and now stands on the Sloat median at 45th Avenue [1].

title: Peeling Back an Airfield to Find a Marsh
place: Crissy Field tidal marsh
hook: In 1999 a channel was cut through the sand, and for the first time in about a century the bay's tides flowed back into Crissy Field.
story: Crissy Field sits on the site of an ancient 130-acre salt marsh where Ohlone people once gathered fish and shellfish. The Army treated it as a wasteland to be dumped on and drained, and later built an airfield on the filled land [1]. When the Park Service took over in 1994, the site was 'a derelict concrete wasteland' [1]. From 1997, crews removed almost 90,000 tons of contaminated material. Between 1998 and 2000 they rebuilt an 18-acre tidal marsh and 16 acres of dunes, digging out more than 230,000 cubic yards of dirt, sand and mud [1]. In November 1999 a channel was opened, and fresh and salt water met there for the first time in 100 years [1]. The Haas family's Haas, Jr. Fund had paid for early planning in 1986. In 1997 the fund and Colleen and Robert Haas pledged $18 million, then the largest cash gift in National Park Service history. In all, the community raised more than $34.5 million [2]. Crissy Field reopened in 2001, and the Crissy Field Center opened that May to bring in young people with little access to national parks [2][3]. Nearly 100 bird species have since been recorded using the marsh [1].

title: A buried creek and a hubcap garden
place: Cotter Street near San Jose Avenue (neighbourhood garden lot described in 2002)
hook: Under Cayuga Avenue runs the south fork of Islais Creek. In 2002 an artist tracked it to a flooded lot full of geese, hubcaps and vegetables.
story: While researching the Balboa Park area for a city planning project, public artist and historian Ann Chamberlain found a 1926 photograph of a railroad bed with a creek running beside it. "What happened to the water?" she wondered [1]. The railroad bed turned out to be today's Alemany Boulevard. The creek was the south fork of Islais Creek, sometimes called the Cayuga River, which runs in a culvert under Cayuga Avenue [1]. Neighbours could hear it through the storm drains, and in the rainy season it squelched underfoot [1]. Its headwaters lie beneath Cayuga Park at the far end of the avenue [2]. Near Cotter Street, behind a plank fence, Chamberlain showed a Chronicle reporter a block-long vacant lot that neighbours had made into a park. It was private land but had no 'keep out' signs. There was hubcap art on the fence, a horseshoe pit, geese in a pen, and vegetable gardens around a circular path [1]. A yellow traffic sign on the fence read "FLOODED". "That's why there is this strange piece of land," she said. "It probably flooded and they couldn't build on it" [1].

title: Boy Scouts Mark the End of the Road
place: Western Terminus of the Lincoln Highway marker, Legion of Honor parking area
hook: America's first coast-to-coast highway starts in Times Square and ends beside a bus stop at the Legion of Honor. Two Boy Scout troops marked the spot, 74 years apart.
story: The Lincoln Highway, dreamed up by Carl Fisher in 1912–13, ran about 3,300 miles from Times Square to Lincoln Park, where its western terminus was dedicated in 1915 [1][2]. In 1925 the new numbered federal highways broke it into pieces [2]. As one of its last acts, the Lincoln Highway Association had Boy Scouts set roughly 2,440 concrete markers along the route on 1 September 1928. Each carried a bronze Lincoln medallion [2]. A San Francisco troop set the one reading 'Western Terminus of the Lincoln Highway' here [1]. The old highway was split among numbered routes, and Interstate 80 later followed much of it [1][2]. The association re-formed in 1992 to preserve the route [2]. On 14 June 2002 San Francisco's Boy Scout Troop 17 set a replica marker a few feet from the original spot [1]. In 2005 the association's California chapter added an interpretive sign. It tells how a young Lt. Col. Dwight Eisenhower crossed on the 1919 Army convoy, and how as president he signed the 1956 Interstate Highway Act [1]. An original 1928 marker survives nearby at 32nd Avenue and El Camino del Mar [2].

title: Collard Greens on a Dumping Ground

In early 2002 Annette Smith and Karl Paige dug up the earth and planted collard greens and flowers [1][2]. Neighbours brought plants from their own backyards. Jeffrey Betcher joined them, and after a community meeting in 2003 the group became the Quesada Gardens Initiative [2]. By 2006 the whole length of the median was a vegetable and flower garden [1], and the project grew to six community gardens, two murals and a weekly newsletter [2]. "People respond differently to everything when they're on a block where they have a sense that people know one another," Betcher said [2]. Paige died in 2007 and Smith moved off the block in 2009. The neighbours who took over still look after the garden the two of them started [1]. Photographs from August 2007 show the median in full growth [3].

title: Laughing Sal Moves to the Wharf
place: Musée Mécanique, Shed A, Pier 45
hook: Evicted from the Cliff House, a century-old arcade of fortune tellers and cackling automatons found a new home among Fisherman's Wharf fish sheds.
story: For nearly a century, coin-operated amusement machines had whirred and clicked at the Cliff House, on the city's far western edge [1]. "All we have to offer here," said manager Dan Zelinsky, "is a good time" [1]. The machines found a new home on the other side of the city, in Shed A on Pier 45 at Fisherman's Wharf [2][3]. The collection had begun with Zelinsky's father, who started collecting at 11 and filled the family's basement near the Presidio [3]. Today visitors feed coins to Laughing Sal, the gap-toothed cackler from Playland at the Beach, to a Ferris wheel made of toothpicks by San Quentin inmates, and to a Wurlitzer organ first installed in a Tennessee merry-go-round in 1917, which Zelinsky, gliding between machines on roller skates, oils himself [2][3]. When the pandemic shut the doors in March 2020, the museum asked the public for $250,000, "or one million quarters," to get through a year [3].

title: Ocean View Park's Promise, Ninety Years Late
place: OceanView Village, 3995 Alemany Boulevard
hook: A 1910s brochure hailed "The Gem of Subdivisions" and promised business lots. The shops finally came in 2002, and a Korean supermarket in 2021.
story: In the 1910s J.W. Wright & Co. sold lots in "Ocean View Park", which it called "The Gem of Subdivisions in San Francisco." The brochure tied the venture, somewhat mysteriously, to the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition, and promised that "Business streets will also develop here" [1]. They didn't. The Ocean Shore Railway cut across the plat on two diagonals, and later Brotherhood Way split it with a gully. Apart from four or five homes from the brochure's era, including two cottages on Belle Avenue near the city line, the tract was built up in the 1930s, without so much as a corner grocery [1]. By early 2002, a new housing and shopping complex, OceanView Village, was rising in the niche between Highway 280, Highway 1, the Daly City BART station and Alemany Boulevard. It promised apartments, a Rite Aid and an Albertsons [1]. In April 2021 the Korean grocery chain H Mart opened its first San Francisco store there, at 3995 Alemany Boulevard. By 2022 it had leased a neighbouring former 24 Hour Fitness to expand its food court [2].

title: The Last Day of Shouting on Pine Street
place: Pacific Stock Exchange, 301 Pine Street
hook: For more than a century San Francisco had a trading floor where brokers shouted orders face to face. Computers ended it, and the floor became a gym.
story: Brokers had traded in San Francisco since the San Francisco Stock and Bond Exchange was founded in 1882 to handle deals tied to the Comstock Lode. In 1956 it merged with the Los Angeles Oil Exchange to form the Pacific Coast Stock Exchange, which traded from this 1915 former U.S. Treasury building, remodelled in 1930 by Miller & Pflueger with Art Deco granite figures by Ralph Stackpole [1]. Ironically, it was among the first exchanges to automate, putting computers on the floor in 1969 [1]. By 1999 the Chronicle reported that the exchange planned to abandon Pine Street, leaving the city without a central stock market for the first time in more than a century; with most trades done by computer, a floor of traders scurrying from post to post was obsolete [2]. "The floor is jazz, the adrenaline in your body," said independent floor broker Frank Gallagher. "I'm not looking forward to sitting in an office. I like my little world" [2]. The exchange sold its equities business in 2000, closed its Los Angeles floor in 2001 and its San Francisco floor in 2002 [1]. The trading hall later reopened as an Equinox fitness club [3].

title: The women's building taken back in court
place: Japanese YWCA / Issei Women's Building, 1830 Sutter Street
hook: Issei women paid for this Julia Morgan building but weren't allowed to own it. Seventy years later, their community sued to get it back.
story: In 1912, Issei women barred from key facilities of the main YWCA founded the first independent Japanese YWCA in the United States [1]. They raised money for a building at 1830 Sutter Street, designed by Julia Morgan, who donated her services and brought antiques from Hearst's San Simeon to decorate it. It opened in 1932 and even had a Noh theatre stage [2]. California's Alien Land Law barred Issei from owning property, so the women asked the San Francisco YWCA to hold the title in trust for the Japanese American community [1]. In 1996 the YWCA, short of money, put the building up for sale for $1.65 million and denied there had ever been a trust [2]. In 1997 Soko Bukai, a group of Japanese American churches, sued, inspired by the campaign for redress for the camps [1][2]. A settlement in February 2002 gave title to Nihonmachi Little Friends, a community child care centre [2]. The building was listed on the National Register in 2020 and is also a San Francisco landmark [1][3].

title: Why the Tutoring Centre Sells Peg Legs
place: 826 Valencia and the Pirate Supply Store, 826 Valencia St
hook: The zoning said the storefront had to sell something. Dave Eggers decided it would sell glass eyes, beard trimmings and planks for pirates.
story: In 2002 the author Dave Eggers and teacher Nínive Calegari leased a space on Valencia Street and hung a sign: "Free Tutoring. Mops. A Pufferfish." [1] The idea was free one-on-one writing help for children, especially those whose parents worked several jobs or did not speak English [2]. The lease came with a catch: zoning required part of the space to be used for retail [2]. Eggers's answer was a pirate supply store selling drawers of glass eyes, peg legs and beard trimmings, "because not all pirates can grow their own," as the store manager said with a straight face [2]. By 2007 the shop had taken $227,000 in a year, and chapters elsewhere copied the trick with superhero, space-travel and secret-agent stores [2]. Eggers told Forbes that writing is "a craft, not thunderbolts and lightning" [2]. The organisation named after its address opened more San Francisco centres and helped launch the national 826 network in 2008 [1].

title: Padlocked on Labor Day weekend
place: Former Real Food Company, 3939 24th Street
hook: Workers at a beloved health-food store asked for a living wage. Days later the doors were chained, and the building stayed dark for years.
story: Kimball and Jane Allen opened the Real Food Company on 24th Street in 1970. In 2002 they sold it to Fresh Organics, a subsidiary of the Utah supplement maker Nutraceutical [1]. In 2003 the staff began organising with the Industrial Workers of the World and asked for a living wage, better equipment and a say in running the store [1]. On Thursday, August 28, the workers on shift were told the store was closing immediately. Shoppers arrived for the Labor Day weekend to find the doors chained and padlocked, and about 30 workers lost their jobs [1][2]. The company said it was a remodel. The ex-workers called it union-busting and filed charges [1]. In 2005 a National Labor Relations Board judge ruled for them on nearly all counts, and a board panel upheld that in 2007 [2]. In 2009 a settlement awarded $371,219 in back pay and interest, but no reinstatement [2]. The building sat empty. Peter Gabel later said the company kept it closed for 15 years [3]. The anger also built something: neighbours started a farmers' market that grew into the Noe Valley Town Square [3].

title: Palm Trees for a Tired Avenue
place: Ocean Avenue at Jules Avenue
hook: Within a month of Dan Weaver moving to the Ingleside in 1978, Ocean Avenue lost its only grocery and its movie palace. He spent years helping bring it back.
story: When Dan Weaver moved to Jules Street in 1978, Ocean Avenue's only grocery store and the El Rey Theatre closed within a month. The street, he said, "looked like a place that was coming undone" [1]. It had been a busy local shopping street: the 1956 merchants' directory listed seven groceries and bakeries, four drug stores, six beauty parlours and barbers, twelve dry-goods shops and thirteen service businesses [2]. Weaver helped found the Ocean Avenue Renaissance Committee. It linked the "front-lawn neighborhoods" north of Ocean with the grid streets of the Ingleside. "We [had] a dozen trees in a mile," he said. "We needed at least a hundred more" [1]. The roadway and streetcar tracks were being rebuilt, and in the late 1990s government money was available. The plan brought better pedestrian access, blue-tinted streetlights and palm trees, which were in the ground by May 2003 [1]. There were neighbourhood battles over details, but everyone agreed something was needed [1]. In April 2005 history panels went up in 29 Ocean Avenue storefronts, from a donut shop to a hobby store, for a month-long OMI History Walk [3].

title: Refugees remake a corner as Little Saigon
place: Little Saigon, Larkin St between Eddy and O'Farrell
hook: Fleeing war and refugee camps, Southeast Asian families filled Tenderloin studios in the 1980s. Two decades later, the city made their Larkin Street official.
story: From the late 1970s thousands of refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos arrived in San Francisco, and the Tenderloin's cheap rents made it their main landing place [1]. Suddenly a neighbourhood with no playgrounds and corner stores selling 'lots of liquor but little fresh food' was home to large families squeezed into studios [1]. Community networks helped families open markets selling vegetables, meat and Asian ingredients, followed by dozens of Vietnamese, Chinese and Cambodian restaurants [1]. In September 2003 the Board of Supervisors unanimously named the two blocks of Larkin Street between Eddy and O'Farrell 'Little Saigon' [2]. About 80 percent of the businesses there were Vietnamese American-owned, from Tammy Pham's Kim Cuong Jewelry to Saigon Sandwiches, where Hang Nguyen made about 400 sandwiches a day [2]. 'Not even San Jose, with its large Vietnamese population, has a Little Saigon,' said task force member Phu Nguyen [2]. Green-and-yellow 'Sai Gon Nho' banners went up. In 2008 two pillars topped with marble ky linh, a mythical creature, rose at Larkin and Eddy as a gateway [2][3].

title: The bear that made a classroom
place: Balboa High School, 1 Balhi Court (Cayuga Avenue side)
hook: Balboa High's rivals were thrown together on camping trips. One night in Yosemite a bear raided their food, and a loner finally found her crew.
story: By the mid-1990s Balboa High drew students from some of San Francisco's poorest neighbourhoods, and ethnic rivalries ran high [1]. In 1995 two young teachers started an after-school 'Unity Club' that took students into the wilderness at weekends. They were history teacher Conrad Benedicto, who came from the Philippines at 13 and grew up near Balboa, and literature teacher Ken Gonzalez [1]. Science teacher Diana Theriault joined them. By 2000 the club had become the Wilderness Arts and Literacy Collaborative (WALC), a two-year program linking US history, literature and environmental science to trips to Mount Lassen, Joshua Tree and Lake Tahoe [1][2]. WALC students ran the school's paper recycling and spent two days a month planting and repairing McLaren Park [1]. Sierra magazine followed the class of 2003. One student, Ashley, had been moved into WALC against her will and kept to herself. On a spring trip to Yosemite she woke to heavy breathing outside her tent, but nobody believed her. The next night a mother bear and her cub raided the camp's bear box. Classmates sympathised, teachers apologised, and for the first time she felt part of the group [1].

title: Two Refugee Shacks Hiding Upstairs
place: 30 Niantic Avenue
hook: Looking for a garden shed, two historians looked up and gasped. The whole second storey of a Niantic Street house was made of 1906 earthquake shacks.
story: Cottages from the 1906 earthquake refugee camps were later moved into the OMI and reused as homes. The neighbourhood's historic context statement lists joined refugee "shacks" as a local building type and notes one at 223 Broad Street, moved from a camp after 1907 [2]. On March 23, 2003, shack expert Jane Cryan and Woody LaBounty of the Western Neighborhoods Project followed a tip from San Francisco Heritage that a shack at 30 Niantic had been turned into a garden shed [1]. Niantic is a tiny dead-end street trapped between Alemany Boulevard and the 280 freeway. There was no shed. Instead a workman on a ladder was hammering at the house's second storey, which turned out to be two "Type A" shacks joined end to end. Original park-green paint still showed where they met. Cryan hugged the owners, Tom and Maureen Ginella [1]. Instead of demolishing the shacks, the Ginellas had set them on a new foundation as their upper floor and were adding a modern level underneath. Upstairs, early walls, floorboards and cove ceilings survived. Cryan amended the city's list of surviving shacks, bringing it to 21 [1].

title: A Methodist first, in the Sunday service
place: Bethany United Methodist Church, 1270 Sanchez Street at Clipper
hook: When City Hall began marrying same-sex couples, a Noe Valley pastor wed two men during Sunday worship. Her church filed a complaint. She later became a bishop.
story: On February 12, 2004, parishioner Michael Eaton called his pastor, the Rev. Karen Oliveto of Bethany United Methodist Church, to say City Hall was issuing marriage licences to same-sex couples. He asked her to marry him and his partner, Sean Higgins [2]. She did. Over the following days she conducted seven ceremonies at City Hall, only for couples she knew as their pastor [2]. On Sunday, February 15, she married an eighth couple, Dan Johnson and Bill Hinson, in Bethany's sanctuary during regular worship. It was the first same-sex marriage held in a United Methodist sanctuary [1][2]. Four days later her district superintendent told her a complaint had been filed for 'disobedience to the order and discipline of the United Methodist Church' [1][2]. At a February 22 news conference, more than 100 Methodists stood behind her [1]. 'I am not doing a holy union,' she said. 'I am doing a legal gay marriage' [1]. She called it 'the most moving thing I've ever done in my ministry' [2]. Oliveto had led Bethany since 1992 [2]. In 2016 she was elected the first openly lesbian bishop in the United Methodist Church [3].

title: Del and Phyllis, first in line
place: San Francisco City Hall, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl
hook: After more than fifty years together, two lesbian pioneers became the first same-sex couple married at City Hall. Then the courts voided it, and they did it again.
story: On February 12, 2004, Mayor Gavin Newsom ordered city officials to issue marriage licences to same-sex couples. The first couple married were Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon, who had moved in together on Valentine's Day 1953 and co-founded the Daughters of Bilitis, the first lesbian-rights organisation in the country, in 1955 [1][2]. About 4,000 couples followed in the next four weeks, arriving from across the country [3]. At a mass reception for 600 newlyweds on February 23, Lyon said it mattered 'for a lot of the people that got married … but also for our friends who didn't get married' [1]. The state Supreme Court stopped the weddings in March. On August 12, 2004, it declared them void [3]. Four years later the same court struck down California's marriage ban. On June 16, 2008, Martin and Lyon were first in line again, married by Newsom himself in the same mauve and turquoise suits they had worn in 2004 [1][2]. Those outfits are now in the GLBT Historical Society's collection [1]. Martin died that August, aged 87. 'We were able to enjoy the ultimate rite of love and commitment before she passed,' Lyon said [1].

title: I Am OMI: A Neighbourhood Tells Its Story
place: Ocean View Recreation Center, Lobos Street & Capitol Avenue
hook: Teen filmmakers, a stage play, a radio drama and history panels in shop windows: between 2003 and 2005 the OMI collected its memories and gave them back.
story: The name OMI is fairly new. In the 1960s residents of Ingleside Terraces made common cause with the neighbourhoods to the east and south to lobby for better services and parks, and "OMI", for Ocean View-Merced Heights-Ingleside, came into use [1]. From 2003 to 2005 the Western Neighborhoods Project ran "I am OMI", using history and shared stories to bridge ethnic, cultural and generational lines and help "an often-divided neighborhood find a unified voice" [2]. In summer 2003, twelve young people in a month-long digital video camp interviewed neighbours and filmed "then and now" shots of landmarks. About 50 people came to their screening on August 1, and each filmmaker was paid $50 [3]. The project set up tables of old photos and free history booklets at the OMI International Family Festival at the Ocean View Recreation Center, Lobos and Capitol [4]. On June 12, 2004, Arts Connection premiered an original play based on neighbourhood stories at City College's Diego Rivera Theatre [4]. In April 2005 history panels filled storefront windows along Ocean Avenue, and in June a radio drama built from the interviews aired on KPFA [2][4].

title: The Labyrinth That Keeps Coming Back
place: Lands End Labyrinth site above Mile Rock Beach
hook: An anonymous car detailer laid stones on a cliff edge at dawn to dodge park rangers. For seventeen years strangers destroyed his labyrinth and a doula kept rebuilding it.
story: On the spring equinox of 2004, Eduardo Aguilera built a seven-circuit labyrinth, in the style of Chartres, on a small plateau above the Golden Gate, using stones from the surrounding area [1]. It was a stealth project. Aguilera, who details cars for a living, spent about 16 hours laying it out at dawn and dusk so rangers wouldn't catch him. 'I wanted to be totally anonymous,' he said [2]. Vandals wrecked it soon after, and he rebuilt it. Around 2008 Colleen Yerge, a North Beach doula, became its unofficial keeper. She carried grapefruit-sized rocks up from Mile Rock Beach in a backpack [3][4]. After it was stripped in August 2015, about 50 volunteers helped her rebuild it, spacing the stones exactly 15 inches apart [2]. Aguilera had warned her not to put her whole heart into it, because it would be destroyed. She kept her compassion for whoever did it [4]. In 2020–21 it was wiped out three times, every rock apparently thrown into the sea. Because the Park Service never approved it, destroying it isn't technically a crime [3].

title: The Lake That Nearly Drained Away
place: Lake Merced boathouse, Harding Road
hook: Lake Merced was once stocked with a quarter of a million fish a year. Then golf courses and cemeteries pumped the aquifer and its boathouse went dark.
story: In the 1950s the state utilities commission gave San Francisco's Recreation and Park Department control of Lake Merced's surface. The conditions were strict: keep the drinking water potable, keep the level up, allow no swimming and no gasoline engines [1]. The city built a first-class urban fishery. At its height stocking reached 250,000 fish [1]. But heavy postwar pumping of the Westside Aquifer by golf courses, cities and cemeteries drew the lake down [1]. As the water fell, stocking all but stopped. The Boat House, once a busy restaurant and bar, closed, and fishing piers were left standing over tule-choked banks [1]. Better management of the aquifer and occasional added water helped the lake start rising again from about 1990 [2]. By 2004 angler Tony Van Houten could report a lake "on the rebound", thanks to CalTrout, the Lake Merced Task Force and the Friends of Lake Merced. There was a new fishing pier, and the state planned to plant 50,000 fish that year [1].

title: When the Excelsior became a Filipino hub
place: Filipino Community Center, 4681 Mission St
hook: Families left a shrinking Manilatown for the Excelsior, and a local barber watched in amazement as they paid cash for their houses.
story: In the 1970 census Filipinos made up just 6 percent of the Excelsior. Within a decade it was one of San Francisco's main Filipino neighbourhoods [1]. There were two reasons. The 1965 immigration reforms ended quotas that had held the Philippines to 100 immigrants a year. Meanwhile redevelopment was wiping out Manilatown, ending with the 1977 eviction of the International Hotel [1]. In 1977 the Excelsior barber Caspare La Rosa told a reporter he was amazed to see Filipino families 'pay cash for the houses they are buying' [1]. The Apollo and Granada theatres showed Filipino films, and Filipino grocers opened along Mission and Geneva [1][2]. In the 1990s, while the archdiocese was closing parishes, the Church of the Epiphany on Vienna Street drew nearly 4,000 people a week to Mass, the most in the city. 'We survived the demographic change because of the Filipino population,' said Father Bruce Dreier [1]. In 2004 the Filipino Community Center opened at 4681 Mission Street [1]. The Excelsior is still one of the city's Filipino hubs [3].

title: A Copper Museum Paid For Privately
place: De Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive
hook: After voters twice refused to pay for a new de Young, a fundraiser simply decided to raise $190 million herself, and a Swiss firm wrapped it in copper.
story: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake badly damaged the old de Young [2]. Around midnight on June 2, 1998, a second bond measure to rebuild it fell short of the two-thirds it needed by 1.7 percent. There was talk of giving up, or of moving the museum out of the park [1][2]. The next morning Dede Wilsey, who chaired the capital campaign, decided, as she put it, "I would simply raise the money myself" [1]. In January 1999 the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron won the commission. Critics called its twisting tower a "huge shed," an "aircraft carrier" and a "Howard Johnson's of the future," and a group called People for a New de Young sued [1]. Supervisors approved the project in January 2002 [1]. Jacques Herzog's idea for the skin came from photographs of sunlight dappling through the park's trees. The result was 7,602 individually punched and embossed panels using 950,000 pounds of copper, some of it recycled drain pipes and wiring [1]. More than 7,000 donors gave $190 million, and the museum opened on October 15, 2005 [1].

title: Broad Street Becomes a Regular Neighbourhood
place: OMI Community Service Center, 103 Broad Street
hook: Streetcars once wouldn't stop at Broad and Randolph. By 2005 the biggest complaint was sidewalk parking, and an old fish market had become a one-stop city hall.
story: The Broad-Randolph corridor, Ocean View's main street between San Jose Avenue and Junipero Serra Boulevard, was once so dominated by gangs and drug dealers that streetcars wouldn't stop there [1]. Police sergeant Michael Williams described "cycle murders": young men who had grown up together, some of whom had coached sports together, killing each other over drugs [1]. From 1996 the Taraval Neighborhood Team of eight officers and a sergeant patrolled the strip around the clock. They made more than 4,000 arrests by 2003, and also took local kids salmon fishing and camping at Camp Mather [1]. There were 12 shootings in 2004 and three in the first months of 2005 [1]. That spring the OMI Community Service Center reopened in a former fish market at 103 Broad Street, near the notorious Broad and Plymouth corner. It housed police, public works, parking, city attorney and probation staff [1]. Not everyone was comfortable: community centre director Nyree Monroe warned against harassing innocent people [1]. Old businesses had helped hold the street together, among them Furlough's Tonsorial Parlor (1955) and Reno's Barber Shop [2]. Bill Reno, the "mayor of Broad Street", found teenagers jobs and lent his back room as a community centre. The Chronicle dates his shop to 1967, a local history to 1960 [1][2].

title: From Parking Lot to Tiger's Playoff
place: Harding Park golf course, 99 Harding Road
hook: In 1998 the city's beloved public course was paved over with parked cars. Seven years later Tiger Woods won a playoff there against John Daly.
story: Harding Park opened in 1925, named for President Warren Harding, a keen golfer [2]. Byron Nelson won the Victory Open there in January 1944 and won again that December, when it had been renamed the San Francisco Open [2]. Johnny Miller learned the game there in the late 1950s. He biked over, fished in Lake Merced by the practice green and hustled middle-aged men for nickels [1]. The PGA Tour left after 1969, and budget cuts let the course decay [1][2]. It hit bottom in 1998, when it served as a parking lot for the U.S. Open at the neighboring Olympic Club [1][2]. Lawyer and former USGA president Sandy Tatum watched it "turning into a weed patch" and rallied the city and the Tour [2]. A $16 million restoration in 2002–03 followed [1][2]. In October 2005 Harding Park became the first municipal course to host a World Golf Championship [1]. Tiger Woods, who remembered it as "basically a clover field", beat John Daly on the third playoff hole [1][2].

title: George Lucas Builds an Empire at Letterman

hook: Where a 10-storey Army hospital once stood, the maker of Star Wars built San Francisco's biggest office project in decades and put a bronze Yoda at the door.
story: The site at the Presidio's Lombard Gate once held the 10-storey Letterman Army Hospital and a 13-acre parking lot [1]. The Presidio Trust had to make the park pay for itself by 2013, and it picked George Lucas over more conventional developers [1]. His Letterman Digital Arts Center opened in 2005, with four buildings holding 865,000 square feet. The Chronicle called it the city's largest office project since 101 California St. opened in 1982 [1]. Lucasfilm paid $5.6 million a year in rent [1]. Critic John King described the result as a 'costume drama' of brick and stucco made to look like older Army buildings. 'I'm very much an advocate of historic architecture,' Lucas said. 'I like to work in a facility that ... looks like it's been there for a period of time' [1]. Landscape architect Lawrence Halprin, then 88, laid out 17 acres of open space with 85 kinds of trees and shrubs, an artificial stream and boulders brought from a ranch near Redding [1]. Outside Industrial Light & Magic's door, Lawrence Noble's bronze Yoda, about 32 inches tall, was unveiled in 2005 [2]. It soon became a pilgrimage spot for fans, school groups and ILM staff on their breaks [2].

title: Mangoes, kabocha and chorizo on Leland Avenue
place: Leland Avenue commercial strip
hook: The valley's main street had boarded-up shops and no fruit market. So a family from Jalisco bought a building and filled it with food for all their neighbours.
story: For years, empty storefronts lined Visitacion Valley's five-block main street [1]. The Lopez family, who came from Jalisco, Mexico, and lived in the neighbourhood, knew what was missing: a place to buy fruit and vegetables. They paid more than $500,000 for a building on Leland Avenue and spent ten months fixing it up. Casa Lopez Produce opened in January 2005 [1]. "We talked to the neighbors, who all said this was a good idea," said Rene Lopez, 18 [1]. The shelves showed who lived nearby. Chinese, Filipino and Central American customers suggested what to stock, so homemade chorizo sat next to kabocha squash, jicama, mangoes, Thai rice and Vietnamese spring-roll wrappers [1]. Across the street, Joaquin Escobar was opening La Loma Produce #2 [1]. Business stayed hard. In 2011, 13 percent of Leland's storefronts were empty and the street closed by 8 p.m. [2]. The valley had gone about 30 years without a supermarket before a Grocery Outlet was due to open in 2014 [3]. Still, in 2015 an urban design critic enjoyed the street fair on Leland. There were "no $14 cocktails" and "no tech buses", and the crowd was local and diverse [4].

title: Mojitos versus the hustlers
place: Former Maye's Oyster House, 1233 Polk St
hook: A $6.5 million restaurant with a Spanish chandelier and a headless Apollo opened on lower Polk, and a fight broke out over who the street was for.
story:
By 2005 lower Polk was changing fast. Restaurateur Myles O'Reilly had turned the old Maye's Oyster House building between Bush and Sutter into O'Reilly's Holy Grail, a $6.5 million restaurant with imported stained glass, a headless Apollo from Rome and a 250-year-old Spanish chandelier, and remade the rundown residential motel upstairs into 14 European-style suites. "I put my life savings into making a statement on this street," he said [1].

The bars were turning over too. The Polk Gulch Saloon, known for drag queens and trans women, became the Lush Lounge; the Hemlock, full of hipsters and live bands, replaced the historic gay bar the Giraffe; Rendezvous, the last male hustler bar, had closed [1][3]. The Lower Polk Neighbors Association welcomed the "cleaning up." The radical group Gay Shame called the association a "brutal gentrification squad" and warned the street would soon be known "more for green-apple mojitos and stretch Hummers than trannies and tweakers" [1].

Historian Joey Plaster argues the clash was one of three major economic shifts on Polk since the 1950s, driven by outside market forces rather than simply homophobia: the same economics that built a gay commercial corridor in the 1960s were now dismantling it [2].

title: Patricia's Green
place: Patricia's Green, Octavia Boulevard between Fell and Hayes
hook: Where freeway ramps once came down, a small park opened in 2005. Months later it was renamed for the soft-spoken activist who fought to get it built.
story: On September 9, 2005, Octavia Boulevard opened with a ribbon-cutting at Market Street [2]. The designers, Allan Jacobs and Elizabeth Macdonald, followed the principle "No one gets everything, but everyone gets a lot" [2][3]. The boulevard has four central lanes for commuters and a slower lane on each side for local traffic [2]. It was planted with 261 trees, including evergreen elms, flowering cherries and pears, and Lombardy poplars [1]. At its northern end, between Fell and Hayes, was a new park called Hayes Green. "This is just an amazing gift for the neighborhood," said Patricia Walkup, the activist who helped lead the fight against rebuilding the freeway [1]. "In a few years, there will be people who will never know a freeway was there" [1]. Walkup, founder of the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association, died on June 6, 2006, at 59. That August the Recreation and Park Commission voted unanimously to rename the park "Patricia's Green in Hayes Valley" [4]. "If not for Patricia, that park would not be there," said her friend Robin Levitt. "If she hadn't done that work, we would have a freeway there" [4]. In December 2006 the American Planning Association gave the project its first award for "hard-won victories" [2].
