title: The Warriors come back across the bay
place: Chase Center, 1 Warriors Way (Third and 16th streets)
hook: The Warriors wanted a waterfront arena on the Embarcadero. A 75-year-old ex-mayor with a battered whiteboard helped push them to a Mission Bay lot instead.
story: The Golden State Warriors first planned an 18,000-seat arena on Piers 30-32 by the Bay Bridge, a project Mayor Ed Lee called 'my legacy project' [1]. Former mayor Art Agnos, 75, led the opposition with a battered whiteboard, a tattered sign-up sheet and a homemade presentation that he took to community rooms two or three times a week. He called it a view-killer 'all dressed up in a basketball uniform', pushed by 'two billionaires, neither of whom lives here' [2]. In April 2014 the team gave up the pier and bought a 12-acre Mission Bay site at Third and 16th streets from Salesforce, which had once planned its headquarters there [1]. The new location avoided a likely public vote, had a Muni stop at its door and satisfied many critics [1]. The Chase Center opened on September 6, 2019, returning the Warriors to San Francisco after almost five decades in Oakland, and seats 18,064 for basketball [3]. In 2025 it also became home to the WNBA's Golden State Valkyries [3].

title: An Olympian's gun shop on Mission
place: High Bridge Arms, 3185 Mission St
hook: San Francisco's last gun store was opened by a Chinese American pistol shooter who went to the 1948 London Olympics.
story:
For decades a faded 'GUNS' sign hung over 3185 Mission Street. High Bridge Arms dates back to the 1950s, when Bob Chow opened it [1]. Chow was born in 1911 to Chinese immigrant parents. He was a ham radio pioneer and a Navy Reserve non-commissioned officer, which was rare for an Asian American at the time. According to a biography quoted by Bernalwood, he was the first Chinese American to compete in Olympic pistol shooting [1]. At the 1948 London Games he finished 13th in the rapid-fire pistol, with all 60 shots on target [2]. He also worked as a movie extra and is said to have taught John Wayne and Roy Rogers to shoot straighter [1].

Chow died in 2003, but the shop kept going under new owners. By 2015 it was the last gun shop in San Francisco. That September its managers announced it would close at the end of October. They blamed a proposed city rule that would have required video of every sale and weekly reports of customer data to police [1]. Many neighbours were glad to see it go. Others missed the old sign as a link to a lost Bernal [1].

title: Fifty Thousand Mirrors Over Kearny Street
place: Portsmouth Square pedestrian bridge over Kearny St
hook: A forgotten concrete footbridge from a hotel to Chinatown's 'living room' was covered in 50,000 mirrors, glued down by the aunties who dance in the square.
story: A concrete footbridge crosses Kearny Street from the Hilton, home of the Chinese Culture Center, to Portsmouth Square. Most days it held a few sunbathers and a skateboarder [1][2]. In August 2015, Austin artist Beili Liu covered it with Sky Bridge: 50,000 brick-sized pieces of mirrored Mylar, each glued to the walkway and walls [1]. On sunny days, visitors were told to bring sunglasses [1]. The biggest group of volunteers came from Chinatown's "Dancing Aunties", women who dance to 1950s and '60s Chinese pop in Portsmouth Square every morning and evening, and they laid the mirrors in what turned out to be the hottest week [1]. Curator Abby Chen said the aim was to highlight open space in the country's second-densest neighbourhood, where "seniors and the children are really kind of trapped in their SROs" [1]. That December, plans were unveiled to turn the 270-foot bridge into a mini-park with planters, benches and a mosaic called Sunrise by Mik Gaspay [2]. "Our alleys and our sidewalks are our front and back yards," planner Roy Chan said. "Portsmouth Square is our living room" [2].

title: The Movie Palace Saved From City College
place: New Mission Theater, 2550 Mission St
hook: It went from movie palace to futon showroom, rave venue and pigeon roost. Then its 70-foot marquee lit up again for Star Wars.
story: In the first half of the 20th century the Mission was San Francisco's second theatre district: at its peak it had 15,000 seats, second only to mid-Market's 25,000 [1]. The 1916 New Mission, with 2,021 seats, was among the last survivors [1]. In 2004 the community rallied when City College of San Francisco, which owned it, sought to gut the building for a campus [1]. Preservationists got it landmarked, and the college sold [2][1]. According to research by Alamo Drafthouse chief Tim League, the last show there was a Carlos Santana concert in the 1980s [2]. After that it was a furniture showroom with futons in the auditorium, then a rave venue, then a home for pigeons [2]. Alamo spent four years planning and rebuilding. It restored the big screen, added four small screens where the balconies had been, and relit the green neon on the 70-foot marquee [2]. The theatre reopened on December 17, 2015, with two premieres of the new Star Wars film [3].

title: Two Mothers and a Staircase of Tiles
place: Lincoln Park Steps, California Street at 32nd Avenue
hook: The old stairs at the end of California Street were cracked, tagged and full of rubbish. Two school parents spent seven years turning them into tiled art.
story: The steps at the western end of California Street date from the early 1900s. They lead from the Outer Richmond up into Lincoln Park, towards the golf course, the Legion of Honor and the Lands End trail [1]. By the 2000s they were cracked and crumbling, and they drew graffiti, dumping and loitering at night [1]. In 2007 Anna Yatroussis and Meg Autry decided to fix them. Both were parents at the Katherine Delmar Burke School right next to the stairs, which was looking for a way to mark its 100th anniversary [1][2]. They founded Friends of Lincoln Park and hired tile artist Aileen Barr, known for the 16th Avenue tiled steps. Other school parents gave architecture and construction management for free [1][2]. Barr's first tiled bench was finished in 2010. Rec and Park put in a $180,000 grant for structural repairs, on condition that the friends raised at least $250,000 privately for the tiles [1]. The Beaux Arts-inspired stairway was formally opened on 28 May 2015 with a ribbon cutting by Supervisor Eric Mar [2].

title: Coming home at 55 Laguna
place: Openhouse at 55 Laguna Street (former Richardson Hall)
hook: An old teachers' college campus became the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming affordable housing for seniors.
story: Richardson Hall was built at 55 Laguna in 1925 as the Kindergarten Training Building of the San Francisco State Teachers College. It is one of three city landmarks on a campus listed on the National Register [1]. After the college left, the University of California Extension used the site until the mid-2000s [2]. More than 20 years before that, two women had begun worrying about where the city's LGBTQ+ elders would live. They were Dr. Marcy Adelman and Jeanette Gurevitch, the founders of Openhouse [3]. Working with Mercy Housing, Openhouse won a landmark decision from the Planning Commission in 2012 for what it describes as the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming low-income housing project [3]. Residents began moving into the renovated 55 Laguna in December 2016. That same year Openhouse opened San Francisco's first LGBTQ+ senior center next door at 65 Laguna [3]. In 2019 residents moved into a new building at 95 Laguna, named for the two founders [3]. Of the 117 apartments, 14 are reserved for formerly homeless people through the federal Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS program. Historic murals are preserved throughout the buildings [3].

title: Drag Queens Buy the Oldest Queer Bar
place: The Stud (1987-2020), 399 Ninth Street at Harrison
hook: Facing a doubled rent and a condo tower next door, San Francisco's oldest queer bar was saved by a co-op of drag queens, DJs and nightlife people.
story: The Stud opened in 1966 on Folsom Street and moved in 1987 to 399 Ninth Street, a kitsch-cluttered room at Ninth and Harrison [1][2]. It welcomed people other gay bars turned away. "Hair fairies, leather daddies - everyone was there on the dance floor," co-owner Honey Mahogany said. Sylvester, Patrick Cowley and Lady Gaga all passed through [2][1]. In 2016 a new landlord raised the rent to $9,000 a month, more than double what owner Michael McElhaney had paid. A huge condo complex was rising next door, and McElhaney planned to sell [3]. Drag performer VivvyAnne ForeverMore (Mica Sigourney) sent out a call to nightlife leaders. A 15-member co-op formed, including Honey Mahogany, DJ Siobhan Aluvalot and promoter Kelly Lovemonster, and raised the money to buy the business [3]. The co-op survived the rent but not the pandemic. In May 2020, with bars shut by COVID-19, it announced it would leave Ninth Street and planned a virtual "drag funeral" [1][2]. "It survived the AIDS epidemic," ForeverMore said, "and now it's the COVID pandemic that's forcing us to close" [2].

title: From gas station to town square
place: Noe Valley Town Square, 3861 24th Street
hook: In 1979 drivers queued three blocks for gas here. Later it was a car park, then a protest farmers' market, and now it's the city's only neighbourhood town square.
story: The square sits on the site of a former gas station [4]. During the 1979 oil crisis, Noe Valley's only service station, Dan's Shell at 3865 24th Street, drew queues from 6 a.m. The line of cars ran up 24th Street and three blocks down Sanchez, and most afternoons the pumps ran dry [1]. The station site later became a parking lot [4]. Then the Real Food Company closed without warning in 2003. Neighbours including Leslie Crawford and Peter Gabel decided to grow their own alternative [2][4]. On December 6, 2003, the Noe Valley Farmers' Market opened in the lot between Vicksburg and Sanchez. More than 2,000 people came the first day, and a live band played every Saturday [2]. Not everyone was pleased: a florist complained that the farmers sold flowers below wholesale [2]. In June 2013 the Recreation and Park Department bought the quarter-acre site. After more than four years of work with a residents' group and Supervisor Scott Wiener's office, Noe Valley Town Square opened in October 2016 [3]. 'There's a utopian dimension to it that I really like,' Gabel said [4].

title: Half the figure eight goes car-free
place: Eastern half of the Twin Peaks Boulevard 'figure 8'
hook: For decades cars circled the summit on a looping figure eight. In 2016 the city handed half of it to walkers.
story:
Twin Peaks Boulevard wraps around both summits in a loop shaped like a figure eight. For decades both halves carried cars [1][2]. In July 2016 the SFMTA and the Recreation and Park Department tried an experiment. The western half became a two-way road, and the eastern half was closed to cars and opened to people walking and cycling, marked off with paint and concrete barriers [1][2]. The results were striking. The number of drivers going over the 30 mph limit fell by 77 per cent. More than 58 per cent of people in a year-long survey wanted the change made permanent [1]. It was, in June 2020 [1].

The summit is 64 acres of open space with three trails, including one named for the Mission blue butterfly [1]. The Chronicle reported that construction was due to start in 2025 on rebuilding the car-free side as a wide promenade, after improvements to the Noe Peak trail and the path down to Crestline Drive [2].

title: The Hospital That Serves Warm Water
place: Chinese Hospital, 845 Jackson St
hook: Chinatown built its own hospital because other hospitals turned Chinese patients away. Bruce Lee was born there. In 2016 it opened a new eight-storey tower.
story: In an era when other San Francisco hospitals turned away or discriminated against Chinese patients, Chinatown looked after its own [3][2]. In 1899 the Tung Wah Dispensary began seeing patients, staffed by Western-trained doctors and Chinese herbalists. In 1925 the community-built Chinese Hospital opened on Jackson Street [1]. Bruce Lee was born there in 1940 [3]. The kitchen serves jook, and macaroni soup with diced ham, and around Lunar New Year grateful patients drop off tea, oranges and mooncakes [3]. NBC News called it the only Chinese-operated and -governed independent hospital in North America [3]. The 1925 building was later judged seismically unsafe. It was pulled down in 2012 to make way for a new tower [1][2]. On April 18, 2016, the hospital opened the eight-storey, $180 million Patient Tower, with hand-painted cherry blossoms in nearly every room [1][2]. "We have the food, we have the language, we know the culture," said CEO Brenda Yee. "Other hospitals give you cold water. We know to provide warm water" [2].

title: The Leaning Tower of Mission Street
place: Millennium Tower, 301 Mission Street
hook: Residents of San Francisco's most glamorous condo tower were summoned to a secret meeting, IDs checked at the door, and told their building was sinking.
story: The 58-story Millennium Tower opened as a home for professional athletes and venture capitalists. Its plans forecast it might settle as much as six inches; by late 2016 it had sunk 16 inches and was tilting, an estimated two to four inches at the base and 14 at the top [1]. A paper trail of concern dated back to early 2009, but most residents knew nothing until they were summoned in May 2016 to a private meeting in a club-level lounge, where identification was checked at the door and they were told what they heard must stay secret [1]. The story broke on the Chronicle's front page that August. In November, City Attorney Dennis Herrera sued the developer, saying it knew the building "had sunk more than it was supposed to" before selling a single condo and didn't tell buyers [1]. After years of litigation, a $100 million foundation fix began in 2020, with the building occupied throughout. In June 2023 crews finished transferring its load onto 18 new piles driven to bedrock; the engineer reported the settlement had been arrested and the tower had risen slightly, undoing some of the 30 inches of tilt to the northwest it had gathered over 15 years [2].

title: The Soil Samples That Weren't
place: Hunters Point Shipyard, Parcel A homes (Innes Court)
hook: The Navy's contractor was supposed to show the old shipyard was safe for thousands of new homes. Instead, regulators found, some of its soil samples had come from somewhere else.
story: From 1946 to 1969 the Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory worked at Hunters Point, cleaning ships contaminated by the Bikini atomic tests and studying fallout. In 1956 alone, 980 tons of radioactive waste were dumped at sea [1]. Decades later, cleaning up the Superfund site was the precondition for turning the yard into a neighbourhood of more than 12,000 homes [2]. Tetra Tech, the contractor hired to measure radionuclides and other contaminants, had been testing soil there since at least the mid-1990s [2]. Whistleblowers inside the firm began speaking out around 2012. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that the company had taken dirt from an area known to be clean and passed it off as coming from another area, where housing was planned [2]. In July 2016 the Navy admitted to Greenaction that it had found 386 "anomalous" samples out of more than 25,000. On 13 September the EPA wrote to the Navy, and land transfers to the developer FivePoint were put on hold [2]. Critics argued that the bigger problem was how much of the shipyard had never been tested at all [3]. By then the first 88 townhomes, built on land handed over years earlier, had already sold out [2].

title: The Year the Famous View Closed
place: Alamo Square Park (Hayes and Steiner streets)
hook: For a year, chain-link fences surrounded the city's most photographed lawn. When the park reopened, its planners wanted it to become the view itself.
story: In May 2016 the 12.7-acre Alamo Square Park closed for a $5.3 million renovation. The work was supposed to take seven months, but it took a year because of a wet winter and extra work that wasn't in the original plan [1][2]. Crews rebuilt the irrigation system, which is controlled by a small device on a nearby flagpole that monitors temperature and rainfall. The park was expected to save more than 2.5 million gallons of water a year, about a third of its use [2]. They repaved the paths, added an all-gender accessible restroom, and planted a rain garden and native plants, using the tennis court as a temporary nursery [1][2]. Neighbours paid for 45 new trees [1]. "Everyone loves the views out of the park," said Recreation and Park project manager Brett Desmarais. "But we want the park to become the view itself" [2]. On the last quiet morning before it reopened, the sidewalk by the Painted Ladies, normally crowded, was empty except for a woman in a bathrobe handing her husband a mug of coffee as he set off on his bike [2]. The ribbon was cut on May 24, 2017, and Board of Supervisors President London Breed called the park "one of the jewels of our city" [1].

title: The art school that swallowed apartments
place: 1055 Pine St
hook: A for-profit art school quietly bought up some 40 buildings, many of them homes. The reckoning turned two Nob Hill properties into housing for low-income seniors.
story:
Over more than a decade, the for-profit Academy of Art University and a web of affiliated companies bought or leased some 40 San Francisco properties, including a cluster on Nob Hill's Bush, Sutter and Pine streets [1][2]. A March 2016 Planning Department memo found at least 33 violated zoning, permit or preservation rules. The city said about 160 affordable homes had been illegally converted into student housing and another 140 units removed from rent control [1].

On 6 May 2016 City Attorney Dennis Herrera sued, calling the academy "one of San Francisco's most egregious land use scofflaws." His complaint targeted properties including 1055 Pine, 1080 and 1153 Bush, and 860 Sutter [2].

That December Herrera announced a settlement valued at over $60 million, then the largest in a city code-enforcement case: $20 million in cash, including $7 million to help low-income tenants stay housed, and at least 160 affordable units [1]. The housing would come from two Pine Street buildings. Students living at 1055 Pine would be moved out and the building renovated, while a new building would rise at 1069 Pine, both for low-income seniors for 66 years [1]. The deal was guaranteed personally by academy president Elisa Stephens, granddaughter of its founder [1].

title: The girl beneath the garage floor
place: Former Odd Fellows Cemetery grounds, near Rossi Avenue (exact house not published)
hook: In 2016 a remodelling crew's shovels hit a tiny bronze coffin with glass windows. Inside was a little girl, a rose still in her hand.
story: On May 9, 2016, workers remodelling a house in the Lone Mountain neighbourhood struck something beneath the concrete garage floor: a small lead-and-bronze coffin with two glass viewing windows [1]. Inside lay a girl of about three in a long white dress, a rose in her right hand and lavender woven into her curly blond hair [1]. She had been left behind when the Odd Fellows Cemetery, which once covered these blocks, was emptied to Colma [1][2]. The medical examiner's office said that because the coffin was on private property, it was the homeowner's problem. Ericka Karner, whose family had lived there since 1976, was quoted $7,000 by one undertaker [1]. The Garden of Innocence charity stepped in, the Odd Fellows paid, and the girl, provisionally named Miranda, was reburied at Greenlawn Memorial Park in Colma on June 4, 2016, with about 140 people attending [2]. In 2017 researchers matched old plot records and obituaries, confirmed by DNA from a descendant of her brother, and gave her back her name: Edith Howard Cook, who died on October 13, 1876, six weeks short of her third birthday [2]. Her father, Horatio Nelson Cook, ran a leather-belting business [3].

title: Julius' Castle Fights Its Way Back

hook: A turreted 1920s restaurant under Coit Tower went dark in 2008. Reviving it took lawsuits, a sliding hillside, a fire and 14 years.
story: On the cliff below Coit Tower, Julius' Castle was built between 1923 and 1928 by the Italian restaurateur Julius Roz and the architect Luigi Mastropasqua. It paid tribute to Layman's Castle, a hilltop folly that fire destroyed in 1903 [1]. Inside, the panelling came from the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition [2]. For generations it was where San Franciscans got engaged and celebrated [2][3]. The whole cast of The Empire Strikes Back once came to dinner. Another night the guests were weathered mountaineers, some missing fingers, gathered to honour Sir Edmund Hillary [1]. It closed in January 2008 [3]. In 2012 the attorney Paul Scott bought it in a bankruptcy sale, outbidding someone who wanted to turn it into condos [3]. Neighbours warned of idling Ubers and drunken revellers, but in July 2017 the Planning Commission voted 7 to 0 to let it reopen. "That is city life," said Commissioner Kathrin Moore. "We are not living in the suburbs" [2]. Then came a building found to sit over the property line, a sliding hillside, and a fire that destroyed a turret [3]. In July 2026 Scott said a chef had been hired and the castle would reopen that September [3].

title: Taking a Name Off the Plaza
place: Embarcadero Plaza (formerly Justin Herman Plaza)
hook: For 43 years the city's busiest waterfront plaza honoured the man who bulldozed the Fillmore. In 2017, residents who remembered finally got his name taken down.
story: From 1974 the plaza at the foot of Market Street carried the name of M. Justin Herman, who ran the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency from 1959 until his death in 1971 [1]. Under Herman, redevelopment displaced thousands of residents, mainly African Americans and Japanese Americans, from 60 blocks of the Western Addition and Fillmore, and moved mostly poor people out of parts of Chinatown and South of Market [1]. In July 2017 Supervisor Aaron Peskin said Herman "personified a dark chapter in modern San Francisco history" and proposed stripping the name [1]. The Board of Supervisors voted unanimously in September; Board President London Breed, who grew up in the Western Addition, recalled living in a community "literally destroyed" by the agency, and noted the new signs would cost about $5,400 [2]. On November 16, 2017, the Recreation and Park Commission made it official, 4-2, restoring the plaza's original name, Embarcadero Plaza [3]. title: The Street That Sold for $90,000
place: Presidio Terrace, off Arguello Boulevard
hook: A gated oval once advertised as the one spot in San Francisco reserved for Caucasians was bought, sidewalks and all, by a San Jose couple. For $90,000.
story: Presidio Terrace began rising in 1905, a private oval of mansions beside the Presidio [3]. A 1906 Baldwin & Howell advertisement boasted that it was 'the only spot in San Francisco where only Caucasians are permitted to buy or lease real estate' [2]. The Supreme Court voided such covenants in 1948, yet a racial clause lingered in the homeowners' bylaws until 1998, when HUD announced an agreement to strike it [2]. Residents over the years included Nancy Pelosi and Dianne Feinstein [1][3]. Then came a twist. The association had not paid the tax on its private street, $14 a year, for two decades; the bills went to an outdated address [1]. In 2015 investor Tina Lam and her husband Michael Cheng bought the street, sidewalks and common areas at auction for $90,000 [1][2]. Lam said it fulfilled her 'simple dream of owning a piece of San Francisco' [2]. When talk turned to charging residents for parking, the neighbours fought back [2]. On 28 November 2017 the Board of Supervisors voted 7-4 to rescind the sale; Supervisor Hillary Ronen, voting no, noted that most people do not have a private street in front of their house [1].

title: The world's first transgender district
place: Aunt Charlie's Lounge, 133 Turk St, in the Transgender District
hook: Half a century after the Compton's riot, three Black trans women set out to make sure the Tenderloin's trans history, and its trans residents, would not be priced out.
story: By the 2010s, the sound of the Tenderloin was construction noise. New cafes and condos were arriving, and rising rents threatened the transgender community that had long called the neighbourhood home [1]. In 2016 the city renamed parts of Turk and Taylor streets 'Compton's Cafeteria Way' and 'Vikki Mar Lane' [2]. In 2017 three Black trans women founded the Compton's Transgender Cultural District, named for the 1966 riot. It is the first legally recognized transgender district in the world [2]. It covers six blocks of the south-eastern Tenderloin and crosses Market Street to take in two blocks of Sixth Street [2]. Co-founder Honey Mahogany, a drag artist and former contestant on RuPaul's Drag Race, met NPR at Aunt Charlie's Lounge on Turk Street, one of the neighbourhood's few remaining gay bars and, she said, 'a centerpiece for the community' [1]. 'People can't put me in the box of male or female, because I'm tall, because I'm black, or whatever, so I get stared at all over San Francisco,' she told NPR. 'In the Tenderloin I find that doesn't happen' [1]. 'With the destruction of these buildings,' she warned, 'we're also losing the stories that go along with them' [1].

title: A Park in the Sky, Closed by Cracks
place: Salesforce Transit Center and rooftop park, 425 Mission Street
hook: San Francisco opened a 5.4-acre garden on top of a bus station. Six weeks later a ceiling installer found a crack, and the whole thing shut for ten months.
story: The Salesforce Transit Center replaced the old Transbay Terminal with a $2.26 billion, four-and-a-half-block-long hall of steel and glass, and a surprise on top: a 5.4-acre public park, planted and landscaped, floating above the streets of South of Market [1][2]. It opened in August 2018. Then on September 25, less than two months later, a ceiling installer spotted a major crack in the bottom flange of one of the huge steel girders carrying the bus deck across Fremont Street [2]. The transit authority closed the entire building, park included, as a precaution after workers found fissures in two beams; Fremont Street was shut and shored, and buses went back to the temporary terminal at Howard and Main streets [3]. The crack in the brittle steel ran through the flange where a hanger slots through it; crews reinforced the twin girders over Fremont and a similar pair over First Street, although inspectors found no cracks there [2]. By May 2019 the repairs were complete and the building was being recommissioned, with fire, safety and elevator systems retested under independent oversight before it could reopen [3].

title: A Bullet in a Skull by the Bioswale
place: El Camino del Mar at the northeast corner of Lincoln Park
hook: A stormwater project to keep Sea Cliff from flooding turned up twenty graves, and a .44-calibre bullet rattling inside a skull.
story: In summer 2019 crews were building bioswales along El Camino del Mar to divert stormwater so the Sea Cliff neighbourhood wouldn't flood. Near the northeastern corner of Lincoln Park they dug up a coffin [1]. With a city-hired archaeologist watching, they uncovered at least 20 graves from the late 19th century [1]. The markers had been removed a century earlier, and the city had no detailed map of the 200-acre cemetery. So the archaeologists turned to historians Alex Ryder and John Martini, who were rebuilding one [1]. The graves turned out to lie in the old plot of the French Mutual Benevolent Society. Several skeletons showed signs of autopsy and other post-mortem study, which was illegal at the time [1]. One skull held a .44-calibre Winchester bullet [1]. Ryder said the team was close to identifying him. A lead in the newspapers: on 15 January 1896 the Call reported that a French doctor, E. L. Molass, had come west hoping to cure his tuberculosis and shot himself at the French Hospital [1]. SF Heritage notes that routine park work often turns up human remains [2].

title: A quake-proof hospital replaces the hotel
place: CPMC Van Ness Campus, 1101 Van Ness Avenue at Geary
hook: On one March weekend in 2019, more than 200 patients were driven across town to a $2.1 billion hospital built where the Jack Tar once stood.
story: California law requires every hospital in the state to meet strict seismic standards by 2030. For Sutter Health's California Pacific Medical Center, that meant replacing its old Pacific and California Street campuses [1]. After some fifteen years of planning and building, and a lot of argument about whether residents would lose services, the answer rose on the old Jack Tar Hotel block at Van Ness and Geary [1][2]. It is a $2.1 billion, 12-storey hospital that fills the whole block. It has 274 beds, all in private rooms, and a 10-storey medical office building next door [1]. About 119 floor-length panels filled with a viscous fluid are built into its frame to absorb shaking like shock absorbers. 'We know this building can withstand a 1906 quake, and possibly more,' a nursing executive told the Chronicle [1]. Over the weekend of 2 and 3 March 2019, more than 200 patients were moved in from the two old campuses, and the new emergency room opened at 7 a.m. on the Saturday [1]. Staff had rehearsed the move with colleagues playing patients. One nurse said of her old unit, 'it can be like a tomb with no windows' [1].

title: Grandma Huang's park
place: Yik Oi Huang Peace & Friendship Park, 251 Leland Ave
hook: For about 20 years she did qigong on the path around this playground. Today the park carries her name.
story: Yik Oi Huang was born in Toi San, China, on February 15, 1930, and had only two years of elementary school [1]. She came to San Francisco in June 1986 with her husband, Ho Wei Huang. She worked as a seamstress, a nanny and a dishwasher, and made her life in Visitacion Valley [1]. Neighbours called her Grandma Huang. For more than 17 years she was an ambassador for the Visitacion Valley Friendship Club, helping Chinese immigrant seniors [1][2]. For about 20 years she did qigong around the edge of Visitacion Valley Playground [1]. On January 8, 2019, she was brutally attacked there during her daily exercise [1]. She fought for a year and died on January 3, 2020, aged 89 [1]. Her attacker had assaulted seven people in two weeks that January; six of them were Asian American [3]. In 2022 the Recreation and Park Commission voted unanimously to rename the playground Yik Oi Huang Peace & Friendship Park [2]. In November 2025 a jury found Keonte Gathron guilty of her murder [3]. "Be something bigger than yourself," her grandson Jeremy Lu said, describing how she lived [1].

title: Rebuilding Sunnydale without moving anyone out

hook: In 2008 a barber called Sunnydale a place with 'no way out unless you die.' Now its wartime barracks are being replaced, with a promise that residents stay.
story: In 2008 the Chronicle described Sunnydale's wartime barracks as crumbling, with black mould in sinks, collapsed stairs, and cable installers who would only come in the morning [1]. "This is like a concentration camp. There is no way out unless you die," said Keith "Kilo" Perry, 55, who ran a barbershop in the development [1]. The Housing Authority's former director admitted the city could not afford to fix it [1]. The plan to replace it comes from HOPE SF. Founded in 2007, it calls itself the country's first large-scale community development effort built around an anti-displacement mission: every current Sunnydale household is promised a new affordable home [2]. Mercy Housing California and Related California are building 1,700 new homes in all [2]. The new buildings are opening one by one. Casala opened in 2019 with 55 Sunnydale families and Malosi in 2022 with 167 [2]. In 2024 Mayor London Breed, who grew up in public housing, marked the topping out of Amani and Nia at Sunnydale Avenue and Hahn Street, with 170 apartments and space for a grocery store and a health centre [3]. Both were finished in 2025, and a new recreation center at the edge of McLaren Park was due to open in January 2026 [2][4].

title: The Murals the Board Voted to Erase
place: George Washington High School lobby, 600 32nd Avenue
hook: A communist painter covered a new school's lobby with George Washington, enslaved workers and a dead Native American. Eighty-three years later, San Francisco fought over them.
story: When George Washington High School opened in August 1936, its lobby held 1,600 square feet of buon fresco by Victor Arnautoff, painted onto wet plaster behind the plasterers, about nine feet a day, over ten months [1]. It was the largest single-artist WPA mural suite on the Pacific Coast [1]. Outside, Sargent Johnson finished the stadium frieze Beniamino Bufano had begun [2]. Arnautoff, a communist and onetime Diego Rivera assistant, showed the first president as a slaveholder and the young nation's westward push over the body of a Native American [3]. Critics, including the American Indian Parent Advisory Council, said students should not be forced to see those images daily; defenders called destruction akin to book burning [3]. In 2019 the Board of Education voted to paint the murals over, then chose to hide them instead [3][4]. The alumni association sued, and in July 2021 Judge Anne-Christine Massullo ruled that no action could be taken without environmental review [3]. In 2022, after three board members were recalled, the Chronicle reported the district had spent $525,000 in bond money on legal fees in the fight [4].

title: A Labyrinth on the Slow Street

hook: A 1905 landmark church on Lake Street ordains openly LGBTQ ministers, opens Pride with a 'Dolly Church' service, and built a labyrinth from neighbours' succulents.

Its welcome today is explicit [1]. Since 2010, it says, it has ordained openly LGBTQ ministers, and since 2014 it has married same-sex couples [1]. In 2018 the congregation affirmed the full inclusion of transgender and non-binary people and went further, lamenting how church policies had driven LGBTQ Christians away [1]. Each June it opens Pride season with a 'Dolly Church' service [1]. It became a sanctuary church for refugees and asylum seekers, and its Harvest Food Pantry feeds about 300 households a week [2]. In 2020, as pandemic walkers filled the neighbourhood and Lake Street became a Slow Street, the church began the Lake Street Labyrinth off the sidewalk, a winding path through garden and pavement [3]. The succulents were donated by neighbours, and painted stones of encouragement dot the way [3].

title: Columbus Comes Down Before Dawn
place: Coit Tower parking circle, Telegraph Hill
hook: The 12-foot bronze explorer had watched over Telegraph Hill since 1957. One June night in 2020, the city quietly took him away.
story: Early on June 18, 2020, city crews lifted a 4,000-pound bronze statue of Christopher Columbus off its pedestal outside Coit Tower [1]. The 12-foot statue had stood there since 1957. Its sculptor, Count Vittorio di Colbertaldo of Verona, had also been an official sculptor for Mussolini's corps of bodyguards [1]. For years protesters had splashed it with red paint to stand for Columbus's conquests, and the city had spent about $70,000 in a single year cleaning it [1]. As protests after the killing of George Floyd spread, it was vandalised three times in a week, and a flyer called on people to march up the hill, pull it down and throw it into the bay off Pier 31 [1]. The Arts Commission said it no longer matched the city's commitment to racial justice, and that a two-ton statue falling from its pedestal was a real danger [1]. The next morning, the Indigenous activist Mariposa Villaluna knelt on the empty pedestal with their four-year-old child. "I felt lighter," she said [1]. North Beach reacted calmly. "The Italian American community doesn't need a statue to tell us who we are," said Dave Barsi of the Italian-American Social Club [1][2].

The operator, District Commons, said the group had no right to live there and filed to remove them [1]. The two sides settled in June 2021, and everyone had left by the end of that year [1].

title: Fire at the Fishermen's Pier
place: Pier 45, Fisherman's Wharf
hook: Before dawn in the pandemic spring, flames tore through a fish warehouse on Pier 45 and crept toward a ship that had sailed to D-Day.
story: Shortly after 4 a.m. on May 23, 2020, fire broke out in a fish processing and storage warehouse the size of a football field near the end of Pier 45 [1]. Alejandro Arellano of La Rocca Seafood was cleaning out a fish locker when it began. "I saw a lot of smoke. A few minutes later, fire everywhere," he said [1]. More than 130 firefighters fought the blaze. The warehouse walls collapsed, the first fire engine to arrive was singed, and a fireboat kept the flames off the SS Jeremiah O'Brien, a Liberty ship that took part in D-Day, which was docked alongside [1]. The fire stayed at the far end of the pier, away from the Musée Mécanique and Alioto's [1]. It came when the Wharf was already shut under the pandemic stay-at-home order. "The seafood industry didn't need this now," said Kenny Belov of the wholesaler TwoXSea, who worried a power cut would spoil the fish in his freezers [1]. Pier 45, the city's longest pier, is where San Francisco's fishing industry hangs on, "still alive, although smaller than in its glory days" [2].

title: Juneteenth Night in the Music Concourse

hook: On Juneteenth 2020, protesters roped and pulled down Junipero Serra, Francis Scott Key and even Ulysses S. Grant. A week later the archbishop returned to pray an exorcism.

Grant, the general who defeated the Confederacy, lay in a roadway splashed with red paint [1]. Cervantes's bust had paint on its eyes, and benches, fountains and a sphinx were damaged too, all beneath an empty Ferris wheel [1]. The Chronicle judged some of the damage to have little to do with politics [1]. On June 27 Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone led Catholics at the site in the rosary and the St. Michael prayer of exorcism. He called the toppling "an act of the Evil One" [2].

title: Last Call at the Edge of the Continent

hook: The Whitneys turned the Cliff House into a roadhouse in 1937. A Greek-American couple ran it for 47 years, until the pandemic and a lapsed lease ended the story.

In December 2020 the Hountalases announced they would close by year's end, blaming coronavirus restrictions and the federal government's stalling on a long-term lease [4]. 'There's something about the place that draws you,' historian John Martini said. 'This is as far as it goes. This is the edge' [4].

In 2021 Supervisor Hillary Ronen brokered a deal giving the nonprofits the right to buy the site for $8.5 million, with the developer promising to save a fraction of the greenhouses if they fell short [1]. title: The Last Chinese Opera House Lights Up
place: Great Star Theater, 636 Jackson St
hook: A 1925 Chinatown theatre that showed Chinese films and staged Chinese opera sat dark behind a roll-down gate. It was revived twice, the second time by two Salesforce engineers.
story: The Great Star on Jackson Street was built in 1925, and Bruce Lee used to watch opera there [1]. By 2010 it had been dark for 12 years. It might have stayed that way if George Kaskanlian Jr. hadn't stormed out after a fight with his girlfriend and walked past its roll-down gate [2]. He found mould, ripped wall fabric and a projection room thick with cobwebs, and he and his partner took a 10-year lease [2]. In the 1970s, filmmaker Ruby Yang recalled, Chinatown had half a dozen theatres showing filmed opera and action movies. The Great Star may be the last Chinatown theatre in America to show both Chinese-language films and Chinese opera. "That place was run by gangs and very dirty, but they were showing some good films there," she said [2]. In June 2021, as the pandemic eased, Alice Chu and Roger Pincombe, a married couple who worked as software engineers at Salesforce, reopened it as a nonprofit [1]. They had put in $150,000 of their own money and donations: new red upholstery after nesting birds ruined the old seat covers, 85 new fire sprinklers, and a traditional altar where actors can pray before going on stage [1].

title: "Where is Nancy?"
place: Pelosi home, 2600 block of Broadway
hook: At 2:27 a.m. an 82-year-old man calmly told a police dispatcher that a stranger was waiting for his wife. She understood what he couldn't say.
story: Early on October 28, 2022, David DePape broke through glass-paneled doors at the back of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's Pacific Heights home. He was looking for the Speaker and shouting "Where is Nancy?" [1]. The Speaker was in Washington. Instead her 82-year-old husband Paul woke to find DePape in his bedroom [1][3]. Paul Pelosi said he needed the bathroom, where his phone was charging, and called 911 [1]. On the 2:27 a.m. call he spoke carefully: "there's a gentleman here just waiting for my wife to come back." He gave the address and the intruder's name, and said the man wanted him to put the phone down [2]. Dispatcher Heather Grives sensed that something more was going on and sent a priority call. Police Chief Bill Scott later called her judgement "lifesaving" [1][2]. Officers arrived to find the two men struggling over a hammer. DePape wrenched it away and struck Pelosi before officers tackled him [1]. Pelosi needed surgery for a fractured skull [1][3]. DePape had planned to kidnap and interrogate the Speaker. In May 2024, after his federal conviction for attempted kidnapping and assault, he was sentenced to 30 years in prison [3].

title: A Park Built on Top of a Freeway
place: Presidio Tunnel Tops, above the Presidio Parkway tunnels
hook: Doyle Drive was one of the city's most dangerous roads. Its replacement went into tunnels, and on top of them the Presidio grew 14 acres of meadows.
story: For decades, Doyle Drive carried Highway 101 along the Presidio's northern bluff to the Golden Gate Bridge. It was decaying, needed seismic work, and was known as one of the most dangerous and congested roads in the city [1]. In 2015 it was replaced by the $1.1 billion Presidio Parkway, which runs part of the way in tunnels [1][2]. The ground on top of those tunnels became a new park. The Presidio Trust hired James Corner Field Operations, the firm behind New York's High Line [2]. First came a long fight with Caltrans over dirt. The Trust wanted soil rich enough for native plants and free of weed seeds and construction debris. 'The heart of our conflict had to do with the disconnect between national park standards and freeway standards,' said the Trust's Michael Boland. 'You can't change the soil once you put it down' [2]. In 2018 three transportation agencies agreed to pay the Presidio a combined $54 million to turn the construction and storage land into parkland [2]. Presidio Tunnel Tops opened in 2022. The $118 million, 14-acre park has lawns, picnic areas and a nature playground, and it makes an easy walk from the heart of the Presidio to the Crissy Field waterfront [1][3].

title: A Subway Station Named for a Fighter
place: Chinatown–Rose Pak Station, Stockton & Washington
hook: She was a chain-smoking power broker who helped make a mayor and fought for a subway. Naming the station after her took six hours of shouting and a 4-3 vote.
story: In 1972, a 24-year-old reporter named Rose Pak was in court against a lawyer accused of punching her during an interview. He called her "extremely pushy." "I was trained to be persistent," she replied [3]. She became one of the most powerful figures in San Francisco politics. She helped put Ed Lee in office as the city's first Asian American mayor, and she made plenty of enemies [2][3]. After the 1989 earthquake brought down the Embarcadero Freeway, a main route into Chinatown, she pushed for a rail line to tie the neighbourhood to downtown [2]. Pak died in 2016 at 68 [2]. In August 2019, after about six hours of public comment, much of it in Chinese, the SFMTA board voted 4-3 to name the new station after her. One supporter called her the subway's "tiger mom"; opponents wanted it called simply Chinatown Station [2]. The station opened in late 2022 as part of the city's first new subway in over 40 years [4][1]. Even then there was a row: the bronze plaque gave her birthplace as Henan, while her funeral booklet said Hengyang, in Hunan [1].

title: A neighbourhood votes for its first landmark
place: St. James Presbyterian Church, 240 Leland Ave
hook: San Francisco had 288 official landmarks and not one of them was in Visitacion Valley. So the neighbourhood held an election to choose one.
story: In 2022 San Francisco had 288 official city landmarks, and none of them was in Visitacion Valley [1]. San Francisco Heritage said landmarking "heavily favor[s] master architects and downtown edifices" and overlooks the places where working people live [1]. So the group held a public vote. There were three candidates: Fire Station 44, built in 1913; the old Sam's Lodge roadhouse on the county line; and St. James Presbyterian Church at 240 Leland Avenue [1][2]. Anyone could vote online until March 1 [1]. The church won [2]. Its congregation formed in 1908 with 69 members, and the present building, designed by Julia Morgan, was dedicated in 1923 [2]. The front has a stained-glass window of the Parable of the Sower. Neighbourhood historian Betty Parshall says it first hung in a church in a Nevada town. When the town and church failed, the St. James congregation "liberated" it [1]. On June 7, 2022, Supervisor Shamann Walton started the process to make the church an official landmark [2].

title: An art school's last lesson
place: San Francisco Art Institute campus, 800 Chestnut St
hook: Deep in debt, one of America's oldest art schools thought about selling its $50 million Rivera mural. The city stepped in, and the school didn't survive.
story: By late 2020 the San Francisco Art Institute owed $19.7 million to the University of California. Its trustees were considering selling the Diego Rivera fresco, appraised at $50 million, and the New York Times named George Lucas's museum as a possible buyer [1]. Alumni and faculty were outraged. On January 12, 2021, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to begin landmarking the mural, a move led by Supervisor Aaron Peskin. Board chair Pam Rorke Levy had asked for a delay. She warned that landmarking would stop the school from using the mural, "SFAI's only significant asset," to secure a $7 million bridge loan. Peskin called the delay efforts "heresy." [1] A planned takeover by the University of San Francisco followed, then collapsed on July 15, 2022, over finances, enrollment and deferred maintenance. The 151-year-old school held its final commencement on July 12 and stopped granting degrees [2]. It filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in April 2023 [3]. In February 2024, a nonprofit backed by Laurene Powell Jobs bought the Russian Hill campus, mural and all [4].

title: Clause 13 and the National Register
place: St. Francis Wood, St. Francis Boulevard fountain
hook: St. Francis Wood's founding rules barred some races from living there. In 2022 its listing on the National Register set off a fight over who gets to live here.
story:
When Mason-McDuffie opened St. Francis Wood in 1912, with Olmsted Brothers streets and John Galen Howard gateways, its founding rules included Clause 13, which kept certain ethnic groups from owning or renting homes [1]. The homes association now calls that clause "discriminatory and inexcusable." The Supreme Court made such covenants unenforceable in 1948, and after the 1968 Fair Housing Act the neighbourhood recorded a declaration that the clause was invalid [1].

On June 30, 2022, after a years-long campaign by residents, St. Francis Wood was added to the National Register of Historic Places [2]. Housing advocates objected. "If you are preserving structures with the requirement that they remain single-family homes forever, when the origin of that single-family home was so Black people and Japanese people and Chinese people could not live there, is that really what you want to preserve?" asked policy expert Annie Fryman [2]. Homes association president Michael Fox answered: "We don't have gates, and we're an inclusive community." [2] One land-use lawyer estimated that the new review would add about $10,000 and three to four months to projects [2]. As of 2016 the neighbourhood was 45 percent Asian and 0 percent Black [2].

title: Roast Pig on the Fairway
place: Kong Chow funerary monument, Lincoln Park Golf Course
hook: Golfers stopped their games while Chinese elders burned incense among the fairways. Under the grass lay thousands of forgotten San Franciscans, and the city was finally about to say so.
story: About 20,000 people still lie under Lincoln Park's golf course. They were mostly immigrants and the poor of the old City Cemetery, and for a century not one sign mentioned them [1]. One visible remnant is the Kong Chow monument. Its inscription calls the graves a temporary resting place for travellers from Kong Chow in south China, whose bones were meant to go home [2][3]. Historian Woody LaBounty urged the new District 1 supervisor, Connie Chan, to make the cemetery a landmark. She admitted she had never known what it was [3]. In October 2021, dozens of Chinese American San Franciscans gathered at the monument for Chung Yeung, the autumn festival for honouring the dead. Golf stopped while they brought incense, paper money and a whole roast pig. 'Some got teary-eyed,' Chan said. It was probably the first such ceremony in decades [3]. Some golfers worried at first that landmarking would hurt the course [3]. In October 2022 the city designated City Cemetery its first primarily archaeological landmark and unveiled the park's first sign telling its story [4].

title: The last manju at Sutter and Buchanan
place: Benkyodo, 1747 Buchanan Street at Sutter
hook: For over a century, three generations of Okamuras made mochi for Japantown. In 2022 the counter where old friends met for breakfast went dark.
story: Suyeichi Okamura founded Benkyodo in 1906. It stood on Geary near Buchanan until World War II forced it to close [1]. The family was incarcerated at Camp Amache in Colorado, where Ricky and Bobby's parents met [1]. Redevelopment later pushed the shop to the corner of Sutter and Buchanan, and ownership passed to Hirofumi Okamura. His sons Ricky and Bobby took over in 1990 [1]. By 2017 they were making more than 800 mochi and manju a day. Ricky started at 5 a.m., and Bobby tasted the beans to check the flavour, his favourite being shiro an, white bean [1]. After two other Japanese confectioners closed in the 1990s, Benkyodo became one of the Bay Area's few remaining makers of mochi and manju [1]. Its counter was a gathering place: 96-year-old Warren Eijima recalled the men who met there for breakfast as "a stick-together bunch" [1]. No fourth generation stepped in. After more than 115 years, Benkyodo closed in 2022, and by 2025 its classic diner interior had been torn out for a new restaurant [2].

title: From parking lot to 131 homes
place: Kapuso at the Upper Yard, 2340 San Jose Avenue
hook: Old Muni storage tracks became a parking lot, then a safe place to sleep in your car. Now 131 affordable homes sit beside Balboa Park BART.
story: Beside Balboa Park station, on the west side of San Jose Avenue, a strip of land once held Muni storage tracks known as the Upper Yard [3]. It later became a Muni surface parking lot. In 2012 the SFMTA board agreed to sell it for affordable housing under the Balboa Park Station Area Plan, and in 2018 it passed to the city's housing office [2]. While plans moved ahead, the site served as San Francisco's first Vehicular Triage Center, a pilot giving people who lived in their vehicles a secure place to park and access to services [2]. Mission Housing Development Corporation and Related California were chosen to build it. It was the first affordable housing project in the city approved under SB 35, a state law that fast-tracks such projects [2]. Thirty-nine apartments were set aside for public-housing families choosing to move from Sunnydale-Velasco [1][2]. Kapuso at the Upper Yard opened on September 28, 2023. It has 131 apartments, a YMCA early-childhood centre, a family resource centre and a bicycle shop run by the environmental-justice group PODER. It cost $119 million [1]. Senator Scott Wiener called it "proof that San Francisco can turn the tide" on housing [1].

title: The Roadhouse the City Nearly Wrote Off
place: Trocadero Clubhouse, Sigmund Stern Grove, northwest of 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard
hook: Less than a year after San Francisco's oldest roadhouse finally became a landmark, an 85-foot eucalyptus crashed through its roof. The news called it "destroyed."
story: The Trocadero was built in 1892 as a Stick-Eastlake roadhouse in a wooded gully. It is the last intact survivor of the roadhouses that once dotted the city's western and southern edges. In 1907 the indicted political boss Abe Ruef was caught hiding there [1][2]. In the 1930s Bernard Maybeck restored it as a clubhouse for the new Stern Grove [2]. After lobbying by neighbors and local nonprofits, it finally became a city landmark in 2022 [1][2]. Then, during a storm on March 11, 2023, an 85-foot eucalyptus fell and ripped through the roof, and the sprinklers soaked the historic interior [1]. Historian Woody LaBounty, whose group had led the landmark campaign, remembers watching the head of Recreation and Parks on the morning news, waiting to hear that the city would save the building. Instead he heard something vague, like "the Trocadero is gone." The Chronicle's headline used the word "destroyed" [1]. LaBounty thinks the new landmark status may have tipped the balance. Money was found, with reimbursement from a FEMA grant. After a restoration by Architectural Resources Group, the Trocadero began taking event bookings again from April 1, 2025 [1].

title: Twenty-Five Million Dollars for a Tiny Cove

hook: Beachgoers told the park service to leave their little cove just as it was. So the rebuild had to keep a palm tree and an old flagpole.
story: China Beach is a small cove with a bathhouse, a picnic terrace and tide pools. At low tide you can walk around to Baker Beach [4]. It has no lifeguards, and swimming is discouraged because the surf is unpredictable [4]. By the late 2010s the retaining walls, road and bathhouse were worn out. The Parks Conservancy dates its feasibility study to 2016 on one page and 2017 on another [2][4]. Hundreds of beachgoers answered surveys, and most said they loved the cove "as-is" [1]. In May 2023 the National Park Service and the Conservancy began a $25 million rehabilitation. It covers the bathhouse, with new restrooms and rinse stations, plus the picnic terrace and the retaining walls. A new arrival plaza keeps a palm tree and the historic flagpole [2]. Beach access stayed open during the work, but the parking lot became a staging yard. As of 2026 the Park Service still warns of very limited parking [2][3].

title: World Leaders Dine in a Downpour
place: Legion of Honor, Court of Honor
hook: Lightning over the bay, aides sweeping water off the red carpet, and reporters in trash bags. This is how Lincoln Park hosted the leaders of the Pacific Rim.
story: On 16 November 2023, during the APEC summit week, President Joe Biden hosted a leaders-and-spouses dinner at the Legion of Honor [1][2]. The weather did not cooperate. A steady drizzle became a torrential downpour around 6:45 p.m., with rare lightning over San Francisco Bay, and Biden's motorcade arrived minutes later [1]. Along its route through the Richmond District, families waved American flags [1]. At the museum, two rows of white-gloved servicemen with swords and rifles stood in formation. A State Department aide pushed pools of water off the red carpet, and soaked reporters were handed trash bags as ponchos [1]. For more than an hour the acting chief of protocol greeted guests who arrived one by one to a military band. Among them were Justin Trudeau, Anthony Albanese, Srettha Thavisin, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Yoon Suk Yeol [1]. Servicemen with umbrellas walked them along a candlelit path to a tent inside the grounds [1]. Xi Jinping was on the guest list but was not spotted at the dinner [1].

title: Goat paths to a hilltop park
place: Panorama Park, summit of Yerba Buena Island
hook: On the summit of the island once named for its goats, the paths of a new park follow the routes the animals once wandered.
story:
Yerba Buena Island was once called Goat Island [1]. In 2024 its summit became a new public park, designed by the Oakland firm Hood Design Studio [2].

Hood's plan, described under the name Hilltop Park, treats the hilltop as a 'cultural + ecological arboretum' and a palimpsest of the island's history [2]. On the eastern high point, native plants reveal the site's ecology, while the western high point focuses on its human past. Trees are planted to echo the outlines of demolished buildings, and fragments of old foundations are left in view. An old water tower has become an amphitheatre overlook. The pathways, Hood's studio writes, were inspired by the meanderings of the goats that once grazed there [2].

The city describes Panorama Park as a three-acre park with 360-degree views of the bay and home to Hiroshi Sugimoto's sculpture Point of Infinity. Next to it is Signal Point, a two-acre overlook of native plants and oak trees [3]. The park also has a permanent memorial to the Port Chicago 50, the Black sailors tried for mutiny on this island in 1944 [4].

He also tried to tax Jewish people to keep them from opening businesses [1]. In 2022 three supervisors urged a new name, and Supervisor Myrna Melgar led the effort [1][2]. Great blue herons nest on Strawberry Hill in April and May, and the department called them a symbol of resilience for the Indigenous community [1]. title: The not-$1.7 million toilet

hook: A single toilet with a $1.7 million price tag made world headlines. In the end it cost about $200,000 and opened with a party called the Toilet Bowl.
story: The town square's 2014 design included a restroom, but it was dropped for lack of money [2]. Neighbours later won state funding based on a rough estimate for a custom-built toilet [2]. Governor Gavin Newsom's office said 'a single, small bathroom should not cost $1.7m' and threatened to withhold the state money [1]. The final bill to the city was about $200,000, mostly labour [1]. Neighbours celebrated in April with the 'Toilet Bowl', where a band called American Standard played. 'When everybody laughs at you, you gotta take the power back and laugh at yourself,' said organiser Leslie Crawford [1].

title: A Highway Becomes a Park, Then a Recall
place: Sunset Dunes (former Upper Great Highway) at Noriega Street
hook: San Francisco turned two miles of oceanfront highway into its newest park. The neighbors closest to it voted against it, and five months later they recalled their supervisor.
story: On April 12, 2025, San Francisco opened Sunset Dunes on the old Upper Great Highway between Sloat Boulevard and Lincoln Way. The two-mile, 50-acre park was the largest pedestrianization project in California history. It has a skate space, hammocks, fitness classes and murals of surfing and sea life [1]. Voters citywide had approved Proposition K in 2024, but most residents living closest to the park voted against it, and many were angry about traffic [2]. The anger landed on Supervisor Joel Engardio, who had backed the measure. On September 16, 2025, more than 60 percent of District 4 voters removed him from office, the first recall of a supervisor in city history [3]. "None of these decisions about us without us," said recall supporter Albert Chow, a local business owner [3][2]. Engardio conceded but insisted, "We are on the right side of history" [3]. A year after opening, city transit officials reported that traffic on the Sunset's main roads was below pre-pandemic levels. Opponents were still collecting signatures to bring cars back at least part of the time [2]. Park supporters point out that the ground under the highway is already washing away: the lower stretch south of Sloat is closed because of coastal erosion [2].

place: Crocker Amazon Playground, Geneva Ave & Moscow St
hook: Samoan cricketers once transformed this neglected ballpark. Now a $50 million, Giants-backed makeover has neighbours fighting over plastic grass.
story: In the 1920s the land at the city's southern edge was still farmland; an aerial photo from about 1923 shows fields where Crocker Amazon Playground would later be built [1]. Michael Arago, who grew up nearby, remembered the park in the 1970s as an ill-kept ballpark more suited to getting drunk than playing ball. Then one Sunday it turned into 'an amazing field of white shirts': Samoan families playing cricket, with picnics that grew bigger every year [2]. Today the gopher holes and soggy fields often close the diamonds for more than a month each spring [3]. In 2025 the parks department proposed a rebuild. In April 2026 the Recreation and Park Commission unanimously recommended accepting $28 million from the San Francisco Giants, which with $22 million of city money makes a $50 million project [4]. A group called Keep Crocker Real opposes the plan to put synthetic turf on five of six ballfields and remove 128 mature trees. Supervisor Chyanne Chen urged keeping real grass on at least two fields [4]. The Board of Supervisors has the final say [3][4].

title: The fight over the Castro's seats
place: Castro Theatre, 429 Castro St
hook: The rows of red seats were almost sacred. When a concert promoter moved to rip them out, the neighbourhood fought it for two years.
story: Timothy Pflueger's 1922 movie palace became Landmark No. 100 in 1976 [3]. In the 1970s programmer Mel Novikoff brought back old films, art-house and foreign pictures, to draw in the neighbourhood's fast-growing gay audience [2]. In January 2022, Berkeley promoter Another Planet Entertainment leased it. Its plan was to flatten the raked floor and remove the permanent seats so the hall could host concerts [1][3]. A 'Save the Seats' campaign argued that the movie-palace seating was part of the building's historic character [3]. After nearly two years of argument, City Hall approved the plan. The theatre closed after a February 4, 2024 screening of 'Victor/Victoria' [1]. It reopened exactly two years and a day later, after a $41 million renovation. More than 1,000 people lined up around the block [1]. Organist David Hegarty rose out of the stage floor as he had for much of the past half century. The Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence celebrated him, and the night ended with 'The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert' on 35mm [1]. About 650 motorised, removable seats now give 1,150 places for films. The balcony was left unchanged [1].
